title: Cognitive and social processes in psychosis: developing more effective treatment approaches.
description: The aim of our research is to advance the understanding of psychosis, in order to improve treatment. Schizophrenia-spectrum psychoses are distressing and disabling for sufferers, place high demands on carers and have high health and social care costs. The effectiveness of medication, the first line treatment, is limited and the risk of relapse is high. Our research strategy is to combine two major outcome trials of psychological treatments with a linked series of explanatory studies. We have developed and evaluated two treatments, cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT) and family interventions (FI). Both are known to be effective, but they have different targets of change and little is known about how they work. Our model of psychosis identifies specific cognitive and social processes which we hypothesise to maintain psychosis and to be important targets of treatment. We intend to test this model to improve understanding of change processes and enhance treatment effectiveness. After five years, we aim to have confirmed that CBT reduces relapse; to have identified processes which maintain psychosis and contribute to relapse; to have identified how CBT and FI work; and to have refined both treatments to meet specific clinical needs.

title: Mechanisms of developmental synaptic plasticity at cortical synapses: normal development and recovery for injury.
description: In this study we will investigate the mechanisms of synaptic plasticity at cortical synapses during normal development, and whether these mechanisms have a role during reactive synaptogenesis following recovery from injury in the adult brain. Using patch-clamp recordings in the in vitro thalamocortical brain slice preparation, the single channel properties of kainate receptors in excised membrane patches from the soma and dendrites from layer IV neurons in the developing barrel cortex will be studied. Pharmacologically isolated kainate receptors will be activated by rapid application of glutamate and compared to synaptic receptors using non-stationary fluctuation analysis. We will also compare wild-type and mutant mice that lack particular kainate receptor subunits. This will provide important information on the properties of native synaptic and non-synaptic kainate receptors and what determines these properties. Such information is critically important for understanding of kainate receptor function in the developing cortex. The involvement of kainate receptors in synaptic plasticity at developing thalamocortical synapses will be studied by investigating whether kainate receptors can directly induce synaptic plasticity or if they modulate the induction of NMDA receptor-dependent plasticity. This will be carried out using electrophysiological recordings of synaptic responses in thalamocortical slices combined with pharmacological and genetic manipulations of kainate receptors. This will allow us to determine the precise role of kainate receptors in developmental plasticity at thalamocortical synapses. We will investigate whether heterosynaptic long-term and short-term depression are important as mechanisms of competition between thalamocortical and intracortical synapses in the developing barrel cortex. The mechanisms of such heterosynaptic plasticity will be investigated. This will provide novel insights into the processes underlying the formation of the topographical thalamocortical projection to ayer IV in sensory cortex. We will study the role of developmental plasticity mechanisms during recovery from injury in the adult brain. To do this we will study the mechanisms of synaptic plasticity during reactive the synaptogenesis observed in the CA1 region of the hippocampus following recovery from kainic acid lesion of CA3. This programme of work will further our understanding of the mechanisms by which synaptic activity leads to the formation of appropriate circuitry in the developing cortex and the involvement of such mechanisms in the synaptogenesis following recovery from injury in the adult CNS.

title: Examination of the neurobiological bases of different symptom dimensions in obsessive-compulsive disorder.
description: Factor-analytic studies have reduced Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD) symptoms to a few dimensions: contamination/washing, checking, hoarding, symmetry/ordering, and sexual/religious obsessions, distinguished by sociodemographic differences, comorbid chronic tics and personality disorders, and antidepressant treatment response. Previous studies have reported in OCD patients, compared with normal and other psychiatric populations: 1. cognitive and motor dysfunction, particularly, impaired motor initiation and execution, executive function, and recognition of facial expressions of disgust; 2. increased neurological soft signs, reflecting impairments in several functional systems; 3. structural brain abnormalities; and 4. dysfunctional fronto-cortico-thalamic circuitry, which improves after successful treatment. There has been little study of the specific neurobiological bases of the different OCD symptom dimensions, which remain unknown. Preliminary findings associate hoarding with more widespread cognitive and motor dysfunction, and abnormalities in related neural structures, and symmetry/ordering and checking with different types of striatal dysfunction. Contamination/washing may be associated with increased experience and recognition of disgust per se, and activation in brain regions underlying disgust perception. With the expertise in the clinical and neuropsychological assessment and treatment of OCD patients, and facilities available for structural and functional neuroimaging of psychiatric populations, at the Maudsley Hospital and IOP, we aim to expand upon these initial findings to determine whether: 1. the different OCD symptom dimensions can be distinguished by the extent of abnormality in the above cognitive and motor functions, and associated neural structures; 2. contamination/washing, but not other symptoms, is associated with increased experience and recognition of the non-symptom-related disgust of standardised disgust-provoking scenarios and facial expressions, and activation of brain regions underlying disgust perception: the anterior insula and striatum; 3. different symptoms, provoked using visual imagery and scenes depicting symptom-related material, are associated with distinct behavioural and neural correlates. We predict that whilst contamination/washing is associated with an experience of disgust of similar intensity to that experienced by all subjects to aversive scenes, and activation predominantly of the anterior insula and striatum, other OCD symptoms are associated with the experience of anxiety, but not disgust, and are distinguished by different patterns of activation within fronto-striatal regions previously associated with symptom provocation in OCD. Our findings from studies 1. and 2. will allow specific predictions to be made regarding these distinctions. Determination of the neurobiological bases of the different OCD symptom dimensions will aid future development of successful treatments for specific OCD symptoms.

title: A Neuroimaging Centre for Developmental Disorders.
description: This proposal is to establish a world-class facility within the Institute of Psychiatry, King's College London (IoP/KCL) for neuroimaging of both aberrant and normal human brain development. The Neuroimaging Centre for Developmental Disorders focuses on IoP/KCL's strategy to translate contemporary, biological science research to improved clinical practice. The centre will provide, under one roof, an interdisciplinary research environment that combines the development of state-of-the-art, high resolution structural, functional and metabolic mapping techniques with our existing expertise in the definition, diagnosis and treatment of psychiatric disorders. The new facility will complement our existing infrastructure in genetic and developmental psychiatry and support our on-going neuroimaging research of both neurological and psychiatric disorders. The primary scientific goal of this interdisciplinary research proposal is to improve our understanding of developmental brain pathology by improved characterisation of functional, structural and metabolic abnormalities, which are associated with common psychiatric disorders. Creation of a Neuroimaging Centre for Developmental Disorders will bring together staff that are currently based in four separate buildings across the Denmark Hill campus into one new facility that will also house all the imaging equipment. The provision of such an integrated centre will expedite the whole process of subject preparation, imaging, neuropsychological testing and data analysis. Furthermore, the local South London and Maudsley NHS Trust have agreed, in principle, to make a substantial financial contribution towards this initiative. This will fund the clinical component of the centre and should lead to rapid implementation of our most salient research developments in the clinical environment. The specification of the research equipment selected (3.0 Tesla MR system) has been chosen to complement the existing, clinically funded magnet (1.5 Tesla). The higher field, dedicated research system will be capable of performing more sensitive MR imaging and spectroscopic studies on both children and adults. The co-location of the two systems will maximise the efficient use of time and space for the whole facility and such a combination of equipment and backup in a psychiatric environment will be unique to the UK. The collaborative nature of this proposal, and its priority within IoP/KCL, is demonstrated by the broad combination of applicants, including scientists with excellent reputations in imaging physics and analysis as well as clinicians of international distinction in their fields of psychiatry and neuropsychology. In addition to providing greater insights into neurodevelopmental disorders, the support of a high calibre medical physicist, image analyst and neuropsychologist will result in the development and refinement of contemporary neuroimaging strategies that will be of benefit to many other centres world wide. The centre will also provide sufficient space and opportunity for enhanced student and postdoctoral training. We envisage that such a centre of excellence will attract both clinicians and basic scientists from around the world as well as providing the firm foundations for continued collaboration with leading scientific colleagues in the UK.

title: Furbishment of the Dorothy Hodgkin Building as an integrated research facility for the University of Bristol Research Centre in Neuroendocrinology.
description: The University of Bristol Research Centre for Neuroendocrinology and Integrative Neuroscience (URCNIN) consists of 9 research groups with common themes at the interface of neuroendocrinology and neuroscience. The URCNIN has a programme of research which spans basic molecular and cellular biology, through integrative physiology to clinical neuroendocrinology, psychiatry and neurology. This rapidly expanding Centre is housed in scattered laboratories in the Bristol Royal Infirmary (BRI) which are now so cramped that there is only 7.2m2 of bench space per member of scientific staff. Equipment has to be housed in corridors and external huts to allow enough work space for day to day use. Our animal facilities are located half a mile away in the School of Medical Sciences, as are those members of the URCNIN who are based in the Departments of Anatomy and Psychiatry. Despite these severe limitations, the scientific output of the members of the URCNIN has been prodigious over the last five years. There is now simply no room either to consolidate our current research groups or to allow for the recruitment of new groups to complement our present activities. Unless we have high quality new accommodation to reinforce the intellectual and technical integration of our research groups, we will not only fail to attract this vital new blood, but we will be in danger of losing our current research teams to other institutions with better infrastructure and facilities. During the summer of 1998 a 7-storey office building, built approximately 40 years ago and adjacent to the BRI, became available. The University recognised that this building provided a strategic opportunity to provide urgently needed accommodation for the URCNIN and purchased the freehold of the building. The strengths of the current application are: (a) the provision of state-of-the-art facilities for the development of our research programmes; (b) an interactive environment in which molecular and cell biologists, physiologists and clinicians can make maximum use of overlapping interests, expertise and technologies; (c) the physical integration of our animal experimental work into the rest of our research programme; (d) our clinical scientists will work in a high class facility within close proximity of their clinical duties, and with easy access to clinical material and clinical investigation facilities; (e) the provision of space for the new research groups recruited to join the URCNIN.

title: Anatomical and functional connectivity between brain regions in twin pairs discordant for schizophrenia.
description: Schizophrenia is recognised as a disorder of multiple aetiological agents. The most widely accepted theory considers that an individual inherits a degree of genetic vulnerability from their parents but that this alone is often insufficient to lead to the development of the illness without the influence of environmental factors. The nature of the neuropathological changes that ensue is unclear. However evidence from neuropathology, and structural and functional neuroimaging suggests that abnormalities affecting the connections between anatomically distant sites within the brain may compromise the normal integration of cerebral function. Objective: I will use Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) and functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) to texamine brain function and the connections between brain regions, in a series of monozygotic (MZ) and dizygotic (DZ) twin pairs where one suffers from schizophrenia. I will compare these subjects with matched healthy control pairs (MZ and DZ). This will allow me to: a) Establish the pattern of connectional and functional abnormalities in schizophrenia. b) Determine the relationship between connectional and functional abnormalities. c) Evaluate the extent to which these are influenced by genetic factors. Method: I will recruit 15 twin pairs to each of the following groups, MZ pairs discordant for schizophrenia, DZ pairs discordant for schizophrenia, MZ matched normal control twin pairs and DZ matched normal control twin pairs. Each subject will be clinically evaluated and examined using DTI and two fMRI paradigms, verbal fluency and verbal self-monitoring. Date will be analysed using established non-parametric methods. Hypotheses: In twins with schizophrenia: a) DTI will demonstrate abnormal anatomical connectivity in the superior longitudinal fasciculus, connecting frontal and temporal cortices. b) Patients will demonstrate functional fronto-temporal dysconnectivity during both verbal fluency and verbal self-monitoring. c) The severity of fronto-temporal dysconnectivity will be correlated to anatomical connectivity deficits detected using DTI. Healthy twins with a schizophrenic co-twin will demonstrate qualitatively similar, but quantitatively smaller deficits, determined by their degree of genetic proximity to their co-twin.

title: Neuroscience.
description: Neuropharmacological investigation of 5-HT-GABA interactions in mood-related brain circuits Theories implicating a role for brain monoamine transmitters in the cause and treatment of major depression have been dominant for over four decades. However, increasing biochemical and pharmacological evidence from animal and human studies supports the hypothesis that mood disorders are associated with low GABA function. Interestingly, new anatomical information regarding the interactions between GABA and the 5-HT system suggest that cortical GABA neurones may be a target for 5-HT potentiating antidepressant drugs like selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs). The purpose of this project is to test this hypothesis using a combination of neurochemical, molecular and neurophysiological methods in animal models.

title: Neuroscience
description: The pathogenesis of synaptic pathology in schizophrenia The student will apply a range of approaches, all in current use in the group, to achieve these aims. Study 1: Morphometric, immunocytochemical and molecular markers will be used to measure the number, size and spatial distribution of 5-HT neurons in sections throughout the dorsal and median raphe nuclei, from 15 subjects with schizophrenia, 15 controls, plus 30 subjects with mood disorders (to serve as 'psychiatric controls'). Study2: Six well-characterised synaptic protein gene products (e.g. synaptophysin, complexins) will be measured in the superior temporal cortex of the same brain series using in situ hybridisation, immunoautoradiography and western blotting. Study 3: The neurodevelopmental genes will be chosen to complement our studies of semaphorin3A and reelin, in that they will be other genes in the same signalling pathways (e.g. disabled, apoR, plexins, neuropilins). The first task will be establishing which of these genes can be reliably detected in adult brains; those which are will then be studied in the case control series, as well as in a series of normal brains from infancy to adulthood. As part of Study 3, the candidate will also use neurodevelopmental expression arrays ('chips') which allow many hundreds of mRNAs to be looked at simultaneously. We are currently developing this technique, with the help of experienced collaborators in Cambridge and the US National Institutes of Health; the student will not work on arrays until the basic methods are working successfully in our lab. Overall, the project will provide significant novel data in three domains of schizophrenia research: synaptic pathology, serotonergic abnormality, and the neurodevelopmental hypothesis. Each study will be of value in its own right, but will also have the added value of the potential integration of the three aspects of schizophrenia neurobiology: As with all post mortem studies, it will not be possible to prove causality between any of the findings - and there are no convincing animal or in vitro alternatives - but it is possible to show a pattern of changes which together allow causal inferences to be drawn and then tested further in other designs.

title: Simultaneous fine-mapping of quantitative trait loci for multiple phenotypes.
description: The potential of dissecting common human disease at a genetic level has so far not been fully realised, largely because the complex genetic architecture of quantitative traits has frustrated attempts to identify genes by standard methodologies. Genetic analysis of laboratory mice can overcome the difficulties inherent in working with human populations. We have developed a novel statistical method that exploits the unusual pedigree structure of genetically heterogeneous mice to map quantitative trait loci (QTL) to a sub- centimorgan resolution. Our approach obviates the need to perform separate QTL detection and fine-mapping steps. Instead, we propose using a single population of genetically heterogeneous mice to find candidate genes that influence variation in asthma, obesity, diabetes, anxiety and cognition simultaneously. Our calculations show that typing 3,000 markers on 2,000 mice provides over 80% power to map loci explaining between 2.5 and 5% of the phenotypic variance into intervals of less than 1 centimorgan. By comparing syntenic mouse and human genomic sequences it will be possible to identify candidate genes in these intervals.

title: Nuffield Council on Bioethics.
description: The Nuffield Council on Bioethics, established in 1991, is an independent body funded by the Nuffield Foundation, the Wellcome Trust and the Medical Research Council. Over the past ten years, its Reports and papers have earned the Council an international reputation. It has produced five major Reports on topics of importance to the public interest and to the information of public policy: genetic screening; ownership of tissue; xenotransplantation; genetics and mental disorders; and genetically modified crops. The landscape of policy- making in bioethics has changed significantly during the Council's ten-year history. Although the UK does not have a statutory national bioethics commission there are a number of quasi-governmental bodies which examine bioethical issues. In this context, the Council's independence of government has become increasingly important as a result of public unease with governmental advisory bodies responsible for advising on and implementing policy in biomedicine and biotechnology. The council perceives its independence as critical to its production work in which the public can place its trust. There is, therefore, a strong case for the Council's continued role, examining and reporting on bioethical issues arising from developments in biomedicine and biology which warrant attention. The council has expanded its capacity significantly over the past two years. New staff, additional accommodation and a larger Council have all played a role. The Council has, as a consequence, been able to introduce new ways of working: organising national and international Workshops and Round Table meetings; establishing Council sub groups; and i9mproving liaison wit other organisations, both in the UK and abroad. The council now seeks to continue and expand its work programme on the basis of five year funding, as opposed to its previous pattern of two-year funding. A five year funding cycle will allow the council to plan its medium and long-term work more effectively and develop programmes for ongoing dissemination of its publications. In this proposal, the need for increased funding to support the Council's work programme for the period January 2002-Decembere 2006 is set out.

title: An investigation of synaptic transmission between monosynaptically coupled layer III and layer IV neurons and the mechanisms underlying experience- dependent plasticity in the visual cortex.
description: The proposed research will utilize a number of techniques to study the receptor mediated and molecular mechanisms underlying synaptic plasticity and experience-dependent development of monosynaptically coupled Layer III and Layer IV neurons in the rat visual cortex. It is well established that cortical physiology is dramatically altered when sensory experience is disrupted. In the visual cortex the behavioural consequences of such manipulations are particularly apparent due to the fact that they result in vision or blindness. Although much research has been carried out to determine the effects of various types of visual deprivation and experience, very little is known about the synaptic modifications and molecular processes which underlie plasticity in the visual cortex. The synaptic modifications will be investigated using ex vivo slices from animals which have had altered visual experience. Electrophysiological recordings will then be made between Layer III and Layer IV neurons, in vitro, to determine the experience-dependent alterations in synaptic transmission compared to in vitro recordings from animals reared with normal sensory experience. In addition to the electrophysiological recordings, experience-dependent changes in the synaptic architecture and the localization of neurotransmitter receptors will be investigated. After completion of this stage in the work the project with go on to attempt to induce the same modifications in acutely prepared visual cortical slices or in visual cortical cultures to determine the molecular mechanisms involved. The project also provides the opportunity to test the long-standing, but unproven, hypothesis that the mechanisms of long-term potentiation and long-term depression contribute naturally to synaptic modifications.

title: The role of brain area 10 in human cognition.
description: The frontal lobes are often described as the least understood area of the brain, and probably the most problematic region of the frontal lobes is BA10. However, recent findings suggest that the processes supported by BA10 are used in a wide range of quite different situations, and are therefore fundamental to human cognition. Moreover, this view receives support from the association between disturbances in this region and common psychiatric conditions such as depression and schizophrenia. Yet there is no coherent theory about the functions of this large region: this is clearly a marked gap in our knowledge about the brain. A second lacuna appears in our understanding of the comparability of evidence gathered from different methods in cognitive neuroscience. For relatively basic cognitive processes (e.g. those involved in early visual or language processing), prediction from the results of one method to another is conceptually relatively straightforward. However this is not the case for more central processes, and especially for those thought to be supported by frontal lobe structures. Understanding the limits of the expected cross-method concordance is crucial for the development of a cognitive neuroscience of frontal lobe function. Two of the most obvious candidate methods are group adult lesion studies and functional imaging, since they use the same subject base (adult humans). Surprisingly, there is only one study in this subject area that has investigated directly the comparability of findings from the two methods, and the results were not encouraging. Recent findings by this investigator and others however suggest that for BA10 at least, there may be greater predictive validity across method than might at first be expected. For instance, three recent PET studies of situations involving the maintenance and execution of delayed intentions have implicated BA10 in this function. The behavioural corollary of a deficit in this domain would be failures of task switching and an inability to follow one's planned actions. Remarkably, a human group lesion study has demonstrated exactly these problems in patients whose lesions involved BA10. The proposed research will address these issues by testing seven plausible theories concerning the role of BA10 emerging from previous work of the investigator and others, and using a discriminant validity approach. A key component of the investigation is that identical paradigms will be used across two methods (lesion work and functional imaging, both with humans).

title: The underlying factors contributing to pragmatic language impairment.
description: The underlying factors contributing to pragmatic language impairment Many developmental disorders result in some type of pragmatic impairment, i.e. abnormality in the appropriate use of language in context. In some cases, pragmatic language impairment (PLI) has no known origin. In others, it is part of a recognised syndrome such as autistic disorder. The proposed research will investigate the nature and underlying causes of PLI by addressing the following questions. Are pragmatic language deficits indicative of impaired social cognition, or do other factors such as delayed language acquisition or impaired executive function contribute significantly? And do the same or different underlying factors result in pragmatic impairment in children with acquired neurological disorders such as hydrocephalus and head injury. In order to address these issues, a battery of measures wil be devised which tap a variety of pragmatic language skills. These will include understanding of non-literal language and humour, lexical ambiguity, inferencing, emotion recognition, and narrative discourse. These are all areas where pragmatic deficits have been investigated in adults with acquired injuries of the right hemisphere and/or frontal lobes, but little work has been done on this topic in children. In the first instance, comparisons will be made between secondary school children diagnosed with typical Specific Language Impairment (SLI) and those with PLI and two groups of typically developing children, one matched on age and the other on language ability, as assessed by traditional non- pragmatic tests that assess areas such as vocabulary and grammar. Group membership will be determined by use of the Children's Communication Checklist (Bishop, 1998). In addition to the 'pragmatic language' measures described above, standardised tests of verbal and non-verbal ability and measures of social cognition, executive function, and memory will be given to all participants. The first question to consider is whether children with PLI will peprform poorly on all the pragmatic measures relative to their age matched peers, or whether their deficits will be evident on only a subset of tasks. A second question is whether they show impairments relative to language age controls or the SLI group. If the PLI group is more impaired than the other two groups, it indicates their pragmatic deficits cannot be explained in terms of general language maturity. This project poses major intellectual challenges, as it will involve developing new assessment methods that are suitable for children, sensitive to pragmatic difficulties and able to distinguish between different underlying causes.

title: Modulation of orbitofrontal - ventral striatal mechanisms by serotonin and dopamine in discrimination reversal learning in the marmoset.
description: Modulation of orbitofrontal - ventral striatal mechanisms by serotonin and dopamine in discrimination reversal learning in the marmoset. Disruption of OFC-VS circuitry and its modulation by DA or 5-HT is implicated in a variety of clinical disorders including Fronto-temporal Dementia (FtD), Schizophrenia, Depression, Huntington's (HD) and Parkinson's Disease (PD). In some, a disruption of this circuitry appears early on in the disorder, i.e. FtD, while in others it appears later, i.e. HD, PD. From the patients' behaviour it is evident that a disruption of this circuitry has profound effects on decision making in the social domain. While visual discrimination learning and reversal is sensitive to OFC and VS lesions in monkey, little is known of the neuromodulation of this circuitry by the ascending DA and 5-HT pathways, although systemic treatment with drugs affecting DA and 5-HT receptors have been shown to either facilitate or disrupt reversal learning. Reversal learning has also been shown to be disrupted in patients suffering from FtD, schizophrenia and also in the later, but not not early stages, of HD and PD. However, a number of different processes contribute to the ability of humans and other animals to alter their responding in accordance with changing reward contingencies. Thus, it is necessary to directly compare specific neural and neurochemical manipulations on a variety of different versions of reversal learning (that differentially tax these processes) in order to differentiate the contribution of the OFC and the VS and their modulation by DA and 5-HT. The project will compare the effects of (i) selective excitotoxic lesions of the OFC and VS and (ii) neuropharmacological manipulations of the DA and 5-HT system (6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA) and 5,7 dihydroxytryptamine (5,7 DHT) will be used to deplete the prefrontal or striatal DA system and dorsal raphe 5-HT system respectively) on a variety of reversal learning procedures. title: Cognitive and neuroimaging abnormalities in schizophrenia: The West London Study.
description: Over the last five years we have conducted a study of first-episode schizophrenia and established that motor, oculomotor and cognitive abnormalities, indicative of dysfunction of fronto-striatal and temporo-limbic circuits, are already present at the time of illness onset. These abnormalities appear to follow different trajectories a year later. Using novel imaging paradigms we have evidence to suggest that subtle brain abnormalities are also present at the illness onset and that these abnormalities may be progressive in some patients. Over the next five years we wish to continue and extend the study to: 1) examine the heterogeneity of cognitive and imaging phenotypes; 2) how these phenotypes mediate clinical and social outcomes; 3) the trajectories they follow over time; 4) medication effects, and 5) include patients with late onset schizophrenia for a comprehensive examination of disease heterogeneity.

title: Susceptibility genes for psychosis in individuals with velo-cardio-facial syndrome (VCFS).
description: Velo-cardio-facial syndrome (VCFS) is usually caused by a deletion of chromosome 22q11. Previously, we and others have shown that people with VCFS have an extraordinary risk of developing psychosis, particularly schizophrenia, that is approximately 30 times higher than the general population. Given that VCFS subjects have such an elevated risk for schizophrenia, and that this is attributable to a single homogeneous risk factor (deletion 22q11), VCFS offer a uniquely powerful opportunity to identify alleles that confer susceptibility to schizophrenia. We postulate that the high susceptibility to schizophrenia in VCFS results from polymorphic haploinsufficiency of genes within the VCFS deletion region. In this application our aim is to test this hypothesis. To achieve this, we will: 1) Recruit a total sample of 100 comprehensively assessed adults with chromosome 22q11 deletions; 2) Screen all genes that map to the VCFS deletion region for sequence variation; 3) Test these variants for association with schizophrenia in our sample of VCFS subjects; 4) Test alleles found to be associated with schizophrenia in VCFS for association with schizophrenia in the general population in the large case-control and family based association samples that already available to us.

title: Characterisation of the neuronal and glial cytoarchitecture in major psychiatric disorders and the investigation of potential mechanisms.
description: Objectives: This research programme is driven by my previous findings of a cortical glial cell deficit and neuronal size reduction in these major depression and schizophrenia. I will address the four main questions: Which glial cell population is responsible for the glial cell deficit in major depression and schizophrenia? This will be done in the candidate cortical regions using stereological methods, immunohistochemistry and tissue donated by the Stanley Foundation Brain Consortium. Are glial cell deficits reproducible in rat models of 'depression-vulnerability', 'depression-like state', and 'stress'? Cell number, size and dendritic aborisation will be evaluated stereologically in candidate brain regions in well-validated rat models. Is exposure to pharmacological agents associated with these changes? This investigation will be done using a human in-vitro primary mixed human cell culture system and will assess the influence of glucocorticoids, lithium, haloperidol and desipramine on neuronal and glial cytoarchitecture. Proteome analysis of the cortical grey matter from the anterior cingulate cortex and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and major depressive disorder. This investigation will allow us to explore the basis of the important and replicated cytoarchitectural changes observed in these regions each disorder in my current fellowship. Together these investigations will address the common aim of improving our understanding of the mechanisms underlying the neuronal and glial changes observed in these major psychiatric disorders.

title: Integrative physiology and behaviour of anxiety: characterisation of an 'emotional motor system' and central autonomic control.
description: In order to investigate the neural mechanisms underlying the autonomic and behavioural components of anxiety and fear, including the role of CRF, CRF- related neuropeptides, and serotonergic systems, an ideal model system would be clinically relevant, would permit a reproducible induction of anxiety from animal to animal, and would minimize influences of the experimenter on the animals. One such model is hypercapnia (high concentrations of carbon dioxide). Several features of this stimulus make it an ideal experimental model, including (1) hypercapnia is a potent anxiogenic stimulus and can induce panic in human patients (Argyropoulos et al., 2002); (2) the use of hypercapnia as a stimulus allows exquisite control over stimulus parameters including intensity, duration, and frequency; (3) the stimulus can be applied and integrated behavioural and physiological indices of anxiety and fear can be monitored in the complete absence of the experimenter; and (4) hypercapnia has previously been shown to selectively activate neurones within the caudal portion of the DRN and a distributed neural system associated with anxiety and fear. In fact, serotonergic neurones within the brainstem raphe and rostral ventrolateral medulla are primary chemosensory (pH-sensing; hy8percapnia- sensing_ neurones, suggesting that serotonergic systems may play a prominent role in the physiological and behavioural responses to this anxiogenic stimulus. In support of this hypothesis, direct activation of chemosensory pathways results in a prolonged increase in respiration that is dependent upon central serotonergic mechanisms. For these studies we will utilise state-of- the art facilities for telemetric measurement of heart rate, blood pressure, body temperature, and behavioural analysis. These studies will provide important new insights into the neural mechanisms underlying the autonomic and behavioural components of anxiety and fear, including the role of CRF, CRF- related neuropeptides, and serotonergic systems.

title: High-density infant event-related potential acquisition and analysis system.
description: Diagnosis of atypical development in specific cognitive domains before the full impairment is manifest remains a challenge for researchers and clinicians, because cognitive systems are defined by their plasticity in development. Infants with developmental disorders may show normal levels of behavioural performance that are in fact mediated by atypical neurocognitive systems ultimately leading to the emergence of observable impairments. We are requesting funds to purchase a system for acquisition and analysis of infant high-density event-related potentials in order to conduct a series of studies to complement ongoing behavioural investigations in specific paediatric populations. Event-related potentials (ERPs) are non-invasive and painless recordings of brain electrical activity measured from the scalp. The ease of recording and relatively robust signal make this technique preferable for use as a functional measure of brain activity in infants, very young children, and patient populations for whom the demands of other imaging techniques may be too great (e.g. positron emission tomography which requires exposure to radiation, or magnetic resonance imaging where minute head motion significantly degrades the signal). While ERPs cannot pinpoint the precise location of neural generators, high-density ERPs can provide a good description of their spatial characteristics and, importantly, can indicate whether the network of neural generators activated during a task is typical or atypical. High density arrays are thus advantageous, but they also present a difficulty. Applying a large number of electrodes quickly is challenging. In traditional methods of application, each recording site needs to be cleansed, abraded and electrodes fixed one-by-one. Even modern electrode 'caps', designed to minimise application time, can take hours to prepare for high- density recordings. Clearly this is not desirable for infants or children with disabilities who would not be able to tolerate this lengthy procedure let alone cooperate with testing once application was completed. For this reason, we are specifically requesting the Geodesic sensor net system, the only system of its kind which allows a rapid and accurate placement of high-density electrode arrays (up to 128 electrodes for infants).

title: Organophosphate pesticide poisoning in Sri Lanka - management, complications and pharmacogenetics. Supplementary funds.
description: Deliberate self-poisoning has reached epidemic proportions in parts of the developing world where highly toxic poisons and sparse medical facilities ensure a high fatality rate. Pesticides are the major problem - the WHO estimates that they cause more than 220,000 deaths worldwide each year. Most deaths are due to organophosphate (OP) pesticides and occur in the young economically active age group. Self-poisoning is particularly important in Sri Lanka where thousands of people die each year and preventing suicide has become a national public health priority. The case fatality rate of OP poisoning in Sri Lanka is ~20% but may reach 60% in some hospitals. Best therapeutic practice is unclear since none of the therapies used in OP poisoning has been subjected to randomised controlled trials (RCT). In addition, the rate of complications and the effect of therapy on their incidence have not been assessed. We propose to recruit a cohort of around 2000 OP poisoned patients and 3000 patients with other forms of self-poisoning to determine whether activated charcoal or pralidoxime reduce mortality following OP poisoning. The incidence of complications and the importance of pralidoxime in preventing the intermediate syndrome will be studied in these patients. The cohort will also be used to assess the importance of polymorphisms in the enzymes that metabolise organophosphate pesticides - cytochrome p450, glutathione S-transferase, and paraoxanase - in determining the outcome of OP poisoning. These enzymes metabolise the pesticides to both more and less toxic compounds - inhibition of particular enzymes prevents toxicity in some animal models. Identification of similar patterns in the OP- poisoned patients may indicate a path for future development of effective therapies.

title: Centre for language, mind and emotion.
description: Our aim is to create a Centre for Language, Mind and Emotion. This will be a centre of excellence bringing together research on normal and disordered cognition, and building on existing strengths in the Department of Psychology. The Centre will act as a focus for scientists and professionals, and will take fundamental theory through to practical application. The Centre will draw principally on the expertise of a core of 9 academic staff from the Psychology Department, who will transfer existing projects to the new Centre and then use its facilities to enhance synergies between their various interests and develop new lines of research where psychological theory is directly engaged with significant practical issues. Topics to be investigated will include: Developmental disorders including dyslexia, specific language impairment, and other forms of communication problem Improving the acquisition of literacy by normal children Language processes in normal and brain-injured adults Social perception in normal and brain-injured adults The relationship between cognition and emotion The emotional make-up of individuals who have committed offences and are regarded as psychopathic in nature Investigation of these practical questions will be underpinned by a strong commitment to linking them to fundamental theory. The Centre will therefore remain heavily involved in basic research, keeping it well-placed to draw maximal scientific benefit from the interplay between theoretical and practical concerns. The support requested is for the construction of a new building to house the Centre, equipment for new projects that will be developed, and the funding of core staff posts for an initial three years.

title: A New Biomedical Sciences Research Building.
description: The proposal is for a new Biomedical Sciences Research Building to house approximately 250 scientists, working across a spectrum of science from structural biology to environmental health, with emphasis on Structural Biology, Cell Signalling and Cardiovascular Science. The MRC Institute of Environment and Health will be incorporated in the building, interacting with Genetic Epidemiology and aspects of Toxicology. The building and the research which it will house are based on the central concept of advancing the science by maximising interdisciplinary interactions between internationally recognised groups, across Departmental boundaries. The particular needs within each scientific area have been incorporated within the design, which includes special accommodation for high-field NMR instruments and a whole-body MRI scanner for small animals. Laboratories for Cell Signalling, Cardiovascular Science, Cancer Biology, Molecular Genetics are based on a flexible, modular design and all include adjacent instrument rooms directly accessible from the laboratories. The laboratories for electrophysiology are based on the same module but have been specifically designed to suit the users. Extensive facilities for animal cell culture include both central services and earmarked cell rooms accessed from specific laboratories. Communal facilities, such as cold rooms, dark rooms, centrifuge rooms, etc. are accessible from a 'laboratory corridor' on all floors. There is strong emphasis on the provision of shared and communal facilities, including a Protein and Nucleic Acid Chemistry Laboratory and a Protein Expression Laboratory. Offices will be adjacent to the laboratories, but physically separated and served via a 'clean corridor' to safeguard the office environment. Activities relating to Cardiovascular Science are strongly featured in the proposal. The Cardiovascular Science group itself will focus on studies of ion channels, receptors and signalling pathways that are relevant to cardiovascular function and disease. Programmes in Cell Signalling and Genetics are also targeted on angiogenesis, signalling pathways and genetic systems that are implicated in cardiovascular disease. Many of the current and planned structural studies will focus on proteins that are relevant to this area.

title: Space, Psyche and Psychiatry: Mental Health/Illness and the Construction and Experience of Space, ca. 1600-2000' conference to be held at Ruskin College, Oxford from 13 to 15th December 2002.
description: In light of a growing interest in the area, it seems an opportune moment to convene a conference on "Space, Psyche and Psychiatry: Mental Health/Illness and the Construction and Experience of Space, ca. 1600-2000". Already in a series of publications, architectural and medical historians, psychiatrists, geographers and sociologists have grappled with common issues such as the ideal of the building as a machine for mental health; power and space within psychiatric institutions; the competing and coalescing politics, economics and ethics of the planning and design of such institutions, and international networks of influence in such contexts. Increasingly, users/patients' own varied and shifting experiences of institutional and other spaces have become a topic of interest, as indeed has the (therapeutic/iatrogenic) psychiatrising of space in the community, outside of the walls of mental hospitals. The main themes this conference seeks to address are as follows: 1. The intentions and ideologies behind the design, planning, geographical siting, architecture and construction of psychiatric/mental health oriented spaces. 2. The role and interaction of various actors, professional/medical and lay/non-medical in the arbitration of such spaces. 3. How space was felt/experienced/mediated by patients'/users; how ownership of space was established, asserted and contested. 4. Others' (e.g. asylum staff) views/experiences and manipulations of "psychiatric space". 5. Psychiatrically-influenced space outside of (as well as inside) institutions (e.g. domestic space, urban space). 6. The spatial environments designed by the mentally ill. 7. Movements into, through, between and out of psychiatric/mental health oriented spaces. 8. The explanation and rationales for broad changes over time in any of the above areas. These themes have been identified and emphasised because they appear to us both to crystallise a range of the major issues in recent research in this field, while also pointing to some significant and discrete directions for research which have been neglected by scholars. Themes were also defined for speakers in this way to ensure some degree of coherence and cross-filtration in presentations, although we have stressed to speakers that we are also open to other suggestions within the general area encapsulated by the conference title.

title: Can investigations of brain function predict the development of psychosis? A follow-up study using event related potentials and fMRI.
description: Can investigations of brain function predict the development of psychosis? A follow-up study using Event Related Potentials and fMRI Aims: (1) To study brain (dys)function in the prodromal phase of psychosis using Event Related Potentials (ERP) and Functional MRI (fMRI). (2) To investigate the use of ERP or fMRI measures to predict which prodomal subjects progress to psychosis. Background: Recent studies claim that early treatment of psychotic disorders may lead to a better prognosis; however, conventional practice is to withhold treatment until frank psychosis has developed. About 40% of 'high-risk' prodromal subjects go on to develop a full-blown psychotic disorder within 6 months. As these subgroups are clinically indistinguishable, could they be differentiated by other methods? Meta-analyses of biological markers of vulnerability to schizophrenia show that the P50 wave has the highest effect size, closely followed by P300 amplitude. Abnormal patterns of asymmetry in the spatial distribution of the P300 wave are also promising. This project seeks to measure such markers at the prodromal stage, and assess whether these may predict subsequent transition to psychosis. Hypotheses: (A) At least 40% of this 'high risk' prodromal sample will develop a first episode of psychosis within 1 year. (B) The subset of prodromal subjects who develop psychosis will display one or more of the following abnormalities compared to controls: (1) Impaired ability to suppress the P50 wave to repetitive stimuli, (2) Deficits in the prepulse inhibition of startle reflex, (3) P300 with smaller amplitude and abnormal asymmetry and (4) attenuated fMRI activation in the superior temporal gyrus while performing the P300 oddball task. (C) Prodromal subjects who do not develop psychosis will perform like controls on the above ERP and fMRI measures. Methods: Subjects will be 50 prodromal subjects and 25 controls. At baseline all 75 participants will undergo a clinical assessment and ERP testing. Half of them will also undergo fMRI testing. After 12 months all 50 prodromal subjects will be re-assessed clinically to ascertain progression to psychosis. The fMRI data will be analysed using established non-parametric techniques. The ERP analyses will involved calculation of amplitude and latency of the above waveforms. Repeated measures (M)ANOVA will be used to compare ERP and fMRI parameters across 3 groups: prodromals who stay unaffected, prodromals who develop psychosis and controls. Implications: ERPs and fMRI may help to identify people at high risk to develop psychosis, who could benefit from early treatment.

title: The role of kainate receptors in developmental synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus.
description: Fast excitatory neurotransmission in the brain is mainly mediated by glutamate. This amino acid exerts its action through metabotropic or ionotropic receptors and have been implicated in synaptic plasticity, neuronal development and neurodegeneration. Three subtypes of ionotropic glutamate receptors have been described: NMDA, AMPA and kainite receptors. Most of the physiological roles of kainite receptors remain unknown. However, with the development of specific pharmacological tools, a work carried out in Dr Isaac's laboratory has shown the synaptic activation of kainite receptors in the somatosensory cortex. In addition to their postsynaptic role, kainite receptors also regulate transmitted release by a presynaptic mechanism. The expression of kainite receptors is strongly regulated during the development suggesting a role in network activity. Unfortunately, most of the functional studies on kainite receptors were performed in adult tissues. To date, only one study from Dr. Isaac's laboratory described the developmental regulation of function of synaptic kainate receptors. Indeed, in the developing barrel cortex, the kainite receptors contribution to transmission decreases. Moreover, they showed that the induction of long term potentiation also causes a reduction of the kainate receptors component. I will investigate the role of kainate receptors in synaptic transmission in the CA1 region of the hippocampus during the development. I will use whole cell patch clamp recordings from neurons in hippocampal slices. I will investigate whether a kainate receptor-mediated excitatory postsynaptic current (EPSC) can be generated at glutamatergic synapses onto CA1 pyramidal neurons in early development stages. This will be done using pharmacological tools: in the presence of a cocktail of antagonists of non-glutamatergic ionotropic receptors and NMDA receptors, the kainate receptor-mediated EPSC must be blocked by the non selective antagonist of the AMPA and kainate receptors (NBQX) and not be blocked by the AMPA receptor antagonist (GYKI53655). Then I will carry out the electrophysiological characterisation of this EPSC in the early stage and during the development. Finally, I will investigate whether kainate receptor-mediated excitatory postsynaptic potential can trigger action potential. Such a kainite receptor-mediated EPSC have been described at glutamatergic inputs onto CA1 GABAergic interneurons in adolescents animals. I will also investigate whether this EPSC exist in early development stages. At glutamatergic synapses onto CA1 pyramidal neurons, in adult animals, pharmacological activation of presynaptic kainate receptors inhibits glutamate release. These receptors also regulate GABAergic synapses onto CA1 pyramidal neurons and onto other interneurons. Then, I will study the role of the presynaptic kainate receptors in early development stages. I will also investigate how these receptors physiologically activated which at present remains is unknown. The role of kainate receptors have been demonstrated in the expression of the long term potentiation at developing thalamocortical synapses and also at the mossy fibres-CA3 synapses. However, to date, the role of kainate receptors in long term potentiation in the CA1 region remains unknown. Then, I will investigate the role of kainate receptors in synaptic plasticity in the CA1 region of the hippocampus during the development. These experiments will be done by applying a long term potentiation or a long term depression induction protocol in the presence and in the absence of the kainate receptor antagonist (LY382884). Some synaptic plasticity are NMDA receptors-dependent. I will also determine if the kainate receptor-dependent synaptic plasticity is sensitive to the NMDA receptor antagonist (D-AP5). Several subunits compose a functional kainate receptor: GluR5, GluR6, GluR7, KA1 or KA2. I will have access to mutant mice lacking GluR5 and GluR6 subunits. I will investigate the role of these subunits in the synaptic transmission and the synaptic plasticity during the development.

title: An empirical investigation of clinical perfectionism.
description: The research project that would be performed exclusively by the student is to empirically evaluate the cognitive-behavioural analysis of clinical perfectionism. The hypotheses to be investigated are: Clinical perfectionism is maintained by: Repeated "performance checking" accompanied by biased evaluation of performance. Re-appraising standards as being insufficiently demanding if they are met Reacting to any perceived "failure" with self- criticism Avoidance and procrastination of tasks in the salient domain. Clinical perfectionism impedes the successful treatment of comorbid psychiatric disorders if the domain in which the perfectionism is expressed overlaps with the domain of the disorder. Clinical perfectionism and self- evaluation are intimately related. Specifically: The self-evaluation of people with clinical perfectionism is overly dependent on the pursuit and attainment of personal standards in a salient domain, despite significant adverse consequences. Clinical perfectionism is maintained by negative self- evaluation. In order to test these hypotheses, Ms Riley will need to further characterise the phenomenology of clinical perfectionism and develop reliable and valid means of assessing it. There are multiple intellectual challenges posed by this research. First, Ms Riley must be cognisant of the academic literature in multiple areas: these include eating disorders, depression, perfectionism and self-esteem; development of assessment measures; and the conduct of experimental manipulations of variables. Second, Ms Riley will need to conduct studies that manipulate specific variables of interest (such as the biased evaluation of performance) in order to determine their effect on perfectionism. This will involve designing specific research studies, recruiting participants, collecting data, analysing data and preparing the findings for publication.

title: Neuroscience
description: WT Studentship Grant Project title: Amygdala-cortical processing in males with social-cognitive dysfunction. The basis of this research investigation is the observation that there is substantial variability in the general population in their ability to recognise accurately the facial expression of fear, to a greater degree than is found in the recognition accuracy of other facial expressions. Individuals who are very poor at accurately classifying fearful facial expressions (usually presented in the form of standardised photographs) are also poor at identifying faces they have seen previously (face-recognition memory). Both these deficits have been reported consistently, as characteristic of people with autism in association with normal-range intelligence. We have shown in pilot work that in the general population, the face-processing problems are associated with self-reported autistic personality traits, and also with impairments on a Theory of Mind task that are characteristic of individuals with autism. In a separate series of studies we have shown that females with a single X-chromosome (Turner syndrome) have characteristic deficits in their recognition of the facial expression of fear, but not other facial emotions. This failure accurately to identify fear is associated with poor face recognition memory, and with impaired Theory of Mind skills. The presumption we have made is that the same neural system, part of the 'social brain', is dysfunctional in 45,X females, autistic patients, and individuals selected from the general population on the basis of deficits in fear-recognition abilities. In other studies we have shown that particular classes of X-linked genes are likely to be responsible for this dysfunction: such genes are exquisitely dosage-sensitive and they are expressed in insufficient dosage in 45,X females compared with 46,XX (normal females.

title: Macromolecular assemblies.
description: The role of BubR1 in maintaining the fidelity of chromosome segregation Prior to cell division, the replicated genome is segregated such that the two daughter cells receive all the genetic information required for further growth and development. Accurate chromosome segregation is achieved by regulating anaphase onset. Chromosome segregation in eukaryotes takes place during mitosis. When a cell enters mitosis, the microtubule organising centres (centrosomes in animal cells, spindle pole bodies in yeast) separate to form a bipolar array of interdigitating microtubules (MTs) called the mitotic spindle apparatus. The spindle checkpoint couples chromosome alignment with anaphase onset. Yeast genetics identified a number of spindle checkpoint including the Bub (Bub1, a protein kinase, and Bub3) and Mad (Mad1, Mad2 and Mad3) proteins and Mps1, another protein kinase. These proteins are conserved in humans and localise to kinetochores, consistent with monitoring KT-MT interactions. Analysis of the mammalian spindle checkpoint. To address these questions, research in my lab is taking a multidisciplinary approach focussing on Bub1 and BubR1. Specifically, we are: 1. Analysing and purifying Bub1 and BubR1 complexes from checkpoint activated cells. We are using small molecules and RNAi to determine what regulates the assembly of these complexes. 2. Inhibiting individual protein, e.g. by RNAi and/or expression of mutants, and analysing the consequences in single cell, microscopy based assays, e.g. DeltaVision, time-lapse etc. 3. Targeting the Bub genes in mouse ES cells to generate in vitro and in vivo models to study the role of Bub1 and BubR1 in the spindle checkpoint and animal development. This project will extend and complement these strategies, thus building upon previous research in my lab. Specificialy, we will develop a novel biochemical assay with which to study the spindle checkpoint.

title: Neuroscience.
description: Efffect of variation in 5-HT transporter gene expression on the behavioural and molecular actions of antidepressant drugs Biological variation in the 5-HT transporter (5-HTT) gene has been linked to altered mood and anxiety-related behaviours and therapeutic response to antidepressant drug treatment. This project will investigate whether variation in the 5-HTT gene expression is associated with i) altered levels of emotional responsivity and neuronal reactivity within specific fear/anxiety circuits and ii) different levels of responsiveness to antidepressant treatment. Experiments will be carried out using behavioural and molecular studies of emotional reactivity in a newly developed mouse model which over-expresses the 5-HTT. A mouse model with the 5-HTT gene knocked out will become available for use in these experiments during the course of the studies. The information gained from these studies will be used to inform neuropsychological studies of emotional responsivity which will be carried out in human volunteers with putative functional variants of the 5-HTT gene.

title: The cellular and molecular basis of disease
description: WT Studentship Project title: Investigation of DISC1 and DISC2, candidate genes for susceptibility to major psychiatric illness. Schizophrenia and related psychiatric disorders are devastating illnesses affecting approximately 1% of the population worldwide. It is clear from family, twin and adoption studies that there is a significant genetic component underlying these disorders, although its nature awaits conclusive identification. It has become apparent that major psychiatric illnesses can be classified as 'common complex disorders' arising from elaborate interactions between few or several genes and environmental influences. However, it is also evident that single genes of major effect are likely to underlie the psychiatric illness that runs in some families, and that such families may be key to identification of the genetic basis and resulting pathology of severe disorders such as schizophrenia. In general, genetic methodologies such as linkage analysis and association studies have been used in attempts to identify the genes responsible for psychiatric disorders. Until recently, however, these have been largely unsuccessful, although promising candidate genes are beginning to emerge. We are taking a different approach to gene identification by investigating a balanced chromosomal translocation between the long arms of chromosomes 1 and 11. This translocation co-segregates with major psychiatric illness in a large Scottish Family, indicating that inheritance of the translocation confers susceptibility to developing severe psychiatric disorders. On chromosome 1 the translocation directly disrupts two genes named Disrupted In Schiziophrenia 1 and 2 (DISC1 and DISC2) that are consequently considered to be candidate susceptibility genes for schizophrenia and related disorders. The function of both genes is unknown, although emerging data on protein interactions involving DISC1 indicates that it may be involved in processes that are important for central nervous system development. DISC2 is apparently a large non-coding RNA gene that is located antisense to DISC1, however, its full extent remains to be identified since we have been unable to determine its size from northern blots. We aim to identify the full extent of transcripts arising from DISC2 and confirm that the gene is non-coding.

title: Psychiatry and primary care in modern Britain, c.1925-1975.
description: The role of psychological medicine in general practice has been described as one of the biggest gaps in the history of psychiatry. It is also one of the biggest gaps in the history of general practice. This project aims to remedy this situation, at least in part, through a thematic survey of the evolving relations between psychiatry and primary care in Britain between the 1920s and the 1970s. Drawing on extensive primary materials, it isolates for analysis four crucial developments, organized chronologically: (i) the impact of psychological theories on differential diagnoses in the inter-war period; (ii) the psychologization of the doctor-patient relationship during and after the Second World War; (iii) the role of general practitioner research in the development of psychiatric epidemiology during the early years of the NHS; and (iv) the work of GPs as frontline psychiatrists and prescribers of anti- depressants in the 1960s and '70s. The study will demonstrate how new psychological and neurophysiological models have modified doctor-patient relationships, leading to new hermeneutic approaches to patient testimony and a renewed awareness of the therapeutic effectiveness of the clinical encounter. It will make clear the reciprocal connections between these intellectual and pharmaceutical innovations and the economic and professional organisation of general practice. Such study is vital in an age in which psychological problems increasingly dominate primary care and in which psychosomatic theories of illness and healing have become central to both the popular understanding of medicine and its recent historiography.

title: Cataloguing of the papers of R D Laing.
description: Research Resources in Medical History: The papers of R D Laing To employ a full-time Project Officer to complete the cataloguing of the papers of R D Laing to our on-line manuscripts catalogue. The papers of Ronald David Laing (1927-1989), psychiatrist, psychotherapist, writer and poet were purchased from the trustees of his estate in July 1997, the acquisition being made possible with the generous support of the National Fund for Acquisitions and the Friends of Glasgow University Library. During the period November 1998 to July 1999, as part of NFF supported cataloguing projects, some 4,000 documents were catalogued and made accessible via our online web-catalogue of manuscripts. This material has already generated considerable interest. Laing's work, especially in the areas of patient care and the aetiology of schizophrenia, are currently undergoing a re-evaluation. Making this key resource more accessible will be of significant service to researchers. On the basis of the earlier cataloguing work it is estimated that the remainder of the collection could be fully described within eighteen months. We are therefore requesting support to employ a full-time Research Assistant to achieve this.
