title: Exploring the anatomy and neurochemistry of frontal lobe function in health and schizophrenia.
description: Delusions are core symptoms of psychotic illnesses such as schizophrenia. Central to our understanding of delusions is the idea that they emerge from a background of abnormal formation of associations. Over the last decade, there has been an increasing understanding of the neuroscience of association formation. This work has emphasised prediction error signal as a drive to associative learning and a guide to allocation of attention and to selection of action. The goal of my proposed work is to test the hypothesis that delusional beliefs arise from changes in association formation as a consequence of abnormal prediction error signalling. In order to do so, I wish to combine behavioural, psychopharmacological and functional neuroimaging studies to: Refine understanding of prediction error-driven associative learning processes in humans Establish the extent and nature of disruption of these processes, (both in terms of behaviour and brain response) a) in deluded individuals and b) under ketamine administration. Test directly the possibility of a link between symptoms of psychosis and disturbances in associative learning by evaluating the extent to which these behavioural and brain responses predict the existence or emergence of delusional beliefs (under ketamine and in psychosis).

title: The relationship between sensorimotor and verbal self-monitoring and psychotic symptoms in schizophrenia: a psychophysical and functional neuroimaging study.
description: I propose to examine the neurophysiology of positive symptoms in schizophrenia using psychophysical measures and functional neuroimaging, incorporating both electroencephalography and magnetic resonance imaging. I will examine healthy volunteers and patients with schizophrenia when symptomatic and when asymptomatic, using a range of verbal and sensorimotor self-monitoring tasks. I propose to test the hypothesis that sensorimotor and verbal self-monitoring deficits in schizophrenia are associated with functional abnormalities in the same cortical networks. The combined use of electroencephalography and functional magnetic resonance imaging will allow both spatial and temporal mapping of neural activity. These investigations will also serve to clarify the neurophysiological basis of sensorimotor and verbal self-monitoring in normal subjects, as well as its role in the pathophysiology of psychotic symptoms. The project will be based at the Institute of Psychiatry (IoP) London, using the local clinical population and neuroimaging expertise, complemented by an extensive training in the psychophysics, cognitive psychology and neurophysiology at the Institute of Neurology (IoN), London.

title: The impact of a water development on parental investment in rural Ethiopia local perceptions.
description: In this project, Abate will test the hypothesis that parents' intentions and behaviour in child rearing have been influenced by a new labour-saving technology. New water-supply developments in rural Ethiopia have dramatically reduced women's workloads by reducing the need to trek long distances daily to collect water. Abate will be gathering local perceptions of how the changes in women's time and energy budgets are influencing both their own fertility, their children's well-being and their own behaviour towards their children. She will be conducting these interviews after a quantitative survey of villages with and without new water points has been collected, which will provide data on a range of biosocial variables that describe the well-being of children in these villages. Abate will be able to test whether the changes that parents perceive are indeed those observed in the quantitative surveys. An earlier study at this site (in which Abate assisted) has already shown that the fertility of the women have increased as a response to the introduction of the water points (Gibson & Mace 2002 a,b). Demographic change is often hard for those involved to assess, as Montgomery (2000) observed for mortality decline. Perceptions of fertility increase have not to our knowledge been previously examined. Also stated sex preferences are not always the same as those observed in data on parental behaviour or child nutrition (as in Cronk 1991, where a preference for boys was stated by Mukogodo parents in northern Kenya, but behavioural biases and nutritional information in fact showed that girls were favoured). Thus it is entirely possible that local perceptions of change will be widely discrepant with what is observed in the quantitative bio-behavioural data. If this is the case, it has relevance to the interpretation of a wide range of qualitative approaches in demography.

title: Medicine Man Exhibition Education Programme at British Museum.
description: Proposal for Wellcome Trust on Wellcome Trust Gallery/'Medicine Man' exhibition Education Programme at The British Museum: This proposal suggests an outline programme that will enable us to engage several of our key audiences and also maximise the opportunities offered by exhibition and gallery especially when running concurrently. To be cross cultural and cross curricular, promoting the Museum as a forum for debate about ideas and current issues as well as displaying visually arresting objects. There are opportunities to explore issues of wellbeing in society as well as developments in contemporary art and their relationship to the ethical, social and cultural context for recent developments in biomedical science. The new gallery will provide a thematic focus for the adjacent Americas, Africa and Asia galleries, and enable us to develop new types of programming for school, college and adult audiences as a result, particularly using drama in collaboration with the Wellcome Trust. Emphasis is on inclusion, with access and community groups. Programmes at all levels will be in partnership wherever possible: with community and access partners such as Kingsway and Barnet colleges (e.g. for adults recovering from mental illness); with adult education such as City Lit and Birkbeck; and with school/teacher education partners such as King's and the Institute of Education. We will develop new areas of the curriculum for the Museum, such as AS Sociology (Health is a term long module) and the Schools Council History Project (History of Medicine is a popular topic with secondary schools), and on linking science, arts and humanities (as we have for the North America gallery for example) and citizenship (we have begun programmes in this area). This gallery will provide a good opportunity to look at cross-cultural ideas of citizenship, particularly in terms of the environment (working with e.g. Oxfam and UNICEF).

title: Genetic analysis of susceptibility to depression.
description: Mapping the susceptibility loci for psychiatric disorders has so far proved difficult because the intensive interviewing necessary for reliable diagnosis has prohibited the collection of the large sample sizes needed to detect relatively small genetic effects. We propose an alternative strategy: to map neuroticism, a major genetic mediator of at least two common psychiatric disorders, major depression and generalized anxiety disorder. Neuroticism is a quantitative trait that can be scored reliably and easily by the completion of a questionnaire, the Eysenck Personality Questionnaire (EPQ). It has been shown that in many cases mapping quantitative trait loci (QTLs) is a more powerful approach than mapping qualitative traits, but even so many thousands of sib pairs are needed to detect loci with low heritabilities. Recent statistical analyses have demonstrated that most of the statistical power comes from sampling pairs that are either discordant or concordant thus making it possible to genotype a fraction of the total sample and yet maintain power. We have used existing estimates of the heritability, mode of inheritance and sibling correlations for neuroticism to simulate sampling strategies. These simulations lead us to propose genotyping 900 sib pairs and the parents of half the sample to detect a locus with a heritability of 10% in the most likely situations with a power of over 80%. To reduce the environmental variance of the EPQ measure, we will use a re-screening strategy. On the basis of a pilot study of our recruitment method, we estimate that by contacting 100,000 patients on the lists of 40 Oxfordshire general practices we will be able to recruit 900 sib pairs for this study.

title: Risk conceptualisation and decision-making in the face of contradictory information: The case of MMR
description: Sample Recruitment (Phase I): 50 affluent and 50 non-affluent (as determined by occupational class and residence) parents of healthy children will be recruited from nurseries, toddler playgroups, and through noticeboards in places frequented by parents of young children (e.g. public mother-and-baby rooms) (Romney et al calculate a minimum sample size of 29 informants is needed to assess cultural consensus at the 95% confidence level of 99% of the questions asked). Data will be collected on education level, household income earners, birth order of children, and acquaintances with cases of autism. Focus Groups and Interviews (Phase I): Three focus groups (of 6-8 participants) will be formed from among the 100 participants, selecting one group of parents with children due for the vaccine, one group of parents who opted for the vaccine, and one group who opted against. All 100 participants will then be asked to participate in a semi-structured interview held at a time and location convenient to them, after an initial pilot study (with 20 participants) conducted to validate and refine the questionnaire. In addition to the questionnaire, parents will be asked to discuss, in their own terms, their perceptions and decisions about MMR, and encouraged to discuss those issues that seem important and relevant to their household. These include (i) steps taken to gather information about the vaccine, (ii) evaluation of the trustworthiness of sources, (iii) factors influencing decisions, (iv) relationships with health professionals, (v) media and health authority treatment of the 'MMR scare', and (vi) possible ambivalence with decisions already taken. Informants will be invited to participate in follow-up interviews, to track possible changes of views at key points in the study. All interviews will be tape-recorded and transcribed. Interviewees and focus group participants will be given £5 vouchers for baby care products. Analysis (Phase I): Data from the questionnaire will be analysed by cultural consensus analysis using ANTHROPAC software. This will create a model of risk as constructed by the informants. I will then test for significant associations between salient aspects of this model, decisions made about MMR, and household socio-demographic characteristics. Population-Based Mail Survey (Phase II): A random sample of 5000 parents of young children in the community will be chosen from NHS data sources. (Ethical permission from the NHS will be sought prior to this phase of the research.) A 1-2 page questionnaire will be developed from the cultural model of risk and decision making that emerges from Phase I. This questionnaire will be mailed to the sample parents, along with a letter explaining the research and a stamped return envelope. A 20-30% response rate is expected, so this sample is expected to generate data for up to 1500 parents.

title: Breaking sex: conceptions and receptions of gender in medical science and massmedia in the UK and US, 1950-2000.
description: Project title: Breaking Sex: Conceptions and Receptions of Gender in Medical Science and Mass Media in the UK and US, 1950-2000. Histories of transsexualism have all but ignored the role of medical science (Herdt, Bolin), whilst specialist medical work has avoided engagement with the cultural discourses of gender identity that necessarily shaped patients' desires. In the later twentieth century developments in plastic surgery (improved skin grafting and pedicle flaps, the use of silicon) allowed medical science to view 'crossing' the gender boundary as a simple matter of physiological alteration. Yet outside the clinic, pop-culture represented such changes in a more problematic fashion, for three reasons: (1) Deconstructing the gender boundary: Medical advances in, and cultural concerns about, Transexual Surgery. (2) Paying for Passage: State Funding, Psychiatry and Patients' Rights in the History of Transsexual Surgery, and (3) Will This Do? The Limitations of Medico-scientific Signification of Gender in Popular Culture. The medico-scientific groundwork for my project will come from the professional journals of plastic/cosmetic surgeons and academic publications by the pioneers in the field. From these sources I aim to construct the developmental/technical narrative of transsexual surgery which I will then re- examine through pop-culture. For mass-media representations of transsexual surgery, I shall look to the print archives of the British Library at Colindale, where I shall make a novel focus upon the tabloid press and the 'lifestyle' magazines so singular to the later twentieth century. Where available, I will also use television archive materials. My project will adopt the social-constructivist position on medical knowledge creation as I believe it better enables the historian of medicine to contextualise their narrative, thus avoiding the trap of assuming medical science operates in a 'cultural clinic'. Postmodern and feminist theories on gender identity will be deployed in analysing the competing claims of medicine and pop-culture, whilst new economic theories on choice and freedom will help explain the reconstructive/cosmetic debates.

title: Genes to cognition.
description: The Genes to Cognition programme (G2C) aims to establish a framework for studying genes, brain and behaviour in order to link basic molecular research from genomes and experimental genetic organisms with human clinical studies of cognition. The G2C programme will collect and integrate data in the areas of psychiatry, human and mouse psychology, cellular neurophysiology and cell biology, proteomics and biochemistry, molecular biology, human and mouse genetics and genomics. Bioinformatics will be used to create new tools for presenting this diverse data in novel relationships that will facilitate mining of information across existing boundaries in neuroscience. The G2C framework will be developed around the current understanding of the molecular basis of learning and memory. We will conduct a systematic study of mutations and polymorphisms in mouse and human genes and explore how these genes influence a broad range of phenotypes including gene expression, protein function, physiology and behaviour, especially cognition. This integrative approach should help close the gap between the shortcomings of psychiatric genetics, which has yet to identify genes for the major psychiatric disorders, and the basic science of cognition in lower organisms that does not, so far, exploit the great strides that have been made in understanding human cognitive psychology.

title: Susceptibility genes for psychosis in individuals with velo-cardio-facial syndrome (VCFS).
description: Velo-cardio-facial syndrome (VCFS) is usually caused by a deletion of chromosome 22q11. Previously, we and others have shown that people with VCFS have an extraordinary risk of developing psychosis, particularly schizophrenia, that is approximately 30 times higher than the general population. Given that VCFS subjects have such an elevated risk for schizophrenia, and that this is attributable to a single homogeneous risk factor (deletion 22q11), VCFS offer a uniquely powerful opportunity to identify alleles that confer susceptibility to schizophrenia. We postulate that the high susceptibility to schizophrenia in VCFS results from polymorphic haploinsufficiency of genes within the VCFS deletion region. In this application our aim is to test this hypothesis. To achieve this, we will: 1) Recruit a total sample of 100 comprehensively assessed adults with chromosome 22q11 deletions; 2) Screen all genes that map to the VCFS deletion region for sequence variation; 3) Test these variants for association with schizophrenia in our sample of VCFS subjects; 4) Test alleles found to be associated with schizophrenia in VCFS for association with schizophrenia in the general population in the large case-control and family based association samples that already available to us.

title: The impact of a water development on parental investment in rural Ethiopia.
description: In this project we will test the hypothesis that a reduction in women's workloads causes them to increase parental investment in their children. A new water-supply development in the Oromiya region of Ethiopia reduced women's workloads by removing the need to trek long distances daily for water. Comparison will be made between children in villages with and without access to the new water points, with respect to their mortality, health, nutrition, workloads and education. Evolutionary life history theory predicts that individuals face trade-offs when allocating energy between body maintenance and reproduction. We have already shown in an earlier study that access to taps has increased female fertility in this population. Thus there may be positive or negative effects of reduced workloads. Mothers may devote more time to childcare and may be able to reduce children's workloads and increase their education. Alternatively, reduced inter-birth intervals could increase competition between siblings for parental resources. A combination of demographic, economic, nutritional and time-budget data should enable us to identify variables mediating changes in parental investment and children's well-being.

title: The neuropathology of a primate developmental model of depression.
description: The rationale for this project comes from three lines of research. (1) Early stressful events, such as parental loss and neglect, are risk factors for depression. (2) Neuropathological correlates of depression have recently been reported in several independent studies. (3) There is a large experimental literature showing that relevant early interventions produce long-term behavioural and physiological effects in rats similar to those reported in depression. This project seeks to integrate and extend these observations by examining the brains of marmosets who had been subject to an early stressor, viz. repeated maternal separation, and in whom there is detailed behavioural, endocrine and cardiovascular evidence of the long-term effects of this intervention. We will therefore test the hypothesis that early environmental events produce structural effects on the brain, and that these differences will be similar in nature and location as those reported in subjects with depression. A range of morphometric and molecular parameters will be measured in candidate brain regions, driven by specific hypotheses. The project will fill a crucial gap between basic and clinical neuroscience, in a key area of mental health. It would also validate in a neuropathological sense this novel primate model, with significant potential for future examination of options for therapeutic prevention or reversal of the effects of early stressful experiences.

title: Short-term health consequences of internal migration in China
description: There are estimated to be between 80 and 120 million internal migrants in China, and the number is rising. Their poor living and working conditions, limited access to health and education, and restricted rights are now recognised by the Chinese government as a potential impediment to sustained economic growth and social stability. City governments have been urged to identify the health, social and educational needs of migrant populations in order to ameliorate the situation. The aim of this study is to determine the health status and needs of migrant workers and their children in Zhejiang Province, and compare these with settled urban and rural dwellers. A cross- sectional study will be carried-out among 3400 migrants, 1700 urban and 1700 rural dwellers and their children. Data to be collected from the adults will include demographic background, health status, including reproductive health and mental well-being, access to healthcare and working conditions and accident/illness rates. Physical examination of height, weight and blood pressure, and fingerprick blood will be taken for HIV, HBsAG and syphilis. Children will be assessed for general health, including atopy, nutrition, immunisation status, school attendance and school achievement. The results are expected to inform policy in the health, education and employment sectors.

title: A double blind placebo controlled crossover trial to assess the efficacy of phenylalanine restriction in adults with previously untreated phenylketonuria (PKU).
description: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is a congenital disorder which can lead to severe learning disability (mental retardation), challenging behaviour and mental health problems, epilepsy, skin disorders and other medical disorders, if untreated. Nowadays, infants are screened for the disorder and treated from very early on, with a low phenylalanine diet, with good results. Those who were never screened and never treated usually have severe learning disabilities and often have challenging behaviour. Recent case studies and small scale pilot studies in the UK have shown that people with untreated PKU nevertheless can benefit from a low phenylalanine diet. Benefits have included improvements in communication skills, alertness, attention span and reductions in challenging behaviour. None of these studies, however, were conducted blind. This study proposes a prospective double blind randomised placebo controlled crossover trial of low phenylananine diet for 30 people with untreated PKU. There will be a baseline of eight weeks, followed by two trial diet phases, each of 24 weeks (with a wash-out period of 4 weeks between the diet phases). One half of the participants will receive phenylanaine-reduced diet in phase 1 and phenylalanine-containing diet in phase 2, while the other half of the participants will receive the two diets in the opposite order (participants will be randomised at the start of phase 1 to the two different orders). Researchers will be blind to participants' diet. Blood phenylalanine will be measured weekly throughout the trial for estimation of phenylalanine and tyrosine levels. Venous blood samples will be taken at five points (at the start of the trial, at the end of the baseline, at the end of phase 1, at the end of the first wash-out phase, at the end of phase 2) for red cell folate, vitamin B12, Ca, phosphate and albumin. The effect of diet will be judged by examining changes in behaviour, across the five time points (at the start of the trial, at the end of the baseline, at the end of phase 1, at the end of the first wash-out, at the end of phase 2). The measures will include standardised assessments of adaptive and challenging behaviour (on the Vineland Scales and on the Aberrant Behaviour Checklist Scales) and direct observation of samples of behaviour at the five time points. In addition, staff ratings of behaviour and symptoms will be conducted daily throughout the trial.

title: Neurochemistry of the imidazoline-2 receptor.
description: Imidazoline-2 receptors are a group of binding proteins found in many species including man. Their density changes in disease states such as depression, Alzheimer's disease and Huntington's chorea and therefore these receptors may provide key information into future treatments or therapies. We've recently discovered, that certain naturally occurring chemicals, the ß-carbolines harman and harmalan bind to imidazoline receptors with high affinity. This project will synthesise a ligand BU99006 which irreversibly binds to the I2 receptor and also radiolabelled forms of harman and harmalan to allow detailed studies on this receptor. Brain microdialysis will monitor the effects of BU99006, harman and harmalan on monoamine turnover in conscious rats to determine the functional effects of these ligands. The effects of BU99006 on monoamine oxidsae activity will be examined to determine what proportion of I2 receptors are associated with this enzyme. The tritiated forms of harman and harmalan will be examined for their ability to bind I2 receptors and also examine if they might act as neuromodulators at this receptor. In addition, this project will enable our group to continue as international leaders in a growing and exciting field of research.

title: Emotion based learning systems, and false beliefs, in schizophrenia.
description: A growing body of neuroscientific evidence suggests that modifications in emotion systems may be central to the production and maintenance of false beliefs, in circumstances as diverse as schizophrenia, dreaming, and the confabulatory states seen in some patients with focal neurological lesions. These findings appear to implicate the over-activation (or non-optimal regulation) of the ventral tegmental dopamine system, including the way in which this emotion system influences executive function through the ventromesial frontal lobes. Our group have assessed a small group (N=8) of schizophrenics on the Iowa Gambling Task, a widely used measure of the influence of emotion-learning systems in complex decision making. We have shown apparently normal learning rates amongst the schizophrenics in a 'standard' version of the task. However, in a novel reversal-learning version of the task, schizophrenics appear to have difficulty modifying to the changing task conditions - suggesting that some of the 'cognitive' deficits in schizophrenics may result from disruption of emotion-based learning systems. This application requests a modest amount of money in order to extend these findings to a larger sample, to establish the reliability of this apparently interesting finding.

title: The development of sex-typed behaviour in boys and girls: a longitudinal studyfrom 20 weeks gestation to 13 years.
description: We propose a longitudinal, population study investigating biological and psychological processes involved in the development of gender identity, gender role behaviour and sexual orientation. We will test the hypothesis that prenatal and neonatal levels of testtosterone predict normal variability within each sex in these areas. In addition, we will examine how postnatal factors, such as the family environment and peer relations, interact with these earlier biological predispositions to influence behaviour. Participants (n=600) have been selected from among a population sample of over 14,000 to represent extreme groups of masculine and feminine boys and girls as wellas random sample of girls and boys with typical gender role behaviour. In an earlier study funded by the Wellcome Trust, we foound that maternal testosterone during preganancy predicted gender role behaviour in girls; mothers of masculine girls had the highest testosterone levels and mothers of feminine girls had the lowest testosterone levels. Although other factors, such as older brothers and sisters, also influence gender role behaviour, the relationship to testosterone remained when these were controlled. The proposed reseach will extend these findings by adding measures of testosterone at birth and by examining additional gender role behaviours, as well as gender identitiy and sexual orientation, in these same children at the transition to adolescence. The importance of variation in early sex-typed behaviour for psychological well-being, family relationships and peer relationships will also be evaluated.

title: A population based twin study on common mental disorders in Sri Lanka.
description: Twin studies of psychiatric disorders allow us to estimate the degree to which such disorders are heritable and the extent to which there are shared or non shared environmental effects within specific populations. Most such studies use volunteer registers of twins, from developed countries. The proposed research aims to identify a population based twin study in Sri Lanka. We have performed an extensive investigation of the feasibility of the study funded by the Wellcome Trust. This work indicates that the most feasible method is to use a combination of key informants and door-to-door interviewing in order to identify the twin sample. We have successfully employed workers from the recent census to do this work, and believe the identification of a population based sample of twins (2000 twin pairs) is feasible. Care will be taken to ensure the sample will be assembled from heterogeneous areas in order to ensure a wide cross-section of socio-economic conditions is represented. We aim also to assemble a parallel sample of 1000 singletons in order to determine whether the twin sample is a representative. Having ascertained these samples we will interview participants on a range of measures, in order to identify the key phenotypes. These will be assessed using a diagnostic interview which will aim to identify current and life-time common mental disorders (CMDs) such as depression and anxiety; and substance misuse and dependence. We will also measure important environmental risk factors for CMDs, such as life events, deprivation, poor educational attainment and early experiences of abuse and neglect. Most of these measures will be translated into Sinhala using techniques which have been developed within the research team. Zygosity will be determined from buccal smears using established methods. The singleton sample will allows us to report prevalence rates of psychiatric disorders. We will be able to compare these rates with the twin sample to determine the twin study is representative of the wider population. We will then use structural equation model fitting in order to estimate the heritability of these disorders and contribution of environmental risk factors. The study will assist in capacity building in Sri Lanka by identifying a population base twin sample which may be used for other phenotypes. The zygosity testing will permit Sri Lankan geneticists to develop their skills in current laboratory methods. The main field work and data analysis will build capacity in psychiatric epidemiology, twin methodology and statistical genetics.

title: Investigating and responding to health, population and social transitions in rural Southern Africa.
description: Health, population and social transitions are dynamic, complex and little documented features of Southern Africa today that impact heavily on the effectiveness of health and public sector systems. Exploiting the capacity of the Agincourt health and demographic surveillance system, sited in a border region of South Africa's rural northeast, work will monitor trends in rural population dynamics with attention to rapidly changing mortality profiles, causes and consequences of an unusual fertility pattern, shifting migration trends particularly among women, and the impacts of these on the composition and functioning of households. To better understand risk factors, inform intervention research and strengthen public sector and policy responses, investigations are underway into stroke and cardiovascular disease in adults, persisting malnutrition (kwashiorkor) in children including associations between social support and child wellbeing, continuing high levels of violence and injury, the immediate and longer term impacts of severe illness on households, and the impact of migration on personal and family health. The proposal seeks to ensure that comprehensive census and vital event update rounds continue annually over the period 2003-2007 and that a high functioning research foundation is secured. This will also support an expanding programme of research training and contribute to multi-site research through INDEPTH, (an International Network for the Demographic Evaluation of Populations and Their Health in developing countries).

title: A contribution towards the cost of a symposium entitled 'First Workshop on Murine Models of Psychiatric Disorder' to be held at Fondation des Treilles, Provence, France in April/May 2003.
description: First Workshop on Murine Models of Psychiatric Disorder, Foundation des Treilles, Provence, France, April/May 2003 Over the next few years it is likely that genes influencing common psychiatric disorders, such as schizophrenia, manic-depressive psychosis, major depression and anxiety, will be identified. Despite the success of some molecular projects, there has been remarkably little advance in our understanding of the biology of the conditions, largely because it has proved extremely difficult to work out the normal function of the cloned genes. One approach to investigating function is to engineer mutations in the mouse homologue of the human gene and examine the resulting phenotype in the animal model. While this approach has been successful for many medical conditions, the same is not true for psychiatric conditions because it is not clear what to measure. How, for instance, are we to model speech deficits in mice? On evolutionary arguments we would expect that abilities specific to humans will have originated from neural systems present in other animals. The problem is that in most cases we do not know what those systems are. We need ways of modelling complex behaviours in animals if we are to benefit from the advances in genetics. By the end of the meeting we aim to obtain a consensus view on the limitations and value of animal models. We hope to be able to answer questions about what they can detect that would be relevant to human behaviour and which tests can be applied to the current and future transgenic models. Finally we hope to address the fundamental question of the extent to which animals provide more complex models than those currently used for learning and memory.

title: Regulation by steroids of neurogenesis in the adult hippocampus: role of dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA).
description: The formation of new neurons (neurogenesis) continues in the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus of rats, mice and humans in adult life. Steroids play a major role in controlling neurogenesis. Glucocorticoids (GCs), such as cortisol (man) or corticosterone (rat) depress it. GC levels are raised in stress and in certain mental illness such as depression. We have found that DHEA both stimulates neurogenesis and antagonises the effects of GCs in male rats. DHEA also improves the survival of newly-generated neurons in the dentate gyrus. Since DHEA levels decline markedly with age in man, and are also reduced by depression, these findings may have important implications for normative process (eg certain forms of memory), the cognitive decline that occurs with age and the longer-term consequences of depression. The proposed work will address four principal questions. Does the stimulating effect of DHEA on neurogenesis depend upon GCs? We will determine whether the effects of DHEA on proliferation is altered by the removing or clamping GC levels. Is the interaction with GCs that determine the effect of DHEA on the survival of new neurons in the hippocampus the same or different from that promoting proliferation? We will study the effects of DHEA on the survival and differentiation of newly-formed neurons. Does DHEA have similar effects in aged rats? DHEA levels decrease markedly in the blood and CSF with age in humans. It is important to determine whether DHEA retains its effects on neurogenesis in older (12-24 month old) rats. Does the stimulating effects of DHEA on either proliferation or survival of new neurons in the dentate gyrus depend upon glutamatergic or gabergic mechanisms (since DHEA is a known GABA antagoinist, and NMDA receptors have been implicated in the way that steroids regulate neurogenesis)? We will determine the effects of giving compounds that block or mimic either glutamate or GABA on the stimulating actions of DHEA on neurogenesis.

title: A quantitative and molecular genetic study of psychological processes as mediators of genetic effects on hyperactivity.
description: We propose to identify psychological processes that mediate genetic influences on ADHD using a multivariate quantitative genetic analysis of 800 pairs of 8-9 year old twins. We further propose to investigate whether genetic variation in genes linked to ADHD is also associated with these processes. Each child will be assessed on experimental tasks that have previously been associated with ADHD/hyperactivity or tap into reward mechanisms. We will also gather behavioural measures of hyperactivity and novelty seeking. The experimental tasks derive from psychological theories of hyperactivity that emphasise the interaction between cognitive performance and factors, such as rewards and presentation time of stimuli, that influence arousal or activation. We will quantify the genetic effects on the psychological processes and the extent to which these are shared with the behavioural measures. If successful, this will provide an empirical basis for the use of endophenotypes in the search for ADHD susceptibility genes, as well as providing a functional understanding of specific genetic variants at the level of psychological processes. Functional analysis of genes associated with ADHD may be facilitated by the identification of experimental paradigms that could be translated to an animal model. At the same time the brain mechanisms involved in humans may be studied by integrating this research with structural and functional imaging studies.

title: Development of the self-controlled case series method for evaluating vaccine safety.
description: The self-controlled case series method was developed by the applicant to evaluate the safety of vaccines in respect of rare, adverse reactions. The method has been widely applied in a range of settings, including measles, mumps and rubella vaccine and autism in the UK, and rotavirus vaccine and intussusception in the USA. The method uses only data on cases, and is controlled by matching each case with itself. As a result, the method is rapid and economical. This is because it does not require denominators or separate controls, as is the case with cohort and case-control methods. Nevertheless, its power has been shown to be only marginally less than that of a cohort study, while the self-matching removes any bias due to fixed confounders or individual heterogeneity. The purpose of the project is to further validate and develop the method in the context of vaccine safety evaluation, and hence encourage its wider use. The specific aims are (1) to undertake a definitive evaluation of the method, including extensive comparisons with cohort and case-control methods; (2) to extend its scope, by relaxing the assumptions upon which it is based; (3) to develop improved methods for controlling for age; and (4) to develop new methods for selecting post-vaccination risk intervals.

title: International workshop on decreases in neural activity and their neuroimaging correlates' at the Wellcome Department oof Imaging Neuroscience, Institute of Neurology, University College London on the 22 March 2003
description: International Workshop on Decreases in Neural Activity and their Neuroimaging Correlates The advent of BOLD contrast fMRI in 1992, with its uniquely precise spatial resolution of brain activation and complete non-invasiveness, stimulated a rapid growth in the field of imaging neuroscience, encompassing many disciplines from neurology to psychiatry. There are sound experimental reasons to believe that increases in BOLD signal indicate increased significant neural activity, corresponding with assumptions made in interpreting PET data for CBF and cerebral metabolism, and EEG and MEG data. Most fMRI studies show focal increases of signal, as compared with a control baseline, that correspond well to hypothesized local increases in neuronal activity. However, there have been sporadic observations of absolute decreases of BOLD signal and CBF that are hard to interpret. Furthermore, careful neurophysiological studies of a small number of neurons in animal brain have shown that increases in neuronal activity can lead to decreases in blood flow. In addition, the existence of evoked potentials observable with EEG or MEG suggests that synchronized neuronal activity has special importance for brain function. In order to clarify these issues and promote a fully informed discussion, the speakers for this workshop have been chosen from among the leading experts in the world in the relevant fields of research. The anticipated outcome is that current knowledge will be shared and experiments will be devised that address the serious gaps in that knowledge.

title: A contribution towards a symposium entitled 'The fMRI Experience V' to be held at the Institute of Psychiatry, King's College London on 10th and 11th March 2003.
description: Meeting : The fMRI Experience V King's College: We have held the fMRI Experience meetings for the past 4 years and have organised another meeting 'The fMRI Experience V' for March 10-11, 2003. The first meeting in 1999 arose from our common need and wish to learn about both the basic principles and some advanced topics in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) research. We sought to bring together some of the international experts in the field and to provide an opportunity for students to make oral presentations and to discuss their research with experts and each other in an interactive and collegial environment. The interest and response from this meeting was overwhelming. Consequently, we have held the meeting again - and again - as we continue to receive such interest and positive feedback from participants. As well, some students have taken up research fellowships with experts whom they have met during the meeting. We have had over 300 registrants for each meeting, with registrants coming from throughout the UK, Europe, USA, Brazil, Australia and China. Again, we shall be combining expert and student presentations. As students are the main 'workhorses' of research projects, this meeting shall provide them with the rare opportunity to give oral presentations in front of a friendly and esteemed audience.

title: Funds to support the REVES 15 meeting entitled 'Socio-Economic Determinants inLife and Health Expectancies'.
description: REVES 15: Socio-Economic Determinants in Life and Health Expectancies Symposia The REVES (Réseau Espérance de Vie en Santé) International Network on Health Expectancy was set up in 1989 by the French National Institute of Health and Medical Research (INSERM, Montpellier, France), the Social Affairs Council, Quebec, Canada and the Center for Demographic Studies, Durham, United States. The ageing of the world population and the lengthening of life have been, and are, monitored by well-established demographic indicators such as the ageing ratio and life expectancy at birth. Similar indicators can measure healthy active ageing and changes in healthy active life to evaluate whether further increases in the quantity of life are accompanied by equivalent increases in quality of life. In other words, the interest is in determining whether or not additional years of life are years spent physically and mentally independent as well as socially integrated. Over the last twenty years, data collection and publication of ageing ratios and life expectancies by the UN have allowed governments, policy planners and other stakeholders to become aware of the ageing of the world population. In the next two decades, these should be supplemented by similar data collection and publication on healthy active life, as a fundamental resource for monitoring quality of life. Although health expectancy as a means of monitoring the ageing process of populations, is well-known in developed countries, it is less known in those countries going through the demographic transition. This is due to two reasons. Firstly, until recently, ageing has not been viewed as of major importance to these countries, and secondly, the nature of the REVES network, with no underlying support to sponsor meetings and where researchers have to fund themselves, discriminates against researchers in developing countries where resources to attend such meetings are scarce. It is envisaged that the topics covered at REVES 15 will be similar to those covered at previous REVES meetings, but with a strong contribution from the host country and Latin America in general. Topics are likely to include: The disability process - how and why; The burden of disease; Measuring disability and health; Regional and socio-economic inequalities in health; Methodological developments in health expectancy; Mental health
recipient: Equipe Inserm Demographie Et Sante, France

title: A contribution towards a symposium entitled Neural Cells, Stem Cells and the repair of CNS lesions, to be held at the Harrogate International Centre on 15th April 2003 (part of 17th National Meeting of the BNA, 13-16 April 2003)
description: Symposia - British Neuroscience Association This gathering allows us to bring together several experts to discuss various methods for the promotion of CNS repair. We will concentrate on repair using cells either present in the host or introduced by transplantation. There has been a huge growth in research supporting the use of stem/progenitor cells for transplant mediated repair, although recently, their potential for repair has become a matter of debate. This is because some recent reports have suggested that the repair may not be as complete as initially thought and that functional recovery is limited. We would like to address this aspect in the symposia with emphasis on three main models used: The first presentation, by Dr Robin Franklin, Cambridge University, will discuss the ability of endogenous CNS progenitors cells to repair CNS lesions. The second, from Dr Sue Barnett, Glasgow University, will discuss functional recovery of CNS lesions using the transplantation of olfactory ensheathing cells to mediate the repair. The potential advantages and disadvantages of using these kinds of cells will also be presented. The third, from Prof Jack Price, Institute of Psychiatry, King's College, London, will discuss the use of neural stem cells in brain repair concentrating on aspects of the mechanism involved. In addition, methods detailing their growth and differentiation of neural stem cells and the resulting pitfalls that might be encountered will be discussed. What is unique about this symposium is that three different approaches will be presented for the repair of CNS lesions and the pros and cons of each will be illustrated, thereby bringing some reality to this burgeoning field.

title: Cognition and health: analysis of data from a series of population-based studies.
description: In the last decade there has been renewed interest in the early life origins of adult chronic disease. In addition to work examining biological determinants such as growth in utero and during childhood, social factors operating during this period, such as parental social class, school truancy, school qualifications and educational attainment, also appear to be related to adult health outcomes. Although emphasis has been given to educational variables in these studies, investigators have tended not to include cognition (as measured by tests of intelligence quotient) in their aetiological models of adult disease. However, given the association of childhood cognition with income, final qualifications, and smoking behaviour in adulthood there is a suggestion that this characteristic may have an influence on adult health. Despite this strong prima facie case, there is a paucity of literature on childhood cognition and later health. The only published report of a population-based sample is a follow-up of a sub-group of 11 year old children in the 1932 Scottish Mental Survey, with the finding that those who had high scores on a test of cognition were at the lowest risk of all-cause mortality in adulthood. The research element of this fellowship aims to systematically address this scarcity of evidence by analysing data from five existing European cohort studies with the capacity to examine the link between cognition and health. The research objectives are: 1. Review the literature on cognition measured in early and later life in relation to adult health. 2. By analysing data from a range of studies, assess the link between cognition and common causes of mortality and morbidity (cardiovascular disease, site- specific cancers and psychiatric illness), and explore the potential role of socio-economic position as a confounding/interacting factor in these relationships. 3. Examine the association of cognition with behavioural and physiological risk factors for disease in adults (a potential mechanism for the cognition-mortality association). 4. Assess the early life determinants of cognition, including growth in utero, gestational age, childhood nutrition (as measured by height and weight in early life), and parental social and educational background. Using existing studies to examine these objectives has two distinct advantages: the project is excellent value for money as no further data collection is necessary, and it is possible to assess the robustness of any associations seen by comparing findings across studies. This research will provide important and unique insights into the life-course determinants of adult morbidity and mortality, in particular the contribution of childhood cognition.

title: Postsynaptic calcium-sensitive protein-protein interactions in synaptic plasticity and ischemia.
description: Synaptic plasticity is thought to underlie learning and memory. In this study I will investigate the role of calcium ions in direct regulation of postsynaptic protein-protein interactions during induction of synaptic plasticity. I will also analyse the role of the same interactions in the processes that lead to neuronal death following stroke. Synaptic plasticity involves changes in the number of synaptic AMPAR by endocytosis or exocytosis, and proteins interacting with AMPARs play roles in these processes. Increased postsynaptic calcium levels are a requirement for most forms of synaptic plasticity, and a crucial question is how calcium transients bring about changes in AMPAR trafficking. By analogy with presynaptic exocytosis/endocytosis of neurotransmitter vesicles, where some protein- protein interactions are directly regulated by calcium, I propose that postsynaptic protein-protein interactions can be regulated by binding calcium ions. PICK1 is involved in AMPAR trafficking and long-term depression (LTD), and these processes also involve increases in postsynaptic [Ca2+]. My preliminary data suggest that PICK1 is a calcium sensor, such that GluR2-PICK1 and SNAP-PICK1 interactions are [Ca2+]- sensitive. [Ca2+]-insensitive PICK1 mutants will be tested for dominant negative effects on LTD in electrophysiological experiments and on AMPAR trafficking in immunocytochemical experiments. My preliminary data indicate that the PICK1 calcium sensor is activated in neurons by phosphorylation. The enzymes responsible for regulating PICK1 phosphorylation will be investigated using chemical induction of synaptic plasticity, and 32P-labelling of neuronal PICK1. Non-phosphorylated PICK1 mutants will be identified and tested for dominant negative effects on LTD and AMPAR trafficking. Post-ischemic cell death involves a reduction in synaptic GluR2 subunit, and it is possible that PICK1 plays a role in this process. The calcium changes in neurons following ischemia suggest that calcium-sensitive protein-protein interactions may be important. I will test these hypotheses in oxygen/glucose deprived hippocampal culture, a widely-used in vitro model of ischemia. Blocking GluR2-PICK1 interactions, or overexpression of PICK1 mutants may be neuroprotective. These studies will further our understanding of the molecular changes occurring during expression of synaptic plasticity and post-ischemic shock, by providing insights into a novel form of regulation of AMPAR function.

title: The ALSPAC study of psychosis-like symptoms in children and adolescents.
description: There has been considerable recent interest in 'non-clinical' psychotic symptoms in adults and children. The Dunedin study, the only birth cohort to have investigated this, reported a prevalence of 14.1% in 11 year olds. There was a strong association (OR 16.4) between psychosis-like symptoms (PLIKS) in children and subsequent development of adult schizophreniform disorder, and PLIKS were also associated with other childhood developmental impairments. The Dunedin cohort was a relatively small (n=761) and low powered study. The 14,138 person ALSPAC birth cohort (now age 10-11) presents a unique opportunity to investigate the nature, prevalence, and epidemiology of psychosis-like symptoms in childhood and adolescence. We will test the hypothesis that PLIKS are an intermediate phenotype for schizophrenia, associated with early developmental deficits, and with familial and environmental risk factors for schizophrenia. We will use an observer rated assessment at age 12 to investigate these associations and to validate and refine a self-report questionnaire, to be used in future sweeps of this population. This study will lay the groundwork for future studies to investigate associations and interactions between biological and environmental exposures, PLIKS in childhood, other intermediate psycho-behavioural outcomes, and adult onset schizophrenia.

title: The social neuroscience of emotion' to be held at the Department of Psychology, University of Portsmouth on 6th and 7th June 2003.
description: 1) Meeting: The social neuroscience of emotion, Department of Psychology, University of Portsmouth, UK, June 6&7, 2003 After a long period of neglect, research on emotions has expanded greatly in the past twenty years. Our understanding of the biological basis of emotion has developed in concert with new and improved technologies such as brain imaging, neurotransmitter tracing and genetic mapping. Research on the social basis of emotion has shown a similar explosion, with advances in our knowledge of how interpersonal and cultural processes affect emotional expression and experience. Unfortunately, researchers within the biological domains and the social domains have worked largely independently of each other. Thus, there has been a lag in the integration of these domains of expertise. Neuroscience has traditionally viewed emotional processes as solidly "within a person" and social psychology has eschewed tackling biological constraints to interpersonal emotional interactions. There is already clear evidence, however, that current domain- specific theories of emotions are inadequate in explaining emerging phenomena, such as the ability of touch to release opioids in the brain. An integrated study of emotional processes has wide-ranging theoretical and practical implications, such as informing child-rearing practice, suggesting alternative rehabilitation strategies after brain injury, and aiding our understanding and treatment of psychiatric disorders. The goal of this workshop, therefore, will be to bring together key researchers in emotion from neuroscience and social psychology, with researchers at the University of Portsmouth's new Centre for the Study of Emotions and postgraduate students, to explore topics and methodologies that will facilitate such integration. Topics: Primitive and higher-level emotional systems in man and other animals. How does the environment affect brain development of emotional systems? How and to what degree do genetics and biology constrain the influence of social factors on the development of emotional systems? What can fMRI and PET studies tell us about the control of emotional processing? Are all emotions "social"? If not, what are the distinguishing characteristics of social emotions? Are these comparable in humans and other animals? What are psychophysiological, behavioural, and experiential aspects of emotions?

title: A contribution towards a meeting entitled 'Understanding IL-1 actions in the nervous system' to be held at the Chancellors Conference Centre, teh University of Manchester, from 23rd to 26th October 2003.
description: Meeting: Understanding IL-1 actions in the nervous system, Chancellors Conference Centre, University of Manchester, UK, October 23-26, 2003 With the exception of small closed meetings, there have been no specific gatherings that focus purely on IL-1 biology in recent years. There has been intense research effort in this area over the last decade and there is now increasing interest in the role of inflammatory mediators in many disease processes. Therefore, the Manchester 2003 meeting is timely, and represents a unique opportunity to gather leading experts in the field here in Manchester, where many important advances in research on IL-1 in the nervous system have taken place. Key topics will relate to basic mechanisms of IL-1, including processing, release and signal transduction pathways. There will also be detailed discussion of the role of IL-1 in several different processes including learning and memory, depression, sickness behaviour, ageing, epilepsy and neurodegenerative disease. This illustrates the diversity of IL-1 actions and the pressing need to fully understand how it acts so that effective therapeutic agents can be developed in the future. Topics are: Stimulus-induced post-translational processing of IL-1; delineating an atypical cytokine export mechanism. Analysis of IL-1 and toll signalling by expression cloning. The IL-1 and IL-1 receptor families in the nervous system. The loss of the atypical CNS inflammatory response to IL-1ß in aged animals. The role of the MyD88 family of adapters in IL-1R/TLR signalling. The role of brain IL-1 in memory functioning and hippocampal plasticity. The role of IL-1 iin age-related deficits in synaptic function. Physiopathological role of IL-1 seizures. Distribution of IL-1 and IL-1 receptor expression in the nervous system: relation to sickness behaviour. Cytokine-induced changes in behaviour: from sickness behaviour to depression. Mechanisms of IL-1 action in acute neurodegeneration. IL-1ra in the clinic for acute ischaemic stroke.

title: Cognitive Development, Genes and the Brain: From Piaget to Cognitive Neuroscience' to be held at the Institute of Child Health on 20 September 2003
description: Symposium in Honour of Professor Annette Karmiloff-Smith; "Cognitive Development, Genes and the Brain: from Piaget to Cognitive Neuroscience", Institute of Child Health, London, 20th September, 2003. In September 2003, Professor Annette Karmiloff-Smith retires from her position as Head of the MRC Neurocognitive Development Unit at the Institute of Child Health. She has been one of the most influential British psychologists over the last 20 years. In 2002 she was awarded the European Latsis Prize for her outstanding contribution to the understanding of cognition and language development in children with genetic disorders. Her career to date has seen the blossoming of the study of developmental psychology from the pioneering work of Jean Piaget (of whom she was a student) to the current multi-disciplinary field of developmental cognitive neuroscience. Reflecting the advances in this field, the objective of this honorary symposium is to bring together leading international researchers from each component discipline to present their latest work, and in particular, to foster a continuing cross-disciplinary approach to understanding the role of the genome and the constraints of brain development in cognitive development. In keeping with this perspective, the symposium combines presentations on brain development, cognitive development, evolution, computational modelling, developmental disorders and genetics. Reflecting Prof. Karmiloff-Smith's work on Williams syndrome, three talks focus on this disorder.

title: Identifying and understanding the actions of autism susceptibility genes.
description: The International Molecular Genetics of Autism Consortium (IMGSAC) will take forward our promising lead in the search for autism susceptibility loci. Our aims are to identify the top 2 susceptibility alleles that underlie Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD's), to identify the next most significant susceptibility region and to establish the interrelationships between individual loci and components of phenotypic expression. We will recruit and assess, using standardised measures, a further 200 affected relative pairs, a new UK same-sex epidemiological twin sample and a further 200 singleton families. To provide convergent evidence for the location of susceptibility loci, we will characterise first degree relatives in the three samples using a combination of interview and observational methods and direct testing of social, language and planning impairments. Qualitative and quantitative information on the affection status of family members will be incorporated in the statistical analysis; the twin sample allowing estimation of genetic and environmental factor covariance from structural equation modelling of the phenotypic measures. The phenotypic assessment protocol and analysis represents the most comprehensive attempt to identify the genetic architecture underlying ASD's yet undertaken. The regions of strongest linkage will be genotyped in the enlarged set of over 400 affected relative pair families. Susceptibility genes will be identified in the top three loci, currently chromosomes 2q, 7q and 16p, using a combination of positional candidate gene analysis and linkage disequilibrium mapping. Susceptibility genes and their associated variants will be tested in all affected relative pair families and in separate sets of singleton families to determine the aetiologic mutations that increase risk for ASD. In the future, the role of these genes and their protein products will be studied in normal brain development and in animal models to determine function; a critical step towards identifying the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying autism and the factors influencing expressivity.

title: Mental health components within the tradition of Chinese pediatric medicine.
description: Mental Health Components within the Tradition of Chinese Pediatric Medicine Traditional Chinese medicine has always been recognised as rested upon principles at variance with other traditions of medicine, including modern health sciences, broadly understood. One of the key elements of this difference is though to be the different ways each of these medical systems relate a human's physical conditions with his/her "mental" or "spiritual" state. In this the special philosophy of a close relation between one's bodily faculties and one's mental state has been widely discussed in the history of Chinese medical ideas and medical theories, although neither any specifics of this "mental health" components within the broader Chinese medical tradition nor the historical development of this lines of "indigenous psychology/psychiatry" has been seriously investigated. I would like to bring this ongoing research project on the mental health aspects of Chinese pediatric medicine to London, to benefit from the institute's good resource in scholarly exchange and library holdings to enhance the comparative perspective of my study. I would also like to be affiliated with the London School of Oriental and African Studies (SDAS) under the direct auspices of Dr. Frank Dikotter. His present investigation on the evolution of criminology and his long-standing expertise on hygiene, health and medicine of modern China compliments well, and will be a best consultation on my research into the mental health of Chinese pediatrics.

title: Understanding persecutory ideation: testing a new cognitive model.
description: WT Studentship: Project title: Understanding persecutory ideation: testing a new cognitive model The proposed research will consist of a series of studies into persecutory thinking. Persecutory delusions are one of the most frequently occurring symptoms of psychosis and are of particular clinical relevance, in that they are associated with high levels of distress, delusional action and hospital admission. We have proposed a cognitive model of persecutory delusions, based on a number of earlier experimental studies, which is developed from our more general model of psychosis (Garety et al, 2001). This builds on the work of Bentall et all (2001) who have also proposed a model of persecutory delusions incorporating attributional and emotional processes, but differs in respect of certain specific hypotheses concerning self-esteem and emotional processes. In brief, our model of persecutory delusions conceptualises them as threat beliefs which develop in the context of dysfunctional prior beliefs (e.g. of the self as vulnerable to threat, others as dangerous), stressful triggering events (perhaps a mugging), anomalous experiences (such as hallucinations, saying 'kill him, kill him') and processes associated with anxiety and depression. We conceptualise persecutory delusions as beliefs formed from an individual's attempts to make sense of experiences, in particular contexts in which threat is perceived. Among the emotions, we propose that anxiety is particularly significant, because the cognitive component of anxiety centres on anticipation of danger and because of the high levels of anxiety associated with psychosis. We also consider that delusions are on an extreme point of a continuum between psychopathology and everyday thinking and that much can be learned by examining persecutory ideas in the general population as well as clinical populations. We have already conducted a series of studies of persecutory delusions (e.g. Freeman et al, 2001), clarified definitional problems and have other studies currently underway in our research group examining attributions and reasoning.

title: Systematic investigation of the neuropsychiatric phenotype in Darier's disease: in search of genotype-phenotype correlation.
description: WT Studentship: Project title: Systematic investigation of the neuropsychiatric phenotype in Darier's disease: in search of genotype- phenotype correlation Darier's Disease: Clinical: Darier's Disease is a rare autosomal dominantly inherited skin disorder with an estimated prevalence of up to 1 in 36 000 (Munro, 1991; Br J Dermatol 27:126-130). It is characterised by warty, brown papules and plaques, present on the back, chest, scalp and forehead, nail dystrophy and pits on the palm. Individuals with the severe form of the disease can be socially and physically handicapped by widespread disfiguring malodorous keratotic plaques. Darier's Disease: Genetic: Darier's Disease maps to chromosome 12q23-q24.1 (Craddock et al, 1991; Hum Mol Genet 2: 1941-3) and has been shown to be caused by mutations in a single gene, ATP2A2 (Sakuntabhai, et al. 1999; Nature Genet 21: 271-7). This gene encodes SERCA2, a sarcoplasmic/endoplasmic reticulum calcium pump which has a pivotal role in intracellular calcium signalling. Over 90 distinct mutations of ATP2A2 have been identified throughout the gene including missense, nonsense, and frameshift and splicing mutations. Darier's Disease: Neuropsychiatric Phenotype: Clinical experience amongst dermatologists suggests that neuropsychiatric abnormalities - both mild and severe - occur at an increased rate in Darier's disease compared with other skin disorders of similar severity and impact upon functioning. Consistent with this, a number of reports of cases and families in the literature have noted the frequent association of Darier's Disease and several neuropsychiatric disturbances, most commonly mild cognitive impairment, epilepsy, mood disorders and suicidal ideation. The student will recruit at least one affected member of 100 unrelated families with Darier's Disease. It is intended that families will be referred by 2 senior academic dermatologists with a research interest in Darier's disease who are in contact with most Darier families known to the services in the UK.

title: Anglo-Dutch-German Workshop: 'Patients' Body Perceptions.
description: Workshop: Anglo-Dutch-German Workshop on 'Patients' Body Perceptions', University of Warwick, 11-13 July 2003 The workshop is one of a series of workshops organised with colleagues in the Netherlands (Amsterdam/Maastricht) and Germany (Stuttgart) and the Wellcome Centre for the History of Medicine in London. The first of these gatherings, initially co-organised by Dutch and British scholars, took place in Amsterdam in 1997 and in 2000 we were joined by a group of German colleagues, forming an Anglo-Dutch-German collaboration. Topics covered in previous workshops include neurasthenia, social psychiatry, the patient in history, and cultures of medicine. For the 2003 workshop we have decided to include the early modern period, to strive for a more ambitious approach to the theme, and to develop comparisons over time as well as between countries. The workshops have urged the participation of established scholars as well as younger colleagues, including graduate students. The workshop is organised around pre-circulated papers and invited commentaries. This formula has worked well in the past, encouraging engagement with the papers, and assisting us to proceed rapidly to publication. The volume based on the 1999 Warwick conference is in press (due 2002). A further volume is planned based on the 2003 workshop.

title: To describe, analyse and explain the scientific and medical uses of the tropane alkaloids hyoscyamine and hyoscine or scopolamine in Europe in the period c. 1830-c.1950.
description: Between 1830 and 1900 a new medical use of hyoscyamine and hyoscine or scopolamine (active principles of nightshades) with a new therapeutic profile was shaped by pharmacists, chemists, physicians, and the pharmaceutical industry (Merck). In this process foundations of the therapeutic use of psychoactive drugs were laid that up to an important point still determine present day developments. This process is still hardly explored in the historiography of psychiatry and pharmacology, especially from perspectives of the interactions between the pharmaceutical industry, the medical profession and the emerging laboratory science; from the perspective of social-cultural developments; and from an international comparative perspective. Dr. Snelders' research project will contribute to our understanding of a field that is relatively unexplored in present day medical history: the origins and development of psychoactive drug therapy in 19th century psychiatry. The project supplements research into 18th and 20th century developments that has been undertaken in the last decade.

title: Psychiatry on the Eastern Front: Russian Psychiatric Service during the First World War.
description: Psychiatry at War: Russian Origins The first psychiatric service in any army was reputedly introduced early in the twentieth century during Russia's war with Japan (1904-05). This war, unpopular with Russians and fought on the distant boundaries of the Empire, allegedly caused a high rate of mental diseases in the Russian army. In addition, also for the first time in psychiatric practice, observers described strange cases of nervous trouble among the officers, later to become internationally known under the name of shell shock. Both public and expert opinion had been made sensitive to the notion of trauma by the industrial insurance law, issued two years earlier, in 1902. For this reason, and because routine life had not been much affected by the war, mental casualties at the front evoked a sympathetic response from both the authorities and the people. State and private medical facilities were made available to the evacuated soldiers, and psychiatrists became actively involved with the treatment and rehabilitation of the veterans. A prelude to twentieth-century disasters, the war with Japan makes Russia a special case in the early history of military psychiatry. The psychological origins of this trauma became widely accepted during the discussion of the nature and causes of shell shock. The folk name for the shell-shocked, which in the Russian medical language was "contused" ("kontuzhennyi"), was "confused" ("skonfuzhennyi") - a slight twist of the word clearly pointed towards belief in the illness' psychological nature. As a result of this early military experience, when Russia entered the First World War, the Army already had a well-established psychiatric service. Another consequence, perhaps, was the fact that Russia arguably displayed the highest percentage of "psychogenic disorders"\- 60% of the 35,000 mentally and nervously ill evacuated from the fronts.
recipient: Institute for the History of Science and Tech

title: The history of pain.
description: This projects aims to describe the process of objectivation of the notion of pain in the period between 1600 and the end of the 20th century. This process is explained by means of the introduction of different methods of visualization, verbalisation, interrogation or measurement of pain. In my understanding, each one of these major sectors is related to an equally relevant process of group formation, like Anatomy in the Renaissance, Anatomia animata in the 17th and 18th centuries, the cult of sensibility in the Enlightenment, or Experimental Physiology and Neurosciences in the 19th century. I argue that, in all these cases, the understanding of pain rests on the homogeneity of society and not of nature. In other words, the progressive centralization of pain depends not so much on the equality of signs, or symptoms, but rather in a social strategy linked to the consolidation of professional bodies both inside and outside the field of medicine. The birth of Pain Clinics during the 20th century, linked to the notion of "chronic pain", can be taken as just another example. More in particular, during my stay at the Wellcome Trust Centre for the History of Medicine at UCL, I intend to conduct research on the mid-19th century definitions of objectivity within experimental physiology and psychology. This involves the examination of the role play by self-registering apparatus, the introduction of measurement scales, experimental research in the transmission and reception of nervous impulses and so on. This will be the last chapter of my forthcoming book, The Measurement of Pain, in which I have been working during the last three years.

title: Insight in schizophrenia: relationship to deficits in brain functions and structures, and responsiveness to cognitive behaviour therapy.
description: WT Studentship Project title: Insight in Schizophrenia: Relationship to Deficits in Brain Functions and Structures, and Responsiveness to Cognitive Behaviour Therapy There is an emerging consensus that insight in schizophrenia is a multi-faceted and potentially complex phenomenon. It can be considered as a multidimensional construct that includes awareness of (a) symptoms, (b) their consequences, and (c) need for intervention for one's disorder with these dimensions having somewhat different implications for the management of, and recovery from, schizophrenia. The psychological, clinical and neural correlates of insight in this disorder are poorly understood. Neuropsychologically, an association between poor insight and deficits on executive functioning measures has been noted but, on the whole, the evidence for a linear relationship between any neurocognitive domain and insight is rather mixed, as patients with relatively unimpaired neurocognition have been characterised by both good and poor insight. There might be a non-linear relationship between insight and neurocognition, mediated by another influence, this being the motivation for positive self-evaluation or denial. In this scenario, the first influence is neurocognitive (good neurocognitive functioning predicts good insight) since insight requires a certain level of neurocognitive functioning. The second influence is psychosocial where (good neurocognitive functioning) patients are motivated for positive self- evaluation or use denial to cope with their problems, and thus apparently manifest poor insight. Clinically, it is not clear whether insight is a 'trait' (stable over time) or 'state' (changes over time) phenomenon At the neural level, frontal lobe deficits are thought to underlie poor insight, but how this association is separate from the effects of symptoms and the effects of deficits in neurocognition remains unclear. An investigation combining neuropsychological, clinical, and neuroimaging techniques is required to develop a model of insight in schizophrenia with practical utility in guiding interventions and predicting outcome in schizophrenia. This is what the doctoral project is designed to achieve.

title: Cognitive mechanisms in suicidal ideation and behaviour: rumination, hopelessness and positive future fluency.
description: Cognitive mechanisms in suicidal ideation and behaviour: Rumination, hopelessness and positive future fluency This research poses challenges in three main areas: research design, recruitment and sampling, and statistical analysis. Tasks must be devised to suit a group with a clinical diagnosis who are potentially extremely distressed. Tasks must be a suitable length, with comprehensible instructions and including appropriate controls. There is an art involved in teasing apart why participants fail tasks, as failure may reflect low motivation or poor comprehension of task instructions, rather than a genuine deficit. Selection of control tasks is particularly important in verifying the specificity of any deficit, as clinical groups typically perform more poorly than controls in many experimental tasks. Samples recruited must be representative and groups appropriately matched, and participants must be followed up with sensitivity and persistence in order to prevent attrition. Once data is attained, analysis will involve complex statistical procedures. The five studies proposed are outlined below. Hopelessness and Positive future fluency: Two studies aim to investigate the relation between positive future fluency and mood, by measuring fluency for future events, and evaluations of these events in terms of valence, with participants in different moods. To test 'future events fluency', participants will be given 30 seconds in which to generate future events of specific valence (positive, negative, neutral) for varying time periods (1 week, 1 month, 1 year, 5-10 years). Studies of fluency will include control fluency tasks. Study 1. Positive future fluency in non-depressed participants in positive or negative mood. Study 2. Positive future fluency in a clinical sample hours after an episode compared to one week later. Rumination: Three studies look at suicidal ideation in terms of its similarity or difference to rumination, and investigate the influence of rumination on poor positive future fluency. Participants will complete the Nolen-Hoeksema's Response Style Questionnaire (to assess rumination), and the Beck Hopelessness and Suicide Ideation Scales (omitting items which refer to rumination).
