Study 3. Association of future fluency scores and ruminative response style. Study 4. Developing a Suicidal Preoccupation Measure. Study 5. Thought suppression and suicidal ideation.

title: Decision making in the rodent and primate cingulate cortices.
description: The study of the neural basis of decision making is a relatively recent departure from more traditional sensory approaches used to study the brain. As such, how the brain chooses between and evaluates the outcome of different courses of action is little understood. It is a particularly important topic, though, as abnormal decision making lies at the core of several neuropsychiatric disorders from substance abuse to mania. During the latter part of my doctorate, I have demonstrated that part of rodent medial front cortex- namely, anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) - is crucial for allowing an animal to put in more work to achieve larger rewards. When rats were faced with a choice between 2 courses of action, one involving exerting effort for a large quantity of reward (high effort/high reward) and the other having a lower energetic demand but also a smaller reward (low effort/low reward), they typically chose the high effort/high reward option. However, following excitotoxic lesions of ACC, the rats switched to selecting the low effort/low reward response on every occasion. This is an exciting result as it is one of the first lesion studies on any brain region to find a specific impairment in decision making. If awarded this fellowship, I would follow up this finding in two novel directions. Firstly, I would validate our rodent studies in a primate model of effort-based decision making. Primates would again be given a choice between two courses of action, one being a high effort/high reward option, the other low effort/low reward, and the performance of a group with bilateral ACC lesions would be compared against a control group. However, the increased memory capacity of primates means that we will be able to test them using stimuli with a range of different effort and reward sizes, allowing us to describe any impairment more precisely than in rodents and to use normative theories of decision making to model and predict performance. Secondly, I would use in vivo voltammetry to monitor changes in glucose and oxygen - indicative of neural activity - in ACC and interconnected parts of the mesolimbic dopamine system while rats are tested on my decision making paradigm. This should enable specification of the role of ACC in overcoming effort-based constraints, and in evaluating and choosing between courses of action on the basis of their relative costs and benefits.

title: 'International Association of Tibetan Studies - Tibetan Meeting' to be held at the University of Oxford from 6th to 12th September 2003.
description: International Association of Tibetan Studies - Tibetan Medicine Despite an increasing number of recent conferences dedicated to Tibetan medicine, a purely academic focus on new research in this field has never been achieved in any international forum. New research concerning the history of Tibetan medicine includes the following topics: The study of as yet untranslated early Tibetan medical texts, the origins of urine and pulse diagnosis in Tibetan medicine, the establishment of western biomedicine in Tibet, and a history of Tibetan public health. Furthermore, the panel will allow for a comparative analysis of public healthcare and other medical practices as well as medical education/professionalisation among Tibetans living in very diverse environments, ranging from the Himalayan regions (Ladakh and Tibetan refugee settlements in northern India and Nepal) to the Tibetan high plateau of the Tibetan Autonomous Region, Eastern Tibet (Chinese provinces of Qinghai, Gansu, Sichuan) and Mongolia. Papers on acute problems in the negotiations between modernity/biomedicine and the Tibetan traditional medical system in both Tibetan and Western contexts, gender issues and psychiatry in Tibetan medicine, pulse diagnosis, and the relationship between cultural concepts/beliefs and medical practice will also be presented to enhance our knowledge and discussion of these controversial issues. All participants are presenting new research material which will then be published for the first time.

title: 'History in Public Health' seminar series from Autumn 2003 - Summer 2005 to be held at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine.
description: History in Public Health The history group at LSHTM have over the last 6 years run 3 seminar series, the first in conjunction with the "science speaks to policy" programme, the second on "public health and history", and the current one on "evidence, health and history." These have succeeded in bringing good historical discussion into the major School of public health and have given history a public role which it did not have before. The outcome of this raised profile for history has been that approval has now been granted for a new Centre for History in Public Health. Membership of the Centre will be provided by the existing nucleus of professional historians who currently form the History Group, as well as by non historians from all departments of the School. The current proposal is for a new seminar series that will look at all aspects of health in historical context, with a particular emphasis on areas that are of current policy interest. It will build on the audience established and the links made through the three previous series, as well as seeking out new audiences. The recent appointment of a Press Officer at the School means that new opportunities for enhancing the public role of history now exist through a closer involvement with the media. Thanks to the interest of the School's Press Officer, the work of the History Group has already attracted the attention of one of the national papers. It is anticipated that the seminar series will further stimulate this interest. This proposal also includes provision for a special seminar with following reception, at which the work of the new Centre will be launched to a multi disciplinary audience. Among the topics to be covered in the series will be: Cancer prevention Environment and health Primary care and the general practitioner Mental health Sexual health Health service organisation
recipient: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine

title: History of psychiatry and sexology, with special reference to Richard von Kraft-Ebing.
description: Project Title: The Krafft-Ebing papers at the Wellcome Library for the History & Understanding of Medicine and Possible research projects based on these materials Dr. Falzeder wishes to visit the Wellcome Library once more, to spend more time assessing the papers of Krafft-Ebing in preparation for a grant application involving extensive work in the papers. He has had a chance to view them for a few hours, but because they are uncatalogued it is important for him to get a more thorough impression of their content and organisation before he can know whether extensive work in them would yield significant results.

title: Children's emotional well-being in 19th & 20th centuries.
description: Children and Grown Ups: Age Relations in English Society since the Eighteenth Century My main project is my book in progress: Children and Grown Ups. Age Relations in Britain since the Eighteenth Century. One of the principal themes of the book is 'children's well-being' which is broadly defined in relation to health (physical, mental and emotional), social welfare, education and standard of living. My current work is on 'children's emotional well-being' and I've recently published two pieces on this topic, one of which was directly supported by small grants from the Wellcome. I am currently extending my interest into the emotional care of young children in relation to the historical provision of daycare facilities and the influences on this provision of the late 19th century Child Study movement and early 20th century developments in the New Psychology, psychoanalysis and the writings of Klein, Bowlby, Winnicott, et al. I'm also hoping to link this to a wider concern with the recognition of the significance of 'emotional' well-being as necessary for 'mental' health, and also as a desirable goal in itself where the 'happiness' of children of all ages is an issue. For example, my essay on hospital visiting suggests that this was not the case for child patients until the 1950s, and only recently has the idea of 'emotional abuse' been incorporated into child protection vis a vis 'child abuse'. Broadly speaking, my interest is in asking when and why does children's emotional well-being come to be regarded as a feature of 'health', 'welfare' and 'self' and what, if any, are the consequences for age relations.

title: Serotonin depletion and vulnerability to panic attacks in panic disorder.
description: Panic disorder (PD) is a common and serious psychiatric disorder characterised by recurrent panic attacks, disabling fear, and avoidance of panic-related situations. This project aims to extend recent studies on the role of serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine, 5-HT) in the mechanisms of panic attacks and in the mode of action of antipanic medications. It uses the new research method of tryptophan depletion (TD) to acutely reduce tryptophan levels and so decrease the synaptic availability of5-HT in the brain. Our recent study of TD in panic patients recovered on treatment with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) and then challenged with the panicogenic agent flumazenil reveal that the therapeutic effect of SSRI was reversed. This strongly suggests that an increase in synaptic 5-HT is critical to therapeutic action of this class of medication. It is now important to determine if this finding could be replicated with another antipanic medication and using differently acting panicogneic challenge. In this work we intend to explore whether TD will reveal a loss of the antipanic action of the most selective 5-HT reuptake inhibitor citalopram to a panicogenic challenge with cholecystokinin- tetrapeptide (CCK-4). CCK-4 is an agonist of the CCK-2 subtype of brain receptors. CCK is the most abundant neuropeptide in the brain and it is strongly implicated in the regulation of anxiety. Effective antipanic treatment, including SSRI citalopram, have been shown to block the CCK-4 induced panic attacks in PD patients but it is not known if this action would be reversed by TD. For this study we will recruit 30 patients with DSM-IV diagnosis of Panic Disorder and treat them during 10 weeks with citalopram according to the standard treatment guidelines. While still on treatment, in the following 2 weeks the responders will be the intensity and rate of CCK-4 induced panic attacks after TD in comparison to placebo (sham depletion). The results of this study should significantly advance our understanding of the neurobiology of the treatment of PD.

title: Role of voltage-gated potassium channels in modulating the release of GABA from hippocampal interneurons.
description: The aim of the project is to characterize in detail the role of different K+ channels in controlling the release of the inhibitory transmitter, GABA, from inhibitory interneurons onto pyramidal neurons in the hippocampus. This is considered to be important because a) the activity of these neurons is crucial to the regulation of hippocampal activity, and to the control of seizures, and (b) some of the channels likely to be involved are also susceptible to regulation by transmitters and intracellular messengers. The majority of experiments will be performed on a low-density primary culture of rate hippocampal neurones. Simultaneous whole-cell recording will be performed from a pyramidal neuron (postsynaptic cell) and an interneuron (presynaptic cell). Pyramidal cells and interneurones will be voltage- and current-clamped, respectively, and inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) in pyramidal neurones will be evoked by direct electrical stimulation of presynaptic interneurons. K+ channel blocking and enhancing agents will be selectively applied by means of local superfusion method either to the somata or nerve endings of a presynaptic neuron and their effects on evoked IPSCs determined, using paired-pulse depression to assess presynaptic effects. Changes in quantal release parameters will be assessed by recording IPSCs evoked by single bouton stimulation, and correlated with measurements of intra-bouton Ca2+ transients. Conjointly, expression of different K+ channel subunits in interneuron somata and processes will be assessed by single-cell PCR, and by immunocytochemistry using antibodies against different K+ channel subunits. Attempts will then be made to determine the effects of acutely-deleting individual subunits on somatic currents and evoked IPSCs by transfecting dominant-negative constructs. Finally, information gained from these experiments on paired-cell cultures will be tested against spontaneous inhibitory transmission recorded in slice preparations of intact adult hippocampus. The project brings together the expertise of the PI in recording and analysis of IPSCs in hippocampal interneuron - pyramidal cell cultures with the interests and experience of the UK partner in the function of neuronal K+ channels. The work will enhance understanding of the dynamics of GABA-mediated inhibition in the hippocampus and the regulation of hippocampal excitability.
recipient: School of Pharmacy, University of London

title: The Protective Role Of The Fear Response.
description: A central tenet of evolutionary psychology is the view that certain behavioural and psychological traits are adaptive. Evolutionary psychologists have attempted to demonstrate the adaptive status of a range of behaviours, including the fear response. For a biological phenomenon to be considered an adaptation, the following criteria should be met: Heritability of variation in expression of the trait. Variation in survival/reproductive outcomes depending on expression of the trait. Survival or reproductive harm resulting from removal of the trait. Homology across species. It has frequently been suggested that fear is an adaptation, especially by clinicians treating individuals suffering with unpleasant levels of fear, or fear which is inappropriate to the stimulus. Variation in expression of the fear response correlates strongly with Neuroticism (N) score on the Eysenck Personality Inventory, and N score is highly heritable. N therefore fulfils the first of Williams' criteria above. There is also evidence of cross species homology of fear and its expressions. There is little evidence from humans for a variation in survival outcomes associated with N. We will perform a cohort study using data from the MRCNSHD, using persistent low Neuroticism score as the exposure variable. The risk set will consist of those survey members who completed all three Maudsley Personality Inventories that were carried out and were followed up for at least one wave of data collecting thereafter.

title: Attention and executive function in Autism: an examination using neuropsychological and event-related functional magnetic resonance imaging (ER-fMRI) techniques.
description: Autism is one of the autistic spectrum of pervasive developmental disorders, that are characterised by specific delays and deviance in social, communication, and cognitive development, with an onset that is within the first few years of life. The disorder is now thought to be biological in nature, with research efforts aimed at elucidating genetic, neuropathological and neurochemical involvements in the disorder. Cognitive and attention impairment may be common in the disorder, and there is a need to integrate explanatory accounts of such deficit with current models of executive and attentional function arising out the cognitive neurosciences. This project therefore aims to systematically investigate executive and attentional impairment in a large sample of children with autism, by employing common paradigms across research centres in Trinity College Dublin and Monash University, Australia. Specifically, we aim to document the nature and extent of an hypothesised executive deficit of attention switching, either within a single modality, or between different modalities. We also aim to investigate the reliability of deficits in spatial attention that have been observed in autism and in particular focus on the ability to shift the spatial scale of attention, from a local level of analysis to a global level. After establishing the reliability of such impairments, we will employ these paradigms within event-related functional magnetic resonance imaging (ER-fMRI) studies to determine the neural correlates of any impairment, focussing in particular on frontostriatal, frontoparietal and cerebellar regions, which are both important for efficient executive and attentional function, and have previously implicated in autism. Collaboration between centres of excellence in Ireland and Australia on this project will allow executive and attentional function in autism to be rigorously investigated, and should contribute significantly to both explanatory and neurobiological accounts of the disorder.

title: Role of NSF and AF2 interactions with AMPA receptors in hippocampal synaptic function.
description: AMPA receptors mediate most fast excitatory synaptic transmission in the brain and dysfunction of AMPA receptor-mediated synaptic transmission has been implicated in the aetiology of disease states, including Alzheimer's disease, epilepsy and trauma. Another reason why AMPA receptors have become such a major focus for research is that they are believed to be a key molecular entity that is modified during synaptic plasticity. In particular, alterations in AMPA receptor properties and the number of AMPA receptors that are expressed at synapses is strongly implicated in long-term potentiation (LTP) and long-term depression (LTD); processes that are believed to engage molecular mechanisms involved in learning and memory. We discovered two proteins that bind to the intracellular c-terminal tail of the AMPA receptor subunit GluR2; namely the ATPase NSF and the protein kinase C targeting molecule PICK1. By defining the interaction sites of GluR2 we were able to design peptide inhibitors and use electrophysiological and imaging techniques to investigate the function of these interactors. We discovered that the GluR2-NSF interaction is required to maintain AMPAR function at synapses. Blocking this interaction acutely led to a rapid reduction in AMPA receptor- mediated synaptic transmission and suggested, fro the first time, that AMPA receptors are rapidly and constitutively recycled at synapses. Blocking this interaction also prevented the induction of LTD suggesting that the constitutively mobile pool of AMPA receptors corresponded to a rapidly modifiable pool. Blocking the GluR2-PICK1 interaction acutely had no obvious effect, however, other data led us to propose that PICK1 may target PKC to phosphorylate GluR2 and lead to AMPAR insertion.

title: Neural correlates of acoustic spatial processing in auditory hallucinations.
description: Neural correlates of acoustic spatial processing in auditory hallucinations Auditory hallucinations (AHs) are a core feature of schizophrenia (WHO, 1973) but lack diagnostic specificity because they also occur in a range of other mental disorders, and in 'non-psychiatric' states such as bereavement. The supposition that people with AHs have a fundamental abnormality of auditory spatial processing is based upon their reported experience of 'voices' as perceptual objects located in external space, in the absence of a speaker or any other stimulus. We have presented functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data that implicates the planum temporale (PT) in the perception of real voices presented as though located 'outside the head', in external space. Additionally, in fMRI and behavioural studies we have found evidence suggesting functional asymmetry for processing spatial aspects of speech in the normal auditory system. Specifically, dominant auditory cortex is more activated by speech stimuli presented on the right than on the left and subjects are more accurate at discerning the spatial location of speech stimuli on the right than on the left. Having already modelled the neural correlates of perceiving the spatial location of hallucination-like actual speech, we will, in the current studies, use fMRI to directly and indirectly examine brain activation during AHs with different spatial properties. We will investigate the behavioural consequences of these neural correlates in a series of outside-scanner psychophysical experiments.This study is clinically important because it addresses the neural basis for a phenomenon, the apparent spatial location of AHs, that is used by clinicians in process of making psychiatric diagnoses. By studying a group of patients that is mixed with respect to diagnosis and phenomenology, we hope to develop methodological probes that may lead to a better understanding of the relationship between psychotic phenomena, diagnosis and brain function, and contribute to the development of more accurate, and biologically more meaningful, diagnoses in psychiatry.

title: Qualitative and quantitative molecular genetic analysis of Catechol-O- methyltransferase (COMT) and Proline dehydrogenase (PRODH) genes in schizophrenia and related traits in a Chinese population.
description: Qualitative and quantitative molecular genetic analysis of Catechol-O- methyltransferase (COMT) and Proline dehydrogenase (PRODH) genes in schizophrenia and related traits in a Chinese population This project aims to investigate an important resource for schizophrenia research, a sample of families with the illness including DNA and detailed clinical and neuropsychological information. 1. To attempt to replicate genetic association with schizophrenia and the Catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) and Proline dehydrogenase (PRODH) genes. 2. To use neuropsychological measures of cognitive abilities as endophenotypes in order to replicate association between COMT allele and performance of the Wisconsin Card Sorting test, and to further refine and understand these genetic associations.

title: Genetic and molecular dissection of the mechanism to ensure chromosome bi- orientation in yeast.
description: To maintain genetic integrity, eukaryotic cells must duplicate and segregate their chromosomes in high fidelity during cell division cycles. For proper segregation of sister chromatids, each sister kinetochore must attach to microtubules extending to the opposite spindle poles before the onset of anaphase. This process is called chromosome bi-orientation or bipolar kinetochore-microtubule attachment. The mechanism for chromosome bi- orientation lies at the heart of the chromosome segregation, but is still poorly understood. Chromosomes could be bi-oriented by pointing sister kinetochores to opposite directions and/or by correcting orientation of kinetochore-spindle connections until microtubule-dependent forces generate tension on kinetochores. To clarify the mechanisms for chromosome bi- orientation, we are designing a genetic screening to identify novel regulators for this process in budding yeast S. cerevisiae. First we will look for temperature-sensitive (ts) mutants that show frequent loss of an artificial marker chromosome. Then we will search the mutants in which both sister chromatids are segregated to the same spindle pole. We will mark two chromosome arm loci, one contromere and spindle pole bodies by different fluorescent proteins and follow their behaviours. Our screening is designed to identify the novel mutants in which kinetochore-spindle pole connections are formed as in wild type cells, but the connections are not properly oriented.

title: Genetic analysis of schizophrenia in SW China: A collaboration between the Institute of Psychiatry, London and Sichuan University.
description: The aims of the project are to collect DNA and detailed clinical and neuropsychological information from family trio, sibling pairs and large, multiply affected families with schizophrenia from Sichuan Province, SW China. This resource will be added to an existing resource of 150 sibling pairs and 400 family trios from the same region, and used for clinical and molecular genetic studies of schizophrenia in the two centres. Specifically, we will test for familiality of symptom dimensions of schizophrenia and related cognitive traits using appropriate statistical methods including Spearman's correlation and partial correlation analysis and perform genetic association analysis on the sample in the COMT, neuregulin and dysbindin genes. In subsequent investigations, the DNA samples from the total of 800 schizophrenic trios and 150 families will be used for LD mapping, positional candidate gene analysis and to replicate positive association findings from other sources. The newly collected 400 schizophrenic nuclear families will also be used to perform quantitative genetic analysis of endophenotypes. Replicated "hot spot" linkage regions (e.g. chromosome 1q, 6p, 8p, 13q32, 15q, 22q11, 22q12-13) will be selected for study, including two claimed associations within 8p (neuregulin 1) and 6p (dysbindin). Fine mapping using family-based linkage disequilibrium approach on these regions and individual DNA polymorphisms (mainly single nucleotide polymorphisms and VNTRs) and haplotypes of targeted regions (or candidate genes) will be used. For associations we find or replicate, we will explore additive and interactive effects between loci and with schizophrenia related clinical and neuropsychological traits.

title: Proteomic analysis of isatin-binding proteins.
description: Isatin (2,3-dioxindole) is an endogenous compound with a distinctive distribution in the brain and other tissues. It is involved in both stress reactions and control of water balance. Low (physiological) doses of isatin in vivo cause anxiety, change of food and water intake, whereas higher doses cause sedation and improve manifestations of symptoms of Parkinson's disease in animal models. In situ isatin influences cell proliferation in different cell lines and antagonises natriuretiuc peptide receptors. In vitro it acts as a potent antagonist of a nitric oxide-stimulated soluble guanylate cyclase, natriuretic peptide-stimulated particulate guanylate cyclase, and monoamine oxidase type B and has minor or no effect on other receptors of major hormones and neurotransmitters that have been tested. Recently, specific isatin binding sites have been found in brain slices in situ, and in particulate and soluble fractions of brain and peripheral tissues. However, the particular proteins which account for this binding, and which form the basis of its rather wide of physiological and pharmacological actions, remain unknown. Identification of the whole spectrum of isatin-binding proteins and the study of mechanisms of their interaction with isatin would allow us to get a clearer picture of the function of this potentially important endogenous regulator. In this project we intend: a) To employ proteomic approaches for the identification of isatin binding proteins in soluble and particulate fractions of rat PC12 cells and human platelets (the particular cells containing the most sensitive targets for physiological concentrations of isatin known to date). b) To analyse protein maps of soluble and particulate fractions of PC12 cells and platelets and to study the effect of isatin on these proteome maps; c) To characterise mechanisms underlying effects of isatin on the biological activity of identified proteins. The employment of various proteomic approaches (2D-electrophoresis, fluorescent imaging, MALDI-TOF MS, SELDI ProteinChip technology) together with affinity chromatography of cell extracts on 5-amino- isatin-Sepharose followed by subsequent trypsinolysis and the resultant fingerprint(s) analysis of by nanoESI MS MS will allow to characterise isatin binding profiles of rat PC12 cells and human platelets and to identify particular isatin-binding proteins. The interaction of isatin with the individual proteins identified in this project, will be further investigated by using biosensor analysis, and traditional binding experiments with [3H]isatin. The final stage of the project will be the study of the effect of different concentrations of isatin on the biological activity of identified proteins.

title: Diffusion tensor imaging in schizophrenia.
description: Background: Studies with functional neuroimaging suggest that there is a disruption of the normal interactions between different brain areas in schizophrenia. This has been termed functional dysconnectivity. There is also evidence of reduced frontal white matter volume in schizophrenia, consistent with the notion that there is an underlying problem with the anatomical pathways that connect brain areas. The recently developed MR technique of Diffusion Tensor Imaging provides a relatively direct means of examining whether this is the case in vivo. Initial applications of this technique in schizophrenia have yielded promising findings, although the number of subjects involved has been relatively small. Hypthesis: Patients with schizophrenia will have lower fractional anisotropy in the major fronto-temporal fasiculi than controls, reflecting a reduction in the uniformity of tract orientation. Methodology: Diffusion Tensor Imaging data have already been collected from 40 patients with DSM-IV schizophrenia and 40 matched controls, using an optimised acquisition sequence. This proposal is designed to allow the applicant to be trained in the methods to be used to analyse these data, which have been developed at the Institute of Psychiatry. He will then apply these and process and analyse the dataset. The analysis involves non-linear warping, tract- tracing, and fractional anisotropy measurement along the white matter tracts of interest. These anisotropy measurements would be compared, at the group level, with those from normal controls.

title: Student electives for Rachel Squires and Safia Debar.
description: Domestic abuse of women remains a worldwide phenomenon affecting all ethnic groups and social classes. This may also occur and worsen in association with pregnancy, with serious implications for the pregnant women and her unborn baby. In the West Indies, little progress has been made in the recognition and management of this problem; this could be justified by poverty, tradition, poor education, religious beliefs and the cultural dependence of women on their man as identified by the stereotyped attitudes about 'ownership' of women and their value and place in the family and in the society. There are both immediate effects on the pregnancy such as blunt trauma to the abdomen and also lasting effects that include women continuing unhealthy habits due to stress, for example smoking. Domestic abuse is associated with adverse birth outcomes such as low birth weight and pre-term delivery due to placental dysfunction. The long-term effects of domestic abuse include post-traumatic stress disorder, the process of childbirth can accentuate this disorder and also the growing child will be less secure if the mother is psychologically distressed. I aim to investigate the level of domestic abuse in a pregnant population in the West Indian country of Trinidad. I aim to raise awareness of these issues, indicate the importance of adequate management through counselling and support services and encourage investments to educate poorly trained and ill-equipped personnel, these are fundamental parts of any programme to support or rescue women from these conditions. I propose to conduct a clinical interview using the 12- item version of the General Health Questionnaire on a 'non-clinical patient' population, i.e. not a specific psychiatric population but it may include a hidden psychiatric morbidity which I aim to determine. I aim to investigate methods used in the UK to treat abused pregnant and non-pregnant patients by contacting patient support groups and aim to relay effective treatment strategies to the health services in Trinidad.

title: Migration, experience of abuse and mental health in the young Thai population
description: Migration, experience of abuse, and mental health in the young Thai population A population-based cross-sectional survey will be conducted in Klong-Luang District, Pathumthani Province. Catchment areas with high rates of rural to urban migration will be identified from data gathered in the pilot study. The assessment comprises two parts: an interviewer administered questionnaire, and a self-administered questionnaire on experience of abuse and substance and alcohol use. The self-report questionnaire will be completed by respondents in private and returned in a sealed envelope to the interviewer. Measures: 1) Exposures - internal migration (defined as geographical mobility within Thailand and assessed in relation to birthplace, age at the time of move, the number of moves before the age of 16, recency of last move, distance of moves, and reasons for moving), experience of abuse and violence - defined as reporting emotional, physical, sexual abuse and domestic violence before the age of 16, using questions adapted from Conflict Tactic Scale. 2) Confounders/mediators - age, gender, living circumstances, education, employment, household income, chronic difficulties, life events, social network and social support. 3) Outcomes a) Common mental disorder (a concept taken to include affective, anxiety, phobic and somatisation disorders, previously referred to collectively as neurosis, and reflecting the high levels of comorbidity encountered in the general population) assessed suing the Clinical Interview Schedule Revised; b) alcohol use assessed by the Alcohol use Disorder Identification Test (AUDIT); c) substance use (tranquilisers, cannabis, amphetamines, opiates, hallucinogens, ecstacy and solvents). Pre-piloting shows that the interview is generally administered in 45 minutes. Analysis

title: Needs of care in the elderly with depression or anxiety disorders in Sao Paulo, Brazil.
description: Needs of care in the elderly with depression or anxiety disorders in Sao Paulo, Brazil A cross-sectional population-based survey will be carried out in a defined geographical area of Sao Paulo, with the main aim of estimating the prevalence of dementia. All residents aged 65 years or more will be eligible to participate in that study, and all those who fulfil ICD-10 diagnostic criteria for depression or anxiety disorder will be invited to participate in the present study. It is expected that some 200 individuals, out of a total sample of 2000 elderly, will fulfil such criteria. Diagnostic assessment will be carried out with the Geriatric Mental State. Socio-demographic and socio- economic information will be gathered with a standardised questionnaire. Activity limitation and participation restriction will be measured by the WHO- DAS II and impact on informal carers with the Zarit Burden Interview. Needs of care will be measured with the Camberwell Assessment of Needs for the Elderly (CANE), a comprehensive needs assessment instrument developed from the Camberwell Assessment of Needs (CAN), which incorporated special needs posed by the elderly. Interviews will take place at subjects homes. Key-informants, preferably informal carers, will also be interviewed. After reciving full explanation about the study, all participants will be asked to sign an informed consent form. Descriptive analysis will be followed by univariate and multivariate analyses. The first two months will be for translation and piloting of the main instrument (CANE). Months two to ten will be for the fieldwork. The MSc course will take place from month 13 to month 24. Months 25 to 30 will be for further analysis and writing up of manuscripts for publication. The findings of the present project will be disseminated in a number of ways: a. Articles published in international specialised journals; b. Presentations in scientific meetings; c. Seminars and workshops for health care professionals.

title: Affective and cognitive disease in urban Pakistan: a population based prevalence study
description: Affective and Cognitive Disease in Urban Pakistan: A Population-based Prevalence Study This study wil be a population-based survey of depression and dementia in a random sample of Karachi's adult population. There will be three survey teams. Each team will comprise one male and one female field worker. A psychiatrist, a family physician, a neurologist, and an epidemiologist experience in the use of the screening instruments and fieldwork will train the field workers. The screening battery will comprise affective (depression) and cognitive (dementia) tests designed to highlight individuals with depression, dementia or both. To screen for depression, we will use the Aga Khan University Anxiety and Depression Scale (AKUADS), an indigenous screening interview administered in Pakistan's national language, Urdu. To screen for dementia, we will follow a cognitive test battery that has been developed in the Hindi language and used in a population-based dementia study in northern India. The cognitive portion of our study will use the following screening tools: Mini-Mental State Examinations in Urdu; a 10-item word list for memory recall; a test of verbal fluency using names of animals and fruits; an Object Naming Test; and a test of constructional praxis requiring the copying of four geometic drawings. A positive dementia screen will be defined as: (i) a score at or below the 10th percentile on the Mini-Mental State Examination; (ii) a score at or below the 10th percentile on the 10-item memory recall word list and on either one of the tests evaluating verbal fluency, object naming, or constructional praxis. Specifically, the following areas of exposure and predisposition will be investigated: age and gender, educational level, socio- economic status, family history, medication history, history of head trauma, marital status and marital history, tobacco and alcohol use, dietary patterns, and co-morbidities. All individuals who are screened positive for depression or dementia by the survey team will undergo expert clinical evaluation for diagnostic confirmation. Each clinical evaluation will incorporate a comprehensive medical and psychiatric history, a general physical examination, a detailed neurological examination, and interview-based assessment by the psychiatrist or neurologist to establish correspondence to the clinical syndromes of depression or dementia. The primary outcome will be the composite outcome of (i) depression defined as clinically-confirmed unipolar major depression, and (ii) dementia defined as clinically-confirmed chronic dementia.

title: The impact of changes in household composition and structure on the well-being of urban South African children within the birth to twenty cohort.
description: Worldwide household structure and composition have undergone dramatic changes in recent years. Consequently, household fluidity has become increasingly apart of family life. Research on the relationship between household composition, and in turn household stability, has been associated with child well-being. It has been suggested that the lack of household stability through continuous shifts in household composition may have negative outcomes for children, such as emotional (depression), behavioural (personality disorders), health (Asthma) and learning prblems (poor academic performance. Furthermore, household instability may heighten the impact environmental influences such as stress and violence may have on the child. The connection between household composition, stability and structure, and child well-being has not been adequately explored within developing countries. Black South African family life has been affected over a long period of time under the social, political and economic pressure of colonialism, a migrant labour system and apartheid policies. Households were in a constant state of flux as members moved between rural and urban households. This situation has not changed much. Recent research indicates that South African households are still fluid as South Africa continues with dynamic population change and rural-urban migration.

title: Prevalence of substance misuse among individuals with a first episode of functional psychosis in Sao Paulo, Brazil
description: Schizophrenia and bipolar disorders are becoming increasingly important public health problems in Brazil and other South American countries. The number of young adults at risk for functional psychosis is rapidly increasing, as a consequence of the fast population aging process. Furthermore, a large proportion of the population has moved from rural areas or small towns to live in huge urban centres, frequently in adverse social conditions. This is important, as a number of recent studies in Europe have shown that being born or brought up in large cities increases the risk of schizophrenia. Moreover, although WHO studies have traditionally shown the outcome for schizophrenia to be better in the developing than developed world, this may not apply to patients living in large urban centres in Brazil. Recently, the Brazilian Congress has approved new legislation on mental health services, focusing on the delivery of community care for severely mentally ill people. However, adequate planning and implementation of community-based care for patients with functional psychoses in Brazil, as well as information about the sufferers' needs for care, the impact caused by the disease on their informal carers and their social network. Therefore, a population-based study of first contact psychosis in Sao Paulo, Brazil, is being carried out. Patients are identified though active surveillance of all public health services which can be contacted by patients in acute phases of functional psychoses in the area studied. Assessments include the SCID, DAS and PANSS. Other aspects investigated using standardised assessments include what are the needs of care when patients first seek help in the health care system, their pathways to care, and the immediate distress imposed on informal carers. A case-control design has been used to investigate a number of risk factors for psychosis: a) family history of psychosis, obstetric complications and childhood dysfunction; b) adverse life events and drug abuse.

title: The environmental impacts on health and well-being of elderly in Thailand
description: During the past three decades, Thailand has proven to be one of the most successful countries in bringing down its fertility level within a short period of time. The total fertility rate has declined from over 6 births per woman in the mid 1960s to below 2 in the mid 1990s. Life expectancy at birth increased from 55.2 years to 69.9 years for men and 61.8 years to 74.9 years for women during the same period. Sharp declines in fertility combined with rising life expectancies will eventually produce unprecedented population aging, commonly measured as the proportion of the population age 60 and older. Based on the latest projections from the United Nations, the growth rate of the Thai elderly population is relatively high, over 3 percent per year, the size of the elderly population will have a doubling times of about 19-23 years. Thailand will become an aged society within the next 10 years, according to the UN's definition. One consequence of the trends already discussed is that the older population, being increasingly long-lived, will also be characterized by extended health problems. This not only adds to the costs of medical treatment, but also places a strain on health care facilities designed for the promotion of health. However, the main objective of health and social systems is to provide health and optimal social functioning for all, to improve health and well-being and not only to prolong life but also to maintain its quality in terms of autonomy as long as possible. Disability must be at the center of interests particularly among the elderly population. Thus, among the aged population diseases or health problems, which affect performance and increase the dependence status must be ranked a high priority.

title: Neural correlates of response to cognitive behaviour therapy in schizophrenia: a functional MRI investigation.
description: Advances in neuroimaging have greatly facilitated investigations of the neural correlates of mental phenomena in psychiatric disorders; for example the study of those functional brain changes associated with symptoms of schizophrenia and their treatment. The study of how successful treatment of schizophrenic symptoms alters brain functions is a promising route to investigate the causes of the illness. The beneficial effects of antipsychotics on the illness are well established. Typical antipsychotics have strong effects on positive symptoms, but have little effects on negative or cognitive symptoms. Atypical antipsychotics are claimed to have some additional effects on negative symptoms, cognition and social behaviour and have also been shown to have beneficial effects on attention and information processing mechanisms and to improve brain functions as compared with typical antipsychotics. However, despite the beneficial effects of antipsychotic treatment for schizophrenia, the outcome for many patients still remains unsatisfactory. This is mainly due to the medication-resistant nature of illness in some patients and inadequate long-term maintenance treatment leading to subsequent relapse and the development of residual symptoms, neurocognitive deficits and functional impairments. In recent years, attention has focused on cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT) as an adjunct treatment to drug therapy for medication resistant patients; among those who fail to show adequate clinical response to drug treatments, about 50% show a significant improvement with CBT. The central aim of this project is to investigate: does successful treatment of symptoms with CBT in medication resistant patients with schizophrenia produce measurable changes in activity in the cortical/sub-cortical and limbic brain regions and, if so, are they qualitatively similar to those induced by successful treatment of symptoms with antipsychotic drugs? In addition, the project will also investigate neural predictors of a clinical response to CBT. In order to achieve these aims, whole brain functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) will be applied to 60 medication-resistant patients with schizophrenia (half of whom will undergo CBT) in a longitudinal within-subjects design during a series of tasks which are known or likely to be sensitive to positive, negative, cognitive and affective symptoms of schizophrenia, to detect patterns of blood-oxygenation-level dependent (BOLD) activity associated with a clinical response to CBT. The resulting patterns of BOLD activity in these subjects will be also compared with that seen in the groups of 20 patients with schizophrenia with a good clinical response to antipsychotic drugs and 20 normal healthy subjects.

title: The neural bases of spatial cognition and memory through the life span in health and disease.
description: This project aims to establish how we internally represent large-scale space and our personal (autobiographical) experiences within it, and seeks to determine how both types of memory can be understood within a unified cognitive-neuroanatomical framework that supports our integrated sense of who and where we are. These goals will be achieved by combining several strategic features. I will continue to develop ecologically value or 'real life' experimental paradigms to directly examine brain-behaviour relationships. Converging evidence will be sought from multiple disciplines including cognitive, developmental and neuropsychology, structural and functional neuroimaging. A lifespan approach will be adopted with participants ranging from children to elderly, involving healthy participants and patients. As well as examining memories at single (static) time points, I will track how they change longitudinally, over short and longer time-scales, as well as through development, and in the context of pathology. Exploring how memories are represented at different stages in life, and the nature of their plasticity may yield clues about how they are structured cognitively and supported neurally. I will seek to establish in greater detail the nature of spatial and autobiographical memory representations, their key elements and their neural substrates. In tandem, and also informed by this work, I will systematically evaluate several extant theoretical frameworks for understanding how the two types of memory might be linked. There will be a fundamental interest in the hippocampus in the project, with the aim of elucidating its role in supporting memory in terms of laterality, and where relevant, its anterior/posterior axis. It is hypothesised that the human hippocampus is involved in combining self-relevance in the context of large interconnected spatial environments (right hippocampus), and in the context of social networks or personal histories (left hippocampus). The wider brain networks supporting memory will also be of interest, including understanding the contributions of brain regions such as retrosplenial and medial frontal cortices, and making inferences at the systems level by characterising inter-regional connectivity. As well as generating theoretical insights into the cognitive neuroanatomy of memory, findings from this project will be used to provide benchmarks for interpreting the effects of pathology on memory representations at different points in the life span (e.g. developmental disorders in children, dementia in the elderly), to aid the development of clinical memory tests for early (differential) diagnosis of pathology and, in the longer-term, to inform treatment and rehabilitative interventions.

title: Neural systems for decision-making and strategy implementation.
description: The human frontal cortex controls attention, learning, memory, language, decision-making, judgment, and planning, in addition to other different cognitive functions. Damage to the frontal lobes is a frequent consequence of stroke and traumatic brain injury. Impairments in frontal lobe function are also common in Alzheimer disease, Parkinson's disease, and frontotemporal dementia, as well as neuropsychiatric disorders such as obsessive-compulsive disorder, mood disorders, and schizophrenia. Clinically, impairments in these functions make it impossible for people with these ailments to live independently. The available data, although very limited, suggests that these different functions may be regulated by different neurotransmitter systems within the frontal cortex. We need to know the neurobiological bases of cognitive functions controlled by the frontal lobe in order to understand the pathogenesis of cognitive impairment in these various conditions and to design therapies that could ameliorate these impairments. The experiments proposed in this programme of research will use sophisticated behavioural assessments of decision-making, planning, and strategy selection in rhesus monkeys, to test the effects of selective depletion of particular neurotransmitters within the frontal cortex on these abilities. First we will identify the subregions within frontal cortex that are responsible for particular aspects of these complex cognitive functions, because there is evidence that different areas of the frontal cortex make different contributions to the regulation of behaviour. Then we will use immunotoxins to remove selectively input from a particular transmitter system (acetylcholine, dopamine, serotonin) to subregions of frontal cortex. The promise of this work is a fuller understanding of the neurochemical regulation of prefrontal cortex function, leading to the development of pharmacological agents that could be used to regulate selectively particular cognitive functions controlled by the frontal lobe.

title: Development and Evaluation by Randomized Trial of a Community-Based Early Multimodal Intervention (EMI) for Depressed Mothers and their Infants in Rural Rawalpindi, Pakistan.
description: Indicators of maternal and child health in south Asia rank among the worse in the world and there is an urgent need for applied research in this area. Rates of postnatal depression in developing countries have been found to be very high and associated with significant disability. Recent epidemiological studies in developing countries show that maternal depression is strongly associated with poor growth and morbidity in infants. Addressing the mental health needs of such mothers could therefore have important bearings on the physical health and development of their infants. This proposal describes the development and evaluation by randomized control trial of an early multimodal intervention delivered by Lady Health Workers (LHWs) to antenatally and postnatally depressed mothers in a rural area of Rawalpindi District, Pakistan, with infant growth as the main outcome indicator. In phases 1 and 2, the intervention will be developed and piloted, and the study design refined, through small qualitative and quantitative studies. In phase 3, the intervention will be compared to routine antenatal and postnatal care by LHWs for mothers ages 17 to 40 years, who have a diagnosis of major depression during the third trimester of pregnancy. Using individual randomization or a cluster design, nine hundred participants living in 200 villages will be randomized by an independent trial centre, and followed up six months, and one year later, by an assessor without knowledge of the treatment given. The primary outcome will be infant growth and other outcomes will include mother's level of depression and social functioning, and economic costs.

title: The assessment of mental capacity in patients with psychiatric disorders.
description: Introduction: We have previously been funded by Wellcome Trust to perform a project on mental capacity in general hospital in-patients. Preliminary results indicate existing methods to make judgments about capacity require some refining, and also that a high proportion lack mental capacity to make decisions regarding their treatment, but this is rarely recognised by medical teams. The proposed research aims to extend this work into a different patient group (psychiatric in-patients and those under the care of a home treatment team). Aims: The main aims are (1) To refine existing measures of capacity; (2) To determine the prevalence of psychiatric in-patients who lack capacity to make key decisions regarding their treatment; and (3) to test a series of hypotheses linking mental capacity with the use of the Mental Health Act, perceived coercion and the presence of cognitive impairment or delusions. Pilot study: We will assess existing measures of mental capacity, checking inter-rater reliability and validity, which will be assessed by a panel of experienced psychiatrists. Main study: A consecutive sample of 250 psychiatric in-patients will be interviewed using the capacity interview, as well as measures of insight, perceived coercion, and clinical status. It will be possible from th is study to determine the proportion of patients judged to lack mental capacity to make decisions regarding their current treatment. All patients will be re-interviewed at the point of discharge, or six months following admission (whichever is the earliest) to determine the proportion in whom capacity is regained over this period of time. Participants who are judged to lack capacity will be compared with those who are thought to have capacity on a range of clinical and demographic characteristics. We will then use univariate and multivariate statistical methods to compare these groups in terms of their legal status under the Mental Health Act (1983), their perception of coercion, and their insight into their condition.

title: The history of Hungarian psychiatry in European context (1867-1918).
description: My Wellcome research project aims at completing a book on the emergence of Hungarian psychiatry, a field hitherto completely unresearched by historians. I reconstruct the process through which the developing science of psychiatry gradually acquired manifold social functions and exerted wide cultural influence by the turn of the century. While highlighting the idiosyncratic features of Central European scientific and social developments (with original research in archives on lands of the former uHuHHhkHungarian Kingdom that now fall on Romanian, Serb, Polish, and Slovak territories), I integrate Hungarian psychiatry into Western trends with its manifold ties to Austrian, German, British and French national psychiatries. My research covers the complex processes of professionalisation and institutionalisation. It also makes use of the invaluable sources (thousands of detailed asylum case histories, patient letters and diaries) that reveal everyday practice and life in mental institutions, as well as the personal experience of madness. Complementing the voice of the patient with doctors' biographies and personal correspondence, I study the day-to-day encounter and negotiation between doctor and patient. By studying the related fields of criminology, sexology, spiritism, experimental psychology, psychoanalysis, eugenics and anthropology, I explore the intellectual climate that favoured psychiatry in its appropriation of a cultural monopoly over a number of issues related to the hygiene of everyday life as well as a 'healthy' society. The project expands my PhD research dedicated to specific psychiatric diseases, institutions and practices in 19th century Hungary.

title: A monograph entitled 'The Connaught District Lunatic Asylum: Land, Power and Politics'.
description: My proposed research relates to the development of the asylum service in Ireland in the late nineteenth and early twentieth century, and its relationship to local and national social, political, and economic developments. I intend to focus upon one institution in particular, in order to establish a solid empirical base from which to explore a range of issues. The principal sources I will use for the project are held in St. Brigid's Psychiatric Hospital, Ballinasloe, Co. Galway, Ireland. This institution was formerly the Connaught District Lunatic Asylum, which from its establishment in 1833 catered for patients sent from the five counties of Galway, Sligo, Roscommon, Leitrim and Mayo. It was one of the largest asylums in the country, and dealt for the most part with pauper patients. The records at Ballinasloe are an invaluable source for understanding nineteenth-century psychiatric practice. They detail admission and discharge rates, treatments, relationships between patients and practitioners, and popular attitudes towards the mentally ill. They also offer a unique insight into social, political, and economic change in Ireland more generally. Events such as the Great Famine, and the subsequent rise in emigration rates in the latter half of the nineteenth- century, impacted significantly upon public perceptions of insanity, and led to a rise in the numbers of patients admitted to Ballinasloe. National political change also effected life behind the asylum walls, altering the relationship between the Lord Lieutenant (the individual responsible for Irish asylums) and the institution, and influencing matters such as the appointment of Catholic staff. The asylum played a key role in the economic development of the region, and was especially significant during the Famine, when it offered both employment, and sanctuary, to the afflicted population.

title: Creating models of health and disease: A facility for integrating production and functional analysis of nervous system plasticity in genetically modified rodents.
description: The goal of this proposal is to build an integrated facility to create, house and behaviourally test genetically modified rodents to gain a new understanding of brain mechanisms of learning, memory and plasticity. Breakthroughs in understanding brain function are dependent on the development of new methodologies, and the application of genetic engineering to neuroscience promises to revolutionise the field. Not only can this technology be applied to understanding the functions of the normal brain, it can be used to produce models of disease with unprecedented similarities to human disease. We propose to create a laboratory to facilitate the modelling of normal and abnormal human behaviour. This bid arises from Cardiff University's strategy of appointing researchers in the adjacent Schools of Biosciences and Psychology with complementary expertise in brain mechanisms of learning and memory. The cohesion and status of this group has been recognised through the award of an MRC Co-operative in "Learning, memory and neuronal plasticity in mammalian systems". This group has been further consolidated by the subsequent appointments of Prof S Dunnett and Dr S Killcross. One special strength of this group is in the development of new behavioural tests for both rats and mice.

title: What is the contribution of neonatal systemic infection to later neurodisability? Follow-up of a randomised controlled trial of prophylactic GN-CSF to reduce sepsis in preterm babies.
description: Diffuse white matter brain injury is now considered the major cause of neurodevelopmental disability in extremely preterm infants. Recent data suggest that white matter injury may be an inflammatory response to infection distant from the brain. We are conducting a UK multicentrre, randomised, single blind, controlled trial, PROGRAMS (PROphylactic GRAnulocyte-Macrophage colony stimulating factor to reduce Sepsis in preterm neonates) to test the hypothesis that the prophylactic administration of GM-CSF for a short period after birth to high risk, preterm neonates, will lead to a reduction ion infection, death and later disability. PROGRAMS is funded by Action Research, the NHS Executive (economic evaluation) and Guy's & Thomas' Charitable Foundation. (laboratory studies). Recruitment of 320 infants, less than or equal to 31 weeks gestation and with a birth weight <10th centile for gestational age, from 26 large neonatal centres, is on target to finish in February 2003. The primary PROGRAMS protocol aims to obtain information by post from local paediatricians about the children's health outcomes at age two-years. This will provide a broad functional categorisation of moderate/severe disability, in particular motor disability, but will not be sufficiently sensitive to detect all clinically important deficits. Preterm infants are at risk of a wide range of neurodisabilities, but an increasing body of recent data show that a broad spectrum of more subtle difficulties (global delay, behavioural, visuo-spatial and learning difficulties, poor fine-motor co-ordination and attention deficit disorders), in keeping with the diffuse nature of white matter injury, are more prevalent than cerebral palsy. Additional later evaluation is important, as the assessment of cognitive and behavioural outcome is unreliable at two-years. This proposal has two aims: 1) to assess detailed outcomes at two and five-years for children randomised to PROGRAMS; 2) to take advantage of the unique opportunity offered by PROGRAMS to examine the long-term impact of systemic neonatal infection, and its contribution to the total burden of brain injury in a vulnerable population.

title: Transcription regulation of apoptosis by p53 in Chromatin.
description: Transcriptional Regulation of Apoptosis by p53 in Chromatin All cells are exposed to potentially lethal stresses, both from the environment in which they reside and from the byproducts of metabolism. These stresses are capable of inducing irreversible cellular damage. In higher eukaryotes a defense mechanism has evolved which serves to eliminate these irreversibly damaged cells through an efficient cellular suicide programme known as apoptosis. Conditions under which control of apoptosis are lost lead to disease. At the hub of this defense strategy is the tumour suppressor protein, p53. p53 is activated in response to a variety of cellular insults and mediates a series of outcomes designed to limit the severity of the threat that the damaged cell poses to the organism. Although p53 is known to have multiple roles in response to stress, the best studied (although not best understood) function is that of p53 as a sequence specific transcription factor. P53 binding sites are found in the regulatory regions of a number of key genes that encode members of the machinery used to execute the cell killing programme. Transcriptional activation of these pro-apoptotic targets is essential for the cell to mount a complete stress response. Although it is clear that p53 is required for the activation of pro-apoptotic genes, the mechanisms by which it accomplishes this are unknown. Interestingly, not all p53 targets seem to be regulated by the same mechanism. A number of cofactors have been identified which allow p53 to selectively activate pro-apoptotic genes, whilst ignoring genes involved in other processes. The molecular basis for this discrimination remains unclear. Furthermore, how p53 navigates and manipulates the chromatin environment of its natural pro-apoptotic target genes has not been addressed.

title: Psychological impact of screening for diabetes.
description: Type 2 diabetes fulfils many of the criteria for screening and is currently under consideration by the National Screening Committee. A trial of the effectiveness of screening for diabetes with intensive treatment of screen- detected cases is under way in 28 Eastern Region primary care teams (the Addition study). The trial provides a unique opportunity to obtain comprehensive information on the psychological impact of diabetes screening. The proposed study will use postal questionnaires to track changes in anxiety, depression and related measures in the short term (3 months) and longer term (12 months) among those invited to participate in diabetes screening (N = 2,500) and in unscreened controls (N = 500). This will enable comparisons to be made between the main groups generated by the screening process: those diagnosed with diabetes; those found not to have diabetes after one, two or three tests; and non-attenders. An additional aim of the study is to estimate the degree to which those who receive a negative screening result are falsely reassured by this information. The findings will inform policy decisions about national screening for Type 2 diabetes and will also contribute to the wider literature on the psychological effects of screening and testing.

title: RCT of Individual Placement and Support (IPS) to improve the occupational outcomes for people with severe mental illness in South London.
description: 1\. This proposal offers people in South London who have severe mental health problems the best proven method of assisting them to find paid employment. The project also carefully evaluates such an intervention's associated costs and outcomes. As a partnership between an experienced non-governmental organisation in this field (Status Employment) and a research centre with the relevant expertise (the Institute of Psychiatry, King's College London), this proposal investigates the cost-effectiveness of this intervention using a randomised controlled trial design. The aim of the project is to establish if individual placement and support is more cost-effective than traditional vocational rehabilitation. The hypotheses to be tested over the three years of this project (comparing an individual placement and support scheme with traditional sheltered occupational schemes) are as follows. After the intervention, individuals in the experimental group, compared with those in the control group, will: be more likely to work be more likely to be working competitively be working significantly more hours each week earn a significantly higher net income make significantly greater (net) contributions to the national economy have a significantly higher quality of life in the domains of work, finance, leisure and social life have more of their needs met.

title: Activity induced functional and structural modification of the Xenopus retinotectal synapses.
description: In the developing visual system, the spatiotemporal patterns of visual inputs play an important role in shaping the connections of developing circuits. Using the developing retinotectal system of Xenopus tadpoles and a combination of in vivo whole cell recording and optical imaging techniques the experience dependent refinement of visual circuits at the cellular level will be examined. In particular I will examine the potential link between activity dependent persistent synaptic modifications, known as long term potentiation/depression (LTP/LTD) and the developmental refinement of visual circuits. I will determine the role of coincidence-based and spike-timing dependent plasticity in the activity-induced refinement of retinotectal connections. I will also examine the effects of visual experience-evoked activity on retinotectal synapses and on the development of the retinotopic map and receptive field properties. These in vivo studies provide unique opportunities to address several fundamental issues concerning the instructive function of sensory inputs in the refinement of developing neural connections, and are likely to yield new information relevant to our basic understanding of physiology and pathology of the nervous system.

title: The attribution of intentions and emotion in Autism and Asperger Syndrome.
description: WT Studentship Project title: The attribution of intentions and emotion in Autism and Asperger Syndrome. This project is concerned with what is known as 'theory of mind' \- our ability to attribute mental states, such as emotions, beliefs and intentions, to ourselves and others. This ability is particularly relevant in the study of autism - a pervasive developmental disorder which causes severe impairment in social cognition and communication skills. Autistic individuals are impaired in their theory of mind, and it may be this that underlies their social impairment. We can attribute mental states, or 'mentalise', using a variety of different cues, including cues from speech, facial expressions, gestures and movement. This study will focus on our ability to use movement patterns to infer mental states. The movement of individuals, either on their own or in interaction with others, is a powerful indicator of their state of mind. We can even attribute mental states to simple geometric shapes, if these shapes move and interact in a way which suggests that they are living, behaving individuals. The crucial factor here is the type of motion involved - if a shape moves in a self-propelled manner, it is perceived as having some degree of agency, and as 'experiencing' mental states.

title: An investigation of cellular mechanisms in cerebellum-dependent learning.
description: An investigation of cellular mechanisms in cerebellum-dependent learning How does the brain encode and store information to control behaviour through learning and memory processes? In vitro work suggests potential synaptic mechanisms but do they underpin the formation of real memories in vivo? An optimal approach is to characterise the activity of a real network of neurons with an essential role in the formation and storage of a memory. The cerebellum has a well-characterised neuronal network architecture and a ubiquitous influence upon behaviour. Classical conditioning of the eyeblink and nictitating membrane response (NMR) is critically dependent upon an identified cerebellar network that is best characterised in rabbits. We will analyse how this network operates to learn and control this representative example of associative learning. The leading candidate mechanism for cerebellar learning is long-term depression (LTD) of the parallel fibre to Purkinje cell synapse (pf-LTD), whose cellular and molecular mechanisms have been characterised in vitro. We will manipulate candidate mechanisms during behavioural learning to demonstrate which are necessary. We will focus on the role of metabotropic glutamate receptor 1 (mGluR1) that is predominant in cerebellar cortical Purkinje cells and essential for the induction of pf-LTD.

title: The involvement of D-Serine metabolism in central NMDA receptor expression and schizophrenia.
description: The involvement of D-serine metabolism in central NMDA receptor expression and schizophrenia To test the hypothesis that D-amino acid oxidase (DAAO) and serine racemase (SR) are involved in central NMDA receptor gene expression, cognition, and schizophrenia. This will be achieved by: 1) directly examining DAAO and SR gene expression in post mortem neural tissue from schizophrenia and control subjects. 2) inhibiting DAAO and SR gene expression in vitro and in vivo, using novel RNA-interference technology, and evaluating gene expression and behavioural parameters.

title: An fMRI and behavioural investigation of the paradoxical effects of early antidepressant drug treatment.
description: An fMRI and behavioural investigation of the paradoxical effects of early antidepressant drug treatment Drugs which prevent the reuptake of serotonin or noradrenaline are commonly used in the treatment of depression and anxiety disorders. Paradoxically, anxiety symptoms are often exacerbated early on in treatment, before therapeutic effects emerge after repeated treatment with these antidepressant drugs. Currently it is unknown what mediates this transient increase in anxiety and why therapeutic effects emerge after prolonged treatment. The reversal in action from acute to repeated administration of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) has also been reported in animal models of anxiety. In particular Le-Doux's group recently reported increased fear conditioning following a single dose of the SSRI citalopram, while repeated (21 day) treatment reduced fear conditioning. We have recently developed models of fear processing to explore these effects in healthy volunteers, which can be used to explore whether findings in rodent models translate to humans. In particular, we have found that acute administration of citalopram facilitates the recognition of fearful facial expressions and the fear potentiated startle (FPS), while repeated citalopram administration reduced fear processing in both these measures. These results suggest that facial expression recognition and the FPS are sensitive models in humans to explore the mechanisms of this reversal in the action of SSRIs. The current proposal aims to explore these effects using a number of different approaches including functional MRI, pharmacological challenges with specific receptor antagonists and cognitive task performance.

title: Kinetochore phosphorylation and chromosome bi-orientation in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
description: WT Studentship Project title: Kinetochore phosphorylation and chromosome bi- orientation in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae Yeast Ipl1p is one of the founding members of a conserved family of serine/threonine kinases, aurora kinases, whose members function in chromosome segregation and cytokinesis. Ipl1p forms a complex with Sli15p and Bir1p in S. cerevisiae, which localises to kinetochores during metaphase and then relocalises to the mitotic spindle at the onset of anaphase. The Ipl1p complex plays a key role in chromosome segregation as the chromosomes of ipl1 and sli15 mutants show high levels of mis-segregation. Recently, it was shown that sister centromeres in these mutants frequently attach to microtubules extending from the same spindle pole, although SPB duplication, DNA replication, spindle pole body function, sister chromatid separation and cytokinesis are not affected in these mutants and both sister kinetochores appeared to be fully functional. In cells that cannot replicate their chromosomes, kinetochores can detach from the old SPB and re-orient to the new or old SPB with equal frequency, but in ipl1 or sli15 mutant cells kinetochores remain associated predominantly with the old SPB. This suggests that the Ipl1p-Sli15p complex facilitates bi-orientation by promoting turnover of kinetochore-SPB connections until tension is exerted on sister kinetochores upon bipolar attachment. How does the Ipl1p-Sli15p complex carry out this re-orientation function? The Ipl1p kinase has numerous cellular targets and they include members of the Dam1p complex, Ndc10p and histone H3. One hypothesis is that Ipl1p may phosphorylate Dam1p to destabilise the microtubule-kinetochore interaction, thus allowing re-orientation to take place. The Dam1p complex, a nine-subunit complex that binds to microtubules and is also an integral part of the kinetochore, is required for chromosome segregation and spindle integrity. This proposal seeks to investigate the role of tension as a regulator of Dam1p phosphorylation, to identify factors required to switch off re-orientation once bi-orientation has been achieved and to gain a better understanding of the function of Glc7p in mitosis.

title: Genetic studies of bipolar disorder and recurrent major depression in a large Scottish family.
description: A study of a positional and functional candidate gene for susceptibility to bipolar affective disorder; PI4KIIß The primary aim of the project is to test the hypothesis that PI4KIIß is involved in susceptibility to bipolar affective disorder. My first task will be to characterise PI4KIIß gene and protein expression. I will begin by using lymphoblastoid cell lines from F22 to determine if there is a difference in mRNA and/or protein expression between disease susceptibility haplotype carriers and controls. To do this, allele- specific quantitative RTPCR and Western blotting will be attempted, respectively. This investigation will also determine whether there are different splice forms or protein isoforms of PI4KIIß. There is a previous brief description of PI4KIIß isoforms and if this is confirmed, it will be necessary to further characterise the isoforms experimentally and with bioinformatics tools. I will also investigate interactions of PIK4IIß by immunoprecipitation. This may identify abnormalities in interactions in the F22 disease susceptibility haplotype carriers. My second and parallel approach is to complete bioinformatics and association analyses of the PI4KIIß locus. Prediction of potential regulatory regions will be undertaken using cross species comparison of conserved regions. Depending on the success of the aforementioned experiments it will be important to explore the role of PI4KIIß in neuronal activity. Using immunocytochemistry and immunohistochemistry techniques, I will investigate the cell types that express PI4KIIß and characterise its subcellular localisation. To support my objectives, I have a substantial contingency plan. If future association studies provide strong evidence of another gene in MRII and the initial PI4KIIß studies prove fruitless, then the focus of my project may change to investigating an alternative positional and functional candidate.
