The study outlined above can be applied to any other functional candidate gene. The approach will also be open to constant experimental review with the aim of using up to date technology, bioinformatics and statistical tools to decipher the candidacy of PI4KIIß.

title: Preservation of mental health archives at Dartford Library.
description: No description available

title: Comprehensive cataloguing of the archive of mental healthcare in Cornwall, 19th-20th centuries.
description: Research Resources in Medical History: St Lawrence County Asylum and other sources for the History of Medicine in Cornwall During 2001, the Cornwall Healthcare Trust transferred the archive of St Lawrence's Hospital, Bodmin, formerly the County Lunatic Asylum. The transfer included records from 1820-1983 and comprised the core administrative records (minutes, accounts and reports), patient records (registers of admission, discharge and treatment, and patient case files) and the archives of the hospital farm. Many of the records, apart from the recent deposit of the St Lawrence archive, have basic lists and reference numbers but there is no indexing and the finding-aids are limited to paper catalogues. The St Lawrence archive itself needs a detailed catalogue, but it is not possible for the Record Office to catalogue the records within a reasonable timetable. Cornwall Record Office has now found a way to retro-convert its existing catalogues but has no way of cataloguing St Lawrence. Cornwall Record Office believes that access to the information is of paramount importance and is committed to finding resources for the cataloguing of its healthcare archives. It is proposed to catalogue or retro-convert records to ISAD(G) compliant standards using existing CALM software and adding the resulting data to our website where appropriate. The schedule would be compliant with other authority file and vocabulary control standards. The project will work within Data Protection and other legislative constraints.

title: Psychological mechanisms in suicidal behaviour.
description: Suicidal behaviour is one of the most serious outcomes of psychiatric illness yet finding effective treatments for patients who engage in deliberate self harm (DSH) is hampered both by the heterogeneity of the behaviour and by lack of knowledge about the mechanisms that underlie it. This programme explores the theory that suicidal behaviour arises from a sense of entrapment (arrested flight), brought about not only by hopelessness about the future but also by deficient problem solving. Elucidating these mechanisms is of critical scientific importance in understanding suicidal behaviour, and has major clinical implications for prevention. Our previous research has linked both these vulnerability factors to an underlying deficit (overgenerality) in autobiographical memory. The programme will investigate the hypotheses: (a) that overgenerality in autobiographical memory occurs as the result of the inhibition of image based material in memory; (b) that increases in suicide risk occur when overgeneral memory combines with inability to imagine a positive future to produce a catastrophic escalation of suicidal ideation when activated by negative mood; (b) that this activation process will be shown in unique 'relapse signatures' that predict suicidal ideation and behaviour for each individual; (d) that such activation processes may be reduced by adapting a new treatment (mindfulness-based cognitive therapy) that has been developed to reduce relapse and recurrence in major depression and applying it to suicidal ideation and behaviour.

title: Contribution of Imperial College London Neurosciences to Brain Awareness Week 2003: Events organised for children and young adults to bring them in contact with contemporary brain research at the Science Museum.
description: "Brain Awareness Week" is a worldwide celebration of research into the brain and its diseases. According to its founders (Dana Alliance for the Brain), "it is an opportunity to let people know what is being done to diagnose, treat and prevent disorders of the brain, such as Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, stroke, schizophrenia and depression, which affect the lives of millions of people. Every March, hundreds of public events to inspire interest in brain research are staged as part of Brain Awareness Week, to draw attention to what is being accomplished in scientific laboratories, and provide information about the brain that everyone can understand. Brain Awareness Week is in its sixth year and has become a major international effort to communicate the achievements of brain research". In 2002, scientists involved in brain research at Imperial College London teamed up with the European Dana Alliance and the National Science Museum in South Kensington to arrange a week of presentations and events organised with and by active scientists which ranged from basic neuroscience to clinical medicine. They were intended to demonstrate especially to children and young adults what contemporary neuroscience research can achieve. The week was a great success with approximately 300 visitors attending the practical presentations that were held during Brain Awareness Week for two hours every day. In addition, a plenary lecture was organised which was excellent but attendances suffered from the fact that the day it took place saw extremely bad weather. It is intended to organise another week of events during this Brain Awareness Week in the same setting as last year. In addition, the presentations are planned to be even more practical, which requires somewhat more personnel and equipment. A lecture will not be presented this year as the target audience will be mainly children, young adults and their families.

title: The nature of panic attack - A photographic and physiological journey.
description: The Nature of Panic - A photographic and physiological journey We plan to create an exhibition of photographs and writing about panic attacks. It is a collaboration between Patrick Olszowski, who has suffered from panic attacks for ten years and biomedical journalist Dr Sophie Petit-Zeman. Patrick's photographs focus on the natural world and explore the physical symptoms of an attack and the emotions surrounding them. The photographic matter and title reflect the belief that panic attacks are an inappropriate extension of a natural phenomenom - "fight or flight". Sophie's writing will include an overview of the physiology of panic attacks as well as excerpts from a discussion with Patrick which challenges the misconceptions surrounding the condition. Sophie is a former Wellcome Trust Prize Scholar who has worked with the Trust on educational (with Peter Finegold) and publishing ventures (with Ian Jones). We are determined that the exhibition be accessible, in location and content. We want to hold it in an area where success and panic too often go hand-in-hand and have thus identified a gallery abutting the City of London. We envisage five key target audiences: 1. Business leaders and workers 2. Panic attack sufferers (estimated 9 million in the UK in 1990) 3. Media 4. Medical, mental health and social care professionals 5. Schools & colleges The main objectives include reducing isolation and stigma and increasing understanding of the condition, both in emotional and scientific terms.

title: Co-sponsor of the Mental Health Media Awards 2003.
description: The Mental Health Media Awards recognise the power of the broadcast media in improving understanding of mental health issues and helping the public understand that mental illness is a fundamentally human and commonplace experience and not one to be feared, derided and stigmatised. Each year the public and programme makers are invited to nominate and enter radio and television programmes which challenge misinformation and stereotypes around mental distress. There are seven categories in the Mental Health Media Awards. Entries are passed to a shortlisting panel which meets in August. Shortlisted entries are then passed to the judging panel which meets in October. Judges for the 2002 Awards provided insights from the worlds of broadcast and print media and psychiatry and perspectives of current and former mental health service users. The Mental Health Media Awards are aimed at a number of audiences. For broadcasters, journalists and programme makers, the Awards set a standard for excellence and encourage more balanced and sensitive approaches and productions. For the general public the Awards aim to foster a better understanding of the negative stereotypes and misinformation which exist around mental health problems. Other audiences of the Awards are those whose awareness of positive media portrayals is formed by their direct experience of mental distress. We look to this group not only to nominate programmes they admire, but also hope they will be inspired to take a more active approach to getting involved with broadcast media. We will be aiming to send out entry forms to 2,200 broadcasters and production companies. We will be aiming to send out 13,500 nomination forms mailouts or response request 100 people to nominate via website. Through press coverage before and after last year's event and using estimates used by the PR industry, over 8.1 million people had the opportunity to hear or read about the Awards. We will be aiming to reach this figure again this year.

title: Wellbeing in Asia; Oriental collections in the Wellcome Library.
description: Wellbeing in Asia; Oriental Collections in the Wellcome Library (working title) It is proposed to stage a major exhibition on Asian medicine in the context of the many cultures and peoples of the East in which it has developed over the centuries. The exhibition will be drawn from the Oriental Collections along with western materials from other collections in the library of the Wellcome Trust relevant to Asia supplemented with artefacts from the Wellcome Collections at the Science Museum. It will expose the public for the first time in a major exhibition to the unparalleled riches and scope of the collections relating to Asia preserved in the Wellcome Library. The Oriental Collections preserved in the Wellcome Library are one of the world's major collections and command an international reputation. Unlike other collections preserved in the Wellcome Library, the Oriental Collections are not confined to medical history and related disciplines but include almost every area of human endeavour manifest in the multiple cultures of the East. It is appropriate that they should, since medicine is an integral part of the social history of Asia and deeply influenced by the cultural and religious milieu in which it developed. As such, the Oriental Collections have been described as the "jewel in the crown" of the Wellcome Library, but to date, there has never been a major exhibition devoted to them outside the Wellcome building where they could be brought to a wider public including the ethnic minority communities, a most apposite constituency, as well as to the general public. The Oriental Collections are particularly strong in South Asian materials with 6,000 Sanskrit manuscripts which include some 2,000 manuscripts devoted to the Jain religion, the largest collection outside the sub-continent. Again, the Wellcome Library can boast the largest collections of Hindi and Panjabi manuscripts outside India, unrivalled by our near neighbour the British Library. The Wellcome Library also holds, Arabic, Persian, Burmese, Thai and Chinese and Japanese collections of international significance as well as many smaller collections in some 43 languages which include items of great rarity and antiquity.

title: The ethical framework for intervention research in those at risk of psychosis
description: Meeting: The Ethical Framework for Intervention Research in Those at Risk of Psychosis, University of Manchester, February 7, 2002. Schizophrenia remains a disorder whose causes are poorly understood. It affects about 0.5-1% of the population, usually starts in early adult life and runs a chronic course. It is the third most expensive disorder for the NHS, after stroke and ischaemic heart disease. A recent shift in focus for research and treatment in schizophrenia has been the early stages of the disorder, particularly the first episode. The possibility is that earlier detection and better treatment will improve long term outcomes, with secondary prevention of chronicity, relapse and complications such as forensic outcomes and suicide. Most recently, a newer paradigm has emerged which raises the possibility of primary prevention, or at least very early secondary prevention. "Prodromal" or at risk symptoms can be identified reliably in some help seeking individuals which increase the risk of later psychosis and schizophrenia. These symptoms are in the nature of subclinical psychosis-like symptoms which are too short- lived or mild to meet diagnostic thresholds. Research in the US, Australia and the UK suggests that 25-25% of such operationally- defined will meet criteria for psychosis by one year. The overarching hypothesis is that appropriate intervention in the prodrome will prevent, delay or ameliorate later psychosis and functional and cognitive disability. The workshop will examine data drawn from several perspectives: clinical; psychological; trial design; epidemiology; psychopharmacology; health economics.

title: Bioethics and the brain in the 21st century - Neuroscience, psychiatry and mental health.
description: Meeting: 'Bioethics and the brain in the 21st century - neuroscience, psychiatry and mental health', London School of Economics, University of London. Sunday 21st September, 2003. The social sciences in Europe and the USA are increasingly researching some of the social, moral and legal consequences of the rapidly developing areas in neuroscience, genomics and psychopharmacology. One of the key dimensions of much of this research has been to find ways of engaging with the science critically, without dismissing its very real effects and social benefits. This conference will provide a significant opportunity for academics, from many different disciplines (including sociology, law, anthropology and philosophy), to share findings and theoretical perspectives. It will raise the profile and significance of this area of research, and highlight many of the broader culture issues that the new biotechnologies are raising. The event will establish an international network of researchers in this field, many of whom are working alongside scientists in collaborative research. It will serve as an opportunity for a growing email discussion group to meet in person, and catalyse further links and research ideas. The general themes of the conference will be: To explore how the rapid developments are potentially redefining illness categories The consequences and experiences of new treatments New models of risk, responsibility and governance. Specific topics likely to be represented by panels of speakers include: Bioethics and governance The growing links between psychopharmacology and genomic research Children and childhood (ADHD, autism) Neuroimaging The promise of psychiatric screening Anti-depressants

title: Ethics in Healthcare Practice.
description: Meeting: Ethics in Healthcare Practice, University College Northampton, Autumn 2003 (September - December). There have been suggestions (Tony Blair at the European Bioscience conference in 2000) that there is an anti-science sentiment growing in the UK, which threatens progress both in terms of business and healthcare. The media is rife with stories on 'Dolly the sheep', cloning of humans, growing body parts in 'test tubes', mistakes over IVF treatment and other human health related issues. Healthcare professionals are required by patients and others to answer questions relating to issues in practice relating to ethics perhaps with little or no knowledge of the underpinning science. Another emerging issue for healthcare professionals in the rapidly evolving NHS is the implication of the introduction of novel therapies especially in terms of the possible ethics involved, not only for the patient but also for the healthcare professionals themselves. This seminar will address some of the current ethical issues in the light of recent advancements in science and technology with emphasis on their implication for healthcare professionals as well as the ethics of the use of novel therapies in a practice healthcare setting. It will be targeted at a multiprofessional audience including allied health professionals, clinicians and managers at all levels. Support is requested to enable conference fees to be kept to a minimum to attract a wide audience representative of the professions involved in healthcare practice. Topics to be covered: Historical influences on ethical issues involved in the advancement of healthcare in the 21st century. The application of genomics and ethics - IVF and other reproductive treatments; stem cell research. Ethical dilemmas in healthcare practice regarding novel technologies and treatments, e.g. larva therapy for wounds; compliance with advanced directives in a resuscitation setting; medication compliance in a mental health medicine; use of restraint when working with individuals with challenging behaviour.

title: Innervations communicating neuroscience through dance.
description: Innervations - Communicating Neuroscience through Dance A collaboration between Hampshire Youth Dance Company (HYDC), managed by Hampshire Dance and Dr Matt Cuttle from the Southampton Neuroscience Group will create an innovative and informative dance work inspired by the science of brain cell communication, neurological disorders, and how to prevent them. The members of HYDC, (20 members aged 13 to 20 years) will be introduced to neuroscience research through a series of workshops, seminars, and laboratory visits to a confocal microscopy facility. Dr Matt Cuttle will provide the group with a background in the basic scientific principles of synaptic transmission, learning and memory, the cellular mechanisms underlying epilepsy, stroke, autism, dementia, short-term memory deficits, and the damaging effects of illegal drugs. Each member of the group will then be given the opportunity to experiment with a confocal microscope to produce their own images that will be shown in parallel with the dance performance. The dancers will then work collaboratively with choreographer Lizzie Swinford and a digital/visual artist to create a performance that reflects their response to the science that will also educate the audience in how the brain works. The work created will be premiered at The Point Dance & Arts Centre, Eastleigh. It will be shown at regional community and youth dance platforms and in non-arts locations such as shopping centres. Hampshire Dance will develop educational work to tour to Hampshire, Portsmouth and Southampton secondary schools with supporting information packs and teachers' INSET. The work will also form the basis of an internet performance piece through collaboration with 'Hypervision', a leading 'motion capture' company based in Hampshire. The wide range of outcomes will engage a broad spectrum of the public at local and national levels.

title: The eden project and truro college gm tie partnership.
description: The Eden Project and Truro College GM TIE Partnership Genetic modification (GM) is one of the most controversial issues of our time. For many people it is an area of anxiety, mystification, even fear. Media images of monstrous cross-species hybrids have captured the public imagination, and the commercial practices of some of the companies involved have provoked widespread cynicism, making a cool appraisal of the real issues almost impossible. Although an increasingly large number of the general public insist on a right to be heard, paradoxically there is a low level of public understanding about the science involved, particularly the extension of GM into the biomedical sciences, including pharmaceutical and vaccine production and nutritional enhancement. In Autumn 2002 Eden hosted a Young Peoples Conference for The Agriculture and Environment Bio-technology Commission (AEBC). The Conference concluded that in order to enter into a debate the public needed more information about GM, including perspectives from different sides of the debate but avoiding the tendency of the media to polarise positions. The participants proposed that a Communication, Education and Public Awareness (CEPA) programme was required to increase understanding, followed by feedback to a wide audience, using locations such as Eden for focused debate. The Eden Project intends to collaborate with twelve young Foundation Degree (FdA) in Performance students at Truro College, the Eden Education Team and an experienced creative team of theatre artists to create a performance and associated role-play workshops. This will tour to Year 9 students and subsequently play in repertoire at the Eden Project. The performance and workshops will explore ethical issues of vested interest and public accountability, as well as demystifying some of the science of genetic engineering. Truro College would like to base their entire final year course work around this project forming the basis for all their practical projects, assignments and work experience. Truro College believe that this project would be a tremendous addition to the learning experience of their students involving them in a project that is actual, rather than a case study.

title: Did you miss me.
description: "Did You Miss Me?" "Did You Miss Me?" is a contemporary physical theatre piece aimed at tackling the immense emotional strain placed on sufferers of memory- loss and those around them. 4Front Theatre Company concentrates on combining text with physicality in an experiment to communicate meaning via body and voice. The project is targeted at young and developing audiences and will tour to various schools within the West Midlands and some across the UK. An event at a local theatre has also been prepared to which schools from Coventry and Warwickshire have been invited. 4Front will also be holding workshops with students in order to develop our theatre language and give students the opportunity to explore their own physicality, whilst educating students about the themes surrounding memory-loss. Our production is presented in collaboration with many artists and organisations including: Local Visual Artists - Creating a visual and interactive front of house display. A Web Designer - Creating an online space for our audience to interact and gain further understanding of the issues raised by the production. A Musician - Creating an original soundtrack for our production. "Headway" \- A National Mental Health Charity, that have supported 4Front in their research. 4Front Theatre Company will also be holding a fundraising event for the benefit of Headway. Confronting human emotion, abandoning the stereotypical view of amnesia and exploring this condition, in a sympathetic manner, with a visually and emotionally realistic style, "Did You Miss Me?" combines reality and illusion, thought and feeling with text and physicality.

title: The place where I live.
description: The Place Where I Live Our project would be called "The Place Where I Live". We have approximately 150 people attending our theatre groups and they range from age 5 to 50 and we would like them all to be involved. We have several special needs children and adults and feel that this sort of project would benefit them greatly. We are a team of four employed by Sefton MBC (on a very part time basis), we have a Director, Assistant Director, Writer and a Dance Animator. Our aim would be to encourage discussion amongst all ages on the various subjects: Mental Health, Different Cultures, Cloning, Genetic Testing and Tropical Diseases. We will carry out workshops in-house to find out what subjects interest them most and which they feel most prepared to tackle, depending on their age. We will then arrange for them to perform to other Youth Groups in the North West and local Schools, as well as to take part in the Summer Street Theatre Festival that takes place in Southport every August. We would also like to run workshops for Schools and Youth Groups, incorporating drama, dance and music, the aim being to get them talking, thinking and taking part in the different issues that surround us today. My full time job is as personal assistant to the Director of Public Health for West Lancashire, so these subjects are already discussed on a regular basis within our environment and the Director has agreed to assist with any research we might require. As a Primary Care Trust we have already engaged a group of professional actors to undertake the subject of Mental Health and I am hoping to watch their performance.

title: Hurrysickness.
description: Third Angel is a partnership that utilises a whole range of media in our numerous works to date from scripted theatre to devised performance, projected images originated as film, video, photographic slide or digital image, durational and task based performance, installation, visual art, original music, sound and lighting design. All of these elements are treated by the artists as tools with which to explore their thematic concerns, and are often combined within an individual project: film and video incorporated into a theatre piece; photography, video, environmental design, soundtrack and live performance combined in a gallery installation. This process invites in a further element of scientific expertise, thinking and opinion which will invigorate the working process and thematic concerns of the project. Advances in technology, and developments in what society expects from the work and social time of individuals are having massive effects on the way we live our day to day lives. Simply put, it feels to many people that the days are getting shorter, because we are encouraged to squeeze more activity in, to do more that one thing at once if possible. People feel a constant pressure and anxiety to achieve more with their time. The Hurrysickness project seeks to investigate what the physiological, emotional and psychological effects of this acceleration of society are on the individual.

title: Cognitive Impairment Access and the Built Environment.
description: The nature of this project rests upon the successful integration of three specialist disciplines; Art (video and installation), Architecture and Development Psychology. At the same time these collaborators have each acquired experience and understanding of further subjects including urban planning and design, material technology, advocacy and consultation. They all, in particular, have unique experience and knowledge of severe and complex disability. Between the team there is contact with a wide range of other disciplines and expertise who can both contribute to the discussion and supply precise critical input. The functionality of space, and its appropriateness to its users, is the primary concern of our research. Within the sphere of disability, which may include physical, visual and cognitive impairment, this embraces aspects of physical access which in turn touch upon issues of social inclusion. We regard these as aspects of entitlement within the broader framework of human rights and therefore of an ethical nature. In a society which aspires towards inclusion and pluralism as desirable ends, we would hope that the potential for practical application of any results we may accomplish would likewise have some social and cultural value, and be able to contribute to these issues.

title: Euthanasia.
description: Euthanasia is a subject that affects the core of the medical profession and is an increasingly important social issue. Recent cases of British citizens dying by assited suicide in Switzerland and those fighting for the right to die by euthanasia in the European court have generated significant media attention. Our project is interdisciplinary in nature in that we will actively seek in the first three months a working relationship with professionals and organisations whose work centres around euthanasia. Our research will be into the arguments for and against euthanasia. By entering into dialogue with other disciplines we intend to stimulate debate around the subject matter whilst challenging our own practice. Central to our research will be the quest for a balance between the social and ethical questions that euthanasia raise, and a visual art language.

title: How to live.
description: How to Live is a highly innovative project which has been under development for 4 years and has received research and development funding from the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation as well as a research award from the SCIART Wellcome Trust. The principle idea behind the project is that Bobby Baker will create a whole new "therapy" inspired by her experience of being treated with Dialectical Behaviour Therapy [DBT], a form of Cognitive Behavioural Therapy [CBT]. This work of art developed in collaboration with psychologist Professor Richard Hallam, will explore the principles lying at the heart of CBT/DBT, the concept of teachable skills, and even the very nature of psychology where it is focused on the examination and transformation of the self. The project will also challenge perceptions of mental health and the whole notion of "ordered/disordered" behaviour. A chapter on the research phase up until December 2002 is included in The SCIART Wellcome Trust book Experiment: Conversations in Art Science to be published in September 2003. The public launch of the project will take place at the Barbican Arts Centre, London in the main theatre, on Friday 12th and Saturday 13th November 2004. There will be a large-scale theatrical production performed by Bobby Baker, with spectacular effects, specially commissioned film, and full use of information technology. On the Saturday a symposium, chaired by Marina Warner and hosted by the Barbican Arts Centre Education Department, on The Psychologisation of Society [working title] will take place in the Pit Theatre and other spaces in the Barbican. The public launch of How to Live will be accompanied by a video (available for purchase) illustrating and summarising the ideas behind the project. This video and supporting printed material will also be marketed through specially created interactive web pages on Bobby Baker's Daily Life website. A scaled down version of the launch show will then tour nationally and internationally to a wide range of venues. A workshop version of the project will also be developed for venues including mental health day centres, businesses and educational institutions. In conjunction with Catherine Bailey Productions Ltd., an application will be made to BBC Radio 4 Drama Department for an audio version of How To Live to be broadcast alongside the launch in November 2004. This will follow Baker's three recent successful Radio 4 commissions.

title: Strategic Award: Health, heredity and environment, 1850-2000'
description: This proposal sets out the focused strategies for developing research in the Centre for Medical History at the University of Exeter for five years between October 2003 and 2008. The proposal provides background details of the Centre and its staff, before articulating the main historical themes and the intellectual and administrative strategies which will direct and sustain a series of integrated research initiatives at the Centre. In broad terms, the designated research theme will revolve around changing constructions of the relationships between health, heredity and the environment in the modern period (1850-2000). More particularly, research initiatives will focus on shifting medical and popular conceptions of the relative roles of nature and nurture in the aetiology and pathogenesis of human disease. In the process, one of the Centre's major aims will be to integrate the history of the environment with the history of medicine, thereby developing historical interest in one of the priority funding areas identified by the Wellcome Trust History of Medicine programme. Within this broad framework, specific projects will focus on (i) the history of environmental and occupational respiratory diseases; the history of mental health; the history of gender, sexuality and the family. Plans to develop research in the Centre along these lines not only build on the current expertise and interests of staff in the Centre but also coincide significantly with on-going developments in other disciplines at Exeter, in particular the recently established ESRC Centre for Genomics in Society (EGenIS) and the new Peninsula Medical School, thereby offering genuine opportunities for productive inter-disciplinary collaborations.

title: Value in People
description: Value in People Awards, King's College London (Including GKT Medical School and Institute of Psychiatry) The VIP award initiative is designed to provide a flexible resource to enable recruitment, career progression and retention of staff who are key to the strategic objectives of the university. VIP awards must be used within the broad aims of assisting Universities in the recruitment, career progression and retention of academic and research staff who are key to the implementation of the University's strategic objectives in the area of biomedical science. Provided awards are applied within these parameters, the Trust does not wish to be prescriptive in how they are used. Examples of how these awards could be used include: Assisting in the recruitment of researchers/technologists/lecturers/professors/re-entry scientists by providing bridging funds until a University post is available or a Fellowship application approved. These bridging funds could include modest consumables costs and non-procured equipment but NOT animal costs. Bridging researchers/technologists on fixed-term contracts Bridging newly graduated post-doctoral scientists until a research post is available Providing short- term support for non-biologists who wish to experience working in the biomedical field. Funding staff to attend short training or up-dating courses. The maximum time a specific individual could be supported would normally be 12 months.

title: The medicalisation of maladjustment - the conceptualisation and management of child behavioural problems, 1928-1975.
description: The Medicalisation of Maladjustment: The conceptualisation and management of child behavioural problems, 1928-1975 This study aims to examine the gradual medicalisation of maladjustment in England, from the introduction of the term maladjustment in the context of child guidance in the late 1920s to the emergence of child-centred policies in the mid-1970s. The first section will examine the emergence of child-guidance theories in Britain in the 1920s following the work of individuals such as Cyril Burt, William Healey and William Moodie. It will show how widespread fears of social degeneracy that had manifested around feeblemindedness in the first decades of the twentieth century became increasingly focused on concerns about rising childhood delinquency and maladjustment. Secondly, the study will explore the shifting influences of individual agents on approaches to, and the treatment of, maladjusted children. It will particularly focus on the competition for control between the medical profession and the education authorities, and the effects of changing administrative structures as a result of the Faversham Report of 1939 and the establishment of the National Health Service in 1948, and legislation, such as the Children Act of 1933 and the Education Act of 1944, aimed at shifting responsibilities for problem children throughout the 1930s and 1940s. The third part will focus on the transformation of attitudes to children and childhood in the 1950s and 60s. It will particularly examine changing approaches to childcare established by the seminal work of John Bowlby in 'Child Care and The Growth of Love' (1953), and his emphasis on the significance of the role of the mother and the effects of maternal deprivation on child behaviour. The final section will explore the reclassification of childhood psychiatric disorders, and the development of new models of behavioural problems, such as autism, attention deficit disorder and attachment disorder, during the 1960s and 1970s. Particular focus will be on the delineation between neurotic and conduct disorders, and the impact of changing nomenclature on social policy in the later twentieth century.

title: A prospective population cohort study of post-natal mental disorder in the rural region of Butajira, Ethiopia, to determine prevalence, predictors, natural course and associated adverse outcomes.
description: Post-natal mental disorder (PNMD) is increasingly recognised as a significant public health issue for infants as well as mothers in low-income countries. We will use the Self-Report Questionnaire to study PNMD in a rural community in Ethiopia characterised by high rates of infant malnutrition and mortality. 700 women will be recruited in the final trimester of pregnancy and they and their children followed through until one year post-partum. The study is powered to detect large (policy-relevant) effects of PNMD on infant mortality at one year, but will also allow ante-natal risk factors for PNMD (at 2 months), and effects of PNMD upon infant growth and development to be estimated with more precision than was possible in previous, smaller prospective studies. The Butajira Rural Health Project (three monthly surveillance of all households in a 37,000 catchment area) allows us to identify a representative population sample of pregnant women, and assures that recruitment and follow-up targets are feasible. Assessments will be completed by experienced Butajira Project survey interviewers. Child cognitive and motor development assessments (Bayley Scales) are time consuming and require special training. These will be complicated at one year on children of all those with PNMD at 2 months, and on a similar number of children of mothers without PNMD.

title: The influence of postnatal psychiatric disorder on child development: the role of maternal preoccupation.
description: There is considerable evidence that maternal postnatal psychiatric disorder has an adverse influence on infant development and that, even after remission of the parental disorder, disturbances in the child may well persist. In attempting to examine the pathways of intergenerational transmission, most research has concentrated on maternal behaviours during mother-child interaction. However, researchers have largely ignored the role of maternal cognition, especially the thought and attentional processes, which underlie maternal behaviours. Elucidating these cognitive processes in important: (i) scientifically, to understand the intergenerational transmission of psychological disturbance and (ii) clinically, to develop effective cognitive- based treatments to prevent the transmission of disturbance. We hypothesise that a particular form of maternal cognition, namely 'preoccupation', is a key mechanism in transmission because it interferes with specific aspects of mental functioning, especially attention and responsivity to the environment; and this, in turn, impairs the mother's parenting capacities, adversely affecting mother-child interaction and child development. Preoccupation is defined as a state of narrowed or self-focused attention in which one's mind is dominated by recurrent intrusive thoughts that are difficult to control, difficult to dismiss, and recur even when dismissed. Preoccupation has been shown to have profound effects on both attention and responsiveness to the environment. It is a key component of 3 common postnatal psychiatric disorders: depression, anxiety disorders and eating disorders. The aim of the proposed research is to investigate the influence of preoccupation, as evident in these maternal postnatal psychiatric disorders, on mother-child interaction and child development. Four groups of women and their infants will be studied: three psychiatric groups - mothers with postnatal depression, generalised anxiety disorder (GAD) and eating disorders - and a healthy control group. The programme will be conducted in three phases. In Phases I and II, a series of studies will examine the effects of experimentally activating or deactivating preoccupation on mother-child interaction and on the infant at ages 10-14 months. Phase III will consist of a longitudinal follow-up study to investigate the impact of maternal preoccupation on infant development t 24 months.

title: Costa Rican health aging: longitudinal study of life course changes in survival, health, and living arrangements and their socioeconomic determinants.
description: Costa Rican Healthy Ageing: longitudinal study of life course changes in survival, health, and living arrangements and their socioeconomic determinants The proposed research program is a comprehensive, multidisciplinary investigation of the health consequences of rapid population ageing in Latin America. The centrepiece of the program will be a longitudinal survey representative of the entire Costa Rican elderly population, complemented with a follow-up survey among Mexican elders. The Costa Rican survey incorporates cutting-edge measurement and research topics, including biomarkers of "allostatic load", about which little is known in either Costa Rica or Latin America in general. Specific aims include: (1) To conclusively determine whether Costa Rican elderly longevity and active life expectancy is indeed superior to that of most developed countries. (2) To document differentials across time, regions, and countries in key indicators of health determinants and well-being, in order to generate hypotheses that will help set the future research agenda for these topics in Latin America. (3) To develop and test causal models of the inter-relations between behaviours and constraints across the life course, the availability of and burdens on social support and health systems, and ultimate effects on population health and longevity outcomes. Throughout this agenda the emphasis is on policy-relevant research designed to better target new interventions, as well as to influence debates throughout Latin America concerning appropriate responses to rapid population ageing. The proposed program, which includes an important training component, will consolidate the development of a population research centre of excellence in the University of Costa Rica, as focal point to disseminate population expertise to the Central American region.

title: Mitotic spindle checkpoint and chromosomal instability.
description: The mitotic spindle checkpoint ensures that during mitosis one chromosome of each pair of sister chromatids is segregated to each of the daughter cells. It does this by ensuring bipolar attachment of the kinetochore of each chromatid within a sister-chromatid pair to the mitotic spindle such that a single unattached chromatid can be detected and leads to the generation of a "wait signal" until all chromatids are attached and aligned correctly. Defects in the spindle checkpoint can lead to chromosomal instability (CIN) and cancer. Even though several components of this checkpoint have been identified, the actual mechanism by which the proteins sense attachment of microtubules, their order of action and the exact nature of the "wait signal" remain to be fully clarified. We have recently found that SV40 T antigen specifically interacts with Bub1, a central component of this checkpoint. The interaction of T antigen with Bub1 activates its kinase activity and causes a partial disruption of the spindle checkpoint such that cells can undergo mitosis even in the presence of low levels of spindle damage. Our aim is to dissect biochemically the mechanism by which SV40 T antigen causes this partial abrogation and determine whether this leads to chromosomal instability and oncogenic transformation.

title: Resource for psychoses genomics, Ireland (RPGI).
description: This application is to establish a resource known as the Resource for Psychoses Genomics, Ireland (RPGI). The RPGI will consist of detailed phenotypic information, DNA and cell lines from 1000-1200 subjects with major psychoses. Taken together, these affect 2% (morbid risk) of the population, causing hallucinations and delusions, and abnormalities of thinking, cognition, behaviour and mood. The psychoses are complex genetic disorders with high heritabilities. Linkage research has identified chromosomal regions containing susceptibility genes to schizophrenia, bipolar disorder or common to both. However, individual gene effects are small (or <2) and may risk genes combined with environmental factors lead to illness. Recently, the first few of these genes have been identified indicating a major step towards understanding mental disorders. The aims of the RPGI are to establish a recourse of genotypic and phenotypic information from 1000-1200 subjects with psychotic disorders matched with 2000 general population controls. Previous work by the applicants and other researchers indicates that the Irish population has particular advantages for resource of this type. The RPGI will be statistically powerful and contain more detailed phenotypic information than would be available to any single group. We envisage that the RPGI will be used over the next 10-15 years for i) Confirmation in this sample of an association detected in a users 'private' sample. ii) Exploration of the relationship between phenotype and genotype. iii) Targeted functional candidate gene or gene family studies. This will enable the production of genetic evidence to support biological hypotheses arising from functional array or animal model studies. iv) Screening a region of the genome in a high- density linkage disequilibrium study. One important advance of the design of the RPGI is the return of the genotypic data to the database that in its turn will become a genotypic resource eventually covering the whole genome. v) Gene: gene and gene: environmental interaction studies. vi) Functional investigations of genetic associations using cell lines. In particular, specific variants or combinations of variants identified in silico could be investigated using in vitro cellular assays. Detailed management structures are in place with a business plan to ensure the long term viability of the resource.

title: The mental health of Afghan youth in the wake of conflict and population displacement
description: The project addresses issues relevant to the appraisal of mental health problems and cultural resilience in Afghan youth, affected by war and forced displacement. It focuses on 11-15 year olds living in Afghanistan and Pakistan (across 6 urban/rural areas), aiming for baseline data on 1800 youth and their families, with follow-up study on a sub-sample. The objective is to test relationships between psychosocial problems, coping resources and physiological outcomes. Analyses will relate exposure to traumatic events to mental health problems and biological markers of stress such as cardiovascular and immune function. They will also evaluate whether psychosocial and physiological variables vary according to gender, socio-economic status, education and social support. This is the first study to screen young Afghans for mental health problems in the wake of decades of conflict and unprecedented population displacement. It uses interdisciplinary methods of investigation and a participative approach with local communities and stakeholders in Afghanistan/Pakistan, to develop suitable tools for screening mental health problems, corroborate psychosocial and biological markers of stress, and qualitatively appraise coping behaviours, with a view to recommend suitable strategies for health service provision.

title: Modulation of neuronal activity patterning by electronic coupling in the amygdala.
description: Neuronal patterning and synchrony is thought to underlie the production of coordinated behaviour in response to environmental modification. Electronic coupling via gap junctions may play a vital role in synchronising activity within populations of neurons. The role of gap junctions in development and pathological neuronal activity, such as epilepsy, has been the subject of a substantial body of work, yet investigation into the strategically significant role that gap junctions may play in the coordination of normal synaptic transmission and plasticity ins still in its infancy, and the role that electrontonic coupling may play in adult neuronal communication remains the subject of debate. The amygdale is an area of the medial temporal lobe that is implicated in the acquisition and expression of emotionally related behaviours, particularly affective behaviours associated with fear and anxiety. Production of these behaviours requires the coordination of neuronal activity passing through the amygdale network to the target organs. We have recently demonstrated the presence of electrotonic coupling within the amygdale. This proposal aims to determine the role of gap junctions and electrotonic coupling in intra-amygdala communication pathways. These experiments will reveal significant details regarding the role of gap junctions in the control of adult inter-neuronal communication and how this activity may sculpt pop8ulatin activity patterning.

title: Mortality, physical morbidity and healthcare utilisation rates in offspring of people admitted for psychiatric inpatient treatment: a population-based cohort study using Danish national registers.
description: Recent Scandinavian research has indicated higher infant mortality in offspring of mothers with schizophrenia (Bennedsen et al, 2001; Nilsson et al, 2002). However, there is a lack of population-based evidence for outcome beyond the first year of life, for effects of exposure to disorders other than schizophrenia or to paternal mental illness, or for outcomes other than mortality, namely morbidity and healthcare utilisation. Primarily, the project will estimate mortality, physical morbidity and healthcare utilisation rates in offspring, born during 1973-98 an aged 0-26 years, of people admitted for psychiatric treatment in Denmark. The secondary aim will be to explore variation according to factors such as offspring sex, parental diagnosis and illness severity, timing of first parental admission n(in relation to offspring birth), mental illness in one versus both parents, and separation from biological parent/s. Following linkage of five national registers (general population and births registers, psychiatric admissions, general hospital admissions, cause of death) the data will be analysed as a whole population cohort. A combination of genetic, antenatal and obstetric factors may explain poorer outcomes among exposed infants, compared with abuse, neglect and adverse domestic environments among exposed children, and early onset of mental disorder, substance misuse, and suicidal behaviour among exposed adolescents and young adults. To date none of these hypotheses have been tested empirically. The topic is sparsely covered in the literature and findings will be applicable to the UK and other European countries.

title: Migration, health and mental health in rural Mexico in the context of globalization.
description: The purpose of this multimethod (qualitative and quantitative), descriptive, cross-sectional community-based research project is to identify general wellbeing, health and mental health status as well as patterns of healthcare practices and service use among rural families left behind of male immigrant workers to the US and compare them with household members of non-immigrant men; all living in small villages (less 5,000 people) located in the intersection of three Mexican states (Guerrero, Puebla and Oaxaca) known for the overlapping of two important factors: extreme poverty and their recent incorporation to the labour migration process to the US. The following members of each domestic unit (selected using a stratified, random, proportional to size sample design) will be interviewed: the head of the household, a woman in reproductive age (13-47); care taker of children under 12, and an elderly person 60 and older. The final goals of this study are: 1) To contribute to the growing body of scientific literature on some of the impacts of globalisation (undocumented international migration and poverty) on the rural poor, 2) To design a program to sensitise health professionals and students interested in health services, research and administration - about the health needs of the rural poor, particularly addressing the needs of families left behind of migrant workers to the US, and 3) To make recommendations for the design of health promotion programs and policies aimed at enhancing their health status and generalised wellbeing.

title: Intracellular trafficking of neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.
description: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs) are pentameric neurotransmitter receptors expressed at both the neuromuscular junction (muscle-type nAChRs) and within the central and peripheral nervous system (neuronal nAChRs). Neuronal nAChRs (the focus of this study) exhibit considerable subunit diversity and are important as both excitatory postsynaptic receptors and presynaptic modulators. Neuronal nAChRs mediate the addictive effects of nicotine associated with tobacco smoking and there is increasing evidence for their involvement in a range of neurological disorders such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, epilepsy and schizophrenia. The proposed research will investigate the assembly and trafficking of neuronal nAChRs. Our aim is to investigate how events such as cell-surface expression and receptor targeting to presynaptic and postsynaptic sites is influenced by subunit domains and sequence motifs. A range of molecular and cell biological techniques will be employed which will include heterologous expression of chimeric and mutated nAChR subunits. The proposed research is timely and important because, despite an increasing understanding of the physiological importance of this receptor family, comparatively little is known about assembly and trafficking events which underlie neuronal nAChR diversity. The influence of receptor subunit composition will be examined by heterologous expression of nAChRs from defined combinations of subunits and the influence of subunit domains (and of individual amino acids) by expression of chimeric and mutated subunit cDNAs.

title: Influencing vulnerability to anxiety through modification of biases in cognitive processing.
description: Anxiety disorders are accompanied by biases in attention and interpretation, such that threatening stimuli or meanings are processed in preference to competing benign information. Recent research in which these biases are artificially induced in the laboratory has enabled, for the first time, experimental confirmation of the hypothesis that biased cognitive processes cause and/or increase vulnerability to anxiety. The present proposal aims to explicate the mechanisms whereby cognitive biases influence emotional vulnerability, and maximise the effectiveness of techniques to alleviate anxiety for those at risk. Extending previous research by the applicant, biases in the interpretation of emotionally ambiguous events, induced by methods varying in the extent to which they involve generative or priming processes, will be compared for their capacity to affect later emotional responses. The more effective and enduring induction methods will then be evaluated for their capacity to reduce vulnerability in groups selected on the basis of elevated proneness to anxiety, leading to the development of techniques applicable to anxiety reduction in more naturalistic settings. Finally, results will inform the modification of existing theoretical models of cognitive processing in anxiety, and allow a better understanding of the origins of the cognitive biases associated with this disorder.

title: Risk patterns and processes for affective psychopathology during adolescence.
description: Adolescence is a key developmental period during which major affective psychopathology emerges. First episode major depressions that arise during this time period carry significant risks for recurrence and social impairment through into adult life. We know little about the pre-adolescent processes, genetic or environmental, that promote psychiatric disorder over the adolescent period. No studies have determined how patterns of earlier adverse factors are influenced by developmental factors within the adolescent. The work proposed in this application is a standard longitudinal cohort design to determine how patterns of risk processes predict the evolving nature of affective psychopathology in post-pubertal adolescents (n=1400) through the age period 13 to 18. Within this we will undertake an embedded experimental procedure to characterise the nature of affective-cognitive vulnerabilities for psychopathology. These 2 investigations will incorporate new techniques and approaches that have only become available within the last few years. The first will measure genetic polymorphisms and early childhood adversities, determine their risk potency over time and in the presence of a changing proximal psychoendocrine environment. The second will use an embedded experimental design on a sub sample (n=320) of 16 year old participants to determine if general vulnerability characteristics (serotonin transporter polymorphism and/or early adversity) are the primary determinants of individual differences mood activation, emotional response and related cognitive sensitivity and performance. The general objective is to understand how far these factors contribute individually to patterns of risk processes, how they interact and influence the formation of psychopathology. Identifying the contribution and potency of these liabilities over time has implications both for understanding causative mechanisms and for developing intervention strategies to forestall emerging mental disorders, some of which are known to carry considerable morbidity and mortality into adult life. The two studies are thus highly complementary.

title: Psychophysiological mechanisms underlying psychological and physical morbidity.
description: Psychophysiological mechanisms underlying psychological and physical morbidity My research combines psychophysiology, neuroimaging and patient studies to examine cerebral autonomic control. My studies implicate specific brain regions in generating and re-mapping autonomic reactions to cognitive, physical and emotional stress: I argued that anterior cingulate cortex is critical for generating autonomic arousal during volitional behaviour, an account that challenges widely-held psychological models of cingulate function. I wish to extend this research in studies of healthy control subjects, neurological and psychiatric patients. First, I will use behavioural psychophysiology to describe adaptive and pathological autonomic response patterns to emotional challenges. Second, using functional neuroimaging (fMRI), I will define emotional brain mechanisms for normal autonomic control and, in specific conditions, underlying maladaptive generation and re- representation of autonomic responses. In selected patient groups (e.g., familial autonomic conditions, e.g. syncope), abnormalities in brain morphology and regional neural integrity will also be explored using morphometric and spectroscopic MR to provide insights into the pathoaetiological basis of abnormal emotion/autonomic interactions. Where appropriate, patients with focal brain lesions will be studied to validate psychophysiological and neuroimaging inferences. Importantly, specific efferent autonomic axes may preferentially express emotional stress. I will examine patients with emotional fainting (neurocardiogenic syncope), sweating (essential hyperhydrosis) and cardiovascular dysautonomia (tachycardia and arrhythmia) to dissect mechanisms for emotional modulation of (respectively) vagal, sympathetic cholinergic and cardiac noradrenergic pathways. Similarly, afferent axes of interoceptive information may differentially contribute to emotional feelings and symptom expression. I will examine patients with cord transection, vagotomy and implanted vagal nerve simulators to dissociate spinal versus vagal mapping of bodily responses and their influences on emotional processes. These investigations will inform parallel psychophysiological and neuroimaging studies of patients with anxiety and panic disorders to address pathological mechanisms of symptom generation. This research programme combines behavioural, neuroimaging and clinical investigations to address questions fundamental to theoretical and basic neuroscience while increasing knowledge regarding symptom expression in somatic and psychological pathology.

title: The molecular cell biology of prolyl oligopeptidase and the causes of lithium sensitivity.
description: Bipolar mood disorder (manic-depression is a common mental illness of major significance for public health. Lithium is the most common treatment for this disorder and offers long-term prophylaxis. However it has associated problems, and there is a need for more potent and specific drugs. The barrier to better design of drugs is our lack of understanding of the molecular origin(s) of bipolar disorder or the therapeutic mechanism of lithium action. There is a significant genetic predisposition for bipolar disorder, but no genes have been isolated. As an alternative genetic approach, we raised lithium resistant mutants in Dictyostelium. We discovered that loss of the enzyme Prolyl oligopeptidase (PO) confers resistance to both lithium and a second mood stabilizer, valproic acid (VPA). Loss of PO elevates the basal concentration of the intracellular signal molecule InsP3, whereas lithium and VPA lowers InsP3. Further studies revealed an unexpected and novel regulatory mechanism where PO activity negatively regulates the cellular Inositol phosphate (InsP) content. We established that this reciprocal relationship exists in neurons, and inhibition of PO activity reverses the effect of the three common mood stabilizers, lithium, VPA and carbamazepine. This suggests that PO and these mood stabilizers converge on a common InsP mediated target pathway. Remarkably, altered PO activity has been associated with bipolar mood disorder and we find that patients with bipolar disorder have significantly lower PO activity. This suggests that lowered PO activity could lead to abnormal InsP meteabolism in bipolar disorder patients and provide a rationale for treatment with lithium and other mood stabilizers. We will now examine how lithium treatment alters Dictyostelium cell behaviour and how Dictyostelium PO (DpoA) modulates InsP metabolism to adjust lithium sensitivity. We have previously shown that lithium effects cell aggregation during early development. We will carry out detailed studies on the chemotactic behaviour of cells treated with lithium or those lacking dpoA and other genes involved in lithium sensitivity. We have also shown that DpoA regulates expression of the inositol synthesis (inol) gene. We will use molecular genetic and biochemical techniques to investigate the role of DpoA and InsP in the regulation gene. Finally, we will carry out an extensive genetic screen for lithium resistant and hypersensitive mutants to identify missing components of the DpoA pathway. Through this study, we aim to produce a conceptual framework to focus future experiments in neural systems and propose candidate genes for clinical genetics and drug studies.

title: The role of polymorphic gene duplication and deletion in complex disorders.
description: It has been shown that 5% of the human genome sequence consists of low copy number repeats (LCRs) where segments of chromosomes of a range of sizes are duplicated in all individuals. There is also a growing number of disorders caused by duplication or deletion of a specific gene or chromosome region which occur in a small number of people. In between those extremes there are a number of published examples of polymorphic sequence duplication involving entire genes, including several which have phenotypic consequences, notably SNCA in Parkinson's and a number of genes in bi-polar disorder. We have recently studied over 700 genes and discovered that sequences from 54 of them are duplicated in what appears to be a polymorphic manner and the duplications do not appear in the published human genome. This has led us to the hypothesis that polymorphic changes to gene copy number are more common than previously envisaged and many such rearrangements may be involved in complex disorders, and may also play a role in human variation. We have developed a novel, very accurate method of studying changes to gene copy number and using our large DNA and RNA resources from patients suffering from schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, Alzheimer's etc., and extensive bio-informatic resources, we intend to study the nature of this phenomenon looking at the frequency and heritability of duplication of the genes mentioned above, the size of the sequences involved, and the functional effect of duplication on gene expression.

title: Health status, well-being and population change in the Middle East: a research network approach.
description: This application seeks funding for a program of research on the health and wellbeing of women and their newborns, the elderly and adolescents in the Middle East. Unified by the research interests of the Centre for Research on Population and Health (AUB Faculty of Health Sciences) we are proposing (i) three interconnected social intervention studies set in a poor "suburb" of Beirut, (ii) a series of regional studies on the medical practices, policy and determinants of childbirth and post-partum care; and (iii) funding for strengthening the infrastructure of a research network to build capacity for population and public health research in the Middle East region. The proposed research will be carried out by a team of researchers, led by Dr Huda Zurayk, at AUB in collaboration with scholars from Egypt, Syria and Palestine directly involved in one element of the research program (i.e. childbirth). Scholars from other Arab countries will participate in and benefit from the consolidation of the CRPH's role as a centre of excellence in research and a focus for academic work aiming to investigate population and health linkages and to test interventions to improve health and wellbeing in the region.

title: Examining the role of the Nek6, Nek7 and Nek9 protein kinases in cell cycle progression and spindle assembly in Xenopus laevis.
description: Cell cycle progression and mitotic spindle assembly depend upon the regulatory action of protein kinases, including Cdks, Aurora kinases, Polo-like kinases and NIMA-related kinases. Fungi contain one NIMA-related kinase that serves multiple roles in cell cycle control. In contrast, vertebrates have multiple NIMA-related kinases, or Neks, which may have more restricted functions in the cell cycle. Previously, we have characterized in detail the regulation and function of the Nek2 protein kinase revealing a role in centrosome regulation. Recently, three other members of this family, Nek6, Nek7 and Nek9, have been implicated in a mitotic regulatory cascade with Nek9 upstream of Nek6 and Nek7. However, the mechanism of action of these kinases in mitosis is not understood. The goal of this research project is to examine the function of these kinases using Xenopus laevis as a model system. Cell-free assays for cell cycle progression, microtubule aster formation and bipolar spindle assembly will be performed in cytoplasmic egg extracts depleted of and reconstituted with individual Nek proteins. In parallel, a proteomic screen for regulators of Nek9 and yeast two-hybrid screens for targets of Nek6 and Nek7 will be performed. Finally, we will examine the expression of these enzymes in human cancer cells. Thus, we aim to define how these kinases participate in the segregation of chromosomes during mitosis and whether their deregulation may contribute to the disease state.

title: Developmental origins of the 'social brain'.
description: One of the major debates in cognitive neuroscience concerns the origins of the "social brain" in humans. The understanding of other people's behaviour, often defined as "Theory of Mind", has been associated with various neural structures (i.e. the amygdale and the temporal pole, the superior temporal gyrus, and the temporal paraietal junction); the neural activity in these regions may reflect different aspects of mental state like understanding of emotions, internationality and of biological motions or actions (Frith, 2001). Nevertheless, although these aspects have precursors in infancy, very little is known about the neural bases of the social brain and its development. For example is there a region-by-region maturation of components of the system, or does the network - develop in terms of increasingly structured interactions between the network of regions involved? I intend to explore this issue through the analysis of the neural correlates of one basic aspect of social cognition, namely "eye gaze processing". The ability to detect gaze direction of another's face is thought to be particularly important in guiding social interactions, and also emerges early in ontogeny (see Farroni ete al., 203 for review). Comprehending the communicative intent of the others begins with understanding their eye gaze behaviour (which, in turn, requires face perception skills) from birth. Recently, Farroni et al., (2002) have shown that even newborns preferentially look toward faces with direct gaze, engaging them in mutual eye contact. This finding reinforces the view that emphasizes the importance of eye gaze perception for successful social development (Kleinke, 1986). However considerable controversy remains with regard to whether the perception of eye gaze is a perceptual skill acquired through experience, or due to innate mechanisms. This controversy is also relevant to the proposal that deficits in eye-gaze perception may be symptomatic of, or even cause, autism (Klin et al. 1999). The primary overall aim of this program is to characterise the typical and atypical trajectory of human functional brain development over the very first period of life in the domain of social cognition. I plan experiments to investigate the early precursors of adult social abilities and their neural bases. I will use converging behavioural (looking time), electrophysiological (ERP), and optical imaging (NIRS) techniques to examine these precursor abilities in typical and atypical populations.

title: 'Bridging the Gap'- The inaugral conference of international mental health at the IoP.
description: 'Bridging the Gap' \- The inaugural conference of International Mental Health at the IoP (26th-27th July) to be followed by workshop on 28th July Given the involvement in our inaugural conference of the executive group of IMH and the additional overseas speakers, we can guarantee a truly international level of participation. As well as the presentations that they shall make in the conference, we will hold two more informal workshops to which they can contribute their insights and experience. We aim to hone our research agenda, increasing its policy relevance, to maximise the scope and value of our projects through broader multidisciplinary input, and to concentrate our methodological and administrative skills. The workshops, held annually on the occasion of our conference, will make a key contribution to this process. Workshop 1 The executive group of IMH is asked to assist our researchers a) in developing a research agenda with strong regional and international policy relevance, and b) in identifying opportunities to further this research agenda. It is proposed that our first meeting will consider the health impacts of migration in developing countries particularly for younger and older people. Mental health status has been considered in crude terms as an outcome, but is more likely to be subtly implicated in complex interrelationships at every stage of the process (including for example the decision to migrate). Executive group members will be asked to prepare discussion papers in advance (from their regional perspective). IoP researchers with an interest in this area will present their study designs. The opportunity will be used to consider methodological issues and propose research questions and study designs. Workshop 2 This workshop, open to all IMH members will consider the topic of research dissemination, a) hearing examples of good practice (e.g. the 'Young Lives' Project, and the Sangath Society in Goa), b) receiving presentations on conducting policy reviews, drafting press releases and policy briefings, and organising local workshops for stakeholders, and c) hearing directly from policymakers and media correspondents.

title: Towards the posthuman condition - Artists, scientists and young people unravel the aesthetics, ethics and future of biosciences.
description: Towards The Posthuman Condition A science and art season featuring a host of innovative activities including an exhibition, symposium and workshops as part of the Edinburgh International Science Festival. It brings together artists, scientists and young people who are passionate about the aesthetics, ethics and future of biosciences. Together they define the posthuman condition and trace the creative impact of the science of genetics on contemporary art and culture. The season will bring to Edinburgh widely acclaimed artworks not seen in Scotland and authored by teams of Scottish artists and scientists. Alongside the exhibition, the season will offer a symposium to debate the issues raised by similar collaborative practices nationally and internationally, as well as creative workshops for young people from ethnic community groups. We will engage with over 10,000 people from well-seasoned audiences to newcomers from diverse backgrounds, with a range of high-quality events, providing insights into creativity, health and wellbeing. Towards The Posthuman Condition represents an alliance of co-producers within the most appropriate context of the Edinburgh International Science Festival. The season will pave the ground for science and art seasons in Edinburgh on an annual basis.

title: Visualising the mind: images of mental life in science, art and popular culture.
description: Visualising the Mind is an artist's residency project in LSE's BIOS research centre with artist Ruth Maclennan. She will work with BIOS director Professor Nikolas Rose and academic research staff on three linked activities: a) research, creation and exhibition of new artworks on the subject of visualising the mind; b) curation of a group exhibition of contemporary art at LSE on this subject; and c) a series of five public debates exploring changing ideas and representations of the mind: the origins, histories, uses and transformation of images of the mind and brain. The public debate speakers will include scientists, artists, cultural commentators, social scientists, curators, and art historians. The project starts form current scientific advances in imaging, representing, and explaining brain activity. It will examine changing interpretations, speculations and visual representations of how the mind works and what it means. The overall objectives are to raise public awareness of the history of visual interpretations of the mind and the uses to which they have been put, and to promote vigorous engagement and debate on contemporary interpretations of these ideas - in science, art, philosophy, social sciences, the media and politics, and in popular culture. At the same time, the project will explore how art and visual culture describe and influence our understanding of the mind. Key audiences will be students and staff at LSE, the Institute of Psychiatry, and other London institutions; contemporary art audiences; other publics; and the artists, scientists, and others who play an active role in the activities.
recipient: London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE)

title: The molecular and functional effects of Type II metabotropic glutamate receptor (GRM2/3) gene deletion in the mouse brain.
description: The molecular and functional effects of Type II metabotropic glutamate receptor (GRM2/3) gene deletion in the mouse brain To characterise the molecular and functional profiles of GRM2/3 double knockout mice. This will be achieved by the following objectives: 1) Evaluating the expression of genes relevant to glutamate neurotransmission (e.g. glutamate transporters and NMDA receptors) in the brains of GRM2/3 double knockout mice; 2) Measuring long- term potentiation (LTP) and pre-synaptic activity in the hippocampus of experimental animals and controls; 3) Examining spatial working/reference memory, anxiety and locomotion in GRM2/3 double knockout mice and controls.

title: Molecular and behavioural characterisation of mice over-expressing type 1 neuregulin-1.
description: Molecular and behavioural characterisation of mice over-expressing type I neuregulin-1 Neuregulin 1 (NRG1) is a susceptibility gene for schizophrenia, and increased expression of the NRG1 type 1 isoform occurs in the disease. The main aim of this study is to establish the extent to which overexpression of type 1 NRG1 in mice reproduces molecular, morphological, and behavioural features of schizophrenia. The work will also begin to reveal the normal neurobiological functions of type 1 NRG1, which are almost entirely unknown at present. Depending on progress, the project also aims to investigate the phenotype of mice overexpressing type IV NRG1, since this alternation is also associated with NRG1's genetic involvement in schizophrenia.

title: Development and validation of a culturally sensitive measure of Health Related Quality of Life (HRQoL) in neurological disease.
description: While medical advancements have diminished the prevalence of infectious diseases, degenerative and chronic diseases continue to abound with increasing longevity. Most neurological diseases are chronic, and their management is complex, posing a major public health problem for developing nations today. The complexities in the management of neurological illness are multi- dimensional, and psychosocial morbidity is an important contributing factor. Quality of Life (QOL) is a function of the conceptual distance between "how I am now" and "how I would like to be" the gap between actuality and expectation. Each neurological disease has independent and significant factors that influence the quality of life of the patient. For example cognitive decline in dementia has a serious influence on the HRQoL, so a HRQoL scale for dementia should establish their responsiveness to change over time. On the other hand seizure frequency and severity are important predictors of HRQoL in epilepsy; aphasia, impairment of ADL, post-stroke depression important predictors in stroke, items that are sensitive to change, thus necessitating disease specific components to any HRQoL measure that is to be applied in these populations.
