Independent measures of HRQoL have therefore been developed for each of these disorders making comparison across neurological illnesses difficult. In developing countries like India the measurement of HRQoL has not been given adequate importance, not least due to the length of conventional assessment procedures. The felt need for a HRQoL measure that is culturally sensitive, disease specific, comprehensive, brief, and easily administrable has thus increased. The current study aims to develop such an outcome measure with specific relevance to Neurological Disease (Demential, Parkinson's disease, Epilepsy, Stroke, Headache).

title: The Organisation and Neural Basis of Social Cognition: Insights from Frontotemporal Dementia.
description: An understanding of the neural basis of social cognition is important in the understanding of both normal human interaction, as well as for disorders such as dementia, autism and brain injury. In frontotemporal dementia (FTD), a neurodegenerative disorder with marked behavioural disturbance and regional brain atrophy, patients perform poorly in tasks assessing aspects of social cognition. We intend to use this as a natural model of a progressive deterioration in social functioning. Formal evaluation of social cognition is poorly developed. The aims of this study are to delineate the neural basis and relationship of the components of social cognition using the model of FTD; to understand the relationship between structural (MRI) and metabolic (FDG-PET) abnormalities in FTD over time; and the development of a clinically applicable battery to assess social cognition. Ultimately we hope that this will provide a framework for evaluating interventions. We hypothesise that defects in social cognition in FTD consist of various combinations of regional atrophy and hypometabolism in the medial frontal and orbitofrontal areas of the brain. 30 patients will be recruited from a longitudinal study of FTD, and compared to two control groups (Alzheimer's Disease and normal volunteers). They will have MRI and FDG-PET scanning performed in conjunction with a comprehensive neuropsychological test battery. The test battery will involve both standard and newly devised components and assess all three recognised components of social cognition: emotional processing, the Theory of Mind and behavioural regulation. 1. Structure-function relationships will be correlated with Statistical Parametric Mapping (SPM) using voxel based morphometry (VBM) with co-registered PET and MRI images. 2. Progression of atrophy and cognitive deficits over a one year interval will be assessed by means of serial scanning and assessments. 3. These results will be used to validate a clinical test battery, which in turn will be applied to a wider FTD cohort as part of an international collaboration.

title: Mood based delusions and the amygdala: emotional memory, false memory and dopaminergic transmission.
description: Background: Delusions may be described as the essence of madness, yet remain poorly understood. They are an important clinical problem, being central to schizophrenia and a frequent accompaniment of violence in this group. A distinction has been made between mood congruent (MC) and mood incongruent (MI) delusional beliefs in terms of understandability and has diagnostic and prognostic implications. The proposed research aims to develop a cognitive neuroscience model of delusion formation by drawing on neuroanatomical, neuropsychological and neuropharmacological models to test a theory of mood congruent delusion formation. It is proposed that abnormalities in the amygdale and its connections, combined with aberrant dopaminergic transmission contribute to delusional interpretations of emotionally arousing events via defective reality monitoring and emotional enhancement of memory. Hypothesis: (a) MC and MI groups will differ in amygdale activation in response to emotional stimuli and in subsequent recall of such stimuli; (b) MC and MI groups will demonstrate different rates of false recall of emotional words in a false memory paradigm; (c) emotional enhancement of memory in healthy volunteers will be reduced by dopamine blockade. Study design: The project is therefore divided into 3 studies: an fMRI study, a cognitive - false memory (FM) - study, and a neuropharmacological study. 15 MC and 15 MI subjects with detailed clinical information have already been recruited from an ongoing 1st episode psychosis study, matched for age and gender with healthy controls and will be available for the fMRI and FM studies. Patients will be assessed using clinical rating scales for positive and negative symptoms of psychosis. In the fMRI study, amygdale activity in response to positive, negative and neutral pictures taken from a standardised and validated set will be compared across groups and correlated with subsequent recognition at 1 week. The study will provide the first step towards an integrated physiological and cognitive model of delusions and will lead naturally to further work and possibly therapeutic interventions.

title: Psychological status of adolescent migrants from Three Gorges to Zhejiang Province China.
description: Built across the Yangtze River in China, the Three Gorges Project is the world's largest hydropower scheme. As a consequence, 1.2 million people have had to be resettled. There is an urgent need for epidemiological research to quantify the impact, not only for resettled populations but also for future migrants, since another large wave of resettlement is planned for 2006-2009. The impact of migration on mental health has been investigated in other populations, but there are unique aspects of the Three Gorges Programme : i) Migration has resulted from a legal imposition rather than conflict, on a voluntary basis or from economic necessity; ii) Migration has occurred at a community (village) rather than individual/family level; iii) Although the resettlement is substantially supported by central and local government and by host communities, and although all migrants were given a choice of destinations in similar settings, the distances involved are substantial (1700 km to Zhejiang), and do not allow migrants to maintain any connection with their region of origin. 9103 Three Gorges Migrants were resettled in Zhejiang Province between 2000-2003. Adolescence is a period of particular sensitivity to stress. It is a key developmental phase in which adult personalities, lifestyles and health behaviours begin to emerge, and in which vulnerability to adult mental disorders first becomes apparent. In a recent epidemiological study of psychiatric morbidity supervised by the applicant in the Zhejiang indigenous population, depression, anxiety and alcohol use disorders were the most common conditions. Smoking is also likely to be prevalent, but other substance use is predicted to be rare. There is little information on adolescent sexual health and behaviour. The proposed project will focus on the prevalence and correlates of these outcomes in adolescent migrants, and in their indigenous peers. The project would address the impact of this particular forced migration upon adolescent mental health, health behaviours and social development. In addition to the focus upon migration, this would be one of the first studies in China of adolescent health and behaviour in the context of rapid economic and social change.

title: Felix Post - a biographical study.
description: Old age psychiatry in England is recognised as being pioneering and leading the world in the development of services for older mentally ill adults. Felix Post (1913-2001) was probably the first doctor ever to practice in old age psychiatry. Both his academic writings and his influence on a generation of doctors at the Maudsley Hospital have had a profound influence on the development of the specialty of old age psychiatry. From the historical perspective, the development of old age psychiatry has hardly been researched. This project aims to investigate the life of Felix Post and his contribution to the development of the specialty of old age psychiatry. The work needs to be undertaken urgently whilst there is still the opportunity for an oral history approach.
recipient: North West London Hospitals NHS Trust

title: An Historical and Epidemiological Analysis of the Medical Examinations of the Colonial Office from 1898-1919.
description: The London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine (LSHTM) has within its archives approximately 12,000 mandatory medical examinations conducted between 1898 and 1919 for men and women seeking employment in the British Colonial Service and for those returning after leave. The Colonial Service administered all the Empire's colonies with the exception of India, Egypt, and the Sudan. Patrick Manson, the founder of LSHTM, was appointed as Colonial Office medical advisor in 1897 and was responsible for most of the examinations until his retirement in 1912. (Haynes 2001). This research project will use this source to analyse patterns of chronic and infectious disease, physical impairment, mental health, alcohol use, reasons for rejection, and familial health as they related to the demographics of the colonial candidate population. Analysis of the group will be used to contribute to the understanding of the British Colonial Service; to the career of Manson and to the interests in medicine and colonialism. The data will also be assessed against wider debates in health, for example that on height and standards of living. The changes in the form and the information required also give an insight into the concerns of turn of the century empire. (Arnold, 1993, Floud et al, 1990). Around the turn of the twentieth century, the demand for overseas civil servants to staff the new territories grew as Britain increased its West African territories (Kirk- Greene, 1999). People entered the Colonial Service as a chance to gain professional status in the colonies not possible at home, in fields that included medicine, education, law, the railways, civil engineering, agriculture, forestry, nursing, public works, and district administration. Both Manson and Joseph Chamberlain, the Secretary of State for the Colonial Office, believed in constructive imperialism, the concept of building strong colonies by sending qualified and health candidates from Britain to build and manage them. The types and volume of questions on the exam forms reflect the need to find healthy candidates.
recipient: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine

title: A Translation and Commentary of Galen, On the Mixtures and Powers of Simple Medicines, books 1 and 5.
description: A translation and Commentary of Galen, On the Mixtures and Powers of Simple Medicines, books 1 and 5 The project is on Galen's nutrition, dietetics and pharmacology. The aim is to bring together the applicant, who is working on the nutritional and dietetic treatise On the Powers of Foods and the Research Assistant, who will work on On the Mixtures and Powers of Simple Medicines ['Simples']. The Research Assistant will assess the major manuscripts of her treatise and will write a translation and commentary of books one and five. This will make available in a modern language for the first time one of Galen's most used treatises. A full translation will be produced in a separate volume. This second volume will be invaluable for those working on Galen and on the later medical tradition and in contemporary Complementary Medicine. The translation and commentary volume meanwhile will make a major contribution to Galenic studies. It studies in depth two of the methodological books of the treatise and will focus in particular on the manuscripts; on Galen's research questions; on his treatment of earlier pharmacological work in medical and other texts; on the relationship of Simples to other Galenic works such as Mixtures; and in particular to On the Powers of Foods. Both treatises share an interest in the actions of foods and drugs on the body and problems of identifying general properties in relation to the condition of a particular patient. There are also major methodological questions of how to order a large body of material according to coherent categories. The project marks an important development in the study of Galen in the Centre for Hellenistic and Romano-Greek Studies in Exeter. Running alongside this work on nutrition and pharmacology, Professor Christopher Gill is writing a book on Galen's psychology and we are organising a conference on Galen's contribution to the intellectual world of the second century AD in 2005.

title: The Maudsley and the Construction of Mental Illness: a history 1916-1948.
description: There are comparatively few studies of psychiatric institutions in the twentieth century and few historical investigations of clinical procedures and outcomes. Using patient records and related management files, this historical study of the Maudsley Hospital and Central Pathological Laboratory will investigate to what extent their ideas and practices served to change the boundaries of mental illness for patients and career psychiatrists. Mapother, Golla, Lewis and their colleagues sought to replace traditional 'moral' approaches by medical models and to establish a physiological basis of mental illness. It is important to ask why they set this agenda, to what extent they achieved these goals and to question the claim that the Maudsley pioneered a novel way of thinking about mental illness. This involves assessing the originality, methodology and impact factor of the institution's publications. Patient records and internal hospital reports will be researched to discover whether new clinical interventions had an impact on lengths of stay, symptoms or physical function. This data will tell us the socio-economic backgrounds of patients, the diagnostic groups targeted and outcomes. In interpreting these results, the Maudsley's individual admissions policy of accepting only voluntary patients has to be acknowledged. The study will also explore how receptive the hospital was to different interpretations of mental illness and to developments in treatment pioneered at other institutions. It is recognised that the identification, classification and treatment of mental illness were conditioned by prevailing models of health and scientific understanding, together with the societal demands, rights and duties places on both doctors and patients. Was, for example, mental illness framed in ways that made it difficult to devise novel therapies? The Maudsley is proposed for study because of its claim to have broken the mould of the asylums in terms of the management and treatment of patients and to have raised the academic status of the discipline to equate with other areas of medicine. This investigation is designed to provide a window on the cultural role of the hospital, to explore the ideas held about the institution, its methods, together with the values and philosophy that drove its strategic development.

title: Conference entitled 'Health in the 'unhealthy' enclaves. Health and Medicine in the Princely States of India' to be held at the University of Southampton, 8-10 July 2005.
description: 'Health in the "unhealthy" enclaves. Health and Medicine in the Princely States of India' Research into the history of medicine in the Princely States is a newly emerging field, as most earlier research on the history of medicine in India has focused on the areas under British colonial rule. The conference panel intends to get together scholars who have started to examine the special issues affecting the development of medicine and health care in these hitherto unresearched areas. It is expected that insights derived from this research will affect also the ways in which we look at colonial medicine in general, which has been a flourishing subject area during the last decade. The following topics will be covered: 'Maternal and infant health in Mysore and Madras' 'Public Health in Mysore' 'Mental Health in Mysore' '"Contributing to the war machine": The First World War and the health of the colonial soldier in the Punjab Princely States' 'Social reform, health and gender in early twentieth-century Bhopal' 'The development of health services in Princely Orissa, 1850-1920' 'The economics of health in Princely Kashmir'

title: 'Insanity and Institutions: comparisons and contrasts' meeting to be held at the University of Limerick, Ireland in April 2005.
description: 'Insanity and Institutions' comparisons and contrasts' The history of psychiatry and allied disciplines are attracting considerable critical attention in Ireland and elsewhere. At the University of Limerick, there is a growing interest in developing the field, and the planned symposium offers an opportunity to draw together individuals working in a variety of medical histories, with scholars from outside the institution. The comparative dimension for the Irish and Scottish cases (still at a relatively early stage of research) is most important, so speakers from Britain and Canada have been invited to offer an international perspective on aspects of psychiatric history. Where possible, speakers have been 'paired' in order to offer points for comparison between countries. For example, Gayle Davis will offer a paper on venereal disease and general paralysis of the insane in Britain, which will be scheduled with Susannah Riordan's presentation on the treatment of soldiers in the Irish army suffering from the same disease; Jonathan Andrews will speak on the topic of the criminally insane in England, a paper that will offer points of comparison with Stuart McKenzie's work on the insane in Scottish prisons. Other topics include: the process of institutionalisation; the importance of W.A.F. Browne in the development of Scottish psychiatry; nursing and the insane, and the process of incarceration in Canada and Ireland.

title: Research on non-commercial factors of development of health care systems, especially in developing countries.
description: In the 20th century the important features of health care systems were their commercialisation and financial limitations. For that reason, the activity of charity organizations and charity trusts in the field of health care is worth of examining. From the Polish point of view three kinds of motivation for charity could be distinguished in the last century: membership to Masonic lodge, religion beliefs, and searching of proper female role in society, which was characteristic for some women's organizations at the turn of the century. The each of these kinds of motivation influenced on health care systems in different way. The Freemason's impact on medicine, especially on psychiatric hospitals, is a little recognized in Poland and carrying out research on archives in London (the British Masonic lodges had international links with many European countries, e.g. Poland) could be significant for better understanding this issue. The different commitment to health care was connected with religion belief. After tens of years of efforts the Christian Health Care Systems provide about 40-60% of medical services in a majority of African countries (e.g. Ghana, Nigeria, Uganda) and some Asiatic countries. The basis of these systems is the charity work. I would like to browse through books in English libraries for completion of knowledge. The interesting issue is an activity of women in charity organizations, which was different in different countries and depended on social and cultural context. The problem of links between charity organizations and funds and health care systems has a very wide range. For example, charity organizations of physicians have played the important role for better access to treatment in Africa in the last decades. These organizations realized the traditional medical ethics based on the Hippocratic oath.

title: All the names' - digitization and online publication of the admission books of Bethlem Royal Hospital (1683-1902).
description: All the names: digitisation and online publication of the admission books of Bethlem Royal Hospital (1683-1902) The project for which help is sought aims to digitise and publish online thirty-nine volumes of Bethlem Hospital admission registers which date from 1683 to 1902. The volumes will be digitally imaged page by page, the images attached to existing archive catalogue descriptions (which provides the metadata necessary to interpret the images), and the descriptions and images launched online on the website of the Bethlem Royal Hospital Archives & Museum. Sample printouts of the images of the registers to be made available online will be appended to a full Research Resources in Medical History application, should one be invited. Bethlem Hospital occupies a unique place in the history of psychiatry. Founded as a religious community in 1247, it has been devoted to the care and treatment of the mentally ill since at least the start of the fifteenth century. Its earliest administrative records date from the sixteenth century, and the admission records which are the focus of this project commence prior to the founding of any other hospital for the insane in England. The records contain the names of patients and their "securities" (sponsors), dates of their admission and discharge, and brief details of diagnosis and patient outcomes. For this reason they are of as much interest to the medical and social historian as they are to the genealogist. This imaging project, dubbed "All the Names", will contribute to the ongoing enhancement of the Archives & Museum catalogue as a whole, but it is self-contained in that the records to be imaged, or the information contained in them, are in particular demand by a discrete group of researchers. The imaging capability of the software used by the Archives & Museum to documents its holdings is currently being utilised in a project, funded by the Marc Fitch Fund, to image minutes of the hospital governors dating from 1559 to 1792.

title: Cataloguing and preserving the archives of the British Psychoanalytical Society.
description: British Psychoanalytical Society Cataloguing and Preservation of the Archives The Archives of the British Psychoanalytical Society are a principal resource for the history of psychoanalysis in Great Britain and internationally. They reflect the Society's role in medicine, mental health and society at large. The project will preserve and catalogue our collections; making these catalogues electronically accessible to all. At present the Institute of Psychoanalysis contributes the salary for an Archives Manager for 18 hours a week. Eight of these hours will be made available for this project. The Institute will also contribute staff for assistance with web design. We seek funding to employ a professional Archivist and purchase preservation packaging. Our collections fall into two parts: 1) Those which we have already begun to catalogue, largely comprising the correspondence and Society records. These will require retrospective conversion in order to meet ISAD(G)2. 2) Other collections require cataloguing from lists or from scratch. In the course of working on 1) we have come to recognise the necessity of employing a professional Archivist to carry out these two tasks. We propose to both catalogue and preserve our Archives.

title: Mechanisms of social interaction.
description: While I am already supported by the Wellcome Trust, my position is currently as a component of the grant awarded to Richard Frackowiak. On the basis of past career and current work it is more appropriate for me to have independent funding. The work I plan will generate a substantial series of linked experiments in a number of cognitive domains. I anticipate that much of the day to day work will be carried out by a series of research fellows and PhD students. Long-term funding for the coordinator of this group is essential to provide continuity and coherence across these projects and to ensure an optimum environment for the training of a new generation of clinical neuroscientists. In addition, a long-term view is needed to ensure that the work of my group continues to feed into and benefit from developments in the other groups that compose the Functional Imaging Laboratory. Functional imaging techniques, particularly fMRI, are going to change and develop rapidly over the next ten years. My past career demonstrates that I have the flexibility to learn and take advantage of new developments as they arise. Long-term funding will obviate the shot-term risks associated with the exploitation of these new developments. My fundamental aim is to increase understanding of brain abnormalities underlying psychosis. Of necessity this is a long-term goal since much work on normal brain function is needed before cognitive paradigms and brain imaging techniques can be applied to the study of psychosis. This work will span at least a ten year period.

title: On the edge - An interactive theatre programme for young people on early intervention in first episode psychosis - with inbuilt research process.
description: "On The Edge" \- An Interactive Theatre Programme for Young People on Early Intevention in First Episode Psychosis - with inbuilt research process Mental health problems are common, affecting one in four people at some time in their life. They are also difficult to face and talk about, attracting widespread misunderstanding and stigma. Psychosis is a particular form of severe mental distress which characteristically begins in late adolescence, and has major consequences for the individual, family and friends. At present help usually arrives late when problems have accumulated and much has been lost. There is increasing evidence that early contact with effective help improves the outlook for all concerned, and yet to date there is little understanding or experience of how to engage young people in thinking more compassionately about these issues, or enable them to feel more able to seek effective help at an earlier stage. 'On the Edge' is an interactive play whose main objective is to engage 16-25 year olds in developing increasing awareness and understanding of those with significant mental health problems by inviting them to participate in an evocative dramatic experience, which sets the development of psychosis in a personal and social context with which they may be able to identify. 'On the Edge' has been written and shaped through a creative collaboration between people with a personal experience of psychosis, mental health service professionals, and students (of a similar age to the characters in the pay) and staff in Applied Drama.

title: An indefinite continuity.
description: Sensual experience can conjure unexpected mental states that appear random but often have recognisable anticedants in the subconscious. This random accessing of dormant memory may also have lineage in psychology, geography, local history, residual genetic material, appreciation of place, coincidence, and synaesthesia. "An indefinite continuity" would investigate where memory exists and these apparently random means of accessing it. Initially the research would begin with site specific inquiries and whether certain locations have a trace memory that plays like a long lost tape loop that can only be appreciated by certain congruent individuals. The project is to research the links between psychology, geography, and memory through a series of field trips, interviews, and site specific evaluation. "An indefinite continuity" will endeavour to connect these seemingly disparate elements. The research undertaken would involve conducting interviews with writers, film makers, exorcists, curators, and habituees of certain psychogeographically significant areas and the feelings and perceptions they have experienced. Recent research suggests that there could be a link between pre cognitive memory and sensual awareness as outlined in prousts "A LA recherché du temps perdu" (Remembrance of things past) or the literal translation 'in search of lost time'. In the novel the hero (Swann) experiences a direct causal link between sensual stimulus and what he had previously regarded as forgotten memories. Another aspect of my research would be an exercise in mental or cognitive mapping as a conduit to accessing dormant memories, subconscious faculties, spatial awareness, artistic interpretation, and imagination.

title: Relative.
description: This proposal is to source and to investigate documentary material towards the making of a film/ installation, tracing histories of psychiatric illness. 'Relative' will be an artistic exploration, and interrogation, of the recent history of 'everyday' madness. Artist filmmaker Tim Shore and his collaborator, Gary Thomas, will conduct an investigation from their own (lay) perspective, and will probe the secrets, mythologies, and hidden narratives of madness that weave through their personal family histories. The project will focus on the experiences of four people - Gary's mother and maternal grandmother, and Tim's father and paternal grandfather. This truncated family tree may help shape the form of the final work. As initial research, we will gather information, to be assessed and considered, to develop an artist's film/installation project. Though the project seeks to document, it is not a documentary or journalistic approach - it is about making some other kind of sense of our own experience of negotiating the space between madness and medical science.

title: Testimony.
description: Testimony Our aim is to: Provide learning opportunities about mental health treatment and care and its social and historical significance. Engage local communities in dissemination. Increase public understanding of mental health treatment in contemporary society by looking at historical treatment and care. By doing this work we will: Raise awareness about the historical treatment of mental health patients. Explore the role of the asylums in the communities they were based. Challenge the stigma associated with being a 'mental patient'. We will do this by: Making MHM archive material available. Producing information to provide historical and social context for the archive. Managing a touring exhibition programme. Producing learning packs for use by schools, colleges and those undertaking life long learning. Promoting the archive and how to access it. Our audience drawn from three groups: Educational Users We will produce material for students in schools, colleges and life long learning, including CPD. Our intention is to produce an integrated set of resources, including an educational pack, CD-ROM/DVD and website, which are flexible enough to be used by different groups. Opinion Formers We will seek to influence debate around the provision of mental health care by making the archive accessible to those working in the media, historians and other academics. Community Groups We will work in partnership with local community groups to develop an exhibition programme suited to particular localities. Our intention is to work with a range of groups including service users, local history groups, architectural groups and local authorities.

title: One night with rats in the service of art.
description: This is an artist-led project that involves aesthetic experiments with rats to make visible controversial, but possibly understandable, practices within scientific research and among owners and breeders of rats. Rats are common but marginalised creatures within western culture. On the one hand, they are the highly social, deeply-loved pets of (often female) owners, whose intimacy with their animals can generate revulsion in people untroubled by conventional pets. On the other, scientists deploying 'the rat model' have been breeding and using rats for over 100 years, often as part of psychology's attempts to understand the human brain. Within these very different cultures are activities which involve the human training the rat to move through a maze and watching how it behaves. Built in are assumptions about what humans can do to animals. The project culminates in a live performance lecture, which will show the results of my training of rats to do drawings and performances, and findings from my research into the science and popular cultures I have investigated, as a way of bringing to the fore ethical questions about these activities.

title: Now you see it, now you don't: change blindness unveiled.
description: This project is a collaboration between a scientist and an artist to explore the possibility of a cross-over in visual material between disciplines. The project focuses on the psychological phenomenon of change blindness, which is a failure to notice dramatic changes to visual sciences, often because the change is outside the observer's focus of attention, or does not conform to their expectations. A series of visuals will be produced, including films and animations, to be used both as experimental material in the psychology lab, and as art works in the gallery. These films will produce change blindness through the use of various visual and cinematic effects. The challenge is to produce films that will function successfully both as a scientific tool, by producing a measurable psychological effect in a laboratory setting, and as artworks exhibited to a wider audience. The project will use a novel and striking psychological phenomenon to expose the fact that our visual experience can differ from visual reality, yet is relied upon for our understanding of that reality. This is the first project in a planned series that aims to use visual art to increase public awareness of scientific research showing the shortcoming of human perception.

title: Exploring the intimate experience of biomedical self-test kits.
description: Exploring the intimate experience of biomedical self-test kits The crisis of health care systems is an ongoing issue, especially in European welfare states. In the UK we currently have a system where we wait for people to get ill before we treat them. A reaction of the individual is the growing movement to self-care. Personal wellbeing concerns are taken to your social network before going to the traditional expert system. Moreover, the progress in biomedical science provides more and more possibilities for self-testing. But little has been explored of how this rich biofeedback from self-test kits affects people's daily health strategies. The project will start by focusing at the change in social behaviour towards reproduction and the use of fertility self-test kits. Female fertility has always been connected to general health, but recently new biomedical products on the market that enable home male fertility testing raise questions about male health. In this sense, masculinity is facing a new era where regular fertility checks can create a whole new experience of age, health and wellbeing lifestyle. How is this biofeedback experienced? The aim of the project is to investigate this area of biomedical self-test products from the point of view of the experience. The research will use time-based tools to explore the subject. The aim of the outcome is to stimulate socio critical debate about the health experience of biomedical products.

title: Dissecting hippocampal function: multiple cellular mechanisms, multiple sub- regions and multiple functions.
description: The relationship between hippocampal long-term potentiation (LTP) and hippocampal-dependent learning requires re-evaluation. GluR-A AMPA receptor subunit knockout mice, lacking CA3-CA1 hippocampal LTP, show hippocampus- dependent, spatial working memory impairments, but exhibit normal hippocampus- dependent, spatial reference memory. This demonstrates hitherto unsuspected yet separable mechanisms within the hippocampus, supporting different aspects of its information processing. This proposal will test the hypothesis that rapid onset hippocampal LTP, which requires NMDA receptors for its induction and GluR-A containing AMPA receptors for its expression, provides a mechanism for the temporal encoding or tagging of "events", which contributes to a rapid, flexible memory system in rodents that may resemble human episodic memory. This will extend initial studies with GluR-A-/- mice by carrying out extensive behavioural phenotyping of both genetically modified mice and pharmacological manipulations that interfere with different components of hippocampal LTP. New constructs with manipulations to subunits of either NMDA or AMPA receptors (generated by collaborators in Heidelberg), will crucially include mice with genetic manipulations that are under both temporal and regional control. This, along with discrete intrahippocampal drug microinfusions, will test the role of different forms of LTP within the different hippocampal subfields to the overall information processing operation performed by the hippocampus. Studies of hippocampal memory processing will not, however, provide a complete description of the role of this brain structure. Selective dorsal, but not ventral, hippocampal lesions produce learning impairments on spatial maze tasks. In contrast, ventral, but not dorsal, hippocampal lesions reduce anxiety using both conditioned and unconditioned tests. This double dissociation suggests the existence of at least two functional sub-regions distributed along the septotemporal axis of the hippocampus. The aim is to obtain a better psychological understanding of not only the mnemonic deficits associated with dorsal hippocampus, but also the anxiolytic effects associated with ventral hippocampal lesions, and to understand how different synaptic mechanisms within the hippocampal subfields contribute to both dorsal and ventral functions. Examination of input and output pathways to and from dorsal and ventral hippocampus and their behavioural functions is likely to be crucial in this regard. The use of techniques such as the newly developed in vivo voltammetry to measure oxygen or glucose utilisation as an index of neuronal activity will allow exploration of these issues. A clearer understanding of ventral hippocampal function will facilitate a precise description of the common underlying hippocampal algorithm.

title: Genetics, ethics and uncertainty; how do the novel uncertainties brought to bear by genetic knowledge affect the justification of medical intervention?
description: The principal concern of my research will be the importance of philosophy of science to bioethics; I believe that problems in medical ethics need to be informed by a broader appreciation of the nature of the claims with which they are occupied. There is a great deal of work existing in philosophy of science that analyses the warrant of knowledge claims. But these analyses rarely critique the particular kinds of claims made in the medical context, which necessitate specific and individualised consideration. These might be diagnostic, prognostic or causal claims, or conclusions as regards the best or most effective course of treatment to be taken. These claims guide action that is ultimately taken, and so their justification is of great importance to the ethical assessment of these actions. My research will ask when we have sufficient ground to conclude that a proposed course of action - to undergo treatment, to make a particular prognosis - is the right course to take; what degree of certainty is needed? I will locate this question specifically in the field of genetic explanations of mental illness, an area that is the locus of deep theoretical divisions that are currently being exacerbated by the trend for geneticisation.

title: Voices beyond the asylum: A Post-War History of Mental Health Services in Manchester and Salford.
description: Voices Beyond the Asylum: A Post-War History of Mental Health Services in Manchester and Salford My general aim is to explore the history and dynamics of the post-asylum mental health services in Britain and to examine the interrelated shifts in location, practice and understandings of mental illness, in the post-war period. The focus will be on schizophrenia. As the most common serious mental health problem, and one which encompasses both positive and negative symptoms, the condition has a major impact on a range of acute and long term services and on the lives of sufferers and families alike. It also has a high profile: although associated with a well established and vocal network of support groups, it is often the object of public prejudice and fear, which, fanned by negative media images, has contributed to the recent emphasis on risk management and compulsory detention and treatment. In terms of location, Manchester and Salford offer a number of advantages. Firstly, as sites of interest, both districts have been involved in a variety of innovative practices, e.g., Salford was one of the first local authorities to develop a community mental health service, and later pioneered the use of a Psychiatric Case Register; Withington Hospital, known as 'the Maudsley of the North' was at the forefront of developments in district general psychiatry; and the psychiatric social work (PSW) course, established at Manchester University in 1946, was the first such course to be located within a Faculty of Medicine. Secondly, in terms of resources, several members of CHSTM have worked on histories of local hospitals, including extensive preliminary work, done in the '80s, on the history of psychiatric services and Pickstone's study of the early development of District General Hospital Psychiatry in the Manchester Region. Thirdly, through my own professional background, I have developed a good local knowledge, and have connections with many practitioners and a number of relevant university departments: Psychiatry; Psychiatric Social Work; Personal and Social Services Research Unit and Nursing.

title: The Construction and Treatment of Childhood Behavioural Disorders in Britain and North America, 1950-2000.
description: The Construction and Treatment of Childhood Behavioural Disorders in Britain and North America, 1950-2000 The proposed PhD project will provide a comparative history of the constructions and treatments of childhood behavioural disorders, particularly ADHD/hyperkinesis, in Britain and North America, 1950-2000. My point of entry is the historical discrepancy between the two countries in the use of stimulants in children, and the apparent reduction of this difference during the 1990s as levels of diagnosis and prescription have increased dramatically on both sides of the Atlantic. I will focus on several strands of medical and social history through which the national differences may be explained, including the institutional structures in the area of child mental health; the professional structures and ideologies together with patterns of training and research; the roles played by the pharmaceutical industry; and the emergence of parent support groups in recent years. Wider social debates on the aetiology and proper treatment of behavioural disorders will also be examined to provide a context to the more technical developments.

title: The Rise of the Slimmers' Disease: A History of Eating Disorders in Twentieth Century Britain.
description: The Rise of the Slimmers' Disease: A History of Eating Disorders in Twentieth Century Britain The thesis will focus on sufferers' and practitioners' experience of anorexia and bulimia nervosa in twentieth century Britain. The aims of the project are: 1. To explore the development of medical ideas on the aetiology and treatment of anorexia and bulimia nervosa after 1900. The psychiatric paradigm will be the primary focus of inquiry, but the thesis will also be framed around the competing professional groups who claimed expertise in explaining and treating the disorder. Psychologists and psychiatrists, counsellors and self-help groups, specialist treatment centres and therapeutic communities advocated different forms of treatment. Physical treatment, the frontline therapy of the 1950s, 60s, and 70s, in line with approaches for other psychiatric disorders (medication, hormone therapy, electroconvulsive therapy, etc) was challenged by advocates of psychological therapies, available in the early twentieth century, but not fully exploited until the 1980s and 90s (psychoanalysis, client-centred therapy, support groups, etc); e.g. from the late 1980s psychiatrists frequently prescribed anti-depressant medication such as Prozac, in particular for those suffering with bulimia, whereas specialist treatment centres recommended psychotherapy. 2. To explore the influence of the mass media on concerns about body image among young women, concerns which in turn could increase their susceptibility to anorexia or bulimia, and to chart the changing body 'ideal' as portrayed through the media during the twentieth century. 3. Medical literature, like the media, often ignored gender issues and this has implications for both research into and the treatment of eating disorders. The increase of diagnoses of eating disorders in men from the 1980s onwards will be explored and contrasted with explanations for the incidence of anorexia amongst women. The creation of a mass health culture in the twentieth century, through the growth of the sport and leisure industries, has been suggested as having had a major impact on male perceptions of the ideal body.

title: M.Phil in the History and Philosophy of Science.
description: M.Phil in the History and Philosophy of Science and Medicine I plan to carry out my dissertation in the field of the History of Medicine, continuing my study of Chinese Medicine, and taking advantage of proposed closer links between the HPS Department and the Needham Research Institute in Cambridge. This specialises in East Asian science, technology and medicine. Research here would help me to build on my personal international interest. My current dissertation study has thrown up many interesting issues that I have not been able to research very thoroughly, this provides a focus for my M.Phil dissertation such as the shaping influence of newly involved large international health institutes (such as American National Institute of Health) on Chinese Medicine in Hong Kong. For the 3 essays required I would like to focus on the area of Science and Technology Studies, specifically the roles of gender and race in shaping modern science; another area I would focus on is the history of modern medicine, concentrating on feminist attitudes within the sphere of reproduction. I would like to concentrate on the role of Psychopharmacology in psychiatry in my third essay, part of the History and Philosophy of Mind area Research in these areas would fulfil and develop my interest in the history and philosophy of medicine, whilst providing opportunities for a broader outlook on science in general.

title: UK BIOBANK
description: UK Biobank is a major national health resource, and a registered charity in its own right, with the aim of improving the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of a wide range of serious and life-threatening illnesses – including cancer, heart diseases, stroke, diabetes, arthritis, osteoporosis, eye disorders, depression and forms of dementia. UK Biobank recruited 500,000 people aged between 40-69 years in 2006-2010 from across the country to take part in this project. They have undergone measures, provided blood, urine and saliva samples for future analysis, detailed information about themselves and agreed to have their health followed. Over many years this will build into a powerful resource to help scientists discover why some people develop particular diseases and others do not.

title: Protein kinase C involvement in u-opioid receptor desensitization and morphine tolerance.
description: Opioid drugs such as morphine produce their therapeutic effects (e.g. analgesia) and unwanted effects (e.g. euphoria and respiratory depression) by acting at the m-opioid receptor (MOR). In the whole animal tolerance develops rapidly to the effects of morphine, even after a single dose. It had been assumed that receptor desensitization was a fundamental component of opioid tolerance. However, morphine, unlike other MOR agonists, does not produce rapid MOR desensitization. This has led to the suggestion that morphine produces tolerance precisely because it does not induce rapid receptor desensitization, but rather because it continues to activate the receptors thus evoking other adaptive changes in the cell that result in the development of tolerance. We, on the other hand, have recently discovered that in mature brain neurones morphine does produce MOR desensitization but only when protein kinase C (PKC) is activated. Thus crosstalk between Gq-coupled receptors that activate PKC and MORs may play a crucial role in MOR desensitization and this potentially may be an important component in the development and maintenance of morphine tolerance. What now needs to be elucidated is:-1. how PKC activation converts morphine into a rapid, receptor desensitizing agonist. 2. whether PKC/morphine-induced MOR desensitization is responsible for the cellular tolerance that develops in neurones on prolonged morphine exposure In this proposal we describe experiments that are designed to address these issues. The experimental approach will be to study MORs endogenously expressed in mature brain neurones. This is important because different cell types (e.g. neurones vs recombinant expression systems) may differentially express the signalling components required for the development of MOR desensitization and morphine tolerance. Furthermore, it is now imperative to confirm and extend theories on morphine tolerance generated from experiments on recombinant systems to mature neurones because it is in such neurones that tolerance and physical dependence actually occur in the intact animal

title: Investigating the role of SUN1 in nuclear positioning.
description: Nuclear migration and anchoring within cells is critical in many biological processes, particularly during development, by establishing polarity and contributing to cell migration. Nuclear positioning is controlled by the actin network and, via dynein, by the microtubule network. Importantly, defects in nuclear-centrosomal attachement have been implicated in lissencephaly, an inherited brain developmental disorder involving defects in neuronal cell migration. Until recently, the nature of the nuclear-cytoskeletal connection was obscure. Studies in C. elegans now implicate a family of nuclear envelope (NE) proteins, known as SUN domain proteins, in both microtubule- and actin- dependent nuclear positioning. We identified murine SUN1 as a lamin-binding NE protein and our studies suggest that SUN1 adopts a novel topology, spanning both NE membranes, and is required for binding of dynein to the NE. This project will study the SUN1 protein in a combined biochemical, structural and functional approach. NE targeting will be examined by electron microscopy, in vitro pull-down and localization studies and membrane dynamics investigated by time-lapse confocal microscopy, FRAP and FLIP. A combination of yeast-two hybrid interaction screens, RNAi depletion and astrocyte cell migration assays will be employed to identify SUN1 binding partners and probe the role of SUN1 in nuclear-cytoskeletal attachment, nuclear positioning and cell migration. These studies will provide important novel information on subcellular organisation and contribute to the understanding of developmental disorders.

title: Environmental changes in Africa and tsetse habitat fragmentation: epidemiological consequences and perspectives for control.
description: The epidemiology of tsetse-transmitted human or livestock trypanosomiasis is to a large extend determined by tsetse density, infection rate and host preference. All three contributing factors vary between tsetse populations and within a tsetse population may, often due to differences in the well-being of the tsetse population, vary in time and space. A major factor, contributing to tsetse population stress is human encroachment and concomitant fragmentation of tsetse habitat as a result of the introduction and expansion of mixed farming systems. Understanding the impact of habitat fragmentation on the tsetse population may contribute to the development of more effective control strategies. Riparian and savannah tsetse species play the major role in disease transmission. Therefore, the project will identify study areas in West and southern Africa, where each group is predominant. In those study areas, the fragmentation of riparian vegetation and savannah woodland will be quantified and qualified using environmental and remotely sensed data. Study sites with different degrees of fragmentation will be identified and the tsetse and livestock populations will be monitored. Special attention will go to parameters that can be used to develop population dynamics and disease transmission models. The models will be used to determine (i) the well-being, dynamics and vulnerability of tsetse subpopulations in fragmented habitats, and (ii) the infection rate of hosts and vectors and the related disease transmission risk. Furthermore, analyses of genetic diversity and gene flow between tsetse populations in habitat fragments will make it possible to determine the effect of different levels of fragmentation on the tsetse's dispersal capacity. This may result in the identification of isolated tsetse populations. Using the findings of the field studies various control approaches will be tested and their appropriateness assessed.

title: Circadian Organisation of Sleep-Wake Disturbances in Schizophrenia.
description: Patients with schizophrenia frequently complain of poor sleep and are commonly observed to shift their rest-activity cycle. Despite the introduction of new antipsychotic drugs, sleep-wake abnormalities remain a major complaint. Of the few previous studies undertaken, all have suggested that abnormal rest- activity or EEG sleep profiles in schizophrenic patients are associated with an increase in severity of psychotic symptoms, a decrease in cognitive performance, and poor psychosocial outcomes. Our preliminary results using long-term simultaneous recordings of rest-activity, light, and hormonal profiles show that both the circadian timing of the sleep-wake profile and endocrine rhythms are either severely delayed or free-running with respect to time of day. The broad aims of this proposal are to determine the extent of sleep timing and circadian rhythm disruption in schizophrenia and to explore potential countermeasures. We will address four issues: (i) Quantify patterns of sleep disturbances and hormonal profiles in patients with chronic schizophrenia; (ii) Correlate patterns of sleep disturbance with medication and neurocognitive function; (iii) Investigate whether abnormal sleep-wake patterns are due to aberrant light exposure or an insensitivity in the photoreceptive mechanisms that regulate the circadian axis; (iv) Apply clinical and pharmacological interventions that have been shown to stabilize patterns of sleep and wake in patients with both circadian rhythm and affective disorders. These interventions will include scheduled sleep, light therapy and melatonin treatment.

title: Design and implementation of large-scale genetic association studies of commondiseases.
description: We propose a pilot study to test the association of 100,000 specific polymorphisms with a range of common diseases using a two stage case-control study design. The study will include diabetes, breast cancer, cardiovascular disease, bipolar disorder, and other diseases (2,000 samples each), as well as two common control groups (up to 3,000 samples total) for further evaluation. Positive associations will form the basis for future biological studies. The results will be used to evaluate how best to optimise the design, implementation, analysis and cost efficiency of large-scale and genome-wide association studies in the future. We will examine features such as SNP selection, analysis methods, population structure, study size, the use of common controls, heterogeneity in sample collections, linkage disequilibrium and SNP tagging. The results will provide independent assessment of the coverage of SNP panels that are available to the community for genetic studies, including the output of the International HapMap Project. The project will help to establish a separate training programme in statistical genetics, and will lay the foundations for the development of an infrastructure for UK research in this area in future years.
