title: Cambridge centre for behavioural and clinical neuroscience.
description: Behavioural and Clinical Neuroscience Institute at the University of Cambridge The main rationale of the BCNC is to translate the basic knowledge of how the brain is organised functionally at a neural system level to the understanding and treatment of the cognitive and emotional sequelae of human mental illness and brain damage. By providing essential infra-structure in several domains, the Centre is introducing or harnessing several functional imaging modalities in rats, monkeys and humans (including fMRI, PET with radioligands in vivo neurochemistry, telemetry, and gene expression) to address specific questions about the functioning and neuromodulation of the cerebral (especially prefrontal) cortex and associated neural systems, relevant to the understanding and treatment of a number of neuropsychiatric and neurological disorders. We aim to enhance existing inter-disciplinary programmes, while also creating new collaborative opportunities to cross-fertilise, and hence enhance synergy between, animal and human research. The current application is made in the following context: a resolution of the outcome of the JIF application; the recent decision to provide funds to the MRC Unit in Brain and Cognitive Sciences (MRC-CBU) for a 3T magnet for functional imaging studies; and certain other developments. These include the urgent need to replace the existing Bruker 3T magnet at the WBIC, the measures taken to preserve existing non-human primate work in Cambridge following the decision not to proceed with the 307 facility, the further opportunities that have opened up through the advance in PET neuroimaging science at the WBIC , recent investigation of genetic polymorphisms at Cambridge and the establishment of a complementary programme at the Sanger Centre in 'Genes to Cognition'; the establishment of an administrative and scientific base for the Centre on the Downing Site arising from two successful SRIF applications; and the exciting scientific progress made during the first 18 months, which has helped to shape the objectives of the Centre. The purpose of this proposal is to seek enhanced funding to consolidate and promote further growth of the Centre over the next five years. In particular, we request support to improve facilities for human fMRI and radioligand PET at the Addenbrooke's site, and for the consolidation of behavioural neuroscience in animals on the Downing Site and at the Innes facility.

title: Impulsivity and compulsion in humans and other animals: neural and neurochemical substrates.
description: The Programme has the overall goal of investigating the neuropsychological and neurochemical basis of two classes of symptom commonly found in neuropsychiatry, impulsivity (behaviour occurring without foresight) and compulsion (excessively repeated behaviour). There are 6 subsidiary goals: To (i) determine the neural and neurochemical basis of processes of response inhibition mediated by fronto-striatal circuitry through cross-species comparisons of rats, monkeys and humans. (ii) define neural circuitry differentially implicated in impulsive and compulsive behaviour, including regions such as the human inferior frontal gyrus, and the primate orbitofrontal cortex (OFC). (iii) validate neuropsychological tests of impulsivity and compulsion in adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) by showing their differential sensitivity to these disorders and relations to symptomatology (iv) understand how monoaminergic modulation affects impulsive and compulsive responding, using various methodologies including functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) in humans, and intra-cerebral infusions of agents with well-defined neuropharmacological actions in animals. (v) understand the neurochemical basis of the anti-impulsive effects of methylphenidate (Ritalin) using pharmacological, neuroimaging and genetic (study of a polymorphism) approaches and (vi) clarify the role of cortical and sub-cortical serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine, 5-HT) in response inhibition and model possible therapeutic effects of serotoninergic treatments on compulsive behaviour.

title: A linkage study on a large ethnically isolated population multiply affected with psychiatric disorders and autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia.
description: We have recruited 96 individuals from a large multigenerational pedigree, of whom 22 members suffer with schizophrenia or affective disorders and 5 siblings are affected with a rare and disabling autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia. This population is from a unique ethnic isolate in Bulgaria with an unusually high rate of inbreeding. We propose to conduct a full genome scan on this pedigree in order to identify loci harbouring susceptibility genes for psychiatric disorders. We expect that due to the high inbreeding, there will be fewer such loci, than in the general population, and they could possibly exert their effect in a recessive mode of inheritance. We propose to use the Affymetrix 10K Array system which which will allow for ~11,000 SNPs across the genome to be genotyped on a single microarray for each individual. This dense saturation of the genome will allow us to construct unique haplotypes and test them for linkage with disease. This should allow us to identify unique shared founder haplotypes that segregate with illness. We also expect to identify the position of a novel gene causing spastic paraplegia, as the already known gene (paraplegin) that causes a similar phenotype, has been excluded as causing the illness in this family.

title: The survival of bacteria under restorations: a paradigm shift in operative dentistry.
description: Dental caries still affects a significant portion of the UK population, especially the poor and disadvantaged, with treatment costing over £1.6 billion for the year 2002. New approaches are required to facilitate dental treatment and this proposal explores the possibility that cavity preparation can be radically altered saving tooth tissue, treatment time and reducing patient anxiety making the restorative treatment of caries less traumatic for the patient. The aims of this study are: (1) to determine whether bacterial survival beneath restorations is influenced by the pre-treatment of the infected dentine with phosphoric acid etching, laser exposure [DentSave] and ozone treatment [HealOzone] during cavity preparation prior to the placement of a restoration, (2) to investigate whether nutrient limitation will significantly reduce the complexity and phenotypic and genotypic diversity of the microflora surviving under restorations and (3) to demonstrate whether the dentine below the restoration will finally harbour only dead bacteria as the nutrient source [serum glycoproteins] is cut off due to sclerosis of the dentinal tubules and formation of secondary dentine within the pulp chamber. These aims are designed to determine the clinical usefulness, efficacy and necessity of available antimicrobial systems designed to kill microbes infecting tooth tissue and to better understand the basis for microbial survival and microbial decline under restorations. The ultimate purpose is to validate clinical procedures that make the provision of dental treatment for carious lesions less traumatic and less destructive of tooth tissue.

title: Interaction of inhibitory control and reward mechanisms in Attention Deficit/ Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD).
description: Current theories of attention deficit/ hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) explain the core symptoms either in terms of an underlying cognitive deficit (responseinhibition and executive dysfunction hypotheses) or a motivational style (delay aversion and reward deficit hypotheses). Separate cortico- striatal dopaminergic circuits are implicated in response inhibition (right orbito-frontal cortex and dorsal striatum) and reward evaluation (limbic cortex, ventral striatum / nucleus accumbens). However, it is not clear whether i) the executive/inhibitory and motivational systems in ADHD are trulydistinct or interact and ii) whether stimulants and reward-based behavioural approaches act via the same dopaminergic networks. The proposed study exploresthe interaction between inhibitory and motivational processes in ADHD by testing whether motivational incentives can reverse abnormalities in response inhibition. We will measure the effect of reward anticipation on a response inhibition task (Stop-Signal task) utilising event-related potentials (ERP) and fMRI analysis. We predict that i) reward will attenuate neural markers ofinhibitory dysfunction, ii) the neural correlates of reward and stimulant medication will be similar and iii) the neural correlates of reward in ADHD will resemble that of younger typically developing children. We also predict that the effects of reward and stimulant medication will be moderated by dopamine transporter (DAT1) genotype.

title: The relation between social and cognitive inflexibility in autism.
description: The aim is to examine the relation between cognitive and social deficits in children and adolescents with autism. Our hypothesis is that children with autism have a limited propensity to identify with other people: often they fail to orientate to, and assume, other people's attitudes and styles of action. We hypothesize that this impairment contributes to the children's limited ability to move spontaneously from one perspective to another within their own minds, so that they become inflexible in thought, communication, andaction. Participants will be 40 verbally able children and adolescents with autism, and 40 age- and ability-matched children and adolescents without autism. We shall administer a set of original experimental tasks designed to highlight associations and dissociations among (a) intact and impaired abilities in imitation, (b) understanding communicative intentions vis-à-vis intentions to act, (c) comprehension of meanings in changing social and non- social contexts, and (d) spontaneous versus prompted thinking in language.The approach is novel in comparing spontaneous and/or socially responsive flexibility on the one hand, and flexible adjustment to environmental cues on the other. The results promise to elucidate how certain social and social- cognitive abnormalities of children with autism relate to specific impairments in flexible thinking.

title: The Attentional Basis of Anxiety Vulnerability.
description: The proposed research will examine the causal basis of attentional bias in the development of anxiety vulnerability. In particular, the research will attempt to establish whether any reduction in anxiety vulnerability produced by attentional training is due primarily to manipulations of the detection or selective engagement with threat, or whether promoting the rapid disengagement of attention from threat stimuli is the key mechanism. A central question concerns whether the effects of attentional training can last for up to one or two weeks. Research to date has only measured the affects of attentional training immediately after the task. If this technique is to be useful in a clinical context then the effects must be demonstrated to be lasting. Of course if the beneficial effects last for say two days, then people could be administered attentional training every couple of days on a home computer or via the internet. Both clinical (GAD patients) and non-clinical populations will be tested. A short version of the attentional training task will be developed and evaluated. It is hoped that this may prove useful as a first step towards the reduction of anxiety vulnerability for those undergoing stressful situations, which could be administered in a primary care setting. Statistical techniques (ANOVA and regression analyses) will be used throughout the project to examine the nature of the relations between engage and disengage processes in addition to evaluating the role of attentional biases for threat in modulating anxiety vulnerability. The effects of attentional training on both attentional biases and anxiety vulnerability will be measured immediately after training, as well as at one week following training. The results of this research will be published in leading international scientific and clinical journals as well as being presented at national and international conferences.

title: The triplet gene in Drosophila: what unifies the female meiotic spindle without centrosomes.
description: Accurate segregation of genetic materials is essential for life. A bipolar spindle mediates this process in eukaryotes. Centrosomes, which nucleate microtubules, dictate the spindle formation during mitosis. However, the formation of a bipolar spindle takes place without centrosomes in female meiosis in animals. Although it is medically important, the molecular mechanism of this spindle formation in female meiosis is not well studied in vivo. To understand the acentrosomal spindle formation in female meiosis, we have carried out a genetic screen in Drosophila. One of the mutants, which we call triplet, shows a defect in unifying the female meiotic spindle into one. Each bivalent chromosome assembles a separate bipolar spindle capable of segregating the chromosomes in the mutant. We have found the triplet gene encodes a conserved protein kinase. We propose to study this mutant and gene product, in order to understand how multiple chromosomes assemble one unified spindle without centrosomes in female meiosis. The key goals include 1) to identify the role of the triplet gene by cytological and genetic analysis of the mutant phenotype including a study in somatic cells 2) to reveal a regulatory mechanism of the Triplet protein, a protein kinase 3) to identify substrates of the Triplet protein.

title: Exploring the roles of tetraspanin extracellular domains in cellular function.
description: Researchers postulate that socio-economic inequities lead to poor health not only through the direct effects of poverty, but indirectly, through both individual and community level factors. These include the subjective experience of marginalisation, and the socially detrimental effects of living in communities that are disjointed and unstable, counting on minimal social and organisational resources. As a result, public health interest in civil society, community empowerment, and "social capital" has peaked. This literature-base: (1) underestimates the importance class struggles and political processes in promoting health, and (2) has failed to develop a multidisciplinary approach for a full understanding of the actual mechanism through which community-level characteristics may impact upon health. The aim of this proposal is to develop an integrated interdisciplinary approach that can investigate the impact recent social and political changes in Pelotas, Brazil, have had on the life course and health of the youth and mothers participating in two birth cohorts studies (1982 and 1993). Social and political changes will be investigated at both the individual and ecological levels, span from the 1970s, and include: (a) socio-economic inequities, (b) rural-urban and within-city migration, and (c) community characteristics, namely the social and organisational quality of the neighbourhoods. Item (c) includes new socio-political opportunities provided by recent community development initiatives. This aim will be achieved by analysing existing data, and by collecting additional quantitative and qualitative data at the individual and ecological levels. Outcomes include psychiatric morbidity, harmful life-style behaviours, violence, and unwanted sexual and reproductive experiences. Results will be fed back to local communities through pre- existing governmental and civic mechanisms, and will involve the participation of 1982 cohort youth.

title: The molecular basis of mesoderm formation
description: The proposed research aims to understand the molecular basis of vertebrate mesoderm formation. Most of the work makes use of embryos of Xenopus laevis and Xenopus tropicalis, in which species the mesoderm is formed by an inductive interaction in which vegetal cells act on overlying equatorial cells. The final objective of the work, however, is ask to what extent the lessons we learn from the frog also apply to mouse embryos. The experiments should identify genes that are involved in human developmental disorders and also assist in efforts to direct stem cells down particular developmental pathways. The project has six aims. These are (i) to observe long range signalling by GFP-tagged inducing factors in real time; (ii) to study gene activation in responding cells and to elucidate the functions of Smad- interacting proteins in this process; (iii) to identify partners of T domain proteins such as Xbra and Eomesodermin; (iv) to study the regulation of gastrulation; (v) to use a novel over-expression screen to identify new molecules involved in mesoderm induction; and (vi) to ask whether the phenotypes of mouse embryos lacking a particular gene resemble those of Xenopus embryos in which translation of the homologous protein has been inhibited.
recipient: MRC National Institute for Medical Research

title: Wellcome Gallery Pilot Education Programme
description: Wellcome Gallery Pilot Education Programme Funding is sought for a pilot programme (6 months) for the Wellcome Trust Gallery commencing January 2005, with a view to developing the programme thereafter. The programme is designed to complement the existing education programmes for the Gallery including the Eye-Opener tours, Gallery talks and schools programme. Schools Arts Programme Objective Explore issues raised by the Wellcome Trust Gallery through the arts How Focus on issues around human wellbeing, such as governance, access to food and healthcare, cultural autonomy with particular regard to the citizenship module of the curriculum Make comparisons between the cultures represented in the gallery and Western scientific approaches Explore the issues through language, literature, role-play, visual and performing arts Study Programme Objectives To provide a forum for debate around issues raised by the gallery and address potentially controversial issues To pilot an approach for future larger programmes including development of teaching materials for student groups How 3 evenings of two hour debates with panel of experts Activities Programme Objectives Provides access to collection through object handling Encourage creativity through adult and family drawing workshops How 10 free workshops and sessions for adults on weekends and families on school days to include drawing, artefact handling and storytelling Residency Dr Liz Lee who made Cradle to Grave exhibit in the Wellcome Gallery to work with visitors in the gallery for 10 days. Film Programme The film programme will provide public access to films that relate to the gallery itself. The films will focus on non-Western responses to problems of wellbeing. Academic Programme The academic programme will support English learning institutions while encouraging public interest in the subject of anthropology.

title: Cultural implications of Genetic Science in Britain, 1930-60.
description: The long-term aim of this project is to write a monograph on the cultural implications of genetic science as it developed in Britain between 1930 and 1960. This was a period in which genetics sought to establish itself as a disinterested scientific discipline and to dissociate itself from the taint of eugenics. However, I wish to examine the extent to which the concepts and models of genetic science continued to be shaped (at least in part) by specific cultural contexts and by the non- scientific beliefs of scientists. Conversely, I wish to consider the extent to which concepts of the gene, gene action and genetic programming made possible new conceptualisations of the 'ideal' human, which in turn affected aspects of social policy. My research will draw on scientific, medical and medico-social texts (the latter in social medicine and psychiatry, in particular); on government commissions and reports; on popular science texts; and on literary and popular fiction, in order to provide a cultural history of genetics in the mid-twentieth century. With respect to this application, the aim is to work on archives which contain material relevant to the following key issues: The relationship between the gene and cytoplasm, differing interpretations of which have implications for the explanatory power of the gene (Waddington and Darlington papers). The conceptualisation of desirable and undesirable genetic traits, with particular reference to IQ (Eugenics Society Archive, Medawar and Burt papers). The definition and management of mental deficiency and physical disability (Fairfield, Blacker, Parkes Weber, Sargent and Burt papers).

title: The emergence of ADHD in European countries: a historical study of child behavioural disorders diagnostic categories from 1950 to 2000.
description: The emergence of ADHD in European countries: a historical study of child behavioural disorders diagnostic categories from 1950 to 2000 This study aims at reconstructing the history of the changes in the medical and psychological conceptualisation and treatment of child behavioural disorders in Great Britain, France, the Netherlands and Italy from 1945 onwards. A special emphasis will be given to the influence of genetic studies and pharmacological remedies on the theory and practice of child psychiatry and psychology. The questions that this research sets out to answer are: How have psychological and biological theories on behavioural disorders among children been interacting over the past fifty years? How did psychopharmacology and neurobiological research change the theory and the practice of child psychiatric and psychological expertise? How did the above-mentioned change influence the public debate and lay perception of child disorders? The proposed research is an extension of my previous study on the history of child behavioural disorders in France, Britain and Italy (But Fidgety Phil/He Won't Sit Still From Instability to Hyperactivity, c.1890s-1990s, PhD. Thesis, University of Amsterdam, June 2001). I plan to study the developments in the psychiatric debate in Italian, British, French and Dutch medical journals, textbooks of child psychiatry and monographies devoted to child behavioural disorders. In addition, I plan to extend my research to the information channels through which medical professionals or other groups (such as parents' associations and pharmaceutical companies) disseminate information about child behavioural disorders among lay people.

title: Naked science: your brain, your life, your self.
description: A series of two dialogue events and three interactive forum theatre events on what we should do with the new knowledge we have regarding the human mind. The target audience is 18-45 year old, culturally active, non-specialist adults. This project aims to increase awareness and understanding of the impact of recent advances in neuroscience upon our everyday lives and the complexities surrounding these, and increase the audience's confidence and skills in taking an active part in biomedicine debate. This series of five events will challenge the audience to consider the ethical, moral, social and economic implications of improved understanding of our brains and what it means to be human. At the outset of the project, representatives from the target audience will be consulted to help decide exactly which issues should be discussed. For instance; how should children with ADHD be treated, is it right to provide early diagnosis of disorders that we can't yet treat or can a criminal with a deviant brain pattern be held responsible for their actions? Their input will help shape the content of two dialogue events exploring the social, ethical and moral implications of the issues they have selected. The dialogue from these events will feed into the creation of an interactive theatre piece for the same target audience. During this piece the audience, working in small groups with the actors, will argue for different courses of action to manage the new knowledge we have regarding the human mind.

title: Wellcoming Dialogue.
description: Welcoming dialogue : Cheltenham Science festival When do you pull the plug on the terminally ill? What makes an addict? Do you have any experience of depression? The Cheltenham Science Festival explores the ethical, medical and historical issues surrounding addition, depression and the treatment of the terminally ill. Each discussion will be an intimate and interactive forum which allows the audience and panel of experts to share ideas and learn from one another. Based on the successful model trialled at the Cheltenham Science Festival in 2004, the multi-perspective discussions will make use of a PRS (personal response system) to allow the audience to express personal opinions throughout the discussion as well as contribute to the debate anonymously. Each event will be guided by the audience, shifting the dynamic and providing a unique opportunity to draw opinion from a broad spectrum of experience. Audiences of no more than 200 will be actively targeted prior to the Festival to seek out advice from special interest groups in the local communities. Each event will welcome audience members as well as speakers who can contribute to the discussion from different personal, cultural and professional perspectives such as medics, carers, family members, scientists, ethicists and historians. Consultation of such individuals before the event will also ensure the most relevant concerns and issues are addressed. Each discussion will be evaluated for its effectiveness in providing a truly interactive forum for public engagement in important biomedical issues ability to provide a transparent window on public opinion and a constructive tool for delivering feedback to scientists, policy makers or the science engagement community as appropriate.
recipient: University of the West of England

title: 'The Science, Culture and Practice of Soviet Medicine'
description: Symposium: The Science, Culture and Practice of Soviet Medicine, Gregynog Conference Centre, Newton, Powys, Wales, 26-29 May, 2005 The symposium will bring together scholars working on the history of Soviet medicine. Cold War Western historiography of Soviet medicine concentrated on institutions and policy. This symposium assesses the new themes and approaches now open to scholars in a post-Cold War world, and builds a network for future collaboration. With the availability of archival sources for the study of Soviet medicine it is now possible to delve into themes such as environmental health, famine and plague, nationality and healthcare, reproductive issues, medical evidence in the justice system, and professional practice. The conference will be the first to take stock of the new currents of research emerging since 1991. In contrast to the 1986 Toronto meeting on the topic that resulted in the respected collection edited by Susan Solomon and the late John Hutchinson, Health and Society in Revolutionary Russia (Bloomington & Indianapolis: Indiana University Press, 1990), this symposium will include a large contingent of Russians, most of them of a younger generation, who have established their credentials with research on these ground-breaking areas. It will enable an exchange with their Western analogues (from the UK, USA, Canada and Japan). Senior scholars (Solomon, Graham, Naiman and Barber) with particular expertise will provide detailed criticism and an interdisciplinary assessment of the state of the field. The symposium will result in the publication of a volume of essays as a companion and successor to Health and Society in Revolutionary Russia. It will establish a new international network of scholars working on the cultural, social and scientific history of Soviet medicine, with significant British leadership and participation, in order to develop collaborative research projects.

title: 'Comparison, Transfer and Histoire Croisee in the History of Psychiatry' conference to be held at the University of Southampton on 3rd and 4th September 2005.
description: Meeting: Comparison, Transfer and Histoire Croisee in the History of Psychiatry, University of Southampton, 3-4 September 2005 The number of comparative historical research projects is increasing - in Britain as well as in Continental Europe. This conference aims at getting together researchers who employ comparative methodologies in the history of psychiatry, psychology and psychotherapy, c. 1800-2000, and provides an opportunity for the dissemination and discussion of individual research project findings. The history of psychiatry has been a vibrant field for over two decades, but the focus has been mainly on individual case studies of particular institutions, disorders, ideas and treatment approaches, resulting in a plethora of more or less self-contained publications and a tendency for each new project to simply add yet another narrowly country-specific case to the existing field. In contrast, this meeting will assess the extent to which comparisons between psychiatries in different countries and cultural and regional contexts add a new dimension to our understanding of the history of psychiatry that cannot be achieved through the traditional single-case and country-specific historical account. The different methodological approaches to comparisons in the history of psychiatry that have been favoured in various national contexts and their scope and limitations will be discussed, and it is expected that the meeting will not only contribute substantial cross-national studies to the extant historiography, but will also enhance and refine awareness of the methodological tools available to historians of psychiatry.

title: 'Nursing History: Profession and Practice' conference to be held at the Mandec Conference Centre, University of Manchester on 18th November 2005.
description: \- 'Nursing History: Profession and Practice' The planned conference will be the first to be held jointly by the UK Centre for the History of Nursing and Midwifery and the History Society of the Royal College of Nursing. As the two professional organisations for nurse-historians in the UK, both felt that it was important to work in cooperation to develop what is now a very rapidly expanding discipline. The conference will be devoted to research in the history of profession and practice in nursing and midwifery, and will address the breadth of practice by exploring the following themes: Specialisation in nursing and midwifery care, particularly in relation to: age groups; mental health; learning disability; sophisticated technology; community and public health The scope and breadth of nursing and midwifery practice Education and training for nurses and midwives Gender in nursing and midwifery Nursing and war Moral values, charity, philanthropy and missions in nursing and midwifery

title: The treatment of Lady Lincoln by Dr. Koreff and Dr. Wolowski in Paris 1837.
description: The Treatment of Lady Lincoln by Dr Koreff and Dr Wolowski in Paris 1837 Lady Lincoln's illness and its remarkable treatment offers an unequalled opportunity to look at the understanding of 'hysterical' symptoms, manifestations of clairvoyance, somnambulism as they were understood in the 19th century, and in terms of a 21st century perspective as well. Lady Lincoln's two doctors belonged to the tradition of therapeutic intervention pioneered by the Marquis de Puysegur - a disciple of Mesmer, who believed that the power involved in his healing work was psychological rather than physical (in Mesmer's case the key element was believed to be a magnetic fluid). For this reason Lady Lincoln's case offers a very useful example of early 19th century therapeutic intervention that presents some of the features of the later psychiatric and psychoanalytical work of Charcot, Freud and others. John-Pierre Peter, with whom I have been discussing his work in the history of medicine for many years, first brought the case to my attention about 18 months ago. I saw the possibility of writing a film script based on the Lady Lincoln case, for which there exists such a detailed day-by-day account, including even specific dialogue between patient and those attending on her. At present I am imagining something of a hybrid between documentary and fiction, with the 'factual' elements anchored in the present work and perspective of the research group in Paris, and the 'fictional' ingredients based on the doctors' reports of the Lincoln case, as well as the interpretations which are made of the text by the historians. There is rich ground for doing something original. I have talked about the project to the commissioning editor for documentaries at ARTE France, the distinguished French cultural TV channel, and he is very excited about the project, and is keen to be kept in touch with developments, though unable to support financially at this early stage.

title: 'Assaulting the Past': Placing Violence in Historical Context' conference to be held at St Anne's College, University of Oxford on 7th to 9th July 2005.
description: 'Assaulting the Past': Placing Violence in Historical Context The fact that this meeting brings together, for the first time, historians of medicine with historians of crime, is very important. Obvious links exist between both of these increasingly influential strands of the historical discipline (for example, the role of psychiatry in defining the 'criminal' and influencing the attitudes of the criminal justice system; the role played by coroners and medical practitioners in identifying crimes against the person; the medicalisation of infanticide; and the growing importance of forensic medicine since the eighteenth century, to name but a few). Traditionally, however, conferences devoted to the history of crime have tended to overlook the role of medicine and the medial profession entirely. Similarly, historians of medicine who address topics related to forensic issues have not embedded their work in the broader trends identified by historians of crime and violence. This conference will thus provide a unique forum for international scholars to discuss and debate interdisciplinary concerns related to the subject of violence in society, explicitly linking medicine and crime through the rise of forensic medicine. In doing so, it seeks to encourage fresh research into this area of study, both in a collaborative and a comparative context, to expand the boundaries of medical and social history, and to open innovative gateways for future research. Specific sessions will be devoted to the following topics: violence and insanity; violence and the body; domestic violence; gender and violence; theoretical assumptions (medical and otherwise) about violence; violence in a colonial context; regional patterns of violence; urban violence; the punishment of violence; trends in violence and criminal justice; and spectacles of violence.

title: 'Enabling the Past: New Perspectives in the History of Disability' conference to be held at the University of Manchester on 17-19 June 2005.
description: Enabling the Past: New Perspectives in the History of Disability History of disability is in its infancy in the UK. There is a need for a conference that begins a dialogue on the nature of 'disability', as a key historical category in its own right. This conference aims to integrate social and cultural perspectives of disability in a way that will allow a more subtle understanding of the part played by medicine, amongst other agencies, in shaping the nature of disability. If we are to develop a new integrated approach to the history of disability and medicine, we need to move beyond just conceptualising disability as a 'pathology' that individualises and marginalises the patient's experience. The conference, therefore, aims to sensitise historians of medicine (and other historians as well) to the potential methodologies and disciplinary frameworks needed for integrating disabled peoples' experiences, views and perceptions. The conference will tackle both broad, historiographical concerns as well as dealing with the specific histories of disability. Papers will be presented on the following topics: Why we need a 'new' other User perspectives on assistive technologies The challenges in historicising disabled agency War and the meanings of disfigurement Masculinity, rehabilitation and reconstruction Learning Difficulties, 'Maladjustment' and Autism 'Medicalisation' and 'Demedicalisation' of disability Analysing images of disability Disability activists are also very interested in the history of the subject; hence, I anticipate that there will be opportunities for outreach associated with the meeting.

title: 'Cultural History of Medicine Seminar Series' to be held at Goldsmiths College from October 2005 to March 2006.
description: Seminar: Cultural History of Medicine Seminar Series, Department of History, Goldsmiths College, Bi-Weekly, Wed afternoons beginning 12 Oct 2005 In recent years, there have been innovative methodological developments in cultural history, in particular exploring the relationship between philosophy, cultural theory and historical practice. In addition, there have been advances in the historical understanding of several fields of medical knowledge, including Chinese medicine, Indian ayurvedics and psychiatry. We believe there is a need to consider the intersection of these two streams of scholarship, and to thus explore anew the boundaries of the 'cultural history of medicine'. While recent scholarship in this field has tended to look at the social and experiential aspects of health and illness, we believe there is room to extend research in this field to include the history of ideas, of 'mentalities', and their intersection with medical thought and practice. Our proposal consists of a series of 12 seminars, held bi-weekly beginning October 2005. Six of the seminars would be given by members of the Department covering topics such as Kant's medical philosophy; Italian psychiatry and the history of ideas; post- war French psychiatry; occult practices in early modern Europe; the intersection between medical uses of animals and the scientific study of animals in the later Middle ages; the history of death in Africa. We envision coupling these six papers with six others, bringing in scholars whose work we feel enriches the debates present in our own research. We hope that the proposed Seminar Series fosters a strong relationship with the Wellcome Trust, whose new presence at Goldsmiths would help generate Research Themes to be explored in future collaborations with Wellcome.

title: The health consequences of orphan mobility in eastern Zimbabwe.
description: Manicaland HIV/STD Prevention Project The research programme being undertaken by the Manicaland Project currently comprises three components. 1. Studies on the temporal dynamics of HIV transmission, impact and control in a widely disseminated maturing sub-Saharan African epidemic. 2. Growing up in an AIDS- afflicted population: the nature, adequacy and sustainability of family and community coping mechanisms in rural Zimbabwe. 3. Epidemiology, mathematical modelling and tools for monitoring the response to the HIV/AIDS epidemic in Zimbabwe. These studies are being undertaken primarily through the conduct of population-based cohort surveys of approximately 10,000 adults and 1,000 children and their caregivers in Manicaland, Zimbabwe's eastern province. For the past two years the candidate has been working primarily on the second of the above studies. This study is designed to provide comparative information on childhood experience and outcomes according to orphan hood status in populations subject to a major HIV/AIDS epidemic. Particular attention is being paid to outcomes likely to affect health, well-being, productivity and fulfilment during adulthood. Specific aspects being investigated include nutrition, physical and psychosocial health, various forms of child abuse, and school education and qualifications. The nature and effectiveness of caregiver arrangements and other forms of support received from the extended family and the local community, NGOs and government sources are being described and assessed. The study design involves the recruitment and follow-up after 6 months, 18 months and 30 months of a cohort of 1,000 children stratified by initial orphan status and initial location of residence (towns, estates, roadside business centres and subsistence farming areas). Children who change households between survey rounds are followed to and re-interviewed in their destination households wherever possible. Recruitment and the first round of follow-up have been completed successfully and the second (18th month) round of data collection is currently underway. The candidate's project would add to this work through an in-depth description of the patterns of mobility and residence experienced by orphans as compared to non-orphans and the implications of observed differences for children's health and well-being.
recipient: London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE)

title: Risk factors for and effects of postpartum depression among women in four districts of the Brong Ahafo region of Ghana: a prospective cohort study.
description: A cohort study of independent associations between perinatal maternal depression and adverse infant and maternal health outcomes (including mortality) in the Kintampo district of the Brong Ahafo Region of Ghana.

title: Assessment of mental capacity in individuals with psychiatric disorders.
description: The project builds on previous work funded by Wellcome. Mental capacity is a cornerstone in the process of giving informed consent. The prevalence, associations and consequences of mental incapacity have not been sufficiently studied in clinical populations. Our first project involved acutely ill general hospital in-patients, and we determined that approximately 40% lacked mental capacity to make key treatment decisions. These patients were older and more cognitively impaired than patients who had mental capacity. We used transcripts of semi-structured interviews to determine that experts rating the interviews had good inter-rater reliability (mean kappa = 0.76). Our second study funded by Wellcome was the pilot study for the present proposal, and indicated firstly that two psychiatrists performing a semi-structured interview 1-2 days apart had good inter-rater reliability (kappa = 0.78). It also indicated that the proposed project is feasible, with satisfactory participation rates. The main aims are (1) To determine the prevalence of psychiatric in-patients who lack capacity to make key decisions regarding their treatment; (2) to test a series of hypotheses linking mental capacity with the use of the Mental Health Act, perceived coercion and the presence of cognitive impairment or delusions and (3) to describe the proportion of mentally incapacitated individuals who regain capacity by the time of discharge from hospital. A consecutive sample of 270 psychiatric in-patients will be approached and interviewed using the capacity interview, as well as measures of insight, perceived coercion, and clinical status. It will be possible from this study to determine the proportion of patients judged to lack mental capacity to make decisions regarding their current treatment. All incapacitated patients will be re-interviewed at the point of discharge, or six months following admission, to determine the proportion in whom capacity is regained over this period of time. Participants who are judged to lack capacity will be compared with those who are thought to have capacity on a range of clinical and demographic characteristics. We will then use univariate and multivariate statistical methods to compare these groups in terms of their legal status under the Mental Health Act (1983), their perception of coercion, and their insight into their condition.

title: Child Guidance in Inter-War Britain: Adopting and Adapting American Psychiatry.
description: The child guidance movement was central to the twentieth century shift in child health from concerns with the body to concerns with the mind. The movement took off after 1918, initially in the USA before coming to Britain in the mid-1920s. It was financed, in both countries, by the American philanthropic body the Commonwealth Fund (CF). Child guidance was to be promoted through designated clinics staffed by psychiatrists, psychologists, and psychiatric social workers. While emphasis was laid on teamwork, the psychiatrist was nonetheless the key figure. It was explicitly intended that this American psychiatric/medical model be adopted in Britain. This project will describe and evaluate the movement in inter-war Britain. Two research trips, supported financially by the Rockefeller Archive Center, have been made to the CF's archives to look at its records on British child guidance. This pilot project uncovered a huge volume of previously unexamined material. This part of the research is thus for the most part completed, at least from the point of view of gathering information. Archival material in Britain has also been worked on, for instance at the London School of Economics. Some archives need to be returned to while others, for example in Dundee, have yet to be visited. Funding is thus sought for one year to enable both the completion of archival research and the opportunity to interpret and write on these sources. The project will provide the first comprehensive analysis of British child guidance during its crucial, early phase; and in a broad, transatlantic, context. Work already undertaken suggests that in important respects the American psychiatric model was adopted here. This reflects two factors: first, the CF's financial support for British child guidance and the Fund's advocacy of the American model. Second, again often as a result of American financial support, British psychiatrists and social workers made observational trips to US child guidance clinics and often returned determined to put what they had observed into practice. However, this adoption was not complete. British psychiatric and social work practice also influenced the shape of the British child guidance movement, as did, especially in Scotland, educational psychology. The project will thus have as one of its central aims an assessment of the extent to which the American medical model was adopted in Britain and, on the other hand, the degree to which British practices were taken on in this new field of 'mental hygiene'.

title: Therapy in Ancient Mesopotamia.
description: The present application is for research leave for the 2005-2006 academic year (for a 12-month period), in order to write a book on Therapy in Ancient Mesopotamia. It is a re-submission. The applicant has a book contract with Blackwell Publishing to include the book within their series, Blackwell History of the Ancient World. The second reason for applying for research leave is to join two medical doctors working at the Cabinet d'Assyriologie of the Collège de France, under the direction of Professor Jean-Marie Durand, who has expressed an interest in my coming to Paris to work with his research group. The doctors, A. Attia and G. Buisson, have published three issues of a new journal, Le Journal des Médecines Cunéiformes. This project will reconsider the rôles of physician (as herbalist) and exorcist (as diagnostician), as well as the fundamental differences between two main genres of texts in Babylonian medicine, the diagnostic lists and therapeutic recipes. Other questions will be examined, such as, what is disease in Mesopotamia? How does one distinguish between disease and symptoms? How important was the 'placebo effect' in Babylonian pharmacology? Therapy in Ancient Mesopotamia will present a new assessment of healing practices, techniques, and psychology in Ancient Mesopotamia.

title: Hans Selye and the biology of stress: pilot project.
description: In 1936, the Austrian-Hungarian doctor and scientist, Hans Selye (1907-1982), described a syndrome characterised by non-specific physiological responses to harmful agents. According to Selye, the syndrome developed in three stages: an initial alarm phase; a second stage of adaptation to injury in which physiological resistance allowed normal function; and a final stage of exhaustion when adaptive mechanisms eventually failed. Selye initially termed this new syndrome 'general adaptation syndrome', but in an extensive range of subsequent publications he increasingly adopted the term 'stress' to explain non-specific physiological and pathological responses to injury. Although not routinely accepted by physiologists, Selye's theory of disease was taken up particularly by clinicians in the fields of allergy, clinical ecology, military medicine, psychology, and occupational health in order to explain the pathogenesis of a wide variety of conditions such as cancer, diabetes, heart disease, arthritis, allergies, and mental illness. In spite of its contribution to modern framings of disease and in spite of widespread public interest in stress, little historical attention has been given to the notion of stress or to its modern biological formulation by Hans Selye. The overall aim of this pilot project is to determine the feasibility of a large-scale project on Hans Selye and the history of stress. The pilot project carries three discrete aims: To identify, access, and survey potential archival sources in Canada, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, and the USA. To contact (and if possible carry out preliminary interviews with) surviving colleagues, family, and friends to Hans Selye. To determine the feasibility of a project/programme on the history of stress.

title: Children's emotional well-being in 19th and 20th centuries.
description: The application is for travel grant: to attend the conference on Health, Heredity & the Modern Home Centre for Medical History to be held at Crossmead Conference Centre, University of Exter, 21-23 March, 2005: Aim: To continue ongoing research for paper/chapter on 'home, mothering and children's emotional health, c1930s-1960s'. This visit is proposed to search Margaret Lowenfeld Papers and those of Susan Isaacs. I'm trying to build up a picture of changing concepts of child-rearing as portrayed by psychodynamic approaches and to suggest that 'liberal' child rearing is paralleled by changing ideas of house, home and mothering.

title: XIXth century origin (Bain versus Bastian) and current development of the controversy between centralist and periphalist theories of sense of movement, body awareness and motor control.
description: XIXth century origin (Bain versus Bastian) and current development of the controversy between centralist and periphalist theories of sense of movement, body awareness and motor control I am currently a temporary member of the French CNRS to conduct a program of research which concerns sensory functions, and in particular proprioception and body image in a historical perspective (XIXth-XXth century), and the relations between internal and external senses. The purpose of the visit is to take advantage of research facilities in London (the Wellcome Library, the British Library) while treating the following related themes: 1. XIXth century origin (Bain versus Bastian) and current development of the controversy between centralist and peripheralist theories of sense of movement, body awareness and motor control. 2. The role of abnormal cases and clinical categories (phantom limbs, allochiria, hemineglect, extinction, and autotopagnosia) in the birth and progress of a neurophysiological and a neuropsychological knowledge of so-called body image and body scheme(s). The question of abnormal beliefs related to the body (as in the case of somatoparaphrenia) considered as a frontier between neurology and psychiatry. 3. The "muscular sense" and the birth of a "proprioceptive system". The relation between (objective) proprioceptive information and (subjective) proprioceptive awareness. The Sherringtonian legacy - in particular, the recent changes both in the physiology of muscle spindles and in the assessment of their functions. 4. Molyneux's questions and the origins of the current interest of cognitive scientists in multisensory processes as a physiological issue - rather than a purely psychological one; the relation between internal and external sensory powers, and their significance for an integrated conception of sensory functions.

title: The role of SynGAP C-terminal variation in synaptic development and plasticity.
description: 1\. The role of SynGAP C-terminal variation in synaptic development and plasticity Abnormal glutamatergic signalling has been implicated in human developmental cognitive diseases, including certain forms of mental retardation, schizophrenia and autism. Therefore investigation of the mechanisms by which synaptic activity regulates the formation of neuronal connectivity is likely to yield insight into the cellular basis of these disorders. N-methyl d-aspartate receptors (NMDARs) are glutamate receptors that regulate synaptic plasticity, the cellular process that underlies synaptic development, learning and memory. SynGAP (a synaptically enriched GTPase activating protein) is a key downstream target of NMDAR signalling. Alternative splicing of Syngap mRNA produces protein isoforms that vary in their C-terminal peptide sequence (Syngap a1, a2, ß and ?). The C-terminus of SynGAP regulates its localisation and activity. Although SynGAP plays a critical role in neuronal development, nothing is known about the spatiotemporal expression profile of the different SynGAP isoforms. Recently we isolated two novel putative C-terminal isoforms that have the known protein-protein interaction domains replaced with peptide sequences with no conserved functional domains. Interestingly these 2 isoforms appear to arise from a non-conventional method of mRNA splicing. This project aims to investigate the regulation of SynGAP C-terminal variation and the possibility of a mechanism of regulation of synaptic plasticity involving non-conventional splicing of mRNA. The special aims of this project are: To characterise the spatiotemporal expression patterns of SynGAP C-terminal isoforms arising from conventional (SynGAP a1 and ß) and non-conventional splicing (SynGAP156 and 66) To determine the function and localisation of SynGAP C-terminal isoforms in cortical neuronal culture. To determine the subcellular localisation of Syngap mRNA and its response to activity.

title: Investigating the role of adult neurogenesis and glutamate transmission in the pathophysiology and treatment of depression.
description: Investigating the role of adult neurogenesis and glutamate transmission in the pathophysiology and treatment of depression Recent evidence suggests that a deficit in adult hippocampal neurogenesis may be critically involved in the pathophysiology of depression and that neurogenic activation may underlie the therapeutic efficacy of a number of antidepressant treatments. The aim of this project is to combine molecular, pharmacological, behavioural and genetic approaches to further investigate the neurogenic hypothesis, and provide a better understanding of the role of the glutamate system in its regulation. This research will increase our understanding of mood disorder aetiology and may provide vital information for the development of much needed novel and improved therapeutic strategies.

title: Walking here and there: movement, memory and delusion.
description: Walking Here And There: Movement, Memory and Delusion 'Walking, Here and There: Movement, Memory and Delusion' is a research and development project resulting from a collaboration between the artist Simon Pope and the neuropsychologist Vaughan Bell. The project aims to investigate the interaction of reference and memory in reduplicative paramnesia, a delusional belief that a place exists in two or more locations simultaneously. It uses video and performance to bring an experience of this otherwise exceptional condition into everyday life, to explore relationships between space, mobility, delusion and memory. Outcomes include audio/video recordings and a lecture/presentation at venues applicable to both disciplines. This project extends the research activity of both collaborators: Vaughan Bell is a Research Associate studying the neuropsychology of delusions and belief formation at Cardiff University and Cardiff and Vale NHS Trust; Simon Pope is a NESTA Fellow investigating walking as a contemporary visual art practice.

title: Khat-out of sight, out of mind.
description: Khat - out of sight, out of mind (working title) Khat - out of sight, out of mind, is a Research & Development project by oh/art looking at the biomedical, social and political implications of the use of Khat within the British Somali Community. Khat, a legally available drug is widely used within the Somali community but little known in the wider community. With a similar chemical component to amphetamine, excessive use can lead to serious mental health problems. This collaboration is between oh/art, a Somali playwright and a Somali-English translator to produce a 30 minute play that will have rehearsed readings in Somali and in English, working with Doctor Eleni Palazidou who specialises in mental health problems amongst Khat users in the Somali community. The project will ask questions about the problems facing the Somali Community, recreational and abusive drug use, the reasons Khat may have been left off government drugs lists and the physical/psychological effects of using Khat.

title: Synaesthesia & sound.
description: Synaesthesia & Sound The project has two broad aims. Firstly, to pre-produce a short animated film and complete a sound-visual orchestration that will have educational and entertainment value to the wider public. Secondly, it will further our understanding at a scientific level of how synaesthesia operates and how it relates to the type of multi-sensory processing that every one of us engages in. We will initially conduct original research utilising animation and evaluating the results. We will then develop the project to encompass more research, simultaneously expanding the animation into an artistic outcome. The culmination of this will be presented at the New London Orchestra's Music and the Mind Festival (May 2006). Synaesthesia & Sound will involve collaboration between: Dr Jamie Ward who heads the Synaesthesia Research Group, Department of Psychology, University College London; the New London Orchestra, in residence at UCL Bloomsbury; and Samantha Moore, animation director and project coordinator.

title: Panacea: the art of wellbeing.
description: Panacea: The Art of Wellbeing Panacea: The Art of Wellbeing is an evolving, expandable and travelling artwork designed to function as a universal formula to cure social, economic and political problems. Once it has reached a destination, Panacea releases its curing powers: a maquette from which evolve a number of artworks, whose forms vary according to the nature of its temporary home, whose effects will be tested by scientific evaluation processes. Panacea: The Art of Wellbeing will be developed in partnership with the John Hansard Gallery by the artists Zoe Walker, Neil Bromwich and Michael Pinsky in collaboration with the medical scientists Dr Mark Down, Dr Steve Warrington and Dr Peter Fraser Down. Panacea: The Art of Wellbeing will tour extensively in the UK and abroad. The artists and Dr Mark Down will explore the effectiveness of this artistic panacea by utilising scientific methodologies used by the medical drugs industry. The resulting investigations will refine and develop the artistic 'solutions' contained within the project.

title: The neurobiological basis of language: insights into late language acquisition and reading from deafness.
description: In my scientific career to date I have explored the impact of altered sensoryand language experience on cognition, language and the brain. In particular myresearch has focussed on individuals born profoundly deaf. During my PhD at University College London (UCL), I employed a cognitive developmental approachto explore the development of short-term memory in deaf children. In 1998 I was employed as the sole postdoctoral researcher on a Medical Research Councilgrant awarded to Prof. R. Campbell (UCL). I had direct responsibility for all day-to-day aspects of this research: participant recruitment, designing appropriate language assessments, designing functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) paradigms, collecting and analysing all behavioural and fMRI data, writing up data for publication (see Q16). This research generated the first and, to date, only fMRI studies of speechreading and British Sign Language processing with deaf participants. In 2001 I was awarded a Wellcome Trust Advanced Training Research Fellowship. This is based primarily at the Institute of Child Health (UCL) sponsored by Prof. Usha Goswami. The fMRI component is based at the Institute of Psychiatry, sponsored by Prof. Michael Brammer. During this Fellowship I have employed a combination of behavioural and neuroimaging methods to address how only a small minority of deaf people become skilled readers of English. As part of this Fellowship, I spent six months in Prof. Helen Neville's lab at the University of Oregon, where I learned the basics of recording event-related potentials (ERPs) using electroencephalography (EEG).

title: European perspectives on end of life decision making.
description: European perspectives on end of life decision making The Assisted Dying For The Terminally Ill Bill (which would enable doctors to perform AVE (active voluntary euthanasia) in strictly limited circumstances) is currently being considered by a House of Lords Select Committee which is expected to report in February/March 2005. This symposium will consider that report and will assess the safeguards built into the Bill, comparing them to those found in the Dutch Termination of Life on Request and Assisted Suicide (Review Procedures) Act 2001 and the Belgian Law Relating to Euthanasia 2002. The symposium will also consider end of life decisions other than active voluntary euthanasia, typically non-treatment decisions particularly in those cases where the patient is no longer competent. Funding is vital for this symposium due to the wide range of participants we are aiming to attract, both from the UK and abroad, and due to the fact that the symposium will be truly multi- disciplinary and therefore difficult to fund from a particular subject area. This symposium will be a conventional academic symposium in the sense that it will bring together professional, public and popular discourses on aspects of end of life decision-making. Topics to be covered would include: An evaluation of the current law and practice of active voluntary euthanasia (AVE) and assisted suicide in England and Wales. An appraisal of the Dutch and Belgian regulation of AVE. Reflections upon the report of the Select Committee on the Assisted Dying For The Terminally Ill Bill. The withdrawal and withholding of life-prolonging medical treatment from an incompetent patient in pursuance of an anticipatory decision. The withdrawal and withholding of life-prolonging medical treatment from an incompetent patient in accordance with the decision of the incompetent patient's proxy decision-maker. The determination of an incompetent patient's best interests in relation to life-prolonging medical treatment.

title: Key conceptual issues in the classification of somatoform and similar disorders: some outline proposals for a revised classification.
description: Key conceptual issues in the classification of somatoform and similar disorders; some outline proposals for a revised classification The need for the workshop comes from the large proportion of patients with somatoform or similar disorders, the confused state of the present classifications and the negative impact, both scientific and social, of this confusion. (Somatoform disorders are disorders characterised by medically unexplained physical symptoms.) There is now a window of opportunity to directly influence future classifications and to propose solutions that are acceptable to patients as well as to professionals. Within the biosciences there is wide recognition that there are serious problems with the classifications currently provided by the World Health Organisation (WHO) in the tenth edition (1992) of the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-10) and by the American Psychiatric Association (APA) in the fourth edition (1994) of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-IV). These classifications are criticised as being based on dubious assumptions and as being ambiguous, internally inconsistent and mutually incompatible. Progressive advances in neuro-biology have accentuated the inadequacies of the present classifications, which are now a great impediment to international research and communication. There have been direct calls for rethinking the classifications in editorials in the Journal of Psychosomatic Research (1998) and in Psychosomatics (2002), as well as in other articles by individual researchers. The symposium will address these difficulties and set out proposals for an improved classification. The topics to be covered include (1) an analysis of the conceptual problems involved in the classification of somatoform disorders, (2) two different senses of "somatisation", (3) the place of "psychological causation" in defining somatoform disorder and whether a satisfactory operational definition can be provided of this concept, (4) whether somatoform disorder should be listed as a mental disorder and the implications of this, (5) whether the category of somatoform disorder should be differently defined or abolished, and most importantly, (6) outline proposals for a revised classification.

title: The ethics of research with children and young people.
description: Research with and about children and young people has had a troubled history and has resulted in occasions where unethical practices have occurred (Shields & Twycross 2003, Aita & Richer 2005). Children and young people have been research subjects in many fields - nursing, medicine, education, psychology, health therapies, to name a few. Recently, research has been done in which children are part of the investigating team (Carter 2001). The ethical issues surrounding research are complex, changing and sometimes quite subtle. They are even more so when children and young people are involved. In the last few years, it has become recognized that developing countries have ethical issues surrounding the conduct of research which are more complex again, especially when children are involved. This conference will address these issues and raise awareness of their complexity and far reaching ramifications over a range of disciplines.

title: Core support for the Wellcome Trust Bloomsbury Centre for Research in Clinical Tropical Medicine.
description: The goal of the Bloomsbury Centre is to support and foster relevant research in Clinical Tropical Medicine that is of the highest quality and has a high potential for impact on international health policy. The LSHTM and our partner institutes provide a supportive environment in which Clinical Research Fellows can develop the international collaborative links and multidisciplinary expertise that are a prerequisite for a successful research career in Tropical Medicine. The LSHTM has particular strengths in multidisciplinary research, provides access to first rate training and ongoing support in research methods in epidemiology and clinical trial design and analysis. Our partner institutions provide expertise in child health, in international mental health research, and in digestive diseases research. Our strategy is to recruit the most talented and committed young clinicians, to provide them with the training they need to become independent researchers, and to support them as they complete their specialist training. In the next three years we propose to work with the Trust to expand the research training opportunities available to clinicians and scientists from our partner institutions in developing countries.
recipient: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine

title: Preserving twentieth-century case notes of the Royal Edinburgh Hospital.
description: Lothian Health Services Archive (LHSA) aims to conserve c25,500 folder-based case notes, 1907-1965, of the Royal Edinburgh Hospital for Mental and Nervous Disorders (REH). £75,194 is requested to cover salaries and materials. All other costs will be borne in-kind. Work will be undertaken over an 18-month period by a Project Conservator and a Conservation Assistant. The records have been prioritised for treatment because they meet a range of intellectual, conservation and access criteria. They are a scarce, nationally and internationally significant, archival resource created by arguably Scotland's most historically important psychiatric hospital. In line with the LHSA preservation and conservation policy, the project seeks to ensure the long- term preservation of the notes and to facilitate safe and easy access for the foreseeable future. Primarily, treatment will include surface cleaning, removal of metal paper fasteners, and realigning of creasing and folding. Treated case notes will then be housed in archival quality folders and boxes, labelled accordingly. They will be accessible to a wide-ranging audience likely to include historians carrying out Higher-Education-based research, doctors pursuing additional professional qualifications, PhD and MSc students, National Health Service staff, and members of the general public undertaking genealogical research, as well as LHSA archivists when answering written enquiries. All such access is managed by LHSA in conformity with current Scottish legislation and guidelines regarding confidential health records. LHSA collections have been held on deposit with the University of Edinburgh since 1981 and the Archive has been in its Main Library since 1988.

title: Beyond the Borderland of Mental Health: creating access to the archive of The Lady Chichester Hospital, Hove, 1905-1987, through a programme of conservation and listing.
description: The Lady Chichester Hospital was opened in 1899 by Dr Helen Boyle for treating nervous disorders in women and girls. Her pioneering work in this field is of international importance: she was among the first to promote the benefits of separating people with recoverable conditions - what she referred to as borderline cases - from the chronically ill. The survival of patient records is extraordinarily good, and of far greater diversity and interest than parallel series from County Asylums. But this extremely significant archive is currently unavailable for lack of useful finding-aids and of the poor physical condition of some of the material. The objective of the project is to preserve the archive, create means of access and make it more widely available. We propose to employ an Archivist and a Clerical Assistant for a year to produce a detailed list of the archive and a database of case-files. Conservation measures will proceed concurrently under the supervision of our Conservator to ensure the archive's long-term survival. The proposal will enable access to a wide range of users: medical practitioners will enjoy enhanced access, both for active work with former LCH patients and for clinical research in the field of mental illness; academic researchers in the history of medicine will have access to the archive for the first time; patients, their families and descendants will benefit from monitored access, particularly in the field of inherited conditions. Work will be compliant with the Data Protection Act 1998.

title: Mechanisms of endocannabinoid signaling and its role in the regulation of synaptic communication.
description: Cell-to-cell communication controlled by cannabinoids has been shown to play a crucial role in several normal and pathological processes, however, the cellular mechanisms underlying the cannabinoid effects are largely unknown. The overall goal of the proposed research is to reveal the molecular logic of endocannabinoid signalling in neuronal circuitries. The first project aims to clarify the identity of endogenous ligands activating cannabinoid receptors under physiological circumstances. The presence of distinct types of endocannabinoids as well as their receptors in the CNS suggests the possibility of the selective control of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic transmission. Second aim is to uncover the detailed mechanisms of endocannabinoid-mediated regulation of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic communication. To achieve this, experiments will be addressed to elucidate the relationship between endocannabinoid- and nitric oxide-mediated signalling. The third specific aim is to determine the interaction among CB1 cannabinoid receptors, 5-HT3 serotonergic receptors and a neuropeptide cholecystokinin know to co-exist at a subset of GABAergic axon terminals. We will elucidate the mechanisms of the release of cholecystokinin and its control by CB1 receptors. These experiments will be performed in the hippocampus and basolateral amygdala, in brain regions where cannabinoids may influence memory formation as well as anxiety.

title: Mind mapping.
description: Mind Mapping Research and Development Project Mind mapping is a collaborative research and development project involving scientists, artists and young all working together to explore neurological research on brain mapping, thought processing and where in the brain different 'subjects' are stored and controlled. We will also look at how our brains are continuously programmed throughout our lives and how this affects our decision making and automatic processing of huge amounts of information. The Mind Mapping project will develop, create and construct an innovative and informative sculptural installation inspired by the science of brain cell communication and neurological functioning. The aim of this artwork is to excite and stimulate young people by providing a graphic interactive experience of how the human brain works. Harriet Murray and Neil Taylor, both practising artists, will support and facilitate the installation. The project will include research and development by the artists together with Dr Bryson Gore, a science educator and Elaine Beattie Lecturer in Bio-Psychology at Goldsmith College, into ways of communicating brain functioning to young people. A cardboard labyrinth will emulate the structure of the brain, while the audience moving through it, represent physical thoughts. Visual art, video and audio stimuli will represent information stored in the brain. This with other sensory materials will influence the paths visitors take. The project will be created by 90-100 local schoolchildren aged 7-15 with the support of artists, teachers and scientists. They will help design, create and construct this exciting installation which will be exhibited for an invited audience of 300-400.

title: Genetics of specific reading and language disorders.
description: Evidence from twin and family studies has indicated a strong genetic component in specific language impairment (SLI) and specific reading disability (dyslexia). We have completed whole genome scans to identify genes giving rise to susceptibility in each disorder using a family based quantitative trait loci (QTL) approach and replicated our linkage results for four loci in independent sets of families. We propose to further analyse the regions of strong linkage with an association strategy to identify susceptibility genes. To achieve this aim we propose to collect 300-500 cases for each disorder to replicate association of specific alleles at candidate genes in the regions of linkage. We have evidence for a candidate gene associated with dyslexia and chromosome 6p22 and propose to identify two other QTLs on chromosome 18 for dyslexia and chromosome 16q24 for SLI. Genes will be further characterised for gene regulation and function based on existing knowledge of these genes and a number of experimental approaches. The overall aim is to understand the neurodevelopmental pathways implicated in the disorders and to provide better diagnostic tools and insight into potential therapies.

title: Genetics of specific reading and language disorders.
description: Evidence from twin and family studies has indicated a strong genetic component in specific language impairment (SLI) and specific reading disability (dyslexia).
