This means transforming the local and regional livestock market systems in such a way that pastoralists can engage profitably with other market-chain actors (e.g., intermediaries, retailers, and exporters), benefit from fairer policies and receive high quality, fee-based animal health services. The overall goal of the project is to contribute to the long-term improvement of livelihoods and well-being of marginalised pastoralists in the state of Kassala in Eastern Sudan. The project will directly benefit 5,407 pastoralists and their families, making the total number of beneficiaries 27,035. Transformations in the livestock market systems in Kassala State have the potential of indirectly benefiting a further 190,000 pastoralists and their families. Other stakeholders involved in the livestock subsector will also benefit from the project. The project is relevant to every aspect of the grant programme. It contributes to the livelihoods of pastoralists, not only through the implementation of a concrete project in Kassala but also through the production of new knowledge for the advancement of community-based, market-based models for the development of livestock markets and animal health in developing countries.

title: Sustainable parasite management and environmental health on livestock farms.
description: The overall goal of the proposed project is the translation of ecotoxicological research outcomes into tangible improvements of animal health management by South African farmers / livestock keepers. We will: establish baseline data of healthy dung beetle communities for reference in assessments of pasture health ; publicise the importance of dung beetles and sound farming practices for healthy agro-ecosystems; communicate our results in international peer-reviewed journals, the popular agricultural press, conferences, workshops and farmers' meetings; establish an internet site for readily accessible information about importance of dung beetles to healthy ecosystems, and about which animal health products have been assessed for environmental safety; expand our network of influential organizations and individuals in the livestock industry in order to lobby on awareness of environmental issues. The target audience will include individual farmers (especially poor, emerging ones), the animal health industry (via the Agricultural and Veterinary Chemical Association of SA), livestock producers' organizations, the SA Government Department of Agriculture and the SA government Registrar of Veterinary Drugs whom we will continue to lobby for changes to the laws on registration of animal health products to include assessment of dung beetle friendliness. The objectives will be addressed by research using dung beetles as indicators for pasture health and the environmental effects of new antiparasitic products (undertaken by our Scarab Research Group, University of Pretoria); workshops targeting the major role players in the animal health sector; training workshops for agricultural extension officers for communicating the information specifically to emerging rural farmers; establishing a database of role players in the animal health industry; producing a dynamic website on which relevant information on the project will be placed; producing hard copy brochures, postures and publications on the subject and research results for dissemination to known interest groups and for public display at agricultural cooperatives and exhibitions.

title: Community-directed brucellosis control by small-scale dairy farmers in Zimbabwe.
description: Brucella was controlled in Zimbabwe until 2001, when the government veterinary services discontinued free vaccinations and disease surveillance due to financial constraints. Small-scale farmers did not seek vaccines from other sources, in part because they were not aware of the benefits of vaccination. Initially, this was not dangerous as brucellosis was absent from small-scale farming areas. Later, uncontrolled cattle movements following the invasions of commercial farms resulted in animals of unknown disease status mingling with the naive, unvaccinated animals. As a result, brucellosis is a potentially serious problem in cattle, and because of the practice of consuming unpasteurized, fermented milk products, also in people. Currently small-scale dairy farmers are served by Dairy Development Project (DDP), which maintains a network of cooperatives for collecting and selling milk throughout Zimbabwe. The PI has worked with DDP conducting courses for small-scale dairy farmers, during which she first recorded the lack of knowledge about, or administration of, brucella vaccinations. Clinical brucellosis in livestock keepers and those handling or consuming raw milk is unlikely to be diagnosed at the local clinics staffed by nurses. They are not expecting brucellosis and lack serological tests to differentiate it. Thus, livestock keepers, primarily women, are unlikely to be treated and will suffer the debilitating effects of chronic brucellosis, including depression and suicide. The project aims to increase widespread use of preventive practices for Brucella. The farmer's knowledge will be evaluated pre- and post-information sessions to assess knowledge dissemination methods. Each community, guided by the research team, will decide suitable health promotion strategies. Community directed disease control is the only sustainable way to control the brucellosis hazard. Any strategies developed will have to be sustained, although after successful, widespread vaccination, the number of human cases is expected to decrease. Maintaining success depends on each community's commitment to pay for the scheme.

title: Personality disorder and moral responsibility.
description: When psychiatrists address the issue of personality disorders, they do so from two standpoints. On the one hand, they try to place these in an explanatory, deterministic context. On the other, they often face the task of deciding when and to what extent patients with personality disorders should be held responsible for their actions. Moral responsibility rests on assumption of free will i.e. that the person could have done otherwise. However, some of history's famous moral statements (e.g. Martin Luther, "Here I stand, I can do no other") make it clear that the freedom or otherwise of actions may not be the critical issue. Instead, we may need to focus on moral character and the extent to which an individual is responsible for this. Theories of free will exist on a spectrum which runs from "hard determinism" at one end, through various "compatibilist" theories (i.e. that free will is compatible with determinism or that moral responsibility is compatible with the absence of libertarian free will) to "radical libertarianism" at the other (Kane, 2002). Determinist theories of action have a clear plausibility but also pose a serious threat to any concept of a moral order and to many of our ideas of what confers value on persons. The present project has two main aims. The first of these is to review recent thinking on free will and to apply this to the issue of personality disorder and moral responsibility. The second is to examine ways in which we might be seen as responsible for our moral characters. This will seek to extend my work on the psychology of aesthetics.

title: Dimensions and social determinants of older people's health and ability to make health maintaining and promoting investments in Nigeria: Implications for policy
description: The proposed research aims to examine, and generate a hitherto non-existent, interpretively based, in-depth understanding of § The dimensions of older people's health, functional status and well-being in the Nigerian context§ The individual, familial/intergenerational and structural factors that determine older people's access to and use of health services and their ability to make other health maintaining/promoting investments (e.g. adequate nutrition)§ The relative capacity of older people compared to younger-generation family members to make investments in their health.In developing such an understanding, the goals of the research are to:Contribute to the building of an urgently needed evidence base to inform the development of strategies to enhance health and health care for Nigeria's growing older population, as part of the broad National Health Policy and Human Development agenda currently pursued in Nigeria. Contribute to key academic debates in social gerontology and public health, specifically on questions of the social and life course determinants of health in old age; the nature of intergenerational justice, resource allocation and old age support in families; the relationships between old age and poverty.

title: Early recurrent pain and its effect on adult pain processing.
description: This project therefore takes a multidisciplinary approach by combining psychological and behavioural assessment of children with recurrent pain together with an animal behavioural study of the effects of recurrent pain in juvenile rats. The student will therefore be primarily supervised by Prof. Maria Fitzgerald with psychological supervison from Prof Amanda Williams, Reader in Clinical Health Psychology at UCL.

title: Changing family relationships and peri-natal depression in Turkey.
description: This study is carried out in the context of rapidly changing family support networks in Turkey as a result of trans-national and rural-urban migration, and the adoption of 'Western' lifestyles. The primary objective is to investigate the associations between quality of family relationships (particularly between a woman, her mother and mother-in-law) and ante-natal (AND) and post-natal depression (PND). The proposed project is a prospective study of 750 women who will be recruitedfrom 20 urban and rural clinics in and around Ankara. Participants will be interviewed in the third trimester and then followed till 2 months after childbirth with an interim examination at 1 month. At each interview, a standard instrument (the Edinburgh Post-natal Depression Scale) will be administered to identify symptoms of AND/PND. Structured questionnaires will be administered to rate the quality of women's relationships with their husband, mother and mother-in-law. As a secondary objective, the study will also investigate the association between male child preference (for the woman, her family, and her husband's family) and PND in women who have had a female child. These findings will be compared between urban and rural sites which, it is anticipated, will differ substantially in terms of family structures and expectations.

title: Adverse childhood experiences among women victims of trafficking deported back to Moldova, and mental health consequences of being trafficked.
description: A rise in the crime of human trafficking is taking place in several countries of Eastern Europe, one being Moldova. Those trafficked are subjected to gross violations which are likely to effect long-term mental and physical health. Recent international protocols call for collaboration in prosecuting offenders, and in providing for the support of victims. The goals are: 1) To use a case-control study to investigate antecedent characteristics of women victims of trafficking, especially adverse childhood experiences. Cases will be drawn at random from those deported home via the International Organisation for Migration. Controls will be non-trafficked women matched for age and district of residence from where the trafficking occurred. 2) To survey women victims of trafficking (VoT) to measure the prevalence of common mental disorders, post-traumatic stress disorder and disability around three months after deportation in relation to level of adversity experienced as part of the trafficking and deportation and to social support after deportation. Better knowledge of the characteristics of women VoT, and of mental disorders consequent to being trafficked, should assist in designing interventions to assist those deported back home.Moldova provides an ideal setting, given the high level of trafficking and the presence of of a system through the International Organisation for Migration for registering repatriated women VoT.

title: Towards a better understanding of the exceptionally low prevalence of DSMIV dementia in a community-based population of South India.
description: The collaboration between 10/66 Dementia Research Group (the research arm of Alzheimer's Disease International) and The Institute of Neurological Sciences- Voluntary Health Services began in 1998 with the appointment of a collaborative fellow in dementia. The instruments for dementia diagnosis were developed or translated and validated through this collaborative fellowship over an 18 month period. Subsequently funding from Alzheimer's Disease International resulted in the development of a cartoon book intervention for caregivers and subsequently in the collection of pilot data on cognitive impairment and depression in the elderly. In 2002 the World Health Organization funded the project initiated by IOP-KCL with TINS-VHS as one of two centres in India. Targeted 1000 community living elderly had been screened for cognitive impairment and depression using an extensive one-stage screening procedure developed and validated by the 10/66 dementia research group. A randomised controlled trial of the cartoon book caregiver intervention for patients with MCI and dementia as well as a number of nested case-control studies examining important risk factors and well as protective factors for cognitive impairment are proposed in this population. The current proposal will draw on this extensive background of local experience in studying cognitive impairment among community living elderly.

title: The role of stimulant drug treatment in children's moral understandings of the self.
description: This study contributes children's voices to the national debates (eg. President's Council on Bioethics) over the ethical implications of rising child psychiatric diagnoses, increasing use of drugs in child psychiatry, and "enhancing" performance with psychotropic drugs. These voices provide an empirical basis for ethical debate, judgement, and decisions in national policy arenas, which had previously not been taken into account. Findings from this study will also inform clinical and parental practices around child behaviour management, diagnosis and treatment.
recipient: London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE)

title: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), Food Additives, and the History of the Feingold Diet, 1970-Present.
description: This research aims to trace the history of the Feingold Diet and to identify those factors that led first to its acceptance and ultimately to its rejection. The project will integrate constructively three different areas in the history of medicine, namely the histories of mental health, allergy, and nutrition. In addition to providing an original academic contribution to the histories of these specific fields, the project will also encourage informed debate about the disorder and about the processes of medical classification and labelling amongst patients, their families, and the medical profession.

title: Psychopathology and Concepts of Demonical Possession in Late Antiquity and the Byzantine Period.
description: The proposed study wants to define the precise relationship between psychopathological and religious and/or demonological concepts of disease. Case studies include ephialtes, in which the patient suffers some form of nightmare, as well as lycanthropy, where the sufferer believes himself or herself to be a wolf. The emergence of such nosological concepts in medical writings shows how popular beliefs, with their origins in superstition, myth, magic, and religion, were embellished with the pathology of humours. The fact that medical authors discuss the conditions mentioned above primarily between 300 and 1100 AD and again between 1550 and 1650 AD dictates the time frame of the proposed PhD. The thesis will consider the entire body of the surviving late classical and Byzantine literature that reflects on the way people suffering from mental illness or demonical possession were treated, or comments on the clinical pictures in question. Such comprehensive textual basis will not least serve to place and thus view the medical texts in their broader cultural context. A separate chapter will be devoted to the lasting impact ancient notions of lycanthropy and ephialtes had on the Early Modern debate on beliefs in demonical possession, incubus, witchcraft and werewolves.

title: Physicke for mind, body and soul: the diagnosis, treatment and experience of melancholy in early modern England.
description: This research will explore the links between early modern medical and religious practices and their respective efforts to diagnose and treat psychological dysfunction associated with discontent and depression. Interdisciplinary in its scope, the thesis will draw upon contemporary medical, theological and literary works in an attempt to understand better early modern perceptions of human interiority and its relationship to the body, mind and soul. This project will include an examination of conditions during the period associated with chronic unhappiness (such as melancholy, grief and despair) and a subsequent analysis of how these various forms of depression were understood within both medical and religious contexts. The thesis will aim to demonstrate how contemporary understandings of sadness and discontent emerged from both medical-physical and spiritual-supernatural teachings on human existence and, in turn, how such a multi-discipline paradigm resulted in a highly eclectic approach to psychological therapy.

title: Student elective for Mark Lawrence
description: Characterisation of sensory neurons produced by pluripotent mouse neural crest-like stem cells The regulation of cell determination is a central issue in developmental biology. There has been much recent interest in postnatal stem cells and their unexpectedly broad differentiation capacity because of the potential therapeutic implications. We established from neonatal mouse skin three immortal, pluripotent stem cell lines that resemble neural crest stem cells and are capable of producing at least three cell lineages (melanoblasts/melanocytes, neurons and Schwann precursor cells).They promise to be valuable tools for study of cell determination. Neuronal differentiation of these cell lines is the least well characterised. We plan to expose pluripotent neural crest-like stem cells to growth/differentiation factors known to control determination of sensory neurons in short-term cultures: brain derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), neurotrophic factor (NT3), fibroblast growth factor 2 (FGF2) and nerve growth factor (NGF). We have preliminary data showing that in the presence of these factors very long bipolar neuron-like cells and large, dendritic cells resembling sensory neurons appear in the cultures. The student will repeat and confirm these observations, analysing and recording changes of cell morphology using photo microscopy. He will also study effect of these factors on cell proliferation by counting cell numbers before and some time after growing the cells in the presence of these growth actors by haemocytometer. To test whether morphologically different cells are indeed sensory neurons he will perform immunocytochemical analysis of these cells by using a marker of sensory neurons (substance P) and neuronal markers (neuronal tubulin beta 3 and a neurofilament subunit).

title: Closing the loop: interactive dissemination and validation of empirical medical ethics research studies.
description: This is an application to fund a project to run workshops, in order to disseminate and validate the results of a set of three Wellcome Trust-funded medical ethics empirical research studies. These medical ethics studies centre on the issue of competence and treatment decision-making in anorexia nervosa. This issue is important because anorexia nervosa is a mental disorder with a high morbidity and mortality, yet patients characteristically refuse treatment in spite of a good understanding of their problems. This presents particular problems to mental health professionals with respect to decisions about whether to use compulsory treatment. Method: This project will achieve its aims through the following strategies: - Literature search and theoretical analysis of issues of dissemination and translation; - Workshops - presentation of results, obtaining feedback and engaging in dialogue and consultations with clinicians, patients and parents, and experts in the field; - Integrating theoretical analysis and outcome of workshops with study results in the form of two written reports, one for publication in a medical education journal and one for open access through the Wellcome Trust website. Outcomes: 1.The publicising of Wellcome Trust-funded empirical medical ethics research to disparate groups of participants; 2.Promoting user involvement in the research process by obtaining feedback on the results, to refine the analysis and validate the results; 3.The publication of two reports: a clinically- oriented peer-reviewed journal paper and a written report for the Wellcome Trust; 4.The development of ideas for the future direction of new research in the field of empirical medical ethics in psychiatry.

title: Imaging neuroscience at the Functional Neuroimaging Laboratory (FIL)
description: The FIL is a prime example of a UK based laboratory that is an established world leader. This application for a Strategic Award is motivated by the need to secure the future of the FIL. The FIL supports a large portfolio of Wellcome Trust (WT) supported programme and project grant research, fellowships and studentships. A Strategic Award will enable the laboratory to retain its highly-skilled core infrastructure support staff; ensure a context of excellence to enable Wellcome Trust funded principal investigators (PIs) to continue producing science that is world class and high impact; and enable the laboratory to provide specific added value. A key example of the latter is in the field of bio-mathematics and data-analysis where our goal is to provide a common platform (extended SPM) for integrating data across distinct imaging modalities including fMRI, magneto-encephalography (MEG) and electro- encephalography (EEG). Finally, a Strategic Award will enable the FIL to provide a theoretical-neuroscience framework that informs both basic and clinically-oriented research into common neurological and psychiatric diseases.

title: Defining the genetic architecture of Crohn's Disease.
description: We propose a pilot study to test the association of 100,000 specific polymorphisms with a range of common diseases using a two stage case-control study design. The study will include diabetes, breast cancer, cardiovascular disease, bipolar disorder, and other diseases (2,000 samples each), as well as two common control groups (up to 3,000 samples total) for further evaluation. Positive associations will form the basis for future biological studies. The results will be used to evaluate how best to optimise the design, implementation, analysis and cost efficiency of large-scale and genome-wide association studies in the future. We will examine features such as SNP selection, analysis methods, population structure, study size, the use of common controls, heterogeneity in sample collections, linkage disequilibrium and SNP tagging. The results will provide independent assessment of the coverage of SNP panels that are available to the community for genetic studies, including the output of the International HapMap Project. The project will help to establish a separate training programme in statistical genetics, and will lay the foundations for the development of an infrastructure for UK research in this area in future years.

title: Mechanisms regulating transmitter release from central noradrenergic neurones.
description: Importance of the central noradrenergic system for human health can be illustrated by just one fact: according to some estimates up to 20% of the Western population may suffer from depression during some periods of their life and numerous studies have linked depression to the brain noradrenergic system. Surprisingly, most of the current ideas about this system are based on studies on peripheral models. This project will establish several fundamental characteristics of the central noradrenergic n eurones using a range of novel approaches recently developed in our laboratories. Noradrenergic neurones in organotypic brainstem cultures will be targeted with adenoviral vectors with a cell-specific promoter which allows visualisation of these cells for patch clamp recordings and confocal Ca2+ measurements in somata, dendrites and axonal varicosities. Mechanisms governing Ca2+ elevations in individual varicosities will be studied and compared with these in dendrites. Release of noradrenaline f rom individual varicosities will be registered using microamperometry under visual control. Viral vectors will also be used to genetically manipulate the properties of these neurones, such as their resting membrane potential. Using these approaches we will investigate the mechanisms which control release of noradrenaline from different parts of NA neurones in response to various signalling events.

title: Predictive genomic and transgenic analysis of tachykinin gene regulatory systems in the amygdala.
description: The products of the TAC1 gene, that include the tachykinin substance-P, are expressed in the amygdala where they play an important role in the modulation of fear and anxiety. Understanding the systems that regulate TAC1 expression in the amygdala may provide an important step towards understanding the causes of chronic depression and anxiety that affect 10% of the UK population at some point in their lives. We have used a novel series of post-genomic bioinformatic strategies in combination with transgenic analysis, immunohistochemistry and transgenic organotypic culture to provide evidence that a remote amygdala specific enhancer drives the expression of TAC1 in the amygdala under the influence of the MEIS-1 transcription factor. We will use our unique transgenic lines, that express a marker gene under the influence of ECR1, and the combined skills of all four applicants to examine 1. the DNA- protein interactions, 2. the signal transduction pathways and 3. the ligand receptor interacti ons that make up the regulatory systems that modulate ECR1 activity in the amygdala in both unstressed and mildly stressed transgenic models. Understanding how these regulatory systems operate will facilitate the identification of novel drug targets and the development of more efficacious and specific anti-depressive and anxiolytic therapies.

title: The Consequences and Outcomes of Convulsive Status Epilepticus in Children.
description: The central hypothesis of this study is that convulsive status epilepticus (CSE) is associated with brain injury, particularly to the hippocampus, which predisposes individuals to subsequent development of epilepsy and associated neurodevelopmental and/or behavioural dysfunction. CSE is the most common medical neurological emergency in childhood with an incidence of 18-20/100,000 children per year. The possible adverse outcomes from childhood CSE include subsequent epilepsy, permanent neurol ogical, developmental or cognitive deficits, or death. The proposed study will characterise structural brain abnormalities and identify early predictors of adverse outcomes, with particular emphasis on the hippocampus and mesial temporal sclerosis (MTS). Understanding the genesis of MTS would provide a framework for development of strategies that could reduce morbidity associated with MTS. My previous studies have shown evidence of hippocampal oedema and evidence of longer-term hippocampal injur y 6 months following CSE, although not all of the magnetic resonance criteria for MTS have been met. In the work proposed, the natural history of MTS and other structural brain abnormalities will be investigated using longitudinal quantitative magnetic resonance imaging in children with CSE. Prediction of morbidities based on magnetic resonance parameters will allow early identification of children who would develop an adverse outcome and promote early treatment.

title: In-vivo and In-vitro Control of Adult Neural Progenitor Differentiation in the Hippocampus by Retinoic Acid.
description: All-trans retinoic acid (tRA) has been widely investigated as a regulator of the embryonic CNS [1], a topic we have extensively studied [2-10]. Much less is known however regarding its influence on the adult brain [11]. We were the first to show that RA influences one aspect of hippocampal neuroplasticity neurogenesis [12, 13] and this proposal tests a new hypothesis that a precise equilibrium of tRA is essential to maintain this process. We will test this hypothesis by disrupting the bal ance of RA either by over-stimulation via treatment with 13-cis RA, used in the anti-acne drug Accutane [14] or under- stimulation using a retinol-binding protein null mutant mouse as a model for vitamin A deficiency. The effects of imbalance will be tested on three defined, quantifiable aspects of neurogenesis, determining: 1) the influence of varying RA concentrations on neuronal birth, 2) candidate cell cycle proteins influenced by RA and 3) RA s influence on neuronal maturation. New modulat ors of neurogenesis are currently sought because of their potential importance in CNS repair and psychiatric disease [15-17] and this proposal will characterize a new neurogenic modulator unique because of its ability to be adjusted by both dietary and genetic means.

title: Functional importance of RNA editing of the 5-HT2C receptor in vivo using a gene-targeting approach.
description: Abnormalities in serotonergic neurotransmission through 5-HT2C receptors (2CR) have been implicated in several diseases of the CNS, namely mood disorders, schizophrenia, eating disorders and Parkinson s Disease. As well as being regulated by conventional mechanisms, ligand availability and receptor number - 2CR signalling is also subject to a relatively rare and novel machanism of regulation, that of RNA editing, carried out by the adenine deaminase enzymes. This results in three different amino acids encoded in the fully-edited RNA compared to the non-edited. In transfected cells, edited 2CR mRNA encodes a receptor protein with reduced G-protein coupling, decreased agonist potency and no constitutive activity. Hence, expression of different edited isoforms, at similar levels to normal expression, could have dramatic effects on 2CR neurotransmission and hence alter behaviour. Evidence exists for RNA editing of 2CR in vivo, but its functional consequences have not been demonstrated. U sing gene-targeted mice that only express the non-edited or edited form of 2CR, we shall determine the cellular and behavioural consequences of RNA editing of 2CR in the whole animal. These studies may identify novel targets for drug intervention where abnormal 2CR neurotransmission has been identified as a contributing factor to disease symptoms.

title: Contrasting immune adaptation in peripheral organs and the central nervous system in response to chronic infection in health and disease.
description: Systemic inflammation or infection leads to the generation of inflammatory cytokines in the periphery that communicate with the brain to initiate cytokine synthesis there. These cytokines in the brain in turn give rise to fever and behavioural changes such as anorexia, loss of activity and depression, known as sickness behaviour. It is well known that repeated or sustained systemic inflammatory challenges lead to a state of immune tolerance in the periphery: an important protective mechanism ag ainst over-activity of the immune system. We will investigate whether there is a state of immune tolerance induced in the brain, after repeated or sustained peripheral inflammatory challenges, using measures of cytokine production and the associated behaviours. We have evidence that, in brain, repeated systemic challenges do not lead to the same state of innate immune tolerance as seen in the periphery. We will investigate the cell types and potential pathways involved in the non-tolerant state. We will investigate whether an immune tolerant state is evoked in brains with ongoing neurodegeneration, in which the innate immune system is already primed by the pathology. We predict that the lack of innate immune tolerance mechanisms in the brain will exacerbate the progression of chronic neurodegenerative disease.

title: Approaching the function of the vertebrate Nipbl/Mau-2 complex by creating and analysing a series of mouse Mau-2 mutants.
description: We recently demonstrated that mutations in NIPBL, an orthologue of the fly developmental regulator Nipped-B and yeast sister chromatid cohesion protein Scc2, cause a severe developmental disorder, Cornelia de Lange syndrome. With Wellcome Trust funding we are currently analysing the function of Nipbl in a mouse knockout model. Our follow-up work showed that NIPBL protein binds MAU-2, a protein encoded by another gene previously unstudied in vertebrates but an orthologue of a cell and axon migrat ion guidance factor in C.elegans. We found that C.elegans and human MAU-2 are involved in chromosome segregation/cohesin loading and that they are homologues of S.cerevisiae Scc4, a protein that interacts with Scc2 to load cohesins onto chromatin. The chromosome segregation function of the Scc2 and Scc4 protein families appears evolutionary conserved from yeast to man, but in metazoans the two proteins have acquired new roles in regulating developmental pathways, some of which are common to the two partners. Using a genetic approach we aim to explore the biological function of the Nipbl/Mau2 complex in a vertebrate model system by creating and characterising an allelic series of mouse Mau-2 mutants that will be referenced against, and tested for genetic interaction with, equivalent Nipbl mutants.

title: Does reducing depression and/or anxiety symptoms of low-income married women (residing in Hay el Sellom) using a community based psycho-social intervention decrease their complaints of medically unexplained vaginal discharge?
description: The main aim of this proposal is to evaluate the impact of a psycho-social intervention on medically unexplained vaginal discharge (MUVD) in a group of married, low-income Lebanese women aged 18-49 suffering from moderate levels of anxiety and/or depression. The intervention components will include structured social support group discussions and trainer-supervised relaxing exercises. Women receiving the intervention will attend 24 weekly sessions. The intervention was chosen based on evidence-based literature on psycho- social interventions on mental health taking into consideration the cultural context of the study and the observed association between mental distress and reported MUVD. The intervention will be compared to usual care using a randomized controlled trial design. A total of 3630 women will be recruited from Hey el Solloum, a southern suburb of Beirut. The primary outcome will be self-reported MUVD after administering a medical exam to rule out reproductive tract infections (RTIs), with anxiety and/or depression acting as the mediating intermediary factor. Women with RTIs or who are severely depressed and/or suicidal will be clinically assessed and referred for treatment. Intention to treat analysis will be used. Findings will be shared with practitioners, policy makers and the media through various dissemination methods, including workshops and meetings.

title: Understanding the mechanisms by which exercise supports coping with stress.
description: Evidence is accumulating that regular voluntary exercise (but, for clarity, not forced exercise or extreme endurance training) improves mental wellbeing and helps to alleviate various mood disorders. Recent studies suggest that the regular performance of exercise enhances the ability to successfully cope with stressful events. The mechanisms underlying these beneficial effects of exercise are, however, currently unknown but may involve adjustments in glucocorticoid responses to stress. We have d eveloped a model of long-term voluntary exercise in the rat which suggests that a major aspect of the exercise-mediated adaptation to stress occurs through modulation of the sympathetic nervous system. Surprisingly, the way(s) in which the sympathetic nervous system modulates adrenal glucocorticoid secretion during stress have not been fully investigated and not at all in exercising animals. Here we wish to investigate the mechanisms through which this occurs by: (1) Studying the role of the sym patho-adrenal system in modulating glucocorticoid responses to physically demanding and psychological stresses, (2) Investigating activation of the central nervous system pathways which regulate efferent adrenal innervation, and (3) Determining the role of the medial prefrontal cortex in stress-induced sympatho-adrenal responses, glucocorticoid responses and neuronal activation patterns in pathways regulating efferent adrenal input.

title: Analysing PLA2 signalling as a potential therapeutic target for branched shortchain fatty acids using the model system Dictyostelium.
description: Phospholipase A2 (PLA2) signalling is attenuated by valproic acid (VPA) in the mammalian brain by an unknown mechanism, and this has been postulated to play a role in epilepsy and bipolar disorder treatment. We have shown that VPA also attenuates PLA2 signalling in the simple biomedical model, Dictyostelium. We have identified a PLA2 enzyme controlling VPA sensitivity in Dictyostelium, and this protein has an uncharacterised human homologue. We will ablate, over- express and mutate the Dictyostel ium PLA2 protein, and use the resulting mutants to examine the cellular function of the enzyme. We will also characterise the upstream regulation and potential downstream targets of the protein. Analysis of the role of VPA in the absence of PLA2 activity will help to identify other VPA targets. We will also complement the Dictyostelium mutant with the identified human homologue to enable the analysis of the human gene in a PLA2 null background. We will also identify structural constraints for PL A2 inhibition in a mammalian model and will test for the incorporation of VPA into lipids. This work will provide a greater understanding of the cellular role of PLA2 signalling, and its role as a target for the therapeutic compound, VPA.

title: The neuropharmacological substrates of stimulus associability in the rat.
description: The salience of stimuli is, on some accounts, identified as an important determinant of their associability or usefulness for learning. The dopamine (DA) system has been identified as a critical substrate of associative learning and we propose to further investigate its role by selective regional depletion and drug microinjections studies. The project has translational relevance because the aberrant processing of stimulus salience and the DA system are both key to our understanding of disorders featuring attentional disturbance (e.g., schizophrenia). We need to know whether the different aspects of salience which arise from intrinsic and acquired properties of the stimulus are equivalent from the associative learning perspective. This question will be addressed by systematically comparing salience reduced in overshadowing and latent inhibition procedures, to test for differences between intrinsic and acquired salience. We will furthermore test for dissociable roles of DA D2 and D1 rece ptor families, in latent inhibition and overshadowing, respectively. Because nucleus accumbens, the key dopaminergic structure for selective learning is functionally heterogenous, we will compare dose-related effects at medial and lateral sites. Novel pharmacotherapeutic implications could follow from the project predictions, for example the use of DA D1 agonists for aspects of the attentional disturbance of acute schizophrenia.

title: Urocortin 3 and the Corticotropin Releasing Factor Type 2 Receptor: Role in HPA axis functions and stress-related behaviours in transgenic mouse models.
description: Corticotropin-Releasing Factor (CRF) and related ligands are major co- ordinators of hormonal and behavioural responses to stressors. Effects are mediated via CRF type 1 (CRFR1) and type 2 (CRFR2) receptors. CRFR1 is dominant in stimulating the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis (HPAA) and anxiety-like behaviours. Studies reveal both potential anxiolytic and anxiogenic roles for CRFR2 and its highly selective ligands Urocortin-2 and Urocortin-3. Effects are seemingly site, time course and paradi gm specific. We hypothesise acute CRFR2 activation in adult CNS promotes HPAA activation and anxiety-like behaviours, while chronic stimulation results in a depressive phenotype. With Professor Wylie Vale (Salk Institute) we have generated transgenic mice with neuronal-specific Urocortin-3 overexpression predicted to provide a unique model of chronic CRFR2 activation. We will exploit these to study acute or chronic effects of CRFR2 exposure to ligand within the CNS. We will detail CNS expression of CRF receptors and ligands, dissect HPAA and sympathoadrenal responses and assess anxiety- and depression-like behaviours under basal, acute and chronic stress conditions. We will use lentivirus-based overexpression of Urocortin-3 or CRFR2 knockdown to further dissect site- specific functions of CRFR2 and consider the potential molecular basis for the phenotypes by examining corticosteroid and serotonergic receptor expression in these models.

title: Child Health, growth and development in relation to maternal disorder in Ethiopia (the C-MaMIE study): a population-based cohort study.
description: A Wellcome-funded population-based cohort (GR071643MA; Perinatal Maternal Mental disorder in Ethiopia, the 'P-MaMiE' study) of 1073 women recruited in the third trimester of pregnancy was established in Butajira Demographic Surveillance Site (DSS), rural Ethiopia to investigate the impact of perinatal common mental disorders (CMD) upon infant outcomes. We plan to continue this cohort for a further two years in the first instance, making this the first longitudinal study from a low-income country to examine interactions between maternal CMD and child undernutrition, development and mortality starting in utero and extending beyond the first 18 months of life. Complex pathways linking perinatal CMD with child undernutrition at two and three years of age will be tested, including direct and indirect effects upon birth weight, subsequent episodes of maternal CMD, maternal disability and impaired help- seeking behaviour in response to child illness episodes. Annual Bayley Scale1 assessments will enable us to examine enduring effects of perinatal CMD upon child motor, cognitive and language development. The potential mediating role of levels of home stimulation will be assessed using the Home Observation for Measurement of the Environment (HOME) scale2. We will also investigate the relationship between perinatal CMD and post-neonatal child mortality, using registration of vital events in the DSS.

title: Impact of a community based RCT to improve mental health of Palestinian refugee youth.
description: The research proposed research focuses on a priority health problem (mental health) in a group of low income urban youth refugees and uses an innovative conceptual framework (positive youth development) with evidence of effectiveness to guide the intervention design. Specifically, the proposed research intends to assess the impact of a social skills and social support intervention on mental health of Palestinian refugee children aged 11-13 years living in Beirut using a randomized controlled trial design. The intervention to be evaluated is informed by evidence-based literature on mental health intervention for youth. The intervention is ecologic as it includes activities tailored to youth, their parents, and their teachers.The outcome will be measured using the CES-D and Strengths and Difficulties questionnaire. Intervention design, implementation, and evaluation is guided and approved by a community based youth committee, thus enhancing relevance, feasibility, and ultimately sustainability if results prove positive. The results of the evaluation will extend the evidence base of mental health promotion interventions to a developing world context, to a refugee setting, and from the school into the community as a setting.

title: School-based intervention to improve the mental health of low-income, secondary school students in Santiago, Chile.
description: This proposal aims to evaluate a school-based, psychological intervention to reduce depressive symptoms among students aged 14-15 attending state secondary schools in low-income areas in Santiago, Chile. This intervention will be tested in a cluster randomised controlled trial involving 20 schools and 1800 students. Students who are severely depressed and/or suicidal will also be clinically assessed and referred for treatment. Dual consent will be sought to enter the trial. Students in the schoo ls receiving the intervention will attend 10 regular and 4 booster sessions of a psychological course based on adapted cognitive-behavioural programmes used successfully in Western countries. The control schools will receive their usual but enhanced counselling classes currently included in the curriculum. Mean depression scores as well as other indicators of functioning levels will be assessed at completion of the course and 3 and 12 months later to estimate the effectiveness of the interventio n. Direct and indirect costs will be measured in both groups to assess the cost-effectiveness of this intervention. Multilevel modelling with an intention to treat analysis will be used in the analysis. Findings will be disseminated through a variety of methods, including media, workshops, and meetings with policy makers.

title: Father involvement and its impact on men's health in a South African population with high AIDS mortality.
description: Men have been largely invisible in African family health scholarship and policy. This gap is a cause for concern because whilst women and children continue to be the main target groups for health and welfare interventions, men have important roles in determining both the economic well-being of families and the health of children and mothers. In addition, young men, particularly in South Africa face an increasing threat to their health due to HIV, violence and accidents. The social and health beh aviours that place men at risk are well known, in contrast little is known about men s positive behaviours and how to promote and support them. This project aims to improve understanding of the form and meaning of men s involvement in families in South Africa, particularly with regard to fathering and fatherhood, and explore how these roles are associated with men s health and health risk behaviours. This work will provide basic knowledge which can inform decisions about possible interventio ns to strengthen men s involvement in families and improve the health of men and their families. Our study takes advantage of existing data collected in a large, longitudinal population-based study in rural KwaZulu Natal. In-depth qualitative studies with fathers will also be conducted.
recipient: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine

title: Biology Zone: Cambridge Science Festival, Schools' Visits and Online
description: We intend to run novel participative Biology Zone activities at the Cambridge Science Festival during National Science Week in March 2007, through school visits and online through interactive content, audio and video material. The Biology Zone will engage school pupils, young people and adults with interactive presentations, demonstrations, and take-home activities on the health, social and ethical dimension of advances in genetic research, stem cell research, the effects of pharmaceutical drugs on the body, nutrition and farming, cancer research, psychology and neuroscience and infectious disease. In collaboration with partners with extensive track records in this area, the Biology Zone will involve scientists presenting interactive experiments, displays and computer presentations, and discussing issues with 3,000 visitors of all ages. Schools visits are planned to reach a further 1300 pupils, focusing on schools in challenging circumstances, with a combination of scientists and artists visiting schools and school groups visiting farms and other sites of interest to support learning in biological subjects. Online activities will bring interactive biomedical brainteasers and puzzles, targeted at 11-18 year olds, on to the Cambridge Science Festival site to give learning an extended dimension. We will also make Podcasts and audio downloads of biomedical content at the Cambridge Science Festival available through our website, in partnership with the Naked Scientists' radio show. Videos of biomedical lectures and of Festival attendees presenting their views will also be made available through our website. These online activities will engage at least 10,000 visitors.

title: Mind over Matter: exploring brain donation and its role in biomedical science
description: Recent scandals surrounding the unconsented retention of bodily parts have heightened public anxiety about the collection of human tissue for use in bio- medical research. This has resulted in a marked decline in willingness to donate bodily organs and tissues for such purposes. This award would fund a groundbreaking multimedia installation that highlights the contribution that Britain's oldest prospective brain donors (now aged in their 90s) are set to make to the 21st century technoscientific project of finding cures for debilitating diseases such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's. Photographic portraits of the donors (unprecedented in the history of such research) will be supplemented by audio recordings of their personal philosophies on life, death, disease and donation. Interactive touch screens will provide scans of their brains and information on the ways in which these, and the brains themselves, will be employed after their deaths. The exhibition will illustrate the vitally important role that brain donation plays in the analysis and cure of neurological disease and celebrate their role in this important project. Audience members will be encouraged to reflect on their own attitudes towards the practice of bodily donation and to record their thoughts and feelings on the subject. The aim of the project is to begin to rehabilitate the practice of bodily donation in the public imagination. The exhibition will be mounted at the Science Museum or ICA and will be accompanied by a catalogue and a website providing an on-going interactive platform for exploration of the project by the public.

title: More Animated Minds
description: 'Animated Minds' is a series of three-minute animated documentaries using real testimony from survivors of mental illness and those with neurological disorders, combined with engaging visuals, to climb inside the minds of the those afflicted with such problems. Windows into experiences rarely seen, each piece draws us in to these people's inner worlds, journeying around the landscape of their minds, and leaving us with a greater understanding of what it is to suffer from mental distress. Originally, 4 episodes were commissioned by Channel 4 in 2003, to be shown after the 7 o'clock news. These films were a resounding success, both winning and being nominated for numerous awards including a Grierson Award, and a Mental Health Media Award for best documentary. These four episodes also received a great deal of attention from schools, universities, hospitals, community mental health centres, as well ass in the voluntary sector, both as a tool for education, as well as communication. To date, four films have explored the experiences of bipolar disorder, psychosis, panic attacks, and obsessive compulsive disorder. These films were made in a particularly unique way, involving the subject at all times in the progress of the film, so that a true collaboration was formed in our attempt to give some relevant visual metaphor to this inner experience. The next series of four films focus on Asperger's Syndrome, Demential, post- traumatic Stress Disorder and Prosopagnosia (face Blindness).

title: Medical perception and treatment of homosexuality in Scotland, 1950-80.
description: In recent years, the social politics and legal and medical discourses surrounding homosexuality in twentieth-century Britain have attracted increasing attention from historians and social scientists. Within the growing literature, the medical perception and treatment of homosexuality and homosexual offences have been treated from a variety of standpoints. Many studies treat the subject as a central aspect of the social politics surrounding either the regulation of dangerous sexualities or the process of homosexual law reform. Others, often from a social constructivist viewpoint, have focused on the competing sexological and psychoanalytical discourses surrounding homosexuality and their impact upon public policy. Anecdotal evidence of medical attitudes and therapies is also scattered in the written and recorded testimonies of homosexuals. However, with the notable exception o the oral history recently undertaken by King, Smith and Bartlett [King et al (2004)], there has been little systematic primary research into the medical perception and treatment of male homosexuality that prevailed in the surgeries, clinics, courts and prisons of the land since the Second World War. This is especially true in relation to the Scottish experience, despite the distinctive traditions of law and medical practice north of the Border, as well as, arguably, Scotland's distinctive civic and sexual culture. My current research seeks to explore the Scottish experience using a range of archives; first, the verbal and written evidence of Scottish witnesses before the Wolfenden Committee on Prostitution and Homosexual Offences (1954-7); secondly, the correspondence and papers of psychiatrists who treated 'homosexual' patients at Scottish psychiatric clinics in the 1950s; thirdly, the medical reports of psychiatrists and other doctors reporting on homosexual offenders in Scottish High Court trials during the period 1950-80; and finally, the evidence of medical attitudes and treatment presented in the archives and newspapers of the Scottish Minorities Group, and of its successor, the Scottish Homosexual Rights Group.

title: Ethical issues in the use of in-depth interviews in health research.
description: Meeting: Ethical issues in the use of in-depth interviews in health research, Sheffield, Estimated: March and April 2007. In-depth interviews are often used by health researchers undertaking qualitative or mixed method research. For example, if one wants to know what it is like to use mental health services it is important to talk to people in that position. Such research is extensively used to inform policy decisions about treatments, health technologies, and the delivery and management of health services. As such, it is important that the findings of such research are sound. However, we believe that ethical issues in the use of in-depth interviews and, more importantly, how they are tackled, have the potential to weaken or undermine the findings of interview-based research. The literature suggests that there a number of ethical issues that arise in conducting in-depth interview. Some of these are generic (such as consent); some are more specific (such as role conflict as when an interviewer is also, say, a nurse). Even the generic issues tend to eventuate in particular ways when applied to in-depth interviews. The literature suggests also that there are different ways of tackling some of these issues. For example, some researchers emphasise the therapeutic nature of interviewing patients following traumatic events whilst others are keen to separate therapy from interview. Clearly, whether one behaves as therapist or not during an interview can have significant effects on one's findings and conclusions. The meetings proposed will, to our knowledge, be the first that are focused solely on this issue. They will also contribute to the development of a research protocol that similarly will be the first focused solely on the issue. The objectives / topics are: Identification and discussion of ethical issues encountered when undertaking in-depth interview research. Discussion of a) different strategies for tackling these ethical issues; b) epistemological and methodological implications. Specifically i) What impact do different methodological and theoretical perspectives have on the way researchers tackle ethical issues? (ii) What impact do the ethical issues and the way they are tackled have on the data collected and the conclusions drawn? c) gaps in current knowledge and whether there is a need for further research or guidelines. To refine the research design of the large-scale empirical study mentioned above.

title: Study of early sixteenth-century Spanish medical ideas about the effect of the passions and pertubations of the soul on physical and mential health.
description: The aim of my project is to provide a systematic study of medical approaches to mental illness in Spain between 1498 and 1555. The project will follow a twofold strategy. Firstly, it will examine the notions of insanity and mental infirmity prevailing in key Latin and Spanish medical and moral treatises available in Spain during that period. To date, no historian or historian of medicine has studied the views on madness offered in the Spanish and Latin medical texts circulating in Spain between the late fifteenth century and the late sixteenth century. The few historical studies of madness which refer to sixteenth-century Spain only provide passing references to some people at the royal court who were deemed to be mad, but make no attempt at discussing what constituted 'madness' at the time, and do not mention how these 'mad people' were diagnosed or whether they were treated. My project will seek to fill that clear gap. Secondly, it will examine actual practices of treating the mentally ill by focusing on the case of Juana I (1479-1555), proprietary Queen of Castile, sister of Catherine of Aragon and mother of Emperor Charles V. Historians have often posed the question whether Juana was actually mad, or whether she was simply the victim of political intrigues. In recent years, the question has been reopened from the point of view of political history. The project will seek to make connections which have so far been overlooked by historians. For instance, some of the documents which refer to Juana's 'passion', 'extreme anger' and 'illness' seem to date from the periods of time when she was pregnant: there are references to her mad behaviour during at least three of her six pregnancies. Yet no study of Juana has taken into account her contemporaries' moral and medical views on the possible effects of pregnancy on mental health.

title: 'Kill or Cure: Water and Health in the Nineteenth Century' workshop to be held in Venice, Italy from 29th to 30th March 2007.
description: Conference: Kill or Cure: Water and Health in the Nineteenth Century, Venice, Italy (Palazzo Pesaro Papafava), 29-30 March 2007 The nineteenth-century public health movement has been well documented; so too has the use of spas and interest in hydropathic approaches after the 1840s. However, until now there has been no attempt to unite the two strands of scholarship to interrogate the multiple ways in which water was represented and conceived as both a potential hazard and an important health resource in the nineteenth century. The workshop participants will question how ideas on pure water were constructed according to nineteenth-century views and protocols, linking with new research on water and environment. It will also examine the domestic uses of water in relationship to hygienic and curing practices. The workshop participants will question how ideas on pure water were constructed according to nineteenth-century views and protocols, linking with new research on water and environment. It will also examine the domestic uses of water in relationship to hygienic and curing practices. The workshop will explore the medium of water as a source of disease and health in an international context, comparing East with West, with a specific focus on Western Europe and Asia. The theme of water has important connections with current debates on the relationship of water and its supply with health and wellbeing, particularly in developing countries. Venice, forming a passageway between East and West, has powerful associations with water, the basis of its wealth through trade and leisure, and more sinister associations with water and disease. It provides a perfect context for this workshop, and will be a convenient location for many of the participants. We will benefit too from the availability of the Palazzo Pesaro-Papafava to Warwick academics and from the funding opportunities offered by the University of Warwick. We anticipate that the workshop will result in an enduring and productive international network of scholars. Topics to be covered include: Concerns about the availability and purity of water supplies The construction of the relationship between water and disease Responses to water-borne epidemics Water as a focus of reform Water consumption and the politicization of water supply and usage The impact of improved domestic water supplies Water and healing practices and cultures The workshop will link closely to the our Wellcome Trust funded Project Grant, 'Healing Cultures, Medicine and the Therapeutic Uses of Water in the English Midlands, 1840-1948', and the organization of what we envisage as a high- impact workshop will strengthen our profile in this area of research, as well as highlighting the potential of a scholarly network based around the theme of water.

title: 'Developments in mental health since 1945: international and local perspectives' conference to be held at the University of Manchester on 23rd February 2007.
description: Developments in mental health since 1945: international and local perspectives The workshop will address a neglected period in the history of psychiatry, offer much needed comparative perspectives and provide a forum for historians and practitioners to exchange ideas and develop common understandings. The workshop, which includes both British and North American perspectives, will focus on two main themes. Adult mental health services, with a particular emphasis on the experimental and non-traditional. Changing concepts of and responses to childhood behavioural and emotional disorders. The topics covered are: - Post-asylum geographies of mental illness - Post-war mental health services in Saskatchewan - Radical therapeutic communites post-68 - North Manchester Community Mental Health Services, 1982-96 - Approaches to Maladjusted Children in Britain, 1945-1955 - Child Therapy and Social Welfare 1945-1980 - The Role of ADHD Parent Support Groups in the US and the UK - Changing Accounts of Bad Behaviour in the American Journal of Psychiatry, 1950-2005

title: Combat Exhaustion and Demobilization in the United States, 1941-50.
description: Combat Exhaustion and Demobilisation in the United States, 1941-50 This proposed research project examines the relationship between medicine and psychiatry within the context of US involvement in World War II. The project will consider particularly the influence of new psychiatric nomenclature in terms of the treatment of illness and injury in World War II, with new terms such as 'combat exhaustion' and 'operational fatigue' replacing the 'shell shock' of World War I. My focus will be on induction procedures in the US armed forces for assessing the mental and physical health of recruits and on the rehabilitation of war casualties. My project will also examine (i) the medical-psychiatric interface by analysing clinical literature and reports written during and immediately after World War II and (ii) how combat exhaustion was represented in the cultural sphere, both in terms of training films made by the US Medical Army Department and the cycle of commercial 'demobilisation films' that were produced between 1946 and 1950. My concern is centrally with the US involvement in World War II, but I will consult British and Canadian military psychiatric texts and assess the changing psychiatric terminology with reference to World War I and the Korean War in the early 1950s.

title: The development of lunatic asylums in the British West Indies in the period 1838-1939.
description: My specific interest in the history of psychiatric institutions in the Caribbean was kindled last summer during a visit to Barbados. Whilst being driven through the outskirts of Bridgetown I observed a set of institutional looking buildings with an unusual colonial-style design. This was 'Jenkins Hospital', formerly the Barbados Lunatic Asylum, constructed in the latter part of the nineteenth century. I became intrigued by the representation of relationship both to colonial and post-colonial Barbadian society and to the history of asylums and mental hospitals in Britain. The study will build on the work of a number of scholars who have studied the history of psychiatric institutions in British colonial societies, notably India, Nigeria, South Africa and Australia. Hitherto there has not been a comprehensive historical study of the development of provision for the insane in the British West Indies. The particular historical, political, economic and social circumstances of the Caribbean islands, notably the consequences of slavery and abolition, make them a fertile field for a research project which has ramifications that are wider than a specific consideration of the development of institutions.

title: Oxford Forum for Medical Humanities Symposium 'Neuroethics'.
description: Neuroethics The symposium will have three sessions, arranged around the ethical implications of the rapidly advancing field of neuroscience, addressing key areas of brain imaging, pharmacological cognitive enhancement and artificial intelligence. We shall also discuss the extent to which new definitions of biological abnormalities within neuroscience may exempt individuals from prosecution or potentially identify them as genetic markers of violence. The first session will consider recent advances in 'SMART drugs' the ethical implications of cognitive enhancement and the social and philosophical issues of recent advances in artificial intelligence. Secondly we shall discuss the ethics of brain reading and the controversy of the spiritual influence of the soul over conscious action. We shall conclude by addressing the responsibilities of individuals in society, the influence of genetic abnormalities versus personal choice and the legal determination of criminal responsibility. Often conferences are focused within one field, although there are clearly many conferences that draw together researchers from law and bioethics. This gathering, held by the Oxford Forum for Medial Humanities will broaden the dialogue beyond this approach, and actively bring into the conversation these other fields - medical anthropology, history of medicine and theology. Similarly, while there are many conferences that cover issues raised by the ethical implications of drug enhancement of intelligence or the influence of genetics over spiritual control, legal implications of psychiatric disease but these usually targeted at ethicists, clinicians and lawyers. This gathering is needed, as it will invite speakers from these other disciplines, to engage in discussion on these issues about life and life choices.

title: Moral and ethical imperatives of health care technologies: scientific, legal and socioeconomic perspectives on use and misuse.
description: Meeting: Moral and ethical imperatives of health care technologies: scientific, legal and socioeconomic perspectives on use and misuse, Convention Centre, National Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences, Bangalore, India, 6-8 December, 2007. Bioethics is an emerging discipline in India. Hitherto, work in bioethics has depended largely on the voluntary efforts of interested individuals. Only a few organisations have contributed to the systematic growth of bioethics. In this scenario, the Indian Journal of Medical Ethics (IJME) stands as unique effort to bring together disparate individuals and institutions, which had no other formal mechanisms for sharing their ideas and experiences. The IJME made a modest beginning in 1993 under the title Issues in Medical Ethics, and in last 15 years of uninterrupted publication, it has gained academic recognition in India and is also Indexed in medline and pubmed. Besides, in last 15 years, it has coalesced around it a strong group of medical professionals, social scientists and health activities working on or interested in bioethics. In November 2005, the first national bioethics conference was held in Mumbai under the umbrella of the journal. It was a resounding success, with more than 400 participants and more than 120 abstract submissions. Also, importantly, it was a unique effort of collaboration between 20 Indian institutions, which came together to organise this conference This conference also gave us an idea about the extent to which concern and interest in bioethics has spread across the country. We had a massive participation even from medical institutions in small mofussil towns, apart from the premier institutions of the country. A sign of the growth of the bioethics movements is that, this time, 33 organisations have already come on board as co-organisers. In the past two years, there have been many more developments in the field of bio-ethics, and we expect the 2nd national bioethics conference to be a larger event. Three major cross-cutting aspects of the main theme and the sub-themes will be discussed: Ethical Challenges in research in healthcare technology Ethical problems in use of technology in healthcare practice, and public health and policy dimensions of healthcare technology.

title: Investigating perceived coercion amongst patients in secure forensic psychiatric wards.
description: This grant requests salary support (£10,124) for one Research Assistant, Malcolm Scoales, for the duration of the study (4 months). The Research Assistant will be responsible for the day-to-day running of the study, including general coordination and the research stages of recruitment, data collection, data analysis, and writing-up of findings. The Research Assistant will be supervised in this role on a weekly basis by the Research Fellow, Kelso Cratsley, and on a two weekly basis by the lead applicant Professor Nigel Eastman. The Research Assistant will be based at the Division of Mental Health, St. George's, University of London, but will also travel to the Oxford Clinic on a regular basis, as well as attending Ethox for advice and supervision. He will gain methodological supervision from Professor Fitzpatrick, also at Oxford. For the purposes of the study the Research Assistant will secure Honorary Clinical Contracts with both the South West London and St. George's NHS Trust and the Trust managing the Oxford Clinic. More specifically as regards the Coapplicants on the study, their responsibilities will be as follows. Professor Nigel Eastman will manage the project as well as providing ethical, legal and psychiatric advice. Professor Tony Hope will provide consultation on the interface between ethical theory and empirical methods, centring on the relationship between theoretical ethical concepts and qualitative empirical data collection. Professor Ray Fitzpatrick consult on the qualitative methodology of the study, with particular emphasis on the analysis of the data collected in focus groups, assisting also in writing up the results. Dr. Seena Fazel will advise on clinical and service-related issues, as well as assisting with patient recruitment at one of the study sites (Oxford Clinic).

title: Scottish Presbyterian Medical Missionary Understandings of Their Work and Issues of Health, Healing and Sickness, in Nigeria and South Africa, circa 1900- 1945.
description: The central aim of this project is to obtain research material that is either very difficult or altogether impossible to access in my current setting. In the London portion of the proposal, I am seeking the use of general written resource at the Wellcome Library. These materials are either unobtainable elsewhere or are not found within the confines of one location. While the number of resources are too vast to exhaustively mention, a few of the general headings and specific collections include: books and articles - Medical Missionary work, 19th c. Scottish Medicine, Colonial Health, Tropical Medicine, African Medicine, and Public Health Education; manuscripts and collections - Alexander Brown (MS 1729/2), David Livingstone (MS 7329), British Social Hygiene Council (SA/BSH), Psychiatry in Nigeria (GC.146), and Jane Waterston (SA/MWF/C.152), just to name a few. This material is crucial to a full understanding not only of British medical work in the Colonial setting, but British medical education and work within Britain. The second aspect of this research project is concerned with travelling to four sites within South Africa, to obtain material directly related to Dr. Neil Macvicar, Mary Balmer, Dr. Sheena Ross, and Dr. George Gale - material unobtainable elsewhere.

title: The Eighth Global Forum on Bioethics in Research: Fostering the Research Ethics Infrastructure in the Developing World/Transition Societies.
description: The Global Forum on Bioethics in Research is a worldwide collaborative effort to strengthen ethical international health research. The theme of the 8th meeting will focus on fostering the research ethics infrastructure in the developing world/transition societies. A special emphasis during this forum will also be made on the ethical aspects of mental health research. In order to provide frameworks for developing global research ethics network, this Global Forum will focus on identification and dissemination of the best practice related to: Establishing Research Ethics Committees (RECs)/Institutional Review Boards (IRBs) at the national/regional/local levels and creating a positive regulatory environment; Models for training in research ethics; Models for establishing supportive networks among ethicists and their organizations at both national and international levels; Enhancing capacity for the ethical review and conduct of mental health research.

title: 'Journeys into Madness: The Representation of Mental Illness in the Arts and Sciences, 1850-1930' conference to be held at the Wellcome Collection Conference Centre, London from 11-12 October 2007.
description: Conference: Journeys into Madness: The Representation of Mental Illness in the Arts and Sciences, 1850 - 1930, The Wellcome Trust Centre, 11-12 October, 2007. In recent years, the territory of mental illness has been re-mapped. In the Sciences, mental life and behaviour are linked to the workings of the brain and the body's neurochemistry. In the Arts, creative genius and madness are interwoven by the belief that mental illness can provide a unique world- view. The diagnosis, treatment and functioning of mental illness has been investigated in select conferences and publications. Yet, these approaches often fail to place mental illness into larger social, cultural, and historical landscapes. We think it is therefore timely to gather scholars from a range of disciplines to explore new directions in this growing field. Our conference theme- the representation of mental illness in the Arts and Sciences- is designed to give focus to this emerging body of work.

title: A Comparative Ethnographic Study of African Fieldworkers in West and East Africa.
description: This project will examine how local fieldworkers employed by the Medical Research Council (MRC) in The Gambia and by Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI) in Kenya negotiate the social and scientific integrity of clinical research. Expanding the focus of current ethical debate from the subjects of research to those who manage its practice, this study seeks to describe medical research as a collaborative endeavour situated within the everyday project of communal well-being. Its approach will c ombine insights from ethnographic research on the social practices of scientific knowledge production (Latour 1993; Geissler 2005), sociological reflection on public attitudes toward science (Wynne 1992; Jasanoff 2005), and anthropological analysis on epistemological assumptions underpinning health care policy (Wolff 2001; Strathern 2005). The interpretive resources of semantic, theoretical, and practice-based models will enable consideration into how the concrete activities of clinical science reflect the imperatives of research institutions, the standards of biomedicine, and the demands of local health care. A comparative framework will highlight the contrasting commitments of these different communities involved in and constructed by international medical research. By attending to the experience of fieldworkers, this open- ended exploratory project aims to elaborate the social, political and economic features of a global clinical research landscape.
recipient: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine

title: Intractable epilepsy and disability - an intensive closed interdisciplinary workshop.
description: Intractable Epilepsy & Disability - An Intensive Closed Interdisciplinary Workshop, Indian Institute of Technology, Chennai, India, 9-10 December, 2006. Intractable epilepsy (epilepsy that is not controlled by the use of anti- epileptic drugs) is a disabling illness. People with IE have significant medical and psychiatry co-morbidity, are less likely to have achieved higher educational qualifications, to be employed or married. IE demands the lifelong use of drugs which have considerable side effects and People with IE also perceive a considerable burden of stigma especially so in developing nations. Yet, IE is not a registerable disability in India and the person with IE is not eligible for various social and economic supportive measures available to others. This workshop brings together epilepsy and disability professionals as well as key policy makers in an effort to initiate meaningful debate and to develop a policy document that will be presented to the Government. Topics: An introduction to the workshop (Convenor) The Concept of Intractable Epilepsy (IE) and special implications in India The WHO Definition of Disability (based on WHODAS) National Policy on Disability: An Overview and Critique Do these concepts apply to IE (behavioural and subjective experience; stationary, fluctuating, progressive)?
