Why should IE be considered as a disability for statutory benefits? IE & Disability - Presentation and discussion of Research Data from Mumbai.

title: Medsin UK Global Health Conference
description: Meeting: Medsin UK Global Health Conference, Sheldonian Theatre, Oxford, 20-30 March 2008. We live in an age of unacceptable global health inequalities. Millions of people die each year from preventable causes of death. We, as students, strongly believe that it is our responsibility to educate ourselves about this reality and take lead in the actions for change. The need is greater than ever to create a network of highly motivated students, connect them with leading thinkers of today, and create a momentum for a concerted effort to reduce the inequalities. Topics we aim to address in the conference are: (1) Can we ever win? - HIV/Malaria/TB (2) Make Mothers Matter - Maternal and Child Health, (3) Global Healthcare Economics - poverty, aid and affordable solutions, (4) Technology - advancement and accessibility, (5) Global Emergencies - disaster relief and epidemics, (6) Mental Health, (7) Health and Environment, (8) The role of universities in capacity-building.

title: Hospitals and the Development of Modern Medicine in Iran from the Early Nineteenth Century until the Beginning of the Second World War.
description: This project proposes to explore the development of modern medicine in Iran from the early nineteenth century until the beginning of the Second World War, testing the hypothesis that social and political evolution throughout this period constituted the driving force in the emergence of modern medicine. The three major factors involved in this evolution were: the military, the Constitutional Revolution (1906-11), and the religious establishment. In the nineteenth century, military modernisation p rovided the major impetus for medical modernisation. In the twentieth century, however, other socio- political factors became prominent in this process: the Constitutional Revolution went hand in hand with the growth of civil society and of nationalism. At this period, medical modernisation responded to the growing consciousness about bodily and environmental health. Under Reza Shah (1925-41), nationalism became the ideological force behind centralisation of power and medical modernisation respon ded both to the centralisation of power and increasing demand for social welfare. It was within the framework of these socio-political developments that waqf (charitable endowments) were increasingly donated for hospital construction and maintenance, while they had mostly been reserved for religious purposes during the nineteenth century.

title: Bedlam - A History of Bethlem Hospital.
description: 'Bedlam - A History of Bethlem Hospital' explores the fascinating relationship between Bethlem Hospital, the oldest mental asylum in the World, and it's mythical "Bedlam" alter-ego. The film investigates whether Bethlem's infamous reputation as the place where "the lunatics had taken over the asylum" had any basis in fact or was the creation of cultural myth-makers whose number included playwrights, artists and journalists. The film chronicles events inside Bethlem between the mid-seventeenth and late nineteenth centuries, a period that saw huge changes in the understanding and treatment of the mentally ill. Our drama-documentary blends poignant reconstructions of Bethlem life with evocative factual accounts from leading psychiatric historians including Jonathan Andrews, Christine Stevenson and Keir Waddington. The film follows a cast of famous Bethlem characters whose personal stories provide a powerful emotional narrative that both educates and informs a nationwide Channel 4 audience. The intended target audience is comprised of a domestic terrestrial television audience on Channel 4, together with a digital television audience on More 4. There is also potential for a significant international audience when the film is distributed to overseas broadcasters. In addition to the film itself, schools, colleges and other organisations will be able to access the accompanying 'Bedlam - A History of Bethlem Hospital' learning packages containing an educational DVD. The film and the DVD will play an important role in increasing public awareness about the origins of modern psychiatry and promote understanding of the social, cultural and political forces that have shaped historical attitudes towards mental illness.

title: Psychiatric Epidemiology and the Pursuit of Serenity in Modern Britain.
description: This project draws upon recent research in the historiography of psychology and statistics, and the work of Lorraine Daston, Kurt Danziger and Alain Derosieres in particular, to examine the creation and deployment of psychological objects in British political life. It argues that the establishment of the new discipline of psychiatric epidemiology has been foundational to this achievement. Although there had been a longstanding interest in the statistics of insanity, the 1930s witnessed new a ttempts to correlate the incidence of mental and psychosomatic morbidity with specific social and economic variables. This project explores the significance of the new approach through six inter-related investigations. These will map out the social, intellectual and institutional origins of the new approach; its use in mediating industrial relations, the management of morale during the Second World War, urban planning, the organisation of mental health services and reconstruction of psychiatri c classification. Throughout the project, careful attention will be paid to issues of co-constitution, demonstrating how the tools of epidemiological investigation led to the development of new models of mental illness and personality, new assessments of clinical practice and new forms of political rhetoric and governmental action.

title: Treating the patients' records: a preservation and conservation project for the Retreat Archive at the Borthwick Institute, University of York.
description: This project will secure The Retreat patients' records from the effects of original poor storage and handling at The Retreat, and enable them to be safely used by medical history researchers. It builds on a successful ResearchResources in Medical History Scheme re-cataloguing project for The Retreat Archive undertaken in 2002-2004, which transformed access to the archive (resulting in a 50% increase in use), and identified many hitherto unknown records, but also brought to light urgent preservation and conservation problems. These must be addressed to prevent further deterioration of already fragile records. The project will focus on the most heavily-used part of the archive: " Case books, admissions, deaths and discharge registers, and other volumes ofpatients' documentation, 1790s-1960s; " Nineteenth-century patients' papers, letters and writings; " Twentieth- century patients' case notes and correspondence files. The project will utilise a number of preservation and conservation measures, including cleaning, repackaging and boxing; and remedial conservation of individual items as appropriate. The end result will be fully conserved and preserved patients' records for thewhole span of The Retreat's history to the 1960s, thereby opening up new sources relating to one of the most influential psychiatric hospitals in the UK for researchers in medical history.

title: Cataloguing the British Psychological Society's History of Psychology Collection, held at Senate House Library, University of London.
description: Cataloguing the British Psychological Society's History of Psychology Collection, held at Senate House Library, University of London

title: Identification of quantitative trait genes in the mouse.
description: The aim of this proposal is to identify genes that are involved in anxiety and depression, thereby providing insights into the biological processes that give rise to some of the commonest and most disabling diseases. The approach is to use animal models of these conditions and builds on the progress we have made in using outbred mouse populations for gene mapping. We have recently completed the first whole genome genetic association study in a genetically heterogeneous stock of mice descended from eight progenitor strains. mouse population; we are now in the position to move quickly to the functional characterization of genes involved in complex phenotypes that include, but are not restricted to, anxiety and depression. Genes will be validated using sequence and expression data, and a gene-knockout interaction test. We will also be able to investigate the phenotypic consequences of copy number variation in our large mouse data set. Genetic variants in candidate genes will be tested for association with depression in a large sample collection from the south west of England. We will also apply ancestral probabilistic haplotype reconstruction to map genetic effects in a large cohort of commercially available mice. This will allow us to increase the number of genes we can identify, to investigate the relationship between transcriptional variation and disease and the relationship between behaviour and neurogenesis in the hippocampus. The studies described here will be a resource for investigating the molecular basis of phenotypic variation, behavioural and otherwise. The breadth of phenotypic and genotypic information combined with expression data provides the basis for a systems biology approach to complex phenotypes in general.

title: Dissection of stress vulnerability through gene-environment interactions.
description: BACKGROUND. The short allele of the serotonin transporter gene (5-HTTLPR) has been linked with vulnerability to disease after life stress exposure. The 5-HTTLPR short allele has also been linked to abnormal neurodeveloment of the cingulate cortex and the amygdala, critical brain regions involved in the cognitive control of emotional and stress responses. However, mechanisms mediating stress vulnerability remain largely unknown. AIMS. To test the direct, modulatory effect of the 5-HTTLPR on the neuroendocrine and autonomic response to psychosocial stress in humans, and its association with cognitive appraisal. METHODS. This hypothesis will be tested in an experimental gene- environment interaction study. Healthy volunteers will undergo a standard stress paradigm, the Trier Social Stress Test. Between genotypes differences in the stress response, state anxiety and cognitive appraisal will be measured. IMPLICATIONS. The results of the proposed project may help to better characterize resilience and vulnerability processes relevant to common stress- related disorders. The translation of genetic findings into clinically useful evidence may help to improve health, by targeting already available cognitive or pharmacological interventions. The focus on the conditional effect of genetic influences on health upon environmental exposure could minimize the risk of genetic stigmatization and promote risk reduction.

title: 'My illness': a series of 5 x 30 minute films for use on TV, Broadband & DVD.
description: 'My Illness' is a series of 5 x 30-minute films about common conditions such as asthma, psychosis (schizophrenia and bipolar disorder), cystic fibrosis, leukaemia and multiple sclerosis. Each film will focus on one individual who will find out the latest scientific thinking on the cause (or causes) of their condition by meeting reseachers and clinicians using state-of-the-art diagnostic equipment and imaging. The emotional impact of living with the illness will be explored through meeting others with the same condition and by experiencing a piece of art on the subject such as photography, dance, poetry, the visual arts or drama. Some of these artworks will be existing Wellcome- funded projects.

title: A Bayesian account of the mirror system.
description: Social interaction depends upon our ability to infer beliefs and intentions inother minds. Impairments of this ability can lead to major developmental and psychiatric disorders such as autism and schizophrenia. Little is known about the neural basis of our ability to read' the intentions of others, but a very likely candidate is the mirror neuron system.These neurons discharge, not only when a monkey acts, but also when the monkey observes someone else performing the same action. However, it is not known how someone else's intentions can be inferred by the mirror system. The proposed research addresses this issue. More specifically I propose that the mirror system is best considered within a predictive coding framework that appeals to empirical Bayes. Within this scheme the most likely cause of an observed action can be inferred by minimising the prediction error at all levels of a cortical hierarchy that is engaged during action observation. This account specifies a precise role for the mirror system in our ability to infer intentions and formalises the underlying computations. Furthermore, it makes specific predictions about the behaviour and organisation of the mirror systemthat can be tested empirically. The proposed research will test these predictions.

title: Sub-second dopamine release during cost-benefit decision making.
description: The mesocorticolimbic dopamine system has been central to many accounts of outcome processing and response allocation. Its dysfunction is also implicated in numerous neuropsychiatric disorders from schizophrenia to addiction. To date, however, it remains unknown what precise role dopamine plays in directing optimal decision-making and what the temporal dynamics of its involvement are. To investigate these issues, I intend to learn how to use fast-scan cyclic voltammetry at the University of W ashington to measure dopamine release in discrete regions at sub-second resolution during behaviour. I will first validate an operant effort-based decision-making task at Oxford University; I will then transfer to Seattle and use voltammetry to explore whether moment-by-moment dopamine transmission in the nucleus accumbens is influenced by expected rewards or response costs. I will next monitor dopamine during cost-benefit decision-making where animals have to decide between investing effort f or large reward or choosing a more easily obtained but less valuable alternative. By electrically evoking dopamine release at discrete times during this behaviour, it will also be possible to test the causal role of dopamine. Finally, I will set up this technique at Oxford and combine voltammetric recordings with cortical inactivation to assess interactions within frontal-subcortical-monoamine circuits during decision-making.

title: Development of biological motion processing in typically developing children and adolescents and in autism spectrum disorder.
description: 1\. To investigate the nature of biological motion processing in healthy adults. 2. To investigate the neurocognitive development of biological motion processing in typically developing adolescents. 3. To investigate the neurocognitive development of biological motion processing in autism spectrum disorders.

title: The magnetoencephalographic signature of genetic and pharmacological variation in catechol-O-methyl transferase (COMT)
description: 1) To identify whether a functional polymorphism in COMT, known to affect dopamine metabolism and cognitive and emotional processing, influences the localisation and/or timing of cortical activity, as measured using magnetoencephalography (MEG) during performance of various dopamine-dependent neuropsychological tasks. 2} To determine the effects of acute pharmacological inhibition of COMT, using tolcapone, in the same experimental paradigm. 3} To explore the molecular correlates of COMT inhibition in rat brain, using acute and chronic administration of tolcapone, followed by gene expression profiling, qRT -PCR and immunochemical studies. The work will test hypotheses, largely arising from fMRI, about how and where COMT impacts on brain function, and will be of direct relevance to the understanding of the role of COMT in various psychiatric disorders, and the application of COMT inhibitors as therapeutic agents.

title: Investigating the role of DISC1/ATF4 interaction in neurons: Is DISC1 involved in regulation of GABAB receptor signalling.
description: To elucidate the functional significance of the molecular interaction between ATF4 and DISC1. We will focus on the potential ability of ATF4-bound DISC1 to modulate the interaction between ATF4 and GABAB receptors, and/or regulate ATF4 stability, sub-cellular localisation and transcriptional activity in response to GABAB receptor activation. We will also ask if, and how, ATF4-GABAB interaction is altered by disease-related DISC1 mutations, with the aim of elucidating potential molecular mechanisms in psychopathology. We will focus upon the following DISC1 mutations: 1) Q31L and L100P mouse DISC1 missense mutations associated with depressive and schizophrenia-like phenotype, respectively in mouse42 2) The common S704C human DISC1 polymorphism associated with schizophrenia, that influence cognition and grey matter density in both healthy and schizophrenic subjects43. 3) Five missense variants of human DISC1 identified in schizophrenia patients but not in 10,000 control alleles (G14A, R37W, S90L, R418H, T603I)44.

title: Assisted self-harm in mental health care facilities: an ethically acceptable approach?
description: The study will involve an analysis of the ethical, legal and practical implications of the use of assisted self-harm in secondary mental health care. The methodology will be a combination of empirical qualitative research, with health care professionals and service users, and normative ethical and legal analysis. The results of the research will be used to develop policy suggestions for the management of self-harm in secondary care.

title: Emotions, ethics and moral heuristics: what are the ethical implications of recent accounts of emotion developed in neuroscience and empirical psychology and how should they relate to moral heuristics?
description: My research will unravel the ethical implications of recent theories of emotion developed in neuroscience and empirical psychology, which emphasise the bodily aspect of emotion and its frequent lack of cognitive penetrability. A typical view, which has considerable currency at present, characterises emotion as an adaptive tool, evolved to solve problems of survival and reproduction in a 'fast and frugal' manner, rather than by using slower cognitive mechanisms. These scientific theories tend to characterize emotions in ways that leave open the question of evaluation of emotion. My analysis will involve considering how we evaluate emotional responses and their role in moral intuition. Theories of emotion have important implications in the actual ways we think morally, and how these ways of thinking are shaped emotionally. Furthermore, there are specific areas in which these implications have practical relevance: in the diagnosis and treatment of mental illness; in the education of the emotions in children, as an essential part of their moral education and socialisation. I will investigate this link between emotion and moral behaviour, exploring the possibility that humans act in accordance with 'moral heuristics', quick and simple rules of thumb that guide moral judgements, and which may be founded in emotion.

title: An examination of philosophy, law and practice in voluntary psychiatric treatment.
description: The central purpose of this project is to examine the philosophical principles underpinning legislation relating to involuntary psychiatric treatment, and to investigate the extent to which, in England, these principles and the legislation are reflected in the realities of day-to-day clinical practice. A variety of methodologies will be employed at different stages of the project. These will include textual analytical methods, philosophical analysis, semi- structured interviews, and observational methodologies drawn from the social sciences. Two outcomes are anticipated. First, an overview of the complex relationships that may exist between the principles underpinning involuntary psychiatric treatment as they are conceptualised in legislation, expounded in policy, and currently operationalised in decision-making. This will inform the development of future legislation and assist in devising guidance and training in the implementation of mental health law that reflects any dissonances between the 'intent' of legislation and policy and the lived realities of psychiatric care. It may also be helpful in developing similar legislation and practice in other jurisdictions. The second outcome will be the setting of a baseline against which the process of full implementation of amendments to the Mental Health Act 1983 can be evaluated over time.

title: Induced attentional bias and the brain.
description: Several lines of evidence suggest that attentional biases represent a route to the development of anxious symptoms. Recently it has been demonstrated that it is possible experimentally to manipulate attentional biases in healthy volunteers. Neuroimaging studies suggest that emotional attention is influenced by both the amygdala-based threat detection system and by frontal control areas. However the roles of these systems in the production of attentional bias are unclear as are their specific roles in the modulation of anxiety symptoms. This project will experimentally manipulate the attentional bias of low and high trait anxiety volunteers in order to assess the effects of the biases on both behavioural measures of emotional processing and fMRI. Imaging the effects of induced attentional bias offers the opportunity to probe the neural structures associated with the biases without the confounding effects of mood. By using repeated training in anxious volunteers this project will a lso provide evidence as to the role of specific systems in the production of anxious symptoms.

title: Acentrosomal spindle formation in female meiosis.
description: Accurate segregation of genetic material is essential for life. A bipolar spindle mediates this process in eukaryotes. Centrosomes, which nucleate microtubules, dictate spindle formation during mitosis. However, the formation of a bipolar spindle takes place without centrosomes in female meiosis in most animals. Despite its importance for human health and understanding basic cellular function, little is known about the molecular mechanism of this spindle formation in female meiosis in vivo. The long-term goal is to understand this acentrosomal spindle formation at the molecular level. I propose to study three key aspects of female meiotic spindle formation, namely, spindle pole organisation, chromosome-mediated spindle assembly and the regulatory network controlling spindle formation by applying genetics-led multidisciplinary approaches. Key goals include determining the assembly mechanism and function of the pole scaffold, establishing the molecular basis of multiple chromosome s organising a single spindle without centrosomes, and systematically identifying new proteins required for spindle formation to uncover their interactions. All together these studies will lead to understanding the regulatory network of acentrosomal spindle formation in female meiosis.

title: Reducing cognitive vulnerability to suicidal ideation in recurrent major depression: using translational research to elucidate risk mechanisms and their modification.
description: Suicidal behaviour is one of the most serious outcomes of psychiatric illness yet finding effective treatments for patients who engage in deliberate self harm (DSH) is hampered both by the heterogeneity of the behaviour and by lack of knowledge about the mechanisms that underlie it. This programme explores the theory that suicidal behaviour arises from a sense of entrapment (arrested flight), brought about not only by hopelessness about the future but also by deficient problem solving. Elucidating these mechanisms is of critical scientific importance in understanding suicidal behaviour, and has major clinical implications for prevention. Our previous research has linked both these vulnerability factors to an underlying deficit (overgenerality) in autobiographical memory. The programme will investigate the hypotheses: (a) that overgenerality in autobiographical memory occurs as the result of the inhibition of image based material in memory; (b) that increases in suicide risk occur when overgeneral memory combines with inability to imagine a positive future to produce a catastrophic escalation of suicidal ideation when activated by negative mood; (b) that this activation process will be shown in unique 'relapse signatures' that predict suicidal ideation and behaviour for each individual; (d) that such activation processes may be reduced by adapting a new treatment (mindfulness-based cognitive therapy) that has been developed to reduce relapse and recurrence in major depression and applying it to suicidal ideation and behaviour.

title: An Eyeful of Sound.
description: An Eyeful of Sound is an exciting collaboration between animator Samantha Moore from the University of Wolverhampton, Dr Jamie Ward from the Department of Psychology UCL and a group of people with audio-visual synaesthesia. The people with synaesthesia who are taking part in this project have a strong visual reaction to sound. When they hear sounds, speech, music or even the phone ringing they experience colours, shapes and movement. This project, culminating in a short film, takes a selection of every day sounds and animates their responses together with the sound that inspired them.

title: Do Not Adjust Your Mind.
description: Film maker and trainee psychotherapist Tom Cotton and film producer Natasha Dack will work with project advisor Professor Del Loewenthal, subject leader for psychotherapy, Roehampton University, to research radical psychotherapist R. D. Laing's Mingsley Hall experimental community, where psychotherapists and schizophrenic patients lived together without conventional patient/doctor boundaries. Although disbanded thirty seven years ago, Laing's findings from Kingsley Hall presented a major challenge to psychiatric orthodoxy and arguably, in light of proposed government reforms of the 1983 mental health act, are more important today than ever. The team's research will take the form of extensive interviews with ex-Kingsley Hall participants, as well as Laing's contemporaries from both psychotherapy and the psychiatric establishment. This material will then be collated, analysed and presented in the form of a screenplay dramatising the events of Kingsley Hall, together with material for an accompanying documentary and book.

title: A clinical, neuropsychological and magnetic resonance imaging study comparing autism spectrum disorders and schizophrenia spectrum disorders.
description: Psychiatric diagnostic categories are defined almost exclusively on observed clinical features. As a result diagnoses often overlap as in the case of autism spectrum and schizophrenia spectrum disorders. The aims of the proposed research are to identify biological markers which distinguish between these disorders and to investigate the pathophysiology of the disorders themselves. Three groups of 30 people will be recruited: individuals with Asperger disorder or high-functioning autism (AD /HFA); individuals with schizotypal personality disorder (SPD) and unimpaired controls. Diagnoses will be confirmed using the Structured Clinical Interviews for DSM Axis I and II Disorders and the Autism Diagnostic Observational Schedule. Participants will also be rated on the Structured Interview for Schizotypy, the Rust Inventory of Schizotypal Cognitions and the Autism Spectrum Quotient. Each participant will undergo neuropsychological testing of domains relevant to the disorders and which are hypothesised to distinguish between them (central coherence, theory of mind, executive function and inspection time). They will also receive a volumetric and a functional magnetic resonance imaging scan based on the results of the neuropsychological tests. The groups will then be compared to each other to identify the features which characterise AD/HFA and SPD and which distinguish between them.

title: MA in the Social and Cultural History of Medicine.
description: The 1940s were a watershed in the development of the Irish health system. The fuel and food shortages caused by WWII and the compulsory medical inspections of Irish immigrants to Britain from 1943 drew attention to the continuing deficiencies in the health of the nation. There ensued a debate on the future of the Irish health system. Various alternatives to the system in place were proposed and resisted by interest groups, most notably the Catholic Church, the government and the medical profession. Central to this discourse was the question of how much power the state should have over the lives and health of families, whose primacy was enshrined in the constitution. This thesis will examine how this debate impacted on the health and welfare of Irish Travellers. In this period the perception and status of Irish Travellers was changing due to modernisation and the strains of post war Ireland. This process culminated in the perception of Travellers as an 'itinerant problem' that needed to be fixed. Hitherto Travellers operated on the margins of the state. This had serious health implications for Travellers who experienced with high birth rates, high infant mortality rates, high suicide rates and low life expectancy. The change in the perception of Travellers in the post war period culminated in the appointment of a Commission on Itinerancy in 1960 to investigate the rehabilitation, education and health of Travellers.

title: MA History of Medicine.
description: For my MA dissertation I propose to investigate how forensic medicine in Britain in the period between 1829 and 1985 has been able to discover the identity of 1) unidentified corpses in cases of murder, accident or suicide; found either intact or in pieces; and 2) living subjects over whose identity questions have been raised, including missing persons, fraud cases, and unknown amnesia cases. This project is not concerned with the identification of criminals who were still at large - much work has been done on the subject of the use of newly developed techniques in criminal investigations of the nineteenth and twentieth century. I am concerned more with the role of forensic specialists using the unknown body to identify an individual, rather than the use of evidence from the scene of the crime to identify an unknown assailant, or to identify a suspect for an investigation. At the most basic level, I am interested in investigating how forensic specialists 'put names to faces'. The project will address the period between the formation of the Metropolitan Police; and the development of DNA analysis in the process of identification. While undoubtedly the most reliable and successful identification technique, I view DNA analysis as a dependence on chemical science, rather than the analytical skills of the specialist and the detective skills of the police- I am more interested in how several different branches of forensic medicine interacted

title: PhD Programme at Wellcome Trust Cenre for Human Genetics.
description: Understanding the molecular basis of common, complex diseases, such as hypertension, diabetes, obesity and depression is a major challenge for medical research in the 21st century. Despite an enormous investment in genomic resources, progress has been slow. It is now clear that tackling common disease will require the collection of large samples (because the genetic effects are subtle), the application of complex analytical techniques (because of the interaction between genes and between genes and environment), and an understanding of gene function (in order to interpret the findings of the genetic analyses and to bring them into the clinic). We are now beginning to see that the conjunction of high throughput genotyping technologies and appropriate analysis will bear fruit: whole genome association studies, in which hundreds of thousands of molecular markers are genotyped on thousands of individuals, are identifying some of the susceptibility genes underlying common disease. Studies now underway (such as the UK Biobank) pave the way to answering fundamental questions in epidemiology and disease aetiology: how and why populations differ in their spectrum of disease-variants; how these variants interact with environmental causes; how information about DNA sequence variants, gene expression and protein content relates to disease phenotype; how we can use this flood of new molecular information to arrive at improved definitions of disease that lend themselves to better diagnosis and treatment. The proposed course exploits the internationally recognized strengths in genetics, statistics and epidemiology in Oxford and gains added value by integration with existing programmes. Last year, two world leading research centres began a process of integration, following the opening of the Richard Doll building next to the Wellcome Trust Centre for Human Genetics. The Richard Doll building (which consists of the University's Clinical Trial Service Unit & Epidemiological Studies Unit, Cancer Research UK Epidemiology Unit and part of the Department of Public Health) contains scientists who have pioneered the design and interpretation of large-scale randomised clinical trials that provide observational evidence to investigate the causes, prevention and treatment of premature death and disability in developed and developing countries.

title: UCL Neuroscience.
description: The United Kingdom has a vital need for well trained neuroscience researchers. We are in a period of astonishing growth of understanding of how the brain works, which will transform our understanding of ourselves and will greatly advance clinical treatments. Mental illness is the leading cause of illness and disability in the UK, accounting for 25% of the government's total payments on sickness and disability benefits, and neurological and psychiatric disorders are predicted by the World Health Organization to become increasingly major causes of death and disability in this century (source: Wellcome Trust Audit of Neuroscience Research Activity, 1999). For the UK to benefit maximally from the increase in knowledge of brain function, and to apply this knowledge to generate clinical benefits, it is essential for the country to have a highly trained pool of outstanding neuroscience researchers. Given UCL's excellence in neuroscience research (documented below), our 4 year PhD programme provides a centre for the very highest quality training in neuroscience, with outstanding strengths across the whole range of molecular, cellular, and systems and imaging neuroscience. Further funding of our programme will help to produce the next generation of creative neuroscience researchers.

title: Neuroscience.
description: Neuroscience has been identified as a top priority by the Oxford's Division of Medical Sciences. Mental illness and neurological disorders have huge personal and economic costs. We believe that the successful neuroscientists of the future will be more interdisciplinary (or at least multidisciplinary) than ever before, and contributing to solving some of the most pressing, yet difficult, of our clinical problems, relying on access to an extraordinary mix of underlying skills and techniques. It also means that the key technologies will be constantly changing, much faster than individual Departments change. Flexible, interdepartmental training networks provide a way to respond to these changing needs. Studentships that bring different skills into the discipline and link different training laboratories through the students' activities are thus a key to the discipline's future. The Oxford 4-year doctoral programme in Neuroscience has demonstrated its ability simultaneously to meet these strategic needs and the specific needs of individual students.

title: Systems Neuroscience: From Networks to Behaviour
description: Rapid technological advances in neuroscience have created a large gap between the skills offered by traditional training in biological sciences and the skills needed to apply new techniques and to exploit complex datasets. For example, neuroimaging and simultaneous multi-electrode recording now require analysis which often goes beyond the analytical and computational skills of students trained in biology, medicine, or psychology. Furthermore, the increasing sophistication of these techniques demands an understanding of the underlying physical principles of operation. Thus, modern neuroscience increasingly relies on researchers from mathematics, engineering and the physical sciences, not only for analysing data but also for developing new experimental and analytical techniques. The proposed Programme specifically targets four areas where there is a growing demand for bridging this skills gap: 1) Understanding complex neural systems requires functional, predictive models of network and whole-brain activity. 2) The synthesis of data from multi-modal imaging and physiological studies on different levels (for example, reconciling optical imaging with cellular recordings) requires extensive analysis and modelling. 3) In the focussed area of fMRI, there is a fundamental need to understand the relationship between neuronal spiking activity and BOLD response, as well as a need for more intensive image analysis and image registration with other modalities, such as EEG and MEG. These advances rely on the interchange between MR physicists, mathematical biologists, computational scientists, and neuroscientists. 4) The development of new experimental and analytical techniques requires significant input from 'hard' scientists trained in neuroscience.

title: Using gene-wide association data to understand the genetic basis of height.
description: We propose a pilot study to test the association of 100,000 specific polymorphisms with a range of common diseases using a two stage case-control study design. The study will include diabetes, breast cancer, cardiovascular disease, bipolar disorder, and other diseases (2,000 samples each), as well as two common control groups (up to 3,000 samples total) for further evaluation. Positive associations will form the basis for future biological studies. The results will be used to evaluate how best to optimise the design, implementation, analysis and cost efficiency of large-scale and genome-wide association studies in the future. We will examine features such as SNP selection, analysis methods, population structure, study size, the use of common controls, heterogeneity in sample collections, linkage disequilibrium and SNP tagging. The results will provide independent assessment of the coverage of SNP panels that are available to the community for genetic studies, including the output of the International HapMap Project. The project will help to establish a separate training programme in statistical genetics, and will lay the foundations for the development of an infrastructure for UK research in this area in future years.

title: Experimental investigation and manipulation of cognitive processes in worry and in maintaining or ameliorating Generalized Anxiety Disorder.
description: GAD is a disabling disorder that leads to severe occupational and social dysfunction. Excessive and uncontrollable worry is the defining feature of GAD. Our first goal is to investigate key cognitive processes hypothesised to maintain worry in GAD. Worry involves a predominance of verbal thoughts (as if talking to oneself about potential problems) with less imagery than when thinking about benign topics. When imagery does occur during worry, it is assumed to be brief, and Borkovec and colleague s have hypothesised that avoidance of imagery during worry perpetuates worry. We will be the first investigators to assess the duration of imagery during worry and also whether more prolonged imagery reduces persistence of worry. Furthermore, we will investigate whether facilitating more realistic (benign) imagery reduces persistence of worry further. Clients with GAD interpret ambiguous information in more negative way than non-anxious individuals. These negative interpretations may influence t he valence of images. Using cognitive bias manipulation methods we will investigate whether enabling high worriers to generate more benign interpretations has congruent effects on imagery content. Our second goal is to use the results to develop a brief intervention to target key processes that maintain worry and assess its impact on people with GAD.

title: A whole genome association study of major depression.
description: We aim to establish a resource for the identification of susceptibility genes that increase the risk of developing major depression (MD). The aetiology and pathogenesis of MD reflects the joint effects of numerous genetic and environmental risk factors and their interactions, making the detection of individual susceptibility genes extremely difficult, even with large sample sizes. Success will require a coordinated activity, with data being combined from numerous groups across the world. Our p rimary objective is to facilitate this process by establishing a large and freely available data set. We seek support to collect 6,000 cases of recurrent lifetime MD and 6,000 matched controls of Han Chinese ancestry in Shanghai, China, one of the few places in the world where it will be possible to acquire such a sample of high quality phenotypes quickly and inexpensively. We will study only females and will train Chinese doctors in the assessment of cases and in the editing of data to ensure h igh quality data. Cases and controls will be genotyped for a whole genome association analysis will take account of the effects of environmental and other non-genetic risk factors. Genotypes, phenotypes and results will be freely available through a web accessible database.

title: Alleviating anxiety through Cognitive Bias Modification (CBM).
description: Examining the causal basis of characteristic cognitive processing biases in emotional disorders has only recently been possible by artificially inducing change using the Cognitive Bias Modification (CBM) paradigm, developed by the PI and others. Creating more positive biases can improve mood and stress tolerance. The present proposal aims to enhance understanding of underlying biases mechanisms, in particular whether they are predominantly driven by action of single or multiple processes. Thi s information can direct treatment programmes as to whether all biases need independent attention and whether negative distortion in one bias predicts similar functioning in another. Development of viable tools for better measuring bias will precede detailed analysis of individual differences in several biases, their inter correlations, relationships to standard emotional status self-report measures and psychophysiological responsiveness, and monitoring of predictors of who most benefits from C BM methods. Comparison of the method with others superficially similar will enhance understanding of mechanisms and relative stability in the face of imposed mental loads. Additional practical advancement of details of the technique and its acceptance in everyday and clinical settings will provide improved understanding of cognitive processes in anxiety and a sounder evidence based and theoretical footing to progress CBM towards clinical translation.

title: Effects of prenatal alcohol consumption and alcohol metabolising genes on child growth and neurodevelopment in the ALSPAC study .
description: Although the association between prenatal alcohol consumption and adverse growth and neurodevelopmental outcome has been the subject of a number of prospective cohort studies, very few of these have focussed on the effects of drinking at low to moderate levels of consumption (less than 10 units per week) or on binge drinking (6 or more units on one occasion) and the current evidence of harm is inconclusive. We plan to use the ALSPAC study to measure the association between prenatal alcohol expo sure and growth and neurodevelopmental outcome from birth through to age 11. We will also use the extended Mendelian randomisation approach to alcohol metabolising genes in the cohort to triangulate these findings. Key goals will be to quantify the population impact of both low-to-moderate and prenatal binge drinking and to test the robustness of the associations.

title: A randomised cluster controlled trial of community level interventions to address social and structural determinants of physical activity, diet and mental well being.
description: Well London is Greater London Authority s flagship project on health, supported by NHS London and 20 PCTs and Boroughs. The project will commence in October 2007 in 20 of most deprived communities in London with 9.42m funding from Big Lottery Wellbeing fund (BLF), delivering complex interventions over 3.5 years, to address poor diet, insufficient levels of physical activity and low levels of mental health/well-being. Interventions are based on existing best practice, designed and implemented with participation of the communities. To properly evaluate interventions requires each area be matched with similar control area with no intervention activity. Well London therefore selected communities for intervention by random allocation from two matched candidate communities in 20 Boroughs, ensuring sufficient statistical power. Health indicators in the matched clusters will be compared at start and end of Well London . Funding for the complex intervention would be provided by BLF. We h ere seek funding for fieldwork in the 20 control clusters and for in-depth qualitative and quantitative studies and biological assays in both intervention and control clusters. This will provide rigorous evaluation of interventions and approach taken to participatory design and thus evidence of the appropriateness of extending this complex intervention in other deprived areas.

title: Depression at 17: ALSPAC.
description: We propose to base the study in the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC), a birth cohort, based in Bristol that has a unique combination of assessments from before birth until 15 years. Previous assessments of emotional disorders and depression have been performed on the participants and we propose a further assessment at 17 years in order to investigate the increase in incidence of depression at this age. We will assess depression and anxiety disorders using the revised clinical interview schedule, that has been widely used in the Psychiatric Morbidity Surveys in the UK and in the last 1958 birth cohort sweep. We will also assess psychological factors that are associated with depression and appear to reflect underlying vulnerability. These are depressogenic cognitive styles and certain neurocognitive tests (affective go/no go and probability reversal with false feedback). These assessments, together with the data already collected in ALSPAC, will allow us to a nswer our research questions. The applicants come from a wide range of disciplines and Universities. This will ensure that these data and those already collected in ALSPAC will be thoroughly exploited and disseminated.

title: Randomised controlled trial of Community Care for People with Schizophrenia in India (COPSI).
description: Study Design: Randomised controlled trial comparing people with schizophrenia allocated to: (i) treatment as usual (TAU), or (ii) TAU and Community Based Intervention (CBI), with 12 month follow-up. Hypotheses: Primary hypothesis: (i) CBI is superior in reducing the symptoms of people with schizophrenia in India compared to TAU, with the primary endpoint at 12 months. Secondary hypotheses: compared with TAU: (ii) CBI is more effective in reducing the disabilities of people with schizophre nia; (iii) CBI is cost-effective; (iv) CBI is more effective in improving the knowledge and attitudes of family members of people with schizophrenia; (v) CBI reduces the impact on care givers; (vi) CBI improves participants adherence to treatment; (vii) CBI reduces participants experience of discrimination. Our ultimate goal is to generate evidence to inform the scaling up of community care for people with schizophrenia in this, and other low resource settings. Setting: Two Indian States : in Tamil Nadu the study will be conducted in rural community clinics; in Goa the study will be conducted in the Institute of Psychiatry and Human Behavior. These sites will improve the generalisability of the findings across different social and care settings, and ensure that recruitment is feasible within the study timeframe.

title: Neural Correlates of Auditory Processing Deficits in Auditory Cortex and Thalamus of BXSB/MpJ Mice.
description: Our aim is to determine whether behavioural deficits in auditory temporal processing are correlated with abnormalities in the responses of auditory cortical and thalamic neurones in BXSB/MpJ mice. These mice are considered to be an animal model for human developmental disorders associated with auditory processing deficits. Approximately half the animals within a BXSB/MpJ litter are ectopic; they have cortical malformations (ectopia) and thalamic abnormalities that resemble those observed in hu mans with developmental disorders like dyslexia. Despite having normal hearing sensitivity, male ectopic mice have difficulty with perception of rapidly changing sounds; such deficits are also typical of dyslexia. We will compare auditory behaviour and auditory cortical and thalamic responses in ectopic male mice with those in non-ectopic males, which do not have auditory processing deficits and therefore serve as genetically matched controls. Key goals are to determine whether neuronal thres holds for gap detection and detection of rapid two-tone oddball stimuli correlate with behavioural thresholds, and whether neuronal minimum response latencies and limits for synchronised following differ between ectopic and non-ectopic mice. These experiments will produce important information about auditory temporal processing in the mouse, and provide insights into the neuronal basis for auditory processing deficits in humans.

title: The mechanism of action and significance of RIC-3, a selective molecular chaperone for nicotinic and 5-HT3 receptors.
description: RIC-3 is a recently discovered selective molecular chaperone of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs) and 5-hydroxytryptamine type 3 receptors (5-HT3Rs). The influence of RIC-3 is illustrated most dramatically by its effect on homomeric alpha7 nAChRs. In many host cell types the alpha7 subunit fails to produce functional receptors. In some, but not all, cell lines this can be rectified by the co-expression of RIC-3. RIC-3 also modulates the functional expression level of some, but not all , heteromeric nAChR subtypes. Importantly, RIC-3 promotes the formation of homomeric 5-HT3A, but inhibits the formation of heteromeric 5-HT3AB, receptors. Accumulating evidence suggests that RIC-3 exerts these effects by modulating receptor maturation, but there is considerable uncertainty about its precise mechanism of action. We will explore the mechanisms by which RIC-3 modulates receptor maturation and function. In addition, we will generate a RIC-3-DsRed knock-in transgenic animal to enab le us to explore RIC-3 function and expression on endogenous receptors. To explore the in vivo significance of RIC-3, we will examine the phenotype of RIC-3 null mutants, using a conditional knockout approach. We will concentrate our initial characterisation on learning and memory, indicators of anxiety and schizophrenia and animals responses to nicotine.
