title: Regulation of Dendritic Spine Morphology by PICK1.
description: Activity-dependent, long-lasting changes in synaptic transmission involve alterations in dendritic spine shape, size and number. Long-Term Potentiation (LTP) involves an increase in spine size and number, whereas spine shrinkage and retraction form a crucial part of Long-Term Depression (LTD). Since spine structure is determined by its underlying actin cytoskeleton, it is crucial to identify signaling pathways linking synaptic activity to actin polymerization. We recently demonstrated that PICK1 , an AMPA receptor (AMPAR) interacting protein required for LTD, inhibits actin polymerization by direct interaction with the actin-nucleating Arp2/3 complex, and that this activity is required for NMDA-induced AMPAR internalisation in neurons. Our preliminary data show that PICK1 overexpression in neurons results in smaller dendritic spines, and that this process requires the interaction with the Arp2/3 complex. This suggests that PICK1 may be involved not only in reducing synaptic AMPAR number , but also in reducing spine size during LTD. In this study, we will use molecular cell biological techniques and confocal imaging to investigate the details of spine size regulation by PICK1 in hippocampal neurons, the role of this mechanism in activity-dependent processes and LTD-induced spine shrinkage, and also explore potential links between receptor trafficking and spine morphology.

title: Combining Diffusion Tensor Imaging & functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging to Investigate Perisylvian Language Pathways in Schizophrenia.
description: It has been proposed that the core neural deficit of schizophrenia lies in abnormal structural and functional connectivity within a distributed network of brain regions. To date, however, structural and functional deficits in connectivity have been examined separately and their relationship is yet to be investigated. Furthermore most studies have been carried out without a detailed clinical characterization, thus making it difficult to understand the relation between deficits in structural or fu nctional connectivity and specific symptoms. The aim of the present project is to investigate the anatomical and functional integrity of the perisylvian language pathways in schizophrenia, using Diffusion Tensor Imaging and functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging. More specifically, we will (i) characterize white matter integrity and functional integration in patients with and without a history of auditory verbal hallucinations; (ii) assess the relationship between deficits in white matter integri ty and deficits in functional integration for the first time. We expect that structural and functional deficits will be apparent in patients relative to controls and will be more pronounced in hallucinators than non-hallucinators. In addition, we expect that deficits in white matter integrity within the perisylvian language pathways will be associated with deficits in functional integration within the same pathways.

title: Cognitive mechanisms of change in delusions.
description: The aim of this research is to investigate hypotheses about key cognitive mechanisms that contribute to change in delusions, in order to identify targets for cognitive behavioural interventions. Psychosis is acknowledged to be a complex disorder with multiple causes. The study of individual positive psychotic symptoms (delusions and hallucinations) has emerged as one way of making progress. Recent advances in understanding, using cognitive models, have identified new candidate cognitive and emot ional processes as causes of delusions, identified with stronger evidence and greater specificity than five years ago. Our focus here is on two key processes, reasoning biases and anxiety-related processes, and their contribution to delusions. We will manipulate reasoning and anxiety processes in two linked experiments, each with one hundred patients with delusions. We will test hypotheses about the effects of these processes on delusions. The work proposed is intended to serve as the precursor for a programme of further cognitive behavioural treatment development.

title: Medicine and human flourishing.
description: It is a commonplace that modern medicine is, in a scientific and technologicalsense, able to do more for us than ever before, yet collectively we do not feel healthier or happier as a result. This implies a gap between the biomedical understanding of human nature, health and well-being, and a non-scientific, personal, understanding of our nature, health and flourishing that is grounded in experience. When we go to the doctor we seek help for experiential problems - concerning how we feel or what we are able to do. Medical solutions are founded on the scientific and technical, but we judge their success in experiential terms because it is experiential problems that these solutions must ultimately address. This divergence, and its implications for medical practice, research and policy, are the prime enquiry for Medical Humanities, especially for a conception of Medical Humanities that recognises and responds to the essentially philosophical character of these questions. No international-class academic centre for such enquiry yet exists in the UK. The present proposal addresses both the establishment of such a Centre, and the undertaking of the necessary programme of sustained intellectual enquiry, beginning by exploring the proper extent of medicine's role in human flourishing.

title: WTCCC folow-up studies for rheumatoid arthritis. No-cost extension granted, orig end date 02/03/09. SA
description: We propose a pilot study to test the association of 100,000 specific polymorphisms with a range of common diseases using a two stage case-control study design. The study will include diabetes, breast cancer, cardiovascular disease, bipolar disorder, and other diseases (2,000 samples each), as well as two common control groups (up to 3,000 samples total) for further evaluation. Positive associations will form the basis for future biological studies. The results will be used to evaluate how best to optimise the design, implementation, analysis and cost efficiency of large-scale and genome-wide association studies in the future. We will examine features such as SNP selection, analysis methods, population structure, study size, the use of common controls, heterogeneity in sample collections, linkage disequilibrium and SNP tagging. The results will provide independent assessment of the coverage of SNP panels that are available to the community for genetic studies, including the output of the International HapMap Project. The project will help to establish a separate training programme in statistical genetics, and will lay the foundations for the development of an infrastructure for UK research in this area in future years.

title: Genome-wide association study of schizophrenia in Ireland.
description: To perform a Genome-Wide Association (GWA) study in a large case-control psychosis sample (n=2,738 cases; n=5,200 controls). This is a scientific collaboration between groups at Trinity College Dublin (TCD) (Corvin/Gill), Virginia Commonwealth University (VCU) (Riley/Kendler), Queens University Belfast (QUB) (O'Neill) and the Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium (WTCCC). The goals being to: i. Identify common genetic variants that contribute to schizophrenia (SZ) in this population. ii. Annotate associated variants and perform systems analyses to extract pathway signals' from noise in the primary data. iii. Perform joint analysis with copy number variation (CNV) data at 2 million-probe resolution, to comprehensively investigate common genomic variation in SZ. iv. Analyse a broader psychoses phenotype to establish if susceptibility extends to related disorders (e.g. bipolar disorders) or maps better to specific illness dimensions (e.g. affective or psychotic symptoms) than to clinical diagnosis. v. Replicate primary or secondary findings in available datasets.

title: A genome-wide association study of psychosis endophenotypes.
description: Psychotic disorders affect 2% of the population and are within the seven leading causes of disability (WHO). Although psychosis is highly heritable and neuregulin 1 and dysbindin are promising candidate genes, no unambiguous risk variant(s) have been identified yet. Psychiatric diagnoses do not constitute optimal phenotypes for genetic research and we propose using endophenotypes as an alternative. Endophenotypes are quantitative biological traits characterising psychosis which are obtained by laboratory-based methods rather than clinical observations. From twin and family studies we selected the most suitable psychosis endophenotypes: (i) cognitive deficits affecting verbal memory, digit span and block design performance, (ii) neurophysiologic deficits in the P300 wave from the human electroencephalogram, and (iii) neuro-anatomical abnormalities in whole brain and lateral ventricular volumes. Through our European collaboration we obtained DNA and clinical diagnoses from 7,098 individuals [1,470 patients, 2,515 relatives and 3,113 controls]. Of these a large proportion had their cognitive, neuro-anatomic and neurophyisologic endophenotypes ascertained. The USA Consortium On the Genetics of Schizophrenia, a comparable independent study, provides an opportunity for replications. We now seek support from the WTCCC to undertake a whole-genome association study of psychosis endophenotypes in this large and well-characterised sample of families.

title: The impact of oxidative and endoplasmic reticulum stress on placental protein synthesis and maternal and fetal wellbeing.
description: Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) and preeclampsia are common allied complications of pregnancy associated with increased fetal and neonatal morbidity and mortality. Our current research, supported by the Trust, has provided the first molecular evidence of endoplasmic reticulum stress and inhibition of protein translation initiation in IUGR placentas. The latter is mediated through phosphorylation of eIF2?. We now aim to test experimentally whether activation of the endoplasmic reticulum ki nase PERK acts as causal link between these phenomena. Protein synthesis inhibition can influence growth through reductions in regulatory proteins, e.g. cyclin D1. We aim to determine whether translation inhibition, mediated through the AKT/mTOR pathway, acts as a convergence point for various stimuli regulating placental growth. Paradoxically placental secretion of certain factors, thought to activate maternal endothelial cells, is increased in preeclampsia. We have identified signalling pathw ays stimulated by oxidative stress mediating their release, and that the protein elongation machinery remains active in these placentas. A key step now is to understand how endoplasmic reticulum stress, oxidative and nutritive stress interact to regulate placental protein synthesis, down-regulating many proteins but up-regulating others. Our novel insights open new avenues for improved diagnosis, clinical management and possible therapeutic intervention in these important complications of pregna ncy.

title: Health, population and social transitions in rural Southern Africa: Elucidating pathways and testing interventions.
description: Rural Southern Africa is in the midst of far-reaching socio-demographic transitions reflected in complex health challenges spanning the life course. The Agincourt health and socio-demographic surveillance system (HDSS), located in a border region of rural South Africa, has tracked and investigated these changes. Findings illuminate a protracted epidemiological transition with worsening mortality from HIV and TB paralleled by increasing vascular disease, particularly stroke, and persistent child malnutrition. Households demonstrate variable capacity to cope, especially with the shock of adult death. This proposal seeks five years further support for the HDSS to secure an exceptional research platform and thereby provide the foundation for a programme to test interventions informed by prior studies, and elucidate causal pathways that affect health outcomes. Enhanced surveillance includes linking project datasets to the HDSS; linking HDSS and clinic records; and an accessible web-bas ed approach to sharing data. Interventions target stunted growth in the youngest; poor mental health and achievement at school; adolescent parenting; phase IIb/III trial site development; secondary prevention of vascular disease with strengthening of chronic care systems; and evaluation of anti-retroviral rollout. Work will vigorously support doctoral/masters and post-doctoral training; and contribute leadership to multi-site collaborations involving the INDEPTH Network of HDSS sites.

title: Narrating the Holocaust: Innovative Approaches to Narrative Analysis of Holocaust Survivor Testimony
description: This qualitative interview study uses Holocaust survivor testimony, collected over two years with the few remaining survivors in South Wales. Data covers hours of extensive research conversations. The study aims to shed light on the value of survivor testimony for clarifying long-term and short-term mental illness, particularly after trauma. I have been invited for six months to Harvard as Visiting Professor to examine these data to understand Holocaust survivor experiences and their impact on health, illness and wellbeing for trauma sufferers. This offers the rare opportunity of working with the world- renowned narrative analyst, Prof Elliot Mishler (Dept. Psychiatry), applying novel analytic approaches such as storytelling and ethnographic narrative representation, whilst gaining a scientific understanding of trauma and its effects. Initial data analyses have led to publications and an award for ethnographic data representations (AAA, Dec 07). The skills acquired will enhance my knowledge base and lead to teaching initiatives towards knowledge transference, research capacity building and network development between the countries. Outputs will include: publications, manuscript preparation and health outcomes around psychological wellbeing in relationship to health after this specific trauma as well as clarifying the application of narrative techniques to survivor testimony, adding to understanding of New Qualitative Methodologies.

title: The performance of medicine : researching the historical writings on the ritual of tarantism.
description: The project for which this grant is being sought, is for proposed archival research into specific aspects of medical history relating to the phenomenon of tarantism. The grant will allow for detailed examination of documents and sources contained within two libraries, the Wellcome Trust Library, London, and the Bodleian Library, Oxford, both of which hold significant material relating to the historical study of the medical writings concerning tarantism, which date from the 15th Century through to the present. The key goals of this archival research are that it will contribute toward the writing of a monograph, Ritual, Rapture and Remorse: the dance of the spider in Salento, under contract with Peter Lang, which is a study of the history of tarantism through different disciplinary perspectives, and includes discussion of the extensive amount of documentation within the field of the history of medicine. This will make an important contribution to dissemination of these writings, each of which demonstrates the shifts in approaches to the body, medicine and scientific and philosophical paradigms, most particularly in Renaissance and Early Modern Italy, but also moving through to the developments in psychiatric medicine during the 20th Century.

title: Psychiatry, murder and M'Naghten in colonial context: The place for forensic psychiatric knowledge in East Africa
description: This research aims to complement some work I did in Africa in January 2008 on the role and status of psychiatry in the insanity defence in colonial East Africa. The aim of this research is to evaluate the treatment of psychiatric knowledge in murder trials in which insanity defences were raised. This research will include examining trial transcripts, (especially that of Charles Ross; National Archive, CO/533/427/5), as well as medical sources (East African Medical Journal), the press (including trial reports in the East African Standard), and legal sources (especially the East African Law Reports). In addition, there is some archival correspondence at the Wellcome Library (Eugenics Society papers) about a prominent insanity trial from colonial Kenya (Ross, 1932) by the leading East African psychiatrist, HL Gordon, which encapsulated some of his eugenic arguments concerning feeble- mindedness in relation to criminal responsibility. Such sources are not available in Scotland. This research will be presented at both medical history and socio-legal studies conferences, and published in a number of academic journals and in an edited collection. It will form the basis of a larger project on this topic for which I will be seeking funding.

title: In Pursuit of the Nazi Mind: The Deployment and Development of Psychoanalysis in the Allied Struggle against Germany.
description: 'In Pursuit of the Nazi Mind' demonstrates how models of the unconscious and cognate clinical techniques contributed to and were reshaped by the Allied struggle against the Third Reich. Important studies of Nazi psychology, centred on the concept of the superego, were mobilised in military intelligence, post-war planning and policy recommendations. My goal is to contextualise and critically assess medico-psychiatric and psychoanalytical endeavours to grasp the irrational wellsprings of N azism, and to show their significance more widely for the history of psychology in western culture. A panoramic survey will cover the emergence of new Freudian approaches to politics in the 1920s, their apotheosis in the 1940s and disintegration in and beyond the 1960s. Five accompanying core cases, for which extensive documentation exists, are designed to illustrate the varied roles and influences of applied psychoanalysis around the war: 1. Testimony of Hess s doctors, in Britain 1941-45, an d at Nuremberg. 2. Studies of Hitler, commissioned by the US Office of Strategic Services in 1941. 3. Experiments conducted upon Nazi sympathisers through the Allied Control Commission, 1945-6. 4. Psychoanalytic materials furnished to the UNESCO project, Tensions Affecting International Understanding' , 1947-51. 5. Clinical evaluations of imprisoned Nazi murderers psychic lives, 1945-1970.

title: No time for panic: British responses to influenza in peace and war, 1889-1919
description: The 1918 influenza pandemic represents the worst outbreak of infectious disease in Britain in modern times. Although the virus swept the world in three waves between March 1918 and April 1919, in Britain the majority of the estimated 228,000 fatalities occurred in the autumn of 1918. In London alone deaths at the peak of the epidemic were 55.5 per 1,000- the highest since the 1849 cholera epidemic. Yet in the capital as in other great cities and towns throughout Britain, there was none of the panic that had accompanied earlier 19th century outbreaks of infectious disease at the heart of urban populations. Instead, the British response to the 'Spanish Lady' as the pandemic strain of flu was familiarly known was remarkably sanguine. As The Times commented at the height of the pandemic: 'Never since the Black Death has such a plague swept over the face of the world, [and] never, perhaps, has a plague been more stoically accepted.' The apparent absence of marked social responses to the 1918 influenza is a phenomenon much remarked on in the literature of the pandemic, as is the apparent paradox that despite the widespread morbidity and high mortality the pandemic had little apparent impact on public institutions and left few traces in public memory. However, to date no one has explored the deeper cultural 'narratives' that informed and conditioned these responses. Was Britain really a more stoical and robust nation in 1918, or was the absence of medical and other social responses a reflection of the particular social and political conditions that prevailed in Britain during the First World War and then medical nosologies and cultural perceptions of influenza? And if the 1918 pandemic was 'overshadowed,' as one writer puts it, by the war and the peace that followed the Armistice, what explains the similarly muted response to the Russian flu pandemic of the early 1890's, a disease outbreak that coincided with a long period of peace and stability in Britain? In this project I aim to show that, contrary to previous studies, both the 1918 and the 1889-92 Russian flu pandemic were the objects of much deeper public concern and anxiety than has previously been acknowledged and that the morbidity of prominent members of British society, coupled with the high mortality, occasioned widespread 'dread' and in some cases alarm. However, in 1918 at least, government departments and public institutions actively suppressed these concerns for the sake of the war effort and the maintenance of national morale.

title: Gender, health and function in older people in Santiago, Chile.
description: The aim of the proposal is to study the main determinants of gender differences in functional limitation in older people from low and medium socioeconomic strata in Santiago, Chile. Using data from the CENEX cluster randomised trial, this study will determine the association of socio- demographic factors, self-reported chronic diseases and access to and use of medical services with gender differences among older Santiago residents. Analysis will be both cross-sectional, using the baseline data on 2000 individuals, and longitudinal using the 24 month follow-up data from CENEX to determine the influence of gender on change in health status over time. Cross- sectional analysis will examine prevalence data, while the longitudinal analysis will permit study of incidence of change in health and wellbeing using sociodemographic and health variables such as education, income, social participation, BMI, chronic disease status, physical activity, access to and use of medical services as independent variables. Findings will be nuanced with focus-group discussions with CENEX participants. The goal is to provide evidence of the factors associated with gender inequalities in older people in Chile which will inform policy makers in the design of appropriate interventions for this age group aimed at reducing gender inequalities in health.
recipient: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine

title: Send in the Idiots
description: SEND IN THE IDIOTS will be a feature length documentary film. Duration - 90 mins approx. based upon Kamran Nazeer's memoir SEND IN THE IDIOTS Or How We Grew To Understand the World, the film will illuminate the world and lives of people with autism from the point of view of someone with autism himself. Using Kamran's own experiences, supplemented by expert contribution and those of his former classmates, to examine topics such as the difficulties of language, conversation as performance, the politics of civility and 'normality', with wit and warmth, the film will explore the way that people - all people - learn to think, feel and make a difference on each other.

title: Cat and her eccentric Uncle Gillies.
description: Cat and her 'eccentric' Uncle Gillies hatch a plan to build a giant firework in which to launch her father's ashes across the sky as an explosive riposte to an ancient family feud. But Gillies is manic depressive and the lithium carbonate used to treat his manic depression is also used to make fireworks. So naturally they decide to put his medication into their firework. Which is when things start to go drastically awry.

title: Autism.
description: Autistic spectrum disorders are estimated by the National Autistic Society to affect one in 100 people in the UK, but there is no biological marker for a condition which can lead to lifelong disability, and huge social and economic cost. Current research in genetics may lead to a clearer diagnosis of susceptibility in the future. But are the fears justified of people on the autistic spectrum who feel that pinpointing genetic susceptibility could mean that in the future people with ASD are screened out of existence by the 'neurotypical'? And what can be learnt about autism using cutting-edge technologies which allow cognitive neuroscientists to conduct in-depth brain research using Virtual Reality, fMRI, MEG and EEG?

title: The Laing Legacy.
description: Documentary- The Laing Legacy (working title) Genius, prophet, poet, philosopher of madness, hero, anti-hero, radical psychiatrist, one-man revolution.......many labels were given to R.D. Laing since he began to question the scientific establishment with his groundbreaking work of critical psychiatry, The Divided Self in 1960. His death in 1989 left the psychiatric profession polarised and irrevocably changed. Using reclaimed footage, this timely documentary reassesses the life, work and legacy of the most influential psychiatrist of the 20th century.

title: Motherhood and Mental Illness.
description: We will use the Wellcome Broadcast Development Award to develop a proposal and shoot footage for a one hour documentary about motherhood and mental illness. This is a progression of our 5 minute 'Science on Film' short documentary (Over my left shoulder) which discussed postnatal depression. This award will enable us to collaborate with an established independent TV production company (Maverick TV) to provide development & production support and expertise. Maverick TV has experience in developing projects related to mental health and securing commissions from large broadcasters. From this collaboration we aim to secure a broadcast platform for our documentary.

title: Biology Zone: Cambridge Science Festival, Schools' Visits and Online
description: We intend to run new participative Biology Zone activities at the Cambridge Science Festival during National Science and Engineering Week in March 2008, through school visits and online through interactive content, audio and video material. The Biology Zone will engage school pupils, young people and adults with interactive presentations, demonstrations, and take-home activities on the health, social and ethical dimension of advances in genetic research, stem cell research, the effects of pharmaceutical drugs on the body, nutrition, cancer, psychology and neuroscience and infectious disease. In collaboration with partners with extensive track records in this area, the Biology Zone will involve scientists presenting interactive experiments, displays and computer presentations, and discussing issues with 3,000 visitors of all ages. Schools visits are planned to reach a further 300 pupils, focusing on schools which receive less science outreach, with scientists visiting schools and school groups visiting the University and research partners to support learning in biological subjects. We will also make short Podcasts and audio downloads of biomedical content at the Cambridge Science Festival available through our website. We will also run an 'Ask a Specialist / Question of the Day' activity through our website, in conjunction with the Naked Scientists. These online activities will engage at least 10,000 visitors.

title: Theatrescience India in London, July 2008
description: IMAGINING THE FUTURE III is the next stage of a science/drama project initiated in Plymouth (UK) in 2003, resulting in a Workshop/Festival of biomedical science-based drama in Bangalore (India) in 2007. It will comprise of two productions (from India) and three play-readings (two from India, one from the UK) taking place in the Drum Theatre, Theatre Royal Plymouth (TRP), in April 2008. The subjects covered in the productions and play-readings are: Science v Religion (in the context of the Ganga - Ganges River), HIV prevention in India, attitudes towards, and causes of, autism, ethics of drig trials in India, ethics of drug trials in Europe/America and Africa. As well as performances and play-readings there will be workshops, seminars and discussions.

title: States of Mind
description: What is consciousness? What does it mean to have consciousness? Is it only humans that experience it? And how can the study of the unconscious help us to understand what it is to be human? Research published in the last year by Adrian Owen at the University of Cambridge is fundamentally changing the way we view consciousness and the contribution of brain scanning to the study of the mind. Our aim is to programme a series of four events and a schools' project exploring altered states of mind and introducing the general public to the latest research and ideas about brain mapping, neuroscience and psychology - and how these disciplines now inform each other. As part of Cheltenham Science Festival 2008, using chaired and informal debates, a creative visual art project and an on-line outreach programme, we will enable a wide range of publics to learn about the latest scientific research in this field, debate the ethical issues and explore the implications of these new ideas and discoveries for how we define ourselves as 'human'. Building on established Science Festival formats and the recommendations of our 2007 evaluation, events will incorporate a substantial amount of formal and informal audience participation, offer detailed 'sign-posting' to further information and present novel formats for taking part in the debate. The intended audience will include our core Festival audience of over-45s but we will also aim to attract a broader range of people through our on-line activities and by working with partners. The bespoke education project will offer schoolchildren not normally involved in the Festival the chance to take part. We believe this project offers an excellent way to strengthen the Festival's programme of bio- medical debate and to share the excitement of brave new research with the general public.

title: Conference: Autism 2020.
description: Prior's Court Foundation is at the forefront of autism provision for five to nineteen year olds. With this event we aim to consolidate developments in autism in both the education and research sectors and stimulate discussion on the future directions for all working with autism. There have been a number of recent conferences specific to autism research, but this conference will give an engaging view of what has led to the current state of the autism knowledge and will be wholly accessible to parents, professionals and practitioners alike. By bringing advancements made since the earliest descriptions of autism together with present trends in research and practice the conference will allow reflection on the direction of Autism in the future, hence the title' Autism 2020'. The conference will be the inaugural vent in the Dame Stephanie Shirley Lecture Series and as founding patron and an influential figure in the autism field, Dame Stephanie will give the opening address.

title: Bodies of Evidence: An exhibition exploring the technologies that make bodies visible.
description: This application seeks support for a vital and fully integrated biomedical component for a major temporary exhibition exploring the human body at the University of Cambridge Museum of Archaeology & Anthropology (Feb 2009 - Nov 2010). The activity is part of a Leverhulme-funded interdisciplinary project based at the University of Cambridge, 'Changing Beliefs of the Human Body', that involves research groups in archaeology, classics, history, social anthropology and the Museum. The exhibition draws further insights from the history of science, biomedical research and artistic practice. The AIM OF THE PROJECT is to challenge common assumptions about the human body and to stimulate diverse audiences to explore ways that bodies are constructed, known, and contested in different time periods, across cultures, and through different disciplinary perspectives. The exhibition and associated activities will provide a forum for reflection and debate around pressing social, cultural and ethical issues to do with the human body, including well-being, race, gender, disability, and disease. Support from Wellcome will highlight and extend the biomedical components of the project and enhance public engagement with the themes of the exhibition. Three multi-sensory exhibits will stimulate interest in biomedical research and challenge visitors to learn about their own bodies. Loans from two National Museums will supplement the rich and diverse collections within the University. The provision of educational resources, a series of workshops and activities for families and community groups, and a catalogue will reach new audiences and encourage new ways of thinking about the human body.

title: Berkshire Historic Mental Health Resources Project: conservation of Broadmoor patient files.
description: The project aims to complete high standard conservation repair work to 7,000 damaged papers from the Broadmoor Hospital archive. They are contained withinthe files of male patients who were admitted between November 1875 and February 1884. This will allow all the Victorian patient files from the hospital to be used by researchers. The papers are currently so fragile from water damage that they crumble when handled. Conservation work will be undertaken by a professional conservator using recognised archival materials and methods. The main bulk of the hospital's significant archive is already the subject of a project funded by The Wellcome Trust. This new application is focussed solely on a discrete part of the Broadmoor collection which had not been deposited with us at the time of the original application, and which we have found subsequently to have extensive conservation needs.

title: Conservation of the antiquarian books and archives of the Royal College of Psychiatrists.
description: The Royal College of Psychiatrists is applying for funding to conserve part of its archival collection, the condition of which has deteriorated due to wear and tear thereby making it unfit for use by researchers. Additional funding is also required to restore the remainder of the antiquarian book collection. The purpose of the bid is to have these two unique collections restored and made available for research purposes without the risk of further damage, and to ensure their longevity and existence as a national treasure. The College archives which will be part of the project amount to forty eight items. They consist of minute books of the Council, Education and Parliamentary Committees of the Royal Medico-Psychological Association, a predecessor body of the College. Included also in the project are asylum records. These comprise of asylum institutional reports, reports of Commissioners in Lunacy, annual reports of asylum committees and medical reports. These archives are in bound volumes whose spines and covers are in poor condition and need to be repaired before they can be used by researchers. The conservation of archives is in line with the College's long-term plan of increasing access to its holdings through website on-line searches. As part of this plan the College recently embarked on a cataloguing programme which uses the Heritage Document Management System software, acquired from the University of Melbourne, Australia. It is planned that as more material is catalogued, it will be placed on the College website as well as other websites such as Archives Hub. The antiquarian book collection contains works which date back to the 15th century. Thirty two books and tracts of historical importance were selected from this collection for this bid.

title: Cataloguing and conservation of Exeter regional mental health records: retrieving and preserving modern mental health records - a project to sort, conserve and catalogue Exe Vale Hospital files for research purposes.
description: The project aims initially to complete a database, begun by Dr Nicole Baur in 2007, of the principal information contained in around 10,000 mental health patients' files, dating from c 1870 to c 1970, received from Exe Vale Hospital(comprising Wonford House Hospital, the Devon County Lunatic Asylum at Exminster, and the Exeter City Asylum at Digby) in June 2006. This will be used to analyse the contents of the records, with a view to assessing their potential to support future research projects, and to establishing a rationalefor selection and retention of these files and other records from similar sources. (It is hoped that a parallel project, to be led by the Centre for Medical History at the University of Exeter, will also inform this process.) Files subsequently selected for permanent retention will be conserved when necessary, re-packaged, and given a permanent location at the Devon Record Office; the remainder will be confidentially destroyed. The records retained will be catalogued using CALM 2000 for Archives, and the catalogue will be made available on the Internet. The principal outcomes will be a corpus of records selected, preserved, and catalogued; support for a CMH medical recordsresearch project; a clear rationale for selection and preservation of patients' mental health files; and closer collaborative links with healthcare professionals and the research community.

title: Troubled Minds: a project to catalogue the papers of psychiatrists Sir Aubrey Lewis (1900-1975), Hilda Stoessiger (1900-1966), Professor John Gunn (b.1937) and archives relating to Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD).
description: 'Troubled Minds' will provide first time access to archives on three key themes in psychiatry, the impact of social deprivation, war and Post TraumaticStress, alongside matchless evidence of the 20th century modernisation of psychiatry education and the advance of integrated provision of public psychiatry services. These comprise the collections of: " Sir Aubrey Lewis, founder of the modern Institute of Psychiatry at King's College London (IOP), and one of the pre-eminent psychiatrists of the twentieth century, [1910-1975] (18 boxes) " His wife, psychiatrist Hilda Stoessiger, [1930-1966] (6 boxes) " Professor John Gunn concerning Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD), special hospitals, public policy in relation to psychiatry and the teaching offorensic psychiatry, [1970-2004] (150 boxes) " IOP clinical studies of juvenile PTSD, [1986-2000] (89 boxes) The project will provide detailed catalogues to the highest professional standards supported by preservation standard repackaging. Processes will be inplace for ensuring that sensitive personal data is anonymised. The project will be delivered by a team with a strong track record of meeting targets of this nature.

title: A Model Family.
description: Research and design for a pilot performance of a larger project A Model Family planned for 2009. Developing from Baker's An Edible Family in a Mobile Home (1976), which examined her family-of-origin through a life-sized edible family - A Model Family will focus on four generations of her family, highlighting periods of trauma, mental illness, emotional conflict and its surrounding events. With a team of consultant who are professionally involved with families, Baker will explore the emotional impact of major world events, societal pressures on families, their potential impact on mental health and the way family experience is transmitted across the generations.

title: Forum Theatre production of Woyzeck.
description: With the assistance of mental health professionals, Cardboard Citizens - the UK's only homeless people's professional theatre company - will develop the famous Georg Büchner play Woyzeck as an interactive Forum Theatre production that will engage audiences in discussions about its themes of schizophrenia, the ethics of human medical testing, and the social isolation of mental illness. We will perform Woyzeck for three weeks at the Southwark Playhouse in London, reaching 1,500 people.

title: Beachy Head.
description: Our project focuses on research and development towards Beachy Head, a new production by Analogue. Beachy Head looks at three stories, indirectly relating and affected by one man's decision to take his own life. We will collaborate with a professor of histopathology and a professor of health and social care to chart the psychological and bio-medical impacts of 'an 8 second fall' from there very different perspectives: the emotional, the clinical and the artistic. Using an innovative, cinematic performance style, mixing 3D animation, object manipulation, text and arresting physical performance, Analogue explores the physical, mental and social repercussions of suicide.

title: New Opera Project.
description: The research and development phase of a new opera exploring the social, emotional and physical impacts of dementia - and specifically Alzheimer's disease. Working in partnership with Professor Simon Lovestone's team at the Institute of Psychiatry, King's College London, The Opera Group will deliver a series of activities which will enable research and development of the new opera and build support and partnerships for the larger project across both cultural and scientific communities.

title: Tranquility is a State of Mind.
description: This project takes the metaphor of the hearing aid as a point of departure, when individuals suffer hearing loss, a range of prosthetic devices and therapies are available to alleviate the symptoms. As a society we have been gradually devaluing our ability to listen in preference to seeing. We would research contexts in which the act of listening itself might be contemplated. The listener might listen to herself listen. Using the idea of the listening aid as a central metaphor the project will investigate notions of noise, tranquillity, health and wellbeing in relation to the perception of sound in the environment.

title: The Kursk
description: The Kursk is a new piece of theatre made in collaboration with playwright Bryony Lavery due to be performed at the young Vic in spring 2009. The inspiration for the piece comes from the tragic submarine disaster in 2000 when the Kursk, a Russian nuclear submarine, suffered catastrophic explosion and sank with all hands. Through this piece of highly experimental theatre we want to examine the psychology of trauma, stress and confinement. Working with naval psychiatrists we wish to create a theatrical environment where we can take our audience on a voyage of the imagination to allow them to experience a microcosm of the submariners' life. We are asking The Wellcome Trust to fund a discrete element of the project - a research and development phase with naval psychologists including a consultation period, 2 weeks of workshopping and creation of the theatrical environment with the full company and a psychological consultant, concluding in three work in progress performances.

title: Genetic, neurological and cognitive determinants of success and failure in learning a first language.
description: This research aims to identify causes of specific language impairment (SLI) at the etiological, neurobiological and cognitive levels of description, and to understand the links between SLI and other neurodevelopmental disorders. A twin study will be conducted with the goal of identifying aspects of the phenotype that are heritable and so might be useful in molecular genetic studies. In addition, bivariate genetic analyses will be conducted to explore associations between impairments, both within the domain of language, and between language and other domains. A longitudinal study following toddlers at risk of language impairment to 4 yr of age will track development of cerebral lateralisation in relation to emerging language skills. Finally, a fine- grained analysis of verbal learning will be conducted in a training study of school-aged children, with the goal of discovering why children with SLI fail to develop fluent understanding of meanings conveyed by word order. We shall consider patterns of learning on different language tasks, and procedural learning in nonlinguistic tasks, to see how far the difficulty is in abstracting rules and/or interpreting word order, or whether it reflects general problems with aspects of learning and retention.

title: Involving mental health carers in research
description: Having completed the first phase of the successful Mental Health Care website, we now have an outstanding platform to further extend and develop this initiative and to engage the public to an even greater extent in the knowledge transfer about research findings from the Institute of Psychiatry, King's College London, and about the best available evidence on mental illnesss worldwide. We now intend to expand the website with users' and carers' input, to improve both the depth of the content and the range of carers included, and to extend substantially public participation activities in our research. This project will aim to update the format of carer case stories (adding audio/video clips); produce new information for young carers in consultation with this group; involve carers in the research process via new mental health carer in research panels; encourage debate about topical issues in mental health and research; encourage the public to make comments on the website; extend the current coverage of research and evaluate the impact and reach of the website, via online surveys and feedback sessions with users. We will produce final published reports of these activities to summarise the project's conclusions, distributing them to the public and the research community, and publish them in peer-reviewed journals We will also directly support the new national anti-stigma campaign in England, Moving People, to reduce the negative connotations and discrimination associated with mental illness as well as working to promote the website to a wider audience, including GPs, community centres, hospital and service users, using targeted publicity.

title: Improving Psychological interventions for Mood Disorder: A translational research approach.
description: The next generation of psychological treatments must directly target improved outcomes and increased availability for difficult-to-treat psychiatric patients. To accomplish this, a better understanding is required of the cognitive and emotional mechanisms causally involved in the onset and maintenance of mood disorders and of the mechanisms of change associated with effective treatments. Further, innovative and effective ways to deliver cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT) to mood disorders need to be established. Accomplishing these objectives will require infrastructure support for collaborative research teams that have established experience in the testing, development, and integration of translational research findings. The Mood Disorders Centre (MDC) is uniquely positioned to be able to accomplish these aims: The MDC has an excellent track record in both experimental and clinical trial research in mood disorders, and has recently recruited international experts who bring experience in translational research paradigms and personality disorders. However, the MDC has outgrown its current facilities. This proposal will develop the MDC's internationally competitive leading-edge research through the provision of (1) a fit-for-purpose Biobehavioural and Virtual Reality Laboratory and (2) a dedicated and specialized Research Clinic. This infrastructure will support the following key objectives: (a) extending MDC research programmes investigating the mechanisms of dysfunctional and disordered affect by adding behavioural laboratory, psychophysiological, neural imaging, and virtual reality technologies to the portfolio of research methodologies, (b) the conduct of large-scale clinical trials to improve the efficacy and accessibility of psychological treatments, and (c) developing and testing novel treatments (e.g., cognitive bias modification, extinction and learning reminders).

title: Oxford Behavioural and Systems Neuroscience Centre.
description: We seek to refurbish and reconfigure space within the Department of Experimental Psychology to provide a state-of-the-art Centre for Behavioural and Systems Neuroscience. The planned layout will optimise capacity for a wide range of behavioural and chronic physiological studies of genetically and neurochemically manipulated rodent models. The floor plan will reflect the different needs of different types of experiments, from rat water mazes to mouse operant chambers or chronic unit recording studies. These requirements differ markedly from those in facilities designed primarily for rodent breeding and holding, or for acute or ex vivo tissue experiments. There will also be (limited) holding space for animals requiring long-running daily testing. The facility will advance our interdisciplinary neuroscience programmes. It will link gene expression, through cellular and systems neuroscience, to behaviour, with the goal of improving understanding of human brain development, neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders. Its complementarity with the new Life Sciences Building, nearing completion adjacent to Experimental Psychology, will allow the inter-departmental expertise of Oxford in mouse genetics, rodent cellular and systems neurochemistry, and behaviour to be maximally effectively combined. This will both widen and deepen existing cross-departmental collaborations. The Experimental Psychology department has major research programmes in primate and human cognitive neuroscience and developmental disorders, and lies within yards of the preclinical medical departments and biochemistry. This will encourage the generation and multi-level analysis of rodent models that we can translate into work on human neuropsychiatric and developmental conditions which have major individual and social impact.

title: Mother-child interaction and the development of imitation in preterm infants.
description: Developmental psychology is an area that has intrigued me for many years. In face it was one of the main reasons to study psychology at degree level. The variety of experiences I have had working with children has encouraged a keen interest in the different ways in which children develop. The majority of my work experience has involved working with atypically-developing children in both school and play settings. I also spent some time in Sri Lanka after the Boxing Day Tsunami, where I volunteered in camps for displaced families, and at an orphanage for children with learning difficulties. All of these experiences have demonstrated the importance of social interactions, and not only biological dispositions, in development. Whilst studying my undergraduate degree at Cardiff university, my interest in developmental psychology was reinforced when I was given a chance to work as a research assistant for the research group headed by Dr. Merideth Gattis. This work allowed me to see the ways in which imitation is a skill which is not only interesting in its own right but helps to uncover other social and cognitive processes as well. Melzoff (1995) presented infants with completed or incompleted actions by humans or machines. When offered the chance to imitate, infants completed the actions which had been performed by human models but not those performed by machines. Therefore the imitation demonstrated that infants replicated intended rather than viewed actions; a result that has been replicated in a number of different studies. This ability to understand psychological processes of others has been suggested to be lacking in children with autism (Aldridge, Stone, Sweeney & Bower, 2000). This idea of individual differences in intention understanding (as measured by imitative response) in different populations is of interest to me due to my work experience with both children with disabilities and a group investigating goal directed imitation. I believe a PhD would allow me to combine aspects of both my undergraduate degree and the extensive experience I have acquired over the past seven years of working with children. Once I have completed my PhD, I hope to continue with research looking at social cognition in both normally and atypically developing populations.

title: A new approach to study chromosome-driven spindle assembly in Drosophila oocytes.
description: A bipolar spindle is assembled without centrosomes in oocytes of many animals including humans and Drosophila. An in vitro system using Xenopus egg extract indicates that a bipolar spindle can be assembled from chromosomes without centrosomes and kinetochores. This project aims to understand how chromosomes drive bipolar spindle assembly in Drosophila oocytes by developing a new approach that combines the power of genetics with the flexibility of injecting chemicals and beads coupled with chromosomal factors.

title: Dopamine modulation of network oscillations in models of schizophrenia.
description: 1\. Determine the magnitude, frequency and synchrony of gamma frequency activity within and between the different regions of PFC. 2. Characterise the role and spike timing of pyramidal cells and fast-spiking interneurons in relation to gamma frequency activity within the different regions of the PFC to determine generator mechanisms used. 3. Determine the effects of dopamine modulation on network oscillations and single spike activity within the PFC. 4. Assess how network oscillations and single spike activity is altered in rodent models of schizophrenia.

title: The role of translation in Wnt mediated spine morphogenesis.
description: This project aims to examine the effect of Wnt signalling in protein translation during the formation of dendrites spines, excitatory postsynaptic structures, in the hippocampus. Changes in spines have been observed during long-term plasticity. Moreover, loss of spines has been associated with disorders like autism, schizophrenia and in neurodegenerative diseases. Our new studies reveal for the first time that Wnt7a, a member of the Wnt family expressed in the hippocampus, stimulates the formation of excitatory synapses with no significant effect of inhibitory synapses. Through gain and loss of function studies, we demonstrated that Wnt7a stimulates the formation and growth of spines. Postsynaptically Wnt signalling stimulates the maturation of dendritic spines in the hippocampus through a mechanism that involves Dishevelled-I (Dvll), a scaffold protein that regulates local Wnt signalling. To begin to understand the mechanism by which Wnt signalling regulates spine morphogenesis we performed a yeast two-hybrid screen to look for Dvll interactors. In this screen we identified Microspherules Protein 58 (MSP58), a novel RNA-binding protein that interacts with fragile X mental retardation protein (FMRP). Interestingly, FMRP has been implicated in spine morphogenesis by regulating local translation. In addition, FMRP binds to microRNAs. These findings suggest the interesting possibility that Wnt-Dvl signaling could regulate local translation through MSP58 and FMRP. In this project, the student will examine: I) The role of translation in Wnt mediated spine morphogenesis. 2) The role of MSP58 and FMRP in spine development and their contribution to Wnt-mediated spin morphogenesis. 3) The function ofmicroRNAs in Wnt-mediated function of spine formation and growth.

title: Novel Schizophrenia Risk Genes and Gene Expression.
description: a) Aims of the project. To characterise the currently unknown mechanisms by which the zinc finger protein 804A gene encoding ZNF804A influences risk of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. Based upon data generated in the host laboratory, the main hypothesis is that ZNF804A functions as a regulator of mRNA expression. To test this hypothesis, and to identify downstream mechanisms leading to disease risk, I propose to determine the consequences of altered ZNF804A expression in the brains of mice carrying truncating mutations at ZNF804A (in mouse, known as Zfp804a). Specifically, I will 1. Undertake a genetics driven approach. Thus, I will use a global transcriptomics driven approach to identify genes whose expression is altered in the brains of the above mice. These will be identified using two approaches. i) Affymetrix Exon Expression Chips (Mouse Exon 1.0 ST Array). ii) Whole transcriptome sequencing ? using the Illumina (isystem). 2. Target genes/systems identified as regulated (directly or indirectly) by ZNF804A will be tested for aetiological relevance in large case-control samples of subjects with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder using single locus and multilocus genetic association approaches. 3. Expression of candidate genes of interest will be examined in human brain mRNA samples, with the aim of linking these changes to the single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) risk variation in ZNF804A, and to associated variants in those genes per se.

title: The role of Prdm8 in mammalian eye development.
description: Although eye development in different organisms produces dramatically different structures, like the compound eye of insects and the camera-like eye of vertebrates, the underlying molecular mechanisms are highly conserved. Animal models have proven to be highly informative of the intrinsic network of transcription factors (TFs) that regulates human eye formation, and mutations in a number of TF genes have subsequently been shown to cause inherited eye and retinal cell type-specific defects in h umans. The aim of the proposed research is to define the role of the putative TF, Prdm8, in eye development and identify its downstream target genes. Adult mice homozygous for a Prdm8 null allele (Prdm8-/-) lack the major class of retinal interneurons, rod bipolar cells. My first goal will be to define the population of genes that are differentially expressed in the developing retinas of wild-type vs. Prdm8-/- mice. My second goal will be to identify the consensus DNA-binding site for Prdm8. Those genes that are: (i) differentially expressed in Prdm8-/- vs wildtype mice, (ii) expressed in the same retinal cell types as Prdm8, and (iii) contain the Prdm8 consensus DNA-binding sequence(s), are likely to be direct downstream target genes for Prdm8, involved in retinal bipolar cell formation.

title: Shock Headed Soul.
description: A cross media project containing a moving-image installation, feature length film and a supporting book and website, based on the writings of Daniel Paul Schreber, whose book Memoirs of My Nervous Illness - 1903 was made famous by Freud's 1911 critical and diagnostic reading. Schreber was raised within punitive systems of discipline developed by his father, and suffering long- term psychosis later in life. Shockheaded Soul aims to convey both the depth of Schreber's suffering and the richness of his literary depiction of the experience of psychosis, exploring the contemporary implications of the labyrinthine inner worlds depicted in Schreber's book in a way that invites audience to engage and empathise with psychotic experience.

title: Situating Medicine: New Directions in the History of Medicine.
description: Building on the Centre for the History of Medicine s (CHM) research strengths, increasingly global orientation, interest in interdisciplinary approaches, and eagerness to reflect critically on our discipline and its relationship with medicine and the public, our second Strategic Award will focus on research under the heading Situating Medicine: New Directions in the History of Medicine . This will be shaped by four contexts which will strongly inform our research projects: 1) reframing our rese arch questions to respond to recent changes within medicine; 2) reflecting critically on the disciplinary context of our work; 3) locating our research in the context of globalisation and global governance; and 4) responding to the changing relationship between both medicine and the history of medicine and the public. Informed by these four contexts, our research programme focuses upon four strands of work: Systems of Medicine and Health , interrogating relationships between the classical an d traditional and health practice and everyday life; Health and Governance , considering how health serves as an object and mode of governance; Histories of Biopower , with particular reference to visual strategies and the global traffic in medical garbage; and Post-war Mental Health in Global Context , focusing on children s mental health and diagnosis of societies.

title: Social Epidemiology of Psychoses in East Anglia [SEPEA] study: disentangling poverty, migration and urbanicity.
description: This study will utilise subject data from two funded, ongoing First Episode Psychoses [FEP] studies to obtain clinically relevant incidence cases of psychoses in East Anglia; the NIHR Understanding Causes and Developing Effective Interventions For Schizophrenia and Other Psychoses study (REF: RP- PG-0606-1335), and the MRC PsyGrid study, an ongoing FEP study in 7 centres in England. I will utilise data available in these studies to address the following key aims/goals: 1-To estimate the inc idence of psychoses in East Anglia for health service planning & causal research 2-To determine in this unique population whether the incidence of psychoses varies by: a) age and sex b) ethnicity c) immigrant status and immigration history d) urbanicity e) socioeconomic deprivation, social cohesion, discrimination, ethnic density and population mixing f) a priori hypothesis-driven interactions between the above factors; for example ethnicity and ethnic density. 3-To understand whether At- Risk Mental States [ARMS] also show variation by socio-environmental characteristics. 4-To develop a prediction tool using clinically relevant epidemiological models to determine the expected burden of psychiatric illness based on the factors outlined in (2). It is envisaged this model can then be used, tested and refined to obtain accurate estimates of the burden of serious mental illness for PCTs throughout Eng land.

title: Centre for the study of incentives in health.
description: Governments increasingly use financial and "payment in kind" incentives to encourage people to act in individually and socially beneficial ways, particularly in the context of health policy. Yet even when effective in changing behaviour, their use has attracted strong criticism for being coercive, and undermining of autonomy, personal responsibility and equity. We propose an integrated programme of research that examines these criticisms from the perspectives of three disciplines-philosophy, psychology and economics - with the aim of evaluating whether financial incentives are an acceptable means by which to improve population health. The central question we propose to address is: When is it right to use financial incentives to improve health? The key goals of the proposed Centre are: To conduct a programme of research, starting from four case examples of current uses of financial incentives in the UK, that combines philosophy, psychology and economics in the analysis of the relationship between financial incentives, coercion, equity, autonomy and behaviour in order to evaluate the acceptability and effectiveness of financial incentives to improve population health II To train post-doctoral fellows and PhD students, with the aim of creating a cadre of interdisciplinary specialists to undertake innovative, substantive research and advise policy makers

title: The Oxford Centre for Neuroethics.
description: Neuroscience is challenging our traditional understanding of consciousness, responsibility, morality and well-being, a challenge that also raises new problems for ethics and clinical practice concerning addiction and criminal responsibility, the treatment of vegetative patients, medical decision-making and the enhancement of normal human capacities. The new discipline of neuroethics addresses these urgent issues. Our goals are to: Establish a Wellcome Centre for Neuroethics at Oxford University, bringing together interdisciplinary expertise from ethics, philosophy of mind, law, psychiatry and neurosciences to contribute to neuroethical research, focussing on four areas: 1. Cognitive and affective enhancement 2.Borderline consciousness and severe neurological impairment 3. Free will, responsibility & addiction 4. Neuroscience of morality and decision-making Conduct applied research which aims to use neuroethics and practical ethics in general to address: (1) advances in neuroscientific technology; (2) ethical issues arising from research and clinical practice in neuroscience. Facilitate neuroethical research internationally by creating a metacentre which brings together leading international researchers from relevant disciplines. Apply the results of our research to specific problems in biomedical policy, law and practice and to disseminate them to influence policy and promote public debate.

title: How did scientific developments in psychiatry and political reforms to health services affect approaches to treatment and the organisation of care at Bethlem Royal Hospital, 1930-1983?.
description: Documentary and oral history approaches will be employed to investigate the variables acting on treatment priorities and service organisation at Bethlem between 1930 and 1983. I will evaluate Bethlem's initial treatment priorities, efficacy and service expansion amidst major changes in clientele and available resources. This will include the uptake of particular therapies and medications, admission of new patient populations and development of dedicated treatment facilities. Furthermore, the study will consider the ongoing interplay of social, legal, financial and political factors in effecting service organisation between 1930 and 1983. I will survey the role of wartime experiences in shaping psychiatry, the administrative and legal changes occurring in 1947-48, notably the influences, research interests and personal ambitions of those running the new Joint Hospital. Moreover, I will assess the wider impact of the early NHS on mental health services, and the dual ideological and economic challenges to institutional care regimes posed by anti-psychiatry rhetoric and community care legislation.
recipient: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine

title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease, Steroids and Affective Disorder.
description: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) is associated with a significant presence of co morbid anxiety and depression with rates estimated as 29% 35% during remission and as high as 80% for anxiety and 60% for depression during relapse. Co morbid depression and physical illness may lead to increased symptoms, surgery, sick leave and hospital stay and 60% of those with co- morbid depression will not be detected. Little is known about biological mechanisms by which these conditions co-exist. As depress ion and IBD are highly heritable, there is evidence that genome-wide association studies show genomic regions of interest for both conditions. Prescribed corticosteroid medication, used frequently in IBD, is known to commonly cause psychiatric side effects. This project will look at the genetic and neuroendocrine factors which may underlie co-morbid IBD and affective disorder. This will be done by a case control study of IBD and Coeliac Disease studying clinical, medication and disease varia bles. It will be followed by replication of known Genome Wide Asssociation areas of interest for unipolar depression and IBD in this population.

title: Wellcome Trust Clinical PhD Programme in International Health (LSHTM): a randomised control trial evaluation of the impact of community care on the experience of stigma and discrimination by people with schizophrenia in India.
description: Persons suffering from schizophrenia, and their families, experience considerable stigma and discrimination. This study seeks to answer the question whether a community-based intervention, primarily aimed at improving symptoms and function in people with schizophrenia, is effective in reducing the experience of stigma and discrimination of patients and care-givers. The study will be nested in the COPSI (Community Care for People with Schizophrenia in India) trial which is comparing two types of treatment for people with schizophrenia in two sites in India (Goa and Chennai). Roughly half the patients will receive treatment as usual, consisting of anti- psychotic medication prescribed in out-patient clinics; the other half will receive treatment as usual with additional Community Based Intervention (CBI). CBI comprises an individualised needs assessment, psycho-education, adherence management, rehabilitation and networking with community agencies such as self-help groups. The study will use a mixed-methods approach combining both quantitative and qualitative data collected from participants, their care- givers and other stakeholders in the Goa site. The.findings will contribute to the limited evidence on interventions to reduce stigma and discrimination for people with severe mental disorders in developing countries.
recipient: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine

title: Cognitive processes in the maintenance and treatment of post-traumatic stress disorder and social phobia
description: This application is for funds to continue a long-term, Trust-funded programme of research on anxiety disorders and their treatment. The proposed studies build on the applicant's success in using a cognitive science approach to improve the understanding of posttraumatic stress disorder and social phobia and to develop effective psychological treatments for these disorders. The aims are: 1) To enhance the efficiency of the treatments in order to make them more widely available; 2) To identify the mechanisms of therapeutic change inorder to test the theories on which the treatments are based and to facilitate refinement of the interventions; and 3) To identify individuals who are at high risk of developing posttraumatic stress disorder after a traumatic event so they can be targeted in future prevention programmes. An integrated programme of treatment development studies, two randomized controlled trials, treatment mechanism studies and a prospective longitudinal study is proposed to achieve these aims. The overall strategy of using a single team to simultaneously investigate two anxiety disorders has provided added scientific value in the applicants' current programme grant.
