title: Nature's Great Experiment - Identity committee.
description: Nature's Great Experiment refers to the phrase that behavioural geneticists use to describe their research with identical twins. Twin studies use comparisons between identical and non-identical twins to explore the contributions of genes and environment to health, disease and behaviour. Behavioural genetics seeks to understand both the genetic and environmental contributions to individual variations in human behaviour. Nature's Great Experiment will be a series of short films, (and a companion website), that use case studies, drawings, audio files, and recorded interviews with behavioural geneticists, Professor Terrie Moffitt and her Twin Research Team at the Institute of Psychiatry, King's College London.

title: Biology Zone, Cambridge Science Festival, Discussion Events, Schools' Visits and Outline.
description: We plan new participative Biology Zone activities at the Cambridge Science Festival in March 2009, as well as research into the impact of biomedical public engagement in science festival settings. Through school visits, a large open hands-on activity day and online interactive content, audio and video material, the Biology Zone will engage school pupils, young people and adults with interactive presentations, demonstrations, and take-home activities on the health, social and ethical dimensions of advances in biomedical science. These will include genetic research, stem cell research, the effects of pharmaceutical drugs on the body, nutrition, cancer research, psychology and neuroscience, epidemiology, biostatistics, pathology, biochemistry, and physiology. Together with the Institute of Public Health, we will offer a guided walk: '8 centuries of death and disease in Cambridge'. Schools visits are planned to focus on schools which receive less science outreach, with scientists visiting schools and school groups visiting the University and research partners. We will offer at least four evening public discussions on biomedical issues. These will include a café scientifique on the ethics of brain imaging, a panel discussion on Alzheimer's research, a presentation on Darwin as a global phenomenon, and an insight into research into consciousness. We plan to run workshops bridging alternative health and scientific pharmacology. Dr Jenny Koenig plans workshops for complementary health practitioners, members of the public and school pupils on two topics: 'herbal weight-loss treatments' and 'medicines for pain and inflammation'

title: How much is enough? A public engagement investigation into sleep timing in a 24/7 society.
description: The main objective of this project is to increase public awareness about sleep and sleep loss using a real-time research paradigm. Within the vibrant scientific environment of the Glasgow Science Centre, our main objective is to engage the public in recognising the signs of sleepiness, and its effects, through the 'Meet the Scientists Programme'. We have planned a series of lectures and experiments, over eight months, and aim to disseminate the findings from the data collected at the Science Centre back to the public during this period. The role of amylase in human physiology and psychology will be explained by interactive modelling that depicts the importance of this enzyme to vital functions, from digestion to stress responses. Visitors to the Science Centre will be informed about how their circadian body clock works and why individual variations, such as 'morning' or 'evening' types, exist. Interactive media will also be used to explain how genes and proteins in the circadian clock interact with the social environment to determine how the 24-hour period is created and managed. Visitors will also be invited to take part in a study that will investigate the magnitude of sleep loss in a 24/7 society. They will complete computerised questionnaires, provide a saliva swab to determine their current levels of amylase, and a buccal swab for DNA extraction, to identify individual differences in their clock genes.

title: Portraits of Doctors and Patients at Bethlem Royal Hospital.
description: Artist Gemma Anderson will collaborate with Forensic Psychiatrist Dr Tim Mcinerny to create ten life size etched portraits of a variety of psychiatric patients and psychiatrists at Bethlem Royal Hospital, London. The portraits will concentrate on transforming psychiatric ideas into narrative imagery embodied within individuals and will be exhibited in both Hospitals and Galleries on a national tour.

title: The Table Turned.
description: This event aims to engage an audience with debates of the 1870's that arose in response to reports of strange phenomena during seances carried out by Victorian spiritualists. Phenomena such as table rapping and levitation provoked a range of responses at the time including accusations of fakery. Scientists varied in their responses- some were profoundly sceptical, refusing to believe that such phenomena could be true whilst others believed an open mind was necessary and stated that scientists must concede the truth of these phenomena if no trickery could be found. The debates that followed invoked some important questions about the nature of scientific knowledge: What is the best method for producing scientific facts? How valid is observation as a method of establishing facts, bearing in mind that the eye can be deceived? Are there some phenomena which are beyond the reach of orthodox science? How should such phenomena be understood? Or, if a phenomenon cannot be explained scientifically is this proof that it cannot really exist? Such questions about the authority of orthodox science are still relevant today in debates about parapsychology and homeopathy. In this interactive event the audience will be witnesses to a Victorian seance (which will be presented as a short film) and then be able to question the characters that were present at this seance. To provide a range of views, the characters will be a medium, a sceptical scientist, a physician, a poet and a politician, all played by the event providers.
recipient: British Society for the History of Science

title: The teenage brain - a work in progress'. An exhibit selected for the Royal Society Summer Science Exhibition 2009.
description: Our research group has been selected to present an exhibit entitled "The teenage brain - a work in progress" at the Royal Society Summer Science Exhibition 2009. The audience includes school parties of adolescents and their teachers, the general public including families with children, and fellows of the Royal Society, ministers, peers and science journalists. The aim of our exhibit is to present to this wide audience the latest research on the adolescent brain. Adolescence is a time defined by change - hormonal, physical, psychological and social. In the past decade, brain scanning research has shown that this period of life is also characterised by dramatic development of the brain. Our interactive exhibit will explore how the human brain changes and how this development might underlie behaviours that characterise the teenage years, such as increased self-consciousness and risk- taking. We will highlight implications of this research for education and medicine. We will evaluate questions such as: How can lessons and teaching be adapted for the teenage brain? Why do so many psychological disorders, such as eating disorders and depression, start in adolescence? With the help of an exhibit designer from the London Science Museum we will build a visually engaging and highly interactive exhibit. Visitors will be able to experience the MRI scanning environment, walk along a neuron and learn about how each part of it changes with age, and see how their own performance on a variety of fun scientific tasks differs according to age and gender.

title: 'Spectrum of Opinion: Genes, Autism and Psychological Spectrum Disorders'.
description: The Progress Educational Trust (PET) will organise two public debates, will draft and produce a resource pack and pilot its use in a secondary school, andwill publish and disseminate a variety of related materials, under the heading'Spectrum of Opinion: Genes, Autism and Psychological Spectrum Disorders'. The project was conceived as a response to autism expert Professor Simon Baron-Cohen's call for an informed public debate about developments in genetics and our understanding of autism, following a media furore in 2009 about the prospect of genetic testing for autism. This episode highlighted shortcomings not only in public and media understanding of the relationship ofgenetics to psychology, but also in the divergent interpretations of this relationship promulgated by experts in different fields. Much of the confusion in this area relates to the concept of the 'spectrum' asapplied to psychological disorders. This is a concept that the project will seek to clarify for the benefit of the public and professionals alike. The project will centre around two public debates, entitled 'From Autism to Asperger's: Disentangling the Genetics and Sociology of the Autistic Spectrum'and 'Marked for Life: Are Genetic Markers Helpful in Understanding Psychological Disorders?'. These will be accompanied by extensive publicity and commentary in PET's BioNews newsletter, and will be followed by publication of a resource pack for schoolchildren containing expert pieces, a glossary of terms and lesson plans for classroom discussion and debate. Use ofthis resource pack will be piloted in Robert Napier School in Gillingham, Kent.

title: ConnectFest.
description: ConnectFest is a live experiment in which delegates at a festival have their networking activities recorded, analysed and fed back to them live throughout the event. It is rare to be able to capture data about how social networks develop and are maintained over time and so we stand to learn useful information about the psychology of social networks that will help us learn how to create more effective networking events in the future. Participants at the Sheffield DocFest (4-8 November 2009) will be asked to take part in a unique social experiment designed to track how they go about building a network of contacts and maintaining them after the festival. As they use the ConnectFest system to see who else is at the festival, arrange meetings and swap contact details the system will automatically analyse their interactions and feed them back to them via large display screens so everyone at the festival can watch as the DocFest social network expands. Meanwhile a resident psychologist will analyse the data and provide regular updates about the psychology of social networks and how this is manifested at DocFest. Furthermore, as each delegate consults their own profile at regular intervals throughout the festival, they will be fed information about their own individual position in the DocFest social network and what this means to them. Towards the end of the festival our resident psychologist will take part in a panel discussion about social networks where he will explain what this experiment can tell us about the evolution of social networks and why such public experiments are useful in expanding our understanding of this emerging strand of social psychology.

title: Replication for blood cell indicies associations.
description: We propose a pilot study to test the association of 100,000 specific polymorphisms with a range of common diseases using a two stage case-control study design. The study will include diabetes, breast cancer, cardiovascular disease, bipolar disorder, and other diseases (2,000 samples each), as well as two common control groups (up to 3,000 samples total) for further evaluation. Positive associations will form the basis for future biological studies. The results will be used to evaluate how best to optimise the design, implementation, analysis and cost efficiency of large-scale and genome-wide association studies in the future. We will examine features such as SNP selection, analysis methods, population structure, study size, the use of common controls, heterogeneity in sample collections, linkage disequilibrium and SNP tagging. The results will provide independent assessment of the coverage of SNP panels that are available to the community for genetic studies, including the output of the International HapMap Project. The project will help to establish a separate training programme in statistical genetics, and will lay the foundations for the development of an infrastructure for UK research in this area in future years.

title: Neurobiological programming of midbrain dopaminergic populations.
description: Based on our neuroanatomical findings that prenatally elevated glucocorticoid levels disrupt the dopaminergic neuronal populations in the adult rat ventral tegmental area (VTA) and substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc), we hypothesize that these perturbations give rise to disrupted connectivity and functionality in the physiologically distinct mesocortical, mesolimbic and mesostriatal systems. Our key goals/objectives are to assess prenatal glucocorticoid programming in terms of effects at molecu lar, cellular, tissue and whole animal levels in these systems by measuring: 1. neuronal positioning and target innervation using quantitative neuroanatomical methods to map structural alterations 2. electrophysiological responses in vivo to establish functional integration and physiological properties 3. whole animal behaviours known to load separately on the three brain DA systems. 4. spontaneous and psychostimulant-induced DA release in freely moving conscious rats, using in vivo micro dialysis to measure directly dynamic neurotransmitter release within the target areas of the VTA (n.accumbens and medial-prefrontal cortex) and SNc (dorsal striatum). 5. sex differences in selected parameters to extend our observations of sex dimorphisms in VTA/SNc and susceptibility to glucocorticoid programming. This work will offer novel explanations of how early experience may disrupt brain pathways that are critical for normal adaptive behaviours and associated, sexually differentiated, neurological/neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: The analysis of three-dimensional facial dysmorphology.
description: This research aims to provide tools to extract important and potentially useful quantitative information on facial shape from three-dimensional images. We plan to identify anatomical landmarks in a more automatic manner than is currently possible, by using techniques of differential geometry to characterize local surface shape and match this with the definitions of landmarks of interest. This will be extended into a quantitative characterization of anatomical curves, and of the entire facial s urface, again using differential geometry and template matching on the image data at its highest resolution. Appropriate statistical models will then be constructed to allow this information to be used to weigh the evidence for effects of interest. Important special cases will be the use of functional data analysis for anatomical curves and the construction of measures of asymmetry. These computational and statistical tools will be applied to two important application areas in the c haracterization of the facial shape of schizophrenia patients and of patients undergoing orthognathic surgery. The first of these will involve cognitive assessment and will provide valuable information on the biological processes which underlie schizophrenia. The second will enable surgical outcomes to be assessed in a quantitative and highly informative manner.

title: Implications of early life and contemporary exposures on body composition, human capital, mental health, and precursors of complex chronic diseases in three Brazilian cohorts (1982, 1993 and 2004).
description: Health and nutrition conditions in middle-income country populations are changing rapidly. Chronic-degenerative diseases, overweight, mental diseases and violence account for a major share of the burden of disease. Populations that suffered from diseases of poverty in early life now face chronic- degenerative conditions as adults, and social inequalities are rampant. Epidemiological findings from developed countries cannot be automatically extrapolated to these fast-evolving populations. We are s tudying three large population-based birth cohorts (1982, 1993 and 2004) in Pelotas, Brazil, each with 4,000+ members; the two older cohorts are currently at their peak of their phenotypic development. We plan to relate key outcomes measured in adolescence and young adulthood - nutrition and body composition, precursors of chronic diseases, mental health and human capital to early-life exposures, including gene-environment interactions, while also collecting high-quality information that can b e later related to future morbidity and mortality. Comparisons across the three cohorts will document time trends in health indicators, relating them to socioeconomic, cultural, environmental and health care changes. Our proposal combines the disciplines of epidemiology, anthropology, psychology, clinical sciences and molecular biology. Young Latin American investigators will be trained in life course studies, and findings will be proactively disseminated to scientists and policy makers.

title: The childhood adversity and psychosis study (CAPsy) study: Integrating society, psychology and biology to investigate links between childhood adversity and psychosis
description: There has been a resurgence of interest in childhood adversity, particularly abuse, and risk of schizophrenia and other psychoses. However, research to date has been limited by methodological problems and it remains unclear why only a small percentage exposed to such adversity goes on to develop psychosis. Using a case-control design, we aim to test a number of hypotheses focusing on the relationship between specific forms of childhood adversity (abuse, adverse home environments and peer bullyi ng) and risk of psychosis, and the impact of three sets of factors in amplifying risk of psychosis in those exposed to childhood adversity (social, psychological, biological). We will recruit 360 cases with a first-episode of psychosis and 360 population- based controls, over a three year period. We will collect detailed information on 1) each form of childhood adversity, using a validated semi-structured interview; and 2) potential modifiers of the relationship between childhood adversity and psychosis (adult adversity, cognitive and affective processes, biological factors). The study has high statistical power to test main and interaction effects. This study will address an important and controversial issue in psychosis research. The findings will have implications for our understanding of aetiology and will inform strategies of prevention and intervention.

title: The neural basis of familiar face perception.
description: 1: What facial information is used to represent identity? Findings from cognitive psychology show that face recognition is a holistic process. We will identify whether holistic processing of identity is characteristic of all face regions, or restricted to those thought to be involved in recognition. We will then demonstrate whether shape or texture cues dominate this representation. 2: Are different neural codes used to represent familiar and unfamiliar faces? The ability to recognise fam iliar faces across a variety of image changes has been integrated into cognitive models of face processing. We will ask whether an image-dependent or image-invariant neural code is used to represent familiar faces. We will then determine whether the neural code that is used to represent the configuration of familiar faces is different to that used for unfamiliar faces. 3: How are dynamic and static cues used for recognition? Because faces can be readily recognized from photographs, most stu dies of face recognition ignore the role played by dynamic cues. However, recent studies have found that movement can play an important role in face recognition. A key question, we will address is whether the same or different brain regions are involved in recognition with static and dynamic cues.

title: Interleaving brain systems for recognition and episodic memory.
description: We will examine the neural substrates of two key forms of memory across behavioural, systems and cellular levels. In particular, we will investigate the specific contributions of different brain regions within both the perirhinal-centred system (for familiarity discrimination), and the hippocampal-medial diencephalic system (for event memory). Of especial note is the introduction of new methods including: new behavioural tests of object recognition memory and scene learning, and new manipulat ions to block the expression of synaptic plasticity long-term potentiation (LTP) and/or long- term depression (LTD). Issues to be investigated include: the importance of regions connected to the perirhinal cortex, including prefrontal cortex and the extended hippocampal system, for different forms of recognition memory the role of thalamic-prefrontal interactions in recognition memory. diencephalic involvement in recognition memory revealed through gene-imaging perirhinal h ippocampal system interactions modelled from neuronal activity measures differentiation of the role of perirhinal cortex in perception and recognition memory whether all components of the extended hippocampal system are required for a key attribute of episodic memory scene learning whether and where LTD and LTP mechanisms are required for different forms of scene learning and recognition memory

title: Does uterine artery delivery of adenovirus VEGF increase uterine blood flow and birthweight in growth restricted fetal sheep?
description: Impaired utero-placental perfusion causes fetal growth restriction (FGR), an important pregnancy complication with high perinatal mortality and long term complications in surviving neonates. There is no treatment. We observed significantly increased uterine blood flow (UBF) short and long term after adenovirus mediated over-expression of VEGF-A165 in pregnant sheep uterine arteries. This study examines whether local over expression of VEGF-A165 in the uterine arteries of pregnant sheep with uter oplacental insufficiency and FGR will increase UBF and fetal birthweight through a combination of NO mediated vasodilatation and angiogenesis. We propose using the overnourished adolescent FGR sheep model in which a significant 40% reduction in UBF is first manifest in mid-gestation and which is strongly correlated with birthweight. In mid-gestation we will inject Ad.VEGF-A165, Ad.LacZ as a non- vasoreactive control or saline into the uterine arteries of normal or FGR sheep. We will measure UBF, fetal growth rate and wellbeing regularly until term. We will assess uterine artery endothelium-dependent relaxation and constriction in an organ bath, and angiogenesis and VEGF expression will be measured. Long term efficacy and safety will be examined in spontaneously delivering FGR pregnancies. These studies will explore the mechanism of action and improve understanding into the pathogenesis of FGR.

title: Deficits in processing of sensory context associated with schizophrenia.
description: Although schizophrenia affects more than 500,000 people in the UK, its neural basis remains poorly understood. What is increasingly clear is that the diverse range of symptoms associated with the disorder are linked by a pervasive problem with the appropriate processing of context. We have reported that people with schizophrenia are largely immune to a visual illusion that relies on suppressive contextual interactions (contrast gain control). The first series of experiments examine contrast gain control in schizophrenia in some depth. We will modify an established combined fMRI-psychophysics paradigm to (a) measure Threshold-versus-Contrast (TvC) functions and so determine if reduced inhibition confers better detection performance in the test group and (b) relate this to the BOLD contrast response function in test and control groups. The second series of psychophysical experiments will determine if gain control deficits extend into domains other than contrast, such orientation and moti on-direction. Finally we will use fMRI and psychophysics to investigate gain-control in another sensory modality: tactile perception. These findings will contribute both to understanding sensory abnormalities associated with schizophrenia and, we hope, in the potential to diagnose it, using psychophysical and fMRI measures.

title: Functional analysis of the sp tzle paralogues in the central nervous system of Drosophila.
description: Disruptions to neurotrophin (NT) function underlie neurodegeneration, cancer and psychiatric disorders. Understanding and manipulation of NTs is necessary for stem cell based central nervous system regeneration. We have recently discovered sequence, structural and functional NT homologues in Drosophila (DNTs). The DNTs belong to a group of six sp tzle paralogous genes (spz-ps). The functions of spz3, spz4 and spz6 are unknown, but preliminary findings indicate that they are involved in the n ervous system. The aim is to investigate the functions of spz3, spz4 and spz6 in the Drosophila nervous system. The key experimental goals are to investigate: (1) their expression patterns and the neuronal circuits involved; (2) the consequences of removing their function, and of expressing them ectopically, in neuronal survival, targeting and locomotion; whether the SPZ-P functions are redundant or not; and whether they overlap with innate immunity; (3) whether the canonical NT downstream s ignalling pathways underlie SPZ-P functions; (5) and the consequences of expressing vertebrate NTs in Drosophila to test functional conservation. The approach is interdisciplinary, combining molecular genetics and image processing to accurately measure the biological data. Our findings will establish a Drosophila NT platform to aid the understanding of NT functions, related brain diseases and repair.

title: A Genomewide association study of anorexia nervosa.
description: Our aim is to find unequivocal evidence of associations between DNA sequence variations and AN. Given its public health importance and consistent evidence of genetic aetiological contributions, GWAS for AN is rational. We propose: 1) Primary GWAS. Conduct GWAS genotyping on 4,015 female AN cases and 4,015 female controls. (Our preferences are the Illumina 1M platform to maximize comparability with an independent AN GWAS and to genotype controls to minimize site, batch, and platform effects). Af ter rigorous QC, association analyses for SNPs and CNVs along with bioinformatic integration will be conducted. 2) Mega-analyses. (a) Within-disorder mega-analysis with an independent GWAS (N=1,900 AN cases, genotyping ~Q3 2009, Illumina 650K), (b) cross-disorder mega-analyses with WTCCC psychiatric disorders (bipolar disorder and schizophrenia), (c) with the Psychiatric GWAS Consortium (including ADHD, autism, and major depressive disorder), and (d) with obesity. 3) Follow-up genotyping. We are collecting DNA samples from an ongoing Swedish National Eating Disorders Registry (current N=5000 cases) which is highly appropriate for replication efforts. 4) Elucidating genotype-to-phenotype mechanisms. For strong/replicated findings, GCAN is well-positioned immediately to pursue genomic, transcriptomic, molecular biological, and epidemiological studies in humans and mouse studies including the Collaborative Cross and activity-based anorexia.

title: Characterising the function of the schizophrenia susceptibility gene ZNF804A.
description: Although there are strong reasons outlined in the application to suggest that ZNF804A is a transcription factor, its function is not known with certainty. Establishing this is central to understanding how ZNF804A influences schizophrenia pathogenesis, and hence to translating the finding to benefits for patients. We will therefore conduct experiments with the goal of characterizing the function of ZNF804A. Our specific aims are: 1. To Identify ZNF804A binding proteins. If indeed it is a transc ription factor, these experiments will identify proteins that form regulatory complexes. If it is not, the identity of its partners will inform us about its other likely functions. 2. We will additionally test the hypothesis that it is a transcription factor by seeking DNA sequences to which ZNF804A (or members of a complex including ZNF804A) binds and thereby genes likely to be regulated by it. 3. Identify genes whose expression (mRNA) is altered in culture by manipulating the expression of ZNF804A. 4. Use the above data to identify functional pathways that are perturbed by altered ZNF804A expression. Such pathways will shed light on possible pathophysiology, inform parallel genetic studies (for which we do not seek support) and may identify suitable potential targets for treatment.

title: Genetic investigation of life course phenotypes of mental health and illness in the 1946 British birth cohort.
description: Using repeated measures collected between ages 13 and 53 years in the British 1946 birth cohort we will test associations between hypothesis-driven candidate genes and novel, empirically derived life-course phenotypes of depression and anxiety, cognition and personality. Our new phenotypes are longitudinal latent classes and latent quantitative traits derived from innovative psychometric approaches that we have piloted (Colman et al, 2007). Goal 1 confirms and 2 extends the phenotypes from m ental health to personality (neuroticism) and cognition ( g ). Goal 3 involves conducting single and multi-marker genetic association studies exploring the impact of sets of genes related to brain development, neurotransmission, cognitive ageing, and endocrine function on these summary measures of life-course risk for health and psychiatric symptoms, personality and cognition. Our overarching hypothesis is that these higher-fidelity, longitudinal measures will represent more valid targets for genetic research than conventional cross-sectional, binary diagnoses. Goal 4 considers the impact of three specified effect modifiers (G x E interaction). These include an early environmental adverse event (childhood separation), pubertal stage (in early teenage years) and a protective factor, educational/occupational attainment. This research will serve as a platform for thematically and methodologically linked collaborative work in other British cohorts, and other relevant samples.

title: Wnt signalling in the regulation of spine morphogenesis.
description: The establishment of an appropriate balance between excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmission is crucial for the normal function of the nervous system. Disruption of this balance is believed to contribute to neurodevelopmental disorders such as mental retardation, autism and schizophrenia. Our laboratory has been studying the role of Wnt signalling in the formation of neuronal connections in the vertebrate nervous system. We found that Wnts promote synaptogenesis in the cerebellum and hippoca mpus. Our new studies now show that Wnt7a preferentially regulates the formation of excitatory but not inhibitory synapses. Accordingly, Wnt7a stimulates the formation and maturation of dendritic spines, protrusions that received most excitatory inputs through a pathway that requires CaMKII, a key molecule implicated in synaptic plasticity. In the present proposal, we are taking a multidisciplinary approach combining cell imaging, biochemical and transgenic techniques to understand the mechanism s that control the formation, the maturation and the dynamics of dendritic spines. Using electrophysiological techniques, we will also investigate the effect of Wnt signalling on synaptic plasticity. Our studies will elucidate the mechanisms that modulate critical steps during the formation of excitatory connections and how these processes affect synaptic function and plasticity.

title: Cardiovascular risk and cognitive function in three ethnic groups - the SABRE- COG Study.
description: The study will investigate associations between mid-life vascular risk factors and later cognitive function in three ethnic groups. It will further investigate the role of cerebral MRI volumetric and microvascular disease measures as potential mediating factors between exposures and outcome. The SABRE study, already funded by the Wellcome Trust and British Heart Foundation, is a 20-year follow-up and re-examination of European, South Asian and African-Caribbean residents in north London (cur rent mean age 70y). The proposed SABRE-COG study will fund additional cognitive assessments, genetic analysis (apolipoprotein E) and volumetric analysis of cerebral MRI data in order to address the core objectives. Examinations will have been completed by the end of Year 2 and data analysis and reporting will be carried out in Year 3. The projected sample sizes in the three respective ethnic groups will be 1000, 700 and 300. SABRE-COG brings together experts in cardiovascular epidemiology at Imperial College, neuropsychology at the MRC Unit for Lifelong Health and Ageing, and neuroepidemiology at King's College London: in particular a team of researchers who, through the WT 10/66 Programme, have developed valid assessments of cognitive function with robust cross-cultural applicability.

title: Conservation of Bethlem and Maudsley Hospital discharge summaries (1967-1993)
description: This project aims to achieve the conservation of Bethlem and Maudsley Hospitals' patient discharge summaries dating from 1967 to 1993. These summaries are part of medical record series that extend back to 1816 and 1923 (for Bethlem and Maudsley respectively). Holdings of medical records of the nineteenth and early twentieth century are relatively common in UK repositories, but (perhaps counter-intuitively) survival of records from the second half of the twentieth century are comparatively rare. The depth of detail in these summaries, and the fact that they represent the work of many key figures in UK psychiatry, make them critical sources for the development of contemporary psychiatry. The summaries were rescued from damp storage conditions in 2001, and those that date from 1967 to 1993 are currently stored in the lever arch files into which they were originally put by the hospitals' medical records departments. This is highly unsatisfactory. A certain amount of damage to the records has already been sustained, and in the absence of intervention more can be expected. They cannot be accessed without the risk of damage, as they are on loose poor-quality copy paper, are in many cases dirty, stapled and in danger of crumbling. As a consequence the research potential of these records has remained untapped to date. These summaries were the top conservation priority identified by the National Preservation Office's Preservation Assessment Survey of the Archives & Museum's collections in 2006. Without intervention to save them, they are likely to perish before the period which they document passes out of living memory. Science

title: Phobia: Constructing the phenomenology of chronic fear, 1789 to the present' to be held at Cardiff on 8-9 May 2009
description: By examining shifts in the constructions of fear and anxiety disorders from 1789 to the present, this interdisciplinary conference investigates the social and cultural appropriations of medical knowledge. It aims to show 1) that changes in the cultural perception of phobias were reconsidered and redefined during periods of change and tension (during the long nineteenth century, at the fin de siecle, during the Cold War, in post-modernity), and 2) that this particular pathological .configuration was enthusiastically adopted, developed and transformed by literary writers, cultural theorists and the media. While the understanding of phobias was historically conditioned, the conference explores in what ways cultural representations of fear and anxiety disorders actively assisted in first disseminating and then transforming medical knowledge and scholarship. The cultural history of phobias is a multidisciplinary one. This conference therefore brings together scholars working in different fields of the medical humanities. It aims to generate a fruitful debate on the interfaces between the social history of medicine, science, literature and popular culture.

title: Health, Well-Being and Commerce 1500-2000' to be held at the University of Wolverhampton on 25 March 2009
description: The main objective of the workshop is to bring together scholars from different historical and other academic disciplines, in order to explore the commercial practices and services associated with health and well-being, from the early modern to the contemporary period. Well-being is defined broadly, including notions of beauty, hygiene and grooming. On the one hand, then, the workshop seeks to provide a venue for the discussion of themes relating to the historical development of retail trades and services associated with medicine- most notably, chemists and the drugs trade. On the other, it also intends to consider the marketing and sale of products and services that sought (and seek) to offer not only physical health, but also mental wellbeing, beauty and 'cleanliness'. Thus, a central theme of the workshop will be the historically shifting relationship between the commercial practices, consumer expectations and regulatory frameworks associated with conventional, science-based medicines and remedies, and those associated with 'life-style', beauty and grooming products.

title: David Skae's 'Lectures on insanity': text and context.
description: A scholarly edition of Skae s 'Lectures on insanity is planned. The text and accompanying historical introduction will make Skae's contribution to nineteenth-century alienism more accessible to further historical scrutiny and also draw out its wider historiographic significance. The goals of the edition are: (i) to prepare an accessible text featuring: a) Skae's final versions of non-clinical lectures, with footnote references to any significant variations found in earlier versions; b) all Skae's clinical lectures, with footnote references to case notes of named Royal Edinburgh Asylum patients. The goals of the historical introduction are: i) to provide background to Skae's life, thought and pedagogy; ii) to explain the significance of his 'Lectures' to current historiographies of psychiatry and medicine, with special reference to Scottish, and English-speaking, developments.

title: R.D. Laing in America: preserving the original, un-edited film record of the 1972 lecture tour to enable access and research
description: The project aims to conserve and transfer to High Definition (HD) digital form at the original, unedited and unseen 16mm film footage and audio track (ca37 h rs) of the 1972 lecture tour of the U.S.A. made by the psychiatrist R. D. Lain g (1927-1989), and other films. The key goals will be to: " repair, clean and prepare for re-formatting, the original 16mm colour film footage " digitally c apture, to the best current standards, the full image quality of the 16mm film " clean up and transfer the audio track to digital format " provide a full tr anscript which will be accessible on-line " provide immediate research access to the content, via DVDs, CDs and transcript, and facilitate the production of an edited, feature length documentary " enable the long-term preservation of the films " describe the contents of the films for discovery via on-line catal ogues of the University of Glasgow and the National Library of Scotland, Scott ish Screen Archive (NLS SSA) " provide permanent storage at the NLS SSA cold s tore for the original film, audio tapes, and the digital masters (at no cost t o the project)

title: The Medical History of British India Online: Mental Illness: Treatment & Research
description: The material we have chosen for this application is a collection of reports from the colonial mental hospitals of India. They relate to the study and definition of mental illness and the development of psychiatry in India. It contains rich detail about the staff and patients, the administration and governance of the institution, and records of treatment and research. The changes in medical practice and the social aspects (including religious aspects) of mental illness are traced through the chronological study of the reports. The objective is to preserve the collection through conservation measures and to protect it from further damage by the production of microfilm copies, and the production of searchable digital copies linked to catalogue records. All images will be hosted on the Medical History of British India web feature. The Library's aim is to add to this useful and interesting feature using this further collection of rare and fascinating documents that will be accessible remotely to medical history researchers and others, and which will also have the advantage of highlighting the diverse range of the Library's collections.

title: Madness, Migration and the Irish in Lancashire, c.1850-1921
description: Through a close survey of the records of the Lancashire asylum system, the project will explore the relationship between Irish migrants and mental illness from c.1850 to 1921, a period marked by high levels of migration into Lancashire and Liverpool in particular. It will explore the linkage of mental disorder amongst the Irish to migration, trauma, isolation, poverty, and social and cultural dislocation, questioning whether underlying explanations of mental illness and its predisposing factors differed from those attributed to English patients, other migrant groups, and Irish patients in Ireland. The project will examine whether there were particular stereotypes concerning the Irish which influenced their admission to the asylum and experiences of care, and how concerns about the very visible rise in their numbers were linked to changing debates about insanity, including the impact of degeneracy, race and gender, at a time of massive growth in asylum numbers overall. Uniquely, this project will situate the experiences of Irish pauper asylum patients and those treating them within a broader canvass of efforts to manage perceived and real problems of disease, poverty, and intemperance amongst Irish migrants. The main outputs comprise a co-authored book, three articles, a workshop, conference and public engagement activities.

title: A cultural history of mental health and the role of Franco Basaglia in Italy, 1960-2008. Pilot research and recce.
description: The aim of this pilot research is to establish the presence and overall of archival and other material relating to mental health reform and the activities of Franco Basaglia in Italy in various Italian locations with a view to an extensive research project application to the Wellcome Trust in December 2009. 1. Overall project Using the research grant funds, a number of cities where large-scale mental health institutions were located, and were at the centre of reform efforts by doctors and activists influence by Franco Basaglia and others in the 1960s and 1970s will be visited. The aim will be to make contact with those who took part in the period of reform and change, and to make a survey of the presence of archival and other material (photographs, newspapers, official material, the structural state and contemporary use of the buildings, film material) with a view to a large-scale research project (application to be prepared for December 2009). These recces will make an overall assessment of the material available, its accessibility and lead to an assessment of the time and resources needed to collect and analyse the relevant material.

title: Health and Masculinity in Post War Britain.
description: This pilot project will provide the opportunity for exploratory archival, documentary and oral research into masculinity and men s health in the post- war period, leading to a re-submission of a fellowship grant application in December 2009. In order to refine the overall direction of a larger project on the apparent rise of psychosomatic and psychological illness in men, it will allow the RA to pursue exploratory research into four specific areas: 1 How men presented with symptoms (by oral te stimonies of retired GPs with experience in this area). 2 Attitudes and values of men relating to work, family and health (qualitative electronic data from social surveys on health and lifestyle and archival records from the GP John Fry) 3 The rationale behind the marketing of pharmaceutical treatments for depression and anxiety to men. 4 Representations of masculinity in popular culture (television, magazines and newspapers). The study will result in one journal article and a number of pu blic engagement activities, as well as a larger research fellowship application.

title: Interviews with post-war pioneers in the field of psychiatry, philosophy and anthropology
description: The proposed research will be facilitated by three meetings: (1) with Dr. Jean Oury of La Borde Clinic, (2) with Emeritus Professor Henri Maldiney in Lyon (3) with Professor Levi-Strauss and (4) time permitting, with the poet and novelist Francois Cheng (Officier de la Légion d'honneur Chevalier des Palmes académiques, Commandeur des Arts et des Lettres).

title: Reality Bites.
description: The science documentary 'Reality Bites' provides an insight into a new condition discovered by Canadian psychiatrists Joel and Ian Gold: The Truman Show delusion - where patients believe that they are starring in their own reality television show. After a decade saturated with TV reality shows, and internet video sites such as youtube, the film will analyse the impact that reality TV has on human psychosis and ask the question: what does the Truman show delusion say about today's society?

title: The practice of obstetric care in Mumbai: an ethical analysis.
description: This study will document obstetric practices in Mumbai hospitals and analyse their influence on professional behaviour, its consequences for vulnerable groups, and its ethical implications for healthcare practice and policy. It will be based on interviews with physicians, nurses and support staff and focus group discussions with a cross-section of women who have used obstetric care in the past one year. It will be supplemented by an analysis of secondary data. The specific objectives are: 1. To document women's experiences of obstetric care in public and private sector services in Mumbai; 2. To document the practices and attitudes of public and private providers andinstitutions in Mumbai towards women seeking obstetric care; 3 To present an analysis of the implications of these practices on the doctor-patient relationship. 4. To document the impact of these practices on women's well-being and rights;5. To consider the ethical implications of these for healthcare practice and policy.

title: The Dual-Use Dilemma in Biomedical Science: An Ethical Analysis.
description: My principal aims will be to: 1. Draw on my medical and philosophical training to rigorously analyse fundamental ethical questions raised by: -The increasing prevalence of dual-use dilemmas in biomedical science. -Recent advances in synthetic genomics/biology. -Recent advances in the neuroscience and psychology of morally-significant behaviour. 2. Develop recommendations on: -Who should regulate dual-use research. -How the risks and benefits of dual- use research should be balanced. -Whether and when science censorship is appropriate. -What kinds of synthetic genomics/biology will require special regulation, and what form this regulation should take. -How scientists and policymakers should respond to the radically new kinds of behaviour modification made likely by recent advances in psychology and neuroscience. 3. Publish my findings in a series of twelve articles in leading ethics, bioethics, science and medical journals. 4. Publish a monograph on the neuroethic s of behaviour modification. 5. Communicate my recommendations to policymakers, scientists, clinicians and the public through involvement in policy projects; publication of editorials and feature articles; submissions to public consultations; contributions to public engagement websites; media interviews; and public lectures and panel discussions. 6. Establish myself as an academic researcher with interdisciplinary and international collaborative relationships, and expertise on a range o f bioethical/neuroethical topics.

title: A phenomenological study of decision-making capacity in psychiatric disorders.
description: This project will seek to investigate how 3 psychiatric disorders (schizophrenia, severe depression, frontal brain syndrome) threaten capacity to make decisions by probing the task of decision as the patient encounters it(the phenomenology). It will focus on the 'use and weigh' ability for mental capacity used by English law because this is both most relevant for these disorders and also most difficult to interpret. The research builds on a completed cross-sectional study funded by the Wellcome Trust that forms the basis for my PhD in which I conducted capacity assessments using the MacArthurCompetence Assessment Tool on 200 patients admitted to psychiatric hospital and again one month later. This project will use a qualitative design with ethical and phenomenological analysis. In depth interviews will seek to clarify how the 'use and weigh' ability can be threatened by psychiatric disorder. Because mental capacity crosses three disciplines: psychiatry, law and philosophy, this research needs to be interdisciplinary. I will bring Professor Wayne Martin - an expert on theories of autonomy and judgement - into collaboration with these interviews and their analysis. I will also consult closely with Professor Genevra Richardson - an experienced mental health lawyer. I have established working relations with both these academics on mental capacity. The goal of the research is both practical (to inform and improve practical assessments of capacity) and theoretical (to inform and enrich philosophical discussions about autonomy through the study of decision- making inability).

title: Wellbeing, consciousness and moral decision-making: key concepts in biomedical ethics.
description: My key goals will be to: (a) Make significant scholarly contributions to ethical questions raised by radical advances in biotechnology and neuroscience, by integrating rigorous analytic philosophy and up-to-date science to address three key issues: (1) Wellbeing, impairment and enhancement (2) Consciousness in severe neurological impairment (3) Implications for biomedical practice of the neuroscience of human decision-making (b) Publish the research as articles in the leading jou rnals for bioethics, philosophy, science, and medicine (around 5 articles per year). (c) Prepare a monograph on wellbeing, impairment and enhancement (years 1-3) and edit a volume on the implications of the neuroscience of morality (years 3-4). (d) Apply my findings to specific problems in biomedical policy, law and clinical practice and disseminate them to influence policy, promote political and public debate, and prevent widespread misconceptions about the ethical significance of scienti fic advances. My long term goals will be to: (e) Establish myself as a expert in biomedical ethics, with special focus on the emerging discipline of neuroethics. (f) Build collaborative links with ethicists, philosophers of mind, neuroscientists, geneticists, social scientists, clinicians and legal experts. (g) Contribute to capacity building by setting up a new graduate course in biomedical ethics at Oxford (years 4-5).

title: Costing mental health care in Uganda.
description: The goal of the research is to generate evidence on mental health financing in Wakiso District. Specific objectives are: 1\. to gather information on policies for mental health care services in Uganda; 2\. to study costing of mental health services both at the allopathic as well as at traditional healer sites; 3\. to disseminate the results in Uganda and more widely. The study will take place at Entebbe Grade B Hospital and Gombe Hospital Mental Health Clinics and at two Traditional Healer's premises in the Wakiso area. The study population will be adults with mental disorders. The dependent variable will be costs of care for the current mental illness episode; independent variables will include socioeconomic status, knowledge and practices in relation to mental disorders and mental health services. The study will use a cross- sectional design and will have qualitative and quantitative components. Quantitative data analysis will include population characteristics, bivariate and multivariate analysis, and qualitative data analysis will use the grounded theory approach. Findings will be disseminated widely in Uganda and the region, through attendance at workshops and conferences and writing articles for peer reviewed journals
recipient: London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE)

title: Pathological Sounds: The History of Music as a Threat to the Nerves.
description: Conceptions of the nervous system had been central to understandings of music throughout the Enlightenment, but it was only at the end of the eighteenth century that the neuropathological model of disease that was developed by figures such as Haller, Cheyne, Whytt, Cullen and Brown started to be applied to music. By 1800 music was being portrayed not just as a means of refining the nerves, but as a potential pathogen in works of psychiatry, dietetics, aesthetics and etiquette. During the nin eteenth century, this discourse was influenced by such things as the theory of degeneration, the neurasthenia diagnosis and the emerging medical discourse of homosexuality. Krafft-Ebing describes three cases of men who connected their same-sex feelings to love of Wagner. As well as physicians such as Krafft-Ebing and critics such as Hanslick, writers like Thomas Mann and Proust also dealt with the theme. Mixed with anti-Semitism and opportunism, this rhetoric of nervous music formed the basi s of the Nazi concept of degenerate music. My goal is to outline and explain the development of the idea of music as a source of pathological nervous strain by putting it in the context of changes in neurology, psychiatry, aesthetics, cultural and sexual politics.

title: Whole Genome Analysis of Copy Number Variation in a Large Case Control Study of Recurrent Depression.
description: This project will analyse for the presence of submicroscopic genomic structural variation (copy number variation, or CNV) between 4,700 cases of narrowly defined unipolar major depression and 2,300 ethnically matched controls. These are already being analysed for SNP variation on the Illumina 610 Quad microarray as part of a larger MRC funded study headed by Professor Peter McGuffin at the IoP. The 610 Quad has additional SNPs specific for detection of CNV. The research will involve advanced t echniques in data mining, normalization of data, CNV calling, statistical testing, regenotyping and sequencing. The goals of such projects are to ultimately identify biomarkers to refine diagnostic specificity and discover new molecular targets for treatment in Psychiatric disorders. This research specifically will aim to identify robust difference in CNV between cases and controls, and at the same time refine and combine methods in data mining, statistical genetics and regenotyping in this most embryonic of research areas. This will identify novel genetic loci for further research into biomarkers for diagnosis and treatment.

title: Psychosis and cortico-cortical connectivity.
description: While psychotic disorders are thought to involve a disruption of cortico- cortical connectivity, it is unclear whether this is a correlate of the disorder itself or is related to risk factors for the disorder. This study aims to examine the integrity of cortical connections and the pattern of cortical gyrification in two unique MRI datasets that have been collected over the last five years: one from a large sample of twins discordant for schizophrenia, and another from a cohort of subjects with prodromal signs of psychosis, scanned before and after the onset of the disorder. Both Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) and conventional MRI data have been acquired. Data will be analysed by using a voxel-brain morphometry approach optimized for DTI, DTI tractography and a method for assessing cortical gyrification. The main hypothesis is that abnormal cortical connectivity will be evident in subjects at high risk of psychosis, but to a lesser degree than in patients with psychosis. This study wi ll provide new information on the relationship between cortical gyrification and white matter integrity, and the extent to which abnormalities in these domains underlie the risk of developing psychosis. The findings should inform the development of new interventions aimed at preventing psychosis.

title: A machine learning approach to the analysis of psychiatric neuroimaging data.
description: The World Health Organization (WHO) states that one in four people experience a mental health problem during their life. The development of technologies for assisting psychiatric diagnosis and predicting treatment responses is extremely relevant to avoid inefficient treatment and to promote mental health. The purpose of this research is to develop models and tools for the application of novel machine learning techniques to the analysis of brain scan data to assist in the understanding, diagnosis and prognosis of psychiatric disorders. Key Goals: 1. Development of new machine learning techniques for the analysis of brain scans including: - Probabilistic classifiers to predict group membership (e.g. patients vs. controls and - responders vs. non- responders); - Hypothesis-driven models of brain alterations in psychiatric disorders (e.g. schizophrenia, depression); - New strategies to extract useful information from neuroimaging data (i.e. feature selection approaches). 2. Developme nt of multi-modal classification integrating data from different techniques (e.g. fMRI, MRI, EEG, genetic data). 3. Validation of the developed approaches using a variety of data sets. 4. Translation of the validated approaches into clinical practice, i.e. development of a toolbox that could be used for aid diagnosis of psychiatric disorders and other clinical/outcome goals.

title: The computational neurobiology of attention.
description: 1\. Work up a plausible model of behaviour in the task, based on the Free Energy Principle and informed by knowledge of cortical structure and neurotransmitter action. 2. Acquire performance and neuroimaging data in the task from normal subjects. Use these data to parameterise and optimize the model, using Bayesian model comparison. 3. Choose one or two psychoactive drugs that are implicated in mental disorder and abnormal task performance in normal subjects and measure performance on this task under these drugs. I will then re-parameterise the model for performance on this drug. The PhD will focus on attention. Patients with schizophrenia seem to be particularly deficient in attentional tasks which involve conflict or identifying which stimulus to attend to (Luck & Gold, 2008; Wang et al., 2005; Maruff et al., 1998). Thus, I will use a modified version of the Posner task (Posner et al., 1978), which introduces conflict, to study this phenomenon. In the Posner subjects are required to foveate a central spot and respond as quickly as possible to the appearance of a peripheral target. The side the target will appear is cued at a fixed interval beforehand. The cue is correct (valid) 80% of the time. Posner found that reaction times to validly cued targets were significantly shorter than to targets which were incorrectly cued. This demonstrated that attention could be moved to salient locations in the absence of gaze shift. Evidence as to the performance of schizophrenic patients in this task is mixed. The choice of this paradigm is based partly on the fact that the groundwork of the modelling has already been done. Moreover, the Posner paradigm yields a wealth of data ? the values parameterising the reaction time distributions to cues with up to three different levels of validity, plus the proportion of correct responses ? which will furnish empirical constraints on key model parameters (e.g., synaptic rate constants and gain). In addition, the cognitive processes engaged by this paradigm are clearly influenced by the pathological process underlying schizophrenia.

title: Separate and interactive effects of COMT and acute tetrahydrocannabinol treatment on frontostriatral dopamine function.
description: The frontostriatal dopamine (DA) system is a key modulator of cognitive function. Dysfunction of this system has been associated with many pathological states including schizophrenia, obsessive compulsive disorder, and cognitive decline in ageing. It has been shown that both genetic and environmental factors can alter frontostriatal DA function. The proposed research project focuses on two of these factors, namely a functional polymorphism in the catechol-0-methyltransferase (COMT) gene and the use of cannabis. It aims to investigate whether COMT and t.-9- tetrahydrocannabinol (THC; the primary psychoactive ingredient of cannabis) have separate and interactive effects on frontostriatal DA function. More specifically, I will examine whether COMT and THC have separate and interactive effects on a) behavioural indices known to depend on frontostriatal DA function b) striatal and prefrontal cortex (PFC) DA levels c) striatal and PFC gene expression. This research will provide valuable information about the effects of cannabis and COMT on normal brain function, both separately and in combination. Investigation of the mechanisms underlying this interaction, which is one of the most promising of the proposed gene x environment interactions in psychiatric research, will help to clarify how individual genetic differences might influence responses to cannabis and why some people may be more vulnerable to psychosis and cognitive dysfunction following cannabis use then others.

title: Expression of ZNF804A, the first genome-wide nd significant psychosis gene and the functional correlates of the risk genotype.
description: 1\. To characterise ZNF804A expression in human brain and establish how this is affected by psychosis and by genotype. IdentifY the regional and cellular expression of ZNF804A in the human brain. Study the developmental profile of ZNF804A expression from fetal to adult life. Compare ZNF804A expression in schizophrenia and bipolar disorder compared to controls, and between risk and non-risk allele carriers at rs /344706. 2. To assess the functional correlates of rs1344706 genotype in the living human brain uSing MEG and complementary imaging methods.

title: Investigating the psychological mechanisms which modulate and the neural mechanisms which instantiate predictive coding in the human brain.
description: This project will investigate predictive coding in the human brain, and the importance of synchronous oscillations in mediating the cortico-cortical interactions which may subserve predictive coding. The combination of an associative paradigm, psychophysical measures of the behavioural impact of predictive relationships between stimuli, and concurrent recording of oscillatory activity using magnetoencephalography (MEG) will allow us to address hypotheses about different forms of predictive coding in an integrated manner. Predictive suppression and top-down facilitation in sensory cortices (see below) have both been investigated using fMRI, but their behavioural effects (e.g. in terms of psychophysical performance) have rarely been investigated, rendering these findings difficult to interpret in terms of functional mechanisms. Moreover, it is unclear which factors (e.g. attentional focus, reward relevance) determine the nature of cortico-cortical interactions. We aim to characterize neural correlates of predictive coding in visual cortex using MEG and a simple associative paradigm, exploiting the high temporal resolution of this technique to investigate the proposal that synchronous oscillations are a primary substrate for the propagation of predictive signals between cortical regions, and the high signal to noise ratio associated with this technique (compared to fMRI) to relate these effects to psychophysical performance on a trial by trial basis. Following the development of associative paradigms, we will use pharmacological manipulations of dopamine to investigate the proposed dopaminergic involvement in modulation of top-down effects on stimulus processing, which is relevant to the neuropathological basis of schizophrenia.

title: Investigating the pathway of centriole and centrosome assembly in Drosophila.
description: Centrioles are cylindrical protein structures present in many eukaryotic cell types .. They are very important cellular structures as they organise two important organelles: centrosomes and cilia. Centrosomes are the main microtubule (MT) organising centre in animal cells, and arEl therefore important in cellular processes such as bipolar spindle formation (essential for separation of chromosomes upon mitosis) and organelle localisation. They are also important locations for the concentration of cell cycle regulators 1. Centrosomes are formed by two centrioles surrounded by the pericentriolar material (PCM), an electron dense protein mass Cilia plays important roles in development and in adult cells. As a consequence, a variety of human diseases have been associated with centriole, centrosome and cilia malfunction. Understanding the mechanism by which centrioles duplicate is therefore important in understanding these essential processes and how they are disturbed in disease. Genetic and RNA interference studies in worms have identified only 5 main players in centriole duplication, SPD-2, ZYG-1, SAS-5 SAS-6 and SAS-44. In Drosophila there are also only 5 proteins involved in this process of which are conserved from worms: DSas-414 and DSas- 615, which are homologues of Sas-4 and Sas-6; and Sak and Ana2, functional orthologues of ZYG-1 and Sas-5 respectively. In Drosophila, DSpd-2 is not necessary for centriole duplication, but an extra player, asterless (Asl) is also involved in duplication. Despite our knowledge of the main players in centriole duplication, however, little is known about how they interact to form new centrioles and to allow these structures to organise the centrosome. I propose here two strategies to better understand some of these processes. Aim 1: Dynamics and regulation of centriole formation using centriole-like structures (CLS). Aim 2: Development of the degron system in Drosophila.

title: Wellcome Trust Clinical PhD Programme in International Health at the LSHTM: 'The roles of non-specialist health workers in mental health care provision in developing countries'.
description: With the significant burden of mental illness in developing countries, the large treatment gap due principally to scarcity of skilled mental health personnel and inequities in their distribution, non-specialist health workers (professionals and non-professionals) (NSHW) are important for task-shifting within mental health care. Growing evidence for NSHWs? use in mental health care highlights the need to systematically examine their roles. India has pioneered decentralised mental health services since the 1970s but so far has had limited success in increasing coverage. Describing programmatic achievements and failures and understanding roles of NSHWs within mental health care are essential for informing policy makers and for building recommendations on effective implementation and sustainability of scaling up community mental health services in India and other low income countries (LICs). This project systematically reviews LIC mental health initiatives, which has not been done before. It explores the history and development of NSHWs? roles in mental health care provision in India through oral and written historical primary source analysis, describes NSHWs current roles through ethnographic observation and interviews and uses Delphi and workshop methods with key international and Indian stakeholders to examine the acceptability and feasibility of non-specialists? roles to inform the development of policies in LICs.
recipient: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine

title: Wellcome Trust PhD Programme for Clinicians at the University of Cambridge: 'The impact of delirium on cognitive outcomes.'
description: Delirium is a neuropsychiatric syndrome that represents a decompensation in cognitive function in response to acute illness. Long-term cognitive sequelae of delirium are not well understood. This study aims to be the most comprehensive analysis to date of the impact of delirium on dementia in the general population. Delirium can be ascertained in part through existing measures of acute cognitive change in population-based cohort studies. These will be refined by data from record-linkage (Hospital Episode Statistics), and retrospective review of hospital records. This delirium exposure measure will then be used to examine rates of cognitive change before and after delirium. In addition, if it is shown that delirium itself contributes to overall cognitive impairment, data on delirium exposure can inform current studies of dementia neuropathology in CFAS. Throughout, there will be a focus on the implications of these models for cognitive health in the general population.

title: African SNOWS: strengthening research capacity in environmental health.
description: The African SNOWS (Scientists Networked for Outcomes from Water and Sanitation) Consortium takes its inspiration from Dr John Snow, who not only founded the science of epidemiology but was also the father of evidence-based interventions for environmental health. He famously prevented cholera in 19th century London by taking something away and changing behaviour (removing a pump handle to prevent its use) as he lacked the funds to provide something, like a better water supply. Ever since then, environmental health has lacked its fair share of resources, and environmental health practitioners have had to use all their creative ingenuity to achieve challenging goals such as behaviour change, as cheaply as possible. Environmental health research has also suffered, particularly in Africa where resources are as scarce as anywhere. At the start of 2008, the International Year of Sanitation, nearly two thirds of the population of sub-Saharan Africa are still without a toilet,and a recent study (World Bank 2008) has estimated that the cost of poor environmental health in child diarrhoea and associated malnutrition amounts tosome 8% of the GDP of an African country. This consortium seeks to begin to redress the balance, by taking advantage of the Wellcome Trust's call for proposals to strengthen health-related research capacity in Africa. Interdisciplinary research into action. The long-term objective of the consortium is to build sustainable capacity in research that leads to improvedpublic health by improving water supply, sanitation and hygiene. We aim to enable African researchers to conduct policy-relevant research on the health impact of environmental interventions, and on how these interventions can be implemented most effectively and taken to scale. We shall do this by building research capacity within the interdisciplinary areas between engineering, epidemiology, environmental microbiology and behavioural sciences, rather thanin water resources or sanitary engineering as such. Key factors (culture, gender, age, perception of disease risk etc.) that motivate or inhibit the sustainable use of sanitary services will also be studied. The sphere of interest will also include problems in situations of stress such as floods, droughts and refugee settings. We will create a sustainable community of active African researchers in durable and enabling institutions by: -Carrying out a participatory needs assessment for individual and institutional capacity-building. -Awarding up to 30 PhD scholarships to outstanding African students, adapting the highly successful Gates Partnership model to our sector's needs. -Promoting research-oriented modules for suitable Master's courses, and the capacity to offer relevant short courses, at African universities which are leaders in our field. -Developing dialogue and collaboration with implementing agencies in the field, to ensure that our research addresses real problems and benefits from stakeholder support, and that our results are applied in practice. -Supporting linked interdisciplinarymulti-centre practically-oriented research projects. -Establishing common field platforms for research from multiple perspectives. -Ensuring continuity of support for post-doctoral and other staff research. -Building and sustaining institutional capacity to manage and conduct research.
