title: Autonomy and mental health.
description: The objectives of the proposed event are threefold: 1. to provide a forum for constructive dialogue between philosophers, mental health practitioners, and legal experts; 2. to spell out key interrelations between two fundamental, yet challenging concepts, that is, autonomy and mental health; and 3. to deepen and expand our understanding of the role of autonomy in psychiatry and promote an inclusive, destigmatising approach to mental disorders.

title: Workshop on Maximising Health Research Communication in Zambia
description: This project aims to develop and conduct a one week Health Research Communication Workshop. The aim of the workshop is to bring together twenty five research scientists, media personnel and public health workers to share experiences and aspirations in the techniques of disseminating health research findings with the view of developing a Research Communication Course or short courses in Zambia. With expert facilitation in the fields of health research, media and public health- the workshop will use lecture, group discussions, a community field trip, and community participation/consultation methods to bring out effective ways of disseminating research findings through a diversity of strategies and communication channels. The course(s) to be developed will help to popularise research communication and enhance public engagement and participation in research that is meant to improve the health of the people and their wellbeing. The course(s) will improve communication of health research findings which will stimulate civil society debate on key health issues, influence policy development in health and spur end users particularly the poor and marginalised and the organisations that work with them to act on new information. Apart from providing evidence and stimulating dialogue between researchers, media and policy makers and users of research results such as non-government organisations and the private sector, the course will contribute to the strengthening of the integration of health research in health sector development in Zambia and eventually in the Southern African region. The workshop will tap into the work already done by other organisations in this field.

title: Self-Directed Research of Public and Environmental Health Problems by Indigenous People in Suriname.
description: The Organisation of Indigenous People in Suriname (OIS), a coalition of indigenous villages, and the Suriname Indigenous Health Fund (SIHF), are proposing a three-year project that will develop the capacity of OIS to independently implement their own public health research and intervention programs. The project will equip them with the technology and training needed to create and promote public health intervention strategies on their own behalf. Currently, their health is impacted by gold mining throughout Suriname's interior region. SIHFund will provide interim administrative and technical support to the OIS until they are able to operate independently. This is a continuation of community-directed projects that began in 2004. Past projects trained indigenous community members to perform their own risk and health assessment studies. The foreign-based SIHF learned how to address their emerging public and environmental health problems. Ethical guidelines and standard operating procedures were developed to assist foreign NGOs who want to work with indigenous communities. The results of these projects were used by participating communities to engage mining companies, local government agencies and international health organisations in discussions that continue until this day. Communities now want to expand their role in the research process so they can eventually take full responsibility for the research process. This project has four goals: 1) promote indigenous public health research projects; 2) develop education strategies that train indigenous researchers; 3) establish relationships that support indigenous research; 4) disseminate research to indigenous audiences through regular contact between indigenous communities and their non-indigenous counterparts.

title: Promoting evidence-based practice for autism in the Arab World
description: Autism is a life-long condition affecting 1 in 100 individuals and interfering with the person's ability to communicate and relate to others. There is currently a clear gap between the level of public awareness of autism and the extent to which scientific research findings are integrated within practice towards people affected by the condition. While this holds internationally, the gap between evidence and practice is much wider in developing countries. Our vision is to promote public engagement with autism research in the Arab world. This is achieved through the integration of the best scientific evidence within the context of characteristics and values of those affected. We view this as a bi-directional learning process. By promoting the use of scientific evidence in practice, stakeholders will have the opportunity to directly articulate their outlook of future research needs and priorities. We will design and implement a series of workshops delivered to families and educators of people with autism. The workshops will be designed with input from leading international figures in autism research and individually customized to maximally benefit stakeholders in each developing country. Local partner organisations in four Arab countries will contribute to the project by facilitating the goals in their communities. Through direct engagement with stakeholders at multiple levels, we will gather critical knowledge about local and regional research needs and priorities. We will disseminate this knowledge locally and globally. By increasing awareness of the state of the science, the immediate impact will be to improve family and educator's practices towards people with autism. The process will also contribute towards deriving future research needs and priorities directly from these stakeholders, with the hope that their vision will influence the global research agenda.

title: Scottish Inebriate Reformatories,1901-1925:The medical role in the response to the last alcohol epidemic.
description: The project will explore the history of the Scottish State Inebriate Reformatories, a short-lived initiative in the management of alcohol abuse, 1901-1925. The existing records of the State Inebriate Reformatory in Perth will be read and surviving records from the local Inebriate Reformatories will also be looked at to address specific questions:- 1) What were the characteristics of the inmate population of these institutions? What was the nature of the therapeutic regime they experienced? 2) What were the backgrounds of the medical men involved in the running of these institutions and how were they connected to the prior campaign for Inebriate Reformatories? What roles did doctors play within these institutions? 3) What were the views of the Scottish psychiatric establishment toward these institutions? What was the nature of the day-to-day relations between the Inebriate Reformatories and the Royal and District asylums. In part this is an exploration of how easy or diffi cult it proved in practice to separate the Inebriate from the Insane , and hence to what extent the problems associated with alcohol use were medicalised. It is hoped that this study will contribute to our understanding of alcohol abuse issues in Scotland today.

title: The neural basis of genetic vulnerability to bipolar disorder.
description: Brain function abnormalities in Bipolar Disorder (BD) suggest involvement of emotional circuitry in the disease development. Unaffected relatives experience subclinical mood instability and emotional difficulties suggestive of an extended phenotype. Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) using emotional tasks that activate circuitry implicated in the pathophysiology of BD could inform our understanding of the neural basis of diagnosable illness and increased genetic liability to BD without the confounds of medication. Aim: To examine brain function in 25 people with BD, 25 unaffected, unmedicated relatives of patients with BD and 25 healthy controls, matched for gender and age. FMRI tasks will be conducted: implicit and explicit event- related emotional recognition for happy, sad and neutral faces. a block-design emotional memory task for emotional scenes followed by associated behavioural tests. Hypotheses: Remitted BD individuals, will demonst rate increased medial temporal lobe (MTL), striatal and decreased prefrontal activation to emotional compared to neutral stimuli. Unaffected relatives will demonstrate disrupted activation in MTL, striatal and prefrontal regions. Functional deficits will be associated with minor degrees of mood instability in otherwise unaffected relatives. Identifying objective biomarkers of disease is likely to be useful in the development and evaluation of new treatments.

title: Functional magnetic resonance imaging of appetite and eating behaviour in obesity surgery.
description: Appetite and eating behaviour changes after obesity surgery are poorly understood. It is likely that alterations in brain reward system play a key role in weight loss. By visualizing activity in brain food reward systems when viewing food pictures, using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), we will be able to demonstrate how brain activation related to food craving is altered by the 2 different surgical procedures. We will also examine whether baseline psychiatric, psychological and fM RI characteristics predict weight loss after surgery. Comparison will be made between obese patients who have previously undergone (i) gastric bypass and (ii) gastric banding surgery, and (iii) un-operated obese patients, and (iv) after temporary reversal of the anorexigenic gut hormone increases seen after gastric bypass surgery. In a prospective study, weight loss at one year post-surgery will be compared between patients with and without binge eating disorder and correlated with other bas eline psychological measurements and fMRI activation in brain food reward systems. Identifying the brain pathways through which obesity surgery works and understanding of the neuropsychological predictors of individual responses to obesity surgery, will aid the use and choice of surgery, and development of novel treatments for obesity, less invasive and risky than surgery.

title: Aberrant novelty and reward salience and the risk of psychosis.
description: BACKGROUND: Current theories propose that the aberrant assignment of salience to otherwise innocuous stimuli is fundamental to the development of psychosis, and reflects dysregulated dopamine function. However, to date studies of salience in patients with psychosis have been limited to its reward aspect and have involved subjects treated with dopamine blocking medication. OBJECTIVES: To use functional MRI to assess both novelty and reward aspects of stimulus salience, in unmedicated subjects experiencing prodromal symptoms of psychosis, and relate this to striatal dopamine function, psychotic symptoms and the risk of subsequent transition to psychosis. METHODOLOGY: Subjects with an At Risk Mental State will be compared to controls while performing tasks that engage novelty salience and reward salience, respectively. Regional brain activation will be assessed using functional MRI. PET measures of striatal dopamine function will be available from the same subjects through another stu dy. Clinical measures will be taken at baseline and at 1 year, and subjects will be monitored for the emergence of frank psychosis. IMPLICATIONS: The present study will clarify the role of different components of salience processing in the development of psychosis. This should inform the development of clinical interventions designed to treat and prevent psychotic disorders.

title: Genetic dissections of hippocampal function.
description: The aim is to provide a unifying account of the hippocampus, using the latest molecular biological techniques, along with a novel in vivo voltammetric approach for recording tissue oxygen concentrations. I will investigate the role of synaptic plasticity in two, distinct forms of hippocampus-dependent spatial memory, and test the novel hypothesis that SRM and SWM reflect associative and non-associative information processing respectively. I will test whether these memory processes can be dis sociated on the basis of (i) the nature of LTP induction, (ii) the mechanisms underlying LTP expression/maintenance, and (iii) the hippocampal pathways recruited and the subfields in which plasticity occurs. I will also test whether the amygdala and ventral hippocampus are differentially associated with fear and anxiety respectively. I will use in vivo oxygen voltammetry to measure haemodynamic responses as an index of brain activity in key regions of interest, and compare this signal to oth er electrophysiological correlates of neuronal activity during behaviour. These techniques will also be combined in genetically modified mice in which key components of hippocampal information processing are disrupted. Finally, I will use this approach to study the contribution of ventral hippocampus and amygdala to emotional processing in pre-clinical mouse models of anxiety and depression.

title: Medicine, Emotion and Disease in History.
description: Recent social-historical research has investigated changing modes and standards of emotional expression and the political implications of these changes (Bourke 2005; Rosenwein 2002, 2006; Stearns, 2003). In medical history new work has explored links between emotion, health and disease (Bound Alberti 2006; Gouk and Hills 2005). Specific themes have included the development of humoral, biochemical and neurological theories of emotion (Dror 1999); psychosomatic medicine (Jackson 2006) and changing technologies of investigation (Hayward 2001; Winter 2003). The proposed research project will bring these developments together. It will do this through the organisation of seminars, workshops and a conference; and also through individual research projects on: medical and legal control of the passions (Dixon); emotional expression (Jones); the humours, madness and the passions (Carrera); psychiatric epidemiology (Hayward); and psychosomatic medicine (Bound Alberti). This collaboration will wo rk towards achieving three key goals. 1. To create a dialogue on the historical role, status and meaning of emotion that will have relevance for contemporary health policy and clinical practice. 2. To provide historians with the medical historical insights necessary for methodological reflection on the historiography of the emotions. 3. To foster public understanding of the historical dimensions of the emotions and the passions.

title: Identifying patterns of genome-wide association in the development of cognitive, behavioural and psychiatric disorders.
description: The research has three primary objectives at three UK centres of excellence instatistical geneticsand computational biology: 1) Methods for multivariate and longitudinal genome-wide association (GWA) in developmental psychiatry at the Wellcome Trust Centre for Human Genetics, Oxford. The applicant will develop multivariate and longitudinal approaches to GWA that also incorporate environmental information to provide more complete models of the developmental aetiology of traits. 2) Visual analysis of genomic information to enhance biological inference at the European Bioinformatics Institute (EBI), Cambridge. The applicant will develop tools tovisually represent high- dimensional GWA data and explore ways of using Ajax technology and the Web to enable collaborative exploration of these rich datasets. 3) Application to developmental hypotheses in TEDS at the Institute of Psychiatry's Social, Genetic and Developmental Psychiatry Centre, King's College London. The applicant will apply methods developed through Objectives 1 and 2 to TEDS GWA data, testing key hypotheses in the development of cognitive, behavioural and psychiatric disorders. Through these aims, the applicant will receive advanced training in the Trust's highlighted strategic training area of mathematical biology and statistical methods, and conduct empirical hypothesis driven research in a large UK population sample towards the Trust's mission of improving human health.

title: Prevalence of common mental disorders and the association with resilience among internally displaced people (IDP) in Puttalam district of Sri Lanka.
description: Data on prevalence of the common mental disorders among the internally displaced people in Sri Lanka is very limited. This study aims particularly to estimate the prevalence of Common Mental Disorders (CMD) and suicidal ideation and will also test hypotheses concerning potential protective effects of higher social support and higher individual ?resilience?. The study will sample the IDP population resident in the Puttalam district of the North Western province of Sri Lanka. The IDPs are mainly resident in 141 welfare camps (Resettlement Camps). Participants will be 18 years old, who had been residing in a district in North and Eastern provinces of Sri Lanka and who have migrated to Puttalam during the last 20 years. A total sample of 316 people will be recruited and interviewed with standard measures including those of CMD, suicidality, post-traumatic stress disorder, pre- and post- migration social status, social support and resilience.

title: Heathen Sufferings: The Church Missionary Society and mental ill-health at Mengo Hospital, Uganda, 1897-1944
description: I will explore constructions of mental ill-health at the Church Missionary Society (CMS) Mengo Hospital, Uganda, 1897-1944, in order to redress a historiographical bias towards discourses of colonial governance in colonial psychiatry. By introducing a medical mission as a distinct context for psychiatric discourses, my research will develop a new framework in which psychiatric practices can be examined.

title: The Emergence of 'Parasuicide' in British Psychiatry and Society c. 1950 - 1980
description: This project examines the emergence of 'parasuicide' (i.e. the 'suicidal gesture') as an organising concept in British psychiatric medicine and wider society between 1950 and 1980. The first goal involves charting the contours of "parasuicide" through an analysis of the psychiatric journal literature. I will examine the practical methods that clinicians used to distinguish parasuicide from other "self-harming" behaviours such as assignment of motives, assessment of method lethality and a series of enduring stereotypes regarding the age and gender of the parasuicidal subject. Second, the influence of institutions and their intellectual contexts (such as the Regional Poisoning Treatment Centre in Edinburgh) will be assessed in order to investigate a sense of spatial (not just temporal) specificity for "parasuicide". The third goal involves investigation of lay and legal renderings of "attempted suicide" (such as those deployed by the Samaritans or in the 1961 Suicide Act) and any conflicts or negotiations that might occur between differing understandings of this behaviour. Finally, the role of material and technological factors (such as the availability of an "artificial kidney" or patient access to prescription drugs) will be examined insofar as they influence different types of discussions about "suicide gestures" at different times.

title: Crossing the boundaries of mind and medicine: Carl du Prel (1839-1899) and his network in the history of dynamic psychiatry
description: The proposed research aims to a) detail du Prel's philosophical-psychological system in the context of emerging mechanistic, monistic, and other theories of mind and body, especially pertaining to issues related to the mental causation of physical and mental health, b) reconstruct the genesis of knowledge claims of opponents of late nineteenth- to early twentieth century psychical research, who held that certain unpopular beliefs and unusual experiences were inherently pathological or based on deviant cognitive functioning, c) evaluate the significance of responses to psychical research in general, and du Prel and his network in particular, for the making of psychology as a university discipline, d) assess the relationship between the theories of du Prel and those of the founder of 'subliminal psychology', Frederic Myers, whose theories informed key concepts in the psychology of the unconscious.

title: A psychological approach to understanding and treating bipolar disorder: investigating new cognitive mechanisms.
description: Given the need to improve our understanding and treatment of bipolar disorder, this research investigates cognitive and emotional processes underlying mood instability. My previous research demonstrated that imagery has a powerful impact on emotion. I have developed a theory of mental imagery s amplification of emotion within bipolar disorder, proposing that this drives mood instability. The research will test hypotheses from this theory (and existing pilot-work), investigating whether biase s in mental imagery form part of the disorder s psychopathology. Treatment of imagery-related abnormalities will be explored. The research goals are to determine whether imagery-related abnormalities: (A) Occur in bipolar disorder and are specific to it; (B) Predict mood fluctuation; (C) Have causal significance; (D) Respond to cognitive behavioural treatment procedures? Each goal is the subject of a specific project. Project A compares imagery biases between clinical and non- clinic al groups. Project B prospectively studies patients with bipolar disorder using SMS (mobile phone) technology to track process changes over time. Project C experimentally manipulates imagery (in analogue samples) to determine whether hypothesised mechanisms have a causal role. Treatment development with patients in Project D will be informed by the experimental work. Project D includes a preliminary uncontrolled evaluation of the new cognitive behavioural treatment.

title: Neurocognitive Mechanisms of Learning and Representation of Numerical Information in the Numerate and Innumerate Brain.
description: This project will examine the neuronal and cognitive bases for acquiring, encoding, and representing numbers in the normal brain and the atypical (developmental dyscalculia (DD)) brain. By using behavioural, neuroimaging, and brain stimulation methods, and experimentally manipulating the learning regime of artificial digits I will examine: 1) The trajectory of functional plasticity (as reflected by whole brain, functional and effective connectivity analyses), and the trajectory of anatomical pla sticity (as reflected by diffusion tensor imaging, and voxel-based morphometry analysis) on the brain network that is involved in learned numerical representation. 2) The effect of explicit vs. implicit learning regimes of numerical information. 3) The commonalities and differences between newly learned numbers and digits, as a function proficiency (i.e., the issue of abstractness). 4) The capability of the DD brain to learn and represent new numerical material when it is explicit and implicit. 5) The effect of brain stimulation on numerical acquisition and representation in non-DD subjects and improving learning in DD subjects. The results will have important implications for many groups of people including the basic understanding of human brain organisation, its typical and atypical development, rehabilitation and education, and for people from the fields of neuroscience, psychology and education.

title: The Lion's Face.
description: The Opera Group (TOG) will produce The Lion's Face, a new opera which explores social, emotional and physical impacts of Alzheimer's Disease. Composer Elena Langer and Poet Glyn Maxwell have been researching this opera with support from Wellcome Trust, including an intensive research phase with Professor Simon Lovestone's team at the Institute of Psychiatry (loP), King's College London. The opera will premiere at Brighton Festival in Spring 2010 and tour to the UK's leading music and theatre venues. In addition, TOG will deliver a programme of associated dissemination activities with each tour venue created in partnership with local scientific partners.

title: Investigating attentional function and cognitive fluctuations in Lewy body disease: a functional magnetic imaging and electrophysiological study.
description: Background: Lewy body dementias (LBD) include Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) and Parkinson s disease with dementia (PDD). LBD are common age-related neurodegenerative disorders and cause considerable disability, morbidity and mortality. They are characterized by fluctuating cognitive and attentional impairment, Parkinsonism and visual hallucinations. The aetiology of the cognitive fluctuations (FC) and attentional impairment is poorly understood; yet such knowledge is essential to develop rati onal management strategies for this important clinical feature. Aims & Methods: 24 subjects with DLB, 24 with PDD, 24 with Alzheimer s dementia, and 24 normal aged matched controls will be recruited. All subjects will undergo detailed physical, neurological, neuropsychiatric, ophthalmological and neuropsychological assessments as well as assessment of any cognitive fluctuations. Aim 1: Investigate attentional function using a visual attentional task. Neural activation patterns during the tas k will be measured on separate occasions by functional magnetic resonance imaging and high density electroencephalography (EEG). Aim 2: Investigate white matter connectivity in LBD using Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) and compare and contrast this with spectral coherence in resting EEG frequency bands between disparate cortical regions. Outcome: Analysis and modelling of imaging and electrophysiological data will provide valuable insights into the aetiology of FC and attentional dysfunction in LBD.

title: Sainsbury Wellcome Centre for Neural Circuits and Behaviour; Interim Director Support.
description: Neuroscience is entering a new and exciting period in which it will be possible to decipher the neural codes underlying cognition and emotion. Our aim is to position the Sainsbury Wellcome Centre at the heart of this development. The convergence of novel genetic, molecular, physiological, optical and behavioural approaches will enable scientists in the Sainsbury Wellcome Centre to monitor activity across genetically-defined ensembles of neurons in behaving animals, and to manipulate this activity in a temporally and spatially precise manner. This will make it possible for the first time to establish causal links between patterns of neural activity and behaviour, and to allow decisive tests of new theories about the computational properties of neural circuits. The new Centre will use model systems including rodents, and perhaps fish, and will maintain close contact with the fly research conducted at the Centre for Neural Circuits and Behaviour in Oxford. The animal models under consideration are excellent candidates for linking activity in neural circuits with well-defined behaviours. Drawing on current strengths at UCL and with the intention of maximizing collaborations with existing UCL neuroscientists, we envisage focusing on neural circuits underlying visual, motor, spatial, social and affective behaviours, during development and maturity, and for experience-dependent plastic changes. One advantage of such behaviours is that they can be studied across multiple species with different levels of complexity, allowing models with simpler nervous systems such as larva and adult zebrafish to facilitate conceptual development. They also provide a tractable methodological testbed before implementation in more complex systems (e.g. rodents). This blue sky research undertaken in the Centre will address some of the key problems in neuroscience and the basic understanding gained will have the additional benefit of providing the foundations for understanding neurological and psychiatric diseases which are emerging as some of the major epidemics of our time.
