Successful commercialisation of these products would enable genetic testing to be offered to all patients with developmental disorders in the UK, rather than the current minority. This project is designed to transform clinical genetic practice for developmental disorders by providing timely, cost-effective and accurate diagnosis for many patients who are currently undiagnosable.

title: Development and application of a targeted array test to diagnose and direct therapy in haematological cancers.
description: Leukaemia and Non-Hodgkin-Lymphomas (NHL) are cancers that arise from bone marrow or lymphoid organs, respectively. Lymphomas are the fifth commonest cancer in the UK. Approximately 20,000 patients are diagnosed with haematological cancers each year. Most types remain incurable, following a chronic relapsing course, thus representing a significant healthcare burden. Treatments vary according to the sub-type of disease but chemotherapy is the mainstay. Novel targeted therapies are emerging but their expense makes it imperative to stratify patients according to genetic response predictors of efficacy. Genomic imbalances are important prognostic indicators for leukaemia. However, current NHS tests for these have limited resolution. Alternative, higher resolution, genomics technologies that detect genomic imbalances as well as other relevant changes have potential to improve diagnostic/prognostic accuracy, but must be specifically developed for clinical diagnostic use. To address this, we aim to develop an innovative microarray-based prognostic test for leukaemia that incorporates new statistical algorithms and software that make it suitable for routine use globally. We will translate this test into the NHS. This novel approach will enable leukaemia treatments to be targeted more effectively, thereby reducing morbidity/mortality, improving patient well-being and lowering the cost burden of this condition for the NHS and other healthcare providers.

title: Psychiatric Reform in Brazil.
description: The Psychiatric revolution which occured in Brazil radically redifined the system of institutionalisation and treatment. The term coined at the time was that of a de-instiutionalisation in favour of more community therapy projects and specialised day centres of rehabilitation and treatment. Although the Italian democratic model of psychiatric reform greatly informed that of Brazil with the notion of doing away with the asylum and its beds , it is not a direct parallel, for Brazilian cultural diversity has played an important part in the strategisation and indeed, the psychopathology of community psychiatric assistance. The pilot, more than being a salvage operation of historical data alone, will be to explore the significance and uniqueness of cultural changes to psychiatry and community assistance in Brazil. The key goals are: (1) to obtain oral historical evidence of Professor Paulo Amarante who spearheaded psychiatric reform (2) to assess the influence of Franco Basaglia's d emocratic psychiatry on Brazil (3) to assess historical parallels (4) to publish the interviews with Professor Paulo Amarante and the Minister of Health Paul Delgado (5) that the pilot findings will form the basis of an extended comparative project focusing on strategies of mental health and community care

title: Imperial iGEM project 2010.
description: The Imperial College iGEM team has always been run according to the ethos of the competition. This allows for free and creative thinking, driven by the students, but guided by the advisors. An important aspect of this is that the final idea for the project comes from the students. Because of this they have both a responsibility and a motivation invested in the idea. This has proved to be a highly effective method for enabling students to think creatively as well as being a highly effective teaching method when supervised appropriately. The overall aim of this project is therefore to provide the environment and resources for students to create a novel biological system, which they can implement during the course of the summer project, and present at the iGEM jamboree at MIT in November 2010. There are also specific objectives within the broad remit of the project. The project must rationally design a novel biological system, based on existing standard biological parts, as well as creating new parts The project must be of biomedical relevance that will improve the well-being of society The project must be considered socially and ethically from inception The project must be inter-disciplinary, involving students from different backgrounds There must be an engineering and modelling component to the project as well as wet biology experiments The design of the system must conform to biobrick standards, which the students must learn about and understand Students will be trained in both wet and dry lab methods

title: Me and My World.
description: A reinvention of the existing, hugely popular Me and My Body exhibition, this project will harness the very latest knowledge and techniques in playful learning to captivate, stimulate and challenge children and their families in science, health and well-being. Me and My World will celebrate children as confident individuals who can live safe, healthy and fulfilling lives. Multi- sensory, hands-on exhibits will encourage them to explore how the body works; imaginative spaces and activities will invite them to enjoy and understand the uniqueness of their own bodies. The experience will be inclusive and accessible to all. Every space and experience will be carefully researched and designed by experts, working hand in hand with children themselves, to capture children's imaginations as they learn and develop through play. The project will inspire children up to the age of 11 tostart questioning their own role in the world and the choices they can make to influence their own futures. It will reach out into the community to enrich the lives of those who are least advantaged, for whom a safe gathering place in which to play, discover and learn about themselves and their bodies is of particular value. This project is the first step of a major redevelopment, which over the next 10-15 years will transform Eureka! The National Children's Museum. This work will reach beyond the existing Halifax site, both through our contribution to the field of play-based learning and through ambitious initiatives such as a new Eureka! in London. Me and My World will serve as a model for a sister exhibition in this London venue.

title: BodyWorks Health & Well-being in the 21st Century.
description: BodyWorks is an exciting new approach to disseminating research outcomes and latest good practice to the general population. This practical hands-on' exhibition will use a combination of interactive exhibits and living lab' experiences to raise awareness of the science underpinning human health & well-being in the 21st century. The exhibition will be a dynamic installation that flows organically throughout the whole of the 700 m2 third floor of Glasgow Science Centre (GSC), taking full advantage of the bright, open, riverside aspect to create an immediate wow' factor. In this impressive spaceinteractivity, engagement, fundamental biology and personal health & well-being are key to the exhibition design. At the heart of this exhibition are 10 Research Capsules' that will showcase cutting-edge developments in biomedical science. Evolving over time through collaboration with research establishments, the capsules will inspire the visitor to learn more through a host of sensory and interactive experiences. The addition of a Live Lab' will provide ample opportunity for the public to engage with practising life science researchers and voluntarily participatein specific research activities. Extension of the exhibition through Web2.0 tools and techniques will enable continued engagement by public visitors, schools and communities and extend opportunities for active participation in ongoing and new research programmes. The exhibition and its associated programmes will run over six years and aims to reach more than 1.8 million public visitors and schoolchildren from across the UK.

title: Mechanism of endocannabinoid signaling and its role in the regulation of synaptic communication
description: Cell-to-cell communication controlled by cannabinoids has been shown to play a crucial role in several normal and pathological processes, however, the cellular mechanisms underlying the cannabinoid effects are largely unknown. The overall goal of the proposed research is to reveal the molecular logic of endocannabinoid signalling in neuronal circuitries. The first project aims to clarify the identity of endogenous ligands activating cannabinoid receptors under physiological circumstances. The presence of distinct types of endocannabinoids as well as their receptors in the CNS suggests the possibility of the selective control of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic transmission. Second aim is to uncover the detailed mechanisms of endocannabinoid-mediated regulation of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic communication. To achieve this, experiments will be addressed to elucidate the relationship between endocannabinoid- and nitric oxide-mediated signalling. The third specific aim is to determine the interaction among CB1 cannabinoid receptors, 5-HT3 serotonergic receptors and a neuropeptide cholecystokinin know to co-exist at a subset of GABAergic axon terminals. We will elucidate the mechanisms of the release of cholecystokinin and its control by CB1 receptors. These experiments will be performed in the hippocampus and basolateral amygdala, in brain regions where cannabinoids may influence memory formation as well as anxiety.

title: 4 year PhD in Neuroscience - Assessing and modelling the effects of antidepressant medication on the learning of emotional and non-emotional information
description: This project will use behavioural and neuroimaging techniques to test two competing models of the time lag in clinical effects of antidepressant drugs. Both these accounts predict improvements in learning with antidepressant treatment but critically expect a different balance of effects on emotional versus non-emotional learning processes. A series of studies will use behavioural and neural markers of learning and plasticity in healthy volunteers to explore the effects of drug treatments relevant to depression and anxiety. Ultimately, the aim of the project is to improve our understanding of the mechanisms of action of antidepressant medication with a view to using this knowledge to inform the early-stage development of novel treatment regimes.

title: Isoform-specific Ras function during development.
description: Ras proto-oncogenes are key signalling intermediates controlling cell proliferation, differentiation and survival. Whilst most attention has focussed on the role of aberrant Ras signalling in cancer, normal Ras function is critical for embryonic development. Intriguingly, this process appears to be differentially dependent on individual Ras isoforms for reasons that remain unclear. Our study will characterise: 1. Tissue-specific gene expression and protein abundance patterns of Ras isoforms during early mouse development. 2. The contribution of Ras isoform-specific signalling networks to early embryonic development. 3. What signalling networks are engaged by Ras mutations associated with developmental disorders compared to those engaged by classical oncogenic mutations. This will allow us to ask whether and how different Ras isoforms contribute to the development of different tissue lineages and lead us to mechanistic insights into the specific pathways regulated by Ras isoforms to promote differentiation versus stemness. In later work we will develop isogenic cell models containing HRAS or KRAS mutations associated with developmental disorders. These mutations are believed to be less potent than oncogenic mutations; we will investigate whether this is the case and how this translates into differential coupling to Ras effector pathways.

title: Systems neuroscience: From networks to behaviour - Modulation of prefrontal cortex circuits in vivo and in vitro in normal animals and rodent models of schizophrenia.
description: The prefrontal cortex (PFC) is involved in many higher cognitive functions including working memory, attention and planning. Neuromodulators, such as the monoamines dopamine and serotonin play a key role in regulating these functions and are also central to many diseases associated with PFC dysfunction, including addiction and schizophrenia. In addition, the neuromodulator systems are also the targets of treatment for these conditions. Despite this key role the mechanisms of how the different neuromodulator systems alter PFC circuit function are still unclear and this proposal aims to further our understanding of the role of these key neuromodulators in the PFC. Specific Aims: 1. Determine how monoamines modulate network activity using in vitro models of PFC oscillations from normal animals. 2. Determine how the above neuromodulators alter single spike and local field potential activity recorded in the PFC in vivo in anaesthetised normal animals and rodent models of schizophrenia. 3. Determine how the above neuromodulators alter interactions between the PFC and the hippocampus and the PFC and the primary auditory cortex in anesthetised rats. Assess how these long-range interactions are altered in rodent models of schizophrenia. 4. Determine the effects of neuromodulators on long-range PFC cortical interactions and local oscillatory activity in freely moving normal animals and rodent models of schizophrenia.

title: Systems neuroscience: From networks to behaviour - Impact of maternal deprivation on cortical gamma oscillations.
description: Early life stress (i.e., a period of social deprivation or neglect occurring in postnatal life) is associated with a variety of neuropsychiatric outcomes in adult life. These include depression, post-traumatic-stress disorder, panic disorder, schizophrenia, attention deficit disorder and an abnormal stress response. Stress exposure in early life is also associated with deficits in cognitive function, including impaired spatial learning and memory. Little information exists concerning the impact of early life stress on cortical rhythms of cognitive relevance. Using a rodent model of early life stress, the ability of cortical circuits to generate neuronal oscillations implicated in cognitive function, will be examined. Specific aims to be addressed in cortical slices from control and maternally deprived rats are: 1) What is the impact of maternal deprivation for gamma oscillation generating circuits in a number of critical cortical regions? 2) Can differences between gamma oscillations in control and MD cortical circuits be explained by a reduction in the expression of specific interneuron subclasses? 3) Assess the longitudinal impact across lifespan of MD for cortical gamma oscillations.

title: Epigenetics and schizophrenia: Integration of chromatin dynamics and animal behaviour
description: The aims of this project are to investigate the connections between environmental stress-induced changes in the euchromatic histone methyltransferase 1 gene (EHMT1), epigenetic regulation and behaviour. Our investigation will be divided into three stages which are designed to establish: 1) The effects of environmental stress on EHMT1 expression and methylation patterns; 2) The identification of EHMT1-mediated methylation patterns and target genomic loci; 3) Whether stress induced changes in EHMT1 expression and methylation lead to subsequent changes in target gene expression. Schizophrenia is a serious psychiatric disorder affecting approximately 1% of the population. Genetic factors are consistently found to account for a large percentage of the risks in developing the disease. Known environmental risks have also been identified. However, progress in understanding the aetiology and developmental trajectory of the disorder is seriously hampered both by the lack of consistency in findings and the entrenched state of the post mortem tissue often used for analysis. The contribution of both environmental and genetic risks suggests that there may be a significant epigenetic component to the elevated risks. A recent copy number variant screen of schizophrenia patients identified increased risks associated with either a deletion or duplication of histone methyltransferase gene EHMT19. EHMT1, also known as G9a-like protein (GLP), is a member of a complex set of site-specific lysine (K) methyltransferases (or KMTs) which transfer the methyl group S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) to lysine residues. GLP protein forms a multimeric complex with several protein families including G9a/EHMT2 in order to mediate monomethylation and dimethylation on lysine-9 of Histone 3 (H3K9me)11. EHMT1-mediate H3K9me2 marks chromatin sites for the transcriptional silencing of individual genes. Kirov et al. also reported several CNVs encoded members of the DLG family of Membrane Associated Guanylate Kinases (MAGUKs). Interestingly, EHMT1 has been found to directly regulate the DLG family members. In addition to finding a handful of highly penetrate CNVs, the case de novos were also found to be significantly enriched for the post-snynaptic density (PSD) proteome. This was further explained by specific enrichment in NMDAR and neuronal activity-regulated cytoskeleton- associated protein or ARC, both of which are postsynaptic signalling complexes9. Kirov et al.'s identification of related gene groups enriched in these CNVs provides a promising biological pathway for analysis. Furthermore their specific identification of NMDAR enrichment in these patients along with a recent report providing evidence that KMTs may directly mediated NMDA subunit expression in a highly specific manner bodes well with leading hypothesis on the role of NMDA hypofunciton in schizophrenia. Accumulating evidence reviewed below points to the direct role of EHMT1 in experience- dependent transcriptional regulation and cognition in both the developing and mature brain. In order to simplify, we will structure our investigation around the Kirov et al. report. We will focus on the DLG gene family and PSD-related gene expression and on NMDA receptor function.

title: Investigating the behavioural consequences of perturbed Cdkn1c expression; developmental programming, dopamine and mental illness
description: The main aim of this project is to examine the role of the imprinted cyclin dependant kinase inhibitor gene, Cdkn1c, in neural development and the resultant behaviour in adult animals when the copy number of Cdkn1c is altered. Furthermore we will assess how manipulation of maternal environment during pregnancy interacts with Cdkn1c expression in the normal animal and how this affects midbrain structure and animal behaviour.

title: Molecular, genetic and lifecourse epidemiology.
description: 1\. Summarise the current literature on the role of 5-HTTLPR on discontinuation from antidepressant treatment (SSRI v. non-SSRI). 2. Compare the adverse effect profile of citalopram and reboxetine treatment in GenPod. 3. Identify any genetic variants, affecting the pharmacokinetics and the pharmacodynamics of drugs used to treat depression, which are associated with the occurrence of adverse effects or discontinuation from citalopram or reboxetine treatment. Initially this will be achieved using a genome wide approach, followed by specific, candidate gene approach investigating the following hypotheses: a) The CYP2C19*2 variant will be associated with general adverse effects causing discontinuation from citalopram: b) The S allele of 5-HTTLPR will be associated with general adverse effects causing discontinuation from citalopram; c) The 178C/C genotype of the 5-HT3A will be associated with Gl adverse effects with citalopram treatment; d) The T/T genotype (-3081AfT) of NAT will be associated with general adverse effects causing discontinuation from reboxetine.

title: The pathology of the emotions
description: My research will show how melancholy in nineteenth-century Britain was conceptualised as a disease of the emotions situated in the brain through the influence of German psychiatry and neurology. There are five main goals to this project: - To address a lack in existing historical scholarship as no comprehensive study of nineteenth-century melancholy exists. - To demonstrate how the understanding of melancholy as a disease of the emotions was facilitated by two key developments: Firstly, the creation of 'emotions' as a psychological category within the emergent evolutionary paradigm, and secondly the growing influence of physiology and neurology on psychiatric thought and practice which involved understanding its functions through the concept of 'mental reflex'. - To show how emotions were produced as symptoms of melancholy and made into a useful psychiatric category. - To explore, through a close reading of case reports and patient letters, - To consider what the implications were of this biomedical cerebral melancholy for how 'normal' and 'pathological' emotions came to be understood and defined in the late nineteenth century.

title: 'Unable to give any account of himself': Male experiences of Stanley Royd asylum, Wakefield, 1880-1900.
description: The project examines the influence and interplay of popular and scientific explanations for male mental illness during the period 1880-1900. My first key goal will be to gather a sample for statistical analysis, enabling me to identify any significant differences between the experiences of male and female patients at Stanley Royd asylum e.g. duration of illness prior to admission. This will allow me to compare and place my findings within the existing historiography, and highlight any points of particular interest that merit further investigation e.g. the reasons given at admission for male/female committal. Secondly, I will examine medical casebooks for insights into the opinions of doctors, families and acquaintances on the situation of the patient: if there are clear judgements on a male patient's state of mind which flow from contemporary ideals of 'manliness', and if treatments draw explicitly upon such ideas e.g. the prescription of strong beer and physical work to remedy a man's 'weak' nature. Thirdly, papers and lectures by asylum doctors will be consulted. As well as investigating the possibility of biological explanations reinforcing or challenging existing gender stereotypes, these will chart the development of biological psychiatry at Stanley Royd that influenced researchers further afield.

title: 'The great class which lies between': Provision for the non-pauper insane in Ireland, 1830-1900.
description: Through a close survey of the records of selected private and district asylums, Commission of Lunacy reports, and official records, the project will explore the domestic and institutional provision for the Irish non-pauper insane from c.1830 to 1900, a period marked by significant socioeconomic change. It will assess whether the emergence of a strong middle-class in this period informed interactions between gender, religion, identity, and insanity, and question whether underlying medical, legal and lay explanations of mental illness and its predisposing factors in this group differed from those attributed to pauper patients in Ireland. The project will reflect on the anxieties that were prompted among local and national authorities, the medical profession and families, inside and outside the asylum, while devising management strategies. It will then assess the impact of these strategies upon patient and family experiences of insanity. This project will consider whether some Irish asylums operated as a mixed economy' of care and will explore how class and religious divisions were played out among the patient and staff populations within the asylums thereby contributing to emerging debates on presence of emotional communities' within asylums. The main outputs comprise a PhD thesis, three articles two policy-related and a workshop.

title: Senility before Alzheimer: Old Age Mental Health in British Medicine, Politicsand Culture, 1840- 1914.
description: This project will explore how 'senile dementia' was understood before Alzheimer in latenineteenth century Britain in medical, political and popular contexts. It will look to the period 1840- 1914 as a time of intense political interest in both the elderly and the mentally ill, and as the time when the word 'senile' shifted, from a value-neutral term describing the general condition of old age, to a more negative term with significant connotations about mental incapacity. Key goals: - To assess how the mental changes of old age were described and explained by psychiatrists. - To examine the relationship between published ideas and practice in increasingly crowded asylums. - To investigate the relationship between the political discourses on pensions, retirement and the welfare of the aged poor, and mental aspects of ageing. - To survey representations of the 'senile' in 'popular culture', and to examine the relationship between these representations, medical models and political concerns. The final product will be a broad survey of the images and meanings of 'old age' in Victorian society and culture, and the place of 'mental capacity and behaviour' within them.

title: PREMIUM: A program for effective mental health interventions in under- resourced health systems
description: The proposed program (?PREMIUM?) aims to define a systematic methodology for the development and evaluation of psychological treatments for delivery by Community and Lay Health Workers and to test this methodology for two mental disorders of global health significance, viz., Depressive Disorder and Alcohol Use Disorders. In the first phase, the program will implement the systematic methodology for development of treatments, derived from three distinct sources of experience and knowledge, to answer two key questions: what are the components of the treatment and how should it be delivered. This phase will comprise a number of sequential steps: synthesis of global and local evidence through systematic reviews and search of the gray literature; determining components of the treatment through consultations with diverse stakeholders; determining an acceptable and feasible delivery model for the treatment through formative research case studies; and testing the intervention in the real world in pilot trials. In the second phase, the clinical and cost- effectiveness of the treatments developed will be evaluated in parallel group randomized controlled trials with primary health care attenders. In the final phase, the findings will be disseminated and a framework for increasing access to these treatments within routine health care programs developed.
recipient: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine

title: The Colombo Twin and Singleton Study (CoTaSS) follow up.
description: We will follow up the Colombo Twin and Singleton Study, a population based twin study of 1954 twin pairs and 2019 non-twins who in the first wave of data collection completed a psychiatric interview to ascertain common mental disorders, alcohol and nicotine use, post traumatic stress disorder and physical symptoms. The second wave of data collection will repeat some of these measures, particularly in relation to depression, and include detailed ascertainment of phenotypes relevant to metabolic syndrome and cardio- metabolic risk, including anthropometrics, BP, fasting lipids, glucose and insulin, an immune marker, heart rate variability, diet and exercise. The twin sample will be extended using the Colombo twin register, to increase the number of individuals with severe symptoms of depression included in the study. Prevalence and 95% CIs for the main phenotypes under study will be described. Heritability will be estimated using conventional model fitting approaches. Bivariate mod els will be used to explore the relationship between dimensions of metabolic syndrome, and the extent to which any overlap between dimensions could be explained by genetic or environmental factors. Similar analyses will be performed to test the hypothesis that any overlap between depression and metabolic syndrome variables can be explained by shared genes.

title: Imaging mechanisms of energy failure following head injury.
description: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) caused over 170,000 NHS hospital admissions in 2008, requiring over 0.5 million acute hospital bed-days, and over 50,000 intensive care unit bed-days annually. TBI is amongst the most important causes of death in young adults. Survivors experience an enormous burden of physical disability, neurocognitive deficits, and neuropsychiatric sequelae. Despite this, outcome following injury has improved through the provision of protocol driven therapy aimed at preventing an d treating secondary ischaemic insults. However, energy failure may be due to mechanisms other than classical ischaemia, and this may explain the failure of pharmacological neuroprotective therapies. The research detailed in this application aims to improve our understanding of the mechanisms of energy failure following TBI using magnetic resonance imaging, proton spectroscopy and positron emission tomography to map the extent and spatial distribution of metabolic derangements. These will differ entiate classical ischaemia, regional hypoxia secondary to microvascular injury and mitochondrial dysfunction. Sequential measurements of n-acetylaspartate, a mitochondrial metabolite, will address whether metabolic derangements are reversible and represent mitochondrial dysfunction, or irreversible and represent on going neuronal loss. Such data may provide important advances in the development and implementation of successful neuroprotective therapies.

title: Reward prediction in health and disease.
description: Our goal is to characterise and extend our understanding of behavioural and brain signatures of prediction-dependent responding in schizophrenia. The behavioural symptoms of schizophrenia, as well as the implications of dopaminergic alterations, suggest that abnormal prediction error signals and predictions may be key to understanding the condition. Several functional neuroimaging studies have provided evidence in favour of this view. However, the functions of prediction errors in learning and b ehaviour are complex and cannot be adequately characterised solely in terms of their presence and magnitude. We hypothesise that a detailed understanding of the adaptivity of prediction error coding and the variability of reward prediction in relation to background environmental characteristics will bring us closer to understanding the positive symptoms of schizophrenia. Our aims are therefore to explore these two features of error-dependent learning using complementary studies in control partic ipants and in patients with schizophrenia. Our specific goal is to identify changes in prediction error sensitivity to adaptation and contingency in patients and to characterise the extent to which these signals in healthy controls are susceptible to perturbations induced by dopaminergic drugs (L-Dopa and sulpiride). In doing so, we will provide critical insights to the neurobiology of positive symptoms of schizophrenia.

title: An investigation on community-level influences on mental health amongst internally displaced persons and returnees in Georgia using innovative methodological and analytical techniques.
description: Evidence shows how persons forcibly displaced from their homes by armed conflict are subject to many negative influences on their mental health. There is far less evidence on what factors may promote their mental health such as community-based factors of housing conditions, security, mobility, social networks, and sources of support. Georgia has approximately 250,000 internally displaced persons (IDPs) who live in a variety of types of settlements in rural and urban areas. No reliable data could be identified on the mental health status of these IDPs or those who have recently returned to their home areas (returnees). We firstly propose to conduct a cross-sectional survey with a representative sample of Georgian IDPs and returnees to collect individual- level data on their mental health and investigate the influence of community factors on their mental health. Secondly, we propose to collect community- level data using an innovative community profiling method to help quantify the extent to which the communities in which IDPs and returnees live may promote their mental health. Data analysis will include multivariate analysis and multi-level modelling; and the validity, reliability and feasibility of the community profiling method. The project will include activities to strengthen epidemiological research capacity on mental health Georgia.
recipient: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine

title: Exploring the link between extrasynaptic GABA-A receptors and behaviour.
description: A central aim of this proposal is to understand how a tonic conductance generated by high-affinity alpha4, beta & delta subunit-containing GABA-A receptors can influence cell excitability, network dynamics and whole-animal behaviour. Stephen Brickley will study the tonic conductance generated in three brain regions that strongly express alpha4, beta & delta subunit- containing GABA-A receptors; layer II/III neocortical pyramidal cells, thalamic relay neurons and medium spiny neurons of the striat um. William Wisden will utilize region-specific promoters to drive Cre expression and enable the deletion of alpha4, beta & delta subunit-containing GABA-A receptors from these neurons. To complement our in vitro assays of cellular/network excitability we will make use of in vivo recording methods developed in Nick Franks laboratory to monitor a variety of extracellular electrical signals in freely moving mice. We are interested in exploring how slow thalamo-cortical oscillations observed durin g non-REM sleep are influenced by thalamic, striatal and neocortical tonic conductances. We believe that this multidisciplinary approach will help explain why disturbances in extrasynaptic GABA-A receptor function are associated with the sleep deficits reported in neurological disorders such as depression, schizophrenia, epilepsy and Parkinson s disease.

title: The Incidence, Course and Outcome of Psychosis in Socially and Culturally Diverse Settings: A Pilot Study.
description: Our understanding of the nature, onset and outcome of schizophrenia and other psychoses is largely based on studies conducted in North America, Europe and Australasia. Few studies have been carried out in other settings. The exceptions, the WHO multi-country studies conducted in the 1960s, 1970s and 1980s, raised a number of important questions about the determinants of cross- cultural variations in the incidence and outcome of schizophrenia that have not been pursued in similarly rigorous and co mparable cross-country studies since. It is our eventual objective to address these questions in a programme of research in three diverse settings: Ibadan (Nigeria); Chennai (India); and Trinidad and Tobago. There are, however, a number of methodological challenges inherent in studying psychosis across diverse settings and there is a consequent need to conduct substantial pilot work. It is this we propose here. Specifically, in designated areas with populations of around 200,000 at risk in our chosen sites, we will test extensive strategies to a) identify and recruit incident cases of psychosis and representative controls, b) follow individuals over time while minimising attrition, and c) establish a core set of cross-culturally valid instruments and procedures to collate data on psychopathology, social and biological exposures, and outcome.

title: Pregnancy changes and future health of mother and offspring.
description: This sabbatical award will support development of a new collaboration to answer the following: (1) What are the relationships between pregnancy characteristics and future maternal and offspring health? (2) What are the pathways that underlie the relationships identified in (1)? (3) Can routinely collected antenatal and postnatal data be used to predict future ill-health and developmental problems? The outcomes that we will specifically focus on are: (i) obesity, type 2 diabetes and cardiova scular disease risk factors and incidence in mother and child and (ii) the child s attainment of developmental milestones, normal growth, cognitive function and educational attainment. There are existing grant funds in each centre that will contribute to the collaboration to examine some parts of the above questions, but to date none of us have had the opportunity to share results, explore whether these replicate in our different studies or work together to look closely across all three questio ns and hence build-up a bigger picture of the links between pregnancy and future health and well-being. By the end of the collaboration we anticipate that there will be at least one submitted publications from the collaboration and that we will have drawn up a strategy for future research requirements.

title: Sheffield Human 3T MR Imaging & Spectroscopy Facility.
description: Part capital-funding for a whole-body, human, in-vivo, superconducting Magnetic Resonance (MR) research system is required to provide a continued, sustainable, leading-edge, multi-nuclear, 3T MR imaging resource based in Sheffield. This equipment will facilitate ongoing and novel investigations. Current key areas of application include: a) clinical neuroimaging - cerebrovascular dysfunction in diabetes - CNS pain matrix associated with chronic neuropathies - schizophrenia fMRI correlates of auditory hallucinations, cognitive status and therapeutic intervention - neuro-oncology lesion characterization - neurodegenerative diseases such as the ataxias and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (emphasis on therapy monitoring) - metal ion exposure sequalae of hip-implant resurfacing - computational neuro-modeling for clinical decision support b) basic science fMRI neuro- - emotion and executive function, notably in dramatic arts - musical rhythm performance - mathematical process ing - mistruths c) Inhaled hyperpolarized 3-He and 129-Xe lung imaging with simultaneous multi-nuclear excitation d) Hyperpolarized 129-Xe labeling and 1-H imaging for linked cardiac and brain perfusion assessment We also aim to conjoin imaging measures of CNS, heart and lung status and function. Provision of state-of-the-art imaging equipment will help to drive and facilitate other areas of research, in particular, in-vivo monitoring following translational research / novel interventi ons, including those developed in the part-Wellcome-funded Medical School.

title: Specific language impairment and comorbidity: development over the first three years of schooling.
description: This research aims to investigate the development of co-morbidity in children identified as having language impairment at school entry and to determine whether behavioural co-morbidities reflect underlying cognitive impairment (endophenotypes). We investigate patterns of language impairment and co- morbidity predicted by neurocognitive theories of SLI. The study design utilises a 2-stage process. In Stage 1, a population sample of children at school-entry is screened for possible SLI and develop mental disorder using a teacher questionnaire. In addition, scores from the Foundation Stage Profile will index the child s educational experience during the first year of school. In Stage 2, a stratified sub-sample of children at high-risk and low-risk of SLI will be assessed at ages 6 and 8. In-depth assessments will tap possible co-morbid deficits at behavioural and cognitive levels in language, cognition, literacy, motor skill, social abilities and attention deficits. Our analyses focus on s tatistical modelling of the developmental relationships between aspects of language and different cognitive and behavioural impairments. These models will explicitly contrast the predicted relationships offered by different neurocognitive theories of SLI. Such analyses will enable us to determine profiles of language impairment at school entry that are predictive of different co-morbidities over the first years of formal schooling.

title: Neurobiological determinants of treatment response in psychosis.
description: Dopaminergic and glutamatergic pathology has been observed separately in patients using PET and MR imaging, but these neurochemicals have not been previously studied in the same patients. A key objective of this study is thus to study both neurochemicals in the same patients and relate them to subsequent treatment response. We will do this in first episode patients who will receive a standardised treatment algorithm and follow-up to determine changes in psychopathology. After scanning, patien ts will start with six weeks treatment with amisulpride. At this point non-responders, determined according to standard criteria, will be switched to six weeks of olanzapine. Patients who remain non-responders after olanzapine will meet UK treatment guideline for treatment resistance. This will clarify the extent to which these pathophysiological factors, and their interaction, are related to treatment response and treatment resistance.

title: Living Links to Human Biology and Medicine
description: We have recently established the 'Living Links to Human Evolution' Research Centre, a University primate research centre built in the heart of Edinburgh Zoo. The primates studied there are 'living links' to our evolutionary past. 'Living Links' was designed to facilitate multiple Science Engagement activities with visitors from the 600,000+ who roam the Zoo annually. A Science Engagement Grant from the Scottish Government supported a first phase exploiting this potential, beginning to furnish a Science Exploration Zone and last year attracting an estimated 400,000 visitors to directly witness and engage with ongoing research and related activities. Our data show that visitors now spend longer in Living Links than normal zoo exhibits. To build on this success, we here apply for support of a second phase to enhance the scope and depth of Engagement, in ways of direct interest to the Wellcome Trust. Three main themes link to the Trust's biomedical focus. The first, 'Living Links to Our Past' will address multiple aspects of what our fellow primates share with us in their basic biology and psychology, the bedrock of biomedical science. The second, 'Evolutionary Medicine' will explore the light an evolutionary perspective throws on illness and medicine, with illustrations from both human and non-human primates. The third theme will focus on the fascinating story of the evolutionary roots of HIV and AIDS in monkeys and apes. A variety of innovative activities will further public engagement with these topics, on a scale few if any venues can match.

title: Unravelling Eve.
description: A collaboration between artist Joan Molloy, biomedical and social scientists, and women who have experienced postpartum psychosis ("PP"). Molloy will complete a period of residency at the MRC Centre for Neuropsychiatric Genetics and Genomics at Cardiff University in order to develop work that reflects upon issues of motherhood and inheritance- the beautiful complexity of the genetic science mirroring the intricacies of the social, ethical and familial implications of the illness. A 2-day workshop will connect the artist with women who have experienced an episode of PP. Molloy will share her work and lead practical art sessions in order to capture the voice of the women. A gathering of women like this is rare and will give scientists an opportunity for qualitative study so that they can improve their understanding of the emotional aspects of the illness. It will be an invaluable opportunity for the women to establish a dialogue with each other and clinicians, to share their stories and highlight the differences in their care. The artist's intention is to create a body of work, including an arresting film, which encapsulates the science and values the personal histories whilst engaging the public via exhibitions in Cardiff and Christies, London, as well as being available on the web.

title: Honeyscribe.
description: Honey scribe is an artistic investigation into the life of the honeybee aiming to find ways to communicate the relationship between honeybee and human health. Ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs document the role of a 'Honey Scribe' tasked to record every drop of honey produced. Shelton will assume the function of contemporary honey scribe, charting current threats to the health of our pollinators and listening to what bees have got to tell us about our own health and wellbeing. Honeyscribe considers three key themes: The relationship between bee health, human health and the environment The medicinal properties of hive products Bee myths and the relationship of myth to human wellbeing Honey scribe emphasizes communication, exchange and diversity. The voices and ideas of scientists, medics, artists, poets, activists, beekeepers, musicians, children, and shamanic practitioners are central to the project and will inspire and invigorate the artwork. Honeyscribe will culminate in new artwork for exhibition, a publication and a symposium.

title: All the King's fools: re-thinking mental health through learning-disabled performance at Hampton Court Palace
description: 'All the King's fools' is a public engagement project. Its main objective is to explore cultural attitudes and medical responses to the fact that many fools and jesters in the Tudor period were what were then described as 'natural fools', but what doctors today would characterise as 'learning disabled'. 'The Misfits', a company of learning-disabled actors directed by professional jester Peet Cooper, will stage six days of performances at Hampton Court Palace in the very rooms in which court fools performed. The theatre company will be supported by academics with expertise on the history of disability, the body, and medical ethics. Through the participation of learning-disabled actors, this vivid re-enactment will give insight into lives of disabled people at the Tudor court, and will stimulate public debate about the historical and present-day treatment of mental ill-health (broadly defined) and its medical context. Its objective is to challenge stereotypical public perceptions arising out of an under-researched history of disability, especially by encouraging reflection on our assumptions about the inevitability of progress in biomedical attitudes. The project will draw on new historical research and explore further the dramatic history of mental disability, including issues such as the purpose of 'foolish' performances, the likelihood that royal fools had learning difficulties, the limits of a fool's licence, and the fools' mental well-being, as well as general attitudes to, and the treatment of, 'natural fools' in the past and today. Longevity will be achieved by developing a broader research and public engagement project in future.

title: WORLDbytes-The School of Citizen TV Science Strand
description: The charity WORLDwrite's award-winning and pioneering online Citizen TV channel WORLDbytes will work with 30 disadvantaged young people (volunteers) aged 16-25 to develop an understanding of biomedical issues and an accessible science strand on the channel starting with a series of 6 programmes. The project's planning and advisory committee will advise staff and volunteers on further relevant scientists and research on selected issues for programmes and ongoing advice. WORLDwrite's media professionals will train and support young volunteer crews through the whole production process developing their understanding of the science and creative approaches to it. This creative educational process will engage young people with scientists and vice versa, media professionals with both, share programme content with local communities and the world and create a novel science strand on a unique CitizenTV channel. The programme series will comprise: an introduction to biomedical science-what it is and why it matters; one based on our popular on the sofa series "Don't Shout at the Telly" with young volunteers grilling an expert on animal experimentation (Stuart Derbyshire, School of Psychology, University of Birmingham has agreed); one utilising our engaging 'View from the Streets' format which asks if a price can be put on life; a collaboration with Timandra Harkness transforming aspects of her ?YourDaysAreNumbered? stand-up show for online TV; the penultimate programme will investigate performance enhancing drugs and specially engineered technologies in sports to coincide with the Olympics and finally we will investigate what happens if a relative leaves their organs to science.

title: Patient's Narratives/Doctor's Cases
description: Patient's Narratives/Doctor's Cases explores contemporary experiences of illness by tapping into medical history. Consultation letters, autobiography and clinical cases will be presented on stage in an informal and relaxing environment. Live performance in the congenial atmosphere of the Storytelling Centre will give people opportunities to discuss medical care and coping with illness. We use historical sources because they encourage people to comment and offer their own interpretation while at the same time maintaining an objective distance which is both beneficial and challenging. The narratives include bodily affliction, mental illness and doctor's case histories from town hospitals and mental asylums. We will present a series of events, each one with varying content to encourage listening and talking about illness. Medical history can vibrantly illuminate present difficulties in doctor- patient communication and the crucial contextualisation of illness and dying. This will not be primarily an analytical, historical project, but one where 'tales of the past' initiate sharing and reflection. We emphasize the 'talking voice' in a theatre setting because this is both public and immediate. The audience can engage with each other and stories told at the performance. The discussion right after the readings is crucial to the project. The long eighteenth century was vivid in its autobiographical writing, in its letter- writing, personal narratives and religious conversion literature (often about illness). Whether hand-written or in print, patient's narratives leap off the page and are vital to how we understand medical advice and patient's perceptions.

title: 'Face to Face with Sports Science.'
description: The Research Institute of Sport and Exercise Sciences (RISES) at Liverpool John Moores University has partnered with National Museums Liverpool (NML) and the Museum of Science and Industry (MOSI) to provide a series of interactive sports science events to engage and inspire the general public. The project aims to engage members of the general public in a challenging, exciting and interactive manner by hosting exhibits at two of the most popular Museums in the UK, whilst also running targeted workshops for secondary schools students. The sports science disciplines of physiology, motor control, biomechanics, performance analysis and psychology will be presented in a format that enhances knowledge through practical 'pods' providing experiential insight into the translation of theory into practice. The project will ultimately inform the general public how key principles of training with elite athletes are related to and influenced by world leading research at RISES. Direct links will be made with major sporting events in 2012 through existing collaborations including: the London Olympic Games; European Football Championships; and national public engagement events such as Sports Relief and the Liverpool Marathon. The project will achieve three main aims: 1. Provide inspiring and interactive public engagement in the science of elite sport performance. 2. Provide a practical interface for the public to engage with the world leading research undertaken by RISES 3. Provide insight and practical experiences for the public and school children demonstrating the link between the practices of elite athletes and activities of the general public

title: 'The Brain and the Mind.'
description: Over the past two decades neuroscience has developed to a point where basic psychological functions are now widely understood in biological terms. How robust is this neurological account of the mind? This is the question at the heart of this project. To answer it, we propose to stage six discussions between neuroscientists, psychologists, psychoanalysts and writers, artists and philosophers. Among the questions to be debated are: How much cognition goes on outside awareness? To what extent is it shaped by emotional and motivational factors? Do we still believe in anything like a Freudian unconscious? How do we acquire the competence to relate to the minds of others? Is it entirely explicable in biological terms e.g. by the activation of mirror neurons? Or is the neurobiological 'hard wiring' itself dependent on certain types of emotional experience? Can disorders such as autism shed any light on these processes? Are male and female brains different from one another? Darwinians sympathetic to sociobiology have argued that there are strong reasons why sex differences will be especially marked in mammalian species such as our own. Does neuroscience bear this claim out? And what is the relation between neuroscience and evolutionary theory more generally? Mirror neurons have been described by VS Ramachandran as 'the driving force behind in the "great leap forward in human evolution"'. Again, is this more than a "Just-so" story? The series concludes with a discussion of the significance of recent discoveries relating to the neurobiology of memory, e.g. for Alzheimer's sufferers.

title: 'The Home Front - engaging the armed forces on mental illness.'
description: The aim of this project is to investigate, pilot and evaluate the effectiveness of using comedy with armed service personnel, as a way of: stimulating interest and engaging them in the biomedical area of mental illness (and related substance misuse); encouraging new ways of thinking about and supporting informal learning about this area. Despite the inherent occupational risk factors for mental illness within the armed forces, there is little engagement of personnel in this area due to: limited understanding of mental illness, the stigma that surrounds this area, and a culture/way of thinking among personnel which associate mental illness with signs of weakness. Engagement and participation will be achieved through: - Discussion sessions with the target group to explore their knowledge around mental illness and help inform the script development (and pitch the content and style of the show appropriately) - Including relevant contributions to the show from armed service personnel to harness the positive effect of peer learning and to help 'normalise' mental health problems, thereby challenging stigma. Evaluation will be designed in collaboration with the Institute of Psychiatry and will gather both pre and post intervention quantitative and qualitative data on armed forces personnel's: attitudes, understanding/knowledge and engagement around the biomedical area of mental illness; and participation in the focus groups and the shows. This innovative project will form new collaborations and partnerships between the armed forces, the arts, academic institutions, and the charitable sector - to pilot this creative approach to engagement, participation and education in mental ill-health.

title: (False) Memories are made of this.
description: Artist Alasdair Hopwood proposes to undertake a residency at the Anomalistic Psychology Research Unit (APRU) at Goldsmiths College, University of London. Hopwood will create a new body of work that aims to increase public understanding about False Memory and current research into the manipulation of memory for medical purposes. The project will include a new website, a talks series and an exhibition that will examine the potential impact of these issues on Biomedical Science and Art, whilst stimulating a debate on the wider consequences of this area of scientific enquiry. Hopwood's co-applicant is Psychologist, Professor Christopher French who leads APRU and has written extensively about the role of False Memory in the reporting of anomalous experiences. In consultation, relevant contacts and collaborations will also be sought across the University of Landor and beyond, particularly with Professor James Ost (University of Portsmouth) and Professor Elizabeth Loftus (University of California, Irvine) who are also at the forefront of research in this area.

title: Site and Smell.
description: Dr Anna Fenemore and Pigeon Theatre (specialists in immersive performance) will create a new performance work that explores the neuroscience and psychology of .spatial and olfactory memory. A complex 'smell-scape' will be developed as the central performance strategy, and the performance will explore how smell links to our processes of long-term memory formation, specifically our memories of space or site. The project will explore how some smells will be associated in the brain with certain places, as in Proust's tea-dipped madeleine. The work will address the importance of the hippocampus in this process, where the association between odour and place/spatial context is coded, and will examine the processes of pattern completion. The immersive and interactive performance will be a collaboration with Cognitive Neuroscientist Dr Colin Lever at the University of Durham, and Cognitive Psychologist Professor Martin Conway at the University of Leeds.

title: And you were in it.
description: Dreaming is mysterious, primal, highly emotional and personal. In the past 100 years, psychologists and researchers have made significant discoveries about the nature of dreams and sleep and have posited a range of theories as to their function. Theatre Studio West will work with Dr Martina Reynolds of Brunei University to educate and creatively explore the psychology of dreams. Young participants will be guided and challenged to explore dreams through their own dream diaries and archive research, alongside creative sessions to dramatise their ideas and findings. This will culminate in a multimedia exhibition/performance created by the young people, consisting of movement and dramatic monologues, film, posters and music in a studio space transformed into a dreaming brain. 'And You Were In It' will ask: can something you dream affect your life? It will also demystify dreams and make the science accessible and relevant to the audience and our young participants.

title: The Use of the Internet to Train Clinicians to Implement Psychological Treatments.
description: Empirically-supported psychological treatments have been developed for a range of psychiatric disorders. If patients are to benefit from these treatments there is a need to develop effective and efficient means of training clinicians to deliver them. A programme of education research is proposed. The primary aim of this research is to evaluate the use of the internet to help clinicians acquire the knowledge and skills required to implement psychological treatments. Two uses of the intern et will be studied. The first (internet-enhanced training) involves trainees being provided with access to a specially designed clinically-rich website which provides extensive information on the psychological treatment together with multiple acted illustrations of its key procedures. Access to the website is followed by an enhanced form of case supervision that makes extensive reference to the website. The second form of training involves access to the website alone with no case supervision ( internet-only training ). This form of training has the potential to be highly disseminable. The effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of these two new forms of training will be compared with that of conventional training (a two-day training workshop followed by case supervision) in a randomised controlled education trial that will employ new measures of clinical competence.

title: The Cambridge-UCL Mental Health and Neurosciences Network.
description: Our aims are to deconstruct current clinical classifications of psychiatric disorders and reformulate abnormal and disabling behaviours in terms of their underlying processing dimensions, based on a neuroscientific understanding of human brain development. We posit that a conventional psychiatric diagnosis is at best an epiphenomenon: the consequence of variability in multiple, developmentally-dependent dimensions of emotion, cognition, behaviour and their associated neurocomputational systems.. This radical and novel approach to characterising mental illness will be realised by defining population variation in key cognitive and behavioural phenotypes and linking these to underlying variation in the development of brain networks measured by structural and functional neuroimaging; the measured characteristics of these networks will be biomarkers for psychiatry. We will focus on the period of youth, 14 to 25 years of age, because this is a developmental epoch associated with major change s in normal cognitive function and brain organization, and (not coincidentally) with a high incidence of serious mental illnesses that continue through the rest of the life course: depressions, psychoses, conduct and personality disorders.

title: Francois Rabelais: Medical Humanist.
description: The project will lead to a monograph: Fran ois Rabelais: Medical Humanist. The primary texts for consideration are Pantagruel, Gargantua, Le Tiers Livre, Le Quart Livre, Le Cinquiesme Livre, despite the latter s contested authorship, and correspondence such as Rabelais s letters from Italy. The first section of the book will analyse the presentation of various medical fields in these texts. Account will be taken of the extent to which Rabelais reflects Renaissance thought and what deliberate mis representation he introduces. Evidence will be taken from Classical, Arabic and Renaissance medical sources to support the analysis and from more modern theories of the body such as those proposed by Bakhtin, Kristeva, Laqueur, Foucault and Merleau-Ponty. The second part of the project will address health promotion via pharmacology, humour and literature as therapy. In the dedicatory epistle to the Quart Livre Rabelais explicitly states how the writer administers to the sick reader in the same w ay that a doctor attends a patient, and how the creation of art fosters health. Theories of humour, studies of doctor-patient relationships and of the therapeutic value of the arts will underpin an investigation of how Rabelais uses his works to encourage physical and mental wellbeing in his readers.

title: Twin Beds: From Hygienic Homes to Healthy Marriages, 1870-1970.
description: This study of twin beds will result in a monograph contributing to the expanding field of the history of the domestic sphere and the place of medical (both alternative and biomedical) interventions in establishing its everyday rules of occupation. Through the examination of documents such as popular medical treatises, domestic sanitation advice manuals, marriage advice books, and household and furnishing magazines, this research will show how medical expertise constituted the middle-class home a s a place where health was to be secured and maintained (Adams, Bashford, Szreter, Tomes). Central to this history of shifting prescriptions about co-sleeping is the generative and regulatory discourse of sexual, marital and familial health and hygiene (Foucault, Bland, Hall, Doan). The study will present the history of twin beds (and their alternatives) as a condensation of multiple and intersecting ideas about what secures and what threatens emotional and physical wellbeing. Examining the adv ent and genealogy of an unremarked and everyday household object between 1870 and 1970, this research will track significant shifts in understandings of the modern married couple, their environment, their intimacy, their exchanges, their compatibility and the balance of power between them.

title: Autism Ethics Group.
description: To identify and analyse the ethical issues raised by.autism To bring to bear on the ethical issues current advances in science, neuroscience and psychology. To enable an exchange of ideas between scientists and Ethicists. To identify the implications for research and intervention of different ethical viewpoints. To facilitate the inclusion in the discussion of those directly affected by autism and their carers : To produce papers for a conference

title: O - The History of Orgasm 3*60' for BBC2/4.
description: This grant is to fund development for a three part television series about the history of the female orgasm. This series is a journey to one of the most complex and misunderstood of human behaviours - the female orgasm. In the company of Dr Alice Roberts we cross millennia and continents, spanning physiology, anatomy and psychiatry, meeting quacks and scientific pioneers, uncovering our most intimate secrets. Ultimately we discover how medicine and science have shaped women's sexuality. This series would ideally coincide with the forthcoming Hollywood movie, Hysteria, scheduled for release in late 2011 starring Maggie Gyllenhaal and Hugh Dancy.

title: The Death of the Asylum in Late Twentieth Century Britain.
description: The project explores the deinstitutionalisation of mental health care in late twentieth century Britain. Friern mental hospital in northeast London - once the notorious lunatic asylum, Colney Hatch - closed in 1993. I was a patient there in the late 1980s. Using Friern's records alongside my own and other people's memories of it, I look in detail at the hospital's closure and its impact on those - patients, staff, and managers - involved in the transition from institutional to community care. I explore the relational life of the hospital and the changes in care principles and practices that accompanied deinstitutionalisation. Mental health services in the UK today are governed by a recovery model that emphasises patient choice and independence, and proscribes open-ended 'dependent' care relationships. I examine the treatment and care principles displaced by this new model, the attitudinal changes that underpin it, and its reception from mental health professionals and service users. My key goal is to provide new insights into the recent history of mental health care in the UK, and to stimulate and inform discussion of this important public issue.

title: Religious melancholy: An interdisciplinary conference' to be held at KCL on 19-20 May 2011
description: It is a founding premise of the medical humanities that the study of the lived experience of disease in the past has. a great deal to teach present-day practitioners and carers, especially in conditions such as melancholy which has held up as a diagnostic category for millennia. Prima facie, religious melancholy would appear to pose a significant challenge to this claim. Few medically-minded workers in mental health today believe religious melancholy is qualitatively distinct from other forms of melancholy. So one aim of the conference would be to ask the question 'why not?' By reviewing the medical history of religious melancholy in its wider cultural context, the conference will attempt to reconstruct the evolution and the eventual withering away of the concept of religious melancholy which dominated medical thinking about the mind from the seventeenth until well into the nineteenth centuries. It is hoped that the end result will supply a model for thinking about the relationship between depression and culture more generally. What might historically grounded scholarship contribute to contemporary medical understandings relating to spirituality and mental health? Why are some forms of religious belief more prone to lead to despair than others? Where do these traditions originate and where do they lead? Thus our primary objective is to bring together experts from medical humanities, history of medicine, literature and comparative literature, religion and theology, philosophy and history to create an interdisciplinary dialogue. This will take the form of a series of plenary papers and discussion panels with contributors from a handpicked group of invited scholars. Our ultimate objective is to produce a publication in the form of a volume of edited essays.

title: Diagnosing Normal.
description: Raymond and Billy are both 5 year old British boys who know they are girls and want to live in their ?real? gender. They are being raised in very different ways. Raymond is allowed to wear dresses, push prams and study ballet. Billy is forbidden any feminine behaviour, or even female friends. Both children have been diagnosed with Gender Identity Disorder (GID), as defined by the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual (DSM). As publication of the next edition of the DSM looms, GID has become a tinderbox in a powerful debate about what behaviour constitutes mental illness and how it should be treated.

title: Mastering the emotions: Control, contagion and chaos: 1800 to the present day' to be held at QMUL on 16-17 June 2011
description: A one and a half day international and interdisciplinary conference, 'Mastering the Emotions' will bring together scholars working on medical interventions to suppress, control or artificially produce emotional states from 1800 the present day. With contributors from the history of medicine, psychiatry and psychology as well as from literature, drama and musicology, (including two keynotes: Allan Young, Department of Social Studies of Medicine, McGill University, and Sally Shuttleworth, Professor of English at St Annes College, Oxford), this conference will open up new avenues of historical research and collaboration on medicine and the emotions. Conceived and organised by the Centre's post-graduate cohort, this meeting also aims to strengthen Queen Mary's links with postgraduates at other history of medicine centres, both in the UK and abroad. In particular, we will strengthen our existing ties with Centro de Ciencias Humanas y Sociales in Madrid. To this end, we are applying to the Wellcome Trust for help with the provision of subsidy for UK and international postgraduates to attend the conference. This conference will build on the Centre's strong record of hosting successful symposia and inviting international speakers, by hosting its first residential conference. This will raise the profile of the Centre both within the UK and abroad, whilst giving an opportunity for the Centre's PhD students (several of whom are funded by the Wellcome Trust) to develop skills necessary for their future careers.

title: Coma, Consciousness and Serious Brain Injury: medical humanities and decision making.
description: How do clinicians and families make serious medical treatment decisions on behalf of people with profound brain damage, such as those in vegetative and minimally conscious states? What treatment pathways, assumptions, laws and policies frame the options available - and how could these best be challenged, implemented, or improved to ensure science and medicine is deployed to maximize human health and well-being? What insights can be brought to bear by a medical humanities approach to this troubling area of biomedicine/health care ethics? This symposium will bring together around 20 key experts in this field - across disciplinary and professional boundaries- to examine these questions in depth and suggest ways forward. The meeting will strengthen emerging networks and establish dialogue across different perspectives - setting the ground work for future joint research bids, publications, and policy debates. In particular the symposium is designed to lead to a subsequent high-profile event in London and journal special issue devoted to these questions. In parallel to this application I am working with a theatre director and playwright to develop a public-engagement project, and also hope this topic could be a subject for a Wellcome 'Witness Seminar', My initial seeping exercise has ensured that the concerns/expertise of a wide range of medical humanities scholars, policy makers and user groups have been integrated from the outset and that key people in the field are enrolled in this exercise. The initial symposium will work with case study material to review the issue around decision-making, drawing on expertise in the Mental Capacity Act 2005 (designed to frame decision-making for those without capacity) and reflections on the practicalities of clinical dilemmas and family experience, policy making and economics as well as reflections from philosophers and experts in medical history, disability theory, bioethics, literature etc

title: Turning the Pages: exploring the history of psychiatry in India
description: Document the histories of asylum care Investigate the patterns of use of hospital services by patients in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries Describe the emergence, and changes to community care models Explore ideas about the psychological aspects of social and political change Collation and comparison of asylum notes from across India will allow us to compare standards of care, patterns of use, and administrative responses to the mentally ill in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. These will be compared across regions within India, and to others in the UK, to explore the spread of disease constructs, and bio-medical approaches. In addition, patient records, and local histories will be explored to better understand the social responses to psychiatric care. The development of community care programs in India, and its engagement with traditional models, as well as incorporation into the medical care delivery system, will be contextualized. We will try and understand how health policy evolved before and after Independence as regards mental health services, and reasons for the changes in direction. In addition, the psychological and psychiatric aspects of the particular trauma of the Partition, and the role of fractured psyches in response to social upheavals, will be explored.
recipient: National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro Sciences

title: Thomas Hardy and Biology: Character, Culture and Environment, 1859-1928.
description: Hardy was deeply interested in Victorian scientific and medical questions, listing among the thinkers who had most influenced him Charles Darwin, T.H.Huxley and Herbert Spencer, and taking notes from Darwin, Galton, Eduard von Hartmann, Huxley, George Henry Lewes, Maudsley, George Romanes, Spencer and August Weismann. Examining his notebooks, correspondence, fiction and poetry, I will also consider his meetings and correspondence with physicians, psychiatrists, eugenists and degenerationists ( including Crichton-Browne and C.W. Saleeby), as well as his critical reception, including the interest in his work by, for example, the sexologist Havelock Ellis. The first key goal of the research is to demonstrate the extent to which Hardy explored in his fiction the ideas which contemporary scientists were researching and debating, on the physical basis of mind, the relation of psychology and physiology, the unconscious, the physiological basis of the emotions, psychological differences be tween humans and animals, the role of instincts in the development of the moral sense, and evolutionary and medical ideas about war. The second key goal is to shed new light on Hardy's novels. The third key goal is to ask what antecedents there are in Hardy's fiction for postgenomic science and medicine.

title: Investigating retrieval control mechanisms.
description: This PhD project is designed to understand the reasons for memory problems in people suffering from schizophrenia. It is likely that these memory problems are at least in part due to failures of memory control processes: that is, failures in processes involved in strategically regulating how information is encoded and retrieved. In pursuing this question event-related potential (ERP), functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and behavioural measures will be employed. ERPs have been shown to index several different kinds of retrieval control processes. Similarly, fMRI measures have been shown to be particularly sensitive to encoding operations. Together, such methods are extremely well-suited to investigations of this type. The overall goal of the project is to understand how memory control operates in people suffering from schizophrenia, and how failures of encoding and retrieval control contribute to their memory problems. This will be accomplished in the following ways: • Identifying robust ERP,fMRI and behavioural markers of encoding and retrieval control operations • Observing how these vary according to schizotypy ratings. • Investigating the effects of intervention/training on memory control processes.

title: Biography and the history of psychology and psychiatry' to be held at UCL in June 2011.
description: To establish an international network of scholars currently using biographical approaches to study the History of Psychology and Psychiatry. To encourage debate and a reflexive awareness about the methodological advantages and problems associated with biographical approaches in general and those that are particularly pertinent to this field of historical research. To examine the historical use of 'patient biographies', in the form of individual case studies, by psychologists and psychiatrists and to problematise such epistemological practices, as a basis of knowledge formation, within these disciplines. To raise awareness of, and discuss solutions to, the 'public engagement gap' between the kind of biographies that are extremely popular with the lay public and those that are deemed 'too scholarly' and unprofitable by publishers. To disseminate the findings and discussions of the symposium to a wider audience after the event. Providing the papers presented form a sufficiently coherent body of original material, publication will be sought in the form of a special issue of a relevant journal, for example, Journal of the History of the Behavioural Sciences, History of the Human Sciences, History of Psychiatry.

title: Pedigree Chums: Science, Medicine and the Remaking of the Dog in the Twentieth Century.
description: The modern dog can be defined as pedigree-bred, convenience food-fed, obedience-trained and medicalised. Historians who have considered this topic have concluded that the modern pedigree dog was a creation of the long nineteenth century. We want to build upon this work, but also challenge it, to show how and why the dog has been continuously 'remade', materially and culturally, in the period since 1920-2009. We will investigate how breeding, feeding, training and treating interacted with, and across, genetics, nutritional science, ethology and psychology and and veterinary medicine to factors that shaped the dog and dog human companionship.
