They cannot be accessed without risk, as they are on loose poor-quality copy paper, are in many cases dirty, stapled and in danger of crumbling. As a consequence the research potential of these records has remained untapped to date. These summaries were among the highest conservation priorities identified by the National Preservation Office's Preservation Assessment Survey of the Archives & Museum's collections in 2006. Without intervention to save them, they are likely to perish before the period which they document passes out of living memory.
recipient: Bethlem Art and History Collections Trust

title: Cataloguing the Kinnier Wilson and Ninian Bruce Neurology Collections
description: Cataloguing the Kinnier Wilson and Ninian Bruce Neurology Collections The Royal College of Physicians of Edinburgh Sibbald Library is requesting £33,063 to employ a cataloguer for 12 months to catalogue 2 important linked neurological print collections. We are also seeking £8,265 to employ an archivist for 3 months to catalogue Kinnier Wilson papers. If these collections were catalogued to the high RCPE standards (including provenance notes etc) researchers (including the neurologists and historians supporting this bid) would gain hugely improved access to two personal collections that cover a particularly interesting era in neurology. The collection of S A Kinnier Wilson In 1996 the RCPE Sibbald Library rescued the collection of one of the most important 20th century British neurologists, S A Kinnier Wilson (Wilson's Disease) when there was no longer any room to house it at the Cairns Library in the John Radcliffe in Oxford. Although we managed to protect the collection (which is in pretty good condition) and house it in excellent environmental conditions we have not managed to catalogue it. Webb Haymaker in his book The Founders of Neurology described Wilson as "the bibliographer of British neurology". Jellinek's 2004 paper describing the un-catalogued book collection used by the bibliographer was published in the Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery & Psychiatry (Appendix 1). No work has been done on the Kinnear Wilson archive which is both more extensive and more interesting than originally thought. The collection of Alexander Ninian Bruce The Sibbald Library also holds the collection of 500 neurology books built up by Wilson's brother-in-law Alexander Ninian Bruce. Bruce's collection contains many psychiatric works and includes rarities like Murrell's photographic study of locomotion. Card records exist for most of the Ninian Bruce books which were partially catalogued in the early 1980s.
recipient: Royal College of Physicians of Edinburgh

title: Fully integrated, real-time detection, diagnosis and control of community diarrhoeal disease clusters and outbreaks.
description: Seventeen million people suffer from diarrhoeal disease in the UK annually. It commonly causes outbreaks - norovirus outbreaks alone are the third most costly healthcare-associated infection in the NHS. Recent severe outbreaks of Escherichia coli O104 in Germany and O157 at Godstone Farm in Surrey are timely reminders that rapid detection, through surveillance, is key to control. We need to identify the nature, distribution and scale of outbreaks quickly enough to lessen impact. The hidden burden of undiagnosed disease is growing as fewer people consult their General Practitioner, reducing outbreak detection sensitivity. We will use syndromic surveillance for cluster detection in the community and targeted sampling, replacing traditional diagnostics with rapid modern technologies, to identify and characterise responsible pathogens rapidly. We will apply targeted microbial metagenomics, using latest-generation genome sequencing for pathogen discovery, and determine phylogeny and evolutionary trends to understand how new agents have arisen. Many diarrhoeal diseases are zoonotic yet medical and veterinary surveillance systems are poorly integrated so we will incorporate and develop veterinary surveillance. An interdisciplinary, integrated, real-time, surveillance/diagnosis/investigation system, placing the patient at its centre, will enable earlier detection of community outbreaks, lessening harm because Health Protection professionals and Environmental Health Officers can intervene faster.

title: Time and decision-making: a study of fluctuating mental capacity and anticipatory decision-making.
description: Mental health law has undergone considerable recent change but problems remain. A parallel change is increasing philosophical interest in the problems of mental capacity and best interests. I am proposing a clinically-based study that investigates contemporary problems for the law and psychiatry and associated philosophical problems of personal identity. The investigation will centre on cases of bipolar affective disorder (also known as manic depression ), cases of people who are in delirium in a general hospital and cases of people attending A&E departments in emotional crisis who have self-harmed. My goals are to advance understanding of problems related to fluctuating mental capacity and anticipatory decision-making (also known as advanced directives ) in healthcare. This project is part of a interdisciplinary research strategy in psychiatry/law/philosophy that I seek to develop which will interface with interface with policy.

title: What are the relationships between the degree of pregnancy intention and key neonatal and maternal outcomes in the Mchinji district of Malawi?.
description: This project aims to assess the relationships between the degree of pregnancy intention and key maternal and neonatal health outcomes. It is hypothesised that unintended pregnancies will have poorer outcomes for both woman and baby. This may be due to the physiological effects of anxiety on the pregnancy or may be mediated by lower uptake of key preventative practices such as antenatal care. The project will be conducted in Malawi where the unintended pregnancy rate is 41%. Data on pregnancy intention will be collected during pregnancy using the London Measure of Unintended Pregnancy, and women will be followed up for in depth interviews one month post-natally. Logistic regression will be used to assess the effect of pregnancy intention on outcomes including birthweight, neonatal mortality rate and postnatal depression and the impact of meeting the unmet need for family planning globally will be modelled. Qualitative research will explore the attitudes of men, women and communitie s to family planning and the provision of family planning in Malawi will be assessed from policy to service user. This will lead to a whole service pathway description to inform discussion on how to reduce the unmet need for family planning in Malawi.

title: Lay perspectives on psychiatric illness and healing and their implications for the management of psychiatric illness in a Tibetan community in India
description: No description available

title: Refining the computer based system for Avatar Therapy and evaluating its effectiveness in a randomised controlled trial conducted by an independent research team in London.
description: About 25% of people with schizophrenia continue to suffer with persecutory auditory hallucinations despite drug treatment. Their capacity to work and make relationships is grossly impaired, often for the rest of their life. We have developed and evaluated a novel therapy based on computer technology which enables each patient to create an avatar of the entity (human or non- human) that they believe is talking to them. The therapist promotes a dialogue between the patient and the avatar in which the avatar progressively comes under the patient's control. A maximum of 7 sessions lasting 30 minutes has resulted in highly significant reductions in the patients' abnormal experiences, enhancing the quality of their life. The recorded sessions are transferred to an MP3 for patients to use at home in perpetuity, resulting in continuing improvement over time. The proposed research encompasses: 1. Refining the system and streamlining the technology to make it more user- friendly. 2. Evaluating the improved system by a randomised controlled trial conducted by an independent team of researchers trained by the originator of the therapy. 3. Recruiting a large enough sample of suitable patients to the trial to identify predictors of a good response using baseline demographic and clinical data.

title: Investigating the sense of agency in human-computer interaction.
description: The proposed research is to investigate the sense of agency in human-computer interaction (HCI). The sense of agency is the experience of initiating and controlling actions in order to influence events in the environment. Agency is well studied from a cognitive neuroscientific perspective because it underlies many cognitive disorders such as schizophrenia and psychosis. HCI involves the study, planning and design of the interaction between humans and computers. Currently there is a paucity of research lookingat agency in the context of technology. However it is a hugely topical and relevant area. There are two key goals of this PhD project- 1) enhance our understanding of agency in various computer/machine interaction contexts, 2) highlight the key considerations regarding agency and control in HCI research.

title: A high-content screen for genes regulating neural differentiation of human iPS cells
description: The aim of the proposed project is to investigate the genetic networks that regulate differentiation of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) into neural cells. We will make use of a library of double knockout hiPS cell lines, currently under development by Dr Bill Skarnes, to study the effect of gene deletion on neural differentiation. We will screen -100 knock-out cell lines in total, focusing on genes which are known to be sufficient for normal neural differentiation, or which are implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders. We will use a 'high-content' approach to study mutant phenotypes. Differentiating cells will be imaged in time-lapse, and automated image- processing tools with be used to label cells with high-dimensional feature sets, allowing us to examine the quantitative effects of gene knock-outs. We will use these phenotypic data, together with newly generated functional genomics data, to cluster mutant cell lines by phenotype, from which we will infer putative genetic pathways. In so doing we hope to find novel gene functions, and to identify the genetic circuits that regulate the dynamics of neural differentiation.

title: Network Informed Investigation of Evolutionary Conserved Neuronal Transport Processes.
description: Neuronal function is dependent on the appropriate conditional release of neurotransmitters at synaptic and motor neurone junctions. The molecular transport processes and regulated secretory mechanisms required to facilitate appropriate synaptic transmission are complex multi-stage events and defects at any step of these pathways may result in chronic or progressive neuropathies, including myasthenia gravis, schizophrenia [1] or neurodegenerative disorders, such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) [2] and Alzheimer's disease [3]. Although the fundamental mechanisms of vesicular transport, neurotransmitter release and endocytic recycling are known, there are many aspects of molecular organisation and regulation that remain unclear.Previous work in the Sanderson lab has identified around 50 novel proteins that are required for effective neurotransmission in C. elegans. This project aims to combine informatics and experimental methods to validate and characterise the role of these proteins, in both C. elegans and mammalian cells. Initially, protein interactions involving novel orthologous human proteins will be analysed using established yeast-2-hybrid (Y2H) methods. The dynamic composition and molecular architecture of the identified protein complexes will then be investigated in mammalian cells using advanced FCCS imaging techniques. Selective 'edgetic' effects of disease-related mutations will also be tested, to provide new insights into the molecular mechanisms of associated neurological disorders. Finally, an improved annotated protein interaction network for evolutionary conserved neuronal transport will be submitted to the IntAct database as an open access public resource.

title: Analysis of Trappc9 functions in brain development.
description: Recently, mutations in six genes have been identified to cause the neurodevelopmental disorder 'autosomal recessive non-syndromic mental retardation' in humans. 'Trafficking protein particle complex subunit 9' (Trappc9), also known as 'NIK and IKK? binding protein' (NIBP), is one of these genes, which leads to a range of symptoms when homozygously mutated, including microcephaly, corpus callosum and white matter abnormalities, speechimpairment and cognitive delay. The molecular basis of Trappc9's role in braindevelopment is not yet known. Some studies implicate Trappc9 in intracellular vesicle trafficking, while other work highlights a role in NF-?B signalling, promotion of neurite outgrowth and cell survival. Since no mouse model for the human disorder has been described so far, we aim to analyse the phenotype of a Trappc9 knock-out line with regard to neuron proliferation and cell survival, establishment of neuronal connections and potential physiological and/or behavioural abnormalities. We also aim to investigate the molecular basis of this disorder by using a range of molecularbiology techniques in PC12 cells and/or primary neurons (siRNA/lentivirus knock-down, NF-?B cytoplasmic-nuclear translocation studies), to clarify the mechanisms by which this protein exerts its functions. Is Trappc9 involved in NF-?B cytoplasmic-nuclear translocation, for example upon signalling from neurotrophin receptors?

title: The functions of postsynaptic density implicated in psychiatric disorders in associative memory formation.
description: Variants in the genes coding for postsynaptic density (PSD) proteins Homer1, DLG1 and DLG2 have been linked to psychopathology and schizophrenia. These proteins are functionally linked to postsynaptic glutamate receptors such asAMPA, NMDA and metabotropic glutamate receptors, and are thought to be key mediators of synaptic plasticity. Since associative learning is dependent on NMDA receptor-mediated synaptic plasticity and is impaired in several psychiatric disorders, we aim to determine the roles that PSD proteins including Homer1, DLG1 and DLG2 have in associative learning, with a view to shedding light on their part in psychiatric pathology To do this, we will a) use in situ hybridization to measure the expression of Homer1 transcription variants, Homer1a and Ania-3, DLG1 and DLG2 during key components of associative learning, including memory consolidation, recall andinhibitory learning, through the fear conditioning of adult rats. b) Use antisense­mediated knockdown of these PSD proteins before consolidation, recall and inhibitory learning, as well as knockout rodent models, to evaluate their function in processes required for associative learning. c) Administer mGiu and AMPA receptor-acting drugs to transgenic animals to investigate gene dependence in associative learning processes.

title: The role of MlR137 and its targets in associative learning.
description: We aim to determine the role of miR-137 and its targets in associative learning by investigating gene expression during contextual fear conditioning, a rodent model of hippocampal associative plasticity. Allelic variation in MIR137 and a sub-set of its confirmed targets has been associatedwith increased risk of schizophrenia in the latest GWAS. The aim is to focus on the regulation of calcium channel genes by miR-137, including the confirmedtarget CACNA1C, as well as other putative targets found to be associated withschizophrenia. Research would progress to explore the effects of local inhibition of calcium channels in the hippocampus as well as characterisation of a transgenic CACNA1C knock-out model. We further aim to confirm or refute predicted targets of miR-137 that may advance our understanding of this potential pathological pathway contributing to the etiology of schizophrenia.

title: Using machine learning algorithms to analyse complex genetic data in sub- phenotypes of psychiatric disorders.
description: The main objective for my PhD will be to apply machine learning methods and algorithms to complex genetic data in an attempt to identify features that characterise different sub­ phenotypes in psychiatric disorders. This will not only look for the contribution of individual genes, but also at possible biological gene-gene interactions and functional pathways. The use of non- parametric machine learning techniques will allow us to go beyond classical statistical (parametric) methods and search for more complex underlying patterns in the data.

title: Maturation of the meiotic spindle in oocytes
description: Chromosome segregation in human oocytes is surprisingly error prone. Indeed it is reported that about 20% of all eggs are aneuploid. This is a major cause of infertility, miscarriages and birth defects including Down syndrome. The machinery of chromosome segregation in oocytes differs from mitosis, including a lack of centrosomes in oocytes. Furthermore, oocytes undergo arrest with a bipolar spindle in meiotic metaphase to wait for fertilisation. The bipolar spindle may require further stabilisation during the arrest, but little is known about whether such a stabilisation mechanism exists and, if so, what is its molecular basis. Our laboratory has found that some microtubule regulators change their localisation during the metaphase arrest in Drosophila oocytes, including the kinesin-5 Klp61F. The PhD project aims to understand how and why the meiotic spindle change the organisation and dynamic during prolonged arrest in oocytes. Firstly, the change of spindle organisation and dynamics will be assessed by live imaging from nuclear envelope breakdown. Secondly, the mechanism and biological significance of

title: Genetic manipulation of MeCP2 in the human neuronal LUHMES cell line with a view to gene therapy of Rett Syndrome
description: Rett syndrome (RTT) is an autism spectrum disorder that is caused by mutationsin the gene encoding MeCP2, a chromatin-associated protein that binds mainly to methylated DNA and brings about gene expression changes. Being a single-gene disorder, whose symptoms are reversed by introducing MeCP2 into MeCP2-null mice, the use of gene therapy for this disease is possible. Recombinant adeno-associated viruses (rAAVs) are an extremely useful tool for gene therapy, demonstrating high transduction efficiencies, a lack of toxicityand the ability to reverse disease symptoms when used in clinical trials. Thisresearch aims to use rAAVs to target homologous donors into the nuclei of neuronal cells in vitro, to mutate the endogenous MeCP2 locus. To encourage homologous recombination to occur between the endogenous locus and the mutation-containing homologous donor; a CRISPR/Cas9 nuclease cassette will be used to nick the endogenous locus. This will produce mutant strains of neuronsthat can be phenotyped to gain insight into the cellular and molecular mechanisms involved in Rett syndrome. Using this rAAV/CRISPR/Cas9 technology

title: Plk1 regulation of chromosome segregation and the mitotic spindle
description: Bipolar spindle formation and chromosome alignment are essential and tightly regulated mitotic processes. Misaligned chromosomes can lead to missegregation and create aneuploidy and genetic instability, a characteristicassociated with cancer cells. Polo-like-kinase-1 (Plk1) is a serine/threonine kinase with multiple mitotic functions from centrosome maturation to chromosome alignment and cytokinesis. Many substrates have been identified, yet the molecular mechanism underlying Plk1-induced centrosome separation and spindle assembly remains unclear. Preliminary results from the Welburn lab suggest that Plk1 regulates microtubule dynamics and microtubule length in mitosis. In addition, the data indicates a role of Plk1 in bipolar spindle formation independent of Eg5, which may involve Plk1-dependent activation of dynein to induce centrosome separation. To show this I will (1) perform a targeted mitotic screen to identify Plk1 substrates (2) test if Plk1 localization is important for mitotic function. Toaddress this question, I will alter the Plk1 localisation to microtubule plus

title: Identification of genetic risk factors and assessing causality of modifiable exposures in adolescent depression.
description: The overall aim of my research is to investigate causal risk factors associated with adolescent depression. My research will first aim to investigate genetic risk factors for aadolescent depression through a combination of genome-wide analysis aapproaches. Next, I intend to investigate environmental risk factors for adolescent ddepression using a Mendelian randomisation approach. Finally, I will also use DNA methylation data to investigate whether risk ffactors exert their effects through epigenetic mechanisms.

title: Life course influences on suicidal behaviour in Low and Middle Income (LAMIC) countries: a cohort study based on 53,000 households in Sri Lanka.
description: My research will investigate the association of socioeconomic positioning (SEP) and suicide risk in low and middle income countries in Asia, by using Sri Lanka as a case study. The research will use data that is being collected as part of a large randomised control trial being conducted in the North Central Province of Sri Lanka. The data from this trial will be analysed both cross-sectionally and longitudinally to investigate associations of SEP measures and suicide. The household data from the cross-sectional survey has been geocoded and therefore I will be able to look at the effect of area levelSEP measures in relation to individual suicide risk, in particular investigatethe importance of status inconsistency. A key goal is to try and gain a betterunderstanding on how SEP is related to different aspects of the suicidal pathway, as this will help in our understanding on how suicidal behaviour develops.

title: Investigating the Regulation of Dopaminergic Neurons in C. elegans.
description: Dopaminergic neurons control many aspects of behaviour in both humans and C. elegans. Therefore unsurprisingly, major human diseases like Parkinson's and Schizophrenia are associated with the malfunction of dopaminergic neurons. The nematode C. elegans is an established model organism to address neurobiological questions like the regulation of dopaminergic neurons. The specific degeneration of these neurons is the major hallmark of Parkinson's Disease and can be recapitulated following administration of the drug 6-Hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA) in mammals and worms (Nass et al. 2010). I used this drug assay to screen for mutants which render C. elegans more susceptible to 6-OHDA-toxicity. In result, 4 hypersensitive mutants were isolated and 3 additional mutants were found that do not properly specify dopaminergic fate. The identification of the corresponding genes and their subsequent characterisation will be the focus of my PhD. To our best knowledge, there is only one other gene known so far to protect dopaminergic neurons from degeneration (manuscript in preparation) and the mutants with defective differentiation promise to contribute to the existing literature. Hence, by characterising the function and molecular mode of action of these genes we expect to make important contributions to the understanding of dopaminergic neuron biology in health and disease.

title: Insight: Research for mental health
description: No description available

title: Professional Interests and the Emergence of 'Child Abuse' in Britain, c.1962 -1987
description: My PhD will research child abuse in Britain from 1962 until 1987. In the long history of child abuse, this period was crucial to the emergence of our modern understanding, and in the explosion of a prolific discourse on child abuse. Various models of explanation and understanding emerged and changed rapidly, and the definition of 'abuse' expanded to incorporate new types of physical, emotional, and sexual abuse. This PhD will develop a distinctive approach, analysing the construction of child abuse as a case of conflict between and within professional groups, including social workers, radiologists, psychiatrists, lawyers, paediatricians, and local and central government. It will raise issues of professional accountability and authority. It will problematise the broad category of child abuse by considering different actors' prioritisation of types of abuse; debates about identification and the signifiers of abuse such as 'failure to thrive'; and the tensions between physical, psychological, and social explanations. As such, I aim to provide a case study of more general significance which uses the subject of child abuse to explore the challenges to medical models and medical authority in a period in which social explanations of well-being were reaching a peak of influence.

title: Medical and Cultural Constructions of Female Mental Illness in Britain and the United States, 1948-1965
description: This dissertation will explore changing conceptions of female depression and anxiety disorders in Britain and the United States to uncover the formative role of different health care systems in the development of psychiatric categories and their popular representation. In doing it will analyse the relationship between internal, national cultures and international cultures within the specific context of postwar gender and medical developments.

title: Understanding the inattentive and impulsive brain.
description: Inattention and impulsivity are complex syndromes that impact significantly on a range of disorders, including focal brain lesions (e.g., stroke), neurodegenerative conditions (e.g., Parkinsons disease, PD) and developmental disorders (e.g., attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, ADHD). To understand mechanisms underlying these behavioural syndromes we need to improve current knowledge of attention, working memory and rapid decision- making under risk, and examine whether they can be modulated effectively by drugs. This programme of research will characterize such mechanisms in healthy people and patients with stroke, PD and adult ADHD. We will: 1. Establish whether one type of inattention might be ultra-rapid forgetting of information held in working memory 2. Determine if one aspect of impulsivity might be hypersensitivity to rewards while conversely apathy might be associated with insensitivity to rewards 3. Define whether some types of inattention interact with rapid decision-making under risk to contribute to impulsivity or apathy 4. Modulate attention and decision-making using dopamine receptor agonists in healthy people and patients with stroke and PD 5. Test a new model that we have developed to see if it provides a better way to understand how information is maintained and protected from loss in working memory.

title: The neurobiology of motivation in health and disease.
description: My goal is to provide a mechanistic account of motivation in terms of its computational and neural structure. To realise this I will focus on how distinct motivational axes, for example those reflecting invigorating and directing effects, impact on behaviour. I see this characterisation of the architecture of motivation in the normal brain as an essential step towards addressing how motivational processes are compromised in disease states. Thus, my focus on motivation will al so afford me an opportunity to pursue an even more challenging goal and address how motivational processes are compromised in psychopathology, for example in clinical depression. This new extension of my research will realise a vision of providing a neuroscientific perspective regarding determinants of behaviour, where motivation is a fundamental component, so as to inform a theoretically enriched understanding of its aberrant expression in psychiatric states.

title: Dedicated computing infrastructure for CUBRIC.
description: The Cardiff University Brain Research Imaging Centre (CUBRIC) is a multi-modal imaging centre (comprising MRI, MEG, EEG and TMS) that opened in March 2006. Our strategic aim is to become the reference site for the development, integration and application of multi-modal neuroimaging methods in health and disease. Our strategy encompasses several key-objectives: (1) to understand the biophysical origin of neuroimaging signals; (2) to optimize data capture/analysis methods to target the most relevant aspects of those signals; (3) to apply these methods to understand the brain in both health and a range of psychiatric / neurological conditions; and (4) to disseminate the tools widely to the neuroimaging community. Current foci include: deeper characterization of tissue microstructure; understanding of individual differences in electrophysiology; memory processes; modulation of attention; neurovascular coupling; pharmacological modulation of brain function; the impact of differen ces in brain chemistry on brain function; and disease applications including: mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimers disease, ADHD, autism, schizophrenia, depression, epilepsy and multiple sclerosis. In response to expanding computational demands arising from our efforts in developing, promoting and deploying cutting-edge multi-modal methods, we are requesting funds to cover the crucial replacement of CUBRICs computing infrastructure to increase computational speed, memory and storage capacit y.

title: Optogenetic dissection and treatment of diseased neural circuitry in schizophrenia.
description: Despite decades of investigation into the molecular basis of schizophrenia, the alterations at the neural network level, which actually underlie the observed symptoms experienced by patients are very poorly understood. The proposed project aims to identify such alterations, especially those, that are causally related to the often pharmacoresistant cognitive and negative schizophrenic symptoms. The experimental strategy is to screen for cell types, whose optogenetic activation or silencing can improve such schizophrenia- related endophenotypes, as assessed in expedient behavioural tests in relevant transgenic mouse models. The key hypothesis of my project is that there are certain types of neurons in the brain, which - when activated or inhibited selectively enough in a well-defined manner - will improve a major share of schizophrenia-related behavioural readouts. The anticipated result is twofold. Firstly, the role of certain cell types and circuits in the emergence of specific schiz ophrenia-related symptoms (and the corresponding normal cognitive function) will be clarified, and the currently dominating circuit- based theory of schizophrenia, upon which this study is based, will be directly tested. This will also help to identify a range of cell types and molecules as pharmacological targets. Secondly, my project will work towards a direct gene therapy of schizophrenic symptoms.

title: A cluster randomized controlled trial of a STEPped CARE intervention for depression in primary care.
description: STEPCARE is a randomized controlled trial to test the effectiveness and cost- effectiveness of a program of intervention for depression delivered by non- physician primary care providers supported by general practitioners using mobile telephony. The trial will compare two arms: 1) an intervention arm in which a manualized intervention package is provided; and 2) a care as usual arm in which an enhanced usual care is delivered. Study will recruit adults with depression of at least moderate severity. Primary outcome, to be assessed at 6 months following recruitment, will be the proportion of cases who recover from depression.

title: Fitness to Plead: A Conceptual and Empirical Study.
description: The concept of fitness to plead is intrinsically interdisciplinary. The final arbiters of fitness are judges, but the courts turn to psychiatrists for expert testimony; in the end the proper standard of fitness to plead is a question of ethics. The study draws on all these disciplines, with the goal of validating an empirically and conceptually sound test for fitness in the population for which it is intended. The study comprises: 1. a quantitative study of targeted populations in the criminal justice systemusing a video- based clinical instrument for assessing fitness to plead which has been recommended by the Law Commission 2. a follow-up qualitative study to probe the decision-making capacity of selected defendants; 3. focus groups with judges and other professionals, using vignettes drawn from the study, to seek expert consensus on the determination of fitness The purpose of this three- stage approach is to test and refine the video-basedassessment instrument, comparing its results with the gold standard of judicial opinion, and generating suggested cut off' scores to define and estimate the prevalence of unfitness'. In addition, the study will generate good practice guidelines for conducting fitness assessments, while also providing empirically robust data about risk factors.

title: 'Centre for the Improvement of Population Health through E-health Research (CIPHER)'
description: The vision of the Centre for Improving Population Health through E-Health Research (CIPHER) is to maximise the utility of routine health-related data on the UK population to support research to improve the nation's health. Objectives are: to provide a focus for innovative research using electronic health records; undertake novel linkage and analyses of large datasets; and build multi-disciplinary research capacity. The Centre will deliver four research programmes in: methodological innovation; injury, the built environment and health; psychosocial determinants of health; and, population aspect of infection. Much of the methodological work will be on enabling data to be used whilst protecting and ensuring privacy. The development of an anonymised data linkage platform will enable previously infeasible, large scale observational and interventional studies to be undertaken. CIPHER will address many scientific questions, including those listed below. How can data linkage improve measurement of the national and global burden of injury? What is the population impact of fall-prevention initiatives, Vitamin D supplements and targeted fire prevention activities? Have energy efficiency interventions reduced excess winter mortality? What is the relationship between urban design, obesity and mental health? To what extent do care and repair services protect health and prolong independent living? Is cannabis, alcohol and tobacco use associated with increased risk of psychosis? What is the burden of mental disorder in the young adult population from substance use? Does opiate therapy in prison reduce risk of death in the period immediately following prison release? Can linked routine data be used to identify opportunities to intervene in pathways to harm for people who self-harm or die by suicide? How can linked data be used to evaluate interventions to reduce antibiotic resistant infections? Does carriage of bowel microflora influence development of bowel disorders?

title: Things that go bump in the night - Sleep disorders in children and young people.
description: An investigation into the science of sleep, sleep disorders and the effects of sleep deprivation particularly elective sleep deprivation in children and young people on concenration, ability to perform tasks and general well-being. Project partner, Dr Adrian Kendrick, of the 'Sleep Unit', of University Hospital Bristol, will lead a student conference and initiate primary research to be carried out by students keeping 'Sleep Diaries' over a 2 months period. A cohort of 2,000 7 - 16 year olds wi ll be involved in the research to identify any links between quallity of sleep with outside influences eg from anxieties at school, exam worries, peer pressure, family or personal relationships. From this initial input and research, Year 10 creative arts and science students will produce an hour long multi-arts performance piece investigating some of the more dramatic forms of sleep disorder, sleep walking, nightmares, narcolepsy, stress insomnia, which will be toured to participating schools a nd then seen at a theatre venue by public audiences. The performance (Working Title - Afraid of the Dark?) is delivered to school students in a day of related creative workshops and is followed for adult audiences by a Question Time session.

title: Dead Mother.
description: There is a strong correlation between psychiatric disorders in adults who have suffered a maternal loss through death as a child or adolescent. The impact of an emotional trauma at this early age is highly relevant to current neurological and psychological research, 'Dead Mother' will address the long term effects of the trauma on the individual in a more subjective manner, an area in which strict scientific rationale is less able to access. Sisters Anne Brodie, a Visual Artist, and Dr Catrio na Brodie, a London GP, will interview and film women of different ages and backgrounds who share their experience of growing up and living with the death of their mother. Using film, photography, and text, the project will attempt to explore the nature and shape of the absence; the efforts and effects involved in accommodating the loss. Of particular interest are the points in the women's lives when they become a mother themselves, and when they reach the age at which their mother died. Scient ific support and collaboration will be contributed by Professor Sarah- Jayne Blakemore, Professor of Cognitive Neuroscience, and leading social neuroscientist of adolescent development, Blakemore lab, UCL: Professor Martin Conway, Neuropsychologist, and specialist in autobiographical memory, Dept of Psychology, City University: Professor Michael Parsons, Writer and Psychoanalyst: Dr Caterina Albano, writer, senior researcher and curator (Artakt, Central Saint Martins College of Arts and Des ign), and will act as Artistic Advisor and Curator. Jo Nolan, Managing Director of Screen South, as Film Advisor and Producer

title: The Anatomy of Melancholy.
description: Robert Burton's The Anatomy of Melancholy was first published in 1621. This project will devise and tour a theatrical adaptation of this extraordinary survey of melancholy, its symptoms, causes and cures. Our project aims to communicate the tone of Burton's engaging book, as well as to clearly set out its theories, in which melancholy is believed to arise from an imbalance in the humours. Once this 17th Century world has been invoked, our principle objective is to compare its apparently arcan e thinking with contemporary biomedical theories of depression. Dr. Erin Sullivan will act as our principle collaborator, ensuring we stay true to Burton's book. Other collaborators, specialists in medical history, neuroscience, psychotherapy, cognitive behavioral therapy and general medical practice are in place to ensure the project remains rigorous in its grasp of biomedical and psychological thinking around the subject of depression both contemporary and historic. The project is being made by Stan's Cafe, in association with the Royal Shakespeare Company who will advise on details of 17th Century dance and drama. The project is commissioned by Warwick Arts Centre who, as part of the commission, will host both the premiere performances and a mini-conference, which will bring together a range of the project's collaborators and advisers with an audience and elements of the show as part of its devising process. The Anatomy of Melancholy will tour to theatres across the UK. Eac h venue will host a post-show discussion around its content. Video extracts of the show and writing about it will be disseminated on-line.

title: Angels and Ghosts.
description: Angels and Ghosts is a crossplatform project centred around a short animated narrative film, website, virals, travelling exhibition, social networks and a series of panel discussions to accompany the film. The project aims to explore the biomedical questions raised by individuals who have a family member affected by schizophrenia. The story is based on the real experiences of one girl who has 2-brothers both who have been diagnosed with schizophrenia. The aim is to use the popular Hollywood narr ative of good over evil, coupled with a well-known actress playing the main protagonist, in order to bring a general audience to the story. The story is told using animation and a fairy-tale world. Through our characters experiences there are key biomedical questions that we will explore. What do scientists think is happening in the brain when someone experiences psychosis? What sort of medication is administered and what does that do to the brain? How do you speak to someone with schizophre nia, particular when they are suffering from psychosis? The implications of the genetics of schizophrenia if a sibling or family member has schizophrenia how likely are other family members to develop the illness? The short film will be distributed via film festivals and a supporting website will provide a hub for extra material. After the film festival circuit has been exhausted the film will be released for free on youtube and via our partner organisation, Rethink.

title: Any One Of Us.
description: Theatre Studio West works with many young people who deal with mental health issues among their friends and loved ones, including some who are carers for parents. In 2010, one of our young participants was sectioned after having gone missing for three days and found wandering the streets naked. This profoundly affected our group; as one of them said: He could be any one of us. Despite their direct and indirect contact, societal stigma and lack of knowledge raises questions of: *Who exper iences mental health issues and why? *How much is known about mental health? *How are mental health issues different in BMER communities? *What happens to the brain of someone with a mental health issue? *How are our opinions coloured by direct experiences, society and cultural portrayal? *What are the similarities between mental health issues and theatrical performance? With this project, Any One Of Us, TSW will engage 35 13-19 year olds to gain a developed understanding of mental healt h through established research, direct experience and personal insight. The culmination will be a performance and audio CD which brings together text, movement and sound into an interactive format, enabling the audience to experience the world created. We will work with: *Dr. Brynmor Lloyd-Evans of UCL who has extensive research in the area of mental health issues in young people *Kim O'Kelly, a support counsellor from Mind, who will provide support and guidance and facilitate visits from volunteers from Avenue House, a local Community Mental Health Resource Centre.

title: Head in the Cloud.
description: This 12-month period of intensive research and development centres on fostering collaborative relationships between three moving-image artists and research scientists spanning neurobiology, clinical neurosciences, psychiatry, health sciences, psychology, bioengineering and computer sciences. This body of speculative and practical enquiry will consider our increasingly intimate, immersive relationship with computer technology, and ask whether a growing reliance on the online world is insidiously changing the way we think. As the ever-expanding Google-shaped 'cloud' fills our cultural horizon, and our individual waking hours, becoming the go-to archive/point of access for both personal and collective memories, the project wonders whether this rapid and seemingly unconditional embrace of the internet is affecting our innate ability to remember, and other forms of thought and behaviour. This hot contemporary topic will be considered from an artistic viewpoint, against an informed scient ific background. Three focused partnerships between artists and scientists will extend to wider critical explorations by the project curators who will build on relationships already forged with co-collaborators Dr Daniel Bor and Professor Dame Wendy Hall, Professor Nigel Shadbolt and Professor David Baldwin. Professor Lindy Holden-Dye (chair, Southampton Neuroscience Group, SoNG) will provide a link to further wide-ranging interdisciplinary collaborations. Internationally respected contempor ary visual arts venue John Hansard Gallery are partners, with an ambition to stage an exhibition of resulting artworks, mooted for 2014/5. Hansard's immediate academic context at University of Southampton is a hotbed of innovative, interdisciplinary thinking and, aptly, is the place where the idea of the internet was conceived by Tim Berners-Lee.

title: The Noise.
description: Building on our award winning track record for innovative collaborations with scientists, Unlimited Theatre will research, develop and produce a new show about sound and its impact on us - physically, emotionally, psychologically. In recent years we have worked closely with scientists (mostly in quantum and astro physics) to research and develop a series of new plays, events and experiences that have been enormously successful in bringing leading edge research in these fields to a large audie nce. For all of these projects, we have also worked closely with a composer David Edwards - better known by his recording name Minotaur Shock. Our work together has led to an increasingly important focus on how music and sound affect and influence our audiences' experience and conversations about what the physical processes of that experience are. This, in turn, has led us to start conversations with Dr Denis McKeown (Senior Lecturer in Cognitive Psychology at the University of Leeds) and Pr ofessor Tim Griffiths (Professor of Cognitive Neurology at Newcastle University and a Wellcome Senior Clinical Fellow) about the neurology of sound, specifically it's impact and influence on Memory and how we remember/recall/forget/store information. For this project, we will work closely with our consultant scientists to make a new show with biomedical science at its heart. THE NOISE is a co-production with Newcastle's Northern Stage and will tour to many of the UK's most prestigious theat re venues including West Yorkshire Playhouse, The Crucible in Sheffield, Royal & Derngate in Northampton and Warwick Arts Centre.

title: Honeyscribe - Florilegium.
description: The 'Honeyscribe' project was established in 2011 by Amy Shelton to explore the relationship between bee health, human health, the environment and the arts. The aim of the project is to create dialogue and exchange about bees between scientists, artists, children and the general public through artistic practice, developing new artworks, delivering workshops and curating public events. Ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs document the role of a Honey Scribe tasked to record every drop of honey produc ed. Artist Amy Shelton has assumed the function of a contemporary honeyscribe, charting current threats to the health of pollinators and listening to what bees have to tell us about our own health and wellbeing. 'Honeyscribe' emphasizes communication, exchange and diversity. 'Florilegium' is a light box installation, which literally illuminates the floral sources of nectar and pollen that sustain honeybee colonies. Melliferous plant samples collected throughout the year are preserved at the peak of their bloom and act as a vibrant palatte with which to create a map of the biodiverse flora essential to honeybee health, making visible the importance of pollinating insects to our own wellbeing. The research and development of 'Honeyscribe' to date has been supported by a Wellcome Trust Arts Award. This proposal seeks to develop the project further, supporting the costs of the public exhibition of 'Florilegium' at a variety of urban venues including Peninsula Arts Gallery, Wellcom e Collection, Southbank Centre, Natural History Museum, as well as to deliver a series of workshops for children throughout 2013/2014.

title: Invisible Heat .
description: Invisible Heat is a UK wide exciting new research project on the health effects of climate change for five artists to develop public realm proposals and for one artist to create a test bed artwork for an estimated 26,000 online and attendee audiences. Collaborations with scientists will enable new scientific ideas and the development of commissions to explore the boundaries of art and new media. Heat is the main catalyst for climate change. Our atmosphere is becoming a giant heat engine causing health problems including disease and displacement from flooding, mental illness, food insecurity and air pollution. In 2009, WHO estimated the effect of climate change on human health and connected mortality was 0.2%. 85% were children. Artists Adam Chodzko, Semiconductor, Burak Arikan, Gordon Cheung, Kasia Molga will produce proposals. Ellie Harrisons new artwork at Manchester University will target 39,000 students. They will collaborate with Professor Paul Wilkinson London School of Hygie ne and Tropical Medicine, Professor Frank Kelly, Environmental Health Kings College London and Professor Kevin Anderson, Tyndall Manchester. Together they will explore health and climate models, predictions of future warming and the consequences. Invisible Heat will be coordinated by Invisible Dust Curator, Alice Sharp who has a track record of delivering high profile artworks exploring our environment. Public realm proposals and community participation projects will be developed with signif icant host partners including Professor Nancy Rothwell, Vice-Chancellor, Manchester University, Hadrian Garrard, Director, CREATE, Rose Wu, Science Festival Coordinator, Newcastle University and Asher Minns, Tyndall Centre, University of East Anglia.

title: Let's talk Neuroscience.
description: We aim to foster informative and engaging discussions on neuroscience subjectsinvestigated by the BCNI with the general public and mental health patient groups. For Brain Awareness Week we will facilitate two interactive events: (a) Focusing on ADHD', during which the audience and a panel composed of BCNI scientists and clinicians and an ADHD patient will discuss the causes, treatments and science of ADHD, and (b) Smart pills, anyone?', a debate on the science and ethical implications of cognitive enhancement with school students, the Naked Scientists (Smarter UK delivery partner) and Barbara Sahakian (BCNI; Chair of Smarter UK Advisory Panel).

title: Ecotoxic.
description: Ecotoxic is a series of research projects by artists Ariel Guzik, Brandon Balleng e, Micol Assa l and Kuai Shen exploring the impact of environmental pollution on animal behaviour and health. The aim is to enrich their current artistic practices, and make credible observations of animal behaviour that may contribute to scientific knowledge. Their research will be conducted in collaboration with scientists working in marine biology, ecology, entomology, and ecotoxicology. Tracing and unravelli ng the often-invisible effects of human activity on other species, the artists aim to draw attention to the impact of noise and toxins on animal wellbeing and health through distinctive artistic practices. Ariel Guzik will focus on the importance of sound in whale and dolphin communication and the impact of underwater sound pollution, through performative actions undertaken in the UK in cooperation with cetacean experts. Brandon Balleng e will work with environmental biologist Dr Alan Scarlett o f Plymouth University to see if it is possible to detect Deep Water Horizon (Gulf oil spill) disaster chemicals in migratory fish species in British markets. Micol Assa l will look into the poetics and dynamics of bee flight trajectories in changing environmental conditions, advised by insect specialists. Kuai Shen will investigate how ant behaviour alters in response to manmade environmental changes, specifically in Yasuni National Park in Ecuador, in collaboration with myrmecologist Dr David D onoso. The aim of this research phase is to arrive at detailed production proposals for a series of original artists works, taking the form of sound performances, installations and films.

title: The Mouse.
description: 23-minute drama. THE MOUSE is a tender love story concealed within a fierce urban thriller. It dramatises the interface of bipolar disorder, psychiatry and deprivation in the life of a vulnerable teenager. The project is a collaboration between filmmaker Theo Baines, adolescent psychiatrist Dr Simon Lewis (clinical lead, Simmons House NHS residential unit) and cinema story- editor Walter Donohue (Paris Texas, 28 Days Later). The film explores the impact of social and economic deprivatio n in adolescence on young people's first experiences of mental illness and psychiatry, and on their subsequent risk of isolation, unemployment and homelessness in early adulthood. A psychotic young homeless man is sectioned by police in east London and taken to A&E. In a psychiatric assessment, Jacob tells his story: Two weeks earlier he travels to London, leaving his medication to begin again without it. He finds work in a kitchen and meets 15-year-old Ayla. They fascinate each other. Ayla loves the mice she sees under the tracks at tube stations. Jacob devotes himself to getting her one by any means possible - in an increasingly imaginative series of schemes. Unaware of his endeavours but alarmed by his unsettled personality, Ayla ends their short relationship. Heart-broken, unemployed and homeless, Jacobs rapid-cycling symptoms of bipolar disorder and anxiety become increasingly serious, and his quest to catch a mouse ever-more urgent. The story ends in a suspenseful enco unter at Aylas family home. To be offered free online and to Key-Stage 4 PSHE teachers. Promotional campaign will target audience of 15-25-year-olds.

title: The Anatomy of Melancholy the Opera.
description: The Anatomy of Melancholy the Opera is a treatment of three relationships in music and drama. 1. The relationship between neuroscientific study and the state(s) of depression. 2. The relationship between neuroscientific study and the effects of music on the brain. 3. The relationship between points 1. and 2.. By plotting these relationships in an operatic exploration of Burton's seminal work, we hope to present current scientific investigation into depression in a new dance-opera, fo r orchestra, electronics, voice and body. This work will be staged in The Peckham Hotel, a new multi-purpose arts venue that will be the largest of its kind in South London, as part of its launch season in summer 2013. By performing there we hope to bring contemporary science and contemporary opera to audiences who may not otherwise find these accessible. We believe that depression is an extremely important issue for both art and science to examine, and by combining the two (with expert guida nce from Wellcome Trust Professor Jonathan Flint) we hope to facilitate much- needed discussion in the more impoverished areas of London. While our research and development phase of the project will undoubtedly highlight particular areas we wish to focus on, we are also keen for this work to respond directly to research we undertake in the community in which the performances will take place.

title: 'The Eradication of Schizophrenia in Western Lapland' - Research and Development for a new play to tour in 2014.
description: Ridiculusmus is planning an 8-week research and development project in order to create a new play entitled The Eradication of Schizophrenia in Western Lapland. The aim of this project is NOT to create a production, but for Ridiculusmus to engage in scientific research, enquiry and dialogue to gain significant understanding of specific medical specialisms, in order to inform the writing of a new play. We will consult and interact with two molecular psychopharmacologists and psychiatrists, and a clinical psychologist and family therapist to investigate the effects of drugs on dialogue in a therapeutic setting. In particular, we are focusing on the treatment of schizophrenia and anxiety disorders, in order to write a script that is anchored in the reality of contemporary medical practice. Ridiculusmus will undertake workshops, rehearsals, sharings and script development alongside ongoing dialogue and exchanges with medical specialists. This project will enable the company to ga ther the knowledge and material to enable us to create a new theatre production in 2014, which will consequently tour in the UK and abroad, stimulating interest, excitement, learning, thinking and debate around pharmacology and therapeutic dialogue, and an examination of the personal, societal and cultural impacts of current medical practices in relation schizophrenia and anxiety disorders. This project will support a research and development process towards this.

title: Overpowered: Is the Science an Art or the Art a Science?.
description: Overpowered is a experiential theatrical presentation using the techniques of stage hypnosis, clinical hypnotherapy, original music and good old fashioned showbiz, to illustrate the transformative power of suggestion to heal. It is a development of the research into both branches of hypnosis undertaken during Christopher Green's tenure as Artist in Residence at the British Library. The Science advisors are Professor David Oakley of the Hypnosis Unit, UCL and Professor Christopher French, H ead of the Anomalistic Psychology Research Unit at Goldsmiths' College. Donald Robertson, principal of the London College of Hypnosis and Hypnotherapy is the academic consultant. The research will inform the show as an entertainment that asks fundamental questions about how we experience our own consciousness and what steps we can take to change our neural pathways, and so alter our behaviour. The show is housed in a tent that feels part revivalist meeting and part medicine show. A variety of stage turns, lectures, and installations support the main show undertaken by Christopher Green's character, who uniquely uses song as the hypnotic induction technique. This travelling show will tour festivals with it's mission to entertain, educate and encourage change for the better. The Singing Hypnotist may be a showman, even a snakeoil salesman, but his skills are based in the latest empirical research. How would it be if he really could help you let go of pain and painful habits? W ho is to say that every word he sings isn't true?

title: Madge Gill: Medium and Visionary.
description: This major exhibition of outsider and visionary artist Madge Gill (1882-1961) is planned as a collaborative project across the arts and sciences. This interdisciplinary project will bring together mental health service users from the Art & Soul group, curators, art critics, art psychotherapists and psychologists to share their reflections and interpretations of Gill's life and work through a film and publication. At the age of thirty-seven, after suffering an illness that left her blind in h er left eye, Gill began to create art passionately and created thousands of mediumistic work over 40 years. She claimed to be guided by a spirit called 'Myrninrest' and often signed her drawings with this name. Her drawings often contain the figure of a young woman, possibly a self portrait. Her work is in all sizes from postcard size to over 30ft. The exhibition will contain loans from Newham Borough Council (who hold rarely seen work by Gill in their collection) and from the Henry Boxer Galler y and will be curated by Roger Cardinal, a leading critic who originally coined the term 'outsider art.' By holding the exhibition in a well-known public art gallery, the project will aim to reach new audiences not normally engaged in history of medicine, whilst at the same time celebrating the benefits of creativity for mental and emotional well-being for those in the present day.

title: Mansions in the Orchard: Space, Architecture and Asylum in the 'Care in the Community' Era.
description: In 2014, the Bethlem Royal Hospital Archives & Museum will move into the hospital's Art Deco administration block. Built in 1930, this building reflects a largely unexplored era of the ancient institution. New research and photography will reveal the history of the hospital at Monks Orchard, which has been overshadowed by interest in Victorian 'Bedlam'. Oral histories, collected from those who worked and lived in the building (at first used as staff accommodation) will supplement textual rese arch and photographic documentation of the architecture, bringing post-war psychiatry to life. By combining archive research with individual stories and new photographic documentation, this project will create a space in which academic historians and current and former staff and service users can work together and share skills and experience to create two temporary exhibitions and a permanent local history archive. The project will incorporate the perspectives of mental health staff and se rvice users at every stage. All members of the core project team have either worked in or used mental health services (or both). This background will enable sustainable opportunities for collaboration between mental health staff and service users and the academic history of psychiatry. Focus groups and events will increase public understanding of mental healthcare, aiding destigmatisation by encouraging audiences to consider their attitudes toward mental illness: in particular, the ongoing prese nce of inpatient treatment in the 'care in the community' era.
recipient: Bethlem Art and History Collections Trust

title: Primary BioSciences.
description: Primary BioScience is a programme to help schools achieve relevant aims of the Northern Ireland Curriculum at Key Stage 2, by developing pupils capabilities related to personal understanding and health, and in the science and technology area of The World Around Us, specifically in the biomedical sciences and bioengineering. In this six school pilot programme, bioscientists from university and industrial biosciences provide expertise, and work with teachers and educational advisers, - to help develop pupils appreciation and understanding of bioscience applications in the world around them, - to help identify areas in the biological sciences appropriate for upper primary pupils, and develop resources for teaching and learning in these areas, including a Primary BioSciences Teaching and Learning Guide to be circulated to all Northern Ireland primary schools, and - to act as inspiring role models to young people, and help identify potential careers in the biosciences. Te achers and their associated bioscientists will work together to develop teaching and learning resources in possible themes from - health and wellbeing: body systems and their potential problems, - perception of the outside world: thinking and learning development, - positive and negative effects of microorganisms, - responding to diseases, for example asthma, cancers and diabetes, - defining conditions for a safe environment, - food science and technology: security, production, pro cessing, packaging, distribution, - discovery in the biosciences: impact on society, - biosciences in the news: developing an understanding of their impact. The programme also develops the communication skills of participating bioscientists.

title: Deciphering the Mechanisms of Developmental Disorders (DMDD).
description: The proposal aims to capitalize on the unique resource of knockout mouse strains being generated by the Sanger Institute Mouse Genetics Project pipeline. Over the next 5 years the MGP primary screen will identify in excess of 250 genes essential for normal development. The DMDD project will employ high throughput imaging ( CT and HREM) of mutant embryos to identify and catalog structural developmental defects. Possible contributions resulting from disturbed placental development will be assess ed. Phenotypic characterization in conjunction with high-throughput transcriptomic analysis at defined developmental stages will provide new information about gene regulatory networks underpinning normal development. The efforts of the DMDD project will be guided by interactions with Deciphering Developmental Disorders and the MRC Developmental Anomalies Consortia, to prioritize generation and analysis of mutants in mouse genes orthologous to disease alleles identified by human genetic studies. The major output of DMDD will be a single, publicly-available database, fully linked into the International Mouse Phenotyping Consortium and designed to facilitate access by the clinical and developmental biology community. Our goals are dissemination of primary phenotyping information, encouraging maximal uptake of mutant strains by laboratories for future in-depth analysis and advancing identification of developmental disease alleles.

title: DEFINE - Defining endophenotypes from integrated neurosciences
description: Our objective is to rebuild the foundations of psychiatry by breaking away from existing diagnostic categories to define a new biology of mental disorders. Recent genomic studies have identified a number of genetic risk factors for neurodevelopmental disorders. These implicate specific synaptic processes but do not respect current diagnostic boundaries and confer susceptibility across a spectrum of clinical phenotypes including schizophrenia, autism, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADH D), and intellectual disability. Thus, in order to identify novel biomarkers and mechanisms, it will be necessary to jettison existing categorical classifications and instead take a radically different approach based on the genetic underpinnings of these conditions. By focusing upon the effects of high-penetrance mutations that each confers risk across a range of disorders we will be able to establish convergent effects on processes involved in synaptic plasticity and associated effects at a cir cuit level. This bottom-up approach will enable us to work across species and levels of complexity to identify cellular, animal and human endophenotypes that are signatures of risk across diagnostic categories. This will enable us to prioritise animal and cellular phenotypes for future drug development and identify biomarkers of fundamental disease processes for patient studies.

title: Centre for the Development and Evaluation of Complex Interventions for Public Health Improvement (DECIPHer).
description: DECIPHer's aims are to conduct research that:1. will lead to measurable improvements in the health of children and young people2. identifies policies and interventions that are readily adopted, implemented and maintained in the real world and areeffective in improving health and reducing health inequalitiesThe principal objectives of DECIPHer in its second quinquennium of Centre funding will be to develop and ensure the longterm sustainability of DECIPHer as:1. a platform for internationally excellent multidisciplinary research in the development and evaluation of complexinterventions to improve the health and wellbeing of children and young people and address health inequalities2. an internationally excellent environment for multidisciplinary public health improvement research career development3. a focal point in Wales and the South West of England for collaboration between academia, policy, practice and the publicin public health improvement research that will maximise its relevance, innovation, translation and impact.

title: Children and medicine; ethics, autonomy and regulation.
description: A two-day workshop that examines the philosophical and ethico-legal problems associated with assessing and respecting the autonomy of children within the context of medical treatment and medical research. Participants will be from different disciplines (philosophy, law, medicine, education) and different legal jurisdictions (England, Scotland, Northern Ireland, Republic of Ireland). We will discuss, compare, and criticise the latest developments in law, policy and practice in both countries, as well as examine and challenge some of the ethical and philosophical presuppositions behind the latest developments. The workshop will comprise seven papers, with ample discussion time, together with a final roundtable. The papers cover important areas such as the problem of defining consent and best interests, the problem of parents disagreeing with physicians, the problem of assessing and communicating risk, and the problem of evaluating and treating adolescent mental health. All 17 particip ants listed in the proposal have agreed to attend the workshop; and all 7 presenters listed as giving papers have provided titles and abstracts for their papers. After the workshop, the organisers will collect revised submissions into a volume for publication. This would further increase the impact of the workshop on policy and practice in both countries.

title: Doing good in chronic and long term care.
description: A two day workshop that brings together ethicists and medical practitioners to investigate how best to conceptualise the aims of medicine and social care when it comes to people with chronic or long-term conditions. The workshop will be split into three sessions. One will focus directly on a theoretical examination of the aims of health care, drawing on work being done in related areas around themes such as quality of life, well-being and capabilities. The other sessions will concentrate on two issues, making resource allocation decisions and the idea of partnerships between care providers and recipients, where the ways in which this theoretical question is resolved has significant impact on practice. In bringing together theory and practice in this way the workshop aims to ground the theoretical discussion in the practical questions facing health care providers, and also to address those practical questions directly. The workshop will include six papers and will conclude with a pan el drawn from across the different disciplines represented. Each paper will be allocated 45 minutes in order to allow time for discussion.

title: Biomedical ethics and the arts; generating dialogue and provoking debate.
description: Sparkle and Dark (S&D) will be touring their show, Killing Roger at the Edinburgh Fringe Festival in August. Their show is focused on Assisted Suicide and has provoked audience reaction around the issues presented. The Mason Institute (MI) at the University of Edinburgh and S&D wish to hold a public debate discussing the issues around assisted suicide and the role of the Arts in these ethical debates. Patrick Harvie (MSP) presenting the proposed Assisted Suicide in Scotland bill, Professor Graeme Laurie (MI) discussing specific legal cases, Dr Calum McKellar (Scottish Centre for Human Bioethics) will discuss the moral issues and Lawrence Ilsley (S&D) will discuss how the arts can influence, shape and inform the debate have all agreed to participate. MI and S&D also wish to hold a joint Arts symposium to discuss how the arts can provoke and generate questions and ideas on biomedical ethical and legal issues around advances in medicine and the life sciences and how can this arti stic input be measured, valued and understood. This event will have writers, poets, theatre companies, artists, animators and others who will showcase examples of relevant artistic work to identify commonalities.

title: Conference Support for Power and pitfalls of psychopathology: Marking 100 years since the publication of Karl Jaspers General Psychopathology.
description: Karl Jaspers' Allgemeine Psychopathologie, published 100 years ago, formed the philosophical foundation of modern psychiatry, particularly in the UK. It was required reading for psychiatrists in training and introduced a number of powerful concepts that continue to divide psychiatrists today. The Maudsley Philosophy Group Trust is a UK educational Charity dedicated to the philosophy of psychiatry. We wish to celebrate the centenary with a one-day conference dedicated to the book, its impact, and its ongoing relevance.

title: In vitro reconstitution of spindle bipolarity.
description: The proposed study aims to answer the key question of what constitutes the mechanochemical core of the mitotic spindle using an in vitro reconstitution approach. Supported by microfluidics, mathematical modelling and experiments in Xenopus egg extracts, I will develop a novel experimental setup, consisting entirely of purified proteins, to test the central hypothesis of how a combination of spatially restricted microtubule nucleation and antagonistic motor activities generates symmetric bipolar spindles of appropriate size. To mimic the role of chromatin and locally promote microtubule formation, I will engineer different molecular gradients inducing microtubule polymerisation around functionalised glass beads, based on the Aurora B and the Ran pathways. Analysing the biophysical properties of these gradients will explain how high microtubule densities form in the proximity of chromosomes in vivo. Second, I will evaluate the role of the main microtubule crosslinking motors, the plus- en d-directed kinesin-5 and the minus-end-directed kinesin-14, in generating bipolar topology. By combining here, for the first time, the anti-parallel microtubule sorting potential of kinesin-5, the pole focussing ability of kinesin-14 and the continous turnover of locally generated microtubules, I will elucidate the relative contribution of each factor in ensuring a bipolar spindle-like state instead of mono- or multi-polar microtubule assemblies.

title: Reanimating faces: Creating an iPad/mobile device application to facilitate rehabilitation following Bell's Palsy
description: A disparity exists in UK facial palsy physiotherapy provisioning, with some centres providing no aid to significantly-impaired patients. With approximately 15,000 new UK cases annually and a proportion receiving no specialist palsy care, a significant unmet need exists for cohesive management of facial muscle dysfunction. Studies support the benefit of physiotherapy to reduce complications and alleviate synkinesis, yet PATH 06/13 Science 8 physiotherapy is not routinely available to all patients and is only provided via 2-4 short therapy sessions per year - benefits only arise from daily practice of prescribed exercise regimes. Our proposed image-based system uses inexpensive, widely-utilised mobile device technology to provide accurate measurements of facial landmarks, allowing: i) avatar, wireframe, or abstract facial representation, dynamically demonstrating asymmetry; ii) tracking of progress over time to provide motivation; iii) data-integration into games for paediatric patients and social interaction with other patients; and, iv) patient progress auto-feedback to health professionals. Daily system use within the home environment, with regular remote data monitoring by the clinical team, will allow exercise regime modification without the need for outpatient appointments. Daily therapy means faster achievement of therapy goals, reducing the burden on expensive NHS surgical services, but most importantly, improving patient health, psychology and quality of life.

title: Wellcome Trust PhD Programme for Clinicians at the University of Dundee: 'Targetting opiod receptor signal transduction to produce sustained analgesia'.
description: Analgesic opioids remain the drugs of choice for treating severe pain despite debilitating side effects including respiratory depression, tolerance, constipation and hyperalgesia. Tolerance, a phenomenon that leads to the requirement for escalating doses in order to sustain analgesia, is arguably the most problematic aspect of opioid use. Dose increases required to overcome tolerance lead to a greater likelihood of additional opioid side effects. The b-arrestins, proteins involved in opioid receptor trafficking and signalling, are implicated in tolerance. A lack of b-arrestin2 in b-arr2-/- mice leads to negligible tolerance and the appearance of basal opioid-independent analgesia1,2. The host lab demonstrated that basal analgesia is associated with constitutive opioid receptor coupling to voltage-activated Ca2+ channels (VACCs) in b-arr2-/- dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons2,3. The latter can berecapitulated in wild type neurons by directly inhibiting c-Src activity implicating tyrosine kinase-mediated phosphorylation3. While opioid receptor signalling becomes persistent in pain circuitry of b-arr2-/- mice, conditioned place aversion studies reveal normal hedonic homeostasis2. These findings led to the hypothesis that b-arrestin2 signalling through c-Src can be modulated to produce sustained analgesia without affecting reward circuitry. We will use molecular, cellular and behavioural approaches to explore differential opioid signalling in pain and reward pathways.

title: Hormones Project.
description: All of us take a rollercoaster ride through puberty and adolescence. If you are a teenager, you have little idea of the huge changes that are going on. This series follows a whole group of teenagers in the midst of their hormonal journey and witnesses their life-changing experiences and rites of passage. It reveals how hormones and brain development shapes every aspect of their health and wellbeing. With the age of puberty getting lower by the decade, the gulf between physical and psychological maturity has never been greater. This series sees our teens take a positive journey of discovery.

title: Classifying Sexuality and Subjectivity in the DSM-5.
description: The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders is the standard reference for the classification of mental disorders, and is seen as authoritative by clinicians, academics, drug companies and policy makers alike around the world. As the first major revision since 1994, the publication of the upcoming 5th edition of the DSM in May 2013 will represent a significant social and medical event. Psychiatric discourses have increasingly struggled with their embeddedness in culture since the pa rtial declassification of homosexuality from the DSM in the 1970s. DSM-5 has responded to this predicament through the proliferation of ever more precise labels. Against this backdrop, the fundamental question that our conference aims to explore is: how do changing classifications of sexuality and gender in DSM-5 navigate wider cultural discourses about morality and human nature? Our conference will bring together an interdisciplinary range of scholars: members of the DSM-5s Sexual and Gender Id entity Disorders Work Group, mental health practitioners, activists, sociologists, political scientists, ethicists, historians and philosophers. We aim to generate new conceptual and substantive work on the interaction between psychiatry and culture, pioneering analyses of the sexual classifications produced by DSM-5, which are expected to be used globally for decades to come.

title: Symposium on 'Reassessing Psychiatric Experiments and Coerced Research under National Socialism, 1933-1945: New Findings, Interpretations and Bioethical Problems'.
