The performance then weaves between Edna's world and Anthony's, reflecting the fluid nature of memory and providing the audience with insight into Edna's deterioration and her strength of character, and Anthony's research and attempts at treatment. We plan to fully develop the project during Winter 2013, and tour the show to rural areas in England and Wales during Spring 2014. A short film of our first R&D is available here: https://vimeo.com/64727552 Information about the company is available on our w ebsite: www.breadandgoose.co.uk

title: SICK! Festival 2014.
description: SICK! 2014 is an ambitious, cross-art form festival that seeks out new ways of talking about physical, mental and social problems and well-being. Presenting a high-quality, international programme of performance, theatre, film, visual art and digital media, across many venues and public spaces, SICK! focuses on 4 themes: Growing Pains: Adolescence & identity Inside / Out: Mental illness & wellbeing in society Running Out Of Time: Ageing & dementia The End: Death & Euthanasia See Additio nal Information: SICK! 2014 Thematics SICK! 2014 Programme SICK! 2014 builds on the experience and support generated through a hugely successful Wellcome Trust-funded pilot event that took place in March 2013 and looks towards the further development of an annual festival taking place in Brighton and Manchester. The project incorporates the first full- scale festival and research towards the strategic development of the festival. The project will include: Presentation of a 3-week long Si ck Festival in Brighton, March 2014 Commissioning of five new artworks Research and development for annual festival to take place in Manchester, Brighton and other cities in the UK. The festival brings together art works that provide a profound insight into personal experience with the expertise of doctors, academics, healthcare providers, charity workers, and the people for whom these themes are urgent daily realities. The festival creates formats and opportunities specifically designed t o enable audiences to share and reflect upon their own experiences and perceptions, engaging with experts and non- experts from a wide range of perspectives.

title: Animated Minds: Post Natal Expression (working title) .
description: Animated Minds: Stories of Post-Natal Depression is a continuation of the Animated Minds project (www.animatedminds.com), and will consist of five short (3-5 minute) animated documentaries using real testimonies of people who have experienced, or who are close to someone suffering from postnatal depression. The project lead on the films will be BAFTA winning director Andy Glynne who pioneered the use of animated documentaries in the UK and has won over 20 awards, including a two BAFTAs, a Me ntal Health Media Award and an RTS Award. Building on Mosaics unique reputation for making award-winning animated documentaries the films will use personal stories (using audio testimony) , combined with engaging animation to address important issues about postnatal depression. With an estimated three in ten mothers suffering from postnatal depression we feel that it is important to make a series of films which help people identify signs and symptoms of PND, and to help understand more abo ut what it feels like from a subjective point of view. During our research we have been particualry struck by the fact that an estimated 58% of mothers, suffering from postnatal depression, do not seek medical help - often due to lack of understanding about signs and symptoms, or the unnecessary guilt and shame that many mothers experience when faced with the new, and often overwhelming presentation of PND.

title: Winter Shuffle - engaging science events.
description: A continuation of the summer Shuffle Festival programme, Winter Shuffle will mix community, arts and science to further explore mental health, the seasons, identity and togetherness in the festive winter period. We aim to explore the history of psychiatric institution, spread awareness and understanding, prickle curiosity and delight the senses by bringing people together to share stories, light and warmth in this festive time. Winter Shuffle will be held in St Clement's, the disused, Grade- II-listed Victorian psychiatric hospital in which Shuffle Festival took place. The grand front building, will host an inclusive programme of storytelling, poetry, comedy, lectures and music recitals. In the surrounding rooms - former outpatient waiting rooms, medical records cupboards and doctor's offices - will be The Science of Christmas exhibition. Integrated through both will be a series of lectures by pre- eminent scientists on our core themes; each scientist will be paired with an artist who will create a workshop in response to their lecture. Artists confirmed include Susan Morris, Anne Brodie, Tessa Garland, Peter Hudson and Bobby Baker. In particular, pairs will be invited to respond to the Wellcome's research on Seasonal Affective Disorder. Three 'science cinema' evenings will pair celebrated film directors Danny Boyle and Nic Roeg with a relevant scientist to discuss the film's plot in a Q+A with audiences, and promote the Wellcome's exciting new partnership with the BFI. Outside, a giant greenhouse will be lit from within by artist projections and film screenings.

title: Seal Boy - Resubmission.
description: Seal Boy will create a wonderful interactive experience, using leading computer game methodology, techniques and tools to encapsulate and explore many of the central issues around society's dependency on complex bioscience, using a state-of-the-art IPhone phone computer game application that will be made freely available for download. Using the experience of Thalidomide as a central element, Mckeown will work with Mat Fraser, the UK's most well-known Thalidomide affected actor, musician and performer, most recently with Cold Play. The game revolves around the main character, roughly based on Fraser, completing and filling in the gaps of his mothers scrapbook/diary. The main character, played and narrated by Fraser, finds this unfinished journal/book in his mothers attic and it sparks an interest in him to research and discover more about his own disability and history. Intriguingly we also experience first-hand his physicality and disability though game play as his 3D character car ries, moves and touches things, in ways unique to his disability. The game play leads into and makes appropriate use of a scrapbook to showcase elements of medical history to provide a wider view of the Thalidomide story, from distribution to crisis and the aftermath of the drugs use, including the stricter drug regulations we see today. Thalidomide continues to be infamous and its modern-day use for leprosy patients in developing countries raises complex issues concerning business, scien ce, health and well-being, morality and choice as well as raising a vivid and on-going historical narrative.

title: Consortium of Neuroimmunology of Mood Disorders and Alzheimer's Disease.
description: We propose to form a consortium of academic and industrial partners to address the therapeutic challenges of Alzheimers disease and mood disorders by a shared, innovative focus on immunological mechanisms of these key neuropsychiatric disorders and their treatment by anti-inflammatory drugs. The industrial partners (Janssen and Lundbeck) will contribute drug discovery know-how and access to anti-inflammatory drugs. The academic partners will contribute expertise in neuroimaging, clinical phen otyping, animal models and informatics. The work will be organised as two programmes, focused on Alzheimer's disease and mood disorders, and four cross-cutting technical platforms (cytometry, proteomics, PET and MRI). In phase 1 (years 1-3), we will validate peripheral immunological phenotypes, e.g., cytokine levels or macrophage transcriptomes, as markers of Alzheimer's disease and mood disorders. We will seek mechanistically to link peripheral immunophenotypes to markers of central (brain) inflammation and microglial activation; to brain function and behaviour; and to longitudinal changes in the clinical phenotypes and animal models. In phase 2 (years 3-5), we will use these biomarkers in experimental medicine studies designed to test mechanism-of-action and / or therapeutic proof-of-concept of anti-inflammatory drugs in immunologically stratified cohorts of patients with Alzheimer's disease or mood disorders.

title: Stratifying Resilience and Depression Longitudinally (STRADL)
description: Progress in understanding the pathophysiology of MDD has been severely restricted by its aetiological heterogeneity. Our contention is that longitudinal and quantitative assessment of individuals stratified by key exposures and course modifiers will reduce dilution across diverse aetiologies, measurement error and capture more of the total phenotypic variation. It will thus enable the mechanisms underlying resilience, depressive symptoms and MDD to be determined. Our goal is to utilise an ex isting cohort of 21,516 individuals extensively phenotyped for MDD and related quantitative traits called Generation Scotland . We will initially reassess this cohort using remote questionnaires and further assessments in the first year of STRADL, whilst completing GWAS on the entire sample. After conducting our baseline assessments, we will then recruit individuals with quantifiable measures of MDD to test key hypotheses about the heterogeneity of MDD. Specifically we will address the follo wing aims: 1. Identify subtypes of MDD and define their discriminating clinical features, cognitive characteristics and neurobiological mechanisms 2. To test for distinct mechanisms, clinical trajectories and treatment responses in these MDD subtypes 3. To test whether resilience can be constructed and quantified 4. To identify the neurobiological mechanisms underlying resilience to MDD

title: Centre for prevention of stroke and dementia.
description: We aim to substantially expand the Stroke Prevention Research Unit (SPRU) to create a new Centre for Prevention of Stroke and Dementia in the first phase of the establishment of an Institute for Preventive Neurology. SPRU has trained several outstanding early career researchers who now require the space to develop their own programmes, exploiting our unique cohort studies, biobanks and imaging facilities. The Centre will provide 1000 square-metres of new research space (laboratory, clinic, offic e), bringing all current SPRU staff together and allowing a major expansion of our programmes. The Centre will house 50 staff at the heart of the hospital, linked directly to areas of patient care and to our Acute Vascular Imaging Centre and will incorporate other key infrastructure, including the Oxford Vascular Study. The research will continue to focus on better understanding of known risk factors and more effective use of existing treatments, developing cost-effective preventive strategies t hat will impact quickly on clinical practice. The Centre will facilitate further integration with other groups in Oxford, including Neuroimaging (Jezzard), Neuroplasticity (Johansen-berg), Experimental Psychology (Husain), Vascular Physiology (Leeson), Bioengineering (Tarassenko) , Global Health (Woodward), Old Age Psychiatry (Lovestone), Primary Care (Hobbs/Lasserson) and Health Economics (Luengo-Fernadez).

title: The Kiss of Light: Nursing and Light Therapy in 20th-Century Britain.
description: 'The Kiss of Light' is an exciting collaboration between a well-established small museum and the Centre for the History of Medicine at Warwick University, principally Dr Tania Woloshyn, a Wellcome Trust-funded Research Fellow and specialist in the history of light therapy. Through a shared commitment to engaging the public by examining historic medical treatments and questioning their contemporary relevance, we aim to show how perceptions of light have changed over time and been shaped by both e nthusiasm and fear. Over the 12 weeks of the exhibition, we will display a diverse range of British images, objects and texts about sunlight therapy (heliotherapy) and artificial light therapy (phototherapy) in a visually inspiring way. Highlighting the role of nurses as key agents and children as vulnerable patients in light therapy's history, our project aims to excavate a forgotten past and to provoke discussion about medical agency and patient care. Through its interpretation and engagem ent programme aimed at the museum's key audiences, the exhibition aspires to prompt visitors to think critically about light's healing powers and risks, about ongoing debates on light for wellbeing, as beautifying, curative or dangerous, and to question the voices disseminating these beliefs. The museum's location in St Thomas Hospital enables us to work with healthcare professionals who use light as a treatment for mental and physical health today. By using the very subject of the exhibitio n, namely light, to display the historic material, we will illuminate this subject both intellectually and aesthetically.

title: The Artful Experts Season.
description: Artful Experts Season is a pilot public engagement programme of exhibitions, music, events and live performances by people with lived experience of mental distress. Curated by arts and mental health charity DLL, the programme will bring together expert collaborators from the fields of mental health, digital media and the arts to explore methods of public engagement, with a view to a larger scale World Mental Health Day 2015 programme. Our Steering Group, Advisory Panel and Creative Collaborato r team will work with an external Evaluator to direct and shape public engagement, evaluative and data gathering methodology; test and critique processes during the programme; and develop material into assets that can inform future public engagement methodology. A two-minute film and formal Evaluation document will be publically shared. Public engagement will be driven by accessible exhibitions and live shows, social media and web activity, including an online animated serial narrated by comic character Dr Bobby. The vibrant programme will culminate in the Artful Symposium. This unusual artist-led event at the Royal Society of Medicine will present invited mental health audiences with art and performances by people with personal experience of mental illness. The aim is that this unique context of a shared mediating experience of art will form the basis for reflection and fresh dialogue around mental health in this historically fraught and polarised field. DLL believes that art can off er a transformative basis for public engagement with mental health, where experts by experience work together with experts by profession.

title: Ida's Diary.
description: At the end of 2010, Indie Film received a package in the mail. The package contained an unedited video diary from a young girl living in a small town in Southern Norway. She told us she wanted someone to tell her story. Ida's Diary will be a moving and complex film which documents seven years of Ida's video diary as a person suffering from Borderline Personality disorder and post traumatic stress disorder. Ida self-harms. Ida's Diary will not be a film that focuses on why people hurt the mselves or why they have mental health issues, it will be a film that creatively explores what it actually feels like; how blistering the cold can feel on a bad day and how precious a moment of contentment can feel in a beautiful place. Ida has been hospitalised and committed to both closed and open wards over 60 times and suffered more than 2000 stitches because of her cutting. In 2010, after many different types of treatments, she enrolled into one of the few psychiatric programmes aimed at self-harmers. Since then, Ida has stopped cutting. The main driving force in this film is Ida's battle for survival. It's a film filled with hope, and which heartbreakingly picks apart the biggest battle one can have with oneself. We hope that Ida's vibrant and honest openness about her illness; her relationship with her medication; and her will to survive will give audiences a new perspective on mental health. Trailer Ida's Diary: https://vimeo.com/47644103 Password: IdaIndie

title: Promoting mental health and building resilience in adolescence: Investigating mindfulness and attentional control.
description: Mental health problems most commonly start during adolescence. Major depression carries the largest potential burden in terms of years lived with disability and this proposal aims to determine how best to prevent it. It is based on the hypothesis that depression, and co-occurring behavioural problems, in part represent a failure to exercise top-down executive control, impairing the ability to recruit effective problem-solving skills in the face of emotional distress (e.g., anger, sadness, fear). Mindfulness training (MT) has been seen to be highly effective in adults. Our key goal is to examine whether mindfulness training is also effective in adolescents in reducing psychopathology in those at high risk, and enhancing well-being in those at low risk. Three interlinked research themes will: (1) use experimental research to characterise the impact of MT (versus control interventions) on adolescents ability to exert executive control in the face of motivationally compelling distr actions and across diverse contexts (Theme 1); (2) evaluate how best to train teachers to deliver a MT curriculum competently, and how best to implement the intervention in schools (Theme 2); (3) investigate the effectiveness, cost-effectiveness and mechanisms of MT in schools using a large-scale cluster-randomised controlled trial (Theme 3).

title: SHUFFLE 2014 - SURVIVAL / NATURE / DEATH.
description: Shuffle Festival will be building on our history of creating cutting-edge cultural and educational happenings across film, visual + performance art, scientific research, public workshops and discussion. This year the summer festival will be held in Tower Hamlets Cemetery Park, the largest area of urban woodland in London. In 2014 we propose to look at Nature, Survival and Death and launch a new short film prize (judged by Danny Boyle) specifically relating to 'Science and the Imagination'. T his application relates only to the science element of Shuffle Festival, which can be broken into three main parts. 1. Day of The Dead (Sunday the 3rd August 2014) A full day of workshops directly related to exploring the modern taboo towards the last stage of life: death. Conducted by leading scientists across the fields of neuropsychology and neuroscience, materials science and sleep science and culminating in a 'Decay Dinner,' a sophisticated curated feast combining cooking and chemistr y and revealing the potential of food in both sustenance and medicine. 2.Still Ill Site-specific theatrical production by local theatre group involving local hospitals and academics to be performed on the Day of the Dead. 3. Science Summer Camp A three day 'Science Camp' for children aged 7 12 run by play workers and with specialist sessions with scientists, naturalists and architects to build dens, discover natural ecosystems in their cities and learn about their own bodies and th e relationship to natural processes.

title: Promoting understanding of the complexities and dilemmas of first episode psychosis through the ethnodrama CRACKED in workshops, performances and caf s scientifiques.
description: This proposal is to fund the production and tour of a new play CRACKED through a creative artistic collaboration between theatre, neuroscience, psychiatry and clinical ethics. The playwright Mike Kenny and the poet Julie Boden have drawn on recent research on first episode psychosis of young adults from ethnically diverse backgrounds (Singh et al 2012). Lay and professional perceptions and explanations of psychosis such as auditory hallucinations (hearing voices) will be explored and visually re presented through projection of both functional imaging (MRIs) and aspects of delusions. The play will address the paradigms of both early detection and intervention and the patho- physiology, and the socio-cultural context that affects patterns of help seeking. It will shed light on the prodromal phase of psychosis when behaviour becomes 'odd' but is contained within families until they seek help in different ways. The play will capture elements of emerging psychosis in the prodromal phase through poetry and verbatim text, framing the inner voices of the young adults and outer lives of the carers with professional actors. The theatre company will rehearse with young adults from community youth theatre groups at each venue ending with public performances that will be followed by post- show caf scientifiques with a panel of experts to stimulate debate and informal learning with the audiences. The tour will cover the Midlands and Scotland between September -October 2014. The play will be performed in theatre studio spaces and will creatively frame socio-cultural issues and current explanations of psychosis in neuroscience and psychiatry.

title: Pyschobible: The Book Behind the Battle in Mental Health.
description: The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) is one of the most powerful scientific books of our time: a 1000-page bible for psychiatrists around the world, giving rise to vicious controversies that reflect deep rifts at the heart of the field. This film tells the story of the people and politics behind the DSM, combining interviews with key figures in the book's development and prominent British psychiatrists, stories of patients whose lives have been affected by DSM diagnose s, and archival and creative explorations of mental-illness diagnoses over time to create a unique social history of modern psychiatry.

title: STATE OF EMERGENCY.
description: A feature film in which filmmaker and his wife intimately document their lives following news of pregnancy after years of IVF. It's as close as we can get to real feelings, as they occur. Joy, uncertainty, guilt, comedy, anxiety over their shifting roles, bodies, responsibilities, the barrage of advice. Then: bad news. One of twin fetuses has a rare genetic condition with severe disability if carried to term. They're thrust into vexed medical and human questions plaguing NRT-era parents- to-be. The film collides documentary, re- enactment, and poetic modes to reach the fullest revelations.

title: The Billion Dollar Bald Spot.
description: The Billion Dollar Bald Spot [working title] is a film designed to explore male vulnerability through the discussion of the science and psychological impact of hair loss. We're applying for a development award to create a trailer/teaser and online presence to attract the attention of UK TV Commissioners by exploring biomedical innovation as it intersects with an intimate investigation of the psychology associated with male pattern baldness. Using interviews and a first-person documentation of my own experience of hair-loss, we'll mix scientific rigour, sensitivity and humour in a visually-striking film that intends to make hair loss less depressing!

title: Irene's Ghost.
description: My mother, Irene, died when I was 3 after a coma. No-one knew the cause, only that she'd been ill since childbirth from a postnatal complication. Growing up, the mental health problems she'd also suffered were hidden from me. Over 30 years later, Im finding out what happened to her, tracing her friends and family to rebuild a picture of Irenes life and death, and exploring the impact of mental illness on new mothers today. Its a film about mental health and about the legacy we leave behin d. A film about memory, love and loss.

title: Illusions of a Beautiful Mind.
description: With unique access to the world of Virtual Therapy, Illusions of a Beautiful Mind follows patients suffering from mental health psychoses as they undergo radical new therapy using immersive virtual reality borrowed from the gaming world. If you look at the anatomy, the structure, the function, there's nothing in the universe that's more beautiful, that's more complex, than the human brain. - Keith Black, Pioneering Neurosurgeon.

title: How To Live Yours.
description: How To Live Yours is a feature film about twin loss and the resultant identity crisis. A comedy drama developed by Creative England and the BFI, it stars Jodie Whittaker, and shoots October-November 2014 This film explores the psychology of twin loss - what happens to someone when they lose a twin, the specific identity crises and loss of a sense of the self that can occur and, crucially, how this affects relationships and friendships. The project aims to stimulate debate and promote learn ing about twin loss through the authentic and humourous voice of the confused protagonist.

title: Three Identical Strangers.
description: Adopted as babies by different New York families, identical triplets David, Eddy and Robert grew up unaware of each others existence. 19 years after their birth, a peculiar coincidence would bring the three of them back together. Overjoyed at their reunion, the triplets had no idea that in chancing upon each other, they had also unearthed a secret scientific study into the effects of nature vs. nurture that they, of all people, were never intended to know about. After decades of no explanation or apology and devastated by the suicide of their brother, David and Robert want answers.

title: Wellcome Trust Engagement Fellowship 2014.
description: How does our individual health relate to the public health messages we receive? Where does this information intersect with our personal understanding and experience and how can individual experiences and behaviour inform research and decision-making? Interrogating these issues creatively, I want to work with audiences to explore the ways in which public health information is conveyed and experienced through language, environments and media. Healthcare environments are hugely variable, yet they have a proven impact on our sense of wellbeing. If our surroundings - manifested in architecture, design, nature and sound, directly affect our wellbeing to what extent do these environments have an impact our experience of illness? Building on my own experience: making site-specific work and collaborating with architects and musicians, I am interested in unpicking the visual and sonic potential of NHS waiting rooms. An extension of this is my interest in how public health information is conveyed and where it is received. Many public spaces are natural theatres where there is a confluence between diverse demographics, visually stimulating information and human interaction. These seem ideally suited as places to experiment, innovate and communicate, through performance, visual 'messaging' and direct interaction. The 'Ageing population time bomb' as defined in a recent United Nations report: 'Ageing in the 21st Century and referenced by our own government and media, refers to us all no matter what our age. Do messages of doom surrounding the aged, or popular media images of mountain- biking 'seniors' represent the 60+ demographic in any resonant way? Using archival material and contemporary interviews I am interested in exploring what it means to age now and how older citizens can use creative means to have their health concerns heard. Digital platforms and film have the potential to make their voices audible in innovative ways. Broadening these questions out to explore the efficacy of different cultural models, does a rural campaign in the developing world have any validity in an urban, first world setting? Can effective, ancient methods such as puppetry and storytelling be re-imagined in more complex 21st Century forms to effectively reach much larger audiences both here and worldwide? Travel and residential research will support this enquiry. Using radio as a creative medium to communicate and explore health information and concerns also enables communities to interact. A powerful means to include isolated groups e.g.: National Prisons' Association Radio, it is also an ideal forum for scientists, artists and other listeners, global or national to come together in creative ways. With Fellowship support I can broaden the reach and scale of my inquiry through projects as physically small as a postage stamp or as dynamic as a film. Technical training will give me access to the new media and languages with which to converse. Access to conferences, talks and mentoring will help me 'step up' my understanding of the issues I wish to explore. Travel and residencies will challenge my understanding of other approaches to engagement, provide stimulus, and broaden my cultural awareness.

title: Wellcome Trust Engagement Fellowship 2014.
description: I will use the Fellowship to learn more about how people learn, about marketing and psychology, and to make strategic connections with science communicators. My goal will be to make that step change in my career and develop the concept of 'Explore More' into a national initiative. The support from Wellcome Trust will release me from the day-to-day operational aspects of running a science centre exhibition and allow me to focus on my personal development. Working with exhibits has provided me with an insight into visitor behaviour, but this practical approach is not based on rigorous educational theory. Specifically I will focus on learning more about how we learn through a bespoke learning and coaching programme to enhance my formal knowledge in this area. To achieve this I will: Create an advisory group - I will work with the Trust to identify suitable candidates to invite to the group with the purpose of advising, engaging, teaching and challenging me throughout the Fellowship. The group will provide me with a platform for discussion and advice throughout the fellowship journey. This formalised process is something that I have successfully managed on projects. Identify best practice - I have a large number of international contacts and people I would like to learn from. The Fellowship will allow me identify other inspirational leaders both in and outside the science centre network. I will travel and work with some of these key people. I am particularly interested in the work of the India science centre network and the Finnish educational system. Build relationships - The UK has a wide range of public engagement activities and resources from a wide variety of practitioners. The Science Learning+ is an important new initiative that will support and develop new engagement approaches and evaluation methods. I would seek to collaborate with any funded projects where appropriate. Organise Coaching Days - I will identify an executive coach and specific experts to act as my mentors and develop my skills. Run a Pilot Project - In preparing this application, I have had discussions with many UK science centre Directors who share the view that there is more to do in this area. These centres range from smaller centres in Cambridge, Bracknell and Winchester, a Millennium funded centre in Newcastle, a devolved government-funded centre in Wales, and a large London based museum. These key institutions will help to inform, devise and test the concepts for 'Explore More' Realise its potential - I will invest time to see how 'Explore More' could be included into other initiatives.

title: Transforming the treatment of schizophrenia: Design & development of AMPA receptor modulators with improved safe profiles as novel drugs for treating the cognitive dysfunction associated with schizophrenia and other CNS disorder
description: In schizophrenia, existing drugs treat the positive symptoms (e.g. paranoia, auditory hallucinations) but have little effect upon the cognitive deficit (impaired attention, memory and problem-solving) and negative symptoms (lack of motivation and impaired social function) which remain a major barrier to the resumption of a normal life. Accordingly, a drug that improves either or ideally both of these illness dimensions will revolutionize the treatment of schizophrenia. While a dysfunction of dopaminergic neurotransmission in schizophrenia is long established, recent pharmacological and genetic evidence implicates glutamatergic disturbances, more specifically hypofunctioning of NMDA receptors, in the pathophysiology of schizophrenia and in particular the cognition and negative symptom dimensions. The AMPA subtype of glutamate receptor is a partner for NMDA receptors and plays a crucial role in the synaptic plasticity associated with cognition, resulting in the Project hypothesis: Increasing AMPA receptor function will improve cognitive function in schizophrenia. Until recently, the cognitive enhancement resulting from increased AMPA receptor function was thought to be associated with a mechanism-based convulsant liability. However, while at GSK, Prof. Ward demonstrated that is it possible to enhance AMPA receptor function without convulsant activity. It is this innovation that forms the basis of the current proposal. Project goal: To identify a safe, well-tolerated AMPA receptor- modulating drug ready for First-in-Human dosing.

title: Understanding the introduction and use of the First Generation Antipsychotic (FGA) drugs in the management of schizophrenia in England, c. 1955 to 1980: The clinicians perspective.
description: The project involves examining published and unpublished primary material and conducting oral interviews with retired clinicians. The published primary material includes contemporary journal articles and drug adverts, the latter being important for understanding the role of the pharmaceutical industry. The unpublished material includes the archives of the British Association for Psychopharmacology (BAP) and the Royal College of Psychiatrists (RCPsych). This includes details of their annual c onferences, major education event in UK clinical psychiatry. These will help illustrate views on FGAs in the management of schizophrenia compared to other therapeutic approaches. The formation of the BAP in 1974, relatively late compared to other national psychopharmacology organisations, will be explored. Dr Haddad will interview 12 clinical psychiatrists who worked in England between 1955 and 1980 to determine their views and experiences of FGAs during that time. He is attending the Wellco me Trust Oral History 5-Day Residential course (September 2013). Interviews will be recorded and transcripts made available for future researchers bringing added value to the project. The key goals include (i) completion and transcription of interviews with clinicians, (ii) reviewing primary material as outlined and (iii) publishing the research so it is available for professional historians, clinical psychiatrists and the lay public.
recipient: Greater Manchester Mental Health NHS Foundation Trust

title: Imperfect choice and the brain: uncertainty, value and decision-making.
description: I will combine theoretical models from economics and psychology with tools from experimental neuroscience to isolate the factors and describe the computational processes that lead to uncertainty in the estimations of value used to guide value-based choice. I will test if the same neural network involved in value computation also represents the levels of uncertainty that emerge during the value comparison process and how uncertainty governs levels of subjective confidence in choice. I aim to diss ect the neural circuit that enables humans to be aware of the level of uncertainty in their value-based decision (measured as level of confidence), an ability that confers the critical advantage of taking corrective actions. I will test how the brain deals with incomplete information when constructing value estimates and more specifically whether (like perceptual decision-making) this fragmented information is combined according to Bayesian (optimal) integration scheme. I will also explore the r elationship between uncertainty and suboptimality in economic or financial choices, testing how noisy value estimates trigger inconsistency in value-based decisions. The ultimate goal of this research agenda will be to produce a coherent and mechanistic account of how we assign values and make choice in a mist of uncertainty.

title: Research IS Relevant to Rural Adolescents and their Educators.
description: "Education is the most powerful weapon you can use to change the world" (Nelson Mandela, 2003). We propose to actively engage rural adolescents in research findings relevant to their own health and wellbeing and excite them about research relevant to their life stage. This will be achieved through developing interactive teaching materials titled "Research IS Relevant" based on research conducted by the MRC/Wits Rural Public Health and Health Transitions Research Unit (Agincourt), South Africa, in a sub-district coveredby a health and socio-demographic surveillance system (HDSS). At workshops involving adolescents and educators, we will discuss results from relevant research already conducted to identify which health needs to include in the materials. These will be aligned with the curriculum of a compulsory school subject "Life Orientation". All Grade 9 Life Orientation educators and learners in the 27 high schools in the Agincourt sub-district will be targeted. Through "Research IS Relevant", adolescents will identify ways to use research results from their OWN communities to change their own, their family or their community's lifestyle choices. An iterative process of evaluation and development involving adolescents and stakeholders, including ateaching materials development consultant, will lead to a template for "Research IS Relevant" materials. This will be straightforward to update annually by the MRC/Wits-Agincourt Unit's LINC Office (responsible for community engagement), in order to target adolescents with up-to-date and relevant materials. This will be part of LINC's ongoing public engagement programme.

title: A cross-syndrome approach to atypical development: Modelling developmental trajectories in children with autism spectrum disorder, attention deficit and hyperactivity disorder and callous-unemotional traits.
description: The key goal of this proposal is to test whether observed overlap in symptoms of autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and callous-unemotional (CU) traits can result from both shared and distinct underlying developmental pathways. To test this hypothesis, I will compare infant social and attentional trajectories by applying advanced statistical methods to existing data from two longitudinal studies: the Wirral Child Health and Development Study (WCHADS) and the British Autism Study of Infant Siblings (BASIS), and newly collected experimental (eye-tracking) and questionnaire data. Study 1 tests the hypothesis that recognising emotional faces will be impaired in 6-year-olds with high ASD- and CU-traits, but infant precursors to social-affective impairment (e.g. face tracking) will differ across traits. Study 2 will test whether executive functions act as protective factors in ASD- and ADHD-traits, through interactions with the catechol-O- methyltr ansferase Val108/158Met polymorphism and behavioural habituation. The final study combines data from BASIS and WCHADS using integrative data analysis techniques in order to compare evidence for cumulative models, in which risk markers work additively to predict outcome, and cascading models, where risk factors interact over development. Characterising developmental origins, rather than just symptomatology, has important relevance for the long-term development of intervention strategies.

title: DSM-5 and the Future of Psychiatric Diagnosis.
description: I recently won funding from the Geneva-based Brocher Foundation to host a 2-day interdisciplinary symposium on the topic: 'DSM-5 and the Future of Psychiatric Diagnosis'. The symposium's purpose is both to analyse the potential impact of the 5th Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (2013), the 'Psychiatric Bible', and form a network of 25 international scholars from multiple disciplines (history, anthropology, literature, philosophy, psychiatry) who will work together to explo re the history and future of psychiatric diagnosis and the nature of mental disorder. Brocher's symposia involve speakers, who present papers, and discussants, who read the pre-circulated papers and provide analysis. Discussants will also play a key role in publishing the proceedings, either co-writing papers in interdisciplinary pairs or providing discussion sections (talks are underway with Transcultural Psychiatry for a special issue). Brocher funds the attendance of speakers and helps with publication, but will not fund discussants. This grant would help the discussants attend the symposium and, given the vital role of discussants in shaping and writing the resulting papers, add considerably to the success of the symposium and future publications, as well as the cohesion of the international and interdisciplinary network that will emerge from it.

title: Two-day international, multidisciplinary workshop on migration and health - particularly mental health - in historical and contemporary contexts, to be held at the University of Aberdeen, April 2014.
description: The application is for support towards the costs of a two-day workshop, to be held at the University of Aberdeen from 10-11 April 2014. The primary theme of the workshop is Migration and Mental Health and it will explore in greater depth issues that were raised at a panel session on migration which was held during the annual Association for Medical Humanities conference in Aberdeen in July 2013. It will also build, more specifically, on a two-day symposium to be held in Halifax, Nova Scotia, in November 2013. The Canadian event, which is being co-organised by the applicant under the auspices of Saint Mary's University, Halifax, and the Gorsebrook Research Institute for Atlantic Canada Studies, is entitled Medicine and Migration: historical & contemporary dimensions. Canadian speakers will be joined by the applicant and another speaker from the UK. Aberdeen University is at the forefront of Medical Humanities in Scotland and the workshop will strengthen that profile. The applicant is e ngaged in collaborative interdisciplinary work with colleagues in Aberdeen, elsewhere in Scotland, the UK, and overseas. The workshop, which is expected to attract approximately 25 participants, will enhance and expand these networks and highlight a marginalised area of study.

title: Scoping London County Council and its Asylums, c.1888-c.1920.
description: The aim of this funding bid is to undertake significant archival research relating to London County Council (LCC) and its Asylums Committee. The LCC assumed responsibility for the Middlesex and Surrey County Asylums following the introduction of the Local Government Act in 1888. In the 1890s and 1900s it built new large institutions at Epsom in a bid to manage demand from the capital for more accommodation for the insane. Despite being the country's foremost provider of institutional provision, both the LCC and its impact on mental health policy have been largely overlooked by historians. Given London's standing on the national and international stage this is an oversight and this project allows an opportunity to consider the complex social and political issues at play in LCC's attempts to manage the capital's 'madness'. The main focus of research in the funding period will be in the London Metropolitan Archives but will include time at both the Surrey History Centre and the Wellcome L ibrary. The project will build on previous archival research and peer reviewed publications completed by the applicant and will lead to new published outputs with a view to a large scale monograph.

title: Gathering Intelligence: the life and work of Professor Sir Godfrey Thomson.
description: The Papers of Sir Godfrey Thomson are currently being catalogued as part of the Wellcome Trust-funded project, 'Documenting the Understanding of Human Intelligence: cataloguing and preserving the papers of Professor Sir Godfrey Thomson' (099432/Z/12/Z). A seminar is planned to communicate the outcomes of the project to the wider academic and archives communities, and to encourage and maintain growing interest in Thomson and his work. The programme of this seminar will be varied, exploring T homson's work in Psychology (especially cognitive testing), Statistics, Education, and Eugenics, with academic speakers from each field. It will also discuss current scientific research facilitated through data sets left from Thomson's work. There will be a presentation on the complexities involved in interpreting and cataloguing the collection itself. Undergraduate and postgraduate students with interests in these fields will be encouraged to attend through bursaries, which will provide tra vel and accommodation The current project budget has allocated 500 for the seminar. However, with bursaries, publicity material, and catering the cost will rise to 5500.

title: Developing indicators for objective well-being in the context of the European Health Policy 2020.
description: The purpose of this grant is to enable the World Health Organization Regional Office for Europe to organize an international meeting involving the Wellcome Trust and bringing together scientists from many sectors outside health to advise the Organization on the on indicators to measure objective and subjective well-being at population level. This is innovative new public health work whose results will have global relevance. The results of this meeting will firstly feed directly into the decision making process of the Regional Committee for Europe and its 53 Member States and determine the monitoring of the newly adopted Health 2020 Policy of the European Region. On the global level, the result of this meeting will feed into the Global Monitoring Framework on Non-communicable diseases. The staff member responsible for follow-up of this meeting will be a scientist seconded from the Wellcome Trust to WHO Europe.

title: Encountering R.D. Laing's Archive: Mental Health, Care and Creativity.
description: 2014 marks an exceptionally significant year in the history of mental health in Glasgow, being the bicentenary of institutional care, and this conference seeks to open up conversations about these issues through the lens of one of Glasgow's most famous psychiatrists, R.D. Laing. These events aim to bring together a number of individuals from across different academic disciplines, professions and communities to share reflections on the changing nature of institutional care. Using the 'Laing Archi ve' as a pivot this event seeks to promote the collections and to set future agendas for working with the 'archive'. A number of interconnecting events at the University of Glasgow are proposed. The first, held in the Special Collections, seeks to bring together a number of participants from across different backgrounds (artists, writers, service users, therapists) to explore materials held in the Laing collection and to generate creative output. The second will bring together leading academi cs from across institutional backgrounds to share, reflect and generate new discussions about mental health care in Scotland and beyond. Finally, the 1972 US Tour Showreel by Peter Robinson will be screened in order to generate further conversations about mental health, the arts and institutional landscapes.

title: Spirituality and Healthcare Research Conference: Implications for Palliative Settings.
description: Issue and invitation to Professor Koenig, a world renowned expert in spiritual healthcare and religion to deliver in Ireland for the first time a seminar exploring spirituality in healthcare and the integration of research into patient care, with particular focus on ageing, mental health and palliative care issues to include Defining the terms religion, spirituality, religion and secular humanism and their use in research and clinical settings Considering how spirituality is currently bein g used in research and clinical practice Appraising the research on religion and mental disorders, positive emotions, health behaviours, physical health outcomes, social health and discuss its application to clinical practice Discussing how to address spiritual needs in caring for patients Discussing chaplains and other health professionals role in spiritual care Providing a unique opportunity for delegates to network, share experiences and gain new insights into spiritual healthcare and research. The target audience includes All health and social care professionals (such as doctors, nurses, social workers, therapists, counsellors, psychologists, chaplains, community clergy), researchers and academics in Ireland with interest in spiritual care and healthcare, particularly in relation to mental health, ageing, and care of the dying

title: Alternative Psychiatric Narratives: a 1.5 day conference.
description: We propose a 1.5 day conference at Birkbeck in London for postgraduate and early career researchers to explore the theme of alternative psychiatric narratives. This aims to investigate new approaches to histories and experiences of psychiatry in its broadest sense, by considering overlooked stories, new sources and approaches, and the very question of narrative in psychiatry itself. We anticipate that researchers across the humanities and social sciences will engage with the topic, that the narratives under consideration will include a range of styles and media, and that there will be challenges to the constructions and uses of psychiatric narratives themselves. We will also welcome discussions of psychiatric encounters occurring outside formal psychiatric spaces, and the engagement of those who fall outside the doctor-patient dyad, such as non-medical staff and activists. The event will include a keynote speech given by an established academic, Dr Mathew Thomson, followed by presentations from junior scholars and a networking reception in the evening. If funding allows, this traditional conference format will be enhanced by a concluding roundtable discussion of invited participants and a final event open to the public.

title: Unseen City: Travelling Psychoanalysis and the Urban Poor.
description: Unseen City: Travelling Psychoanalysis and the Urban Poor examines the institution of psychoanalysis and its underdeveloped relationship with race and urban poverty, as seen in the context of Mumbai, London, and New York. The outcome will be a monograph, which draws on a range of literature, cinema, art, and image archives to explore the following: prevalent psychoanalytic practices in global cities; state policy on poverty and mental disease (and viable alternatives); the dialogue between cultu ral and social discourses and medical initiatives on poverty. This multidisciplinary project requires knowledge-sharing. I will use the grant money to conduct scoping exercises and field research in India in July-August 2014: 1. I will conduct interviews at a) The Association of the Mentally Challenged and b) The All India Institute of Mental Health (current NIMHANS), based in Bangalore. Both run mental health clinics for the poor. 2. I will interview members of the Indian Psychoan alytical Society, Kolkata, and also conduct interviews with Professors Santanu Biswas and Josodhara Bagchi, who work in social welfare collectives. 3. I will gather video and audio data in the Dharavi slum of Mumbai. I will be collaborating with URBZ, an urban research and action collective in Mumbai, for this work.

title: 'Early Modern Women, Religion, and the Body' international conference: 22-23 July 2014, Loughborough University.
description: This two-day international conference on 'Early Modern Women, Religion, and the Body' will take place on 22-23 July 2014 at Loughborough University. Funding is needed to cover the travel and accommodation costs of one of the plenary speakers, Professor Mary Fissell (Institute for the History of Medicine, Johns Hopkins), who will be flying in from the United States. The conference will bring together academics (established, early-career, and postgraduates) working on the histories of medical and religious thinking from the period 1500-1780, and discuss the importance of considering both of these contexts in when seeking to understand spiritual and bodily health and wellbeing in the early-modern period. We have accepted 48 proposals from delegates all over the world (including the US, Canada, Australia, Israel, Italy, Germany, Spain, Ireland, and the UK), with three plenary sessions, and one public lecture by popular historian Alison Weir. Additional funds are sought to provide six fee-w aiver bursaries for postgraduate delegates, and to produce leaflets publicising the conference and its aims to those attending the public lecture by Alison Weir.

title: A conference on Galen s newly discovered Peri alupias (Avoiding Distress): ancient psychology and self-therapy in the Roman Empire.
description: This conference will bring together for the first time in the UK a distinguished panel of speakers to illuminate the multiple facets of the Peri alupias (Avoiding Distress), a medical work written by the great Galen of Pergamum (129-216AD), and only recently discovered in a Greek manuscript. The treatise is essentially a remarkable attempt to address the difficult problem of managing grief and anxiety at the turn of the 3rd c. AD by the best physician of antiquity. It also offers a wealth of evi dence on Galens life, work, thought and entourage, on Roman history, and on medical and cultural history more broadly. The aim of the proposed conference is, by gathering scholars of complementary areas, to explore key aspects of this exciting new text. The speakers will consider Galens approach to psychotherapy, his self- portrait, his ethics, the medical books and resources which he tells us he lost in a great fire in 192 AD, and the way he plays with generic, rhetorical and linguistic constrai nts to explore the fundamental problem of controlling emotion and grief. Finally, our special guest and discoverer of the lost treatise, Antoine Pietrobelli, will discuss the reception of the text in Arabic medical-philosophical literature.

title: Vertigo in the City: Conversations between the Sciences, Arts and Humanities.
description: What is vertigo? And how does it relate to the city? While in medical terms vertigo is understood as a symptom of balance system disorders, in the arts and humanities the word is used, far more loosely, to evoke various forms of disorientation and dizziness that are often associated with modern urban life. Today, as over half of the human population lives in cities, we still largely ignore the full impact of increasing heights, density, and speed on our experience of space. The proposed symposiu m will be the first event to bring together academics and practitioners from the sciences, arts, and humanities to discuss the socio-cultural as well as the psycho-physiological aspects of vertigo with a specific focus on the urban environment. By fostering knowledge sharing and discussion, the event aims to open up new perspectives on this topic while also addressing its implications in terms of public wellbeing. Prior to the symposium, the research team will carry out a scoping mission that wi ll include a series of meetings and field trips, and the design of a dedicated website. The proposed activity is intended to prepare the ground for a larger research project with an emphasis on public engagement activities.

title: Opening Locked Sources in the History of Radical Psychiatry: Conserving, Digitising, and Cataloguing 148 Institute of Phenomenological Studies raw reel-to-reel recordings
description: This project aims to preserve, digitise, catalogue, and make available a unique collection of reel to reel tapes, in order to make a significant contribution to the research resources available for an influential group of late 20th century radical psychiatrists, the pivotal Dialectics of Liberation Congress they organised, and a key moment of global political and intellectualchange. The recordings will be processed by a highly experienced audio engineer and audio archivist, who has been identified, using appropriate equipment and to the highest standards. On initial assessment the master recordings are in goodcondition. Evidence of mold or oxide shedding throughout the collection will be treated professionally to ensure the best preservation of the tapes, and torecover all the information they contain. The tapes will be catalogued and stored in pH neutral/lignin-free archive boxes. The digital files will be stored on a dedicated external hard drive, as well as in the existing Archive digital storage system with its multiple automated back-up provision.

title: An Exploratory Pilot Study to Map the working practices and experiences of Internet based Sex Workers in the UK.
description: This small research project will act as an exploratory pilot study to investigate the experiences and working practices of sex workers who operate through the Internet. We have little knowledge of their experiences of sex working, how it differs from working in a brothel or on the street, and moreso how they experience crimes, particularly violence. We will conduct a survey, hosted through Bristol Online Surveys, to the individual membership of the National Ugly Mugs, who have signed up to recei ve information about health, safety and wellbeing issues as sex workers. The pilot study will aim to capture some core demographic information, as well as map types of sex work, and ask about issues such as stigma, isolation, safety, contact with health services and crimes experienced. The survey will be analysed to expose core data about this population from which a larger mixed methods study can be designed. We will present a written report, a briefing for specialist sex work health projects, and hold a Learning Event symposium where practitioners are brought together who work directly with sex workers, as well as national policing representatives who work with the NUM scheme.

title: WHO International meeting on the cultural determinants of well-being - PART 1 (Project Costs)
description: This application will help to part fund an innovative, international meeting at the WHO Regional Office for Europe in Copenhagen. The meeting will provide a unique opportunity for medical humanities researchers to contribute insightsand expertise to WHO's work on well-being in the context of the new European policy, Health 2020. The outputs of the meeting will have a clear pathway for impact on policy, via a short promotional film as well as via reporting outputs that will be circulated to member states. Lessons learned from the meeting will also be included in WHO/EURO's flagship publication, the EuropeanHealth Report (to be prepared in 2015). We anticipate that this meeting will kick off a more wide-ranging initiative in the medical humanities at WHO, under the banner of Cultural Determinants of Health (CDH). The meeting intends to examine the importance of cultural contexts when measuring well- being, in order to provide country-level guidance for governments on implementing the WHO recommended well-being indicators. In the past, WHO's efforts in this regard have looked primarily to statisticians and social scientists. However, insights from the medical humanities are vitalif culture variation is to be taken seriously. Therefore, this meeting will bring together a wide range of intersectoral and interdisciplinary experts whose work focusses on the cultural determinants of well-being.
