A standard way to do this is using high-throughput microscopy, which is a rich source of quantitative data, with thousands of pixel values measured for every cell. The main problem in making use of this large-scale information is extracting meaningful features. There are many existing software packages that are able to generate numbers from each cell image, ranging from area and shape characteristics to values for Zernike features and Gabor filters, but these hundreds of numbers rarely correspond directly to a biologically interpretable signal. Alternatively, a desired biological characteristic can be modelled and quantified from the images, but this requires extensive feature engineering. A promising alternative to the abundant local and scarce broad global image features is to extract them from deep neural networks. These models are able to make use of large-scale data to learn spatial correlations that are not easily inferred from standard parametric models. In the last years, this class of methods has outperformed alternatives on most image processing tasks, ranging from object detection to semantic embedding. I will explore a collaboration available to me with AstraZeneca, on using image analysis to optimise their virtual screening process. Once a potential drug target or mode of action for a disease is identified, assays are designed, and massively parallel high-throughput drug screens are conducted to identify compounds that successfully interfere with this drug target and achieve a positive assay result. I aim to detect automatically and at an early stage the outcome of a compound for a given trial from an intermediate image that is taken of the assay, reducing the number of false positive results that are carried forward for expensive and time-consuming counter screens, and potentially even obviating the need for them. Related work has shown it is possible to characterise complex cellular phenotypes [1] using deep learning [2], and has also discussed its use in virtual screens [3]. Linking genetic variation to cellular phenotypes The methods established in Aim 1 allow extracting interesting features from many unrelated individuals in the HIPSCI [4] project. The next natural problem is linking genetic variation in them to these features after genotyping and identifying causal mutations, as well as sharing of the underlying mechanisms via colocalization approaches. I am interested in genetically linking cellular traits, and methods that have been developed for finding causal SNP configurations after genotyping. I intend to use stochastic search algorithms as proposed by Brenner et al [5] to find causal configurations on large candidate gene-set ranges. I’m interested in how these methods can be optimised for this use case where I anticipate heritability to be higher. Furthermore, I’m interested in using colocalization methods [6] to investigate the existence of shared genetic basis between phenotypes. In my rotation report, I implemented modern day techniques which cross-multiply independently generated posteriors, and I will look to optimise these techniques for cellular traits. I am also interested in extending these further to detect whether traits in question share a genetic basis only partially. Here I will be interacting with Oliver Stegle and his group which has extensive expertise in statistical genetics. In addition, conducting CRISPR screens with Leopold Parts’ group will allow me to investigate the cellular effects of gene knockouts. Finally, collaborating with drug companies like AstraZeneca will give me the opportunity to investigate the cellular consequences of administering drug compounds. Integrative methods to identify drug targets Given the ability to extract useful cellular features from images, and to model their sources of variability, it is possible to attack the central problem in cell biology - forming a mechanistic chain from genotype to high-level phenotypes via cellular traits. I aim to integrate disease GWAS summary statistics, along with intermediary causal layers like eQTL studies, to look for shared cellular trait QTLs and understand disease pathways at a more granular level. I want to be able to decipher whether genetic mutations impact diseases or traits directly, or whether they do so indirectly by impacting gene expression and other cellular traits. Recently published methods [9] have integrated GWAS summary data with eQTL studies and use mendelian randomisation to account for confounding non-genetic variables. In this way, variants can be better classified as causal, pleiotropic or linked. These questions are important to address in minimising false positive leads and optimising the interface between highlighting potential causal SNPs, and further investigation with functional knockouts, and I intend to extend these methods by incorporating cellular traits. In this way, I aim to build causal models to suggest drug targets. Since this work integrates many different data-layers, I’m interested in investigating whether they can be used as inputs in more complex models. Working as part of Open Targets, a collaboration between the Wellcome Trust Sanger Institute, the European Bioinformatics Institute, GlaxoSmithKline and Biogen, I will be able to collaborate between research and industry to work on the most pressing problems in drug development. Conclusion In conclusion, I’m interested making use of cellular microscopy images, a data types that is increasingly prevalent in understanding cellular systems. I intend to extract features from these images, model them, and link these models to genomic data to understand complex traits and aid drug discovery. I will use available data from HIPSCI, AstraZeneca, novel CRISPR knockout data as part of Leopold Parts’ group, and publically available omics data from Open Targets. This field is set to explode with the advent of high-throughput cellular screens and gene-editing and I look forward to developing the next-generation methods to intelligently handle the volume of data output.

title: Investigating the role of the psychiatric risk gene SETD1A in brain and behaviour
description: Many psychiatric disorders are, in part, heritable. Identification of specific genetic variants that increase risk for these disorders are providing valid leads to investigate their pathogenesis. Recent advances in exome sequencing methods have led to the discovery of risk genes that are highly penetrant for complex brain diseases. Members of the MRC Centre for Neuropsychiatric Genetics and Genomics in Cardiff were part of an international team that identified loss of function point mutations in SET domain 1a (SETD1A) as a highly damaging rare variant contributing to schizophrenia and other developmental disorders. SETD1A encodes an activating histone methyltransferase subunit that is widely expressed in several tissues. Currently, however, the specific brain functions of SETD1A remain unknown. In this project, we will; i) characterise brain expression of SETD1A during development, ii) examine gene expression patterns following SETD1A knockdown in vitro, iii) generate a Setd1aNestin-Cre/+ conditional heterozygous null mouse line (with reduced dosage confined to the brain), iv) conduct in vivo functional characterisation and cognitive phenotyping of this model, and v) investigate the neurobiological consequences of SETD1A knockdown. This work will provide novel insights into the pathogenic role of SETD1A loss of function, both at the molecular and behavioural level.

title: Molecular heterogeneity and functionality of human cortical interneurones in development and neuropsychiatric disorders
description: An imbalance of excitation-inhibition within the brain has been implicated in the aetiology of neurodevelopmental disorders, including attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Cortical interneurones represent a diverse class of inhibitory cells that share a common role of maintaining excitation- inhibition balance within the cerebral cortex. We aim to study how cortical interneurones derived from human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) and foetal medial ganglionic eminence develop in vitro. We will carry out single-cell transcriptome analysis to determine how gene expression changes during differentiation into distinct classes of cortical interneurones. This will allow an unique gene set to be determined for the different subtypes. From this candidate genes can be identified and tested for their ability to programme hESCs into particular interneurone classes. Finally, we will test the ability of enhancing inhibitory input in the cerebral cortex to rescue the ADHD-like behaviour of hGFAP-Cre Foxp1 knockout mice by transplanting cortical interneurone progenitors. The transplantation would take place at two different developmental stages, embryonic and adulthood, to determine if there is a restricted timeframe to rescue the mutant phenotype. If the behaviour was significantly improved this would provide evidence for cortical dysfunction driving ADHD-like phenotype, thereby leading to novel approaches for ADHD treatment.

title: Investigation of gene-gene interactions associated with schizophrenia in 22q11.2 deletion syndrome in human ES cells
description: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, which spans at least 48 genes, may account for as many as 1-2% of cases of schizophrenia, and so can be used as a starting point to potentially understand the causation of schizophrenia in general. Schizophrenia is a complex polygenic disorder with multiple genes working synergistically to confer risk. DGCR8, a gene deleted in 22q11.2DS, has been previously investigated using homozygous and heterozygous knockout hESCs that have been successfully differentiated into neural progenitor cells (NPCs). Firstly, using previous schizophrenia GWAS and exome data, epistatic gene-gene interactions will be identified between genes within the 22q11.2 deletion and with other CNVs or common variants (SNPs) outside of the deletion. Any candidate genes will be knocked out in DGCR8 KO NPCs by transducing with guide RNA CRISPR/Cas9 lentiviruses. NPCs and further differentiated neuronal cells generated will then be characterised using various ‘omic’ approaches and cell biology and function assays. Assessing the effect of additional gene losses in DGCR8 KO cell lines allows us to investigate the mechanisms by which these hemizygous gene deletions are resulting in neuropsychiatric phenotypes.

title: Liverpool, Cellular and Molecula Physiology.
description: 1\. Aims of the Project My hypothesis is that endogenous non-LTR retrotransposons (TEs) can be mobilised in the human genome, resulting in novel insertional mutations, linked deletions or translocations that can affect the progression of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) by acting as germline predisposition variants and/or somatic CNS de novo mutations. To test my hypothesis, I will use data generated by our group using Retrotransposon Capture Sequencing (RC-Seq) to map TE variation in the genome both in lymphocytes and CNS. I will determine if a) Increased or novel retrotransposition events occur in the motor neurons (MNs) of individuals with ALS which correlate with the neurodegeneration of these neurons. b) Specific germline insertions from analysis of lymphocytes are a predisposing factor for ALS I will focus on TE mobilisation on the X chromosome for reasons outlined in section 2. 2\. Previous work which has led to this proposal The incidence of ALS is 5 per 100,000 people and occurs more frequently in males than females. Familial ALS (FALS) accounts for 5-10 % of all ALS with several causative genes identified whilst Sporadic ALS (SALS) also has a strong genetic component [1]. The missing heritability in ALS could be accounted for by rarer variants with relatively large effect. However I propose a complementary explanation based on the mobilisation of endogenous mobile genetic elements, allowing them to ‘jump’ around the genome, in particular non-LTR retrotransposons resulting in both predisposition and de novo mutation that affects the progression of ALS. Their mobilisation is associated with neurodegeneration [2], ataxia telangiectasia [3], schizophrenia [4], ALS [5] and fronto-temporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) [5]. Furthermore one of the major endogenous modulators of TE mobilisation is the ALS risk gene, TDP-43 [5]. A further complication in GWAS analysis is often data for the X and Y chromosomes is delayed or not interpreted. This is due in part to the complexity of X inactivation in females [6] and therefore it is difficult to determine which allele would be functional and relevant for analysis. Therefore limited data is available on genetic risk factors for diseases which are associated with domains on the sex chromosomes. Indeed TEs have been implicated as a regulator of X inactivation [7]. I will utilise data generated by a technique termed retrotransposon capture sequencing (RC-Seq) to address TE involvement in ALS [8, 9]. RC-Seq allows us to enrich for TE insertions in the genome [8, 9]. I will focus analysis on the X chromosome. This study will complement ongoing GWAS data being performed on the X chromosome for ALS by a current collaborator of Professor Quinn on ALS, Ammar Al-Chalabi (KCL) [10, 11]. Any novel germline ALS associated TEs can be validated by targeted PCR in larger cohorts (1000s of individuals) with ALS if required via current collaborations with the KCL MND Care and Research Centre (MCRC). 3\. Approach and methods to be used 3.1. Validation of TE variation in ALS identified by RC-Seq analysis Our current RC-Seq data will identify TE insertions that are potentially associated with ALS. This will identify both germline and somatic variation. The number of individuals in this analysis is shown in Figure 1. Figure 1. The tissue selected for RC-Seq analysis Cohort Sporadic ALS patients Familial ALS patients Control ALS tissue/(no history of ALS) Tissue lymphocyte Lymphocyte DNA x7 Tissue MN ALS tissue x10 (Motor Cortex) ALS tissue x10 ALS tissue x5 Tissue Other Cerebellum; not involved in ALS x10 Cerebellum; not involved ALS x10 Cerebellum not involved ALS x5 Total RCSeq 27 20 10 This RC- Seq data from the cohort in Figure 1 is currently being analysed by Dr Savage (University of Liverpool and Professor Schumann, Germany). I will be given information on the potential TE variation found in the X chromosome. I will then validate by PCR that these insertions are present in the same DNA as used in the RC-Seq libraries. Both germ line retrotransposon insertions and somatic brain tissue-specific insertions detected by RC-Seq will be validated by PCR. In the case of suspected germline TE variation then lymphocyte DNA (100s-1000s) is available. Once validated these TE insertions will be converted into a BED (Brower Extensible data) files for analysis in the UCSC genome browser http://genome.ucsc.edu/. I will overlay my data on the UCSC browser with Encode data to compare site of TE insertion with various parameters that would be indicative of regulatory properties as part of my preliminary analysis to determine how such insertions could modify genome function. I am particularly interested in SVAs as they are known to be polymorphic, predictably in the Variable number tandem repeat domain of the SVA. I will address potential SVA variation in up to 3 novel SVAs. Independent of which TEs are eventually analysed for genetic variation, such polymorphism could be associated with the severity/progression of ALS as shown recently for Alu variation and cognition [12]. Further genetic variation may be helpful in section 3.2 in defining active alleles on the female genome. 3.2. Methylation status of the loci targeted by somatic insertion The original cohort DNA will be subject to an immunoprecipitation protocol to address DNA methylation. The female DNA may be the most interesting as it may be affected by X chromosome inactivation which could be reflected in differential methylation status which has been attributed to TEs [13] [14]. The precipitation will use the commercially available methylation binding domain protein (MBD) to enrich for methylation sites using a commercial antibody against MBD. This enriched DNA will be the substrate for PCR over the somatic insertions identifying the methylation status and to determine if the insertion has modified the methylation status of the allele/locus and secondly if allele specific methylation is observed in the female. 3.3. Integration of TE insertion with X chromosome GWAS I will be given a BED file of ALS GWAS on the X chromosome to overlay on the data that I have generated in section 3.1. I will determine if the GWAS SNPs are in linkage with the novel TEs I will have identified. This will prioritise TEs for further functional analysis as modifiers of gene expression based on their association to GWAS SNPs. 3.4. Analysis of the TAF1 SVA associated with XDP Individuals with X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism (XDP) have dystonia of varying severity and Parkinsonism. The mechanisms with give rise to the disease are unknown but there is an association with an SVA in the intron of the TAF1 gene on the X chromosome. I will use this association as a control for my analysis of TE and if appropriate SVAs found in the ALS analysis. To this end at the beginning of my PhD I will have access to a cohort of 85 individuals with XDP and known to have the ‘novel’ disease related SVA. I will use this to optimise my analysis of SVA PCR and potential polymorphic regions within the SVA that might be associated with XDP. I will also use this DNA to optimise my ChIP with MBD in SVAs that are found to be polymorphic in the female samples to address differential allele methylation. 3.5. Function of novel TE insertions The bioinformatic analysis of TE insertion (sections 3.1 & 2) with the association of GWAS data (section3.3) should highlight TEs with germline or somatic mutations potentially associated with ALS. We will address the function of these TEs to modulate gene function in the context of a reporter gene cassette. Depending on site of insertion, I will address the ability of the SVA to modulate gene expression in reporter gene constructs either directly as a conventional transcriptional regulator [15, 16] or as a modulator of RNA splicing [17]. 4\. Contingency Contingency plan in the absence of data from the ALS cohort would be to continue my initial analysis of the SVA in the TAF1 gene associated with XDP. This would involve genotyping of any variation in larger XDP cohorts, using not only PCR of the SVA but linked GWAS or other SNPs. Functional analysis (section 3.5) would correlate the ability of the SVA to modulate gene expression in reporter cassettes in cell line models. 5\. Timetable and milestones: GANTT chart

title: Genetics and urban environments in the development of autistic spectrum traits
description: Cities are now home to more than half the world�s population and this number is expected to increase dramatically over the century. Previous research has shown that urban living is detrimental to mental health conditions such as autistic spectrum traits, so it is now more important than ever for us to understand the environmental causes of this increased risk and how our genetic background exacerbates or mitigates environmental influences. My PhD will use complementary methods to triangulate on these causes with data from UK and international population cohorts. The methods I will use include structural equation modelling of geocoded twin and DNA data, and Mendelian randomisation analyses to investigate causal influences. The results of my project may inform policy and health service provision for the next generation of urban planners.

title: Oxofrd, Genomic Medicine and Statistics.
description: One goal in the post Genome Wide Association Study (GWAS) era lies in characterizing gene-environment (G-E) interactions. These interactions are typically defined as a joint effect of one or more genes with one or more environmental factors that cannot be explained by their marginal effects. It is thought that better characterization of these interactions could be utilized in several ways [1]. By allowing populations to be stratified into subsets based on their response to certain environments, it may allow more informed public health decisions. It may also provide an answer to the question of missing heritability [2]. More optimistically, it may lead to the discovery of novel genes that act in concert with either the environment or other genes to change disease risk, but have no demonstrable marginal effects themselves. To date there has some interest in testing for G-E interactions in animal models, for example looking at schizophrenia in mouse models [3-5], but there has been limited success in uncovering examples of G-E interactions in humans. This is partly due to the problem of exposure assessment [1]. The exposure intensity of many environmental factors (for example, the composition of harmful particles in air pollution) varies over time. Even if this is not the case, disease risk is still likely to be modified by temporal factors such as the age at exposure or duration of exposure. In short, outside of animal models it has historically proved difficult to obtain data that accurately summarizes the environment of a number of individuals over a lifetime. The release of data from the UK Biobank in 2016 changed this. The UK Biobank is a major collaborative research project with data on over 500,000 volunteers aged 40-69 from the UK. The project aims to provide a comprehensive and reliable quantification of the combined effects of lifestyle, environment, genes and other exposures on health outcomes [6]. The UK Biobank not only represents a 2-fold increase in the number of participants that have typically been involved in genomic studies, but it also contains one of the most comprehensive databases on environmental factors collected to date – including detailed work history, full body MRI, dietary questionnaire responses and medical history. This PhD will focus on developing scalable statistical methods to detect G-E interactions, using the UK BioBank as a model dataset. (b) Previous research done on this topic area within the Marchini Group includes an investigation into using Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) to estimate missing heritability [7]. This approach was tested on 46 yeast phenotypes, and found that over 70% of the total known missing heritability could be explained from common genetic variants. Using a technique known as Automatic Relevance Determination [8], this method can be adapted to act as a classifier to identify environmental & genetic covariates that are associated with the trait. Initial results suggest that this method is also able to detect non-linear associations. A rotation project implemented this approach in the statistical programming language [R] during the first year of the GMS programme. (c) Approach and Methods to be used This project will follow a Bayesian methodology in attempting to infer G-E interactions. We will first start by testing known models on the dataset, such as multivariate linear regression (in effect a null model) or a random effects model, before progressing on to fitting a model based on GPR. As the size of the dataset presents a significant computational challenge, the majority of this will be programmed in C++. (d) Contingency Plans We cannot guarantee that we will uncover novel G-E interactions in the UK Biobank dataset, although due to the size of the dataset we think the chance is high. If not, then these results will still be of great interest to the community. Simulation studies will also be used to assess the power of the methods under different conditions, which will inform study design. (e) Initial milestones for the project include: \- Developing expertise with the programming language C++ \- Gaining familiarity with the UK BioBank and collating a first test dataset. We have identified that the blood pressure phenotypes will be good candidates for testing due to their continuous nature, large number of known marginal genetic associations and likelihood of environment playing a role in the phenotypes. \- Gaining an understanding of mathematical derivation of possible methods. \- Extending knowledge of the literature. Beyond this, over the next twelve months we aim to have implemented several approaches, including a multivariate linear regression and a random effects model, on the UK BioBank in time for the transfer of status viva.

title: Women and HIV/AIDS in South Africa: Medicine, Art, Activism.
description: Following World AIDS Day 2015 we propose a public lecture and one-day symposium with two interdisciplinary panels; the first provides perspectives from experts in the arenas of policy, social psychology, anthropology and the history of medicine. The second focuses on memorialization and representation, featuring South African photojournalists and women's community art activists whose work will be shown in Birkbeck's Peltz Gallery. The event concludes in the evening, with a public keynote lec ture by Edwin Cameron, Justice of the Constitutional Court of South Africa, followed by a reception at the Peltz Gallery. The next day delegates will participate in a walkabout and discussion with participating artists and the curator Professor Annie E. Coombes in the Peltz exhibition, Positive Living: Art and AIDS in South Africa which features work from photo journalists, fine artists, youth print workshop initiatives (to promote safe sex) and community activists engaged today and during the height of AIDS denialism. Our hope is that this symposium will stimulate a more integrated approach to the challenges of HIV and act as an incentive to health professionals and policy makers to recognize the value of working collaboratively with artist-activists and historians of the pandemic.

title: Regulation of KIFC1 expression and centrosome clustering by deubiquitylases
description: KIFC1 (HSET) is a minus-end-directed kinesin whose depletion promotes multipolar mitosis in cancer cells carrying additional centrosomes. Centrosome amplification often occurs in breast and ovarian cancers where KIFC1 is also frequently overexpressed. While cancer cells usually overcome the presence of additional centrosomes by clustering them into two groups to form pseudo- bipolar spindles, they lose this ability in the absence of KIFC1. As multipolar mitosis is usually lethal, targeting KIFC1 may selectively kill cancer cells without affecting non-transformed cells. This exciting hypothesis currently lacks systematic validation. Here, the KIFC1 requirement for normal mitosis and survival will be addressed in a panel of cancer and non- transformed cell lines. Stability of proteins in cells may be regulated by a family of ~90 deubiquitylase (DUB) enzymes, which recently aroused interest as potential drug targets. Targeting a DUB that stabilizes KIFC1 would be predicted to promote KIFC1 degradation and multipolar mitosis. In this project we will identify DUBs that maintain cellular levels of KIFC1, then characterize the effect of their depletion and their mechanistic interaction with KIFC1. Lastly, we will assess the clinical relevance of our findings, by evaluating expression of KIFC1 and its regulatory DUBs in breast cancer patient tissues and performing clinicopathological correlations.

title: Social media and adolescent mental health: A preliminary qualitative exploration of the potential use of social media for promoting mental health and wellbeing among 12-18 year olds.
description: The World Health Organization recognised that there is no health without mental health (WHO, 2005). Despite this, research from many countries has demonstrated that there is a high level of unmet need for mental health (Schomerous & Angermeyer, 2008). This is particularly concerning for children and adolescents. It is well-known that mental health problems increase during mid-to-late adolescence (Burns et al., 2009). While it remains unclear why young people are reluctant to seek help, barriers have included stigma, trust of professionals, and concerns about the characteristics of the provider (Gulliver et al., 2010). In a contemporary digital society it is arguable that social media may be a way of providing information to adolescents and to promote help-seeking behaviour. However, despite the potential, research is only just starting to grapple with the possibilities. It is therefore important that we have a greater understanding of this by exploring adolescents views and engaging me ntal health professionals in the debate. By consulting with these two groups though focus groups and interviews we can gain a better understanding of how adolescents use social media and provide an analysis of the potential benefits and limitations for social media as a mental health promotion tool.

title: The Psy Disciplines and Secularization in Postwar Asia.
description: Four weeks' of exploratory archival and interview work in Tokyo, Kyoto, Osaka, and Tohoku, helping establish the basis for funding applications towards a new project: 'The Psy Disciplines and Secularization in Postwar Asia'. This is a case study-led analysis of the shifting relationships between psychiatric and psychotherapeutic discourses and practices, on the one hand, and those associated with religion and spirituality on the other, in postwar Japan and India. My proposed activity: 1. Exploring the archival and institutional basis for two potential project case studies in Japan, to complement my India case studies. 2. Consulting with colleagues and major figures connected with these two projects 3. Exploring the archival basis for a more general contextualized account of religion-psy dialogue in postwar Japan to complement these case studies: national media, government health policy documentation, journals published by Japanese psy organizations. Having published proof-of-concept articles and book chapters [Harding 2015b, 2015c], this exploratory work in Japan will be an important step towards making competitive applications for the full project. Relevant funding opportunities include: Wellcome Investigator Award, AHRC Fellowship, Leverhulme Research Project Grant, British Academy Mid-Career Fellowship, and Templeton project grant.

title: Strengthening South Africa's health system through integrating treatment for mental illness into chronic disease care (Project MIND)
description: Integrating mental health care into primary health care services could reduce the impact of both chronic communicable and non-communicable diseases (NCDs). Like many low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), South Africa (SA) is challenged with how to reduce the high prevalence and impact of communicable diseases and NCDs, including mental disorders for which there are limited services available. Mental disorders are important to address among patients with chronic diseases as these problems are associated with poor adherence to treatment, more rapid disease progression and treatment failure. As treatment failure increases the use of health services and consequently health service costs, chronic disease care in LMICs must be expanded to include mental health care. The integrated delivery of mental health services and chronic disease care has been shown to improve access to mental health care and the mental health of chronic disease patients. However in LMICs such as SA, integrating mental health care into chronic disease services has been delayed by a lack of knowledge of how to include mental health care in chronic disease services so that these services are acceptable to providers and patients and feasible to implement with few resources. The provision of integrated mental health and chronic disease services has also been delayed by questions about whether mental health services should be vertically integrated into chronic disease care (that is provided by dedicated staff who only provide mental health services) or horizontally integrated (that is provided by general health practitioners who also provide chronic disease care). The goal of this project is to answer these questions by assessing current capacity and barriers to integrating mental health services into chronic disease care and by comparing the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of a vertically integrated and horizontally integrated model of service integration among patients receiving treatment for HIV or diabetes and at risk for treatment failure in Cape Town, SA. Through this project we hope to identify a feasible, acceptable and effective model for integrating mental health services into chronic communicable and non-communicable disease care for patients that is applicable to other LMICs. Findings from this study are likely to be highly relevant for application in other LMICs given similarities between the burden of disease, treatment populations, and treatment systems in SA and other LMICs. The study will comprise two phases. In the first phase, we will conduct 69 in-depth interviews with a range of healthcare providers in HIV and diabetes services to assess barriers to integration and the feasibility and acceptability of our proposed models of service integration (Aim 1). Findings from this phase will be used to adapt our evidence-based mental health service package for optimal integration into chronic disease services. In phase two, a clustered randomised controlled trial will be conducted. We will select 24 HIV and 24 diabetes clinics to randomise to a vertically integrated arm, horizontally integrated arm, or treatment as usual (no integration). We will recruit 25 patients at risk for treatment failure from each of these clinics (total 1200 patients). After study enrollment, a baseline assessment will be completed by a fieldworker. Participants recruited from clinics randomised to either the vertically integrated or horizontally integrated arm will then receive their intervention sessions. All participants, irrespective of their intervention arm, will be tracked for 6- and 12-month follow-up interviews. At these interviews, fieldworkers blinded to their intervention arm will re-administer the baseline assessment and biological specimens will be collected to assess for chronic disease outcomes. Findings from this phase will be used to evaluate the relative effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of our proposed models of service integration.

title: Synaptic and Neuronal Autoantibodies in Psychosis (SNAP): clinical significance, neuroimaging correlates, infective/immune risk factors.
description: Anti-neuronal surface autoantibodies (ANSAs) such as antibodies to the NMDA receptor can cause encephalopathies that feature psychosis alongside neurological symptoms. ANSAs may also cause a purely psychiatric phenotype that is a phenocopy of first episode psychosis (FEP). Moreover, ANSA prevalence in FEP cohorts is between 5-10%, suggesting they might underlie a significant proportion of FEP. These findings have however often been derived from relatively small or heterogenous samples, and the c linical significance of ANSA-positivity in psychosis remains uncertain. I will address this by assessing the prevalence of multiple ANSAs in large samples of FEP patients and individuals at ultra-high risk (UHR) for psychosis. I will examine how ANSA status relates to i) presenting symptomatology; ii) the main clinical outcomes in these groups: onset of psychosis in UHR subjects and response to treatment in FEP; iii) neuroimaging measures of brain structure and chemistry. In order to investiga te a neurodevelopmental model of autoimmunity in psychosis, markers of previous infection with neurotropic viral/other organisms will be measured, along with measures of blood-brain barrier dysfunction. Finally, I will assess the utility of using these autoimmune markers as a means of stratifying patients in the early phase of psychosis according to future clinical outcomes.

title: An investigation into the neurocomputational role of brain oscillations in human motor control for health and disease.
description: The role of brain oscillations in health and disease remains undetermined. I aim to understand how oscillations influence the human motor system, contribute to Parkinson's disease (PD) and can be modulated for therapeutic effect using novel adaptive deep brain stimulation (DBS) techniques. Beta oscillations (12-30Hz) have been proposed to carry movement-relevant information in health and be abnormal in PD. Their precise function however is unknown. I will investigate this by examining the spe cific role of beta oscillations during action selection and execution using high precision magnetoencephalography (MEG) in healthy subjects and electrocorticography (ECoG) in PD. Next, I will causally test these relationships using a technique I have developed that can selectively cancel beta through the precise temporal delivery of DBS. Finally, I will test prolonged disruption of beta in PD to determine how dysfunction in action selection/execution mediates motor symptoms and whether re-tuning the beta network can lead to long-lasting improvements in motor function by reducing excessive cortico-subcortical connectivity. This will validate a novel method for investigating oscillatory neural networks using subcortical stimulation but additionally advance a new principled neurostimulation approach to disease that could be applied to understand and treat a range of neuropsychiatric disorders.

title: Multicenter RCT to evaluate the clinical and costeffectiveness of a culturally adapted therapy (C-MAP) in patients with a history of self-harm
description: Design: A multicenter Randomised Control Trial to compare Treatment As Usual (TAU) plus the Culturally adapted Manual Assisted Psychological therapy (C-MAP) with TAU in patients with a recent history of self-harm.There is a built in 12 months internal pilot phase with clear stop/go criteria to prove viability to proceed to a full trial across all the study sites. Setting: Participants will be recruited from general practices, emergency departments and medical wards of participating hospitals. Health Technologies being assessed: A culturally adapted brief psychological intervention, based on the principles of Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT). The intervention has 6 sessions, approximately 50 minutes each, and its feasibility has previously been established. Sample Size: This trial will use repetition of self-harm as its primary outcome measure because it is a strong predictor of completed suicide. Brown et al (2005) saw a reduction from 41.6% to 24.1% in the rate of repetition of self-harm over an 18 month period. The sample size calculation assumes an event rate of 27.7% in the control arm and 16.1% in the talking therapy (C-MAP) arm of the study, an ICC of 0.05 and a 75% follow-up rate. Under the these assumptions a sample of 624 randomised patients will be required for a cluster adjusted test of proportions to have 80% power to detect this difference assuming a 5% significance level. Measurement: The statistical analysis of the primary outcome measure repetition of self-harm episode and binary secondary outcome measures will be based on a cluster adjusted test of proportions. Economic analysis will estimate costs of primary, secondary/tertiary health care use, Disability Adjusted Life Years (DALYs) and quality adjusted life years (QALYs). Qualitative methods will explore patient and professional experiences. We will use an established approach in order to understand what factors block and facilitate successful delivery of the programme.

title: The development of neuronal circuits controlling sleep/wake behaviour in zebrafish models of autism.
description: The main goal of the proposed research is to understand how the development of hypothalamic neuronal circuits that control complex behaviours such as sleep is disturbed in zebrafish models of autism. For this purpose I will harness a combination of powerful genetic tools available in zebrafish, cutting edge neuroimaging techniques and high-throughput behavioural analysis. The Rihel lab, in collaboration with the Giraldez labs at Yale, has identified diverse sleep/wake phenotypes in zebrafis h mutants harbouring mutations in genes associated with autism. I will test the hypothesis that these sleep phenotypes are due to the altered development and functionality of hypothalamic sleep circuits. I will examine the specification, patterning and connectivity of sleep relevant neuron population located in the hypothalamus, basal forebrain and brain stem using in situ hybridisation, immunostaining and transgenic zebrafish lines. Furthermore, I will image and compare the dynamic activity of developing zebrafish brains of wild-type and mutant larvae to determine the functional integrity of sleep circuits. Differentially active neurons will then be laser-ablated or optogentically/pharmacologically manipulated to directly test their specific sleep/wake circuit function and their contribution to the autism sleep phenotype.

title: A genetic study examining sex differences in the prevalence of ADHD and other neurodevelopmental disorders.
description: Neurodevelopmental disorders, such as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), autism spectrum disorder and developmental delay, are highly heritable and more commonly diagnosed in males than females. The reasons for this difference in prevalence are unknown. Several recent family and genetic studies suggest that females may require a higher burden of genetic risk factors to manifest these problems. However, there is conflicting evidence, sample sizes of genetic studies have been small a nd alternative hypotheses need to be considered. The primary hypothesis of this proposal is that females require a more extreme loading of genetic risks than males to manifest neurodevelopmental problems. This hypothesis will be tested in collaboration with the world's largest clinical ADHD genetics consortium, as well as with an internationally-leading genetic epidemiology research group, who will provide access to a large genotyped population twin sample. A related hypothesis, that the geneti c architecture of ADHD differs by gender, will be tested in the clinical ADHD dataset. A third hypothesis will be tested in the population sample; this will be to determine whether females at increased genetic risk for ADHD are more likely than at-risk males to show a variable phenotype manifestation beyond neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: Understanding variations in self-harm rates between deprived areas in London.
description: This project investigates the spatial epidemiology of self-harm in a diverse and deprived urban setting, exploring reasons for differences to the relationship with deprivation seen in national data. It aims to: (1) Map incidence rate ratios (IRRs) for self-harm presentations to A&E, controlling for individual risk factors, and compare them to overall A&E use and long term limiting illness prevalence. IRRs calculated by Poisson regression, smoothed with Bayesian methods, using data from ele ctronic health records for four London Boroughs, with individuals mapped to lower super output areas (LSOAs). (2) Identify area-level characteristics associated with high and low levels of resilience to the effects of deprivation on self-harm. Areas of varying resilience identified using spatial clustering analysis. Exploratory case studies, using focus groups and interviews, adding to and refining hypotheses in the literature explaining area-level health resilience. Testing of hypotheses u sing routinely available data for all the LSOAs in the study area. (3) Develop a typology of areas based on characteristics related to self-harm identified in (2) that identifies areas with differing rates of self-harm and validate its utility. Typology generated using k-means cluster analysis and validated using data from four different London Boroughs.

title: Living with Autism Second extension
description: Living with autism: development of a DIPEx (personal experiences of health and illness) website Autism spectrum disorders are of particular concern to parents and professionals because of difficulties recognising the problem, the spectrum of disorders involved, and the media coverage concerning their possible association with immunisations. To present a balanced picture this project proposes to establish and market test a web resource, as part of the award winning DIPEx project www.dipex.org We will collect and analyse narrative video and audio tape recorded interviews with parents of children with autism spectrum disorders (ASD) and from a range of young people with ASD and Asperger's syndrome. These interviews will be with people throughout the UK from a broad range of ages, social and cultural backgrounds, and covering experiences of different levels of disability, support, educational provision and attainment. The interviews will be analysed, and supplemented with evidence based information about the conditions, their management and the available treatments. Like other DIPEx health and illness modules, the web site on ASD will include approximately 250 video and audio clips, 25-30 thematic summaries of issues, questions most important to the respondents and links to other information, resources and support groups. Some of the young adults with ASD and Asperger's will be invited to be trained and supported to make a short video diary of their everyday lives and the problems encountered. The website will provide support and information for those concerned that their children might have the condition, families who have children with the condition, and will also provide an invaluable training resource for professionals.

title: The melanopsin signalling pathway in ocular, circadian and sleep physiology: mechanisms to clinical application.
description: Our broad vision is to: Provide a detailed understanding of how melanopsin- based photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (pRGCs) encode and signal light information for the regulation of ocular, circadian and sleep physiology and to translate this knowledge into clinical and public understanding for the improvement of health. A seven-year programme of work is summarised in Figure 1. These aims align very closely with two of the Wellcome Trusts major challenges: (i) Understanding the brain; (ii ) Maximising the health benefits of genetics and genomics. Aim 1: Define the impact of ocular disease on human sleep/wake timing and mood. Despite the critical importance of the eye in regulating human circadian rhythms, sleep, alertness and mood [1], these critical behaviours are rarely addressed in clinical ophthalmology and specific guidelines relating to the disruption of these faculties in ocular disease are entirely lacking. To redress this omission, a Wellcome Trust Enhancement Aw ard allowed us to initiate such a study in January 2013. We have established the recruitment protocols and developed the infrastructure for both primary [2] and advanced [3] phenotyping of sleep and circadian abnormalities across a broad range of ocular diseases. As of June 2014 we have the following patient numbers recruited into the study: Cataract (n=961); Glaucoma (n=191); AMD (n=326); Diabetes II (n=446); Anophthalmia (n=12); RP (n=46). The results from the continuation of these studies wil l permit us to: -Build a comprehensive database linking specific ocular diseases, and disease states, to sleep and mood problems. -Establish which interventions are the most effective in improving these abnormal sleep states (see Aim 6). -Develop national evidence-based guidelines for clinical ophthalmology. We stress, disrupted sleep is closely linked to the added susceptibility of a range of co-morbid pathologies, including cognitive decline, depression, attentional failures, metabo lic and immune problems, and heart disease [4]. Thus ocular disease not only results in visual dysfunction but has the potential to inflict multiple additional pathologies, all of which can lead to major deficits in health and quality of life. Aim 2: Address the role of melanopsin in ocular light protection. The eye has several mechanisms to protect itself from light damage [5; 6], but the photopigment systems that activate these responses remain poorly defined. We reasoned that OPN4 may play an important role. Microarray studies were undertaken on the retinae of mice either lacking melanopsin (Opn4-/-) or wild-type controls (Opn4+/+) following light exposure. Multiple genes that normally protect the retina from light damage were highly up regulated in Opn4+/+ mice but this response was absent in Opn4-/- mice. Building upon these striking findings we will address: -Are Opn4-/- animals more susceptible to light-induced retinal damage? Following different light treatments the e ye/retina of Opn4-/- mice will be examined histologically and using TUNEL staining to detect DNA fragmentation and other markers of light- induced damage. -How is OPN4 mediating this protective effect? Light mediates an increase in retinal dopamine, which may or may not be mediated by OPN4 [7; 8]. We

title: A Novel Small Molecule-Based Therapy for Schizophrenia.
description: Schizophrenia is one of the most costly mental disorders in terms of human suffering and societal expenditure. A significant body of preclinical and clinical literature indicates that activation of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors holds tremendous promise for the treatment of the disease. Numerous pharmaceutical companies have made efforts at developing muscarinic agonists but none of these programs has advanced to market. The problem companies encountered was that the compounds that activate d the M1 and M4 receptor subtypes in the central nervous system (CNS), which mediate agonists therapeutic effect, also activate the M2 and M3 receptor subtypes in the periphery, which produce unacceptable side effects. Karuna is pioneering a novel approach that combines the most promising known muscarnic agonist (xanomeline), which has human proof-of-concept data in schizophrenia and Alzheimer's psychosis, with a generic, peripherally restricted muscarnic antagonist (trospium chloride) to decrea se xanomeline's side effects. Like other muscarinic programs, xanomeline was discontinued by the originator despite promising efficacy due to unacceptable side effects. Karuna has licensed xanomeline and has designated the combination of the agonist and antagonist KP7634. In this study, Karuna aims to determine whether KP7634 combination therapy has a superior safety profile to xanomeline alone.

title: Exploring the neurocomputational mechanisms of adaptive and pathological anxiety.
description: At present the majority of people with anxiety fail to respond to their first treatment. Refining our understanding of the mechanisms underpinning anxiety, as well as the process by which adaptive anxiety becomes maladaptive is critical in order to improve diagnosis and treatment outcomes. To this end, the objective for this collaborative doctoral research project between UCL and the NIMH is to investigate the neurocomputational basis of adaptive and pathological anxiety. Specifically, what are the decision-making variables involved in adaptive and pathological anxiety and what are the underlying computations in the neural level?

title: Beyond Diagnosis? Novelty, Need and the Normative in Twenty-First Century Psychiatry.
description: Psychiatric research is today being transformed by new strategic funding initiatives (e.g. from the Wellcome Trust and the US National Institute of Mental Health). Some of these urge scientists to go beyond diagnosis in investigations of mental illness, and move away from diagnostic texts like the World Health Organization's ICD and the controversial US DSM-5. Many studies instead seek to contribute to new classifications of mental disorders, based on biology, and which could enhance innovation in drug discovery. This University Award project seeks to understand the rationales underlying these strategic (and contested) initiatives, their impact on laboratory research, and their effects on how psychiatrists understand and treat their patients. It uses qualitative methods to do so. Broader questions can then be investigated throughout the Award: about the role of science in generating disease constructs; the place of diagnosis in research and practice; the relationships between the labor atory and the clinic; and the ways in which ascriptions of novelty, need and the normative come to shape, direct and propel biomedicine. The project draws on and contributes significantly to STS and medical sociology concepts, generating findings of relevance and import to a range of audiences within and beyond academia.

title: Chronic Disease in Sub-Saharan Africa: a critical history of an 'epidemiological transition'.
description: According to the WHO, Africa is the latest region of the world to be on the cusp of an epidemic of chronic disease, with rising rates of mortality and morbidity from cardiovascular disease, stroke, diabetes, chronic hepatic and renal diseases as well as cancer, mental illness and HIV/AIDS (now widely viewed as a chronic condition). It is projected that by 2015, a quarter of all deaths on the African continent will be caused by such diseases and their concurrence with infectious diseases. High-le vel meetings have produced a plethora of policy documents directed at the very significant challenges that this apparent epidemiological shift poses for already fragile health systems on the continent. A variant of modernisation theory, the historical framework of the epidemiological transition has been widely criticised, but its broad parameters remain at the heart of current policy-making. Accumulating evidence from different regions of Africa, as well as comparative work on India, China, Lati n America and the historical experience of Europe, suggest that this linear model of change may need more radical re-thinking. Recognising the real importance of these issues, this project has two central goals. Firstly, it will take a step back and ask some critical questions about the definitions and measurements of 'chronic' and 'non-communicable' diseases and examine the evidence for their longer history in sub-Saharan Africa. Secondly, through a set of case studies it will provide much-need ed in-depth research on the current situation in sub-Saharan Africa, paying particular attention to 'co- morbidities'.

title: Managing Medicine and Species: Biotherapy and the Ecological Vision of Health and Wellbeing.
description: This project will produce the first rigorous account of the multiple contributions that nonhuman forms of life make to human health and wellbeing in medicine and society. It explores how, why and to what consequence nonhuman life contributes to human clinical medicine, health and wellbeing outside the biomedical laboratory. Research provides historical context to recent attempts to construct a coherent field of 'biotherapy' from a heterogeneous collective of long-standing techniques that use whole living organisms to enhance human health. Historically, these newly converged 'biotherapies' occupied separate and varying positions within medicine, being alternative, complementary and integral over time. Examples include the use of bacteriophage, maggots and leeches to aid healing. The training of animals to improve human mental and physical health (animal-assisted therapy) and the use of animals to recognize life-threatening conditions such as diabetic crisis. This project challenge s representations of biomedicine that emphasize biological individuality, differentiation of normal from pathological and the eradication of disease. In contrast, 'biotherapies' promote health by maximizing co-operative 'symbiotic' relations (e.g. antibiotics vs. probiotics). By innovatively integrating recent interdisciplinary, posthumanist, and multi-species approaches with the medical humanities, I will reveal historically subjugated aspects of biomedicine that encourage thinking in co-depend ent collectives rather than individual, independent organisms, thereby placing emerging ecological approaches to health into historical context. My research will also enhance our understanding of the contribution of nonhuman life to medicine, moving beyond the focus on animal experimentation to investigate how nonhuman life enhances human health in clinical medicine and everyday life.

title: The Cross-Disciplinary Invention of Sexuality: Sexual Science Beyond the Medical, 1890-1940.
description: This project represents a fundamental rethinking of the emergence of the scientific study of human sexuality in the c19th and reconsiders how modern understandings of sexuality were constructed. We critique the hitherto dominant assumption that 'sexology' existed as a clearly understood and primarily medical field of knowledge. We present a new account of the rise of a cross-disciplinary 'sexual science' driven by dissatisfaction with exclusively medical approaches. From the 1890s, medical docto rs argued that a properly scientific understanding of sexuality required input from additional areas of knowledge (e.g. anthropology, sociology, history, literature). This project offers the first full investigation of the conceptual and cultural factors driving the evolution of a cross-disciplinary sexual science: the desire to understand the global variety of sexual behaviour; an interest in historical and cultural variation; and a new focus on the 'normal' and 'healthy' alongside the 'path ological' and 'abnormal'. We examine the ways in which these studies challenged biological explanations of sexuality, raising questions about the 'nature/nurture' divide, and brought imperially-shaped debates about race, the primitive, civilization and degeneration into the heart of sexual science. Thus the project sheds new light on the evolution of a range of categories that are central to understandings of human behaviour in the modern world. Interdisciplinary collaborations will produce m onographs, journal issues and edited collections. A stakeholder-led engagement programme will raise broader questions about the relation between medical and non- medical forms of knowledge in the past and present to address contemporary challenges surrounding sexual health and wellbeing.
