title: Investigating early life stress in infants enrolled in SPRING intervention trial in rural India
description: The 'first thousand days' from conception are critical to healthy brain development and provide a foundation for healthy physical and mental health throughout the lifecourse. Early life stress (ELS) without adequate caregiver buffering exacerbates the impact of any early deprivation and leads to build- up of allostatic load which impacts negatively on the nervous, endocrine and immune systems. We aim to develop/refine techniques for measuring ELS in 600 infants in rural India, including a questionnaire for mothers, observation of contextual stressors such as parental-child interaction and measurement of cortisol (the end product of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal stress system) in saliva (measuring diurnal rhythm) and hair (measuring chronic secretion). This study is linked to the SPRING cluster randomized controlled trial and will: (i) evaluate the impact on ELS of the SPRING home visits intervention promoting early child growth and development; (ii) elucidate risk factors for ELS; (iii) assess the role of ELS in the SPRING causal pathway of impact on growth and development at 18 months old. The project is of great relevance to health in low and middle income countries, adding to our understanding of ELS worldwide and the ability of a scaleable, sustainable intervention such as SPRING to mitigate against it.
recipient: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine

title: Information processing deficits in multiple sclerosis.
description: This fellowship will use measures of information processing from experimental psychology andpsychophysics in combination with theory-based mathematical (diffusion) models toquantitatively dissect fundamental cognitive processes in multiple sclerosis. This will be used tounderstand how fundamental cognitive processes relate to brain pathology as well as to higherlevelcognitive abilities and real world deficits.The following specific questions will be addressed:1)Which fundamental cognitive processes underpin impaired decision making in MS?2)How do specific information processing deficits relate to the burden of white matter pathology,as well as to higher-level cognitive abilities and real world deficits?

title: PRIDE (PRemIum for aDolEscents).
description: Mental disorders are the leading cause of the burden of disease in adolescents both globally and specifically in India, with up to a third of the total burden of disease being attributed to these conditions. The most common mental disorders in adolescents are depressive, anxiety and conduct disorders which account for over 75% of the burden of mental disorders in this age group. More than 50% of the burden of adult mental disorders has its onset in adolescence. While there is a robust body of e vidence pointing to the effectiveness of psychological treatments for adolescent mental disorders there is little implementation of this evidence in the global context. Notable barriers impeding the effective coverage of evidence based psychological treatments are the lack of skilled human resources and the generalizability of interventions developed in western cultural contexts. The applicants PREMIUM program, supported by his current SRF, has constructed a systematic methodology for the develo pment of psychological treatments which address both these challenges. This methodology will be applied to develop a trans-diagnostic intervention targeting emotional and behavioural disorders in adolescents and to evaluate its effectiveness in reducing symptom severity and improving recovery rates. PRIDE will build on PREMIUM in several ways: by developing an intervention which adopts a personalized approach for adolescents and which addresses the contextual factors associated with mental diso rders; by developing a computerised version of the intervention to promote self-help; and by working with vulnerable (i.e. out of school) populations.

title: Noise in neural codes: consequences for memory, exploration and decision- making.
description: Working memory (WM) refers to the nervous system's capacity to internally maintain information about the external world over short periods, and manipulate that information in support of behaviour. WM is considered fundamental to many if not all cognitive functions, and its impairment by age or disease has far-reaching consequences for human health and well-being. This research programme aims to understand how a fallible WM system arises from noisy neural coding, and how WM errors affect human ab ility to explore the environment and make decisions. The key goals are: To develop a detailed computational model of storage and retrieval from WM, based on empirical results obtained with elementary visual features. The aim is to go beyond a simple model of errors, to provide a neural account of binding failures, decay, time to decision, and the confidence assigned to memories. To investigate the impact of WM errors on value-based decision making. Here the internal representation is of the co sts and rewards associated with different possible courses of action. Using gambling tasks, we will investigate the nature of errors in representation of value, how these errors affect decisions, and what compensatory mechanisms mitigate their impact. To understand the most frequent decision made by the nervous system: where to direct gaze. Specifically, we will address how eye movements are selected during visual search, a microcosm of human choice behaviour that draws on WM both for visual pa rameters (where have I looked?) and for reward (where should I look next?).

title: A revolution for health? An exploration of detecting meaning and sentiment in user-generated social media and web content.
description: A growing number of people use the net to find information on medical problems, to chat in online health forums, and even self-diagnose and self- medicate. This has created new, very large data sets of unregulated user- generated health data. This study will explore whether this data can be exploited to: 1) spot trends in citizen-generated unregulated health data online, using a pilot study drawn from mental health. 2) provide useable and robust insight for health professionals and clini cians that will in turn enable them to: a. Quickly spot emerging trends b. Provide early warning signs where there might be a lack of official provision, and use online data to inform a response c. Better understand public and patient attitudes and feedback towards certain types of prescription and treatment d. Understand the risks and opportunities to patients of these source of information e. Understand the potential uses of this information by clinicians and health services f. Exami ne the ethical, regulatory and legal implications 3) demonstrate the potential for further and wider application of these methods within mental health, and beyond.

title: Towards agri-system thinking: An integrated approach to problems of modern livestock production.
description: This project aims to produce an ambitious plan of work to address problems of livestock health, productivity, welfare and the environment which are commonly associated with intensive farming. In contrast to previous studies, which examine these problems in isolation, it will break new ground by focussing upon the nature and dynamics of the agricultural systems that give rise to them. This approach is essential if we are to confront the threats that these problems pose to food security, ecologica l sustainability, animal well-being and the public acceptability of modern livestock farming. Led by scholars from history, social science and epidemiology, the project will span the historical emergence and characterisation of these problems, their present-day manifestations, and how they might evolve in future under a drive for sustainable intensification. There will be two facilitated workshops, bringing together stakeholders and scholars from a range of backgrounds for a frank exchange of vi ews on these problems, the deficiencies that exist in their understanding, management, governance and communication, and how these could be addressed through an integrated, inter-disciplinary program of work. The core team will use these discussions as a basis for drafting a Wellcome Trust Collaborative Award application and two publications.

title: Waiting Times: Waiting and care in the time of modernity.
description: Seed funding is sought for the development work that will lead to a joint Investigator Award Application by Lisa Baraitser (Birkbeck) and Laura Salisbury (Exeter) that investigates waiting time in relation to mental health, clinical contact time, and care. The project will bring together perspectives from medical humanities, medical history, psychosocial studies, literary studies, and new studies of temporality, to think critically about waiting times in mental healthcare provision, the time-spa ce of the GP encounter, and practices of care for the very elderly. Using an emerging scholarship that reformulates the speed and mobility commonly associated with modernity by emphasizing slowness and stilled, impeded or suspended time, the project investigates contemporary experiences of waiting in clinical and care encounters in what are felt to be increasingly frenetic times. Seed funding will enable a) a scoping study to be completed on the history of managing waiting in the NHS, from 1948- present day; b) the development of the conceptual resources on temporality that will underpin the Investigator Award Application through teaching buy-out, meetings, networking and conference attendance by the two co-investigators; c) the development of partnerships with those who will have a stake in the research outputs of project.

title: Finding the right ingredients: Improving mental health and wellbeing through food-centred activities .
description: Nutrition and social interaction can play an important role in prevention and recovery from mild to moderate mental health problems, and also address the obesity-related comorbidities caused by mental health medication. Community- based services are well placed to intervene through these means, as food is a universal preoccupation and thus well-suited to engage the widest possible range of people. However there is a glaring lack of evidence-based food- centred interventions for mental health patie nts at the community level. We therefore wish to conduct early-phase research to develop an intervention for people who access services through community-based mental health organisations. A novel intervention-development method will be used to create a food-centred intervention, grounded in both theory and the experiences of the target population, who will work with us to test and refine logic models (linking activities to outcomes). This study will inform subsequent pilot phases that will test recruitment and data collection procedures, and generate data to determine sample size. The aim is progression to a fully-powered realist randomised controlled trial to assess the mechanisms of action, effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of the community-based food-centred intervention for mental health and wellbeing.

title: Seeds for Survival: A Global History of Seed Banking.
description: I intend, within the next four years, to launch a major multi-year, multi- researcher project on the history of seed banking as a global conservation practice. The project will seek to understand: how the genetic diversity of plant species came to be seen as a critical but imperiled resource essential to human survival; how seed banks came to be seen as the obvious solution to the threat of losing such diversity; and the consequences of these ideas - and the institutions and activities they inspi red - for global food security and human wellbeing in the present. This is a large, complex, and mostly uncharted history. The activities proposed as part of this application will enable me to put forward a thorough and achievable grant proposal at a later date. A postdoctoral research assistant will assist in identifying the relevant archival resources and living individuals who might be future sources of oral histories. A series of short archival reconnaissance missions will allow me to ass ess the richness of the available materials, and to target sites for case studies. Finally, a small workshop will bring together relevant expertise from other universities and serve as the first meeting of a continuing research network.

title: Towards an epidemiology of health conspiracy theories.
description: We plan to develop novel, interdisciplinary approaches to the cultural epidemiology of health conspiracy theories. These include beliefs about secret agendas behind vaccination programs, the side effects of medical treatments, and cover-ups by the government or pharmaceutical industry. Such theories are widespread in many countries around the world and can have highly detrimental and far-reaching effects on the health and wellbeing. The requested funds will be used to develop pilot projects that link micro-level factors, affecting the virulence of these theories (e.g. the psychological properties that make certain beliefs particularly catchy and memorable) and the susceptibility of individuals (e.g. attitudes and prior beliefs), to macro-level, ecological factors that shape the context and vectors of transmission. The projects include designing controlled cultural transmission experiments and a series of ethnographic feasibility studies carried out in five field sites. They will be dir ected by the PI with the support of the CoI, a full-time RA and members of Durham Universitys Special Interest Group on Conspiracy Theories in Health. The goals of the project include establishing proof of concept for the epidemiological approach, a publication setting out future research agendas, and a large grant application.

title: Suicide Voices: Narratives of Trauma in the Globalised Workplace.
description: This project examines the 'epidemic' of suicides within the globalised workplace during the 2000s and asks why work or conditions of work can push some individuals to take their own lives. It aims to bring a critical humanities perspective based on a close reading of suicide testimonies in their social, cultural and economic contexts, to bear on emerging public health research on the rise of economic suicides internationally. The project investigates what suicidal individuals' own testimonies ca n tell us about the social conditions that motivate self-killing in work and therefore provides a critical alternative to current epidemiological approaches to suicide in public health. Building on an emerging collaboration between humanities and public health researchers in the UK and France, the project breaks new ground in its interdisciplinary, methodological and international scope. It has three main goals: 1. To create a new interdisciplinary and transnational research network that expand s and deepens our understanding of the workplace suicide crisis internationally. 2. To publish two peer-reviewed articles that draw on the projects findings and target both English and French-speaking academic audiences. 3. To develop a joint funding application (with Prof Martin McKee) for the Wellcome Trust's Senior Investigator Awards.

title: Investigating the provision and conceptualisation of Social Prescribing approaches to health creation.
description: Social prescribing (SP) is a mechanism for linking patients in primary care with non-medical sources of support within the community, e.g. providing arts based activities instead of prescribing anti-depressants for patients with depression. Innovating approaches to reduce social inequalities and the burden on primary care is an NHS priority. Whilst some SP initiatives are addressing this priority, many variations exist in the interpretation of SP hence consensus on the definition of SP, and a critical exploration of the theoretical underpinnings is urgently needed. This project will scope the provision of SP and review the theoretical underpinnings of SP in the UK and Ireland. A network of SP service providers, medical professionals, academics and patient representatives will be formed. They will be tasked with reaching a consensus on the definition of SP through debate and discussion. These activities will culminate in the dissemination of learning from the scoping exerc ise, and a position paper on the conceptual underpinning of SP. Furthermore, a research collaboration will develop a larger funding application to Wellcome to address the urgent evidence gaps in the research on comparative and economic effectiveness of SP.

title: The Corpse Project Phase 1.
description: The Corpse Project aims ultimately to improve options for the body after death, through multidisciplinary research and public engagement. Our starting points are that burial and cremation as currently practiced are, generally, poor versions of ancient practices and fail to return the body to the natural cycle. The environmental implications of current and alternative practice are under-researched and poorly understood. This matters, given threats to soil health and wider ecosystems pressures. As important, the UK seems particularly affected by a loss of rituals around, and acceptance of, the dead body, which have historically provided a way to mourn, and to be reconciled to, death. The Corpse Project will aim to establish whether human and ecological well-being can benefit from a more open and informed consideration of the corpse. For the development year, key goals are: 1. Public knowledge and attitudes to the treatment of the corpse and 'ashes' surveyed, to include young pe ople and diverse communities. 2. Literature review (ecosystems and cultural). 3. Public exhibits around decomposition developed. 3. Networking, policy checking and other activity to prove project concept and build sustainability of future work (see below).

title: The rise and fall of executive functions: Modelling the neural mechanisms of age-related changes in higher cognitive abilities.
description: This research aims to determine how changes in prefrontal structure and function affect executive functions across the lifespan. This project attempts to address three challenges that pervade the literature on neurocognitive ageing: Small samples, cross-sectional data and predominantly univariate statistical approaches. This project hopes to overcome these limitations by access to, and close collaboration with, three unique developmental studies: NSPN in London, Cam-CAN in Cambridge and BASE-II at the MPI in Berlin. I will use psychometric models and longitudinal, multimodal neuroimaging to address four key questions. First, I will use Latent Growth Curve Modelling to determine optimal neurodevelopmental trajectories in adolescents. Second, I will use hierarchical MIMIC models to capture the cascade of effects of white matter changes on processing speed and reasoning. Third, I will examine task- based functional connectivity of the prefrontal cortex following prefrontal atrophy to provi de a critical test of the scaffolding hypothesis. Finally, I will use equality-constrained multifactor MIMIC models to determine and compare prefrontal structure and function between healthy and non-healthy cognitive agers. Together, the unique nature of the datasets and novelty of the statistical approaches promise to greatly increase our understanding of neurocognitive development and ageing.

title: Biological markers of stress and inflammation across clinical stages of schizophrenia: from early at-risk states to chronic illness.
description: The proposed study will utilise five existing cohort studies, providing access to individuals at progressively advanced illness stages: (i) at-risk children who present a family history of illness or subthreshold psychotic symptoms and other developmental risk markers, assessed biennially from childhood to age 17-18 years, (ii) individuals displaying features consistent with the prodromal phase and first-episode psychosis (FEP), and (iii) FEP patients followed-up five years later. Across all fiv e cohorts, I propose to collect/re-collect saliva and hair samples for cortisol analysis (providing information on hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal [HPA] axis function, the primary system coordinating the biological stress response) and blood/buccal samples to determine the status of gene expression factors that converge to influence inflammation (e.g., transcript levels of C-reactive protein and cytokines). These data would allow me to address three objectives. Firstly, I will be able to determin e whether greater increases in cortisol over time characterise at- risk children who progress to the putatively prodromal phase of illness. Secondly, I will examine whether salivary cortisol profiles among FEP patients predict clinical outcomes at a five-year follow-up. Finally, using data from all five cohorts, I will investigate the extent to which stress and inflammation biomarkers are differentially expressed across the clinical stages of schizophrenia.

title: Image-guided neurosurgical treatment of epilepsy
description: a) Over 50 million people worldwide are affected by epilepsy which is uncontrolled in 1/3, causing physical, psychological and psychiatric disability and death. Neurosurgical treatment of refractory focal epilepsy is potentially curative, greatly improves quality of life and is cost-effective. Accessibility is impaired and delayed by the complexity of the work-up and concern about adverse effects. b) An image-guided solution to the whole epilepsy surgery pathway, including computer-assisted planning and robotic placement of intracranial electrodes, and 3D image-guided resections. c) (i) Software to automate planning of intracranial electrodes placement, including libraries of cerebral target and entry points. (ii) Integration of software with robotic system for placing intracerebral electrodes, and with widely used neurosurgical navigation software. (iii) Software for visualising intracranial EEG results and designing 3D resection volumes, with planning of craniotomies.

title: Baby talk and baby blues: harnessing technology to investigate mechanisms of influence of parental wellbeing on infants.
description: Post-natal depression (PND), clinical levels baby blues, occurs in 10-20% of new mothers, and is associated with adverse long-term consequences for children. Parents with PND are likely to be less responsive and sensitive during parent-infant interaction. Furthermore, PND negatively impacts parental baby talk, a specialised form of speech used by adults when speaking to infants. Impairments in baby talk have long-term adverse effects on childrens social, emotional and cognitive development. The current project proposes an investigation of a cost-effective and efficient means to collect and code baby talk and parent-child interactions, which is currently extremely labour intensive. We propose to use LENA, a talk pedometer worn by babies to collect and code their linguistic environments, and EMOTIONSENSE, an application that tracks emotion over time. This information will then be used to examine differences in low-, medium- and high-risk PND groups in; (1) baby-talk; assessed via traditi onal gold standard methods and novel technologies; (2) the links between pre- and post-natal parental wellbeing in parents; (3) the links between parent-infant interaction quality and emotional, cognitive and social development in early toddlerhood.

title: SlowMo: Using wearable technology to improve outcomes of psychological therapy for paranoia in psychosis.
description: This study will develop innovative wearable technology to improve outcomes of a talking therapy, 'Thinking Well', which targets thinking habits related to paranoia (or worries about others intentionally causing harm) (Waller et al, 2015). A digital redesign of the intervention has recently been completed in collaboration with clinician academics, technology specialists and inclusive designers. The proposed project aims to augment this work and is the first to investigate therapeutic wearable t echnology for psychosis. Paranoid thoughts are common and associated with anxiety (Freeman et al, 2015). Psychological interventions to address the devastating impact of psychosis have modest effect sizes and need to be improved (Garety & Freeman, 2013). A key obstacle to effectiveness is empowering people to make use of interventions in daily life. Wearable technology may provide a means to overcome this challenge. Automatic biofeedback on paranoia-related anxiety could trigger i ntervention prompts, reducing the demands of self-monitoring. Qualitative methods will be used to develop a prototype for iterative service user testing, to establish acceptability and usability. An application to the MRC DPFS is planned for further prototype development and a pilot trial.

title: Protocadherin 19 in cortical development.
description: Mutations in Pcdh19, a delta-2 protocadherin encoded on the X chromosome, lead to epilepsy with cognitive impairment in heterozygous females. The early disease onset suggests a neurodevelopmental basis for the disorder, but the function of this gene is entirely unknown. We propose to use the developing mouse brain to analyze early roles of Pcdh19 in neurogenesis, migration and circuit formation. Data from expression studies, anatomical analyses and the unusual inheritance mode of the disorder, w ith unaffected hemizygous males, support a role of Pcdh19 in these processes. We will first perform a comprehensive molecular and hodological characterization of Pcdh19 expressing cells at different developmental stages. We will then analyze a Pcdh19 null mouse mutant and assess whether neurogenesis and/or migration are affected. Using in utero electroporation, we will directly interfere with Pcdh19 function, either by shRNA to cause an acute reduction of its levels or with mutant forms of the p rotein. Synapse analysis in embryonic stem cell-derived neurons and electrophysiological recordings in brain slices will complete the analysis. Our results will provide insight into the roles of Pcdh19 during corticogenesis and form a useful basis for subsequent studies.

title: ASTERISK: Addiction Services Treatment Evaluation of RISK.
description: This proposal is the first stage of Addiction Services Treatment Evaluation of Risk (ASTERISK), an interdisciplinary project combining the latest methodological advances in electronic health record (EHR) and risk prediction research to develop innovative tools for stratified care in drug and alcohol addiction treatment. This initial project provides a foundation for further research by addressing two goals: 1. Create phenotype algorithms for extracting clinically meaningful EHR data rele vant to patients treated for addiction; 2. Identify liver disease risk factors in a cohort of addiction patients using data extracted by applying these algorithms to EHR data from a large UK mental health treatment provider. Liver disease will be used as an exemplar to establish the viability of ASTERISK, but the strategy developed will subsequently be applied to other clinical outcomes. The research outlined in this proposal will form the basis of a project grant expanding ASTERISK from risk factor identification to development of clinical prediction tools. It will use EHR data for: (i) prediction model development; (ii) model validation studies; (iii) clinical impact studies. The outcome of this larger project will be novel tools for implementing stratified care, embedded in EHR systems.

title: AMARI: African Mental Health Research Initiative
description: Mental, neurological and substance use (MNS) disorders are a leading, but neglected, cause of morbidity and mortality in sub-Saharan Africa [1]. MNS disorders account for >25% of all years lived with disability globally, more than cardiac disease or cancer [2]. The treatment gap is vast, only 10% of people with MNS disorders in low-income countries access evidence-based treatments, compared to 33% in high-income countries [3]. Reasons for this include low awareness ofthe burden of MNS disorders and limited evidence to support development, adaptation and implementation of effective and feasible treatments. While pockets of mental health research excellence exist in Africa, MNS research capacity is generally limited, particularly in mental health intervention, service and system research. Mental health research excellence is currently undermined by restricted opportunities for training and mentorship, unclear career pathways, lack of integration in general medical settings, limited multi-disciplinary collaboration and the lack of a critical mass of MNS researchers and leaders. The overall goals of the African Mental Health Research Initiative (AMARI) areto build an African-led network of MNS researchers in Ethiopia, Malawi, South Africa and Zimbabwe, equipped to lead high quality mental health research programmes that meet the needs of their countries, and to establish a sustainable career pipeline for these researchers with the emphasis on integrating MNS research into existing programmes such as HIV/AIDS, maternal and child health. The objectives are to: 1. Select and train MNS research fellows from a range of disciplines at masters (n=25), PhD (n=20) and post-doctoral (n=6) levels in research excellence; 2. Build leadership skills of 26 fellows through adaptation of KCL Career Development Series on Leadership, Management and Mentoring; 3. Design and test an advocacy and systems change strategy for each country, aimed at building sustainable career pathways in MNS academia; 4. Develop a web-based support platform for training, supervision and networking. In year 1 we will undertake preparatory work to inform course development, thedesign of the advocacy and systems change strategy and gather baseline data for each country, for evaluation purposes, conducting qualitative and quantitative interviews with local policymakers and service users to identify needs and priorities through a theory of change map. We willtrain local supervisors, run pre-application workshops for potential applicants and assess existing training materials. . In years 2-5, fellows will begin higher degrees and courses as relevant. Trainingwill be mostly in Africa and using a) joint supervision by local and external supervisors with multidisciplinary expertise, b) taught modules in advanced MNS research methods, writing, and engagement with policy makers, and c) undertaking high priority MNS research. The underlying ethos of AMARI will be to ensure LMIC partner capacity is strengthened progressively towards self-sufficiency to ensure sustainability longer term. AMARI will be led by University of Zimbabwe College of Health Sciences (UZ-CHS). All consortium institutions will provide course facilitators and supervisors, with the Centrefor Global Mental Health (CGMH), University of Cape Town (UCT) and University College London (UCL) providing external supervision, research experts and materials for adaptation.

title: Afrique One- African Science Partnership for Intervention Research Excellence (Afrique One-ASPIRE)
description: Building on the successful model established by Afrique One, Afrique One- ASPIRE will significantly expand research capacity in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) through a structured programme of scientific training across five Thematic Training Programmes (TTPs) bound together with an Engagement and Learning Platform (ELP) comprising three cross-cutting programmes, including support for developing Core Research Skills, Research Governance, Management and Administrative (RGMA) skills, and Policy Engagement and Impact (Figure 1).The proposal has three distinctive features: focus, geographic axis and methodological approach. Focus is provided by five TTPs addressing zoonoses: rabies, brucellosis, mycobacterial infections, food-borne diseases, and surveillance-response systems. The geographic axis includes the critical, though nascent research partnerships embedded within the Economic Communities of East and West Africa. The methodological approach is that of 'mutual learning for change', building on the concept that we often have sufficient knowledge to be able to plan and implement relevant interventions that will generate health benefits and enhanced understanding. We focus on endemic zoonoses, which cause millions of illnesses and several hundred thousand deaths in the human population annually, considerable production losses and reduced food security worldwide1-4. The highest burden falls on low-income countries (estimated to account for 99.9% of illnesses and96% of deaths caused by zoonosis), particularly on impoverished livestock-dependent communities across SSA where humans and animals live in close proximity5. The programme will equip African scientists with expertise in planning, monitoring and evaluating interventions through well-implemented integrated 'One-Health' research with the aim of tackling zoonoses and hence improving human and animal health and well-being, as well as food security. This capacity will make important contributions to formulating future health policy and intervention plans based on novel financial instruments. This is particularly timely given the alignment of this proposal with the Sustainable Development Goals, which focus on achieving global health and well-being through preventative interventions, and food security through sustainably managed food production.6 This proposal is developed around three important innovations: Firstly, the programme addresses head-on the challenge of linking emerging research institutions in East and West Africa, mirroring complementary research capacity and experience across the continent in order to train the next generation of young African scientists in intervention research for prevention of zoonoses at the animal-human-environment interface. We will linka core group of 7 African and 2 European institutions with an additional 7 collaborating African institutions. Secondly, we deliberately select disease systems where our current knowledge is distributed along a continuum that ranges from estimating the burden and accurate characterisation of the agents of disease, through morbidity and transmission control, to disease elimination strategies, including public engagement. Only through such a broad research- training portfolio can we collectively provide early career researchers with the full range of experience and expertise required to confront a contemporary One-Health research agenda. Finally, the programme will take advantage of the rapidly increasing broadbandlandscape in Africa to support the installation and management of informatics infrastructure and the development of mobile- health approaches, in particular using mobile technology to increase surveillance and response opportunities, and cross-consortia learning.

title: Longitudinal evidence on the longer-term impacts of environmental change on population health and nutrition
description: Little is known about long-term effects of environmental disasters on population health. We will measure impacts, after 10 years, of the 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami on biological health risks leveraging data from the Study of the Tsunami Aftermath and Recovery (STAR), an on-going large- scale longitudinal population-representative survey of individuals who lived (when the tsunami struck) along the coast of Sumatra, Indonesia. Baseline interviews 10 months pretsunami are combined with 5 annual follow-ups and a 10-year follow-up. We have interviewed over 96% of the 30,000 surviving baseline respondents. To provide rigorous evidence on the disaster’s longer- term impacts, this pilot study collects key biological health and nutrition markers implicated in major non-communicable diseases, and links them to the roles of stresses from tsunami exposure and compromised psycho-social health. Moreover, we investigate behavioural adaption in response to the environmental destruction of the tsunami and reconstruction after the tsunami. Looking forward, this research program provides an ideal platform to develop an international inter-disciplinary model laboratory, leveraging STAR with other resources, to investigate the consequences of environmental and climate- related changes and also conduct interventions to provide the evidence-base necessary to design innovations likely to have a sustained impact on population health and well-being.

title: Optimization of health and sustainability goals for low income housing
description: Housing has a crucial influence on health and well-being. In most settings, energy use in the home and for residential construction also accounts for a sizeable proportion of overall greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. The form and quality of housing is a crucial target both for health protection and for the attainment of sustainability goals in relation to energy and GHG emissions. However, housing varies markedly in the degree to which it protects health, especially for low income households, while the evolving risks of climate change and need to meet mitigation targets often require substantial adaptations in the housing sector. Our vision in this project is to use case studies from four contrasting settings around the world to develop and apply methods to improve the design, refurbishment and operation of housing for low- income households that is low cost, low in environmental impact, high performance and improves quality of life and wellbeing. Lessons learned from these case studies will be used to inform the methods and approaches that can be applied in these and other settings.
recipient: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine

title: The Politics of Misery: A philosophical investigation of the political relevance of mental suffering.
description: This project is an interdisciplinary work of political philosophy, history of political thought and psychiatry, and philosophy of medicine. It will employ philosophical analysis and historical research methods to investigate how the relationship between misery and political agency has changed in the United Kingdom over the past century and evaluate the implications of any changes. I have identified three emotions that are prima facie aspects of misery: sadness, anxiety and anger, which have al l been medicalised to various degrees in the past decades. These emotions will be the focus for two discourse analyses. First, I will analyse the historical relationship between political agency and these emotions during the Second Industrial Revolution, in the nascence of democracy. I will then examine the role of these emotions in the late 20th century, and contrast these findings against the historical analysis to theorise the effects of medicalised misery upon agency. The goals of this res earch are three-fold: (1) to increase our understanding of the relationship between negative emotions and political agency; (2) based on this insight, to propose how we can enhance the political agency of democratic citizens; and (3) to recommend actions that individuals and governments can take to this end.

title: A Face to Die For: Acne, Accutane and the Quest for Perfect Skin. 1950s-present.
description: Acne is a blight on the social and emotional lives of many adolescents, often leaving both physical and psychological scars.But how far have adolescents, physicians and pharmaceutical companies been willing to go in order to treat it? This project is the first to recount the history of acne and its most controversial treatment:the prescription drug Accutane.Although Accutane prescriptions dominated the treatment of acne by the 1980s, the drug also caused many dangerous side effects, ranging fro m gastrointestinal and neurological symptoms to birth defects in pregnant patients.It has also been linked to over 100 suicides and has been the subject of 5,000 lawsuits worldwide.While Accutane has been withdrawn for sale in the United States by its manufacturer, Roche, it is still available for sale in the UK under the trade name Roaccutane. Key goals: 1) chart how acne became the subject of such medical concern following the Second World War and how physicians and patients understood its causes and treatments 2) examine how physicians and pharmaceutical companies turned to the perceived health needs of adolescent patients 3) analyse how the risks and benefits of Accutane and other acne treatments were perceived by both patients and physicians

title: Violence, Mental Health and the British School Child: from theory to practice in an era of war, peace and social change, 1944-1980.
description: Focusing on primary and secondary state education in England from the Education Act of 1944 to 1980, the project will examine thought and practice on the relationship between violence and children. This will entail, in the first instance, exploring the connections between theory and practice and the ways in which psychological ideas were mediated by the range of actors who commented on, and were active in debates about, the problem of violence in schools. Secondly, beginning its time-frame with the Second World War, the research offers a valuable opportunity to assess whether the conflict affected thinking about children as well as providing scope for examining the effect of the new tripartite education system and its post-war extension of secondary education to all children. Finally, the research will consider the differences in how a range of professionals thought about this subject, particularly psychologists and teachers, but also social workers, parents, and popular commentators. It will trace differences in practice according to the age of children, gender, class and ethnicity, and explore the effect of ideas about moral decline associated with the permissive society (evident in alarm during the 1950s about the existence of a 'blackboard jungle').

title: What did they do all day? Patient work, psychiatry and society in England and France 1900 - 1940.
description: The main aim is to recover the day-to-day culture of work-related activities and therapy in mental hospitals in England and France during the period 1900-1940. In particular, the aim is to elucidate the rationale of work therapy and to examine its development, refinement and application in six key institutions. The key goals are: 1. To analyse how the organisation and perception of work, non-work and unemployment in England and France affected ideas and practices of therapeutic work and p astimes within mental institutions. 2. To examine the impact of war on the role of work and activities as rehabilitative treatments for mentally ill patients, both during the war and in peacetime. 3. To highlight the tension between (a) medical rationales for work as therapy and contemporary socio-economic conditions (such as high rates of unemployment) and (b) particular medical ideologies (such as eugenics and mental hygiene). 4. To demonstrate how knowledge, ideas and practices flowe d between French and British psychiatrists regarding work and activities as forms of treatment. 5. To discover whether mentally-ill patients and their families experienced work and activities as empowering, entertaining, educational, punitive, coercive or rehabilitative.

title: Frequent detainees under Section 136 of the Mental Health Act: An exploration of the phenomenon of repeated detention and practitioner developed innovations using realistic evaluation.
description: The goal of this PhD is to produce a unique and comprehensive analysis of the psychosocial characteristics of those repeatedly detained under Section 136 of the Mental Health Act. A systematic review will first be conducted, drawing on relevant bodies of literature relating to Section 136, values based practice, frequent attendance at other frontline services, complex psychological and social needs and relevant policy and guidance documents. The next goal will be a detailed investigation into a range of interventions that have been developed by practitioners in order to reduce repeated detentions. This will incorporate interviews with those involved in the development or delivery of the interventions, as well as those with experience of using these services or partaking in the interventions and their carers. In line with the realistic evaluation model, the focus of these interviews will be on the change achieved by these interventions and the context in which they operate. The data wi ll be reviewed in an interpretive workshop involving interviewees and other public engagement panel members. Finally, this will lead to the production of an overarching programme theory that expounds the mechanisms and context in which reductions in repeat detentions are being achieved.

title: Translational control of neuronal mRNAs in autism spectrum disorders.
description: Translational control is a powerful homeostatic mechanism to regulate gene expression in neurons. We showed that increased translation led to enhanced excitatory(E) and inhibitory(I) synaptic transmission in CA1 pyramidal cells, which caused autism-like symptoms in mice. Genetic deletion of the eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E (eIF4E)-binding protein 2, 4E-BP2, induces exaggerated eIF4E-dependent synthesis of neuroligins causing an E/I imbalance and engendering autism-like behaviors. The E/I balance is restored and autism- like behaviors reversed by blocking cap-dependent translation or knocking down neuroligins. We hypothesize that 4E-BP2 regulates different pools of mRNAs in excitatory and inhibitory neurons, and this is a key mechanism regulating the E/I balance and autism-like behaviours. Now, using novel conditional-knockout 4E-BP2 transgenic mice in excitatory or inhibitory neurons of the cortex and hippocampus, and compounds modulating translation, we will study the ro le of translational control in the maintenance of the E/I balance through aberrant translation of specific mRNAs. To achieve this we will identify the translatome regulated in excitatory and inhibitory synapses of the forebrain using RNA sequencing. The proposed research can lead to the development of novel therapeutic approaches taking advantage of the selective regulation of translational control on a subset of mRNAs in mouse models of ASD.

title: Elucidating the aetiology of psychopathology: Taking a multigenerational approach to genetically informative data.
description: Aim Investigate genetic and environmental mechanisms underlying the intergenerational transmission of psychopathology using large, genetically informative, multi-generation datasets. I will develop novel biometric models capable of distinguishing genetic from environmental routes of transmission in longitudinal children-of-twins (CoT) data, population databases, and genomic samples. I will study associations between parental depression and offspring outcomes across the lifespan, considering bid irectional effects, assortative mating, and psychiatric comorbidity. Objective 1 Develop longitudinal CoT models and apply to the Intergenerational Transmission of Risk Project - the world's first longitudinal CoT sample. Objective 2 Develop intergeneration models for use on Swedish population data taken from the national registries. I will develop multivariate models, take a life-course perspective to the impact of parental depression, and investigate the role of assortative mating. Objective 3 Apply structural equation models to genomic data, evaluating genetic vs environmental routes of transmission and assortative mating using genetic information, complementing my work using biometric models to identify latent factors. Objective 4 Develop my own CoT sample using the world famous Twins Early Development Study as a basis. This will result in a novel dataset comprising two generations phenotypes since birth, providing a rich resource for future research.

title: Dedicated MR equipment for optimised imaging of the structure and function of the human brain.
description: We seek funding for a research-dedicated high gradient strength 3T-MRI scanner to expand our MRI capabilities at the Clinical Imaging Sciences Centre (CISC). This equipment will support the implementation of sophisticated neurochemical, microstructural, and functional imaging techniques that will extend our existing capacity to provide deep insights into human brain function and neuropathology for translational benefit. Our vision is to become a truly world-class centre for clinically-oriented human imaging neuroscience. To this end, our objectives are to: 1) optimise advanced microstructural MRI techniques sensitive to subtle brain abnormalities; 2) integrate functional neuroimaging with detailed multi-axis measurement of bodily physiology; 3) develop advanced functional connectivity analyses for causal characterisation of inter-regional neural interactions; 4) apply these methods to the mechanistic understanding of specific neurological and psychiatric disorders, and adaptive brain processes in healthy individuals, and; 4) disseminate these techniques and research findings. The centre is currently equipped with 1.5T MRI scanner which is nearing the end of its operational lifetime. The new scanner will launch a new era for CISC and enable us to pursue our objectives for the next 10 years.

title: Towards understanding and treatment of MeCP2-related disorders.
description: Mutations in the MECP2 gene are responsible for two autism spectrum disorders (ASDs): Rett Syndrome[1] (loss of function) and MECP2 Duplication Syndrome[2] (over-expression). Involvement in monogenic ASDs has prompted intensive study of MeCP2 protein, but its functional role remains uncertain. As either too little or too much MeCP2 protein leads to profound intellectual disability, understanding how this protein contributes to brain function is a priority. A prominent view is that MeCP2 is a multifunctional hub protein implicated in diverse pathways. A simpler alternative, suggested by the restricted distribution of Rett syndrome (RTT)-causing mutations, is that MeCP2 is primarily a transcriptional repressor that binds methylated DNA[3] and recruits a co-repressor complex[4]. This research programme is designed to distinguish these hypotheses through a series of experiments that challenge each. It will use the resulting basic knowledge to develop small molecules that may be used therapeutically. The following component questions will be addressed: 1. What are the determinants of MeCP2 binding to chromatin in vivo? Although the protein has been shown to bind methylated DNA, additional determinants have been proposed. 2. Is the ability to bind both DNA and NCoR/SMRT sufficient for MeCP2 function? Our previous work suggests that these two discrete interaction domains are of over-riding functional importance for MeCP2 function. We will create mutations in mice that test this hypothesis. 3. How and why is gene expression affected by varying levels of MeCP2? The reported effects of MeCP2-deficiency on brain gene expression are inconsistent, rangingfrom no clear effects, to mostly activation or mostly repression[5]. We will use homogeneouspopulations of cultured human neurons to resolve this question. 4. Can we identify therapeutic options for treatment of Rett syndrome and MECP2 Duplication Syndrome? Our earlier work established proof-of-principle that Rett syndrome is a reversible condition and therefore in principle curable[6]. So far, however, there are no effective treatments for any MeCP2-related condition. Based on our molecular insights into thebiochemical consequences of specific Rett mutations, we will collaboratively seek small molecules that stabilise or disrupt the structure/interactions of wildtype and mutant MeCP2.

title: Fractionating the functions of primate ventromedial prefrontal cortex of relevance to depression.
description: I wish to understand how the primate ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) contributes to the regulation of positive and negative emotion. Specific questions are: What are the cognitive functions of these regions relevant to emotion regulation? How do they interact in decision-making to bias behavioural choices? How is that interaction instantiated in cortico-cortical and cortico-subcortical neural circuits? Are these neurocognitive circuits differentially modulated by current pharmacotherapies of depression and how is the balance of control between cortical and subcortical nodes in these circuits modulated by the monoamines? How is the development of these circuits influenced by genetic risk factors for neuropsychiatric disorders? Answers to these questions will inform our understanding of the aetiology and neural basis of the diverse symptoms of depression and guide personalized treatment strategies.

title: Ancient histories of phrenitis.
description: Considerable attention is paid in ancient medical sources to the disease called phrenitis yet very little work has done on it by modern scholars. The project will produce a comprehensive analysis of the illness symptoms and medical contexts in the major authors of antiquity. I shall offer an interpretation of the uses of the term in the medical writers from the fifth and early fourth century to Celsus De Medicina, Galen, the nosological authors of the early Imperial period and late encyclopaedic works. The close analysis of these ancient medical sources will be concluded by a short exploration of the afterlife of the disease, in particular its connection to the rise of pre- modern and modern psychiatry from the sixteenth century onwards. Research questions: 1) What causation and physiology did ancient medical authors attribute to phrenitis? 2) What symptomatology and patient typology characterise phrenitis? 3) In what respects do the various accounts of phrenitis differ in various authors? 4) What relationships exist between phrenitis and other mental diseases across the history of ancient medicine? 5) How do the treatments of phrenitis vary through history? 6) How was phrenitis represented in popular or non-medical cultures?

title: Understanding the health and wellbeing challenges of UK food poverty and food aid: a qualitative study.
description: Food poverty poses significant concerns for health and social justice. People on low incomes are far more likely to be forced into unhealthy diets and suffer from diet-related diseases. The combination of lowered incomes and rising food prices means that more people are turning to charities for emergency food aid parcels, via a primary care referral system. Food poverty is a long standing problem for the most disadvantaged UK households. And yet, neither its long term effects nor the experiences of involved healthcare professionals have been investigated. This three-year qualitative study aims to explore the health challenges and inequalities of food poverty by interrogating the insights of different actors and clients in the food aid system. The project comprises two main elements. Firstly, a two-wave longitudinal study with eight food aid workers and 15 client families. Family interviews, accompanied food shopping trips and video diaries will be used at both waves. Secondly, a series of interviews with 25 healthcare professionals. Data will be subject to a narrative analysis and synthesised within a Strong Structuration Theory (SST) framework. The goal of the project is to inform improvements in health and social care and structural responses to food poverty.
recipient: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine

title: Invisible Dust enhanced programme and resilience.
description: At the end of the Sustaining Excellence grant period Invisible Dust will have made a significant step change. We will have strategically grown the organisation to transform it from a small project based company employing freelancers to a sustainable organisation with an increased profile; enhanced understanding of its audiences and a diversification of income. The organisation will have a resilient business model with more non-project based income, improved digital capacity and a better understanding of how to reach and engage audiences. Our vision for our organisation is to be a powerful champion for its sector. We will have enhanced our award-winning programme of artists’ projects developed with scientists. Working with high calibre artists Adam Chodzko, Kasia Molga, Mariele Neudecker, writer China Miéville; and their biomedical advisors, we will deliver exciting and thought provoking artworks on health and the environment with an estimated total audience of 75,550 at EuroScience Open Forum, Manchester 2016 and Hull City of Culture 2017; and developed a new project on women’s health and the environment. We will have deeper engagement with audiences. Advised by Education Consultant Bridget McKenzie we will develop, pilot and deliver projects that engage audiences on a personal level. We will also deepen relationships with biomedical advisors. Professor Frank Kelly, Environmental Health, King’s College London will host a residency for artist Molga; Professor Ian Wilkinson, London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine will support his students in designing schools workshops; Professor Alex Rogers, Oxford University, will lead a Schools initiative on ocean health and art; and young women biomedical scientists will advise on our women’s health project.

title: Moving Medicine: A National Programme
description: Over 5 years award--winning performance company Clod Ensemble will collaborate with medics, scientists, artists and cultural thinkers who share a deep concern for the human body and questions of wellbeing, to present an outstanding programme of performances, talks and workshops in six towns and cities across the UK. A powerful and compelling dialogue will emerge encouraging people to have a deeper appreciation of their own flesh and bones and inspiring them to reimagine the place of medicine in our culture now and in the future. At the core of the programme will be the revival of two critically acclaimed large--scale performances An Anatomie in Four Quarters and Under Glass. Through an on--going research and development process the company will also create two new pieces of work and enhance aspects of their existing repertoire so as to engage even more people with interdisciplinary work of the highest quality. The performances will be presented as part of ‘Performing Medicine Seasons’ – which encourage deep exploration of critical debates within biomedical science through talks and workshops, inviting different institutions and individuals to come together, share practice, collaborate and exchange. Continuing to build its network of people interested in what science has to offer the arts and vice versa, Clod Ensemble will their develop professional training ‘Reboot’ programme to stimulate a new generation of artists to engage in interdisciplinary practice.

title: A Theatre of Emotions: The Affective Landscape of Nineteenth-Century British Surgery.
description: This project will transform historical understandings by exploring the emotional landscape of civil and military surgery in the nineteenth century and beyond. Historians have generally emphasised the importance of emotional detachment and affective restraint in surgical practice. However, this project suggests that the affective repertoire of the nineteenth-century operating theatre was more complex than this and encompassed a wide variety of feelings from fear and anxiety to pity and sympathy. This project will draw upon a range of sources and methodologies to paint a rich historical picture and will stimulate debate between academics, practitioners and the public about the place of emotion within the increasingly detached and technologized world of modern surgical practice. This project has four distinct but complementary strands. The first, undertaken by the Principal Applicant, explores the emotional world of civil surgery. The second, undertaken by a Senior Research Fellow, considers the place of emotion in military surgery from the Napoleonic wars to the First World War. The third involves a PhD, jointly supervised with a colleague from the Department of English and Creative Writing, who will examine the representation of the surgeon as affective being in nineteenth- century literature. Finally, a fourth strand involves a Research Fellow/Engagement Officer working on the emotional world of contemporary surgery. The key goals of this project are to produce two mon ographs, five peer-reviewed articles and a PhD thesis, to organise one conference and two workshops, including one centred around engagement, and to stage an exhibition and associated public lectures.

title: Exploring Diagnosis: Autism and the Neurodiversity Movement.
description: Vision: This investigation will contribute to the field of 'Sociology of Diagnosis' using autism as a case study. This nascent field focusses on the role that diagnosis plays in individual and professional understandings of health and illness. Sociologists consider diagnosis to have the following roles: i) A way of categorising people (as ill or healthy) ii) An intervention in itself with consequences for health iii) A social transactional process which clinicians, patient and carers m ay negotiate. Diagnosis may/may not be disclosed according to circumstance. While some patients seek diagnosis, others resist the use of diagnostic labels and argue diagnosis can be used as a form of social control. Building on previous work, I will explore adults' experiences of the utility and consequences of diagnostic categorisation using autism as a case study. Autism diagnosis is particularly relevant because the label is increasingly applied, the diagnosis has clear costs and benefits, and its application is frequently contested. Main method: An analysis of qualitative interview data, especially experiences of adults in the neurodiversity movement together with those of adults who have actively sought a clinical diagnosis of autism. The neurodiversity movement comprises politically mobilised adults with autism who frame neurological difference as a valuable aspect of human variation and argue against medical diagnosis claiming it pathologizes normal behaviour. Outputs : A series of five academic articles, a book and three short films exploring the themes of Diagnosis, Neurodiversity and Treatment.

title: Lindsay Seers.
description: Lindsay Seers' 'Every Thought There Ever Was' is a moving-image installation that explores the phenomenon (and the problem) of consciousness, evoking the apparently miraculous complexity of this mysterious feature of our existence while also suggesting its mutability, its uncertainty, even its multiplicity. Displayed in an atmospheric constructed space over three moving robotically- controlled projection screens, the piece reflects and dramatises the shifting, fluctuating nature of our perception s of reality, and some of the blind spots and ambiguities inherent in the images we form of ourselves. The piece draws from a wellspring of philosophical ideas and from contemporary scientific thinking about the workings of the brain, and its malfunctions and disorders. A particular focus will be on current and historical perceptions/representations of schizophrenia, and the light that neuroscientific study of this and related conditions might shine on the elusive, variable nature of consciousne ss in general. As part of a three-way curatorial collaboration between Film and Video Umbrella, Whitworth Art Gallery, Manchester and Talbot Rice Gallery, Edinburgh, the work will be exhibited in long-run slots that coincide with major arts festivals in both cities. A symposium will showcase expert contributions from academics at the universities to which the galleries are attached. The work will have different iterations at the two venues, while sharing common material. At Edinburgh, Seers will consider the biography of surgeon James Miranda Barry, whereas in Manchester she will focus on another historical figure from the Musgrave Kinley Outsider Art Collection, held by the Whitworth.

title: Evaluating new immersive technologies for improving mindful awareness.
description: Current immersive technologies present visual information in an unnatural way, often forcing us to narrow our field of attention to the central area of vision, thus ignoring most of the peripheral field. We know that narrowing awareness and attention can have negative effects on health and wellbeing. Yet the very same immersive technologies that can cause these negative effects are increasingly being used to treat them. For example, the therapeutic use of virtual reality systems in mindfulne ss training is showing promise in reducing pain, anxiety, and dependence on medication. We have developed a new form of visual perspective that overcomes a major limitation of current immersive technologies. Our method can represent visual information in a more perceptually natural way by using the full field of view, including the periphery, to broaden the focus of awareness and attention. We will work with experts in science, art, the humanities and medicine to evaluate this new form o f visual perspective. Our goal is to determine whether it can improve technologies used for mindfulness training by broadening the focus of attention to the whole visual field. We will gather evidence through focus groups, workshops and a seminar.

title: Dark River
description: Dark River will be the third feature film from acclaimed writer/director Clio BarnardDark River explores the complexities of trauma and memory; what forms us, damages us, untanglinglayers of the past through an abusive adult sibling relationship in the present. It examines theresentments and cruelties of sibling relationships in a family where lines have been crossed and thefamily regime was corrupted.A 90 minute feature film for theatrical and digital distribution. Script developed with finance fromFilm4 and BFI. Production finance will come Film4, BFI, Screen Yorkshire, UK Tax Break & TheWelcome Trust. Our main project collaborators will be:Emily Holmes: Programme Leader; MRC Cognition and Brain Sciences, CambridgeEmily’s research into mental imagery in emotion and emotional disorders directly relates to theoverarching themes of Dark River.http://www.mrc-cbu.cam.ac.uk/our- research/holmes/http://www.psych.ox.ac.uk/team/emily-holmesAlso work as part of Emily’s teamDr Martina Di Simplicio: Psychiatrist and CBT therapist working in the Emotional Disorders andMental Imagery group at MRC Cognition and Brain Sciences, Cambridge.https://www.mrc-cbu.cam.ac.uk/people/martina.disimplicio/

title: Unleashing Healthy Communities
description: This grant will be used to scope a systematic, rigorous evaluation of the Bromley by Bow model with a view to a possible application for a Wellcome Trust Collaborative Award. The underlying purpose in this work is to define a longer term evaluation of the distinctive Bromley by Bow approach. The project will create a framework for a study of the design, performance and results of the Centre’s holistic, integrated model in improving health and wellbeing, social determinants of health and reducing health inequalities. It will assess the effectiveness of the mechanisms and complex interventions and their appropriateness for deprived communities and consider how the model can inform policy and practice related to tackling long standing health inequalities in communities across the country. The objective of this initial nine month phase is to establish the basis by which the research and evaluation project is developed over subsequent years. Key outcomes include: \- establishment of Project Team and Reference Group \- development of collaborative relationships with key partners \- agreement of project intention, scope, research questions, phases \- creation of research governance framework \- review of Centre model, assumptions, theory of change \- definition of research methodologies and data requirements \- development of proposals for subsequent project stages

title: Reading Well Books on Prescription
description: Development of the following areas of Reading Well Books on Prescription in year 1 \- Delivery of a young people's mental health scheme ; With future development in year 2 and beyond of \- The common mental health conditions scheme \- A long term conditions scheme ( diabetes, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease); \- A healthy living scheme (diet, obesity, alcohol awareness, addictions etc.). Development priorities for year 1 include: \- Core delivery and development capacity to: \- Support the research and development of new lists \- Refresh, embed and sustain existing lists \- Create and manage partnership networks \- Expand the delivery framework \- Develop support resources \- Resourcing to build a sustainable business model and create flexibility to allow for the production of low cost/free materials \- To support activities to animate the programme \- To enable the development of an evaluation proposal by an accredited external agency and build the case for a clinical impact study \- To research new digital opportunities for Reading Well Books on Prescription aligned to the Society of Chief Librarian’s work on a Universal Digital Presence. There is already significant interest in the idea of a mobile phone app \- To facilitate workforce development to raise standards and build consistency

title: Wild!; a one person show, that unravels the story of a boy with Attention- Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)and the emerging science.
description: tutti frutti's Artistic Director Wendy Harris and Playwright Evan Placey are to create a one person show, Wild!, that unravels the story of a boy with Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). ADHD is common affecting approximately 5% of children worldwide, so on average there is a child with ADHD (diagnosed or undiagnosed) in most classrooms. It is evident from an early age and can have an enormous and life changing impact on school and family life. tutti frutti create carefully c rafted, imaginative, meaningful productions which help children make sense of the world through the safe and shared experience of theatre. Working with the Centre for ADHD and Neurodevelopmental Disorders across the Lifespan (CANDAL), tutti frutti are uniquely placed to bring insight and understanding to this complex topic, allowing the audience to identify with the boy and go on a journey of his experiences, in a sensitive, empathetic but fun and accessible way. In partnership with Professo r David Daley from CANDAL and his team and researched with ADHD patient groups, the play will explore emotions and behaviours associated with ADHD, with support material in the programmes, online and at theatre display stands outlining current biomedical science and explaining the use of medication and behavioural intervention. Wild! will be performed to children aged 3-8 years, their teachers and families across the UK from Spring 2016. Original music will be composed by Dominic Sales and pe rformed live on stage. Movement choreographed by Joanne Bernard, design by Kate Bunce and digital imagery by Fresh Label.

title: Opening Skinner's Box.
description: Opening Skinner's Box will be a mid-scale touring theatre production created by Improbable. Using the book of the same name by Lauren Slater as a starting point, the show will tell the stories of ten great psychological experiments of the 20th century. It will also tell the stories behind the experiments: the people who created them, the historical context from which they emerged, the impact the results had on the world and the controversy Lauren Slater has prompted by revisiting them. This adaptation will be devised and presented with an ensemble of 7 who will play all the characters and tell all the stories. This theatrically flexible approach will enable us to distance ourselves from any single viewpoint and allow the multi-layered meanings and opinions on these experiments to all come through. We will collaborate with two scientists from the Wellcome Trust established Institute of Neuroscience at Newcastle University, whose fields echo the narrative arc of the book, from be haviourism to neurosurgery: Dr John Lazarus is an evolutionary biologist and psychologist and Dr Quoc Vuong is a neuroscientist. Working with them through rehearsals will deepen our understanding of the scientific material and ensure its presentation is accurate. They will participate in the process of creating and presenting this work and their input will be included in the piece, perhaps in the form of a new experiment on the psychology of performance, audience or the interaction between them.

title: Brainy - Research and Development for a new aerial theatre performance collaboration between Scarabeus Aerial Theatre and the Neuroscience in Psychiatry Network (NSPN).
description: Scarabeus Aerial Theatre would like to collaborate with NSPN neuroscientists on a new theatre project entitled Brainiac, part of a three-year trilogy of work created for and in cosultation with young people aged 14-25. We wish to work with the team in order to understand the structure of the teenage brain and use the results of the U.Change programme in a creative and visually attractive way to present these results to a performing arts audience. We would like: -to look at the structure of the healthy teenage brain using the latest neuroimaging techniques and data on measuring feelings and thoughts; - to understand the relationship between the structure of the brain and certain types of behaviour in teenagers and young adults, with a particular emphasis on mood and conduct disorders, risk taking, sense of belonging and loneliness; - to use this information to research and begin developing a new aerial theatre production with a cast of four performers representing four char acters impacted in different ways by the above. We envisage that the performance installation incorporating aerial dance and visual theatre, multimedia projections and a unique set design, to immerse the audience into the inner workings of the teenage and young adult brain.

title: Hysteria 2017: Research and development for four arts commissions: visual arts, moving image, music , performing/live art .
description: The main aim of this project is to conduct research and development for four arts commissions on the theme of Hysteria for a forthcoming Hysteria 2017 public engagement festival. Four commissions in visual arts, moving image, music and performing arts will explore the various iterations of hysteria; from its emergence as a diagnostic category in the 19th century that was mostly applied to women and the contemporary understanding of conversion disorder. As the highlight of the forthcoming public engagement programme the four commissions will examine different aspects of hysteria in light of contemporary society in order to engage audiences on the relationship between psychological trauma and physical illness. The commissions, involving close collaboration between artists and clinical specialists, will explore the history of hysteria as one that charts the efforts of psychological medicine to understand how traumatic experiences can be experienced as problems with the motor and sen sory functions of the body. The project aims to work with leading artists, clinicians and a medical historian to develop the four commissions. Artist filmmaker John Akomfrah will work with Dr Tracey Loughran, Medical Historian at Cardiff University; Artist Cally Spooner will collaborate with Dr Isabel Valli from the Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology and Neuroscience at Kings College London. We are developing two other commissions in performing art with Dr Victoria Tischler Honorary Associat e Professor in Behavioural Sciences at the Institute of Mental Health, University of Nottingham and in music with composer Jocelyn Pook.

title: 'When Cells Misbehave' - Teaching Children about Cancer
description: One in two people in the UK born after 1960 will be diagnosed with some form of cancer, which means children are now increasingly likely to be affected by cancer in their families/communities. Children have a lack of understanding about cancer that encourages anxiety and fearful responses. Professionals have responded to this need by designing an educational and creative package for children to be delivered within schools. A collaboration between science communicators, cancer research scientists, cancer clinicians, and artists will pilot an interactive show about the science of cancer to children aged 8-11 years in primary schools in London. The show will help them understand how and why cancer grows, how patients are treated, and ways to keep their own cells healthy. Learning will be facilitated by using engaging, high quality, artistic methods, such as giant textile models, and stop motion animation. Written and digital resources will be provided making information accessible to children’s families. Teachers and pastoral care staff will be trained to support their children’s learning. The show will also be delivered within Maggie’s Centre and two London Hospitals and performed at the Big Bang Science London Festival 2017.

title: Irene's Ghost
description: Irene’s Ghost is a part animated cinematic documentary about maternal mental illness, telling the story of a son’s search for information about the mother he never knew. The film deals with the historical and contemporary treatment of maternal mental illness, focusing especially on postpartum psychosis, a serious post birth mental illness that affects 1 in 500 women. It also deals with the impact of such illnesses on families. The film is funded by the Wellcome Trust, the BFI, Creative England, the Maudsley Charity and BBC Storyville. A synopsis of the film is attached. The film will have a theatrical release, be shown at festivals and also broadcast on UK TV by the BBC. We are keen to promote and support the release of the film with an outreach project which helps to engage and educate the public and health professionals about the issues raised by the film. This project is the subject of this funding application and includes public and professional screenings, conferences, Q and A sessions, partnership building and an online and social media engagement plan. Current Sample/Rough Cut: https://vimeo.com/135035882 pw: irenesghost Taster:https://vimeo.com/133354997 pw: irenesghost

title: Talking Mental Health (working title)
description: “Talking Mental Health…” is a creative, collaborative project working with children and young people to: \- Co-produce an accessible and engaging 6-minute animation for 9-11 year olds on how to talk about mental health \- Produce a series of support materials for key stage 2 teachers (e.g. lesson plans) and ‘leave behind’ products for children and parents. Collaboration and participation are at the heart of this project. Children and young people will be involved at every stage: shaping the content, tone and style of the animation and supporting materials in workshops and focus groups. There are few resources to support young children to communicate with others if they are facing mental health issues.
