title: Re-Examining the ‘Global’ in Global Mental Health: African Understandings of Mental Disorder and Intellectual Disability
description: Global mental health stands at an important juncture: recent research and policy reveals substantial challenges in closing the mental health treatment gap in low- and middle-income countries. However, worries persist that global mental health represents cultural colonisation by Western psychiatry/pharmacology, exacerbated further by the expansion of psychiatric genomics in African contexts. The project establishes a UK-Africa consortium which seeks to resolve dual ethical imperatives of addressing genuine challenges to mental health care in African settings alongside respect for African cultural thought and practice. The grant will enable: (i) a three-day workshop investigating (a) biomedical/non-biomedical explanatory models of mental disorder and recovery; (b) cultural conceptions of personhood and genetic identity; (ii) an international conference which explores African bioethical contributions to global mental health; (iii) knowledge exchange drop-ins which establish a deliberative forum for 'bottom-up learning'; (iv) published outputs that (a) critically reflect on psychiatric classificatory models and the DSM-V Cultural Formulation interview; (b) the launch of a research and practical agenda for improving dialogue between biomedical and non-biomedical models of mental health. This will establish a collaborative programme of work devoted to future project proposals that advance cross- treatment dialogue and ‘joined-up’ thinking amongst practitioners and researchers of African mental health care.

title: Planning a Global Study on Sexual Health-Related Practices and Behaviours
description: Sex and sexuality are integral parts of being human, and sexual health and wellbeing is an integral part of overall health and wellbeing. However, the behaviours and practices associated with sex and sexuality are almost universally sensitive subjects. A global survey of sexual health related practices and behaviours would provide needed information to challenge gender and social norms around sex; decouple sexual practices from certain populations; and ensure that health systems are informed to provide adequate, quality information and relevant sexual health services. However, a rigorous global study of this nature has never been undertaken – a substantial number of political, social, methodological, and financial feasibility challenges provide significant obstacles. As such, this application seeks funding to bring together global sexual health experts and innovative researchers to brainstorm the feasibility of conducting a global study of sexual practices and behaviours. Two sessions are proposed: 1) a session to identify and describe both comparable and regionally-distinct understandings of sexual behaviour, vulnerabilities, and needs; and 2) a session to define a financially feasible, robust methodology for the assessment. Should this global study of sexual practices and behaviours be deemed feasible, the study will rolled out in subsequent stages.

title: Health Inequalities: Participative Research with Children and Young People
description: CiS will deliver a participative research project with children and young people aged 10-18. Young peer researchers in areas of high deprivation in Glasgow and Dundee will be supported to research how community and place impacts on their health and the choices they make about this. CiS will provide young peer researchers with participative training on health, wellbeing and health inequalities. They will be supported to collect data from their peers in their own communities on how their local area impacts on their health. The young peer researchers will then use this data and their experiences of their local area to conduct ethnographic field research. They will take case notes and visually document the factors they have decided to explore. The young peer researchers will then conduct an analysis of the findings to identify what it is about areas of high deprivation that negatively impact on the health of the children and young people who Page 6 of 10 live there. A report will be produced to make key policy recommendations to support local and national government to develop communities that support better more equitable health. The children and young people will be involved in the dissemination of the findings.

title: REFLECT: Understanding experiences of mental health in deprived coastal communities
description: During our research in a deprived seaside town following a spate of suicides, people expressed an urgent need for a deeper understanding of how mental health can change - and be changed by – living by the sea. Research shows that blue spaces have mental health benefits(1). But individuals’ lived experiences often jar with this; the sea is seen as a place of cruelty; and the site of that most final of mental health outcomes. This project aims to tell the stories of people in mental health treatment living by the sea, and to weave these stories - told through words, music and visual art - into a rich tapestry of their emotional experience of their environment. The sound and art installations co-created by local people with a lived experience of mental health in one deprived setting (Bude, Cornwall), will be taken to a second setting (Newhaven, East Sussex) to test whether new understanding of mental health and the sea translates. We hope the project will empower the individuals involved - who often feel forgotten next to their urban counterparts - and give voice to their experiences in a de-stigmatising manner; and that their insights will drive health research projects.

title: Relate, Create, Integrate
description: We want to enhance the Dragon Café arts and health programme and engage at least 1,000 people with lived experience of mental ill-health over a 2-year period. Providing opportunities for arts practitioners with lived experience to create six productions in collaboration with health researchers and professionals. We will engage at least 500 researchers, arts practitioners and health and social services professionals with this creative programme and employ at least two of our volunteers to support delivery. Digital content will be produced and shared via our digital channels and national and international arts and mental health networks. We will also investigate partnerships with broadcasters. We will build on our successful pop-up Dragon Café model and develop one new pilot in Oxford in partnership with people who have lived experience of mental ill-health. Opportunities to share our model in one other location outside of London will also be explored. Our aim is to empower people with lived experience to set up their own community spaces and play an active role in developing creative engagement programmes connected with mental health research. An evidenced model of our work will be shared through key arts and health networks and events.

title: Examining the associations between educational experiences and mental health from childhood to adulthood
description: Educational achievement is important to children as individuals as well as to society in general. For children, educational achievement, especially the exam results channel them towards different educational and professional trajectories. However, little is known about the effects of this high-stakes educational system on children’s mental health. Childline, a free counselling service for children in the UK, reported that children's top concern is stress and anxiety related to school work and exam performance. These educational pressures can lead to mental health problems that may cast a long shadow later in life for children. This project aims to identify the associations between educational experiences and mental health establishing both aetiology and causal direction, using epidemiological and genetic tools in studies from the UK, Sweden and Estonia. Finally, I aim to develop individualised prediction models for adverse mental health outcomes using both genetic and environmental risk factors. Knowing individual-specific genetic predispositions and understanding how certain environmental factors may dampen or amplify the genetic predictions will improve our understanding of mental health. This knowledge is critical in order to best target future intervention efforts by identifying those children who are at greater risk of developing mental health problems early on.

title: New approaches to understanding Social-Cognition in Anorexia Nervosa
description: Anorexia Nervosa (AN) is a complex disorder with substantial treatment resistance and high mortality rate. It has been suggested that social- emotional difficulties maintain the illness by increasing social isolation and anxiety. Although a few studies have examined the brain processes that underlie social-emotional difficulties in AN, the small sample sizes, outdated paradigms and statistical methods limit the conclusions that can be drawn from these studies. Thus, there is need to improve current methodology to better understand these challenges in AN and their role in illness maintenance to reduce the devastating impact of this disorder. My aim is to develop new, ecologically valid paradigms to assess social-cognition in and outside of the MRI environment as well as novel statistical methods to model neuroimaging data from the naturalistic tasks and identify biomarkers of illness maintenance in the multimodal data. These new methodologies will be applied to a large study examining the brain and behavioural correlates of social- emotional processing in 140 emerging adults with and without AN. This project will test the hypothesis that people with AN show atypical emotional reactivity and negative interpretation bias, and that these difficulties contribute negatively to poor prognosis.

title: Mapping dynamic trajectories of development in autism spectrum disorder: gaining new insights into aetiology and heterogeneity
description: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by substantial behavioural heterogeneity. Although differences in neurobiological functioning are found in individuals with ASD, much of the extant work has used cross-sectional designs and is therefore ill-equipped to answer questions of directionality. I will use advanced statistical techniques to model directional pathways between brain functioning, cognition and behavioural outcomes. First, I will obtain a detailed characterisation of brain functioning across the early developmental period in infants at high and low risk for developing ASD (Objective 1). I will model different trajectories of early brain development that may precede a diagnosis of ASD, and test whether these differ from those found in individuals without a diagnosis, and whether they predict later profiles of cognitive functioning and behavioural symptoms. Next, I will integrate one sample from Objective 1 with longitudinal data from a large sample of individuals with an established diagnosis of ASD to comprehensively test uni- vs. bi-directional pathways between neurobiological functioning, cognition and behavioural symptoms (Objective 2). Better understanding of these pathways may allow for interventions to be targeted towards mechanisms underpinning specific symptoms, rather than global diagnosis. Given the heterogeneity within ASD, this may lead to more effective interventions.

title: Temporal Aspects of Gaze Perception in Autism
description: In our everyday life, the ability to perceive the occurrence and duration of brief mutual gaze interactions provides us with essential social cues. The human eye, with its great prominence of a white sclera against a dark pupil, seems to provide an optimal cue for this task, the importance of which is underlined by the existence of dedicated brain mechanisms that are tuned to the direction of other's gaze. Individuals diagnosed with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) have been reported to struggle with tasks based on gaze information and, in particular, with the detection and interpretation of gaze direction. However, their ability to estimate gaze duration has not been studied yet. In this project, we aim to conduct a systematic behavioural and electrophysiological investigation of the temporal aspects of gaze interactions in ASD and neurotypical participants. We intend to measure duration discrimination for brief intervals containing gaze stimuli, and, simultaneously, record eye-movements and event-related potentials (ERPs). The analysis of these data will allow us to test the existence of a predictive relationship between the autistic traits and changes in gaze time perception and to decode perceived duration from ERP recordings using multivariate pattern analysis.

title: Neurobiological foundations of flexible social behaviour
description: A core aspect of healthy social function is the ability to map our private beliefs onto those that we express publicly according to the social context. It may be socially appropriate to express gratitude for a gift we do not want, or remorse for an action we do not regret. My goal is to understand the neurocognitive mechanisms supporting context-appropriate social behaviours and how they are altered in neuropsychiatric conditions. I will use a novel social interaction task which requires subjects to learn a repertoire of context- dependent mappings from private to public beliefs. I will first apply computational modelling to reveal how subjects solve this problem, identifying ‘prediction-error’ signals that drive changes in ‘private-public’ mappings. I will then relate these time-varying components to voltammetric recordings of dopamine and serotonin in human striatum during task performance. These neuromodulators are relevant because they are known to support learning and are implicated in neuropsychiatric conditions with prominent social dysfunction. Finally, I will complement the voltammetric recordings with non- invasive whole-brain OPM-MEG recordings, to identify neural areas which provide contextual ‘inputs’ for updating private-public mappings and are the ‘targets’ of such updates. This work promises to enhance our understanding of possible routes to social dysfunction.

title: Using multiple data sources to stratify depression and identify more targeted drug treatments
description: Depression is a heritable disorder with a highly polygenic architecture. Progress in obtaining genome-wide significant findings has been slow, but over the last few years large cohorts have become available and have started to yield valuable insights. I will combine information from these cohorts to uncover the genetic underpinnings of the disorder and develop individual-level risk prediction of depression using polygenic risk scoring. The inclusion of non-genetic risk factors for depression is also likely to further increase accuracy of prediction using multifactorial risk scores. This will also allow me to investigate novel methods for identifying modifiable risk factors for depression. Depression is clinically heterogeneous and comorbid with a range of other health conditions. The derived multifactorial risk scores offer the opportunity to stratify depression into subtypes using machine learning methods. I will analyse the genetic and non-genetic risk factors involved in each depression subtype which will improve our understanding of the underlying biology of each subtype. Gene-set analysis will reveal potential drug repositioning opportunities offering more targeted treatments for patients in each subtype. The efficacy of anti-depressant treatment response for specific subtypes will be estimated using currently available electronic health record linked data.

title: Auditory structured sequence learning on multiple timescales
description: Regularities play an important role in analysing auditory scenes; for example, by exploiting the predictable sounds of the car engine, a driver can effortlessly ignore this irrelevant noise, freeing cognitive resources to focus on the road. Regularities also play an important role in language, dictating the relationship between syllables in word or the order words in a sentence, and have been studied to better understand language acquisition and evolution. Despite the critical importance of regularities to both language- motivated and auditory scene-motivated research there are few direct interactions between them. Integrating these previously separate fields, this fellowship will test the hypothesis that sequencing abilities studied within the context of scene-motivated and language-motivated sequence learning will depend on common brain mechanisms. Creating novel stimuli consisting of sequences of rapid (scene-motivated) and slower (language-motivated) stimuli, governed by the same complex relationships, sensitivity to regularities will be assessed using behavioural, pupillometry and electroencephalography studies. Sequence processing proficiency will then be compared to other cognitive abilities and used to explore neurodevelopmental language disorders, e.g. dyslexia. This work will develop novel avenues for understanding the role of sequence processing in the brain and provide potential insights into how these neural processes are disrupted in language disorders.

title: Psychological wellbeing of health workers in low- and lower-middle income countries: A mixed-methods study of levels, determinants, and consequences for turnover and performance across twelve countries in Sub-Saharan Africa.
description: A healthy and productive health workforce is central to a well-functioning health system. However, health workers are at high risk of poor psychological wellbeing due to their particularly strenuous work demands. While a well- researched issue in high-income countries, tangible evidence from low- and lower-middle-income countries (LLMIC) is largely lacking. The few existing studies hint at poor psychological wellbeing of health workers being a substantial concern, compromising patient care in already heavily constrained health systems. Against this background, the study aims to assess psychological wellbeing of health workers and to explore determinants and consequences at the individual, organizational, and broader health system level, across twelve LLMIC in Sub-Saharan Africa. The study will employ a sequential explanatory mixed methods design. The quantitative component relies on comparable secondary data from large, quasi-representative samples, including data from structured health worker surveys, direct observations of clinical consultations and health facility management and resources, and patient interviews. Psychological wellbeing is measured with the WHO-5 Wellbeing Index. Data will be analyzed using multiple group multi-level structural equation modeling. Qualitative methods will then be employed to further explore and explain emerging quantitative results, likely using a case study approach. Key words: health workers, psychological wellbeing, Sub- Saharan Africa
recipient: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine

title: Mindreading, Psychopathology and Social Adjustment in Middle Childhood
description: Approximately 10% of children aged between 6 and 12 have a diagnosable mental health disorder (Beardsmore, 2015). Mental health problems are the leading cause of disability in middle childhood and are linked to peer relationship problems and poor social adjustment at school (e.g., Erskine et al., 2015; Szekely et al., 2016). Our proof-of-concept study asks whether difficulties understanding others’ thoughts and feelings (or ‘mindreading’) explain why children with mental health problems in middle childhood experience adverse social outcomes. We adopt an innovative group-administered mindreading test to collect data from a large community sample of 8- to 12-year-old children to investigate the links between teacher-rated psychopathology symptoms (e.g., emotional problems, hyperactivity, aggression, autism traits), mindreading, and teacher- and peer-rated social adjustment. We apply a dimensional approach to investigate the specificity of the relations between mindreading and psychopathology, and the extent to which mindreading deficits contribute to social adjustment problems among children with psychopathology symptoms. We use machine learning to create an automated scoring procedure for rating children’s text-based responses to tests of mindreading. The project provides crucial evidence and new methods for a future longitudinal investigation of the developmental links between mental health problems, mindreading and social adjustment in middle childhood.

title: iAWARE: Work-Based Online Psychoeducation for the Enhancement of Employees’ Mental Health Literacy and Workplace Wellbeing
description: This project encompasses development of online work-based mental health training using co-production with employees at participating organisations, and testing feasibility of incorporating this tool into organisational strategies for improving employees’ mental wellbeing. iAWARE would be unique in that it would be designed within a complex intervention framework with the explicit objective of forming one component within a systemic approach to workplace wellbeing. This would be achieved by a) allowing for material to be tailored to particular organisation contexts and b) including a reporting function whereby data generated non-reactively through use of the programme is used to inform employers for development at the organisational level. Future will involve robust pilot testing and evaluation, subject to progression criteria, namely indicative positive changes in mental health literacy from baseline for participants in the first phase study, and proven feasibility of integration into diverse complex organisational settings.

title: Worcestershire's Health Record
description: The project proposes to increase the variety of sources available for the study of medicine, health and welfare in Worcestershire by cataloguing and conserving a range of collections from our backlog and retroconverting old paper catalogues relating to hospitals and health professionals and organisations pre and post the formation of the NHS. This will build on our previous project cataloguing the mental health records of Barnsley Hall and Powick Hospitals. The project objectives are: To create catalogues of our unlisted health related collections to international standards for use by medical professionals and researchers and the general public, subject to any limitations imposed by the confidential or sensitive nature of the material. The catalogues will be available at http://www.worcestershire.gov/CalmView/ To retroconvert our pre CALM paper catalogues relating to health/hospital records so that they can be accessed online. To clean, preserve, repackage into appropriately sized boxes and folders and repair fragile items in the collections To promote the project as it progresses and raise awareness of our medical and health records holdings by means of social media, articles in relevant newsletters, an exhibition, presentations at workshops/day schools and a health walk To produce an online guide outlining our main health archive collections

title: Unboxing the boxer: cataloguing papers relating to sport at De Montfort University Special Collecitons
description: This project will facilitate access to a number of significant collections relating to the history of sport in the United Kingdom held in De Montfort University Special Collections, which are not being used to their full potential because they are difficult to retrieve and access. These comprise papers of the Amateur Boxing Association, Sir Norman Chester, Ski Club of Great Britain and the Special Olympics. Together these collections reflect research themes including widening participation in physical activity for health and wellbeing, elitism, exclusion and the place of minority groups in sport, and addressing societal ‘illness’ such as violence and aggression. The item-level cataloguing of these collections will provide invaluable teaching and learning resources for the university and open up the archives for investigation by the international research community. The objectives of the project are to: \- create an item-level ISAD(G) compliant catalogue of each collection, hosted online \- rehouse the collections in appropriate archival packaging \- identify at-risk items and seek conservation treatment if necessary \- conduct migration to different formats where necessary \- publicise the project to internal and external research audiences and the general public \- assist the Heritage Centre Coordinator with a sports heritage exhibition

title: Body Language: movement, dance and physical education in Scotland, 1890-1990
description: Our successfully completed Research Enrichment activity will be as follows: \- A three-month free exhibition, 'Body Language' at the Edinburgh University Main Library Exhibition Gallery (26 July-26 October 2019), which has attracted high visitor figures, publicity, positive feedback and a high level of engagement. Weekly curator tours of the exhibition have been delivered for public, student and school groups. Visitors will have enjoyed the exhibition, engaged with historic collections which they may not normally get the chance to see, and been encouraged to participate in diverse events and to think about their own health and wellbeing; \- Successful delivery of a diverse programme of free public engagement activities around the exhibition, including: movement and dance and art/textile workshops for the public and specific groups, including families and people living with dementia and their carers; screenings of films and live performances inspired by the collections, and a series of public talks from inspiring speakers which encourage debate and discussion around topics raised by the exhibition. \- Creation of a successful legacy beyond the lifetime of the project, including the engagement of new audiences and ongoing and productive partnerships forged with cultural and community organisations. NB: Due to the exhibition programming for the Edinburgh University Main Library Exhibition Gallery, the exhibition will run from 26 July-26 October 2019. We are aware that this overruns the end of the 'Body Language' project, which runs until 17 September 2019. However, all costs requested here are for activities which will begin and end before 17 September 2019.

title: Information-seeking in health and disease
description: People spend a substantial amount of time seeking out information (e.g., reading, asking questions, internet browsing). It is theorized that common psychiatric conditions, including depression and anxiety, are characterized by abnormal information-seeking patterns. These patterns could potentially be measured and used to facilitate diagnosis and treatment selection. However, the precise links between information-seeking and psychopathology are unknown. In fact, we know little about how to quantify information-seeking or the mechanisms that control it. My aim is to understand (i) how people decide to seek or avoid information and (ii) how those decisions relate to mental health. I have developed tasks to quantify key drivers of information-seeking (including valence of information, uncertainty, instrumental utility). I will test participants to assess whether psychopathology symptoms are linked to abnormal influence of these drivers on information-seeking. I will also combine pharmacological manipulation with neuroimaging to examine whether the influence of these drivers is dependent on dopamine – a neuromodulator that malfunctions in several conditions in which information-seeking is theorized to be altered- and identify the neural computations involved. I will assess whether these drivers are over/under expressed in individuals diagnosed with affective disorders, and conduct experiments to determine how these alterations impact well-being.

title: Organising knowledge for flexible behaviour in the prefrontal-hippocampal circuitry
description: Humans and animals can find new solutions to existing problems, and generalise existing knowledge to new situations. This flexibility relies on internal models of the relationships and causes that govern our world. Despite the importance of world-models to a wide class of behaviours and thus likely relevance to psychiatry, little is known about how they are represented in the brain. Recent evidence suggests rapid progress can be made by comparison to the field of spatial cognition. Specific neuronal mechanisms are shared between spatial and non-spatial model-based behaviours, and new theories suggest links between spatial and non-spatial knowledge. We will study and manipulate hippocampal, entorhinal and prefrontal activity in rodents performing model-based tasks bridging spatial and non-spatial domains. Using unusually rich but precisely specified tasks, we will characterise neuronal representations of world models quantitatively, enabling formal mathematical description. We will therefore provide new data describing how internal-models are represented in neuronal activity in service of flexible behaviour, and how these representations generalise knowledge across different tasks. These data will be crucial for developing theories of how our brains represent and generalise knowledge for flexible behaviour, and will lay essential groundwork for studies of how these representations go awry in clinical populations.

title: Common Variant Genetics of Autism and Autistic Traits (GWAS) Consortium
description: Autism is a life-long developmental condition with a prevalence of approximately 1%, and heritability estimates of between 64-92%. It is polygenic, with variants across the frequency spectrum (from rare to common) contributing to risk. Considerable progress has been made in identifying rare variants in autism, but the largest genome-wide association study (GWAS) of autism (18,000 cases, 28,000 controls) identified only five loci associated with autism, compared to 179 in schizophrenia (40,000 cases, 65,000 controls). Polygenic scores account for 2.45% of the variance in autism, despite 30-50% of the variance in risk for autism being attributable to common variants, suggesting many more common variants remain to be found. Additionally, autistic traits are normally distributed in the general population, but there is no well-powered GWAS of autistic traits. The proposed research aims to accelerate the discovery of common, low frequency, and copy number variants in autism and autistic traits. Specifically, we will: (1) Establish a UK-wide Autism Biobank (N = 10,000 cases), with links to electronic health records and who can be recalled by genotype; (2) Conduct a GWAS of autism in 100K cases from around the world; and (3) Conduct a GWAS of autistic traits in the population in 250K individuals

title: Evaluating Health Impacts of Climate Adaptation Strategies
description: Focus Area 3: Adaptation to climate change This research will develop a new evaluation tool for sustainable adaptation that will comprehensively incorporate direct and indirect health effects of adaptation interventions. It will explicitly focus on the wider effects of adaptation for the health and socio-economic wellbeing of the most vulnerable populations. The research will integrate insights from climate and hydrological sciences, social sciences, and health and economic sciences of disease burden and well-being. The evaluation tool will be developed through cross-disciplinary interaction on concepts and methods, and then calibrated through empirical study of existing adaptations, focused on flooding. Flood risk is a prevalent climate impact globally and diverse adaptations currently being implemented globally. New empirical insights into flood adaptation will be generated focussing on three adaptation interventions for: flood infrastructure, planned relocation, and catchment-based planning across Ghana, Ireland, and UK. The project will undertake proof-of-concept evaluations for these interventions to develop the tool, generating specific lessons on flood adaptation and wider lessons on climate change adaptations more broadly. The research will engage with UK stakeholders and other national and international agencies to ensure the tool, evidence and planned user interface will be policy-relevant for adaptation planning at the global scale.

title: Towards personalized cognitive brain stimulation for depression
description: Non-invasive brain stimulation is a new family of treatments for depression. Efficacy is established for TMS to dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and under evaluation for tDCS. Recently efficacy has emerged for two additional targets: dorsomedial prefrontal (DMPFC) and lateral orbitofrontal cortex (LOFC). In the current state of the art, resting-state neuroimaging is being tested to personalize TMS target selection. My vision is to further improve treatment by targeting stimulation based on cognitive function. My project aims to lay the scientific foundations to achieve this. In depression, cognition and emotion are biased towards negative information. According to theory, when drugs and cognitive therapies work, they do so by rapidly reducing negative bias. I will test if this cognitive mechanism mediates TMS treatment and explains individual differences in clinical response. With repeated treatment, people gradually experience the world more positively, which slowly improves mood. This is thought to depend on reinforcement learning. Using tDCS I will stimulate DMPFC to increase learning from positive outcomes. I will stimulate LOFC to reduce inappropriate self-blame for negative outcomes. My scientific aim is to establish proof of concept that this cognitive targeting will improve DMPFC and LOFC stimulation. My long-term goal is to improve treatment.

title: UK Human Developmental Biology Initiative
description: The goal of the Human Developmental Biology Initiative (HDBI) is to be an enabling initiative to support wider research in human development. The UK is well positioned to take a lead in this, given its expertise in model organism developmental biology, the successful operation of the Human Developmental Biology Resource (HDBR) and clear regulation of human embryo research. HDBI will develop a set of core experimental and computational methods for studies in embryonic and foetal tissues. It will do so by focusing on generating foundational data on cell lineage in human development. To promote wider access to human developmental biology research techniques, HDBI will work closely with HDBR to develop the required technologies, creating two research hubs in proximity to the HDBR sites in London and Newcastle. Understanding developmental cell lineage provides an essential basis for comparative studies of development between species, as well as a context for understanding the developmental origins of disease. In addition to technology development, HDBI data will complement insights from Wellcome’s Deciphering Developmental Disorders program, the Human Cell Atlas and the MRC Regenerative Medicine Platform, and provide baseline data for validation of in vitro differentiated human tissue models.

The UK is well positioned to take a lead in this, given its expertise in model organism developmental biology, the successful operation of the Human Developmental Biology Resource (HDBR) and clear regulation of human embryo research. title: BRAINCHART: Normative brain charting for predicting and stratifying psychosis
description: Our goal is to advance normative modelling or ‘brain growth charting’ methods towards clinical utility in psychiatric disorders. Psychiatric disorders are all extremely heterogeneous, which is a major barrier to understanding their pathophysiology and developing better treatments. Yet, the dominant case- control paradigm assumes that clinical groups are homogeneous and well- defined. We recently introduced normative modelling as an alternative tool to map biological variation across clinical cohorts at the level of individual participants, whilst cutting across classical diagnostic classifications1. Using normative modelling, we showed that by focusing on the ‘average patient’, case-control analyses conceal considerable inter-individual variability in patients with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder2. Now, we aim to convert the brain ‘fingerprints’ provided by normative modelling into a stratification of individuals. This will enable us to take the next step in developing normative modelling as a tool to bring precision medicine to psychiatry. We will: (i) capitalise on ‘big data’ cohorts to define normative brain growth models across the lifespan; (ii) use these models to predict the onset and outcome in early psychosis at the level of the individual and (iii) develop a prototype software tool for research and ultimately to assist clinical decision-making in many disorders.

title: AUTOMATED ANALYSIS FRAMEWORK FOR FDOPA PET IMAGING AS A BIOMARKER FOR TREATMENT STRATIFICATION IN PSYCHOSIS
description: Having completed several successful experimental medicine studies using FDOPA PET imaging in psychosis, we are now working to translate this imaging modality into clinical practice. This scheme will allow us to develop the analytical tools necessary to make it possible. Specifically, we will develop an automated optimised analysis framework to: i) quantify abnormal dopamine synthesis from FDOPA PET imaging, and ii) develop and validate a prediction model for treatment stratification in psychosis. The approach will include all relevant clinical variables and account for experimental variability and patient heterogeneity in the prediction. This project will take advantage of our unique, existing FDOPA PET datasets. Once completed, the tools developed from this project will facilitate the evaluation of FDOPA PET imaging in a multi-centre large-scale clinical trial with clinical collaborators from KCL and other leading clinical research centres. Our vision is to deliver a mental healthcare technology which is cost effective and informed by the underlying neurobiology. Incorporating FDOPA PET imaging into an automated analysis pipeline could be game changing in the management of patients with psychotic disorders and would augment traditional clinical assessments for psychosis, leading to biologically-informed diagnosis, monitoring and treatment of individual patients.

title: Developing an E-Mental Health Detection Tool for Early-Stage Psychosis in the Community
description: Our vision is to extend the benefits of early interventions for young people with emerging psychosis (1), including those with a Clinical High Risk state for Psychosis (CHR-P) (3) and those with a First-Episode of Psychosis (FEP), to the wider community. This is because currently only a minority of young people have access to specialized services (2) and as a result, emerging psychosis is only detected at later stages (4). To achieve this vision, we will develop a novel E-Mental Health detection tool. While some risk estimation models are available to improve the detection of CHR-P and FEP individuals, these models tend to be complex and their scalability is limited. We believe that to improve the detection of emerging psychosis at scale, a cheap and simple detection tool is needed. We feel that digital tools could critically address this issue. We expect that this funding will provide a potentially ground-breaking approach towards better identifying young people with emerging psychosis in the community through the use of E-Mental Health. In our view, this approach could also pave the way for widespread use of E-Mental Health applications for an improved detection of emerging mental disorders beyond the psychosis field.

title: LAMP – REP: Learn, Assess, Manage, Prevent for Relapse in Early Psychosis
description: Reducing the mental health access and treatment gap in all countries around the world, especially in low- and middle-income countries (LMIC), requires innovative approaches to care. This project will form the foundation for a scalable and sharable digital health solution that offers novel ways to both assess personal risk of relapse in schizophrenia and also immediately respond to that risk with real time evidence based adjunctive interventions. The LAMP (Learn, Assess, Manage, Prevent) smartphone application proposed here represents a patient centered, transparent, and collaborative approach to digital health – a vision in contrast to so many proprietary digital health platforms today. We plan to openly share all resulting code, apps, and results so others can expand and build upon our work. The partnership between sites in the United States and two unique sites in India represents our team’s vision for global mental health solutions that are broadly applicable and informed by patients, family members, and clinicians from diverse cultures and backgrounds.

title: The overlapping genetic architecture of platelet granularity and neurodevelopmental disorders
description: Platelets are blood cells needed for clot formation. Neurons are brain cells which transmit information through chemical signals. Although they have different roles in the body, platelets and neurons both function by releasing tiny substance-filled packages called granules. Previous research has shown that similar genes control this process in both cell types. Autism is a neuron disorder which affects the way individuals interact with the world. The genes causing autism are poorly understood but are thought to be involved in the formation of neuron granules. Platelet genes are better understood. I plan to use the similarities between platelet and neuron granules to identify new genes causing autism. In the longer term, we hope this research leads to improvements in diagnosing and treating the disorder. My research builds on data showing that differences between healthy people in the number of granules in platelets are linked to subtle changes in genes. I will analyse lists of these genetic changes and select those most likely to be involved in both platelet granule formation and autism. For the most promising genetic change, I will alter this gene in cells in the laboratory to see if this affects granules, and therefore could contribute to autism.

title: Determining the molecular basis of newly discovered developmental disorders identified in genetically-isolated communities
description: Developmental disorders such as intellectual disability and developmental malformations are a frequent cause of long-term disability during childhood. Many of these conditions are caused by changes in our genetic code, affecting how we grow and develop. Unfortunately, as the causes of developmental disorders are wide-ranging and complex, many children may never receive a diagnosis. Knowledge of how genes go wrong may aid scientific understanding of normal development. This in turn may benefit a child's on-going treatment and, in the longer term, could prevent other children having similar problems. The Amish are a community descended from a small numbers of individuals. The unique genetic make-up and distinctiveness of the Amish population provides an opportunity to overcome some of the difficulties encountered by researchers defining the causes of inherited disorders. Importantly, almost all conditions identified amongst the Amish have been identified outside the community, enabling benefits to be provided for children with similar disorders worldwide. This study aims to learn more about the genetic causes of developmental disorders amongst the Amish. This will provide important health benefits including improved diagnostics and clinical management strategies for the Amish and other families worldwide with these conditions, alongside aiding scientific understanding of human development.

title: Exploration of the relationship between social cognition and PTSD in the pre, peri and post-trauma period.
description: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a disabling psychiatric illness that can occur following a very distressing event, such as sexual assault or war. People with this illness experience very upsetting, intrusive memories and nightmares, have a heightened sense of threat, and try to avoid reminders of the event. However, not everyone who experiences a traumatic event will develop PTSD; this project tries to better understand why that is, by examining the role of social cognition in both the onset and recovery of PTSD. Social cognition is the ability to understand emotions in yourself and others, and it has been hypothesised that difficulties with social cognition may increase the risk of developing PTSD. Using data from the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC), a large study of children born in 1991/1992, I will examine whether difficulties with social cognition in childhood lead to an increased risk of PTSD in adults. I will then undertake a study of around 50 adult patients with PTSD and assess their social cognition and review their progress after several months to see if social cognition deficits affect recovery from PTSD. This study could have implications for the way that we understand and treat PTSD.

title: The role of sequential neuronal replay in inference and decision making using MEG
description: In order act appropriately to achieve goals the human brain needs to represent not only the objects in the environment (e.g. people), but also the relationships between them (e.g. friend or foe). Such a representation has been termed a ‘cognitive map’, and is essential for flexible goal-directed behaviour and inferences about the ‘structure’ of the environment.1 Recently, work has focussed on how the brain uses cognitive maps to plan actions, but less attention has been devoted to studying the neural processes that support the creation and updating of the maps themselves.2 One proposed mechanism for consolidating and updating internal maps involves the rapid ‘replay’ of experienced events in during rest periods, originating in the medial temporal lobe.3–5 This is a central question for neuroscience and psychiatry, where many symptoms can be thought of as arising from maladaptive representations of the world. Examples include an inference of immediate threat in anxiety and psychotic disorders, and maladaptive schemata in personality disorders. Notably, animal models of schizophrenia implicate abnormal hippocampal replay and remapping.6,7 I will study the neural processes underpinning the creation and updating of cognitive maps in humans using non-invasive brain imaging, with a focus on fast sequential activity (replay).

title: An inflammatory biomarker study of psychosis: a longitudinal study in an at risk population
description: Psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia are illnesses characterised by symptoms such as delusions, hallucinations and loss of contact with reality. These disorders are associated with severe disability for affected patients. We know that in many cases the onset of the disorder is preceded by symptoms that do not meet clinical criteria for disorder, but are nevertheless troublesome for those affected and can predict a poorer outcome. Intervening in this critical period may reduce the impact of the disorder or even prevent its onset. However, relying on symptoms alone can be problematic and we need to develop a better understanding of the underlying causes. Recent research is highlighting the influence of inflammation and the immune system in the development of many mental illnesses such as psychotic disorders and depression. In this study, we will analyse blood samples and data from participants in the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC) to examine the association between inflammatory blood proteins and the development of psychotic experiences and depression. This will help us to better understand how this relationship develops over time and whether early inflammatory signals can help to predict the onset of such symptoms.
recipient: Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland

title: The effects of antipsychotics on glial cells, neuroinflammation and demyelination.
description: Schizophrenia is a severe mental disorder that affects how a person thinks, feels and behaves. It can be very disabling and reportedly one percent of the population is diagnosed with the condition worldwide. It, as well as other mental health conditions can be treated with antipsychotic medication. There are many different antipsychotics, all appear to function by changing the level of the neurotransmitter (a signalling chemical released by nerve cells) dopamine. However, their exact mechanism of action is still unknown. Other non-nerve cell types called glia play a role in schizophrenia and may be effected by antipsychotic medication. These cells serve many functions in the brain including supporting nerve cells, forming myelin (an insulating sheath around nerves) and influencing immune responses. I aim to examine the effects of antipsychotic medication on glial cells with the goal of understanding and exploring the ways these drugs may act via non-nerve cells. I will especially look to see whether these drugs influence the development of myelin and/or protect against demyelination. The overall ambition of this work is to elucidate new molecular and cellular pathways that may guide future antipsychotic drug research and development eventually benefiting patients with schizophrenia and other neuropsychiatric disorders.

title: The Efficacy of, and Mechanisms underpinning, Pramipexol as an Antidepressant
description: I will be investigating the mechanisms by which Pramipexole, a drug which mimics the neurochemical dopamine, alters depressed people's reactions to positive and negative feedback. I will be doing this so that we can increase our understanding about the brain mechanisms that underlie the ways in which depressed people perceive and react to the world. My hope is that understanding these mechanisms will help us to make more effective, targeted and individualized treatments for depression.

title: Validating 5HT4 agonism as a novel antidepressant mechanism
description: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) produce a generalised increase in brain serotonin levels, which leads to multiple side effects and several weeks’ delay for a clinical effect. Previous work indicates that medications activating only one type of serotonin (5-HT) receptor might be effective and rapidly-acting antidepressants. Therefore, I plan to examine the effects of drug treatments with specific activators of 5-HT4 receptors on a range of measures affected in depression, including how people see different facial expressions Firstly, I will examine the effect of 5-HT4 activators compared to SSRI and/or placebo on measures of emotional processing including a brain scan (fMRI), both in healthy volunteers and in un-medicated patients with depression. I will determine if, like clinically-effective antidepressants, 5-HT4 agonists produce positive biases in how people process emotions. I will also examine the effect of a 5-HT4 activator compared to placebo in healthy volunteers, examining both behavioural and brain responses to a reward/punishment task using fMRI. I will assess if this medication appears to reduce negative responses to anticipation of punishment. I will also assess for any early adverse effects. The key goal of this translational project is to confirm whether specific 5-HT receptor agents may have potential as antidepressants.

title: The effects of anti-inflammatory drugs on emotional and reward processing
description: The purpose of these studies is to investigate whether anti-inflammatory drugs change how the brain deals with emotional and rewarding information, with a view to improve treatments for people suffering from depression. There is growing scientific evidence that some people who do not respond to conventional antidepressants may benefit from taking anti-inflammatory drugs. Our research has previously shown that antidepressants affect how people experience certain kinds of information, for example by making them focus on positive facial expressions more than negative ones. These effects on ‘emotional processing’ can be found very early on in treatment, even before a patient ‘feels better’; however, we can measure these early changes and use this information to predict whether the treatment will actually help people feel better in the long term. The drugs we are investigating are called tofacitinib and atorvastatin. These are licensed drugs which has been shown to be generally safe and well-tolerated. We will test whether tofacitinib and atorvastatin can alter emotional processing in the same way as standard antidepressant drugs, comparing them with placebo (dummy tablet). Since reward processing and inflammation have been linked to depression, we will assess the effects of these drugs on these measures too.

title: How do males of South Asian origin with long-term conditions understand, experience and seek help for emotional distress?
description: One of the greatest challenges facing healthcare today is treating people with multiple long-term health conditions, a term known as multimorbidity. People with multimorbidity of both physical and mental illness fare worse; they have a worse quality of life and die earlier. People from ethnic minority communities are more vulnerable to mental illnesses such as depression and anxiety; they are under-diagnosed, under-treated and health outcomes are worse. South Asians (SAs) are the largest minority group in the UK and are at a much higher risk of certain conditions such as diabetes and heart disease. Little is known how SAs with long-term conditions understand, experience and seek help for emotional distress, in particular for SA males. A systematic review will initially be undertaken to summarise the current research around SAs with long-term conditions and their experiences of depression of anxiety. A qualitative study will then be done, interviewing SA males with long-term conditions and primary care clinicians in areas with high numbers of SAs. The research will explore how SA males understand, experience and seek help for emotional distress, and what the facilitators and barriers are to primary care clinicians in treating them.

title: Alcohol consumption and brain health
description: Exposure to alcohol is widespread but potentially modifiable. Whilst heavy drinking is recognized as detrimental to the brain, the impact of more moderate intake remains unclear. This project seeks to better understand the relationship between alcohol intake and brain health. Specific aims: \- Examine the causal relationship between alcohol intake and dementia. \- Investigate the causal association between drinking and brain imaging markers. \- Identify mediating pathways between alcohol and brain health. The proposed studies will triangulate large-scale electronic health records with neuroimaging and genetic data in UK Biobank (n=500,000) and Million Veterans Program in the US (n=760,000). The project will include complementary observational and pseudo-experimental (Mendelian randomization) approaches, and examine for consistency of findings across methods. Outcomes: This work will comprise the largest and most in depth study of alcohol’s association with brain health. It has extensive application for the study of other exposures relating to psychiatric phenotypes. The findings are likely to be of widespread interest and relevance to scientific and clinical fields, as well as policy-makers and the public.

title: Study of Neuronal Antibodies in Peadiatric Epilepsy
description: In patients with new-onset refractory status epilepticus, 48% of have an autoimmune aetiology. Moreover, neuronal autoantibodies (e.g. N-methyl-D- aspartate receptor antibodies (NMDAR-Abs)) are found in 10-30% of children and adults with less severe epilepsy, most commonly in focal drug-resistant cases. These data underline the scale and the seriousness of autoimmune epilepsy (AE). Immunotherapy is the mainstay of treatment, but is often slow to work (a key issue in refractory status, where time is critical) and risks significant side-effects. In my NMDAR-Ab AE model, receptor-specific treatment with the neurosteroid pregnenolone sulphate (PS) counteracts the autoantibody effect at the neuronal membrane level leading to rapid and specific reversal of NMDAR-Ab mediated electrophysiological changes. Pregnenolone, the precursor to PS, has been successfully used in clinical trials as an adjunctive treatment in schizophrenia patients [33-35], demonstrating its safety, and highlighting the potential for future drug trials. My proposed research will investigate other neuronal antibodies, e.g.to the gamma-aminobutyric acid A receptor, elucidate their pathogenicity and epileptogenicity using AE models, and treat them with receptor-specific, existing, licensed treatment. This approach directly addresses the unmet clinical need for rapid intervention in autoimmune epilepsy, reduced side-effects from immunotherapy and prevention of persistent cognitive problems, thereby improving long-term paediatric outcomes.

title: Scientific Literacy in Nigeria: Boosting Science Communication and Journalism
description: Nigerian’s health and wellbeing are being affected by a lack of science culture in the country and little interest in science journalism, resulting in absent or inaccurate reporting of health research in the media. This project aims to address this problem by bringing together local scientists and journalists to encourage accurate scientific reporting. We want people in Nigeria to value and trust the role of health and science research in order to improve their health outcomes through empowering journalists by providing training in science journalism and access to experts in health research while educating researchers on how to talk to journalists and the general public. Collectively, this project would inspire a change in the perception of science and health research in Nigeria by promoting awareness about health-related research, enhancing trust through visible science role models and improve the use of healthcare treatment based on scientific research. Ultimately this will contribute to a shared value of science, increased collaboration between scientists and journalists that would eventually result in increased visibility of health research and accurate dissemination of research outcomes.

title: SWEET DREAMS; understanding the importance of sleep for children
description: Research shows that sleep is vital to good health for young children, yet this is not widely recognised or understood. Sleep deprivation has a serious impact on emotional, physical and mental health and is a growing problem in families. tutti frutti plans to respond to this through the development of an imaginative play about the benefits, wonders and fears associated with sleep for 3-7 year olds, based on scientific research augmented with sleep workshops in schools. On tour they will engage with audiences to research the subject of children's habits and perceptions of sleep. The show will tour schools and theatres across the UK, reaching up to 4,000 young children and their families. Sleep Practitioners will attend key theatre venues to offer post show parental ‘surgeries’. Dubit will devise digital methods to collect audience data on understanding how children think about sleep. This will feed into a piece of SCH research on understanding the TCSC sleep intervention approach that leads to long term behavioural changes in children and families. These findings will be presented at the BSS 2021 Conference. A successful application would also allow the company to optimise a one-off opportunity of ACE matched funding secured until August 2019.

title: 4.48 engages the deaf community nationally with mental health debate
description: With the 2018 production nominated for multiple awards, reaching 1, 713 people in person and 11, 808 online, 4.48 will upscale in 2019, actively engaging marginalised deaf communities in four UK localities with new deaf mental health research and debate. The 2018 project broke a significant ‘taboo’ around openly discussing deaf mental health, which affects 50% of the deaf community. Academic involvement revealed widespread ignorance around use of BSL/sign in psychosis, minimal available bilingual support, a need for more deaf-qualified professionals and no recent deaf sector statistics. Delivered with 4 national organisational partners and 4 academic researchers, 4.48 will grow debate and research, with its fulcrum a revival of 4.48 PSYCHOSIS delivered alongside an extended auxiliary event programme. 4.48 will transport deaf mental health debate to locations where it has never been discussed, enabling more extensive deaf engagement and ongoing advocacy. The project’s legacy will be three-fold. New resource materials will be available. A national online network will link all 4 regional communities in advocacy and debate. A combined Vlog from academic researchers will identify recommendations for change around use of sign, regional needs and improvements to bilingual provision, growing awareness of this vital issue in creative and relevant ways.

title: Unified modelling of structural and functional imaging for accurate brain connectivity mapping in health and disease
description: Diffusion and functional magnetic resonance imaging(dMRI/fMRI) offer unique non-invasive possibilities to study brain connections and organisation in- vivo, and explore dys-connections associated with mental disorders. However, existing technology has significant limitations. As MRI probes connectivity indirectly, computational models are needed to infer connections from images. A key bottleneck is that this inference is modality(dMRI/fMRI)-specific. Complementary information is ignored and,as each modality has independent assumptions/limitations, errors and ambiguities arise that hinder research reproducibility and uptake into clinical applications. Our goal is to develop a unified modelling framework that allows brain connectivity estimation with unprecedented accuracy and precision. Given the complementarity in dMRI and fMRI, which probe differently grey matter regions and white matter bundles, we will devise an integrated biophysical approach, where multiple modalities inherently constrain and augment each other. The project will deliver to end- users(neuroscientists/clinicians) new computational methodology, ready for proof-of-concept applications in characterising individual variability of brain organisation, where accuracy is key. The approach will be directly applicable to existing large-scale datasets(e.g. UK-Biobank) and will pave the way to progress connectivity mapping to the next level.The project is the first step towards the long-term aim of personalised brain mapping and a stepping stone for the PI to establish scientific independence.

title: Dynamic functional connectivity in neonates during active and quiet sleep
description: Dynamic functional connectivity (dFC) during resting functional (f)MRI captures the constant neural adjustments which control different brain states and support cognition and behaviour. Abnormalities in dFC are linked to neurodevelopmental disorders (NDD) such as autism spectrum disorder in adults; but no-one has examined infants. This is essential; the foundations of cognition and behaviour are established, and pathology linked to NDD emerge, in early life. Hence, my primary goal is to establish a reference dataset of ‘normative’ dFC during fMRI in natural sleep from a large cohort of neonates. Subsequently, I will generate Proof of Concept that anomalous dFC can be identified in neonates at-risk of NDD. The design exploits the fact that neonatal sleep comprises 2 brain states. First, I will confirm that respiratory indices routinely acquired during sleep-fMRI differentiate 2 sleep phases defined by simultaneous EEG. Then, I will characterise dFC within and between each (respiratory-defined) state. Establishing the maturation profile of neonatal dFC, and identifying early deviation, will seed larger studies to i) examine if/how genetic and/or prenatal environmental insults disrupt the emergence of typical dFC; and ii) determine whether early abnormalities in dFC predict outcomes. This will inform future tailored preventions and interventions to optimise infant health.

title: Understanding the Role of Protein Disorder in Amelogenesis Imperfecta
description: Amelogenesis imperfecta (AI) is a genetically and clinically heterogeneous group of congenital conditions, characterised by generalised dental enamel defects to both primary and permanent teeth. It ranges from mild discolorations to severe loss of tooth structure, requiring extensive restorative treatment. Amelogenin, an intrinsically disordered protein (IDP), is the major extracellular protein in developing enamel and is thought to be critical for the formation of the hierarchical architecture of enamel. Mutations in the gene encoding amelogenin are one of the key causes of AI. It is unknown how the mutated amelogenins generate the defective structure of human enamel in AI. We aim to study the structural differences between mutated and non-mutated amelogenins in respect to their conformation, size and charge, including their interactions with calcium phosphate in solution. Then, scaffolds based on mutated amelogenins will be fabricated and mineralised to investigate the role of amelogenin disorder-order interplay on mineralisation within a bulk environment. This will determine the physiochemical properties of the hierarchical mineralisation as guided by mutated and non-mutated amelogenins. The generation of these in-vitro models will not only represent a critical leap to elucidate the mechanisms of amelogenesis imperfecta, but also to provide strategies to tackle this enamel developmental disorder.

title: Investigating a common developmental origin for sensory issues and disturbed sleep, in Autism
description: Sensory hypersensitivity is one of the earliest predictors of later social and cognitive impairments in Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD). We have limited understanding of the mechanisms linking hypersensitivity to poor learning. Here, we propose that a failure to filter out sensory input during sleep interferes with the critical role sleep has in off-line plasticity and learning consolidation, with knock-on effects on cognitive development. To understand the mechanisms and full developmental impact of disturbed sleep, we will establish a cohort of infants at familial-risk for ASD to undergo deep- phenotyping of sensory processing during sleep and wakefulness. We will focus on the function of particular sleep EEG features, such as spindles and slow oscillations, known to be critical for gating the sensory deafferentation during sleep. During infants’ habitual naps we will use cutting-edge on-line spindle detection algorithms to experimentally probe their sensory gating abilities and measure the impact on off-line consolidation of newly learned vocabulary. This project will establish the “poor sleep” biomarkers needed for assessing the impact of early interventions aimed at enhancing the learning function of sleep oscillations. It will also open new avenues for investigating the mechanisms underlying sensory impairments and their impact on learning, in neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: Feasibility of a large-scale, international, clinical-genetic study of postpartum psychosis
description: Postpartum psychosis represents a unique opportunity to study the effects of reproductive factors on the human brain. One of the most severe and dramatic psychiatric illnesses, it affects ~1 in 1000 women soon after childbirth, in many cases unexpectedly.Genetic factors may be involved, but its causes remain poorly understood. The lack of official recognition and definition have hindered research and negatively impacted sufferers. For the first time this project will harness pre-existing international collaborations and datasets to establish cross-culturally valid definitions and standards of assessment of postpartum psychosis and create a pipeline for data acquisition, quality control and harmonization. Genome-wide analyses will provide metrics and preliminary evidence for a larger study. New collaborations and additional datasets will be sought. This study will lay the foundation for a postpartum psychosis international consortium. It will provide data beyond the lifetime of the funding and a robust, systematic approach to uncover the biology of psychosis triggered by childbirth. It will potentially give clues into new, fast-track targets for translational and pharmacological research and improve risk prediction. Moreover, it will contribute to the de-stigmatization of mental disorders related to female reproduction by providing evidence-based, accessible information to the public.

title: Adrenal dysfunction and obesity in Down Syndrome
description: Obesity is a common problem in Down Syndrome (DS). The reason for DS-related obesity is poorly understood. MRAP is located in the chromosome-21 DS-critical region and the majority of DS individuals have 3-copies of MRAP. We have previously shown that MRAP affects glucocorticoid (GC) production from the adrenal gland. Too little GC is fatal and too much results in a myriad of complications including weight gain, obstructive sleep apnoea, osteoporosis, depression/anxiety, cataracts and glaucoma. Interestingly, these GC excess phenotypes are overrepresented in DS. We have data to suggest that fasted DS- mice have higher GC production. The purpose of this proposal is to generate data to demonstrate adrenal hyper-responsiveness due to an extra copy of MRAP and propensity to obesity in DS-mice. These data will then form the basis of future grant proposals to study adrenal function and metabolism in DS individuals. The project is a new direction of research for the applicant, which is directly translational and utilises her clinical expertise. The project will cement new collaborations to study innovative DS mouse models and the LonDownS cohort of DS participants. The work could transform understanding of adrenal function and obesity in DS and hence provide therapeutic options in the future.

title: Sleep and emotional dysregulation: enduring effects of chronic sleep loss in adolescence
description: Chronic sleep loss is common in modern societies and is epidemic among adolescents. Prefrontal cortical networks, which are integral to decision- making and emotion regulation, are some of the most susceptible brain regions to sleep loss. Convergent lines of evidence suggest that, since cortico-limbic interconnections continue to develop until young adulthood, chronic sleep loss during adolescence could interfere with the development and integration between these brain regions. I hypothesize that altered connectivity between medial prefrontal cortex and amygdala underlies the association between sleep disruption and increased risks of emotional dysregulation, anxiety and depression in adolescents and adults. I aim to: (1) establish a novel protocol of chronic sleep restriction (CSR) in adolescent mice; (2) begin characterising persistent effects on medial prefrontal cortex-amygdala connectivity, using confocal and electron microscopy and (3) investigate the long-term consequences on emotional sensitivity by using two established assays of stress-coping behavior. This research will lay the groundwork for a larger programme designed to define cellular, network and behavioural consequences of sleep loss during development, illuminating mechanistic understanding of the functions of sleep and informing policy and practice in relation to sleep hygiene.

title: Deep Learning of Cerebral Cortex Microstructure
description: My research aims to bridge the gap between in vivo neuroimaging and underlying brain microstructure. MRI can inform us of shape or signal intensity changes in neurological and psychiatric diseases but has limited interpretability with respect to underlying neurobiological disturbances. Currently such specific measurement of neurobiology is only accessible through ex vivo histological techniques. I wish to further our understanding of how in vivo MRI reflects microstructure through three interrelated projects. 1) I will map the distribution of microstructural properties, including cytoarchitecture, myeloarchitecture and receptor-architecture to whole-brain reference atlases, thus representing these features in the space of brain scans. 2) I will create deep learning frameworks for analysing cerebral cortical structure. 3) I will use computational tools to link in vivo MRI cortical structure to its underlying microstructure in health and disease. I will use high-resolution and multi-modal structural MRI data to link interregional and interlaminar MRI differences to their underlying microstructural source. I will apply deep learning to a large cohort of patients with a form of surgically remediable epilepsy, focal cortical dysplasia, which is characterised by abnormal microstructure. This work aims to solve the clinical challenge of identifying subtle epileptogenic structural abnormalities from a patient’s presurgical MRI scan.

title: Applying causal inference methods to investigate the impact of adverse childhood experiences on mental health
description: Children exposed to abuse, neglect, and dysfunctional home environments (e.g., parental substance abuse, mental illness, domestic violence) have an elevated risk of developing costly and impairing mental health problems. However, as highlighted in a recent report by the UK Science and Technology Select Committee, the extent to which these adverse childhood experiences cause mental health problems is not known. This is because children exposed to adversities are likely to have other genetic and environmental risk factors for mental health problems, which may confound previously observed associations. I will apply causal inference methods to disentangle the effects of adverse childhood experiences on mental health from genetic and environmental confounds. In doing so, I will make use of data from three large population-based cohorts of children from the UK, Sweden, and Norway, with measures of adverse childhood experiences, mental health, and potential confounding factors (including genetic data). By examining whether findings converge across different causal inference methods with different assumptions, I will be able to draw more confident conclusions about the effects of adverse childhood experiences on mental health. In turn, the findings will indicate the extent to which interventions targeting adverse childhood experiences could prevent children from developing mental health problems.

title: Paternalism, Health, and Public Policy
description: It is a widely-shared assumption that we ought not to treat rational adults paternalistically. In particular, we should respect agents’ decisions about their own medical treatment. Yet in certain public health contexts it seems more appropriate to focus on promoting citizens’ well-being, rather than on respecting choices. Indeed, in some contexts it is not obvious what respecting autonomous decisions would require. For example, when dealing with diverse groups with conflicting preferences, or when implementing public health policies for populations whose autonomous capacities might be called into question, such as children and disabled individuals. Do we still have a responsibility to avoid paternalism in these cases? Is paternalistic treatment even possible here, if we cannot identify the autonomous will of these individuals or groups? The philosophical literature has produced sophisticated models of paternalism, but typically focuses on small-scale interactions between individuals. Thus, it fails to adequately engage with these more complex, but practically important, cases. Over four inter-disciplinary workshops, the proposed project aims to rectify this. We will stimulate new collaborative research to ground the philosophical discussion in the problems that are animating public and professional debate, as well as developing theoretical frameworks that can inform and structure potential policy responses.

title: MedEnv: Intersections of medical and environmental humanities
description: Our key goal is to establish a network and programme of activities that explore the intersection between medical and environmental humanities. Our ambition is to lead research in this field from an historically-informed humanities standpoint and to develop future research collaborations to consider the rich nature of human and non-human interrelationships and their impact on health and wellbeing. A series of thematic workshops will focus on the key challenges of Climate, Animals and Healthy Cities, and a biennial conference will be established to further research on the complex relationships between health and environment from a humanities perspective. We aim to develop new collaborative research proposals as well as build capacity. Therefore the network will use the programme of activities to support and encourage postgraduate students and postdoctoral researchers who work in these fields.

title: Global Environmental (in)Activism: a Multi-sited Ethnography of Industrial Pollution, Illness and Community Resistance in Italy and Taiwan
description: The research proposed is a multi-sited ethnographic investigation into the relationship between industrial pollution as a health threat and the ongoing social, political, and moral struggle of two communities living in close proximity to polluting sites. Through a comparative study of the people of Taranto, Italy, and Tainan, Taiwan, this project seeks to explore the political dimensions of environmental health degradation and exposure by conceiving pollution as a complex symbolic configuration assembled at the crossroads of historical, scientific, legal, and interpersonal trajectories. Understanding how these communities make sense of their polluted worlds is fundamental in order to grasp their political aspirations and their self- collocation within local and global narratives of environmentalism. This project expands and builds on Anna Lora-Wainwright's (2017) notion of resigned activism and seeks to scale up its theoretical framework to non-Chinese contexts of environmental degradation. Environmental justice research currently focuses on the local dimension of suffering, and calls for theoretical tools empowering marginalised communities to connect globally and participate in policy making at the international level. This research responds to this call and moves the field toward a global narrative of environmental health injustice, generating tools for the incorporation of ethnographic evidence into policy making and implementation.

title: What separates us? Reimagining Life Together Beyond the Psychiatric Asylum Model. A Study of Uruguay's Deinstitutionalisation Process Through Audio- Visual Practice.
description: This practice-based research engages with Uruguay’s ongoing deinstitutionalisation process bringing together spatial theories of coexistence and participatory art.
