We aim to recruit 36 CHR-P individuals aged 18-40 to take part in this double-blind, within-subject, crossover, placebo-paired experimental medicine study. We will use functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) and Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy (1H-MRS), to test the effects of a single dose of the antiepileptic medication levetiracetam on neuroimaging measures. The primary objective is to evaluate the acute effect of levetiracetam on hippocampal cerebral blood flow (rCBF) in CHR-P. We will also determine if levetiracetam (vs. placebo) will improve hippocampal resting-state connectivity, improve fMRI activation during a scene processing task and modulate levels of cortical GABAergic and glutamatergic metabolites.

title: Brain neurocircuitry features of resilience to mental health conditions in young people
description: Childhood adversity is experienced by over half of children and adolescents and is a significant contributor to mental health conditions. Understanding resilience as a dynamic process, where individuals with mental health conditions can still exhibit positive outcomes despite adversity, is crucial. This project leverages the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, a longitudinal dataset of approximately 11,000 North American children, to explore resilience across various adversity-mental health domains. The study aims to identify brain features that can be fortified through non- invasive, non-pharmacological interventions to promote resilience in youth. The first part involves a systematic review to identify existing literature on MRI features of resilience amenable to behavioural interventions in children and adolescents. The second part uses exploratory factor analysis and linear regression on the ABCD dataset to identify dimensions of adversity and their associations with mental health outcomes. The third part assesses if identified MRI features are moderators across different adversity-mental health dimensions, utilising high-performance computing for data analysis. Ultimately, the goal is to identify behavioural health interventions to promote mental health resilience in youth, providing a foundation for future interventions in educational and community settings. Keywords: childhood adversity, mental health, resilience, neuroimaging, behavioural interventions

title: What happens to the Mental Health of Children and Young People whilst they wait for Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services?
description: Prioritising early intervention in children and young people’s mental health is important because most mental health difficulties begin before the age of 18. Currently Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services (CAMHS) are facing many challenges including increasing numbers of referrals and long waiting times. We know from studies in adults and adolescents that there are significant inequities in the mental health of people from Black and Minority Ethnic backgrounds. These likely begin in childhood but has been less studied. My study aims to understand what happens right at the beginning of a young person’s journey when they are waiting for a CAMHS assessment. I will use routine healthcare data linked with education data to look at whether racially minoritised children and young people do worse in terms of their mental health, engagement with healthcare and at school. I will then look at which combination of factors might put people more at risk, and whether support at school or at home whilst waiting might be protective. Better understanding these risk and protective factors will mean that clinicians can straight away identify those who may would benefit the most from early intervention to reduce inequalities in mental healthcare.

title: Sleep disturbances in young people with ADHD: understanding the associations, treatments, and improving identification using digital technology
description: Sleep problems have profound effects on young people, impacting their health, quality of life and the lives of their carers. Young people with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), a neurodevelopmental condition affecting approximately 5% of young people, are particularly affected by sleep problems. Up to 75% have them, however, the relationship between sleep and ADHD, and their treatment is not well understood. A specific issue is that first line treatments for ADHD often worsen sleep. Sleep problems are overlooked in clinical practice. National guidance is unclear on how to monitor and treat sleep problems in young people with ADHD, and little is known about current practice in the UK. I aim to tackle important clinical questions, addressing these gaps in the evidence. First, I aim to improve clinical practice by developing a novel digital approach that could enhance the detection and monitoring of sleep issues, and enable better treatment decisions. Secondly, by combining data from existing trials, I will examine which ADHD medications are associated with worsening sleep problems. Finally, I will use very large health datasets to study how many young people with ADHD are receiving treatments to help their sleep, and how practice varies across the UK.

title: World Health Summit: Enhancing Global Health Through Inclusivity and Global Reach
description: Since its inception in 2009 the World Health Summit (WHS) has become an important platform and convener of diverse stakeholders from all sectors to catalyze better solutions for a healthier world. The WHS’s role is especially important in times of concurrent crises across the globe that affect global health on multiple levels. Over the past years, some cross-cutting themes have emerged as key issues that need to be addressed in this context, among them climate change and health, antimicrobial resistances, mental health, but also diversity, equity, and inclusion. The WHS provides a safe and open space for intersectoral discussions among key stakeholders on these issues through a range of different formats, including the annual main conference in Berlin, the WHS Regional Meeting which is held in various locations around the globe, and smaller by-invitation-only dialogue formats taking place in Berlin and other cities. With the support from partner organizations including the Wellcome Trust, the World Health Summit aims to “bring the right people to the table”, i.e., those who are key to designing and implementing solutions to these critical issues, including people with lived experiences and especially from the global south.

title: Pathways to Healthy Pregnancy in Women Living with Obesity
description: Maternal obesity is an increasing global concern, which is associated with increased risk of both short- and long-term adverse outcomes for mother and child. In the UK, 18-25% of women commence pregnancy with BMI ≥30kg/m2. Within the NHS and other maternity systems worldwide, pregnant women with BMI ≥30kg/m2 are offered increased surveillance, testing, and intervention during antenatal care. However, as obesity rates rise, including in low-resource populations, it becomes increasingly expensive and burdensome to offer additional antenatal care to all women living with obesity, especially as the majority of these women will not experience adverse pregnancy outcomes. Clinicians may cause unintended harm by offering additional testing and interventions to women living with obesity who would otherwise have a healthy pregnancy, including psychological harm from increased anxiety and stigmatisation. Thus, a more nuanced approach to risk stratification is urgently needed. We aim to investigate causal mechanisms and identify potential biomarkers to improve identification of pregnant women with BMI ≥30kg/m2 who are at highest risk of short- and long-term adverse outcomes. The over-arching project aim is to identify the sub-group of mother-child dyads most at risk of adverse outcomes, allowing focused and timely interventions whilst ensuring lower-risk individuals avoid unnecessary interventions.

title: Refining and optimising an online interpretation training intervention to reduce fear of cancer recurrence in people living beyond breast cancer
description: By 2030, there are expected to be 4 million people living with and beyond cancer in the UK (Macmillan Cancer Support, 2019). Breast cancer is the most common. Approximately 75% will survive 10 years or more post-diagnosis (Cancer Research, 2020). Amongst breast cancer survivors, fear of cancer recurrence (FCR), defined as ‘fear, worry or concern relating to the possibility that cancer will come back’ (Lebel et al., 2016), remains the most common unmet need (Ellegaard et al., 2017). Higher FCR has been associated with increased anxiety and depression and poorer quality of life. Effective, scalable interventions must be developed. Specific thinking habits maintain psychological distress. Targeting these using online training (Cognitive Bias Modification, CBM) can improve wellbeing. Preliminary findings indicate that CBM may reduce health worries in those living beyond breast cancer (Lichtenthal et al., 2017). It is important to maximise the acceptability and adherence of new interventions before proceeding with larger trials. We will develop new psychoeducation materials, with breast cancer survivors, and incorporate this into the training. We will then conduct an experiment to compare CBM, with and without the new psychoeducation component, to determine whether the new component improves acceptability and engagement in CBM.

title: Prescribing in autism: trends, inequalities, and outcomes
description: Aims 1A: Describe time trends in psychotropic and lipid-lowering medication prescribing in autistic adults. 1B: Assess whether adverse medication effects are more likely to be recorded for autistic adults, compared with non-autistic adults. 2: Quantify possible drug-gene interactions in an autism cohort. 3: Characterise the overlap between autism and cardiovascular risk factors and outcomes. Methods 1A&B: In population-based British and Swedish data, I will compare psychotropic and lipid-lowering medication prescribing trends in autistic adults against non-autistic adults. I will then examine cardiometabolic outcomes in autistic adults prescribed these medications compared to groups stratified by autism and prescribing status. I will triangulate results from complementary study designs to determine the strength of evidence for i) psychotropic prescribing causing adverse cardiometabolic outcomes in autism and for ii) cardiometabolic conditions being undertreated in autism. 2: I will quantify the presence of clinically relevant pharmacogenomic alleles in two genotyped autistic cohorts and identify the proportion of individuals that have been prescribed medications for which international pharmacogenomic guidelines recommend treatment modifications. 3: I will use complementary approaches on genome-wide summary statistics to identify genetic variants, genes, and biological pathways that may contribute to the association of cardiometabolic outcomes with autism.

title: Developing feasible metrics for tracking mental health policy implementation
description: The Covid-19 pandemic and its consequences highlighted the inadequacies of mental health systems around the world. In this digital era, data around mental health services and programs are increasing and are being routinely collected. Yet it is unclear how policymakers can best make use of these data to monitor mental health policy implementation and optimize health outcomes. The current project has two objectives. The first objective is to develop a list of consensus indicators for assessing the implementation of mental health policies in resource-limited countries. We will do a scoping review of the literature and work with international experts to identify high-priority, feasible indicators that are linked to datasets that are likely to be available in most countries. The second objective is to work with stakeholders in Uganda, Nepal, and Colombia, to evaluate these proposed indicators for feasibility and relevance and identify mechanisms for using local data systems to measure them routinely. The findings of our work will be used to influence discussions around mental health measurement in advance of a United Nations High-Level Meeting in September 2025. The project will also generate preliminary data and proof-of-concept tools that can be developed further in country projects, beyond the proposed research.

title: The ACCEPT study. Developing a complex intervention to improve the process of disclosing Adverse Childhood Experience (ACEs) for service users and staff: an experience-based co-design study
description: Background: Experiences of abuse, neglect, domestic violence, severe bullying and community violence in childhood are very common among people who use mental health services. These often have long-lasting impacts on people's mental health. When a person decides to talk about these traumatic experiences it can help healing. However, mental health staff often lack confidence and organisational support to ask about adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) and struggle to know how best to respond. Research method A research method called experience-based co-design (EBCD) will be used to find ways of supporting staff to have safe conversations about childhood trauma with service users. EBCD involves: 1\. Exploring experiences of service users and staff through in-depth interviewing and observations. 2\. Creating a short film of service users' experiences to stimulate discussions with staff and service users 3\. Staff and service users working together to explore solutions and ways to implement these. Community Mental Health Team staff will be trained to use the intervention which will be tested and refined based on feedback. Anticipated impacts: For service users: Improved experience of disclosing ACEs; improved access to trauma treatment and improved therapeutic relationship; For staff: Improved confidence and competence to engage in conversations about ACEs

title: Strengthening Climate Change and Health Thought Leadership with Africa in Focus
description: Climate change poses immense threats to human health and wellbeing. The sixth assessment report (AR6) of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) highlights significant impacts on physical, physiological, and mental health, with about half the world’s population (3.6 billion people) living in highly susceptible areas. Projections indicate that between 2030 and 2050, climate change will cause approximately 250,000 additional deaths per year due to undernutrition, malaria, diarrhea, and heat stress. The 2024/25 goal will be to influence climate change and health policies while strengthening the health sector's capacity for UNFCCC negotiations through capacity building, thought leadership, and technical assistance, starting with Kenya and Malawi. The Pan Africa Partnership on Climate and Health (PPCH) will address climate change's health impacts through various initiatives, including developing and implementing a curriculum for training health negotiators in collaboration with the Africa Group of Negotiators Expert Support (AGNES). Key activities include leveraging existing Pan-African regional convenings, refining the Pan- African Common Position on Climate Change and Health, and enhancing coordination between health and environmental sectors in Kenya and Malawi. Events such as the African Union Multi-stakeholder Annual Event, AMCEN, and New York Climate Week will be instrumental in promoting climate-health integration.

title: Etalem (እታለም): Exploring the Sexual and Reproductive Health of Women in Ethiopia with Severe Mental Illness
description: The project will study the sexual and reproductive health and rights of women with severe mental illness in Ethiopia. A mixed methods study will combine quantitative and qualitative methodologies to describe and explain the sexual and reproductive health and rights disadvantages faced by women with severe mental illness in Ethiopia across domains of gender-relations (including gender-based violence), sexual health, family planning and reproductive health. A feasibility study will be carried out for a longitudinal matched cohort of pregnant women with severe mental illness in Ethiopia. This study seeks to determine the feasibility of community-based case detection and the collection of reliable maternal and child outcome data in this population.

title: DNA Replisomopathies and Immunodeficiency
description: Defects in DNA replication are a rapidly emerging class of disorders that can be associated with inborn errors of immunity (IEI). It is not understood why lymphocytes are so disproportionally affected in some patients with these disorders. Recurrent or severe infections are frequent and an often-recorded cause of death even for patients in whom neurodevelopmental and growth defects have dominated clinical presentation. Our team have identified novel links between replisomopathies and immunodeficiency that are ripe for further investigation in patients presenting with severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID). We hypothesise that defects in these essential DNA replication factors contribute to the immunodeficiency phenotype seen in these patients. We hope to use findings from this project to investigate a wider group of patients with DNA replisome defects. In this project I will be using state-of-the-art phenotypic, functional and genomic assays, well established in the supervising laboratories to investigate the pathomechanisms by which replisomopathies impact the immune system. This knowledge is a prerequisite for molecular diagnosis and precision medicine in affected families, with the potential for improved patient outcomes.

title: The role of therapeutic alliance in depression symptom reduction: a mixed- methods study of adults receiving face-to-face and digitally delivered psychological therapy through the Friendship Bench in Zimbabwe.
description: Depression is the leading cause of disability worldwide. Task-shifted brief psychological therapies are WHO recommended as first-line depression treatment in low-resource settings. A renowned example is the lay-health-worker delivered Friendship Bench in Zimbabwe. Whilst patients benefit compared to usual-care, over half do not achieve depression remission (similar to other first-line psychological treatments globally). A key ‘active ingredient’ potentially explaining this variation in outcome is the patient-provider relationship (therapeutic alliance). Little is known about alliance in low- resource settings, particularly in digital therapy despite growth in use. Aim: Investigate the role of therapeutic alliance (alliance) in depression symptom reduction across face-to-face and digitally-delivered psychological therapy for adults with depression through Friendship Bench in Zimbabwe. Mixed-methods approach: 1\. Qualitative exploration with in-depth interviews (patients and lay-health-workers), participant observation, and thematic analysis. 2\. Naturalistic observational study following STROBE guidelines, with three-month follow-up, across eight clusters and estimated n=500. Random-effects multilevel multivariate linear regression will assess association between alliance and primary outcome (depression severity,PHQ-9), adjusting for patient/provider-level factors known to predict outcome. Propensity methods will also be used. Impact: Optimise alliance (therefore depression outcomes) by informing training and supervision, thereby facilitating scale-up of depression care delivered through Friendship Bench and other task-shifted psychological therapies worldwide.

title: A Phase II randomised double blind, placebo-controlled trial of oral ketamine as an augmentation treatment for treatment resistant bipolar II depression
description: Our project will conduct the largest phase II randomised clinical trial of ketamine in adults with bipolar depression, to assess the safety and preliminary efficacy of abuse-deterrent oral ketamine in underserved patient population. Bipolar depression II (BD-II), characterized by recurrent episodes of hypomania and depression, is a prevalent subtype of bipolar disorder (BD). Up to 1 of 4 BD-II cases are treatment-resistant (TRBD-II), where prior courses of therapy fail repeatedly. While low doses of the anesthetic ketamine have shown rapid and robust antidepressant effects in adults with TRBD-II, no comprehensive, systematic clinical studies of this intervention have been conducted. Meanwhile, access to intravenous or intranasal ketamine in general is limited by safety, financial and logistical challenges. Given these unmet clinical needs in TRBD-II, Neurocentrx has developed a novel abuse-deterrent capsule formulation of oral ketamine. Our clinical study can confirm whether abuse-deterrent oral ketamine may provide a new effective treatment option for TRBD-II. We will also validate a new clinical care protocol for oral ketamine, where administration starts in clinics and then transitions to home treatment settings. In total, our proposal can help provide a new treatment approach to improve accessibility and expand treatment options for TRBD-II patients.

title: All-optical dissection of schema coding circuits in mouse prefrontal cortex
description: When we cook a new dish or take a train in a new town, we can imagine possible steps we may need to take (e.g., cutting and then seasoning vegetables or buying a ticket and getting on a train). Recent neuroscience studies hypothesize that this is because we can build a schema: a cognitive map of actions that are related to each other. This abstract understanding of “what actions one should take after each step” could allow us to instantly guide our decisions in novel situations. However, it has been unknown whether our brain carries out such complex computation. In my Ph.D. studies, I aim to address this question by recording and manipulating the neurons in awake mice performing a cognitive task. I will build a microscope for an all-optical strategy, a cutting-edge light microscopy technique that can readout and control the activity of each neuron simultaneously, and use this technique to map which neurons generate schema and reveal the wiring diagrams between them. This study will help to understand how animal brains make decisions using schema, and ultimately how such schema formation is impaired in psychiatric disorders.

title: Timing effects in mental health: is there an effect of time with experiencing positive and negative events and how does it manifest?
description: Sensitive periods are conceptualized as specific windows of time in which an individual is particularly malleable in response to an experience due to the development of key functions occurring at that particular timepoint. For example, studies have identified infancy as a critical time for the development of sight. After infancy, vision can no longer be developed if this period of development is missed. However, there is conflicting evidence about whether sensitive periods are relevant for mental health. Furthermore, if relevant, it is unclear when in the lifespan these periods occur. One hypothesis posits that the impact of experiences “fades out” during the lifespan. For example, interventions to support learning in children have demonstrated improvement immediately after the programme, but no differences in the longterm. Another hypothesis states that only the most recent experiences have an impact on outcomes assessed. During this PhD, I will explore the impact of timing effects on mental health by looking at different experiences, both positive and negative, on mental health outcomes. My first study will investigate the timing of bullying victimization across childhood using a novel life course modelling approach. By better understanding timing effects, we can optimize when and for how long to intervene.

title: Physical basis of sister kinetochore monoorientation in meiosis I
description: In meiosis chromosomes from a diploid parent cell are duplicated and then segregated in two consecutive divisions to produce four genetically distinct gametes, errors in which can lead to fertility issues and developmental disorders in humans. In the first division of meiosis sister chromatids co- migrate to the same spindle pole. The kinetochore complexes that are assembled on the centromeres of sister chromatids face in the same direction in meiosis I to direct co-migration, a property termed monoorientation. In budding yeast, the main requirement for monoorientation is crosslinking of sister kinetochores by the protein complex monopolin, however how crosslinking is made specific to sister kinetochores is unknown. Mechanisms independent of direct sister kinetochore crosslinking by monopolin may also be sufficient to enforce monoorientation, potentially by interfering with the surveillance pathways that normally detect tension during cell division. Using budding yeast we will identify the molecular mechanisms that regulate sister kinetochore monoorientation. A combination of live cell imaging and in vitro biophysical studies will reveal whether direct crosslinking of sister kinetochores is required for monoorientation. Phosphoproteomics will be used to investigate the composition and regulation of the kinetochore, to identify how monoorientation is specifically restricted to sister kinetochores in meiosis I.

title: Exploring the link between mind and skin: understanding the neurocutaneous axis in atopic dermatitis
description: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a significant health burden, resulting in chronic inflammation and itching of the skin. AD has the highest prevalence in children and is often accompanied by various comorbidities such as food and respiratory allergies, sleep disorders and neuropsychiatric conditions (e.g. anxiety and depression), which can have long-term consequences, thus further increasing the health burden of AD. The combination of chronic cutaneous inflammation and pruritus aggravate scratching behaviour which further damages and worsens inflammation of the skin. Moreover, this itching-scratching cycle also leads to significant sleep disturbance. Poor sleep quality during early childhood could severely alter neurodevelopment, increasing the risk of neurological conditions seen in AD sufferers, such as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Additionally, chronic skin inflammation in the patients could lead to systemic and even neuroinflammation which has been implicated in sleep disturbances and altered neurodevelopment. In this study, we aim to delineate the multi-directional relationships between inflammation, sleep, brain structure, functional connectivity and cognitive functions in AD patients. This will be achieved by employing advanced computational analysis methods, including machine learning. In the future, novel treatment approaches can be designed to target these new mechanisms to reduce the long-term health impact on these patients.

title: Restoring Vision through Photoreceptor Transplantation: Mapping Structure to Function in the Repaired Connectome
description: Approximately three percent of the UK population suffers from sight loss. Common causes of blindness include age-related macular degeneration, retinitis pigmentosa, and diabetic retinopathy, all involving photoreceptor degeneration. To restore a healthy retina, various therapeutic approaches have been taken, including cell replacement therapy. My host lab has reported proof-of-concept for restoring visual function by transplanting human stem cell-derived cone photoreceptors. We now seek to improve the efficacy of this approach by unravelling the repaired connectome in retinal transplants and finding ways to improve the functional connectivity of transplanted cones. I will use synaptic viral tracing combined with RNA sequencing to characterise the restored connectome and examine the differences in the transcriptomic profiles of integrated and non-integrated transplanted cone photoreceptors, focusing on synapse formation and photoreceptor maturation/function. The second part of my project will be focused on exploring the potential for improving donor-host connectivity in three ways: 1) by developing an in vitro model of photoreceptor-bipolar cell synaptic connectivity to test out potential promoters of synapse formation, 2) by building on preliminary data on the potential photoreceptor axon guidance molecule WNT9A, and 3) by the minimally invasive approach of environmental visual enrichment, known to promote synaptic plasticity in the retina.

title: Developing hiPSC-based models to investigate the role of microglia in schizophrenia and underlying heterogeneity in treatment response
description: Emerging evidence suggests that microglial dysfunction plays an important role in the pathophysiology of schizophrenia, but it remains unclear whether this is a cause or consequence of other cellular and molecular mechanisms implicated in schizophrenia. Furthermore, up to 30% of individuals with schizophrenia do not adequately respond to antipsychotic treatment. In this context, whether and how microglia contribute to antipsychotic treatment resistance and if antipsychotics influence microglial function, is also unknown. The present study will address these gaps in our knowledge by characterising the molecular and functional profiles of microglia, at baseline and upon inflammatory challenges, using human-induced pluripotent stem cell models derived from healthy donors and individuals with schizophrenia stratified by their antipsychotic response: responders vs treatment-resistant. The development of microglia-neuronal co-cultures from the same groups will also enable the identification of relevant phenotypes regarding their interaction in the context of schizophrenia. Furthermore, by challenging microglia monocultures and co-cultures with antipsychotics and addressing whether and how antipsychotics influence them on a transcriptomic, proteomic and functional level, this project will contribute to a better understanding of the mechanisms of action of these drugs, as well as aid in the identification of novel therapeutic targets and potential biomarkers of treatment resistance.

title: Understanding and Measuring the Role of Third Sector Organisations in Advancing the Mental Health and Wellbeing of Asylum Seekers and Refugees in the UK
description: Asylum seekers and refugees (ASRs) face a disproportionately high risk of mental health challenges, and whilst entitled to NHS mental health services, mental health support for these groups is disproportionately sought from third sector organisations (TSOs). This research aims to investigate the mechanisms through which TSOs effectively delivery mental health support, identify barriers and facilitators, and evaluate the impact and cost-effectiveness of their interventions. This project will begin with a literature review, followed by interviews and focus groups with ASRs, representatives from TSOs and wider stakeholders. To gain a quantitative understanding of the role of TSOs, we will collaborate with a relevant TSO to analyse existing data on mental health outcomes, specifically exploring the use of patient reported outcome measures (PROMs), and then pilot a number of different PROMs to quantitatively explore their effectiveness and robustness in measuring the impact of interventions of ASR mental health. The research will involve collaboration with TSOs, asylum seekers, refugees, and other stakeholders to ensure that the findings are relevant and impactful. By understanding the role of TSOs in providing mental health support, this research will contribute to evidence-based policy development and improve the wellbeing of asylum seekers and refugees in the UK.

title: The mechanisms underlying the relationship between depression and inflammation
description: Increasing evidence suggests that inflammation is a proximal marker of depression that may play a causal role in its development. Inflammation is therefore a potential mechanism which could partly explain the effectiveness of interventions targeting inflammation on depression. My PhD will focus on the role of inflammation as a mediator in such interventions, including exercise and inflammation-targeting drugs. The first study will examine how engagement in physical activity, specifically aerobic exercise, is linked to improvements in depression via changes in inflammation, through a randomised controlled trial of 250 patients. Participants will be randomised to eight weeks of either aerobic exercise (active intervention) or stretching/relaxation (control intervention), three times per week. Changes in immune-metabolic markers and performance in cognitive tasks will be assessed. In my second study, I will use genomic methods including Mendelian randomisation applied to proteomic and transcriptomic data to identify proteins that are causally related to depression among those that are targeted by anti-inflammatory drugs. This study has the potential to identify drugs that could be repurposed for treating depressive symptoms that are a result of inflammatory activity. This project will help answer key questions about the role of inflammatory processes in the treatment of depression.

title: Precision Gene Therapy for mTORopathies: Targeting Epileptogenic Cells to Ameliorate mTOR-Driven Seizures
description: Over the past two decades, hyperactivation of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) signalling pathway has been linked to intractable epilepsy in focal malformations of cortical development (MCD) and epileptic encephalopathies without MCD, collectively known as “mTORopathies.” Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC), caused by mutations in TSC1 or TSC2 genes that inhibit mTOR signalling, leads to seizures affecting up to 90% of patients. Focal cortical dysplasia (FCD) type II involves mutations in mTOR pathway genes causing dysplastic lesions with intractable seizures. Hyperactive mTOR signalling alters dendritic morphology and diminishes long-term depression of action potential firing, causing neuronal overexcitation. Traditional treatments, such as anti-seizure medications, mTOR inhibitors, and surgery often fail due to treatment resistance and the complexity of safely inhibiting mTOR signalling, highlighting the need for innovative therapies. This project aims to design genetic therapies that eliminate seizures in models of mTOR- related epilepsy by reducing mTOR activity in relevant cells. Goals include investigating cell-selective promoters to drive expression in epileptogenic cells and exploring methods to reduce excitability and mTOR hyperactivity. The resulting therapies will be assessed in vitro and in vivo to validate efficacy, paving the way for groundbreaking epilepsy treatments to improve the lives of those affected.

title: Development of a Therapeutic Genomic Screen for Identifying ASO Targets in Haploinsufficient Neurodevelopmental Disorders
description: Rare diseases impact 3.5% to 5.9% of the global population[1], yet over 95% lack an approved therapy[2]. Rare neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) often result from autosomal dominant, loss-of-function de novo mutations in haploinsufficient genes[3],[4]. Antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) show promise in treating haploinsufficient NDDs, by upregulating the remaining functional gene copy [5]. However, systematically screening ASOs against target genes is expensive and time-consuming[6]. Recent CRISPR-based genomic screens using pooled lentiviral gRNA libraries offer a high-throughput and cost-effective opportunity to identify therapeutic targets[7]. This approach could be tailored to identify ASO targets by using the recently identified catalytically inactive Cas13b protein (dCas13b), which binds mRNAs without cleavage, sterically blocking regulatory regions[8]. I will develop a multiplexed CRISPR/dCas13b genomic screen to identify target regions in the 3’ untranslated region (UTR) of haploinsufficient NDD genes, determining which are amenable to ASO therapy. Using a bioinformatic target prioritization strategy, I aim to target three regulatory mechanisms within the 3’UTR to upregulate gene expression: (1) microRNA binding sites, (2) polyadenylation sites, (3) splicing regulatory elements. Taking the top targets identified in the screen, I will design ASOs to validate these predictions in disease- relevant cell models, with the ultimate goal of developing novel therapies to treat haploinsufficient NDDs.

title: Deep phenotyping and developmental trajectory of anxiety in neurodevelopmental disorders
description: Despite well-known associations, anxiety is not well managed in children and adults with autism or genetic neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs). This indicates an unmet clinical need to address anxiety in these populations and the need for research into how best to meet this clinical gap. This project seeks to elucidate the relationship between genetic factors, age, and anxiety to better understand the causes of anxiety in children with NDDs and to determine the most effective strategies for treatment. To do this, the study will compare behavioural and physiological phenotypes of anxiety in juvenile and adult rat models of NDDs and anxiety, as well as determining the impact of treatment for anxiety on these phenotypes. Capitalizing on the translational potential of behavioural and physiological symptoms of anxiety, a pipeline of behavioural assays to measure anxiety will be paired with physiological experiments probing the hormonal or neuronal basis of anxious behaviour in juveniles and adults. Evidence of a difference between anxious phenotypes in these models would suggest divergent biological underpinnings for anxiety, with implications for our understanding of anxiety as well as for current treatment paradigms.

title: Intestinal Inflammation in Malaria and Malaria-Schistosomiasis Co-Infection.
description: Diarrhoea is a less-recognised feature of malaria, yet the underlying mechanism remains unknown. To investigate this, the cellular and immunological pathology of intestinal inflammation in malaria will be characterised using two murine models: P.chabaudi AS (‘uncomplicated’) and P.chabaudi CB (‘severe’). Changes in cellular populations and gene expression in the small intestine will be determined by flow cytometry and single-cell genomics. As co-infection with malaria and Schistosomiasis mansoni is found in >90% of Ugandan children, the impact of co-infection will be explored in a novel P.chabaudi/S.mansoni murine co-infection model. Serum cytokines and faecal biomarkers of inflammation will be assessed using Olink cytokine multiplexing, traditional ELISA and flow cytometry. While animal work is ongoing, a cross- sectional field study of Ugandan schoolchildren will be undertaken from an area with endemic malaria and schistosomiasis. For the first time, faecal biomarkers of inflammation will be assessed in acutely infected children to determine the clinical features associated with human malaria-induced diarrhoea and its impact on S.mansoni co-infection. Overall, this project seeks to understand the mechanistic basis of the gastrointestinal immunopathology of malaria and malaria-schistosomiasis coinfection which could lead to the development of new therapeutic strategies to restore intestinal health promoting childhood well-being.

title: Examining social-transactional pathways from childhood adversity to mental health outcomes
description: Background: Childhood adversity is one of the most consistent predictors of mental health problems in later life. There has been significant research on how childhood adversity confers risk for mental health problems by impacting neurobiological systems, however the pathways from childhood adversity to mental health problems are likely to be mediated by social processes as well. Objectives: This project aims to advance the conceptual understanding and empirical evidence for socially mediated pathways from childhood adversity to mental health problems by (a) reviewing the extant evidence for these pathways (b) examining longitudinal relationships between childhood adversity, social architecture and mental health (c) examining alterations in candidate mechanisms impacting social functioning in populations with a history of adversity and (d) providing proof-of-concept for mechanistic interventional work with this population. Methods: The following methods will be used to address each objective: (a) scoping review methods (b) dynamic network modelling of existing cohort datasets (c) quasi-experimental design to collect and analyse primary data from populations with a history of childhood adversity and (d) designing and piloting a lab-based intervention.

title: Metabolism and mental illness through a circadian lens
description: The proposed research seeks to explore the complex relationship between metabolism and mental illness. Specifically, the interplay between metabolism and behaviours that disrupt circadian rhythms will be examined in relation to mental health outcomes. Additionally, the influence of sex-specific differences on this relationship will be explored. This will be achieved by firstly performing a systematic review to summarise the available literature on the relationship between insulin resistance and mental health. Secondly, large health datasets will be interrogated to generate hypotheses regarding the relationship between metabolism and mental health. Lastly, a deep- phenotyping 12-month prospective study will be conducted in 90 young adults with severe mental illness (schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and severe depression) as well as 30 control subjects with no history of mental illness. Clinical and metabolomic assessments will be performed at baseline and at four prospective time points. Alongside this, various biological, lifestyle, environmental, and behavioural factors will be measured, including performing continuous sleep monitoring throughout the 12-month period. The overall goal is to gain insight into novel mechanisms driving mental illness and identify prognostic biomarkers that may inform clinical decision-making. Key terms: Mental illness, metabolic biomarkers, circadian disruption, sex-specific differences, insulin resistance, systematic review, machine learning, prospective study.

title: Investigating brain and peripheral signatures of myelin changes in healthy and perturbed neurodevelopment
description: Myelination, the ensheathment of neuronal axons by a lipid- and protein-rich membrane, is a developmental process that proceeds into the sixth decade of life. Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDD) and preterm birth are closely associated with cognitive impairment and altered myelination, including atypical white matter volume and microstructure, as revealed by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Additionally, these MRI outcomes associate with peripheral Omics markers as early as in infancy. However, no studies have investigated the myelin proteomic changes in healthy and perturbed neurodevelopment and whether peripheral markers can predict myelination- associated cognitive impairment. I hypothesise that peripheral and brain Omics markers capture signatures of myelin development. First, I will analyse associations between peripheral epigenetic scores (EpiScores; DNA methylation- based proxies for protein expression) and MRI white matter measures in large neonatal and adult cohorts. Second, time-course analyses of the myelin proteome in wild-type and NDD model rats will identify neurodevelopmental changes in myelin composition. Third, myelin proteome analyses in post-mortem brain tissue from neurologically healthy and affected young individuals will support cross-species validation. Overall, this study will evaluate EpiScores as diagnostic tools for identifying infants at risk of myelination-associated neurocognitive impairment, and determine myelin proteomic changes in perturbed neurodevelopment, thereby identifying potential therapeutic targets.

title: Social and Community-based Determinants of Young People's Mental Health Globally
description: Social determinants profoundly shape mental health outcomes throughout the life course, with adverse social conditions increasing the risk of poor mental health. While the mental health literature typically focuses on determinants like race, ethnicity, gender, and socioeconomic status, many children and young people (CYP) live in parts of the world where other important social determinants such as religion and caste can affect mental health. This applies to some low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where formal mental health services are often scarce, and research into social determinants and community support remains limited. This thesis aims to fill this gap by investigating religion as a social determinant, and the potential of the broader social environment as a protective factor for CYP’s mental health in LMICs. Using a mixed methods approach, I will combine quantitative analysis of multi-country and longitudinal datasets with qualitative interviews. I will also conduct a bibliometric analysis to investigate inequalities in research capacity for CYP’s mental health between high-income countries and LMICs. The goal of this thesis is to deepen our understanding of key social determinants and community-based support systems for CYP, while emphasising the need for equitable global mental health research.

title: Loneliness and social relationships in severe mental illness: a mixed methods study
description: Loneliness, a common and distressing experience for individuals with severe mental illness (SMI), is linked to poor mental and physical health outcomes and increased mortality. This PhD project aims to explore the socioecological factors contributing to loneliness in individuals with SMI and examine interventions that foster lasting social connections. The first study will map socioecological factors associated with loneliness using data from the UK Adult Psychiatric Morbidity Survey. The second study will employ qualitative interviews to explore friendship experiences and barriers, particularly how relationships formed through social interventions can become lasting friendships. Finally, a rapid realist review will determine which interventions are effective for whom, synthesising findings from the previous studies and existing literature. The overall goal is to inform the development of sustainable social support strategies to reduce loneliness and improve mental health outcomes in people with SMI. The mixed-methods approach, incorporating both structural and individual perspectives, will ensure the research is comprehensive and applicable in real-world settings. Key words: Loneliness Severe mental illness (SMI) Social relationships Socioecological factors Mental health outcomes Friendship Social interventions Social determinants of loneliness Community and mental health

title: Heart-brain interactions in schizophrenia and hallucinations
description: Our bodies and brains are interconnected: the brain regulates internal bodily processes, like heartbeats or breathing, and is in turn influenced by them. These bodily processes, and how the brain senses and interprets them (interoception), are often disrupted in various mental health conditions. Schizophrenia is associated with abnormal perceptions (hallucinations), but also autonomic nervous system changes, including reduced heart rate variability and elevated resting heart rate, which is a predictor of future psychotic episodes. Interestingly, cardiovascular medications appear to have a protective effect against psychosis, although the mechanisms are not well understood. Heart signals also influence cognitive and emotional processes. Studies show that memory, fear processing, and perception of visual stimuli vary depending on whether the heart is contracting or relaxing. Given that schizophrenia involves disruptions in both perception and interoception, it is plausible that altered heart-brain interactions contribute to symptoms. Altered interoception may distort how sensory signals are integrated in the brain, potentially influencing the misperceptions characteristic of hallucinations. This PhD aims to investigate how heart-brain interactions inform cognition, emotion, and hallucinations, shedding light on the role of the heart-brain axis in mental health. We hope this paves the way for innovative therapeutic approaches, bridging physical and mental health.

title: Care in the courtroom: Trauma-informed specialist courts and the medicalisation of justice
description: This interdisciplinary project will investigate the role of trauma-informed care and the influence of neuroscience in transforming trial procedures, courtroom environments, and the treatment, questioning and wellbeing of victims of sexual violence. It will do so through an in-depth empirical study, comparing the pilot of Specialist Sexual Violence Support (SSVS) project courts in England with the creation of a trauma-informed Sex Offence Court for Scotland. The Lead Applicant will work closely with victim-survivors and UK government throughout project phases and will help shape policy and best practice while specialist courts evolve and embed. Literature on the nexus between health and justice mainly focuses on defendants, recidivism, and the root causes of crime. This research will make a substantial and timely contribution to theory and praxis by exploring medico-legal interventions aimed at promoting procedural justice and wellbeing for the victims of traumatic crime. It will be the first study to locate the emergence of 'trauma-informed justice' among the literature on alternative justice theories and to interrogate its manifestation in the UK from the perspective of victim- survivors. It will generate new knowledge and stimulate research into the assimilation of medical epistemologies within criminal justice systems, specialty courts and understandings of therapeutic justice.

title: No pain, no gain: Investigating the influence of punishments on reward learning
description: Most of us can relate to the unusually rewarding experience of a warm bath, especially immediately after enduring freezing temperatures. This rapid interplay between rewarding and punishing experiences, and how people learn from them, is critical for adaptive behaviour. Yet, despite extensive research on reward and punishment learning, their underlying dopaminergic mechanisms have mostly been studied separately, overlooking their potential interplay. This oversight is particularly relevant for addiction, where negative events seem to paradoxically amplify drug-seeking behaviour. To address this, I propose a novel framework to examine the neural mechanisms by which punishments enhance how people learn from rewards. I hypothesise that punishments amplify subsequent dopaminergic reward signals. Across five experiments, I will combine novel tasks with state-of-the-art methods. Neuroimaging and pharmacological manipulations establish the critical role of dopamine. Behavioural paradigms and computational modelling quantify the extent to which punishments dynamically influence reward learning, and how this relates with personality traits and addiction severity. Ambitious multimodal neuroimaging at ultra-high spatio-temporal resolution provides crucial neurobiological insights into how punishments amplify immediately subsequent reward signals. This bold research programme will transform our understanding of how people learn from rewards in combination with punishments, with vital implications for mental health and well-being.

title: Pathways to cardiac dysfunction in psychosis: building a cross-platform understanding
description: People with psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia die 15-years prematurely, mainly due to cardiac disease. Converging lines of evidence point towards a genetic overlap between psychosis, cardiac inflammation, and heart failure, with immune pathways implicated. However, there is also evidence for cardiac inflammatory effects of antipsychotics, the main treatment for people with psychosis. The relative contributions of these pathways to cardiac dysfunction in psychosis are unknown. Characterising these roles will further our pathophysiological understanding of psychosis and its shortened life expectancy, and identity novel therapeutic targets. To test the relative contributions of psychosis and antipsychotic-treatment, I will conduct a cohort study using cardiac MRI to test if there is myocardial inflammation in antipsychotic-naïve people with first-episode psychosis compared to controls. I will then examine cardiac changes following 1-year of antipsychotic- treatment. To explore the contribution of immune and other biochemical pathways implicated in cardiac dysfunction in psychosis, I will measure circulating cytokines and metabolites and test their relationship with cardiac changes. To further explore antipsychotic cardiotoxic effects, I will analyse cardiac MRI data from the large-scale UK Biobank resource. I will compare myocardial inflammatory measures in antipsychotic-treated versus antipsychotic-naïve participants and examine if variations in antipsychotic pharmacology predict cardiac alterations.

title: Using immunopeptidomics and spatial genomics to determine the autoantigen, presenting cells and responding CD8 T cells in ankylosing spondylitis
description: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a debilitating autoimmune disease affecting patients globally with limited and often costly treatment options. Diagnostic delay and higher disease activity are also correlated with poor mental health, especially in young, female and lower-income patients. The strong association of the MHC-class I gene HLA-B27 with AS has led to the arthritogenic peptide hypothesis of disease, where self-peptide presented by HLA-B27 is recognised as foreign by CD8 T cells, thus leading to autoimmunity. My proposal leverages the latest advancements in immunopeptidomics to identify peptides presented by HLA-B27 in AS joint tissue, and establishes which of those peptides are immunogenic in patients. Spatial and droplet-based single-cell sequencing are then used to co-locate and phenotype both cells presenting immunogenic peptides, and their cognate pathogenic T cells. This research could lead to a completely new category of targeted (potentially tolerogenic) therapies and diagnostic tools being developed for AS that require knowledge of AS autoantigen. By also focusing on cells directly participating in the autoimmune response I may further identify druggable targets that would be highly selective for those cells and minimise potential side effects.

title: UNITED NATIONS MENTAL HEALTH IN HUMANITARIAN SETTINGS RETREAT
description: The UN Secretary-General has prioritized mental health as a critical issue for the wellbeing of people around the world and as a pivotal element to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). In 2018, he co-convened a roundtable discussion with WHO and Wellcome Trust which resulted in a Global Mental Health Roadmap 2020-2021. Given the pressing need, this retreat is being convened by the United Nations Deputy Secretary-General building on the Secretary-General’s priorities, co-hosted by Wellcome and UN Office for Partnerships and in collaboration with WHO, UNICEF, and OCHA. Building on these foundations and the continued efforts of the United Nations to accelerate the SDGs and in improving multilateralism to address the pressing issues of today and tomorrow i.e., Pact for the Future and UN 2.0, this retreat will convene key decision-makers and experts from across sectors and regions. The retreat will host focused, solution-driven dialogues to unite and coordinate multisectoral action and leapfrog mental health outcomes for people in humanitarian settings facing gender-based violence (GBV). This retreat will serve as an immersive catalyst to align around a shared vision to strengthen partnerships, identify critical gaps and accelerate implementation of scalable evidence-based and innovative mental health solutions for humanitarian settings.

title: Inclusive dialogue and exchange for smallholder climate preparedness and human wellbeing
description: Smallholder farmers contribute to human food and nutrition, but are vulnerable to climate and environmental change and face challenges that prevent their participation in the mainstream economy. The proposed project aims to build on the relationships and understanding developed through the Sustainable and Healthy Food Systems (SHEFS) project, funded by Wellcome Trust. A key outcome of which was recognition of the limited participation of smallholders in the commercial poultry sector. It will facilitate cross-country learning between India and South Africa, specifically providing space for including smallholder farmers in the dialogue in a way that recognises the knowledge and contextual understanding that they will contribute. The project will use the topic of smallholder poultry farming and potential positive and negative impacts on human and environmental health to develop and scale best practices in stakeholder engagement and co-learning. By linking smallholders with government, academia, and civil society and enabling a dialogue that values different knowledge sources equally, the project will develop capabilities that can in turn foster better outcomes for human and animal health, environmental sustainability, and climate resilience. The platform will focus on developing platforms that generate evidence of the benefits of co-learning and inform future policy and programming.

title: Advancing Community Research in Rural Communities
description: Lwala Community Alliance (Lwala), through our community-led health model, unlocks the potential of communities to advance their own comprehensive well- being. To deepen our impact, we aim to strengthen community engagement in our research, namely the Lwala Household Survey (LHS), which provides evidence of impact and informs future programming. The LHS, a repeated cross-sectional survey, tracks key indicators of health and wellbeing over time. Through this project, we will engage diverse knowledge communities throughout the research cycle—from design and implementation to analysis and knowledge management. Key knowledge communities will be: community members and influencers, Lwala staff, academic researchers from Rongo University and North American institutions, local and national government officials, including marginalised populations. We will host workshops to enhance these groups' understanding of the research process, conduct collaborative data analysis, and gather feedback to inform the 2028 survey. We will deliver: a knowledge-sharing framework, learning reports, community data documentation, a draft manuscript, and a knowledge management platform. We will also share this knowledge with peers at the national and global level, including the Centres for Exchange(CfE) cohort. This work will create a new norm for conducting community-engaged research at Lwala, as well as inform the broader health research space.

title: Bridging Gaps in Care Ecologies: Knowledge Architecture and Adaptation in Mental Health Care
description: The project aims to reconceptualize how knowledge is created, shared, and applied in mental health care settings to better serve marginalized populations. The project is located in two sites where Emergency Care and Recovery Centres, a crisis intervention to community re-entry intervention for homeless people with mental illness, run by The Banyan in India. The goal is to bridge the gap between formal, codified knowledge and the tacit, experience-based knowledge of care providers and service users. Using a participatory action research approach, the project will involve care providers, service users, and researchers in co-creating knowledge about effective mental health care practices. Key activities include collaborative shadowing, narrative sessions, and workshops to capture and integrate informal care practices into formal protocols. The project will involve capacity building for participants, including training in ethical considerations, transdisciplinary learning, and collaborative inquiry techniques. Researchers, care providers and service user will work as part of Participation Action Research teams to observe and reflect on care interactions and document care practices. Outcomes will include improved staff capacity, a care practices repository documenting field experiences and diverse scenarios, and a process framework for integrating informal practices into formal care systems.
recipient: Banyan Academy of Leadership in Mental Health

title: Uncovering Affective Dynamic Mechanisms in Mental Health: a bio-behavioural data driven approach
description: Mental health disorders like depression affect one in four individuals and cost the UK alone over £105 billion annually. Atypical emotional function is a key transdiagnostic factor in mental health, with conditions like depression characterised by shifts in habitual patterns of emotion experience and expression. Despite this, we lack a comprehensive understanding of the underlying emotional mechanisms, which is crucial for improving diagnosis and treatment. Traditional methods for studying emotional function rely on self- reports which are inadequate for capturing the dynamic nature of emotional experiences and how they vary in health and disease. This research will explore a novel approach to uncover objective bio-behavioural markers of typical and abnormal emotional function in depression, leveraging advances in wearable biosensors and machine learning to generate and analyse novel datasets in both laboratory and naturalistic contexts. These insights will enhance our understanding of emotional mechanisms in mental health and inform new approaches for research, diagnostic and treatment. The project will also stimulate interdisciplinary synergies with academic and industry partners at the forefront of wearable bio-behavioural sensing and data-driven mental- health research. These collaborations will build research capacity to accelerate the understanding and discovery of bio-behavioural mechanisms for mental health research.

title: Black Joy as Anti-Racist Praxis: Navigating Structures of Health, Healing and Empowerment within Black British Communities
description: This project investigates the potential uses of Black joy – a term used to describe demonstrations of happiness, humour, and cultural pride within Black diasporic communities – in promoting health and wellbeing amongst Black Britons. It explores the health-promoting benefits of Black joy, as well as its limits and potential harms when used to promote individual action in response to anti-Black violence. Through qualitative research and thematic enquiry on the uses, limits, and potentials of Black joy, this project addresses four research questions: 1\. To what extent does Black joy foster and promote health amongst Black Britons? 2\. How is Black joy pursued to counterbalance the detrimental effects of anti-Black violence within Black British communities? 3\. What are the limits and harms of conceptualising Black joy as a health-promoting resource? 4\. How has Black joy historically been used to promote health across Black diasporic communities, and what insights does this provide about its contemporary uses and significance? By exploring the lived realities and perspectives of Black Britons, along with histories of joy-centred approaches to health and holistic forms of anti- racist health promotion, this project will transform understandings of culturally-grounded wellbeing practices and expand possibilities for future anti-racist, community-based health interventions.

title: ‘Just who do I leave my worldly possessions to, darling?’: A Study of Queer Inheritance
description: Inheritance - the right to bequeath one’s estate to whomever one chooses is at the heart of end-of-life wellbeing and a cornerstone of a ‘good death’. This project examines what inheritance looks like and means for queer people and communities, and asks why inheritance, and indeed disinheritance, are such meaning making sites - beset with traumas, fears and anxieties – and at the same time, foundational to Queer survivance, joy and wellbeing. The key goal of the project is to establish QUEER.UK; a radical space for transformation and societal impact rooted in scholarly explorations of queer health, death and wellbeing that is at its core, intersectional, cross generational, focused on multiplicities of ethnicities, genders, religions and classes. The research network QUEER.UK will focus initially on the question and practices of queer inheritances: what and how queer people pass onto others and how this can contribute towards a sense of queer wellbeing that bridges life and death. QUEER.UK will allow me to create a meaningful scholarly environment through the time, resources and networking opportunities allowed by the Grant and build a portfolio of publications and KEI events, apply for further funding and to build the case for career promotion.

title: For the many, not just the few: Improving help-seeking for Obsessive Compulsive Disorder among UK-based ethnic minority adolescents
description: Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD) is a distressing mental health disorder that, in Western contexts, is just as prevalent among ethnic minorities as White individuals. Despite this, rates of service use are much lower among ethnic minority adults and adolescents with OCD, highlighting a considerable treatment gap. Findings from the US have highlighted several barriers that ethnic minorities may experience when seeking help for OCD, yet very little research has been conducted in the UK, particularly among adolescents. As almost half of individuals with OCD begin to experience symptoms before the age of 18, adolescence is a key period of potential intervention. However, to improve help-seeking among UK-based ethnic minority adolescents with OCD, we first need to understand their lived experiences and the barriers and facilitators they may face. Therefore, this proposal comprises a programme of four work packages which use qualitative, quantitative, and arts-based participatory methods to address this gap in our knowledge, with research training and skills development that will contribute to my growth as a researcher.

title: Improving Black women’s health and wellbeing in the UK through the development of an evidence base
description: Whilst there is a large and growing evidence base on Black women’s health and wellbeing in the USA, the information on Black women’s health and wellbeing in the UK is limited and disparate. There are similarities between Black women's health in the USA and the UK, but also specificities based on the history, geography, migration patterns, housing circumstances and differences in health and social care services and structural racism. The aim of this proposal is to develop a robust evidence base on Black women’s health and wellbeing in the UK. The proposed programme of work comprises three parts: 1) Scoping review, 2) Development of an intersectionality-informed protocol for an empirical study on Black women’s health and wellbeing undertaking secondary data analysis on existing cohort studies; and 3) Undertaking a feasibility study on establishing a Black Women’s Health and Wellbeing Research Centre in the UK. Such a Centre will ensure that the evidence on Black women’s health and wellbeing can be brought together in one place and is accessible to future researchers, policymakers and practitioners. For the purposes of this proposal Black women are defined as African, Caribbean and Black Mixed Heritage women living in the UK.

title: Perturbing the crosstalk between microglia and neurons uncovers mechanisms underpinning neuronal damage and repair in HIV central nervous system infection
description: A central nervous system HIV-1 latent reservoir occurs due to poor drug penetration and weakened immune surveillance. Implications are: 1) aetiology in HIV-associated brain injury (HABI), 2) viral rebound if treatment ceases, 3) barrier to cure and 4) implications for neurodevelopment in babies born to mothers with HIV. Microglia are immune cell types in the brain. Regulated crosstalk between microglia and developing neurons is essential for normal neuronal development. I hypothesise that disruption of this crosstalk by either HIV replication in microglia and consequent neuroinflammation or through interaction with C-C chemokine receptor type 5 expressed on various brain cells or other CD4-independent pathways, causes aberrant intracellular signalling, which alters cytokine and chemokine levels, leading to inflammation, calcium influx and apoptosis in neurons. Additionally, this crosstalk can be perturbed by epigenetic modifications including histone acetylation and methylation. Building upon research in my PhD, I will utilise biobanked specimens from characterised clinical cohorts and physiologically relevant models; 2D iPSC-derived microglia/neuron co-cultures and 3D brain organoids, as well as develop new skills in multiomic approaches, to uncover host-pathogen interactions underlying HIV neuroinflammation. This will give me a platform to develop an independent research program on therapeutic targets for HABI and viral-mediated neurodevelopmental problems.

title: DIALOG: Understanding Disorganisation: A Language-focused Global Initiative in Psychosis
description: Social connectedness is critical to recovery from psychosis in mental disorders and underpins vocational success. Persistent disorganisation of speech and language powerfully disrupts social interaction and perpetuates stigma, yet we know little about its causes. DIALOG, an international interdisciplinary initiative co-conceived with lived-experience experts, aims to address this and provide clarity on the neurobiological underpinnings of disorganisation. By focusing on patients’ everyday language use, rather than traditional clinical ratings, DIALOG seeks to identify the predictive computations implemented ‘on-the-fly’ by our brain when we interact with others, and how they break down to cause disorganisation. We leverage state- of-the-art Large Language Models (LLM) to extract objective markers of disorganisation from naturalistic speech, sampled longitudinally from patients with severe mental disorders. Combining LLM with large-scale new and legacy data from neuroimaging tools (MRI/PET/MEG; >3,000 patients) for the first time, we will identify the cardinal neurophysiological processes (synaptic density, neuronal connectivity and oscillatory dynamics) that underlie the computational failures behind disorganisation. In parallel, we will catalogue potential treatments and build the capacity for their multi-site evaluations, facilitating future trials and accelerating clinical translation. DIALOG will pioneer a computationally informed, molecular-to-systems-level account of disorganisation, identifying the precise mechanisms that can be targeted with novel treatments.

title: The Neurocognitive Mechanisms of Repetitive Negative Thoughts
description: Repetitive negative thoughts (RNTs) are a risk factor for the development and maintenance of anxiety and depression and are the target of treatments for these disorders. The neurocognitive mechanisms that produce RNTs are not well understood. While a number of processes have been associated with them it is not clear: 1\. Whether the identified neural systems are necessary to perform the cognitive computations associated with RNT 2\. Whether changes in the neurocognitive computations are sufficient to produce meaningful changes in RNT This application will address these questions for three candidate neurocognitive processes; the ability to adapt learning to volatility, the tendency to develop habits, the expression of automatic avoidance tendencies. A series of experimental studies will be conducted in non-clinical human participants, including those selected to have higher levels of RNT. Neurocognitive processes will be modulated using transcranial ultrasound stimulation, transcranial magnetic stimulation, pupil-based biofeedback and a cognitive training intervention. Behavioural, neuroimaging, cognitive and symptomatic outcomes will be analysed using reinforcement learning models. The translational role of these processes will be tested in a larger study. Educational and best practice resources will be co-produced with PPIEP members. This application will provide evidence of the causal neurocognitive mechanisms of RNTs.

title: Goal-planning in Psychosis: a study across humans, mice and neural networks
description: People with a schizophrenia diagnosis (PScz) have enduring impairments in planning-to-goals, which profoundly affect functioning. However, underlying brain mechanisms are unclear. Our labs have developed behavioural paradigms and computational tools that allow directly inferring planning algorithms from neuronal activity in the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus. We will leverage these tools to precisely pinpoint the computational basis of planning-to-goal impairments in schizophrenia. We propose a cross-species, multi-scale programme. We will use the same goal-planning tasks and neural measures across human PScz, mouse models and artificial neural networks. In mice, single neuron resolution recordings and optogenetic manipulations will reveal the mechanistic minutiae of computational impairments, and their permanent rescue using known pharmacotherapy. Human functional neuroimaging will translate mechanisms to PScz. A connected language study of hundreds of PScz across four continents will probe the same computations using clinically-scalable behavioural measures, helping demonstrate cross-domain generalizability and catalyse mechanistically-informed patient stratification. Artificial neural network models will bring this all together, teaching us how circuit-level dysfunctions in PScz impact computations behind planning, using simulations and neuroimaging analysis. Together, these three strands will synergise to provide unprecedented computational insight into one of the most important symptoms and recovery targets in schizophrenia.

title: Testing a computational model of the role of cortical circuits in auditory hallucinations in people with psychosis
description: People with lived experience of psychosis (PWLEP) identified auditory hallucinations (AH) as a top research priority. Computational modelling of functional neuroimaging data in PWLEP with chronic AH indicates that disinhibition of pyramidal neurons could underlie AH. However, this has not been tested at first presentation of AH. We will address this key gap in knowledge. Multiple lines of evidence indicate that reduced activity of parvalbumin-expressing interneurons (PVI) contributes to the disinhibition. We will test this mechanism using a drug that augments PVI activity in PWLEP and AH. We will probe mechanism further using chemogenetic mouse models to alter firing in cortical circuits in a cell-type and regionally specific manner and measure the effect on neural oscillatory activity relevant to the studies in PWLEP, and test effects of drugs to target oscillatory abnormalities during neurodevelopment and in a genetic model. This will determine the contribution of pyramidal, PVI and other neuronal sub-types to the loss of inhibition and other alterations seen in PWLEP and the potential for preventive interventions. These data in PWLEP and mice will be used to refine the computational model of AH, and test whether a network model can explain the lived experience of AH.

title: “The glue that holds the pieces together”: Unlocking Cognitive Health in Psychotic Disorders
description: Psychotic disorders like schizophrenia have a strong neurodevelopmental component, yet symptoms often do not emerge until adolescence or early adulthood. Cognitive impairments are among the earliest and most disabling symptoms. Intriguingly, our research reveals that many brain alterations linked to these impairments resemble those associated with premature ageing, such as brain atrophy and advanced brain age. Understanding the neurodevelopmental pathways of these cognitive impairments is crucial for creating effective early interventions. We aim to combat cognitive impairment in psychotic disorders as early as possible by: 1) Understanding the developmental features of brain age acceleration in psychotic disorders and what risk factors might exacerbate these, using large-scale neuroimaging datasets and computationally advanced methods; 2) Characterising the cellular changes associated with advanced brain age, using experimental mouse models for schizophrenia; 3) Identifying proteomic treatment targets that could prevent or slow down cognitive impairment in psychotic disorders, using prospective proteomic samples (of individuals who later went on to develop psychosis). Our goal is to unravel advanced brain age at a cellular level, embed this within a neurodevelopmental framework, and identify effective treatment targets for early intervention against cognitive impairments in psychotic disorders to mitigate cognitive impairments at the earliest stages of the disease.

title: From premature to protracted decision-making: Neural mechanisms underlying transdiagnostic biases in deliberation
description: Deciding when to decide is challenging, and disrupted deliberation processes are central to several mental illnesses. On one extreme, overconfident jumping-to-conclusions (JTC) is common in schizophrenia (SCZ) and may drive delusions. On the other, a pervasive indecisiveness (IND) and doubt is common in obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and is linked to compulsions. Despite the importance of this JTC-IND symptom dimension – and its life-changing impact highlighted by our lived-experience representatives (LERs) – these biases are not commonly targeted in therapy, and their underlying neural mechanisms remain mysterious. In this interdisciplinary, translational, and transdiagnostic project, we will investigate the nature and plasticity of the behavioural, neural, pharmacological and computational mechanisms underlying this JTC-IND spectrum in multiple patient populations and healthy volunteers. By combining approaches from neuroimaging in patients to rodent optogenetics, we will pin down the neurocomputational mechanisms causing deliberation biases in mental illnesses, and by probing how these processes can be changed, we will develop novel interventions targeting these mechanisms. With clinical practitioners, LERs, and experts in computational modelling and neuroscience, we are ideally placed to understand this critical transdiagnostic symptom spectrum with its direct translational potential, helping both those drawing hasty decisions as well as those trapped in their hesitations.

title: Neurocomputational mechanisms underlying anergia: a bidirectionally translational approach.
description: Anergia, the reduced propensity to expend effort leading to the avoidance of rewarding activities, is a key symptom of a wide range of psychiatric, neurological and systemic disorders. Despite its prevalence, the neurobiological and computational mechanisms underlying anergia are still lacking. Filling this gap of knowledge could help inform new treatment strategies.
