We hypothesize that: 1- anergia can be behaviorally and neurally deconstructed into fundamental computational components: a disruption in “perceived effort” exerted towards previously goal-directed activities (now perceived as being more effortful), encoded in the release of glutamate from the ventral hippocampus to a major hub of the reward circuitry, the nucleus accumbens (NAc), or an impairment in “perceived reward-rate” of the environment (now perceived as impoverished), encoded in the release of dopamine to the NAc; 2- chronic stress induces anergia by hijacking the specific neurobiological motifs within the NAc that encode perceived effort and reward-rate; 3- behaviorally distinguishable mechanisms underlying anergia can be translated to stratify depressed patients into behavioral-computational phenotypes; -4 such stratification will help tailoring cognitive-behavioural interventions to patients. By bridging the gap between basic research and clinical application, our study aims to revolutionize the treatment landscape for depression, offering hope to millions worldwide.

title: Bridging the Neurocomputational Explanations of Paranoia: From Cognition to Clinic
description: Paranoia, a persistent and distressing symptom of psychosis, involves the fear and belief that others intend harm. It significantly impacts patients, causing distress and isolation. Yet, the science often overlooks how the brain encodes social interaction, critical to understanding paranoia. This gap limits the development of effective therapies directly addressing patient concerns. Our goal is to change this. We will decode how the brain maps social interactions using advanced interactive paradigms, mathematical models, and neuroimaging. By administering THC, the psychoactive component in cannabis, to healthy volunteers we will induce temporary, reversable paranoia. This allows us to study the shift into paranoid states and compare the findings with data from individuals receiving clinical support for persecutory delusions. EXE will be involved in all stages of the research from designing, advising to dissemination of the findings. Our research will cover the spectrum from neurotransmitters to neurons and computational markers to clinical settings. We will share our results freely, and integrate our models into the free, browser based Hypatia platform, fostering the international development of new tools and therapies. This work aims to lay a foundation for innovative treatments and support options for those suffering from severe paranoia.

title: Wellcome Discretionary Award - Coalition for Mental Health Investment (CMHI
description: African Venture Philanthropy Alliance (AVPA) respectfully requests GBP75,000 amount over 15 months to support the Coalition for Mental Health Investment (CMHI), in partnership with Kokoro Change, Wellcome, the Clinton Global Initiative and McKinsey Health Institute. Together, CMHI organizing partners will accelerate current efforts, galvanize additional partners and contributions, and deliver results and impact on both the implementation and financing sides of the mental health equation. This funding will enable AVPA to hire and equip 1 staff member to serve as a liaison with CMHI partners, and lead the delivery of work agreed through CMHI. Through its involvement in CMHI, AVPA will: • Provide expertise in innovative financing mechanisms based on track record and active engagement of mechanisms in health and other sectors • Support in providing access to a network of investors, experts, and implementors across Africa and, where feasible, other geographic markets, that could be relevant to progress CMHI’s vision and objectives • Lead on incorporating mental health into AVPA’s catalytic pooled funds and / or other innovative financing mechanisms as relevant • Offer space to highlight mental health investment issues and opportunities as well as CMHI at relevant regional and sub-regional conferences and events.

title: Insight to Impact: Accelerating Global Measurement, Accountability and Action for Child, Adolescent and Caregiver Mental Health and Psychosocial Support
description: Investing in the mental health of children and adolescents is crucial for enhancing their ability to learn, work, build meaningful connections, and positively contribute to their communities. Despite its importance, mental health remains a neglected area of data, research and evidence generation, with profound implications for individual and societal wellbeing. This proposal outlines three workstreams to drive action, aligning with UNICEF’s Mental Health Acceleration Initiative and the broader UNICEF strategic plan: \- Workstream 1 accelerates Child and Adolescent Mental Health (CAMH) data and measurement, equipping countries with timely, high-quality data by advancing contextually appropriate, reliable, and validated tools like Measuring Mental Health among Adolescents and Young people at the Population level (MMAPP), supporting data generation, collation, and use to guide informed action on child and adolescent mental health. Notably, this also includes the establishment of a multi-stakeholder engagement platform through a global Technical Advisory Group (TAG). \- Workstream 2 establishes an accountability mechanism to monitor global CAMH policy commitments, driving policy progress through increased government ambition and implementation. \- Workstream 3 empowers data-driven decision-making, builds capacity among stakeholders, including communities (specifically, youth with lived experience), and governments to foster sustainable data ecosystems.

title: A novel approach to record, stimulate, and untangle the function of the serotonergic system in the primate brain.
description: Serotonin is a key neuromodulator in the primate brain. However, its role in cognition and behaviour remains unclear. This is because we lack appropriate methods for causal manipulation of the neuromodulatory systems in primates. This proposal aims to deliver a fundamental new understanding of the serotonin system using an emerging non-invasive technology: blood-brain-barrier opening and targeted drug delivery with transcranial ultrasound. Having established the feasibility and safety of this method for manipulating the serotonin system in non-human primates, I now aim to apply it to understand serotonin’s role in key cognitive functions. I will address the following questions:  1\. How does targeted manipulation of the serotonin system in the primate frontal cortex influence behaviour?  2\. How does it influence patterns of brain activity?  3\. Where in the brain do any observed effects of serotonin on behaviour originate?  4\. Does perturbing the serotonin system influence cellular-level representation of behaviour? I will answer these questions by measuring changes in behaviour and brain using behavioural modelling, functional magnetic resonance imaging and spectroscopy (fMRI/MRS), and single-unit recordings. This will provide an integrative account of serotonin function in the primate brain and can have a substantial impact given the role of serotonin in mental health.

title: Mental health community mobilisation: Influencing the UN High-Level Meeting on NCDs
description: The Fourth High-Level Meeting (HLM) of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) on the prevention and control of non-communicable diseases (NCDs), due to be held in September 2025, is a critical opportunity to advance mental health at global and national levels. It is important that this process is informed by the voices and experiences of local mental health advocates, people with lived experience and civil society from across the world, regardless of location, size and power. They must be given the best opportunity to influence the HLM for national and sub-national progress, as well as shaping the global health architecture. The Global Mental Health Action Network (GMHAN), a global community of over 5000 people from 150 countries, is uniquely placed to play this critical role of mobilising the global mental health community to create a growing momentum that cannot be ignored by the HLM decision makers. We will do this through convening an HLM Mental health Taskforce, convening the HLM Short-Term Action Group, and through civil society consultations. The cost to the GMHAN of leading these efforts will be £369,589 over a one-year period.

title: BLOOMS (Babies' Longitudinal 'Omics, Outcomes, and Milestones Study)
description: We address the challenge of improving life-course trajectory through early detection of antecedents of poor health and educational outcomes. Infants admitted to neonatal intensive care units (NICU) are at high risk of adverse health and educational outcomes, including ~30% chance of not meeting expected national educational targets aged 5. We will link multi-omic data, clinical and developmental deep-phenotyping, and routinely collected national health and educational records in a 1000-trio prospective cohort of NICU graduates. The resulting platform, managed within the UK NIHR Bioresource, will be continually updated to maximise phenotyping, maintain cohort engagement, and make data accessible. We will enhance diversity and validate key results through a Singapore-based mirror-cohort. Inclusivity of our approach is assured through co-design with our PPIE team and basing recruitment in ethnically-diverse and socio-economically deprived East of England cities. Families will receive clinical results reports to ensure bidirectional benefits of participation. Findings from the study are intended to (i) enhance diagnosis and maximise predictive value of neonatal whole genome sequencing (WGS) combined with multiomic-derived biomarkers and detailed phenotypic information, (ii) identify risk-markers allowing targeted early interventions to promote children’s health and developmental potential, and (iii) elucidate fundamental mechanisms leading to adverse physical-mental health and developmental outcomes.

title: Prisons, Drugs and Mental Health: an interdisciplinary global study
description: We and others have researched colonial and post-colonial criminal justice systems and drugs cultures. However, there remain crucial gaps in knowledge about drugs/addiction in prisons and their relationship to mental health. This is important because evidence suggests that drug laws and enforcement disproportionately affect already marginalised populations, and drug users in prison have poorer health and socio-economic outcomes, but we do not yet fully understand their historical genesis or impacts. Our interdisciplinary programme will research the production, supply, use, and lived experience of drugs among prison communities, c.1800 to the present day. Our team will conduct case study research on former British slave colonies in Guyana, the Caribbean, and Indian Ocean – multi-ethnic societies presenting varied prisons and drugs cultures and mental health challenges. We will also establish and support an international network to research other British, European, and South/Latin American colonies and successor independent polities, extending our global reach through co-production of findings and outputs. Integrating the two components of our programme will produce historicised knowledge, insights, and concepts to address a significant scholarly gap and meet the urgent imperative to reduce long-term health challenges and inequalities associated with drugs and their burden on criminal justice systems globally.

title: Cognitive Rewards: Mechanisms, Development & Well-Being
description: Cognitive activities (e.g., reading, solving puzzles) are often pleasurable. This hedonic response is crucial for motivating education, innovation, and enhancing well-being. What makes cognition intrinsically rewarding? What happens when this association breaks? Preliminary studies suggest that mental health is linked to ‘cognitive reward’ sensitivity more than to primary or secondary rewards. Yet, despite an extensive neuroscientific literature devoted to the latter, the concept of cognitive rewards has received limited attention. Our proposed research will alter this status quo. It will provide a new theoretical and empirical basis for understanding why, when, and how cognition becomes rewarding. We will bring together scientists studying human adults, children, monkeys and artificial agents. Using different techniques, but overlapping tasks, we will identify core features, developmental trajectories and neural fingerprints of cognitive rewards. We will examine whether individual differences in sensitivity to cognitive rewards is related to well-being and how such sensitivity changes with environmental statistics and development. The new knowledge, tools and tasks will trigger innovative research in neuroscience, psychology, and computer science. The findings will inform the design of curious artificial agents, the creation of educational programs that consider cognitive features children find rewarding, and mental health treatments that target cognitive rewards.

title: Democratising Neuroimaging Research with MRI
description: Our mission is to democratise MRI-based neuroimaging for all communities regardless of economic status. Neuroimaging research is crucial for understanding the brain in health and disease. One key approach, microstructural MRI, detects changes in cellular architecture, (e.g., myelination, axonal density), essential for studying brain development, ageing, and neurological/psychiatric disorders. To ensure its benefits reach everyone, it must be conducted in diverse populations by local researchers. We will develop high-quality, affordable, and sustainable mobile low-field MRI to take MRI-based neuroimaging research to regions where it is unavailable through: 1\. Developing sustainable low-cost, low-field MRI hardware designed specifically for neuroimaging research in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), 2\. Maximising image quality by combining novel acquisition, post- processing and AI-based image reconstruction techniques, 3\. Creating an efficient data-handling infrastructure, incorporating satellite-based internet access and portable data-storage devices, facilitating robust data transfer and integration in areas with unreliable connectivity, 4\. Harmonising MRI data collection and processing across systems with different field strengths and performance characteristics (including our own scanner design), enabling large-scale, multi-centre imaging studies in LMICs, 5\. Demonstrating effectiveness through proof-of-feasibility studies at three African sites. Ultimately our work will transform access to research-standard MRI and foster sustainable neuroimaging research in resource-limited countries.

title: Co-Creative MiND: The Inner Lifeworlds of MND
description: This multidisciplinary project will establish the world’s first ethnographic and participatory investigation into the interior lifeworlds of Motor Neurone Disease, combining medical-anthropology, computer-science, and co-creative practice. Affecting 1/300 people, MND encompasses the loss of speech, movement, and facial expression. Many people only have limited communicative means, e.g. eye-gaze technology. The substantial barriers between internalised consciousness and public expression means important thoughts, concerns and experiences remain unexpressed, exacerbating isolation, with profound psychosocial impacts. Increasing longevity indicates pressing need for life quality interventions. By necessity, MND comprises a rich, complex inner lifeworld, encompassing streams of thought, reflection, storytelling and imagination that constitute daily lived experience. We propose these vital forms of internalised expression are the most immediate and accessible means through which people can negotiate illness, redefine existence, and improve mental wellbeing. The project will enhance social-life, extend communicative capacity and enable people to share their internalised lifeworlds through Co- Creative-MiND: a national hub that will develop, test and advance new communicative technologies, body-computer interfaces and creative tools to facilitate social interaction, creative expression and investigative research, delivering advances in ethnographic and medical knowledge, demonstrating how life with MND can be transformed through co-creative practice aligned to people’s specific embodiments, temporalities, and interests.

title: Neuroscience Capacity Accelerator for Mental Health (NCAMH) 2.0
description: The Neuroscience Capacity Accelerator for Mental Health seeks to strengthen global neuroscience research capacity on anxiety, depression and psychosis by supporting high potential, LMIC-led projects. Building on the success of its inaugural cohort, NCAMH 2.0 will fund a minimum of 20 innovative, collaborative research projects over two nine-month periods, with grants of up to £50,000. NCAMH 2.0 will strive to address systemic barriers to mental health research in low-resource settings, promote equitable collaboration, and integrate LE perspectives into scientific discovery. Projects will emphasize culturally relevant, regionally impactful approaches while contributing to global advancements in mental health neuroscience. The program will also provide grantees with professional development opportunities to strengthen research skills and ensure sustainability. Selected projects will generate pilot data for future large-scale studies, expanding research networks and fostering long term collaborations. A transparent, inclusive selection process will ensure diversity and alignment with program goals, while structured evaluation will measure project milestones, long-term impact and professional growth. NCAMH 2.0 is uniquely positioned to advance global neuroscience, create equitable opportunities, and drive transformative progress in understanding and addressing global mental health challenges. Key words: mental health, neuroscience, LMIC, anxiety, depression, psychosis, capacity building, lived experience, collaboration

title: Sainsbury Wellcome Centre Core Grant Renewal
description: Together, the Sainsbury Wellcome Centre and Gatsby Computational Neuroscience Unit seek to understand mechanisms of intelligence in brains and machines, by leveraging synergies between neuroscience and machine learning. To achieve our goal, we have assembled outstanding experimentalists, theorists, mathematicians and engineers, in an exceptional environment that promotes collaboration, bold science, innovation and progressive research culture. Our discoveries are helping explain how individuals perceive, make decisions, reason, navigate, organise knowledge, choose goals and act in dynamic environments, and how learning shapes these processes; while simultaneously advancing algorithms and theories behind their artificial analogues. This knowledge is prerequisite for understanding cognitive and psychiatric symptoms and developing more robust, ethical AI systems. Our impact extends beyond scientific discoveries and new technologies. We are committed to nurturing the next generation and increasing diversity in STEM through unique, interdisciplinary PhD programmes, early career support, and targeted outreach across the UK and Low- and Middle-Income countries. Our successful knowledge transfer has seeded the creation of companies at the forefront of solving health and educational challenges. These externally-engaged, cross- disciplinary efforts address the global challenges of understanding how brains generate cognition and behaviour, shaping the future of intelligent systems and improving research culture, thus driving positive societal impact.

title: Randomised Controlled Trial of a Ketogenic Diet for Bipolar Depression (“Keto- BD”).
description: Emerging evidence suggests that a metabolic/nutritional approach - specifically a ketogenic diet - may be effective in treating depressive symptoms in bipolar disorder. Ketogenic diets are low in carbohydrate and high in fat and cause mitochondria in the brain to make use of ketones rather than glucose as a primary source of energy (as such, they may represent a more efficient mode of energy delivery to brain tissue). We recently completed a pilot study of the ketogenic diet in euthymic people with bipolar disorder. This intervention was feasible and well tolerated and was associated with both improved mental health and metabolic outcomes. The goals of the "Keto-BD" trial are: a) to determine the efficacy of a ketogenic diet in comparison to the NHS Eat Well diet for bipolar depression; b) To assess whether changes in Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy markers of brain energetics represent a mechanism of action of the ketogenic diet; c) To assess the healthcare resource use consequences and associated costs of the ketogenic diet intervention; and d) To assess the acceptability, feasibility and fidelity of the ketogenic diet intervention intervention. This study represents the first adequately powered randomized controlled trial of the ketogenic diet for bipolar depression.

title: An ethnography of joy, satisfaction and challenge: subjective wellbeing and occupational justice for disabled children and youth in South Africa
description: Children and youths with disabilities, particularly those with complex communication needs, are at the centre of this longitudinal ethnographic study. In contexts like South Africa, the study setting, social exclusion, poverty, and ableism profoundly limit access to critical services, resulting in poorer outcomes across the life course for these young people. Most related research and intervention focuses on deficit and basic survival. This persistent emphasis on difficulty, however, overshadows other aspects of the lives of these young people - and when non-disabled decision-makers cannot see beyond disabled children's struggles, their limited expectations constrain what is possible. Additionally, the persistent exclusion of young people with intellectual and developmental disabilities from direct research participation, ostensibly to “protect” them, impedes understanding of their needs and preferences. Combining observation and participatory in-depth data collection, I will work with various initiatives focused on psychosocial and physical wellbeing for children and youths with intellectual and developmental disabilities, and their members. My aim is to generate co-created knowledge about what makes life feel satisfying and fulfilling for these young people, and to affirm that while material deprivation must be addressed, meaning, belonging, and connectedness are also critical (but often deprioritised) determinants of their health and wellbeing.

title: DDT Relations: Tracing chemical alterlife in South Africa malaria control
description: Insecticides are the mainstay of global health interventions to address vector-borne illnesses such as malaria. With the ramp-up of malaria control in the last 30 years, insecticides — such as dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (DDT) — are increasingly used in indoor residual spraying programmes across Southern Africa. However, DDT remains controversial for its adverse effects on human and environmental health, described both as a ‘magic bullet’ as well as a ‘poison’. Yet there is little attention to the meanings of DDT amongst those living with it every day, including the communities in sprayed areas where DDT becomes entangled in intimate spaces and the vital substances of life. Through a multi-sited ethnographic project over five years, I will explore DDT through its relations and entanglements in different sites in South Africa: A) Communities that receive indoor residual spray with DDT; B) researchers studying the intergenerational effects of DDT exposure; C) policymakers (past and present), state officials, and government workers who arbitrate its usage, procure DDT, and spray it in homes. In understanding DDT, its meanings, and its effects, this project will contribute new knowledge on chemically driven global health interventions, its politics and its consequences, as well as providing novel theorizing on accountability.

title: Re-knowing self-harm: community and creativity
description: Self-harm is increasingly a common experience across the UK; however it continues to be poorly understood and responded to both within and beyond healthcare. Re-knowing self-harm responds to existing failures of care to reclaim and re-think the relationship between culture and self-harm through re-centring lived experience – moving beyond the quantitative, risk-centric approaches which dominate the field. Re-knowing self-harm accomplishes this through four strands of inter-related intellectual and practical intervention, which mobilise collaboration and innovative creative methods to impact care for self-harm across community action, healthcare practice, and policy. The first engages with and responds to dominant discourses of ‘contagion’, through a reflective reading group with lived-experience co-researchers followed by an interview study. The second strand uses collaging as a way of reflecting on, communicating, and understanding self-harm as a culturally-located experience. The third strand draws on fiction as a space for ‘imagining otherwise’ to articulate a new, radical vision of what ‘care’ means in the context of self- harm. Running through the project, a collaborative fourth strand will work with a Lived-Experience Advisory Group to co-produce the research and build meaningful cross-sector relationships. This will culminate in a series of workshops exploring implications of the research for policy and practice.

title: Archives of Care: Histories of Mental Health & Immigration Control in Scotland
description: This project investigates the imbrication of immigration controls and mental health care, through an empirical study on Scotland's asylum and immigration system. It historicizes this system within legacies of colonial and racialised mental health assessment, looking at how key NGOs, volunteer health care workers, and informal care networks interpret this history. The project uses a novel combination of ethnographic and archival methodologies to collaboratively generate ‘alternative archives’ that speak to this history, whilst exploring the practices, beliefs and motivations of people involved in providing contemporary mental health assessment and care. Here, divergent understandings of ‘care’ can overlap and come into friction, whilst different institutional and personal histories are drawn upon in evidencing and treating mental health conditions. The study takes its point of departure in Glasgow, a significant location due to its history as Scotland’s only asylum dispersal city, a ‘second city’ of the British Empire, and a key site for mental health intervention with migrant populations. Through detailed analysis of this case study and the cultivation of a new set of interdisciplinary methodological tools, the project will generate important ethical, conceptual, and practical interventions in the study of mental health, care, and colonial history.

title: Mental health provision for young people with experiences of sexual violence or abuse: inequalities, effectiveness and acceptability
description: Childhood sexual violence or abuse (SVA) is a widespread experience that is known to adversely impact many young people’s mental health. However, it is unknown what provision young people with experiences of SVA (YESVA) receive from Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services (CAMHS) and whether such treatments improve their outcomes. It is also unclear whether mental health professionals and young people themselves view CAMHS as accessible, equitable and effective. This survivor-led, intersectional, mixed-method research project will be the first to draw on an unprecedented administrative dataset to quantify types of CAMHS provision for YESVA and the impact it has on their mental health outcomes. I will qualitatively analyse case notes from this dataset to understand whether CAMHS provision differs by type of SVA and other intersectional factors. Finally, I will interview both YESVA receiving support from CAMHS, and mental health professionals to understand the strengths and challenges of CAMHS’ response to SVA. Embedded within a broad coalition of experts-by-experience, academics and practitioners from the sexual violence and mental health sector, these findings will underpin sector-wide discussions of how to improve the delivery of care. I will coauthor reports with leading national organisations, and report my findings to a Parliamentary Roundtable.

title: United for Global Mental Health climate change, environment, and mental health strategic plans (2025-2027)
description: UGMH is focusing on integrating mental health across actions to respond to climate and environmental threats through four work packages (WP) (2025-2027). WP1: Data, evidence, and awareness of the impact of climate change on mental health increases, especially amongst key policy actors (e.g., via products such as advocacy briefs, case studies, by strengthening partnerships within both the climate and health sectors, and by developing consistent messaging on climate and mental health). WP2: More governments and other relevant stakeholders include mental health as an integral part of their actions to address climate threats (e.g., adaptation, mitigation, and L&D policies). A tentative subset of priority countries includes: Pakistan, Ghana, Brazil, India, Philippines, Romania. Priority policy mechanisms will include NAPs and NDCs. WP3: Mental health is considered for integration within climate financing plans. We will achieve this by strengthening existing relationships with financing bodies (e.g., Global Fund), build new relationship with organisations (e.g., Adaptation Fund, Green Climate Fund etc.) and explore entry points for mental health within climate financing mechanisms (e.g., L&D fund). WP4: Mental health receives increased attention at key climate and environment moments (e.g., COPs) in a way that reflects the priorities of communities most affected and people with lived experience.

title: MOST-Nexus: Transforming Global Youth Mental Health with Hyper-Personalised, Adaptive Scalable Digital Care
description: Digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) offer a promising solution to the youth mental health (YMH) crisis, but poor engagement limits real-world scalability, sustainability, service integration, and impact. MOST (Moderated Online Social Therapy), a multi-award-winning platform co-designed with young people and services, is a proven effective and scalable solution. Now integrated into 400+ YMH services, it combines evidence-based therapy, peer support, and remote clinical care. To scale MOST globally, we will tackle four key challenges: 1\. Delivering scalable, data-driven personalisation. 2\. Balancing human support and cost-effectiveness 3\. Bridging the research-to- real-world gap. 4\. Developing innovative, sustainable models. Driven by world-class research, industry, and lived experience (LE) experts, we will leverage our unique infrastructure to create, evaluate, and scale MOST-Nexus, the world’s first hyper-personalised, adaptive digital platform for YMH. Phase 1 will create MOST-Nexus, integrating AI-driven hyper-personalisation (Work Package (WP)1) and optimising human support (WP2) for enhanced engagement, cost-effectiveness and real-world scalability. Phase 2 will adapt and evaluate MOST-Nexus internationally (WP3; Netherlands, Germany, Spain), and build a sustainable model for global expansion and equity (WP4). MOST-Nexus will transform YMH outcomes globally, delivering a scalable, cost-effective solution that integrates with overstretched services and operates independently in low-resource settings, driving the next generation of DMHIs.

title: Scaling access to care through a user-centred adaptation of a Digital Mental Health Intervention (Wysa) for adolescent girls with symptoms of anxiety and/or depression in rural India
description: The proposal aims to ensure the scalability and sustainability of a digital mental health intervention (DMHI), Wysa, for adolescent girls with symptoms of anxiety and/or depression by enabling adoption, access and engagement. Adolescent girls in rural India are among the most invisible, and vulnerable populations to mental health risk. They experience compounded socioeconomic disparities and cultural restrictions such as familial gate-keeping and barriers to literacy that limit their effective access to DMHIs. The study will culturally and contextually adapt the evidence-based intervention through the following three aims: (1) identifying and prioritising individual and contextual-level barriers to Wysa; (2) iteratively developing and testing adaptations to the intervention and implementation strategies to address these barriers (3) testing the adapted intervention and multi-component implementation strategy through a type 2 hybrid effectiveness-implementation design. Conducted in India, with its cultural diversity and large adolescent population, the study uses an ideal test bed to develop a solution that can be replicated in low-resource settings globally. The work will result in a (1) responsive, adapted DMHI and implementation plan for adolescent girls with anxiety/ depressive symptoms in rural settings (2) reproducible approach to adapting interventions and implementation strategies for low-resource settings.

title: Sustaining and Scaling Online Support and Intervention (OSI) for child anxiety problems in diverse international settings
description: Online Support and Intervention (OSI) is a brief therapist-guided, parent-led online Cognitive Behaviour Therapy platform for treating anxiety problems in children aged 5-12 years. OSI was codesigned with children, parents/carers, and clinicians in England, has proven clinical and cost-effectiveness in the UK, and is now being implemented in English child mental health services by Koa Health. Using OSI reduces therapist time required which, coupled with excellent outcomes achieved by non-expert practitioners, underscores the potential to scale this approach in diverse settings. This collaboration between researchers, commercial partners, lived experience experts, and key stakeholders from the UK, Japan, Chile, Pakistan, the Philippines, and Thailand aims to work across countries to maximise the intervention's applicability to diverse contexts, ultimately increasing its global reach while ensuring cultural relevance, stakeholder engagement, and rigorous evaluation across settings. We will: 1\. Adapt OSI for new settings and populations. 2\. Refine identification and assessment procedures for varied contexts. 3\. Test the feasibility of adapted procedures. 4\. Evaluate real- world clinical and cost-effectiveness 5\. Conduct pooled data analyses to maximise insights. 6\. Establish the conditions for rapid at-scale implementation. 7\. Promote collaboration and shared learning, lived experience and wider stakeholder involvement, and research capacity building throughout.

title: Improving Cognitive Health in Early Psychosis and Depression with AI assisted Cognitive Remediation
description: For individuals with mental health conditions, cognitive difficulties often stand as a major barrier to achieving recovery and independence. Over the last three decades, Cognitive Remediation (CR), an evidence-based psychological intervention, has been shown to improve both cognition and functioning. At King’s College London, we developed CIRCuiTSTM, an innovative CR programme that integrates key elements such as task practice, therapist support, strategy teaching, and support for generalisation, while also focusing on metacognition, a critical factor in accelerating learning and skills transfer. Independent studies confirmed the benefits of CIRCuiTSTM in young people with psychosis, with growing evidence supporting its efficacy in other conditions. Despite robust evidence for CR, global adoption remains limited due to the significant therapist time required, posing challenges to implement it in resource-constrained clinical settings. This research addresses this gap by developing an AI chatbot to support the safe, effective, and efficient delivery of CIRCuiTSTM. Co-produced with experts by experience and computer scientists, the AI-supported CR will be trialled with young people experiencing psychosis and depression. In partnership with industry, we will the conduct an observational study to provide the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence with evidence for broader implementation of CR in health services.

title: : A lay health worker delivered digital intervention for depression in Zimbabwe – optimisation and effectiveness trial with embedded testing of mediators.
description: Digital interventions for depression are hardly available in Sub-Saharan Africa despite high mobile penetration. The Inuka app is a chat-based digital platform based on the successful Friendship Bench model developed in Zimbabwe. Its advantages for scalability over face-to-face therapy include better access for clients and lay counsellors, better reach for a wider sector of the population, and in-built quality control for fidelity. Pilot studies in African countries suggest Inuka is feasible for implementation and improves depression. However, high data costs and a lack of robust evidence on effectiveness impede broader adoption. We will optimise the Inuka app for scale in Zimbabwe and other low-resource settings by expanding existing partnerships with lived experience experts and organisations which can take Inuka to scale and co-producing a data-lite version of Inuka which is acceptable and feasible for end-users and lay counsellors. We will then conduct a randomised controlled trial in Zimbabwe to test if Inuka is at least as effective as enhanced usual care for depression, to test its mechanisms of action, and to describe its costs. This research will leverage the global Friendship Bench network to expand Inuka's reach across Sub-Saharan Africa and beyond, enhancing mental health support for low-resourced users.

title: British Academy Leadership and Advancement SHAPE Programme Supported by the British Academy ECR Network
description: The British Academy is the UK’s national academy for the humanities and social sciences. We have been working with Wellcome since 2020 on two of our core programmes – Small Research Grants and Conferences – supporting researchers working across SHAPE disciplines with a focus on health and wellbeing. Our organisations have been in discussion for several months about supporting SHAPE Researchers utilising the British Academy Early Career Researcher Network as a platform for delivery. The Network is an inclusive, researcher- led membership body accessible to all UK-based early career researchers (ECRs) working in the humanities and social sciences – regardless of their funding source or background. The Network currently numbers over 5,000 ECRs in six regions with plans to extend nationally by summer 2025. This document sets out a Leadership and Advancement Programme supporting the British Academy and Wellcome ECRs. The programme responds directly to the needs expressed by the community, which we believe, will also benefit Wellcome ECRs working in SHAPE disciplines. The Programme aims to provide and enhance leadership opportunities, which will empower ECRs to build confidence, to be competitive and resilient in their careers, to equip them with the research skills, to develop professionally and to thrive in the job market.

title: EOI Climate & Health Science and Policy Centres Africa
description: The unique convergence of vulnerabilities; high disease burden, fragile health systems, and increasing climate variability, in the West African sub-region are well-known. However, there are gaps in knowledge with respect to the effects of climate change on the health systems and the health systems' resilience to the climatic events such as flood, health, precipitation and winds and their associated health burden ranging from incidences of respiratory diseases, vector-borne illnesses, malnutrition, and mental health challenges to socio-economic dimensions. These require inclusive, transdisciplinary and multisectoral approaches to climate-health policy design and implementation to improve population health. We propose a consortium model to garner diverse expertise to share, discuss and leverage existing structures at KNUST and partner institutions to enhance research and develop models for analyzing, and predicting the effects of climate on health to catalyze the realization of the global health goals such as universal health coverage. The aim of this proposal is to build a consortium with diverse expertise and stakeholders across West Africa to develop a full proposal for the establishment of the Climate and Health Science and Policy Centre in West Africa to effectively respond and mitigate the challenges imposed by climatic variabilities-induced events on the health system.
recipient: Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology

title: Lonely Minds - Characterizing the neurocognitive effects of social disconnection in adolescence
description: Social disconnection is increasingly affecting adolescents. Brain development in this developmental stage is particularly sensitive to social cues, and loneliness in adolescence has been associated with mental health problems. Yet, the neural pathways of how social disconnection impacts brain function in adolescence are not clear. While animal studies provide important insights on the effects of social disconnection on adolescent brains, it is unclear to what extent these findings can be directly translated to humans. I will combine experimental methods, neuroimaging, as well as longitudinal and large- scale data analyses to 1) test the causal effects of social disconnection on neurocognitive processes underlying reward and aversive processing in adolescents; 2) study longitudinal links between adolescent real-life social disconnection, alterations in functional and structural brain measures and development of mental health problems; and 3) investigate interactions between social disconnection and social media use in adolescents. The proposed research aims to provide a step-change in our understanding of the impacts of social disconnection on young people and open new avenues for interventions at the time point of greatest likely impact.

title: Supporting the Data for Health in Africa Meeting
description: The DS-I Africa Coordinating Centre seeks discretionary funding from the Wellcome to host the Data for Health in Africa Meeting from August 23-29, 2025, at the University of Ghana. This event, designed to foster collaborative engagements between DS-I Africa and Wellcome grantees, aims to address urgent public health challenges in Africa by developing innovative data science solutions through cross-continental partnerships. Building on three years of Wellcome’s involvement in DS-I Africa’s annual gatherings, the meeting is pivotal for refining strategies to enhance data diversity and representation of African data. Key objectives include: 1\. Strengthening coordination of data science in Africa through the formation of new strategic partnerships, thematic sessions on initiatives like open data ecosystems, mental health research, and climate health impacts. Networking opportunities will align African tech leaders and funders to support collaboration. 2\. Enhancing the data ecosystem by promoting the adoption of data science outputs, establishing effective data governance and AI regulations, and facilitating training and capacity development. 3\. Convening a multi-stakeholder forum to benchmark and strategically advance data science for health in Africa via joint knowledge exchange and coordinated funding efforts. This initiative aligns with Wellcome’s commitment to interdisciplinary research and innovative, data- driven solutions addressing global health priorities.

title: Unlearning 'Excited Delirium': Acute Behavioural Disturbance, Race, Mental Health and Policing
description: The intersection of race, mental health and policing is a critical public health issue. Black people in the UK are more likely to be diagnosed with a mental health condition; less likely to receive treatment; seven times more likely to be killed by police restraint than white people. Research and policy at this intersection have been compromised by two interrelated concepts: ‘Excited Delirium Syndrome’ (ExDS) and Acute Behavioural Disturbance (ABD). ExDS is a discredited, racist pseudo-diagnosis popular in the US, describing victims of police violence as exhibiting ‘superhuman strength’ and being ‘impervious to pain’, echoing colonial ‘race science’. ABD is its inheritor in the UK. An interdisciplinary team will examine the historical, social, legal and spatial dimensions of restraint-related police killings attributed to ExDS/ABD in the UK, through the prism of casework-led ‘forensic architecture’ research methods. The project seeks a national reckoning with ABD and police restraint, through new approaches to an urgent, public health, social justice and human rights issue. We will pioneer community-led co-production models to advance Wellcome’s strategic goals by working closely with civil society leaders and individuals with lived experience to disentangle the biological, social and cultural factors of the topic, towards better future health outcomes.

title: The role of genes and life experience in the neural modulation of threat sensitivity
description: The ability to appropriately respond to threats is crucial for survival and requires precise calibration - too little sensitivity leaves individuals vulnerable to danger, while excessive reactions to harmless situations can lead to social isolation and impair quality of life. Individuals show natural variation in threat sensitivity, shaped by both genetic background and lifetime experiences, with disrupted threat processing underlying psychiatric conditions including anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorders. This project investigates how genetic variation and experience shape neural circuits to set threat sensitivity, comparing different mouse subspecies with distinct threat sensitivities while tracking individual behaviour and neural activity over extended periods. Using escape from imminent threats as a model system and focusing on a spatially restricted midbrain circuit, we will identify the algorithmic principles by which the superior colliculus and periaqueductal gray transform sensory stimuli into escape decisions, and how these computations are modified by experience and genetic background. We will determine the cellular and circuit mechanisms implementing these changes and identify key genes regulated through evolution and experience to control threat sensitivity. This research will identify key neural mechanisms regulating threat sensitivity and advance our understanding of individual variations in threat processing. Keywords: threat, escape, midbrain, mouse, experience, genes

title: Mental Health Access Initiative: Expanding global access to psychotropic medication for severe mental disorders
description: Mental health accounts for ~16% of global disease burden, with four disorders – schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, major depression and anxiety – contributing ~80% of this burden. Severe mental disorders remain underprioritized despite driving most mental health disability. Governments in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) dedicate 70% of people with psychosis receive no care. Safe, effective medications available in high-income countries remain inaccessible in many LMICs. Building on consensus-based momentum from Wellcome’s recent mental health convening, we propose a 12-month pathfinding program to expand access to treatment for schizophrenia, major depression, bipolar disorder, and anxiety in up to 5 LMICs. Our strategy is two-fold: 1\. Cost-effectiveness analysis: Develop open-access cost-effectiveness tools – built in collaboration with country and lived-experience partners – to drive action towards high-impact interventions, beginning with those for psychosis, in focus LMICs. 2\. Market shaping: Deliver targeted access gains for proven, quality-assured psychotropic medications. Engage manufacturers and policymakers to support the rapid, cost-effective introduction of newer treatments. Secure supplier commitments, improve pricing transparency, and provide framework for scalable access agreements. By achieving early access gains and delivering tools for action, our efforts will help catalyze a future where all people with severe mental disorders can access the best-available treatments – reliably and affordably.

title: Market shaping for mental health treatment in priority markets: Scoping study to inform future innovative financing interventions
description: Mental health conditions affect 1 in 8 people, but remain underfunded, under- treated, and under-prioritised—especially in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). National health budgets in LMICs allocate less than 2% to mental health, with countries like India and Kenya spending as little as 0.06% and 0.01% respectively. Most mental health care costs fall on patients and their families, and at a high cost. MedAccess seeks $447,011 to conduct a global landscaping study to identify how market shaping actions can improve availability and affordability of medications for depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia in LMICs. This project will build on, and complement CHAI’s Pathfinding programme. The project will be implemented over a 12-month period in three phases: 1) Market mapping (months 1-3) to engage with suppliers and stakeholders, map and validate psychothropic medicines for database 2) Market analysis of supply and demand barriers (months 4-6), including product availability, pricing, policies, manufacturer willingness, and in-country findings, to prioritise interventions and essential medicines 3) Partnerships and consensus building (months 7-12) to formalise engagements and identify market-shaping tools based on broad stakeholder consensus to address treatment gaps. The project will provide a shortlist of mental health medications and market shaping strategies for future interventions.

title: The birth of an African Population Cohorts Consortium to mobilise longitudinal data and research for impact
description: This proposal details the establishment of the African Population Cohorts Consortium (APCC), a collaborative effort to unlock the potential of longitudinal data from African cohorts for impactful research and policy influence. The APCC aims to unite African cohort leaders and researchers, fostering networking, best practice exchange, and innovative approaches to data sharing and harmonisation. The project's core goals include setting up a secretariat hosted by the Science for Africa Foundation (SFA), formalising cohort membership, and convening the inaugural annual meeting. Additional goals centre around the development of three strategic research programs: health and wellbeing across the lifespan, climate change and health, and leveraging cohorts to enhance universal health coverage. To facilitate ethical and efficient research, the APCC will develop harmonised ethical guidelines, data-sharing protocols, and a "TRE-in-a-Box"—a secure, cohort-level trusted research environment. This will be complemented by a federated workspace at the Africa Bioinformatics Institute (ABI) to streamline data access and analysis of multi-cohort data. By enhancing African research capacity, promoting scientific breakthroughs, and informing evidence-based policies, the APCC seeks to contribute to equitable universal health coverage and sustainable development across the continent.

title: AVATAR therapy in the Real World (AVATAR-RW): A process evaluation, effectiveness and cost-effectiveness study in routine care of AVATAR therapy, a digitally supported therapy for distressing voices.
description: Background: AVATAR therapy is a highly effective digital therapy for distressing voices in psychosis. Following two successful randomised controlled trials and in line with a NICE-EVA recommendation for generation of Real-World Evidence (RWE) the next steps are to test AVATAR therapy in routine care. Aims: This project will test, for the first time, AVATAR therapy when delivered within routine psychological therapy pathways, across diverse NHS settings. We will generate RWE on effectiveness and cost-effectiveness as well as uptake and acceptability across different stakeholders. Specific aims: 1) To optimise AVATAR therapy for real-world deployment. 2) To establish effectiveness and cost-effectiveness in routine care. 3) To conduct a process evaluation of AVATAR therapy implementation. 4) To establish a reliable and sustainable method for real-world outcome monitoring. 5) To deliver a strategy to support AVATAR therapy spread and sustainment. Methods: We will conduct a prospective controlled cohort study with 12-month follow-up (N=140), delivering RWE on clinical and cost-effectiveness across diverse routine care settings. We will identify barriers and facilitators to sustainable implementation. Anticipated Impact: The outputs will support evaluation for a full NICE recommendation and strongly position AVATAR therapy for wide-spread NHS adoption within the next 5 years.

title: Parent & ecological influences on social cognitive development, and its association with social functioning and functional neuroanatomy in BaYaka and Bantu children
description: Social cognition – the mental processes which allow people to understand the behaviours and intentions of others – is implicated in a variety of psychiatric disorders and their treatment. Emerging evidence suggests that cultural-level factors – such as social norms, value preferences and parenting characteristics – may influence social cognitive development and its link with mental health. However, the previous literature has only studied a small subset of human cultural diversity, and existing evidence is overwhelmingly drawn from Western and/or post-industrial populations. To address this gap, this project will study the timings and trajectory of social cognitive development in the BaYaka, a hunter-gatherer population residing in the rainforests of northern Republic of Congo. Given the BaYaka community pursue obligate group-living and strong alloparenting behaviour (both typical of this subsistence pattern), such a context provides rich variation in the cultural- level factors which are implicated in differences in social cognitive development. Therefore, this project will allow us to ascertain the extent to which social cognitive development is influenced by cultural-level factors. Furthermore, it will examine whether our knowledge of the predictors, neurological correlates and functional outcomes associated with social cognitive development are externally valid beyond Western, industrialised populations.

title: Exploring and Modifying BarrieRs to enhance ACcess to mental health support for Ethnic minority Children and Young People in acute paediatric settings (EMBRACE).
description: An increasing number of Children and Young People (CYP) with Mental Health (MH) issues are presenting to acute paediatric settings, which investigations have shown are unsuitable for managing high-risk mental health behaviour. Ethnic minority CYP have the worst access and outcomes for mental health services but are under-researched. This research project aims to address this through a mixed-methods approach consisting of a realist review and primary realist evaluation. The realist review will explore how, why and in what context MH support is effective for ethnic minority CYP and develop an initial programme theory for the barriers and enablers that ethnic minority CYP may face when accessing MH support in acute paediatric settings. The subsequent primary realist evaluation will explore the programme theory further through case studies & interviews with CYP, their parents/carers and relevant stakeholders across three acute paediatric hospitals in England. The project output will be a list of practical recommendations for optimising access to MH support for ethnic minority CYP in acute paediatric settings. Applying these recommendations to clinical practice would reduce racial inequalities in access to mental health care for CYP and the consequences on healthcare services and CYP in later life. Keywords: CAMHS, ethnic minority, paediatric settings.

title: Predictors of NeuroDevelopmental Disability (NDD) diagnosis, functioning and participation in preschool children in Malawi
description: Neurodevelopmental disabilities (NDDs) are disorders of brain development including autism, ADHD, cerebral palsy, epilepsy, and intellectual disability. NDDs may be caused by early childhood infection, birth trauma, prematurity and malnutrition - all more common in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Surveys using simplistic data tools estimate that NDDs affect 1 in 13 children under 5 years globally, with 95% living in LMICs. There is limited data from Malawi. Current tools to identify NDD are expensive, time-intensive, and often require highly trained professionals, making it challenging to diagnose NDDs in LMICs, with few children receiving early interventions. A new tablet-based assessment tool (Scalable Transdiagnostic Early Assessment of Mental Health [STREAM] tool) has been developed for use by non-specialists in LMICs but not tested for its ability to predict future NDD, functioning or participation. I will conduct diagnostic assessments for NDD and assess functioning and participation in 420 children in Malawi at 5-7 years who were assessed three years previously using the STREAM tool. I will investigate predictors of NDD, functioning and participation using baseline measures from the STREAM study. I will also explore perspectives of children with NDD and caregivers regarding barriers and facilitators to functioning and participation in daily life.

title: Examining the relationship between alcohol-attributable conditions, multimorbidity, adverse outcomes and experiences of care
description: Multimorbidity affects more than 30% of individuals in their lifetime, and is associated with poverty, increased disability, worse mental well-being, and increased mortality. An estimated 7% of the world population live with alcohol use disorder, and harmful alcohol use causes 3 million deaths annually. Overall, 5.1% of the global burden of disease is attributable to alcohol, which causes over 200 health disorders, and impacts disease outcomes. Alcohol use disorder and its’ relation to multimorbidity has been scarcely explored. This project aims to investigate the prevalence and patterns of multimorbidity in individuals with alcohol-attributable conditions, how these relate to demographic factors and healthcare outcomes, and explore the healthcare experiences of affected individuals. We will use a combination of a systematic review, analysis of large-scale electronic health records and qualitative methods. Understanding multimorbidity clusters in the context of harmful alcohol use, the morbidity development over time, and their effect on outcomes, could have important implications from clinical (screening, prioritise effective referral and follow up), policy (resource distributions) and research (intervention development) perspectives. A better understanding of the care needs and outcomes of individuals with unique multimorbidity profiles will allow a move towards person-centred healthcare, away from a disease-centred approach.

title: Relationships and Mental Health During Transitions in Adolescence
description: Adolescence and emerging adulthood are critical developmental phases characterised by dynamic brain changes, heightened vulnerability, and opportunities for growth. This period coincides with significant life transitions whilst this can be a time of excitement, it is also marked by stress, loneliness, and mental health challenges. Seventy-five percent of mental health problems emerge by age 24, recent evidence shows rising distress among young adults, exacerbated by societal stressors such as the Covid-19 pandemic and the cost-of-living crisis. This research will explore how family and friend relationships impact young people’s mental health and well-being during this transition. It will apply ecological systems theory and attachment theory in a mixed-methods longitudinal study to analyse the protective and challenging aspects of these relationships. The study will include quantitative surveys linking young people and their families, followed by qualitative interviews to deepen understanding. Key questions focus on perceptions of social/emotional support, relationship dynamics, and the impact on well-being. Findings will inform a pathway to impact, including systemic workshops and attachment-based programs in educational and community settings, promoting resilience at individual, family, and societal levels. The project seeks to improve mental health outcomes by enhancing relational understanding and support systems during this pivotal life stage.

title: Understanding and addressing the impact of mental-physical multimorbidity
description: BACKGROUND// Mental-physical multimorbidity – the coexistence of mental and physical long-term conditions – has a significant impact on individuals and healthcare services, especially in deprived areas where it occurs much earlier in life. In particular, common mental disorders, like depression and anxiety, are a major contributor to the overall burden of mental-physical multimorbidity, including healthcare utilisation and costs. Interventions to improve outcomes in people with mental-physical multimorbidity involving common mental disorders are therefore a priority for patients and policy makers. AIM// This aim of this project is to develop a complex intervention to improve outcomes in people with mental-physical multimorbidity involving common mental disorders. APPROACH// A systematic review of existing interventions for this group will identify effective intervention components. Analysis of a large population dataset will provide further insights into the epidemiology of mental-physical multimorbidity. These steps will inform a co- design process involving stakeholder consultation, co-production workshops, and the formulation of an intervention design including programme theory, evaluation strategy and feasibility study design. As such, this project will lay the groundwork for future work to test and implement a new complex intervention for people whose lives are impacted by the coexistence of common mental disorders and physical multimorbidity.

title: Understanding the micronutrient influence on neurodevelopmental outcomes of low birthweight infants (LBW) born at Queen Elizabeth Central Hospital (QECH)
description: Over half the children born in Malawi are at increased risk of faltering development; contributory factors include antenatal and perinatal factors as well as under-nutrition and stunting. 18% of babies in Malawi are born prematurely or Low Birth Weight (LBW). As more children survive the neonatal period and we provide better care globally, estimates demonstrate that by 2035, 99 million neonates will have a disability/ lost developmental potential. Micronutrients make up the central nervous system structure and play major functional roles: stimulate nerve cell development, migration and differentiation during the first 1000 days. Current evidence surrounding the nutritional care of LBW infants in low resource settings such as Malawi is limited. Greater knowledge is required in the importance of adequate micronutrient intakes and status into the diet of these LBW Malawian infants to improve neurodevelopment. There is an urgent need to strengthen public policies and develop nutritional strategies focused on neurodevelopmental outcomes amongst LBW infants. During this fellowship, I will have collected data on 200 LBW infants, which will provide evidence to answer to the question as to whether, Malawian LBW infants post-natal micronutrient status and/or other factors related to feeding, when measured at two timepoints is associated with neurodevelopment.

title: Sleep disturbance as a predictor of mental health and functional outcomes following traumatic brain injury
description: The focus of the study will be to determine: Whether sleep data acquired longitudinally over the months and years following traumatic brain injury (TBI) predicts longterm mental health and functional outcomes. The overarching aim is to improve the care and treatment that people with TBI experience, by understanding the predictive value of sleep disturbances. TBI has a profound impact on an individual’s functioning, resulting potentially in life-long impairments. In England and Wales, 1.4 million hospital visits occur each year for people with head injuries. Patients often experience prolonged symptoms such as depression and sleep disturbances, which negatively impact their quality of life (Kyle et al. 2010). Sleep disturbance following TBI is prevalent – some estimates suggest that approximately 50% of patients are affected (Saksvik et al. 2020). Research into sleep disturbance shows that symptoms can become chronic and profound, lasting years post-injury and contributing to poorer outcomes (Kempf et al. 2010).

title: Emotion dysregulation in children and young people with ADHD: Utilising digital technology to understand clinical and educational correlates, and personalise assessments
description: Emotion Dysregulation (ED) is one of the leading causes of mental health referrals in children and young people (CYP). Emerging evidence suggests ED is highly increased in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), one of the most common childhood conditions, and can cause significant impairment. There are effective ways to address ED once identified, however, it is often overlooked in ADHD clinics: Routine ADHD questionnaires cannot detect these symptoms adequately. Furthermore, we know little about the risk factors and real-world impact of ED, including in education. My projects aim to address these gaps to improve assessments and care-planning for CYP with ADHD: Firstly, guided by my review of previous studies about ED assessment/screening, I will co-design digital approaches with service users for remote ED assessments. This will improve the accurate identification of ED. I will then develop Natural Language Processing (NLP) approaches to detect ED symptoms from large healthcare datasets linked with school records. I will use this data to examine ED’s risk factors and impact. Finally, I will combine NLP and digital approaches to build a new automated system for tailored assessments: This system will automatically guide service users to necessary assessments once it detects ED symptoms on electronic records.

title: How can we better predict those at greatest risk of developing depression following a cancer diagnosis?
description: Depression is common, yet remains both under-diagnosed and under-treated in people living with cancer. It is estimated that between 8 to 24% of people go onto experience a depressive illness following a cancer diagnosis. There is a pressing public health need to better predict and identify individuals with cancer who are at risk of developing depression. The stigma associated with depression, lack of physical–mental healthcare integration, and fragmentation of care have been identified as barriers towards targeted screening and diagnosis. The aim of this PhD is to improve the identification and understanding of the impact of depressive disorders in people living with cancer. We will use routinely collected data (including the Clinical Practice Research Datalink) to discover clinically relevant risk factors, develop and evaluate statistical models to estimate individualised risk, and then undertake early translational research using a mixed-methods approach. The specific objectives are to: 1) Collate data on risk factors for developing depression following a cancer diagnosis using routinely collected data, 2) Develop statistical models to estimate individualised risk of depression following a cancer diagnosis and an adverse outcome, and 3) Understand how risk estimates can be used to improve under detection.

title: Examining inequalities in mental healthcare for people with experience of forced migration: a mixed-methods approach
description: My aim is to explore inequalities in mental healthcare for people with experience of forced migration living in the UK, including refugees and people seeking asylum, among others. This population are at high risk of mental health difficulties, and previous research has shown that they face many barriers to accessing mental healthcare. However, it is not known whether those who do access services receive different care to other service user groups. First, I will use electronic health records to identify people with experience of forced migration who have accessed secondary mental health services in Southeast London. I will describe their characteristics (such as age and ethnicity) and aspects of care (such as referral pathways and treatments received) and compare these to service users who have not experienced forced migration, to reveal any discrepancies. Secondly, I will interview service users with experience of forced migration to understand their experiences of care, as well as mental health professionals, to understand the challenges they face when caring for this group. The findings will reveal specific service user groups, services, and clinical outcomes to focus future research. They will also allow inform recommendations for changes to health systems and clinical practice.

title: Creating a culturally tailored internet-based public mental health intervention to improve wellbeing for Black communities
description: Black communities are more likely to experience coercive pathways into the mental health system. There are many reasons for this, including finding services stigmatising and discriminatory, as well as not being able to recognise when additional support might be warranted. Working in partnership with a range of stakeholders, I will design an online intervention specifically for Black communities to address this inequality. The intervention will contain psychoeducational information about mental health, strategies to improve wellbeing, and provide participants with routes to seeking help. The content of the intervention will be designed in consultation with people from Black communities. I will then work with a web developer/company to design the final intervention. I will assess the feasibility of delivering the intervention to the target audience, for example assessing the acceptability of the intervention to participants, as well as measuring improvements on a range of outcome measures. I will partner with local voluntary organisations and businesses to recruit interested people to take part in the study. The expected impact of the intervention is to develop a culturally specific intervention which promotes wellbeing in Black communities, which will be ready to be scaled up into a larger randomised controlled trial.

title: Does psilocybin reopen sensitive period learning in adult humans?
description: Psychedelic-assisted therapy (PAT) is an emerging mental health treatment with significant potential. However, precisely how psychedelics influence learning and cognition remains unknown, particularly in the ensuring days and weeks. A recent animal study suggests that psychedelics reopen a ‘critical period’, a period of enhanced learning usually seen exclusively in childhood (e.g. language acquisition). This suggests there may be a discrete period after psychedelic use characterised by increased neuroplasticity and an enhanced ability to learn new information. This study will investigate whether psilocybin reopens sensitive-period learning in healthy adults using a randomised, double blind design. Following psilocybin (or placebo), participants will complete an absolute pitch learning paradigm, combined with dynamic causal modelling of EEG data to understand corresponding changes in neural pathways. This will shed light on cognitive and neural changes in the week after psilocybin.

title: Diversity in Major Trauma
description: Major trauma is caused by injuries from mechanisms including road traffic collisions, stabbing, falls or self-harm. Resulting in significant mortality and morbidity. Over the past decade, outcomes have improved for major trauma patients as a result of specialisation of hospital services and an emerging evidence base. However, most trauma research studies involve younger male populations, and trauma clinical guidelines are based on these findings rather than the population as a whole. Therefore, the understanding of how other factors such as gender, ethnicity, sexuality or disability affect major trauma patient outcomes is limited. Aim: In adult major trauma patients, which diversity characteristics are associated with their risk of injury, in- hospital recovery, and longer-term outcomes A prospective multi-centre mixed methods study will be conducted at the 4 London Major Trauma Centres. Routine in hospital clinical data will be collected from consecutive adult major trauma patients along with a self-reported diversity questionnaire and established quality of life questionnaires. Participants will be followed up at 6 months to complete further quality of life questionnaires. A sub-group of patients will be invited to semi-structured interviews to explore their experiences of recovery after discharge from hospital.

title: Strengthening whole-family support and outcomes for ethnically and racially minoritised families where parents engage with community mental health services.
description: Ethnically and racially minoritised communities face deeply rooted health inequalities, disadvantage and poor outcomes through continued cycles of systemic discrimination, racism and bias¹. The aim of my research is to co- design a strategy that promotes effective whole-family support and improved outcomes for families from ethnically and racially minoritised communities where parents engage with community mental health services. Co-design is essential in healthcare innovation by helping to discover barriers apparent to people receiving services². I have consulted with service users experienced in adult mental health services and safeguarding who confirmed this as a priority area for research and development. The anticipated research outputs and impact include, but are not limited to, improved health and wellbeing of ethnically and racially minoritised families, improved experience and social acceptance of using support services, increased professional confidence and knowledge of working with ethnically and racially minoritised families in adult mental health settings.

title: MORU Wellcome Major International Programme Core Grant Renewal 2025-2032
description: MORU’s research programme aims to improve the health and well-being of people living in low-resource settings across the tropical world through high quality science and its translation. We will conduct clinical and laboratory research on diseases that disproportionately affect disadvantaged communities. Through discovery research we will identify and understand these health threats, and then innovate affordable and deployable solutions to counter them. We address health challenges along the entire patient pathway, from the village health worker to the intensive care unit. We will address major challenges, with the aim of benefitting hundreds of millions of people. We will focus on infectious diseases and maternal and child health, and the emerging health threats of antimicrobial resistance and climate change. We are committed to ethical research practices and community engagement to ensure our work is relevant. We will improve the techniques to assess and optimise new and existing antimicrobial treatments, and then conduct high-quality clinical trials to assess them. We will strengthen stakeholder partnerships and collaborations to ensure our research agenda is equitably set, and our research is translated into impact. We will develop local research leaders and build research capacity to improve health outcomes and contribute to a more equitable world.

title: The Malawi Liverpool Wellcome Research Programme
description: Our vision is improvement of the health of all in Malawi and southern Africa through transformative research addressing critical global health challenges. Over the next decade, our aims are to: 1\. Pursue excellent research, delivering 1.1. reduced infectious disease burden through enhanced epidemiological and pathogen surveillance, understanding of disease mechanisms, optimising vaccine programmes, and evidence-based interventions underpinned by health data science; 1.2. reduced maternal, neonatal and childhood morbidity and mortality by defining the causes and creating interventions to improve their prevention and management; 1.3. methods for health systems to become resilient to climate shocks and pandemic threats; 1.4. knowledge of how to harness people’s actions and social interactions for optimal health outcomes; 1.5. a mental health initiative to understand the interaction with maternal and child health and climate. 2\. Create an enabling research environment with enhanced platforms and outstanding support. 3\. Provide world-class training to develop African and global health research leaders. 4\. Increase the local, regional and global impact of our research through strategic partnerships. The 2025-2032 core funding underpins this agenda by strengthening our research and training infrastructure, culture, partnerships, public engagement, thereby expanding our impact as an international centre of excellence in interdisciplinary health research and training.

title: Orchard OCD Research Workshop
description: Orchard OCD proposes a landmark two-day scientific workshop in London (Autumn 2026) to accelerate the development of new and more effective treatments for Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD) and improve early detection. Bringing together 400 global participants-including leading researchers, clinicians, people with lived experience (PWLE), early-career scientists, industry, and policymakers-the workshop will foster co-production of research priorities and solutions. Structured through dynamic keynote presentations, panel discussions, interactive breakout sessions, and Delphi-style consensus- building, the workshop will prioritise actionable solutions. Core themes include novel molecular and neuromodulation targets, precision medicine leveraging cognitive, EEG, neuroimaging, and genetic biomarkers, innovative psychotherapy approaches (including EMDR and VR-enhanced therapies), and developmental distinctions between child, adolescent, and adult OCD. This multidisciplinary approach incorporates rigorous co-production methods, embedding PWLE throughout, to ensure outputs directly address patient needs. Tangible outcomes include a collaboratively developed research priority roadmap and accessible, professionally designed dissemination materials.
