By embedding health-economic expertise, the workshop will generate actionable strategies to accelerate translation of research advances into clinical practice, aligned with MHRA and NICE regulatory frameworks. Orchard OCD’s proven leadership in patient-centred research and international collaboration ensures delivery of a high-impact event aligned with Wellcome Trust’s commitment to equitable, transformative mental health research.

title: Role of heat related gut-microbiota-brain-axis changes in psychosis (HEATMAP)
description: Higher ambient temperatures (HAT) and heatwaves have a detrimental impact on the morbidity and mortality associated with mental illnesses, particularly psychoses. Individuals with psychoses are more likely to be admitted to hospital and die during HAT and heatwaves. However, little is known about the mechanisms through which heat precipitates or exacerbates psychoses. High temperatures affect gut microbiota composition. Gut microbiota influence brain functioning through neural and biochemical mechanisms. Differences in gut microbiota may have a causal role in psychoses. Our goal is to understand how heat-related changes in gut microbiota precipitate or exacerbate psychoses. We will measure gut microbiota composition, microbial metabolites, inflammatory markers in stool and blood, and neurometabolite concentrations using magnetic resonance spectroscopy, in people with new-onset or relapse of psychoses under varying degrees of heat-stress. We will combine meteorological data, microclimate measurements, dietary habits, clinical profiles, gut microbiome, stool and blood metabolites, and neurometabolite data to build predictive models of heat-stress related gut-microbiota-brain-axis changes in psychoses. Simultaneously, we will explore the experiences and perceptions of individuals with psychoses on the impact of heat on their mental health, behavioural adaptations, and potential interventions. Our work will provide the basis for potential interventions and feasibility of their uptake.

title: Heat Resilience and Mental Health: Engineering Pathways to Reduce Depression and Anxiety in Schools in Nepal and Sri Lanka
description: Schools are critical environments for adolescent development, providing unique contexts to investigate how extreme heat impacts depression and anxiety among students. This project would implement sustainable, culturally and contextually tailored engineering interventions (e.g., enhanced natural ventilation, shading, greening) for heat reduction in secondary schools in Sri Lanka and Nepal, offering an opportunity to develop a causal framework to understand how mitigating heat exposure influences depression and anxiety. We hypothesise mitigating heat exposure reduces depression and anxiety via improved emotional regulation (e.g., reduced irritability and aggression), cognition (e.g., enhanced attention and memory), and social engagement (e.g., increased peer interaction and reduced isolation). We will closely monitor physical environmental changes—e.g., reduced indoor temperature, humidity and improved air quality to understand how they drive proposed mechanisms. We will conduct qualitative interviews and body mapping workshops with youth in Nepal and Sri Lanka to refine hypothesised mechanisms and associated assessments. A pilot cluster-randomised trial in eight schools in Sri Lanka and Nepal will implement the engineering interventions and focus on feasibility, acceptability, appropriateness and assessment of proposed mechanisms. We will generate preliminary insights into mechanisms linking extreme heat to depression and anxiety and provide a framework to enhance resilience of school environments to heat.

title: YUCA: Youth in Urban Centres across the Americas: Understanding and addressing heat impacts on mental health
description: This project will characterise mechanisms at the environmental, social, physiological, and biological levels linking heat exposure to mental health among urban youth (16-35 years) in the Americas. We will establish longitudinal cohorts of youth experiencing at least mild symptoms of depression, anxiety, and psychosis and who may benefit from mental health care in Montréal (Canada), Querétaro (Mexico), and Buenos Aires (Argentina). We will monitor temperature exposure, primary outcomes of anxiety, depression, and psychosis symptoms, secondary mental health outcomes, and a range of potential mechanisms, including air pollution and other environmental factors, social isolation, cognition, sleep, physical activity, cardiovascular health, psychotropic medication use, brain function and tissue properties, and demographic characteristics. We will develop a rodent model of heat stress to causally examine the relationship between heat exposure, brain volume and tissue properties, and depression and anxiety using longitudinal imaging and cellular assays. We will adapt existing mental health services to integrate intervention components that protect mental health in the context of heat and have been co-designed with youth. Our project will generate novel datasets from middle- and high-income countries across diverse contexts for systematic examination of heat exposure, mental health outcomes, and potential mechanisms from the cellular to population levels.

title: Behavioural, economic and social mechanisms underlying the association between chronic high temperatures and depressive symptoms among farmers and farm workers in India
description: Farmers are one of the most vulnerable communities to both heat exposure and depression. India, where nearly half of the workforce is engaged in agriculture, is no exception. Extreme heat can reduce crop yields, lower cultivation incomes and potentially increase risk of depression. Whilst studies to date have focused almost solely on this yield-income pathway, agricultural household income is increasingly diversifying away from cultivation. We therefore need to explore other causal pathways. The overarching aim of our project is to determine the relative importance—based on both farmers’ perceptions and quantitative data—of different causal pathways between heat and depression among farmers in India, and to translate these findings into scalable solutions. The project will be based in the dryland regions of three states: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Karnataka. WP1 involves participatory learning activities to understand how farmers conceive of the impact of heat on depression. WP2 involves causal mediation analysis using longitudinal data from an ongoing study in Andhra Pradesh—including PHQ-9—supplemented with weather data. In WP3, we will co-develop a heat- informed depression intervention programme, targeting causal pathways identified in WPs 1 and 2. WP4 will pilot this programme in a two-arm parallel cluster randomised pilot trial.

title: Mechanisms Mediating Summer Heat Effects on Mental Health: Examining Sleep, Physical Activity, and Cognitive Pathways in Young Adults with Affective Disorders
description: As climate change drives rising temperatures, research shows heat affects mood, particularly in young adults. Sleep-wake disturbance, cognition, and physical activity may mediate this relationship and offer ideal targets for interventions given they are measurable and modifiable. We propose to study the relationship of temperature, sleep, cognition, and physical activity on mood using a two-pronged approach combining nationwide monitoring and controlled laboratory studies in US young adults with depression and/or anxiety. We plan to measure 1) the direct relationship between ambient temperature and mood, 2) test sleep-wake disturbance, cognitive performance, and physical activity as mediators of this relationship, 3) measure differential effects of daytime and nighttime heat on mood, and 4) assess how heat affects mood and cognition during nocturnal wakefulness. Our interdisciplinary team combines expertise in young adult mood disorders, atmospheric science, sleep research, biostatistics, ecological momentary assessment, heat physiology, cognition, and monitoring through wearable devices. Young adult lived experience experts have helped develop this project and will help conduct the research and create multimedia resources to educate their peers about our findings. This project aligns with this call for proposals to study mechanisms by which heat affects mood disorders in vulnerable populations, with potential for developing targeted interventions.

title: Heat Exposure, Sleep, Cognition and MentAl Health: Mechanisms of Climate Change ImPacts on VulnErable Groups in Two Sub-Saharan Africa Countries – HEATSCAPE-Africa
description: HEATSCAPE-Africa seeks to understand how the impact of heat exposure on depression and anxiety is due to sleep and cognitive functioning, in Ghana (lower middle-income) and Zimbabwe (other low-income). Current evidence suggests that heat exposure disrupts sleep and impairs cognitive function—both of which are essential for mental health. However, research in low- and middle-income countries has been scarce, despite these populations being particularly vulnerable to climate-induced heat stress. 15% and 60% of primary healthcare attendees in Ghana and Zimbabwe respectively report depression symptoms. In both countries there is limited understanding of the mental health needs of vulnerable populations such as adolescents, women of reproductive age, and older adults. The project will focus on three key themes: a) contextual understanding of heat and mental health; b) methodological advances to identify causal mechanisms through a two-year prospective cohort study; c) community/health system readiness. The project has four deliverables: empirically-informed framework on mechanisms of heat exposure on depression/anxiety; a core mediator/moderator set for use in heat- mental health studies in LMICs; a community and health system readiness package of care; and a cohort of young researchers with lived experience. HEATSCAPE-Africa is a partnership based on expertise from Ghana, Zimbabwe, United Kingdom, and Canada.

title: Heat matters; mechanisms impacting maternal and offspring mental health
description: Every human begins life in the womb. Concerningly, pregnant women are particularly vulnerable to extreme heat exposure due to unique biological and psychological factors. These effects of heat exposure during pregnancy can extend across a woman’s lifespan and inter-generationally, influencing cognitive and affective functioning of mother and child. Despite this, the mechanisms linking heat exposure during pregnancy to mental health outcomes remain poorly understood. This research addresses this gap by investigating how extreme heat exposure affects stress, inflammatory signalling, and placental function—key vulnerabilities for poor mental health. Using mice, we will perform longitudinal physiological and behavioural studies, integrating computational modelling of cognitive tasks to uncover mechanisms behind anxiety and depression. Complementing these experiments, we will analyse data from a Wellcome-funded perinatal mental health study in Sydney—a region with significant temperature variability—integrating local weather and personal exposure data to examine the effects of heat on mothers and their children during pregnancy and postpartum. Harmonizing outcome measures across species will ensure translational impact. Finally, in collaboration with women with lived experience of perinatal mental health problems, we will co-design strategies to mitigate the adverse effects of extreme heat exposure during pregnancy, safeguarding maternal and child mental health in a changing climate.

title: Investigating the pathways linking heat exposure to mental health outcomes: mechanisms and interventions in a Ghanaian cohort (HEAT-MIND)
description: Perinatal depression affects 50% of women in Ghana, with suicidal ideation rates at 13-17%. Heat is a risk factor for depression and anxiety, but little is known about impacts on perinatal mental health. We will employ three approaches to causally examine mechanisms linking preconception, prenatal and postpartum heat exposure to maternal depression and anxiety. We integrate persons with lived experience (LE) as core research team members to develop the study approach, contextualize findings and maximize impact. In work package WP1, we leverage the extant Ghana Randomized Air Pollution and Health Study (GRAPHS) where higher prenatal heat exposure is associated with maternal stress and an extensive data repository allows investigation of multiple plausible mechanistic mediators. In WP2, we develop a new pregnancy cohort to understand how biological, social and psychological mechanisms link prenatal heat exposure to maternal depression and anxiety and examine effect modification by other exposures. In WP3 we pilot a heat warning system to reduce the impact of ambient heat on maternal mental health outcomes and investigate impacts on the mechanistic pathways identified in WP1 and WP2. This work will support a causal association between prenatal health and maternal depression and anxiety, elucidate mechanistic pathways, and identify novel interventions.

title: Resilient Emotion Regulation Development in a South African Birth Cohort
description: Resilience—successful development despite adversity—is mostly studied in high- income countries (HICs); however, most at-risk children live in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). This study addresses that gap by examining emotion regulation (ER) resilience in adolescents from the Philani birth cohort in Cape Town, South Africa. This deeply characterised, longitudinal cohort includes youth exposed to significant adversity, with protective and risk exposures comprehensively tracked from birth. We use longitudinal multimodal brain imaging, behavioural assessments, and a prospective design to explore how environmental factors shape ER and mental health outcomes at the behavioural and neurobiological level. Our goal is to identify mechanisms of resilience that can inform scalable, culturally grounded interventions. Aim I identifies brain circuitry associated with resilient ER in 525 adolescents (aged 13–14). Aim II identifies how protective factors promote brain development over two years to strengthen ER, preventing anxiety, depression, and PTSD. By integrating advanced statistical methods and machine learning together with this rare adolescent sample exposed to cumulative high adversity, we seek to improve the precision and inclusivity of resilience research in LMICs. This work aligns with Wellcome’s Mental Health strategy to reveal multi-level causal mechanisms and accelerate impact in underserved settings and global inequalities.
recipient: The Trustees of Columbia University in the City of New York

title: Georgetown-Lancet Commission on Faith, Trust, and Health
description: The Georgetown-Lancet Commission on Faith, Trust, and Health brings together a leading group of faith actors, government leaders, public health practitioners, researchers, and influential media voices. The Commission will create a shared platform for policy dialogue, research, and collaboration to build trust between faith and health partners to advance health and well-being globally. The Commission’s work covers three primary goals: Agenda-setting on faith, trust, and health: Reframe and prioritize the intersection of faith, trust, and health by analyzing the evidence base, generating thought leadership through multidisciplinary dialogue, and leveraging high-profile Commissioners to champion this work. Shaping policy and practice: Develop strategies and tools that strengthen public trust in health through improved policies and practices with health and faith actors and their communities. Collaboration and network-building: Strengthen relationships and networks between diverse groups in faith and health by fostering mutual respect and collaboration at local, national, and global levels. With Wellcome’s support, the Commission will generate actionable insights and tools—including a flagship Lancet Commission report synthesizing evidence across disciplines with case studies, alongside policy briefs, educational modules, and practitioner toolkits to foster collaboration and embed lasting trust-building approaches in faith and health systems globally. Keywords: Faith, Trust, Health, Policy Dialogue, Partnerships.

title: Madness in Medicine: Psychotic experiences and innovative approaches to mental health care in the UK
description: This community-engaged clinical ethnography investigates psychotic experiences and mental health care within the UK’s National Health Service. Experimental psychedelic-assisted therapy mobilizes psychotic experiences as therapeutic in clinical trials. Yet these trials exclude people with a history of psychosis, a highly stigmatised condition that disproportionately impacts racialised and disadvantaged communities. At the same time, conventional psychosis treatments—antipsychotic drugs—are increasingly recognised as insufficient, and cutting-edge psychosis clinics are foregrounding new approaches to managing psychotic illnesses. This project bridges divided research on psychedelics and psychosis to investigate psychotic experiences across these disparate clinical contexts and discover how innovative treatment approaches that mobilize or manage psychotic experiences are transforming mental health care. Through clinical ethnography, participatory arts-based research, and collaborative codesign with patients and clinicians, this research will provide insight on how therapeutic value, safety, and efficacy are changing in the context of the burgeoning ‘psychedelic renaissance’ and global mental health crisis. This project will advance scholarly debates in anthropology and science and technology studies, with implications for destigmatising ‘madness’ and developing more equitable mental health care policy and practice.

title: Caring about Care: Coproducing intersectional understandings of how caregiving relationships impact the mental health of care-experienced young people
description: I am proposing an ambitious, coproduced research project to understand how caregiving relationships can be harnessed to address the mental health crisis faced by care-experienced young people (CEYP). We know CEYP are at greater risk of poor mental health, including psychological distress, psychiatric diagnoses (e.g., depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder), and suicide, and are less likely to access formal mental health services. Harnessing existing caregiving relationships (e.g. with foster carers) to improve CEYP mental health is a government priority and acknowledged as a promising intervention area. This fellowship addresses the limited evidence- base to meeting this priority, developing evidence needed to refine theoretical understanding, informing policy and practice while amplifying CEYP’s traditionally marginalised voices. Specifically, my research aims to identify active ingredients and describe mechanisms by which caregiving relationships promote CEYP mental health using an intersectional approach through four linked studies co-produced with CEYP, caregivers and professionals. WP1 explores intersectional narratives of how caregiving relationships impact CEYP mental health; WP2 and WP3 investigate identified active ingredients in these relationships and how they link to CEYP mental health longitudinally using quantitative and ethnographic approaches respectively; WP4 synthesises findings through co-producing logic models for how identified active ingredients in caregiving relationships impact CEYP.

title: Shared Genetic Etiology Between Cardio-metabolic traits and Mood Disorders: A Genome-Wide Pleiotropic Analysis in Sub-Saharan African cohorts
description: Mood and cardio-metabolic disorders are commonly considered risk factors for each other and represent a significant burden to society. There is evidence suggesting a shared genetic etiology between cardio-metabolic disease risk factors (such as blood pressure, lipids, and glycemic traits) and mood disorders (depression and bipolar disorder). However, the nature of this overlap remains unclear in Sub-Saharan African populations. This study aims to explore the nature of the common genetic etiology between cardio-metabolic risk phenotypes and mood disorders. A genome-wide pleiotropic association study will be conducted using bioinformatics methods to investigate the shared genetic basis between cardio-metabolic disorders and mood disorders, utilizing summary-level data from African-ancestry cohorts. The study will incorporate existing and new data on cardio-metabolic and mood disorders from African cohorts, contributed by African researchers and global partners. The expected outcomes include the identification of pleiotropic genes, biological pathways, and causal effects between mood disorders and cardio-metabolic traits in African populations. This research has the potential to address a critical knowledge gap in cardiometabolic-psychiatric genetics research, particularly in African populations. Furthermore, it will provide a foundation for future multi-trait genetic studies in African populations, who have historically been underrepresented in mental health research.

title: Memory and Materiality in Conflict Landscapes: Psychological Impact of Spontaneous Memorials in the Russian-Ukrainian War
description: This project integrates approaches from mental health and conflict archaeology to study the phenomenon of spontaneous/grassroots memorials and their psychological impact. Amid the ongoing Russian-Ukrainian war, spontaneous memorials are created as the primary spaces for bereavement and remembrance. This research explores the potential psychological benefits of such places and the relationship between material culture, memory and counter-memory. Using an interdisciplinary methodology, the study combines structured and non- structured methods, including self-assessment questionnaires, oral interviews along with spatial and material analysis of sites. A longitudinal study design will trace changes in sites conditions, their public perceptions and impact on mental health over time. Citizen science approach will play a central role, encouraging individuals to share personal experiences and examples of how the war has transformed their environments and well-being. These contributions will be featured on a digital platform, functionng as a Digital Museum to document and represent these lived experiences. This study is particularly important as it is being conducted during an ongoing war. Its findings could benefit researchers across various fields studying human responses to war, conflict and trauma recovery.

title: Wellcome Mental Health Data Prize 2.0
description: The Wellcome Mental Health Data Prize 2.0 will provide grant funding and a comprehensive support programme to a cohort of interdisciplinary teams to unlock innovative digital tool development for mental health research. Key goals include: \- Cultivating interdisciplinary collaborations of researchers, data experts, technologists, lived experience experts and practitioners, contributing to a thriving mental health science community; \- Supporting the development of impactful digital tools with potential to scale; \- Inspiring use of existing mental health datasets to drive insight and action around early intervention; \- Strengthening the skills of Prize teams; \- Integrating lived experience throughout design and development to shape decision-making at both programme and team level. The Prize will be structured around two key phases: 1\. Prototyping Phase (9 months): supporting 6 teams to develop and test prototypes of their digital tool concepts; 2\. Sustainability Phase (9 months): supporting 3 teams to build out their digital tools and develop a robust roadmap for sustainability. As delivery partner, Social Finance will administer and monitor grant awards to participating teams.

title: Scoping Phase of Greentree Acceleration Plan
description: The Greentree Acceleration Plan aims to scale up global mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) in humanitarian settings beginning in Chad and Lebanon, fostering systemic, sustainable change. This proposal seeks support for a scoping phase of the Greentree Acceleration Plan Grant Proposal, with a special focus on building scientific readiness in country. A core component of the Plan is its contribution to the IASC’s MHPSS research agenda (MHPSS-SET-2) as well as to the broader field of global mental health research. The scoping exercise will examine how multisectoral, multilayered approaches to MHPSS can be effectively designed, implemented, and scaled across contexts. The first countries to take part—Chad and Lebanon—were carefully selected for their contrasting contexts: both face acute humanitarian needs but are at different stages in developing their MHPSS systems and capacities. This reflects the Plan’s commitment to fostering cross-context learning, leveraging diverse experiences to generate adaptable models that can strengthen MHPSS efforts worldwide. With the Wellcome Trust’s support, this scoping initiative will build the groundwork for a transformative research program that advances the understanding of effective, context-sensitive, and integrated MHPSS interventions.

title: Climate Stories That Work
description: Heard is a UK-based charity that drives narrative change through popular culture. Our mission is to shift public attitudes on urgent social issues by equipping media professionals and sector organisations with research-backed storytelling tools. For over 17 years, we’ve inspired impactful stories seen by millions across TV, journalism and entertainment. Our Climate Stories That Work programme, focuses on embedding well framed climate stories into TV to help audiences see the connection between a healthy planet and their own wellbeing. In partnership with Wellcome, we will build on this work by supporting production teams with tailored workshops, creative consultancy and story development across scripted and unscripted TV. We aim to reach non- traditional climate audiences - from hospital shows to gardening formats - and guide them to see that human health goes hand in hand with the planet’s health, boosting understanding, concern, and support for policy change. Our long term goal is that people support and embrace the changes we need to make to address climate change, protect nature and improve human health. We know one of the most important ways to do this is to make sure people hear well framed stories about the reality of climate change and the solutions to it.

title: Africa Psychosis Research Network: Inaugural Meeting
description: This application supports the inaugural meeting of the Africa Psychosis Research Network, a continent-wide collaboration of researchers, experts by experience, clinicians, and policymakers working to strengthen psychosis research in Africa. Taking place on 13 November 2025 in Cape Town, following the Global Mental Health Summit, this strategic one-day meeting will identify shared priorities, build trust, and lay the groundwork for a sustainable, inclusive Africa-led network. The network responds to longstanding fragmentation in psychosis research across the continent and the need for African leadership in shaping future agendas. Funding will support equitable participation, particularly for delegates from low-income countries (LICs) and people with lived experience of psychosis, who are frequently underrepresented in research and policy discussions. The meeting will include structured sessions to map ongoing efforts, highlight gaps, and co-develop a shared framework for collaboration. It will also establish working groups to take forward specific themes and prepare for a larger convening in 2026. Outputs will include a network structure, a summary of agreed priorities, and a follow-up plan for joint activities and future funding opportunities. Keywords: psychosis, Africa, research network, lived experience, equity, mental health.

title: Strengthening Mental Health Science III
description: WHO proposes to increase commitment, information and evidence to inform mental health policy and practice through an integrated set of activities. At its core, the initiative will advance commitment to mental health through strategic advocacy to position mental health in high-level agendas and organization and hosting of the first African mental health summit to enable regional leadership. These activities are supported by efforts to strengthen the evidence base and enhance availability of effective interventions, including through a series of activities to monitor implementation of a scalable psychological intervention; enhance access to essential psychotropic medicines; and transition WHO's mhGAP guidelines’ evidence base to a more accessible format, while scoping those most urgent for living reviews, to ensure recommendations remain current and practically accessible. The work is underpinned by systematic meaningful engagement of people with lived experience across all activities - ensuring both sustainable resourcing and authentic incorporation of lived experience perspectives throughout. Together, these interconnected workstreams will help strengthen the availability and use of mental health science while achieving shared goals between WHO and Wellcome.

title: Exposing Hidden Heat: Mapping Heat-Driven Health Disparities and Advancing Policy Implications for Climate-Resilient Urban Development in Dhaka, Bangladesh
description: Extreme heat is an escalating climate threat in Dhaka—one of the world’s most densely populated and rapidly urbanizing cities. This transdisciplinary, mixed-methods study seeks to make the health effects of climate change visible by mapping hyperlocal heat disparities and linking them to health outcomes. We will conduct a temperature monitoring campaign using both stationary and mobile sensors to generate granular urban heat data, which will be linked to geocoded emergency department visits for heat-related illnesses to assess disparities in health impacts. To identify structural and environmental drivers of urban heat, we will apply advanced machine-learning techniques integrating satellite imagery, land use data, OpenStreetMap, and Google Street View. Co-created by environmental health scientists, climate and GIS experts, urban planners, architects, and local policymakers, this project prioritizes actionable, locally relevant solutions. The study will evaluate the feasibility of targeted interventions—such as street planting, rooftop and balcony gardens, mobile cooling stations, and community cooling spaces—using GIS and urban design methods, including a pilot implementation of mobile cooling stations. Focus groups with residents, community leaders, NGOs, and policymakers will identify opportunities and barriers to implementation. By revealing the heat-health disparities and co-developing scalable interventions, this project aims to catalyze equitable climate adaptation in Dhaka.

title: Climate-Health Action through Research, Mobilization, and Engagement of Stakeholders in Kenya (CHARMES- Kenya)
description: Climate change is accelerating health risks across Kenya, with the greatest impacts felt in arid regions, informal settlements, and rural communities. Despite national commitments through recently enacted climate policies, limited Kenya-specific evidence impedes effective adaptation planning and implementation. CHARMES-Kenya project will leverage the government-owned platform, a trusted 20-year longitudinal health surveillance system covering diverse ecological zones, together with public, community, and policy engagements, and a transdisciplinary team of researchers, to close these evidence gaps and catalyze climate policy implementation at national and county level. First, we will generate community-informed evidence quantifying climate impacts on respiratory, diarrheal, and febrile illnesses, adolescent mental health, and healthcare access, using longitudinal health, demographic, and climate data. Second, we will co-develop policy tools with decision- makers, including a Health Impact-based Early Warning System (HIbEWS), site- specific vulnerability assessments, and economic modeling frameworks to support county and national health adaptation planning. Third, we will promote evidence-to-policy translation through technical working groups with the Ministry of Health, policy briefs aligned to national review timelines, county health leadership workshops, and feedback forums via community advisory boards. This project will drive evidence-based decision-making, strengthen health system resilience, and build a scalable model for climate-health policy action across Kenya and sub-Saharan Africa.

title: Strategic Health Integration for Equitable and Localized Decision-making (SHIELD) in a Climate-Stressed Humanitarian Setting in Turkana, Kenya
description: This project will transform how climate-health risks are recognized, prioritized, and addressed in Turkana County, Kenya—a climate-stressed, refugee-hosting region that remains under-represented in national health and development planning. Building on established relationships with refugee and host communities in Kakuma and Kalobeyei, we will co-produce actionable evidence on three initially identified climate-health threats—heat stress, vector-borne diseases, and climate-related mental health impacts—which will be further refined through participatory engagement with local stakeholders. These threats remain absent from policy and planning processes due to fragmented data, limited community voice, and siloed systems. We will address these gaps through a strategic, three-track approach: (1) co-producing knowledge with communities and decision-makers using participatory methods (seasonal calendars, storytelling, photovoice, body mapping), (2) generating empirical evidence through environmental sensors, wearable health monitors, health surveillance, and vector ecology, and (3) integrating these insights through policy-oriented systems modeling to support decision-making. Our transdisciplinary, locally embedded team includes researchers, county planners, humanitarian partners, and community leaders. Guided by the Rapid Outcome Mapping Approach (ROMA), we will deliver policy-facing outputs including dashboards, policy simulators, and visual narratives. These tools will inform the County Integrated Development Plan , budget decisions, and early warning protocols, amplifying lived experience and enabling anticipatory governance in Turkana.

title: MINDCLIMATE: Integrating Mental Health into Climate Change Policy in Zimbabwe: A Multisectoral Approach
description: Our goal is to ensure that Zimbabwe’s climate policy response integrates mental health by generating policy-relevant evidence on links between mental health and climate change and potential policy responses. We hypothesize that chronic and acute climate impacts, mediated through agricultural disruption and food insecurity, contribute to increased anxiety, stress, and depression, but can be mitigated through community-based interventions such as the Friendship Bench. We will combine high-resolution environmental data, historical survey data and a cross-sectional survey in 8 districts complimented by the installation of remote weather monitoring stations to enhance climate data granularity and community knowledge to examine associations between climate variability and mental health outcomes. We will apply human-centered design methods to co-develop community-led adaptation strategies and work with policymakers to translate evidence into climate- resilient mental health policies and integrate mitigation strategies into community platforms such as the Friendship Bench model. Public awareness activities, including multimedia campaigns, will promote climate and mental health literacy at community and national levels. This work will fill critical evidence gaps, inform national climate adaptation planning, and promote inclusive, resilience-building approaches that integrate mental health into Zimbabwe’s broader climate resilience strategies.
recipient: Zvitambo Institute for Maternal and Child Health Research

title: Salinity and Reproductive Health: Exploring the impacts on reproductive health and psychosocial health of women and adolescent girls in coastal Bangladesh
description: Climate change-driven salinity intrusion is silently but profoundly damaging the reproductive and psychosocial health of women and adolescent girls in coastal Bangladesh. Exposure to saline environments increases risks of infections, preeclampsia, emotional distress, and stigma, threatening health and dignity in some of the most climate-vulnerable communities. This project offers an urgent, community-powered response. Through interdisciplinary research, we will assess reproductive and mental health impacts, identify service gaps, and pilot sustainable, locally-led solutions — such as solar- powered water kiosks and peer-supported psychosocial interventions. Our integrated approach will generate new evidence linking climate stress to women's health, a critical and underexplored area in global health research. The outcomes will directly influence the revision of Bangladesh’s National Population Policy and guide scalable health adaptation strategies. Our findings will strengthen primary care services, build emotional resilience, and deliver low-cost, gender-sensitive innovations for safe water services. Community voices are at the heart of this project. Using participatory research frameworks, women and adolescents will co-design tools, lead peer education, and drive local change. Together, we will not only document climate impacts — but also create pathways of hope, dignity, and resilience for generations to come.

title: THRIVE: Transforming Health, community Resilience, and Inclusion in Vulnerable Environments affected by extreme weather events – Shaping local policy and action to improve nutrition, mental health and well-being in Malawi
description: This research investigates the complex interlinkages between extreme weather events, nutrition and mental health in smallholder farming and fishing communities in Malawi. In these settings, community resilience is stretched to a breaking point by increasing food insecurity and serious socio-economic and environmental stressors. We propose transdisciplinary, mixed-methods research to advance evidence-based policy-making and local action. The research adopts a systems lens, combining indigenous knowledge with community health, mental health, nutrition, health policy/systems, economic, anthropological, epidemiological and climate modelling expertise. Findings from a citizen ethnographic study and new insights from existing literature and country-wide datasets will feed into the co-creation and evaluation of community-based resilience strategies. Our collaborating partners, the Malawi Government and Save the Children, will use our findings on the feasibility, costs and effects of these resilience strategies to inform the development of Malawi’s National Health Adaptation Plan, and the design and implementation of district health adaptation plans in two study districts. Learnings will inform national scale- up of district health adaptation plans prioritising locally relevant resilience strategies to improve nutrition and mental health outcomes. This scale-up is embedded in the first-ever health-focused Green Climate Fund grant in Africa, led by the Ministry of Health and Save the Children (2025-2029).

title: Making a silent killer visible: Catalysing policy action to protect school students’ health and wellbeing from extreme heat amidst a changing climate in Latin America
description: Extreme heat is a silent and growing threat to students' cognitive function, health, wellbeing, and future potential across Latin America, yet this impact remains invisible and poorly unaddressed in public policy. This project aims to make these health effects visible to catalyse urgent and evidence-based policy action for adaptation in the health and education sectors across Peru, Chile, and Colombia. As a transdisciplinary team, we propose five work packages (WPs): WP1 will map current policy landscapes across countries to identify critical policy gaps and opportunities. WP2.1 will quantify current and future heat exposure in schools nationwide. WP2.2 will generate exposure- response curves by longitudinally measuring ambient heat/humidity versus student cognitive performance (using reaction time via PVT) in a 10-month school cohorts. WP3 will understand lived experiences in schools under extreme heat through phenomenological research with students and teachers. This evidence generation packages will directly inform the generation of targeted communication strategies via diverse channels (WP4) and the co-development of actionable policy outputs –including policy recommendations for HNAPs, heat- health alert thresholds, and practical school guidelines– created with policymakers (including MoH Peru and local authorities), communication experts, civil society organisations, and school communities in each country (WP5).

title: Salinity and Reproductive Health: Exploring the impacts on reproductive health and psychosocial health of women and adolescent girls in coastal Bangladesh
description: Climate change-driven salinity intrusion is silently but profoundly damaging the reproductive and psychosocial health of women and adolescent girls in coastal Bangladesh. Exposure to saline environments increases risks of infections, preeclampsia, emotional distress, and stigma, threatening health and dignity in some of the most climate-vulnerable communities. This project offers an urgent, community-powered response. Through interdisciplinary research, we will assess reproductive and mental health impacts, identify service gaps, and pilot sustainable, locally-led solutions — such as solar- powered water kiosks and peer-supported psychosocial interventions. Our integrated approach will generate new evidence linking climate stress to women's health, a critical and underexplored area in global health research. The outcomes will directly influence the revision of Bangladesh’s National Population Policy and guide scalable health adaptation strategies. Our findings will strengthen primary care services, build emotional resilience, and deliver low-cost, gender-sensitive innovations for safe water services. Community voices are at the heart of this project. Using participatory research frameworks, women and adolescents will co-design tools, lead peer education, and drive local change. Together, we will not only document climate impacts — but also create pathways of hope, dignity, and resilience for generations to come.

title: Support for At-Risk Academics
description: Cara was founded in 1933 to provide a lifeline to academics persecuted by Nazi Germany. Over 90 years later, a decline in academic freedom caused by a growth of conflict and the expanse of authoritarian regimes has increased the demand for our work. In response we have built a network of 135 UK university partners who provide sanctuary for at risk academics and their families. This grant will support up to 60 academics working in the field of Biosciences, with a focus on health and well-being, enabling fellows to continue and expand their research which is often connected to their home country and its eventual recovery; the funding will leverage the financial contribution of UK hosting universities who are unable to cover the full costs of each placement. The placements also benefit UK universities by making them more inclusive and increasing international research collaborations which strengthen their ability to contribution to global challenges. Moreover, this grant will strengthen Cara’s sustainability through a deeper understanding of impact that Cara fellows contribute to global knowledge and learning and within their host institutions. This will lead to funding diversification and further embedding of support for at-risk academics in the UK higher education sector.

title: Clean Land, Equitable Air, and Resilience (CLEAR): Advancing Health Equity by Addressing Waste-Driven Climate Risks
description: India has 3084 garbage dumpsites that emit Short-Lived Climate Pollutants (SLCP) and other pollutants, leading to significant health problems. Unmanaged waste in India contributes to 4% of total GHG emissions and emissions of volatile organic gases. Chronic exposure to pollutants from dumpsites contributes to respiratory issues, increased cancer risk, oxygen deprivation to vital organs, mental health issues, and reproductive impairments. Vulnerable communities like residents near dumpsites and informal waste pickers bear the brunt of such environmental degradation. India’s national regulations, complex environmental governance, and programmes like Swachh Bharat Mission 2.0 promote circularity in solid waste management to address climate and health risks from dumpsites. However, the progress is slow and India’s health sector response such environmental health issues is weak. India needs comprehensive public health data on the implications of open dumpsites and its mitigation efforts. In this context, the M.S. Swaminathan Research Foundation (MSSRF) proposes to undertake transdisciplinary action research aimed at 1) generating comprehensive data on environmental health, 2) strengthening the health system to improve preparedness and responsiveness to environmental issues, 3) provide support to selected States in improving solid waste management and 4) empower the vulnerable communities associated with dumpsite.

title: Mangrove Conservation for Planetary Health: Quantifying Climate, Health, and Socioeconomic Impacts in Protected Mangrove Ecosystems
description: Mangrove ecosystems play a central role in climate change mitigation and offer a wealth of co-benefits that support human health and local livelihoods. However, ongoing deforestation and fragmented conservation efforts threaten these benefits, exposing communities to health and economic vulnerabilities. This project will assess the impacts of mangrove conservation on climate regulation, health, and socioeconomic outcomes, using Ramsar-protected mangroves in Malaysia as a model. Structured around six integrated work packages, we will combine environmental, public health, and socioeconomic outcomes to understand the full range of conservation impacts. This includes measuring greenhouse gas fluxes, sediment carbon stocks, and microbial functions; investigating health outcomes related to respiratory and mental health, heavy metal exposure and antimicrobial resistance; and examining how conservation influences livelihoods, wellbeing, and community responses to environmental change. Hydrodynamic modelling will assess the role of mangroves in mitigating coastal hazards, while participatory research will explore local knowledge, adaptation barriers, and risks of maladaptation. Findings will be co-produced with local communities and national stakeholders to raise awareness, inform decision-making, and support conservation efforts. By linking climate, health, and development outcomes, this project will strengthen the case for mangrove conservation that contributes to planetary health and resilience in Malaysia and beyond.

title: Impact of Green Energy for Cooking and Heating on Household Air Pollution and Health in Rural Communities of Pakistan
description: A significant proportion of rural households in Pakistan rely on biomass fuels for cooking and heating, contributing to household and environmental air pollution and health risks. Biomass combustion releases harmful pollutants, including PM2.5, CO, and volatile organic compounds, linked to respiratory, cardiovascular, skin, and eye illnesses and adverse pregnancy and birth outcomes. Green energy presents a sustainable alternative, particularly for low-income populations with limited access to cleaner fuels and sustained electricity. This cluster-randomized trial will evaluate the effectiveness and feasibility of green-powered (solar and/or hydro-powered) electric stoves and heaters in reducing household air pollution and improving health across two regions of Pakistan. Villages will be randomized into intervention and comparison arms; intervention households will receive battery-operated electric stoves/heaters, powered by centralized/decentralized solar or micro- hydro sources. Comparison clusters will continue using biomass fuel. Air quality will be monitored biweekly using advanced equipment and laboratory measures, and health assessments will include respiratory function, blood pressure, skin conditions, eye symptoms, and pregnancy and mental health outcomes. Feasibility will be assessed through compliance, acceptability, and cost-effectiveness. The study will model the impact of scale-up on air pollution, health, and economics at national level to support policies for shift to renewable energy and climate mitigation.

title: Clean Land, Equitable Air, and Resilience (CLEAR): Advancing Health Equity by Addressing Waste-Driven Climate Risks
description: India has 3084 garbage dumpsites that emit Short-Lived Climate Pollutants (SLCP) and other pollutants, leading to significant health problems. Unmanaged waste in India contributes to 4% of total GHG emissions and emissions of volatile organic gases. Swaminathan Research Foundation (MSSRF) proposes to undertake transdisciplinary action research aimed at 1) generating comprehensive data on environmental health, 2) strengthening the health system to improve preparedness and responsiveness to environmental issues, 3) provide support to selected States in improving solid waste management and 4) empower the vulnerable communities associated with dumpsite.

title: Blue Anthropocene Wellbeing: Coastal Dwelling Skills and Multispecies Disease Entanglements under Climate Change in the Pacific
description: Pacific artisanal fisherpeople hold ancestral knowledge about adapting to extreme weather events and cohabiting with zoonotic vectors. However, climate change is now challenging long-held wisdom of how to live well in a fast- changing environment. This project will explore the adaptability of coastal communities, transforming our understanding of climate impacts on multispecies dwelling and disease entanglements in the Blue Anthropocene. Utilising a bold and original multidisciplinary biosocial approach through international collaboration between medical anthropology and marine biology in Peru and Chile, I will address the following questions: 1\. What are the emerging politics of entanglement (multispecies interactions in a situated environment) between humans and non-humans in the Blue Anthropocene, considering the changing profile of disease vectors and zoonoses/panzootics? How do these politics influence prevention and control of infectious zoonoses outbreaks? 2\. In what ways have new multispecies dwelling skills (biological and cultural adaptions produced over time within populations inhabiting a specific ecosystem) transformed and/or adapted in the face of climate change? How do these interact with existing ancestral skills/wisdom and the ability to live well within the wider ecosystem? The project outcomes will enable us to better support global coastal communities who may be experiencing ‘new’ unanticipated weather and health events.

title: ASCEND-HD: Advancing Support and Care for Emotional Needs and Distress in Huntington's Disease
description: Huntington’s disease (HD) is a neurodegenerative, inherited condition with typical onset between 30-50 years. It causes physical, cognitive and emotional deterioration, and premature death. UK HD prevalence has doubled since 1990, with 8,000 people affected and 32,000 at risk. Worldwide, HD affects five people per 100,000. HD severely impacts mental wellbeing, including depression, anxiety, and suicidality. However, these difficulties are inadequately understood, affected individuals and families struggle to access informed, effective mental healthcare, and routes to meaningful systemic change are lacking. As an HD-specialist clinical psychologist and researcher, with lived experience of HD myself, I am uniquely placed to change this. I will lead ASCEND-HD, a transformative multi-methods programme of much-needed discovery research employing a Theory of Change model and co-production with experts by experience. Combining well-established and highly-novel methods, we will develop comprehensive understandings of how HD affects wellbeing of individuals and families, and of barriers and facilitators to a step-change in HD wellbeing support. I will then co-produce novel evidence-based guidance and resources for understanding mental wellbeing and support needs among HD families. Working with research, clinical and third-sector networks, these transformative tools will shape future interdisciplinary HD wellbeing research internationally, informing innovative new research and real-world change.

title: What can bureaucratic justice do for mental health?
description: Primary health services are an essential part of the response to the UK’s mental health crisis. Although service delivery may seem secondary to treatment, our early engagement with those navigating primary care pathways for common mental health problems has shown us how accessing and engaging with support often involves struggling with bureaucratic processes, and leaves them with a sense of unjust treatment. This is more than just frustrating or a problem in principle; research across disciplines suggests that perceptions of just treatment can significantly impact treatment outcomes by affecting engagement, deterring future support-seeking, and exacerbating inequalities. This research programme pioneers the application of the theory of ‘bureaucratic justice’ in primary mental health services. The proposed programme will deploy an innovative combination of a longitudinal quantitative and qualitative study with participatory storytelling methods to produce a new understanding of the nature and relevance of just treatment in the context of how people interact with frontline administrative processes in primary care mental health services. It will also build an interdisciplinary community of researchers and provide a platform to embed lived experiences of seeking mental health support into research practices in innovative and engaging ways.

title: Precise mapping of human brain function and connectivity for diseases of neurological network disruption
description: Neurological diseases and neuropsychiatric conditions constitute a looming crisis for ageing societies, including the UK. Many of these diseases involve pathological alterations to deep brain “nuclei”, which cascades into disruption of larger brain networks. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a promising technology for studying, monitoring, and developing therapeutics for these diseases. Specifically, we can measure brain activity with functional MRI and structural connectivity with diffusion MRI. However, current functional and diffusion MRI methods are limited in spatial resolution (>1mm) and cannot precisely measure early changes in many small nuclei and their associated networks. The proposed research will develop novel functional and diffusion MRI technologies to map brain function and connectivity with unprecedented spatial precision and accuracy. The main goals are to: i. develop novel technologies to enable sub-0.5mm diffusion MRI for precise mapping of brain structural connectivity. ii. develop novel technologies to enable sub-0.5mm functional MRI for robust detection of brain activity. iii. apply the developed methods to improve the accuracy of targeting and response measurement for transcranial ultrasound stimulation. iv. translate prototype methods into robust tools and investigate future technical and clinical research directions. These new methods will enable previously unfeasible clinical and basic science research to be performed.

title: Translation-associated quality control of protein secretion.
description: Secreted and membrane proteins (secretome) comprise one-third of our proteome, and are translated at the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). We and others recently discovered a quality control pathway that acts at the earliest stages of secretome biogenesis. Mechanisms underpinning this ER-localized Ribosome- associated Quality Control (ER-RQC) pathway that eliminates stalled ribosomes and aberrant nascent proteins remain largely undefined. Loss of ER-RQC is associated with neurodegenerative and developmental disorders, but the basis for these specific disease outcomes is unknown. This proposal aims to elucidate how ER-RQC maintains secretome integrity by (i) mapping the factors that initiate and resolve ER-RQC, and the proteins that are subject to this pathway; (ii) elucidating the mechanisms that resolve stalled ribosomes and the cellular consequences of defects in this process; (iii) identifying broader translational regulatory pathways that influence secretome biogenesis. We will use state-of-the-art cell engineering to build secretory cell models that link secretome quality control with specific cellular physiology. Our team’s complementary multidisciplinary expertise in structural biology, biochemistry, cell biology, proteomics and genetics positions us perfectly to dissect the pathways that maintain secretome integrity. Our work will advance our understanding of protein quality control, linking the molecular mechanisms underlying these processes to specific failures that cause disease.

title: Africa Oculomics Research Programme: harnessing ocular biomarkers to transform health
description: Our vision is to unlock the potential of Oculomics to better understand, predict, diagnose and manage systemic and ocular disease, to improve health outcomes and equity for African populations. Oculomics is the emerging field of study into relationships between the eyes and systemic health and disease. It is being transformed by advances in high-resolution ocular imaging coupled with recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning. We will conduct ocular phenotyping and imaging studies, repeated five years apart, nested within an existing general population cohort in Uganda. In parallel we will collect clinical, laboratory and image phenotyping data for systemic health states (cardiovascular, neurological, renal, liver, musculoskeletal, mental health), alongside genotyping data. We will use these data to develop, tune and validate AI foundation models to analyse images from this African population for multiple systemic disease and ocular diagnostic tasks. We will investigate cross-sectional and longitudinal relationships between ocular biomarkers and major health conditions, to determine their diagnostic, prognostic and predictive potential. Finally, we will conduct prospective studies to investigate the utility of oculomics supported diagnostics in general health care settings, assessing the suitability and performance of AI-assisted diagnosis, when paired with novel low-cost imaging equipment.
recipient: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine

title: Wellcome UK Mental Health CSO Discretionary Grants: Political Engagement
description: Accelerate collaborative influencing across mental health civil society, to increase political support for mental health in Westminster. This will include streamlining political monitoring and stakeholder management across CSOs, expanding the number and impact of political champions for mental health and building strategic partnerships with political influencers. This will be enabled by funding additional public affairs capacity for the sector alongside dedicated budget to deliver consistent mental health events and engagement with Parliamentarians, including Ministers, backbench Labour MPs, and Opposition Parties. Central to this will be the development of a new ‘sector pitch’ to government, which builds a stronger political argument for increased mental health ambition, identifies opportunities for mental health breakthroughs during this parliament and sets out how the sector can support this. This will include increasing our understanding of current public attitudes to mental health and identifying target audiences to engage. Through insight and message testing we will build a new messaging framework to reach and engage target audiences and increase public pressure on UK Government.

title: Policy Solutions
description: The grant will support collaboration between civil society organisations (CSOs), to build the evidence base required to make a compelling political case for increased mental health ambition in the UK. This will include jointly commissioning pieces of new analysis in response the current political context and prevailing evidence gaps. Policy analysis priorities will be informed by a joint political influencing strategy, with a likely focus on increasing available data and evidence on early intervention, mental health waiting lists and economic activity. The grant will also enable more responsive and reactive policy analysis, providing capacity to draw on and synthesise new insights generated by a sector data hub. The new sector hub will bring together data from multiple sources, including unique data held by CSOs, to build a more nuanced picture of the current mental health context. The data will be used to enable real time and coordinated influencing targeted at MPs, Ministers and No10.

title: UK CSO Mental Health Influencing: Data and Evidence
description: The grant will support collaboration between civil society organisations (CSOs), to build the evidence base required to make a compelling political case for increased mental health ambition in the UK. This includes bringing together mental health data held across CSOs into a central data hub, to build live insight into mental health need and trends across the UK. Data collection will be informed by a joint political influencing strategy, with a focus on increasing available data on early intervention, mental health waiting lists and economic activity. A newly established sector data and evidence network will analyse available data on an ongoing basis to inform joint sector policy and influencing. The data will be used to enable reactive and coordinated influencing targeted at MPs, Ministers and No10.

title: Wellcome UK Mental Health CSO Discretionary Grant: Constituency Engagement
description: Current UK Government plans fall short in addressing the urgency and scale of mental health need across the country. Given the complex political landscape and economic constraints, securing major new investment in mental health care will be difficult without increased, consistent political and public pressure. To drive change, public pressure—particularly from those directly impacted —is essential. However, sector-wide funding cuts have made it difficult to build and sustain the pressure needed to secure government action. At the same time, current media narratives risk undermining progress we’ve made in shifting attitudes to mental health. This grant will amplify the public support we know exists across the UK for transformational changes in mental health care. This will include supporting young people aged 16-25 who are currently most impacted by negative media and political narratives to engage directly with decision-makers, share their perspectives and advocate for and inspire positive change. The grant will enable young advocates to explore and utilise a range of public engagement tactics — including media, PR, and creative advocacy —to begin to increase public and political cut-through for mental health.

title: Unraveling Biological Pathways and Health Impacts of Air Pollution Components to Inform Climate Mitigation
description: This research program addresses the urgent need to quantify dose-response relationships of real-world air pollution exposures on biology to inform climate mitigation. It directly tackles critical Wellcome Trust research gaps: understanding cumulative and combined pollutant exposures and identifying critical exposure thresholds for adverse health effects. The program is structured around two integrated projects. Project 1 (Mechanistic Studies) will characterize source-specific PM2.5 from urban hotspots to define their toxicological profiles and disease pathways in 3D human airway models. This includes assessing susceptibility in diseased airway cells (asthma, COPD) and investigating systemic links to cancer, immune dysregulation, and cardiovascular diseases. Project 2 (Population Studies) will develop high- resolution US air pollution models (PM2.5 components, NO2, O3) to link with nationwide health datasets (Medicaid, Medicare, HCUP). It will produce pollutant-, mixture-, and source-specific dose-response functions for respiratory, cardiovascular, neuropsychiatric, and cancer outcomes. This novel, integrated approach provides essential, policy-relevant evidence, including an interactive online tool to quantify potential health benefits of mitigation activities, enabling policymakers to effectively target hazardous pollutants and optimize public health outcomes. Keywords: Air pollution, PM2.5, climate change mitigation, health impacts, dose-response, cumulative exposures, pollutant mixtures, source apportionment, toxicological profiling, epidemiology, policy relevance, public health, computational modeling, environmental health.
recipient: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health

title: SAFER-MH: Improving Safety Evaluation and Regulatory Capacity for AI-Enabled Mental Health Care
description: In this proposal, we aim to address three key challenges to ensure that AI has safe and equitable impact in mental health (MH): we and our partners will collaborate with the South African Health Products Regulatory Agency (SAHPRA) to create a regulatory pathway for AI-enabled (MH) products; we will define a taxonomy of potential harms caused by AI-enabled MH products and develop new ways of detecting those harms; and we will establish a standard for how information about user engagement is recorded so that we can draw better links between products and real-world outcomes. Taken together, these three strands of work will help developers monitor and maintain user safety, regulators understand how to evaluate the safety of AI applications, and patients access quality care. More succinctly, our work will reduce the friction, complexity, and cost associated with regulatory compliance, making it easier for developers to innovate safely. Our focus will be to deliver these solutions in low-resource settings, but since the application of AI to MH and the field of regulatory science for AI-as-a-medical-device is so nascent, many of our outputs will have global relevance for advancing these fields.

title: Rooted in Resilience: A Child-Centered Inquiry into Climate, Health, and Wellbeing
description: Young children’s understanding of climate change and related phenomena (extreme weather, increased heat, air pollution, biodiversity loss) is generally unexplored. Despite evidence that families discuss significant climate-related events, and that environmental curricula are part of formal learning for children as young as 6, little is known what children are learning and how they are making sense of these issues as they develop their sense of self and understanding of the world around them. Working under the assumptions that 1). certain dispositions learned during childhood can endure throughout life and influence environmental behaviors, and 2). carefully- crafted educational media can help shape those dispositions and behaviors, we intend to elucidate young children’s understandings of environmental issues in order to create powerful messaging to improve their understanding of environmental processes (environmental literacy), build their sense of self- efficacy as environmental agents of change (environmental stewardship), and enrich family conversations around environmental issues and behaviors. We are seeking Wellcome Trust’s $1,000,000 investment to conduct a foundational research study, findings from which will enable us to create globally relevant, joyful, and appealing children’s media that encourages positive environmental behaviors, helping children build the skills they need to thrive in a world reshaped by climate change.

title: ‘Together for Mental Health: African Leadership, Global Impact’ conference
description: ‘Together for Mental Health: African Leadership, Global Impact’ (working title) conference will spotlight African-led research, innovation, and policy solutions in mental health. The conference, scheduled for spring 2026, will be structured around thematic tracks reflecting key priorities in African mental health (such as mental health in the context of climate change and crisis, integrated care, substance use, youth mental health, lived experience leadership, and innovations in African mental health research). The scientific programme will include keynote addresses, thematic sessions, quickfire plenaries, poster presentations, and a curated innovations fair showcasing cost-effective, scalable mental health interventions. Site visits to local programmes and interactive workshops will provide practical, context-rich learning opportunities. Lived experience leadership will be fully integrated from conference design to delivery, ensuring accessibility, inclusion, and relevance. The event will prioritize community-building and developing lasting partnerships through networking, coordinated meetings, and alignment with other global health initiatives. Key goals of the conference include increasing the visibility of African-led mental health initiatives at national, regional, and global levels; convening diverse stakeholders for meaningful knowledge exchange and collaboration; promoting South-to-South learning, shared leadership, and new partnerships; and support evidence- informed policymaking and the scale-up of effective interventions through linking implementers and policy actors.

title: Supporting people with psychosis: a real world deployment of CareLoop in the US.
description: This project proposes a real world evaluation of the CareLoop platform in a mental healthcare setting in the US. The CareLoop product has been developed in the UK to support people with severe mental illness. It has an expansive evidence base and has been extensively tested through a series of clinical trials. The CareLoop product is now NICE-recommended through the Early Value Assessment process in the UK and is registered as a Class I medical device with the UK Medicines and Health Regulatory Authority. However, it has never before been used in the US. This real world project will collect data on clinical outcomes, user acceptability, and implementation. We will work closely with service users and healthcare professionals to identify and overcome the practical barriers and enablers to adoption. The data we collect will inform iterative improvements to the CareLoop product and implementation model. Crucially, the project will support the development of the CareLoop commercialization strategy, bringing critical insights to the CareLoop approach to the U.S. and global markets. The project will also inform the CareLoop strategy to low and middle income countries (LMICs) where affordability, infrastructure limitations, culturally sensitive technical adaptations and health system constraints are key.

title: CORE-MH: Strengthening Capacity for Research Excellence in African Mental Health
description: The Africa Global Mental Health Institute (AGMHI) is a collaborative network dedicated to advancing mental health (MH) research, education, clinical care, advocacy and policies across Africa. Through a pilot program launched in 2023, AGMHI has successfully provided mentorship, foundational research training, and professional growth opportunities to early career African MH researchers. The proposed CORE-MH program builds on this pilot, targeting predoctoral researchers needing foundational support to advance in low-resource settings. CORE-MH is structured around two tracks: 1) a two-year intensive fellowship offering individualised mentorship, practical research training, and flexible funding; and 2) broad-based professional development comprising a series of on-demand learning materials offered through AGMHI's resource hub. Led by Stellenbosch University and University of KwaZulu-Natal, CORE-MH includes five core components: 1) individualised mentorship; 2) fundamental research training; 3) biostatistics and epidemiology support; 4) neuroethics training; and 5) flexible funding for research projects, upskilling, and conferences. These components work together to strengthen research capabilities, academic skills, and career development. Expected outcomes include increased capacity to secure grant funding and conduct rigorous, independent research, career progression to doctoral programs or other leadership roles, and sustainably building a network of skilled MH researchers across Africa to promote equity in global MH science.

title: Hypatia Health
description: Many psychiatric and psychological treatments don’t work for everyone, and when they do, it’s often unclear why. In routine care, there’s a gap between symptom-level and brain-level understanding. As a result, patients are left navigating trial-and-error approaches with a clinician to find what works. Computational models can help close this gap. These models support mechanistic phenotyping, offering better ways to shape treatment plans, structure therapy sessions, and develop new treatments. But current methods are inconsistent across teams and lack a simple, user-friendly interface for clinicians, researchers, and service-users. Hypatia Health aims to change that. We’re building a scalable platform that gives scientific and clinical teams easy access to gold-standard computational models and matching gamified tasks. Researchers worldwide can simulate and predict human behaviour, while clinicians can use interactive games to generate computational phenotypes for service users. By making these tools accessible, we reduce wasted time and resources—and bring care closer to the causes of mental ill health.

title: The Translocator Protein (TSPO) as a Multimodal Target for Generalised Anxiety Disorder
description: Generalised Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is a prevalent and debilitating mental health condition. Current pharmacotherapies suffer from delayed onset, side effects, or poor long-term efficacy, highlighting the urgent need for novel, mechanism-based interventions. The Translocator Protein (TSPO) is a promising, yet under-investigated, target for GAD due to its dual role in neurosteroid synthesis and neuroinflammation regulation, two key pathways implicated in GAD pathophysiology. Despite compelling pre-clinical evidence, TSPO’s therapeutic potential remains unproven due to critical knowledge gaps, particularly regarding the impact of the single nucleotide polymorphism (A147T, rs6971), which impairs TSPO function and druggability, affecting up to 50% of the Caucasian population. Our project will deliver the first comprehensive target validation of TSPO for GAD using a novel pharmacological approach. Using ground-breaking ligands developed in our laboratories that bind both wild-type (WT) and A147T TSPO with nanomolar affinity, we will assess steroidogenic and anti-inflammatory functions in clinically-relevant isogenic iPSC-derived glial cells. In parallel, we will evaluate behavioural and molecular outcomes in WT and A147T TSPO mouse models. This integrative strategy will rigorously define the functional relevance of TSPO in anxiety regulation and its tractability as a therapeutic target, paving the way for the development of genetically robust, fast-acting treatments for GAD.

title: Zinc transporter-3 as a novel target for fast and long-lasting antidepressant actions
description: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) is a leading cause of disability worldwide, with up to 30% of patients developing treatment-resistant depression (TRD). There is an urgent need for novel therapeutic targets that drive rapid and sustained antidepressant effects. Zinc transporter-3 (ZnT3) is a novel and unexplored target. We recently showed that psilocybin enhances proliferation and survival of human hippocampal progenitor cells and promotes neurogenesis and neurite outgrowth. Single-cell RNAseq indicates stage-specific ZnT3 expression, suggesting a role in neurogenesis. In mice, we showed that ZnT3 expression and the activation of adult-born neurons are required for psilocybin’s rapid and lasting antidepressant effects. This project will validate ZnT3 as a novel therapeutic target to elicit rapid and long-lasting effects without hallucinogenic effects, by examining its role in neuroplasticity using preclinical models and patient-derived samples. First, we will assess ZnT3 expression in adult-born neurons following chronic stress and antidepressant treatment, in mice and brain-derived exosomes from MDD and TRD patients. Second, we will determine whether modulating ZnT3 or increasing intracellular Zinc elicits antidepressant-like effects. Targeting ZnT3 will offer a new therapeutic approach for MDD, with the potential to provide rapid and long-lasting benefit to patients resistant to existing treatments.

title: Validating novel, selective CaV2.3 inhibitors as oral, small molecule therapies for posttraumatic stress disorder
description: Post-traumatic stress disorder is a prevalent mental health condition with significant unmet medical need. Over 5% of trauma-exposed adults worldwide develop PTSD during their lifetimes, with those exposed to certain types of trauma such as combat and assault carrying a particularly high burden. The few approved drug treatments (e.g. paroxetine and sertraline) have limited efficacy and significant side effects. A recently published multi-ancestry meta-analysis of genetic data from >1 million individuals exposed to trauma reported significant risk of PTSD associated with the CACNA1E gene which encodes a voltage-gated calcium channel (CaV2.3) with high expression in brain areas (hippocampus, amygdala, anterior cingulate and prefrontal cortex) involved in memory, emotional regulation, and stress response. Genome-wide analyses of transcription indicated that the highest risk alleles are linked to significantly higher expression of CACNA1E, suggesting that inhibition of CaV2.3 function has potential therapeutic benefit. Lario Therapeutics has developed first-in-class, small molecule inhibitors of CaV2.3 which are potent, selective, and brain-penetrant. This collaborative proposal aims to validate CaV2.3 as a target for PTSD and to test potential CaV2.3-targeted therapeutics in mouse models of PTSD including stress-induced alterations in anxiety, fear conditioning and in paradigms showing learned flexibility of instinctual fear behaviours.
recipient: TCG Centres for Research and Education in Science and Technology

title: Validation of the complement C4-C1s interaction as a novel therapeutic target to modulate synaptic plasticity in schizophrenia
