description: Imbalanced complement activity, particularly excessive complement C4A-driven synaptic pruning, has been associated with disrupted neurodevelopment and schizophrenia onset. Genetic studies have identified increased expression of the complement C4A variant, relative to C4B, as a risk factor for schizophrenia. We aim to validate complement C4A as a novel drug target for schizophrenia, focusing on modulating excessive synaptic pruning, a process that eliminates extra synapses during brain development. Our hypothesis is that rebalancing C4A:C4B activity will mitigate excessive synaptic elimination and its associated neuropathology (Figure 1). We have developed a panel of small molecules that modulate complement activity, with selective effects on C4. This project will validate the C4A variant as a suitable target to rebalance synaptic pruning and normalise synaptic plasticity in patients with schizophrenia. We use established molecular and cellular assays and validate plasma C4A:C4B as a biomarker to determine the relevance and druggability of C4A for drug discovery. By specifically modulating C4A activity, this approach has the potential to reduce or prevent brain changes in individuals with C4A:C4B imbalance, alleviating symptoms, halting disease progression or even preventing schizophrenia onset. This work aims to enable early intervention strategies and contribute to a broader understanding of complement-mediated mechanisms in psychiatric disorders.

title: CRF1 Receptor Agonists as an Adjunct Treatment for Major Depression and Treatment-Resistant Depression
description: Major depressive disorder (MDD) affects ~16% of the global population, yet existing treatments like SSRIs/SNRIs are slow to act and leave ~30% of patients treatment-resistant. Although ketamine offers rapid antidepressant effects, its efficacy varies widely. Our preclinical work demonstrates that acute activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, particularly through corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF), is essential for ketamine’s behavioral and synaptic efficacy. We show that CRF facilitates ketamine’s behavioral and cellular effects, while CRF1 receptor (CRF1R) antagonism blocks them, highlighting the therapeutic potential of transient CRF1R activation, a largely unexplored strategy. We propose a novel approach using CRF1R agonists as adjuncts to enhance antidepressant response. Aim 1 will validate the efficacy of CRF1R agonists in combination with ketamine, examining behavior, pharmacokinetics, and circuit-level engagement. Aim 2 will test whether CRF1R agonists can accelerate or enhance SSRI response in a chronic stress model. Aim 3 will generate a detailed safety profile of CRF1R agonists, including CNS and gastrointestinal effects, and use bioinformatic tools to assess translational relevance through human data. Our multidisciplinary team integrates expertise in neuropsychopharmacology, bioinformatics, and drug discovery. This work will advance CRF1R agonists as promising fast-acting, adjunctive treatments for early intervention in treatment-resistant depression.

title: TargetMDD: Validating microRNA-186-5p as a molecular target for early intervention in Major Depressive Disorder
description: This project aims to validate a novel therapeutic strategy for Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) by targeting miR-186-5p, a microRNA elevated by chronic stress and linked to synaptic dysfunction in the prefrontal cortex. Targeting this upstream, stress-responsive microRNA offers a distinct approach compared to conventional treatments focusing on downstream neurotransmitters. Our approach combines chronic stress animal models and human iPSC-derived neurons with data from post-mortem brain, serum, and cerebrospinal fluid of MDD and other stress-related psychiatric patients. We will assess if miR-186-5p inhibition reverses neuronal and behavioural changes caused by stress, establishing its therapeutic potential. In vivo validation will utilize i) light-activatable nanoparticles to deliver inhibitors with precise temporal control and ii) small extracellular vesicles loaded with the miR-186-5p inhibitor, with translational value. By correlating peripheral miR-186-5p levels with patient clinical data, we further aim to establish its potential as a patient stratification biomarker. This strategy holds promise for early intervention by potentially halting disease progression before symptoms become severe, but also for refractory MDD cases, where synaptic disruption is critical. The inclusion of animal models and patient samples from both male and female subjects addresses the significant sex bias in MDD prevalence, enhancing potential impact on all patients.

title: Neuroinflammation in Schizophrenia: Targeting IL-1ß Signaling with NLRP3 Inhibitors
description: This proposal aims to validate the NLRP3 inflammasome as a novel therapeutic target in a biologically defined subgroup of schizophrenia patients with neuroinflammation, marked by elevated IL-1β. Schizophrenia affects 1 in 100 people worldwide, yet current treatments are only partially effective, highlighting the urgent need for new therapeutic strategies. Emerging evidence implicates NLRP3–IL-1β signalling in immune dysregulation within a subset of patients. This study will use patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) models to recreate brain-like environments and validate the NLRP3 inflammasome as a potential therapeutic target in schizophrenia. Specifically, we will (1) investigate aberrant NLRP3 activation in patient-derived iPSC models and (2) assess whether brain-penetrant NLRP3 inhibitors can reverse the deleterious effects of neuroinflammation. Shaped by input from people with lived experience, the project prioritises biologically informed, early-stage interventions. Overall, this work will generate a key dataset that could accelerate the translational pipeline for immune-targeted treatments in a subset of patients who are not well served by current therapies.

title: Target Validation of Interleukin-4 Receptor Alpha for Major Depressive Disorder
description: We propose to validate interleukin-4 receptor alpha (IL-4Rα) as a novel immune target for major depressive disorder (MDD). IL-4Rα is the shared subunit of the IL-4 and IL-13 receptors and modulates the T-helper 2 (Th2) immune pathway. To our knowledge, IL-4Rα has not been investigated in psychiatric drug development, representing a novel mechanism for therapeutic intervention in MDD. Our rationale stems from converging evidence across immunology, psychiatry, and translational biology. Our proteomic analyses show that MDD shares immune signatures involving Th2/Th17 pathways with inflammatory skin disorders, and that the immune signature specific to MDD is reversed by dupilumab, an anti-IL-4Rα monoclonal antibody approved for atopic dermatitis and asthma. We will use dupilumab as a repurposed tool compound in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial to evaluate whether IL-4Rα inhibition modulates the MDD immune signature and reduces depressive symptoms. Study outcomes will include peripheral immune changes, depressive symptom improvement, safety, and exploratory behavioral measures. This proposal focuses on a patient group with high unmet need. Given the favorable safety profile and tolerability of dupilumab in real-world populations, this study offers a low-risk, high-impact opportunity to de-risk a novel immune pathway in MDD and enable biomarker-driven development of IL-4Rα-targeted therapeutics in psychiatry.
recipient: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai

title: Validating novel, selective CaV2.3 inhibitors as oral, small molecule therapies for posttraumatic stress disorder
description: Post-traumatic stress disorder is a prevalent mental health condition with significant unmet medical need. Over 5% of trauma-exposed adults worldwide develop PTSD during their lifetimes, with those exposed to certain types of trauma such as combat and assault carrying a particularly high burden. The few approved drug treatments (e.g. paroxetine and sertraline) have limited efficacy and significant side effects. A recently published multi-ancestry meta-analysis of genetic data from >1 million individuals exposed to trauma reported significant risk of PTSD associated with the CACNA1E gene which encodes a voltage-gated calcium channel (CaV2.3) with high expression in brain areas (hippocampus, amygdala, anterior cingulate and prefrontal cortex) involved in memory, emotional regulation, and stress response. Genome-wide analyses of transcription indicated that the highest risk alleles are linked to significantly higher expression of CACNA1E, suggesting that inhibition of CaV2.3 function has potential therapeutic benefit. Lario Therapeutics has developed first-in-class, small molecule inhibitors of CaV2.3 which are potent, selective, and brain-penetrant. This collaborative proposal aims to validate CaV2.3 as a target for PTSD and to test potential CaV2.3-targeted therapeutics in mouse models of PTSD including stress-induced alterations in anxiety, fear conditioning and in paradigms showing learned flexibility of instinctual fear behaviours.

title: Harmony – An AI tool for contextual data harmonization, translation and cooperation in research
description: For decades governments, and funding bodies have invested considerable amounts of money and resources to collect valuable data, which have been instrumental in driving scientific progress, addressing important social and health problems. However, much of the world’s data are under-utilised and the opportunities that these data resources can offer are widely untapped. There is great potential in retrospectively harmonising, pooling and re-using datasets from existing sources to answer new research questions, however current workflows to achieve this are slow, error-prone and subject to human biases. With Harmony we have shown that AI can facilitate fast, efficient, accurate and reproducible harmonization. Harmony (https://harmonydata.ac.uk/app/) uses large language models (LLMs) to screen meta-data and identify semantically similar survey questions from different sources. This proposal aims to build on our success in Wellcome’s Mental Health Data Prize and increase our impact on the global research community by transforming Harmony into a commercially viable, end-to-end data harmonization product. Our pathway to success will focus on a) product enhancements, b) expanding our evidence base (e.g. validating Harmony across languages and cultures) and c) developing our operational business model and bringing the tool to market to create consistent revenue streams that will support Harmony’s future growth.

title: Hijacking Hinges: Cracking the coiled-coil code to control intracellular transport
description: Kinesin and dynein motors transport cargo bidirectionally along microtubules. Proper regulation is essential for cellular health, and its disruption is linked to neurodegeneration, cardiac disease, and cancer. Motor proteins and adaptors are autoinhibited and activated by specific motor-cargo–adaptor interactions. Coiled-coil domains are highly conserved in motors and adaptors and are emerging as dynamic regulatory elements. This project tests the hypothesis that “coiled-coil hinges” are fundamental regulatory elements in transport systems and can be manipulated to target motor dysfunction in disease. Our proof of concept work on kinesin 1 uncovered a novel autoinhibitory mechanism involving a coiled-coil hinge. I designed a conformational switch, triggered by a cell-penetrating peptide, to activate kinesin-1 allosterically. I will extend this approach to BicD2, the most intensively studied dynein adaptor. Mutations in BicD2 cause neuromuscular and developmental disorders and viruses and bacteria hijack BicD2 to subvert dynein; however, its regulatory mechanisms remain poorly defined. I will elucidate the mechanisms of coiled-coil regulation in BicD2, engineer switchable variants to control dynein activation, and explore how coiled-coil adaptors regulate bidirectional transport more broadly. This work will deepen mechanistic understanding of motor protein regulation and pave the way for novel therapeutic strategies for diseases associated with motor dysfunction.

title: Brain bioenergetics and the menopause in bipolar disorder (MENO-BD)
description: Bipolar disorder (BD) is a common and severe mental illness affecting at least 1 in 100 people. The perimenopause is a time of risk for new onset or relapse of BD, but mechanisms are unclear. Key to this proposal is the novel idea that disrupted brain bioenergetics represent a point of pathophysiological convergence of BD and menopause, specifically, reduced brain energy (adenosine triphosphate (ATP)) reserve, driven by mitochondrial dysfunction. My overarching hypothesis is that brain bioenergetic changes during the menopause drive mental health symptoms in women with BD. This is a co-designed observational study incorporating menopause as a “natural experiment”: prospective clinical cohort study in healthy people and people with BD who are pre, peri, post menopause (n= 75 per group, total n = 150), assessed at baseline and 12 months. Aims a) Quantify brain bioenergetics (phosphocreatine/ATP ratio, lactate) across menopausal stages using Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy. b) Test associations of brain bioenergetics with perimenopausal mental health symptoms (cognition, mood), and c) Explore putative compensatory mechanisms by quantifying metabolomic changes across menopausal stages. This innovative approach to understanding metabolic mechanisms of relapse in women with BD represents a novel potential avenue for intervention in a highly morbid but currently under-served patient group.

title: Neural representations of compositional elements in flexible behaviour.
description: Flexible behaviour depends on the brain’s ability to extract structure from experience and apply it to novel situations. This is thought to rely on latent states – internal representations that capture hidden structure in the world and serve as behavioural frameworks for planning and decision-making. To support flexibility, these models must also be compositional – generalise to new scenarios by combining and rearranging their individual components. While growing evidence suggests that the hippocampus encodes abstract latent states and organises simple representations into sequences, the neural mechanisms underlying the development and compositional use of abstract latent states remain poorly understood. This project will investigate how latent states are constructed and used compositionally and uncover the learning algorithms and neural mechanisms that support their development. Using a complex spatial navigation task in mice, I will combine high-density electrophysiology, two- photon calcium imaging, and causal manipulations to track the emergence, organisation, and compositional use of latent state representations in the ventral hippocampus. I will test how hippocampal replay and dopamine signalling shape and update these representations. This work will establish a mechanistic account of how the brain abstracts experience into compositional elements to support flexible behaviour – core process of complex cognition often disrupted in mental illness.

title: Feeling the credit crunch: The intergenerational impact of problem debt, 1980 to the present
description: Feeling the Credit Crunch will comprehensively connect lived experiences of problem debt and mental health to changing welfare logics and cultural discourses of credit use in Britain since 1980. Through intergenerational participatory workshops, oral histories and archival research, the project will generate a new evidence base to drive more integrated policy responses to problem debt and mental health in the present. From 1980, the liberalisation of consumer credit facilitated a credit boom. In less than a decade, levels of problem debt – characterised by the inability to meet credit commitments – soared across Britain. As access to consumer credit expanded, state welfare support contracted, and personal debt became an essential means by which some families maintained a basic standard of living. Contemporary research demonstrates a growing awareness of the effects of indebtedness on mental health amidst ongoing cost of living crises, but in what ways is this relationship reciprocal, and how has it been experienced across generations against the backdrop of shifting political, welfare and cultural climates since 1980? Only by understanding the lived interconnections between problem debt and mental health in the longer term can we begin to address issues that continue to affect families, healthcare and the economy today.

title: A Life in Sound: Transforming Understandings of Health and Wellbeing through Music, Sonic Arts, and Modes of Listening
description: This practice-based project explores how music, sound, and modes of listening can transform understandings of the human body. It establishes a new theoretical framework of corporeal acoustemology: a mode of embodied, auditory knowledge of the body as sonic field. Using the compositional methodology of artistic sonation, biomedical and experiential information is creatively transducted and expressed through music and sonic arts. At the intersection of health humanities, sound studies, and composition, this project asks how non- lexical sonic artworks might express physiological processes; how corporeal listening can foster affiliation and address health misinformation; and how these approaches can be ethically and creatively evaluated. Outputs include a monograph, composition portfolio, listening events, a radio documentary series, and an interdisciplinary conference. The project also engages with medical sound archives, illness narratives, and develops engaged research events involving participants from boroughs with significant health inequalities. While sound and music are often associated with therapeutic practices and creative health activities, the objective of this project is to extend beyond these applications, positioning sonic artworks and musical compositions as significant psychosocial resources and interventions in their own right which, in turn, help people better understand their bodies and foster beneficial, relational, corporeal listening practices.

title: Advancing methods for pharmacological fMRI to improve discovery and development of treatments for mental health
description: This project aims to advance pharmacological functional magnetic resonance imaging (pharmaco-fMRI) as a robust and reliable tool for accelerating the clinical development of novel mental health treatments and to develop pharmaco-fMRI-based precision approaches for predicting individual responses to drugs. Treatment effectiveness in psychiatry is often unpredictable due to varied responses and subjective diagnoses, contributing to high drug trial failure rates. Funders and regulators now promote objective measures, such as functional neuroimaging, to improve precision drug development. Pharmaco-fMRI is a validated method for quantifying brain function changes in response to drugs, but small sample sizes have limited its impact. This fellowship will aggregate existing datasets, already pledged by over 15 leading PIs, harmonise the largest pharmaco-fMRI dataset to date, and establish a consortium to facilitate sharing with researchers. Using this dataset, this fellowship will develop novel methods to characterise subject-specific drug effects free from confounds like scanner and acquisition sequence, enabling drug response prediction from resting-state brain function. This will be done using a new foundation model of brain function, BrainLM. The project will also validate advanced methods like Receptor Enriched Analysis of Connectivity by Targets (REACT), which provides molecular insights from fMRI scans without the need for costly PET scans.

title: Southern Africa Consortium for Climate Change and Health
description: Southern Africa faces increasingly severe extreme heat and precipitation events. The Centre aims to overcome the knowledge, policy and financial barriers that constrain progress with health adaptation and mitigation. Using a transdisciplinary and multisectoral approach, we address extreme heat in South Africa and Zimbabwe, and flooding in Malawi, with a focus on pregnant women, children, older people and those with chronic conditions. We adopt a policy-cycle framework to: quantify, track and cost climate-health impacts; test adaptation innovations, including anticipatory cash transfers, supports for mental health resilience and complex-cooling interventions; and drive step-changes in regional stakeholder coordination and policy influence. Quantifying health costs of Climate Change informs allocations of domestic financing, estimates of Loss and Damage, and strengthens arguments for mitigation. We support expansion of national climate and health programmes, through proactive policy influence and technical inputs into climate finance applications. We will develop novel-mitigation strategies based on traditional public health levers for controlling health-harming industries, including legal reforms. Throughout, we will include lived experience expertise, and prioritise diversity and inclusion. Together, our activities will catalyse the expansion of national programmes on Climate Change and health, and strengthen African leadership, both critical pathways to securing a liveable future.

title: Transitioning Health Policy Watch to a Sustainable Global Public Good
description: Health Policy Watch (HPW) aims to consolidate its transition to a sustainable, globally relevant public-interest news platform. The funding will strengthen institutional stability by expanding our donor base; securing predictable support for senior editors and core editorial functions; and extending our network of Global South journalists who connect lived realities with global policy debates. HPW provides open-access, interdisciplinary reporting that links complex health challenges—climate change, infectious diseases, AMR, NCDs, mental health, and emergency preparedness—with political, financial, and governance decisions. This proposal includes: engaging a development director to implement strategies for structured donor diversification and enhanced reader support of the open-access model; gradual expansion of our network: and enhanced mentoring and training of reporters in under-represented regions. Wellcome’s partnership will ensure succession and building upon more than CHF 600,000 invested since 2020. At a time of geopolitical uncertainty and rising global health misinformation and disinformation, and rapid advances in generative AI—where information increasingly circulates through AI-mediated systems—independent, evidence-based journalism is essential to foster informed, democratic debate. This grant will enable HPW to remain a trusted, representative media institution and strengthen its long-term resilience—expanding evidence-based reporting, elevating Global South voices, and reinforcing global health decision-making through timely, accessible, and impactful journalism.

title: Decoding Mechanisms of Early Antipsychotic Response in First-Episode Psychosis: A Multimodal Approach
description: Psychotic disorders affect more than 3% of the global population and rank among the most disabling health conditions worldwide. Over 40% of individuals with first-episode psychosis (FEP) do not respond to first-line antipsychotic therapy; however, the neurobiological basis for early-treatment non-response remains poorly understood. Converging evidence points to differences between responders and non-responders across multiple brain systems—including dopaminergic, glutamatergic, and large-scale neural networks—however, integrative studies at illness onset are lacking. This project will use a multimodal approach to understand the disease mechanisms underlying early- treatment non-response in FEP. Participants will undergo neuromelanin- sensitive MRI (to probe dopamine system integrity), magnetic resonance spectroscopy (to quantify glutamate levels in the anterior cingulate cortex), resting-state fMRI (to examine large-scale network dynamics), alongside neurocognitive assessment. Structured clinical assessments will determine treatment response at six weeks, with plasma antipsychotic levels to confirm adherence. Healthy controls will provide normative reference data. The study will generate preliminary effect sizes, evaluate feasibility, and identify candidate markers for future mechanistic models. An international placement at a centre of excellence will support training in multimodal data integration and explainable machine learning. This work will lay the foundation for a more personalised and mechanistically informed approach to psychiatric care.

title: Co-designing culturally sensitive youth-centred mental health services in Malawi with young people and stakeholders
description: Substance abuse which includes harmful drinking and drug use among young people in Malawi is on the rise. Like many African countries, Malawi faces treatment gaps and severe workforce shortages, leading to substance abuse being managed under the broad category of mental, neurological and substance use (MNS) disorders within under-resourced mental health services. Only 2% of Malawi’s health budget is allocated to mental health, and there are virtually no specialist services for children and adolescents. As a result, young people with MNS disorders are disproportionately affected and underserved. This reflects a broader global trend in which African populations are systematically underserved by mental health services. My project will explore how to establish much-needed youth-friendly mental health services in Malawi by: 1) conducting a situation analysis of existing infrastructure; 2) using participatory action research (PAR) with adolescents and caregivers to explore community-level understanding of substance abuse; and 3) co-designing a culturally relevant intervention framework with young people to appropriately address mental, neurological and substance use (MNS) disorders. The Wellcome Accelerator Award will support my mid-career researcher progression, consolidating findings from my previous research with this proposed project to inform culturally grounded mental health interventions for young Africans locally and globally.

title: Magnetic Nanoparticle Mediated Alignment of the Internal Architecture of Brain Organoids for Parkinson's disease modelling.
description: Parkinson’s Disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder affecting over 150,000 people in the UK in 2023, with prevalence projected to rise to 173,000 by 2030. Beyond classical motor symptoms, PD patients suffer from falls, swallowing and speech impairments, depression, and anxiety. Current pharmacological treatments have limited ability to modify disease progression. Whilst cell therapy techniques have been developed as an alternative to pharmaceutical interventions, these techniques have shown limited efficacy to date. This project aims to use iron oxide magnetic nanoparticles (MNP) to directionally influence axon growth on induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) derived neurons and brain organoids to help understand and address challenges in cell therapy for PD. Functional changes in neurons and organoids subjected to MNP mediated forces will be characterised using high throughput micro electrode array (MEA) analysis, spatially resolved single cell transcriptomics, RNA sequencing and proteomics. Engineering structurally textured organoids relevant for PD research will enhance their physiological relevance for producing structured cell therapy grafts with improved integration potential.

title: Human Air pollution exposure and Variation in neurochemical Activity (HAVA) Study
description: This project investigates how long-term exposure to nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) - a traffic-related air pollutant - affects brain chemistry in healthy adults. Using advanced magnetic resonance spectroscopy (¹H-MRS) and quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM), the study will examine whether individuals living in areas with higher NO₂ exposure show measurable differences in glutamate levels and brain iron accumulation. Modelled air pollution data from Imperial College London will be used to classify residential exposure across South London, and participants with at least 10 years of stable residence will be recruited. This pilot study will generate preliminary effect sizes and assess the feasibility of integrating environmental modelling with neuroimaging. The findings will inform future research into the environmental determinants of psychiatric vulnerability, supporting the development of early detection strategies and policy-relevant evidence on air quality and brain health.

title: Extension - Effective regulation and evaluation of digital mental health technologies
description: As the UK safety regulator for healthcare products, we (the MHRA) are undertaking a programme to deliver bold improvements to the regulatory framework for software as a medical device. Further work was needed to translate these broad requirements into specific and accessible requirements for digital mental health products, and the initial grant enabled us to initiate significant activities to support this vision. Additionally, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) are prioritising digital technology evaluations and mental health continues to be recognised as a priority area. The aim of the original project was to enable access to safe and effective products, to help improve mental health care and sought to achieve this by ensuring that digital mental health products are regulated in a risk proportionate manner and evaluated consistently. We successfully achieved much of this ambitious aim by collaboratively working with NICE and other key stakeholders however have identified that further work is required to realise the full potential of the original project aims and objectives. We are therefore proposing an extension of the existing project to complement the work achieved to date outlining a DMHT Airlock, International engagement and regulatory compliance impacts.
recipient: The Secretary of State for Health and Social Care acting through the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency

title: Mental illness in perimenopause: Longitudinal predictors and preventive treatment opportunities
description: Perimenopause is increasingly recognised as a high-risk period for mental illness. Yet, despite its relevance to a global population of ~725 million middle-aged women, it remains strikingly under-investigated. This project aims to transform early prediction and intervention by identifying women at heightened risk of first-onset or recurrent anxiety, depressive, bipolar, and psychotic disorders during perimenopause. We will leverage four large-scale longitudinal cohorts—the Danish Nurse Cohort, Danish Twin Registry, Swedish Women’s Lifestyle and Health cohort, and Swedish Twin Registry—linked to national registers in Denmark and Sweden. Our three aims are to: (1) quantify risk of psychiatric disorders and functional impairment during perimenopause compared to pre- and post-menopause and the general population; (2) develop and externally validate dynamic prediction models for perimenopausal psychiatric episodes; and (3) emulate a target trial estimating the effect of hormone therapy (HT) on mental health outcomes. Key deliverables include population-level psychiatric risk estimates across menopause stages, two web- based risk calculators to support clinical decision-making, and evidence-based guidance on HT for psychiatric risk reduction. Drawing on multidisciplinary expertise and lived experience, this project addresses long-standing sex- and age-related disparities in mental health and delivers actionable tools to support early detection and personalised prevention, advancing healthy ageing in women.
recipient: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai

title: Accelerating the detection and treatment of perinatal depression and anxiety in low- and middle-income countries through advanced analytics
description: Perinatal mood disorders (depression and anxiety) are common worldwide and have major negative consequences for parent and child. Expanded screening, personalized medicine and risk-guided care have the potential to transform early identification and treatment of perinatal mood disorders, but research is needed in three areas. First, among women without antenatal depression, can risk-guided care that tailors the intensity of follow-up improve early identification of incident postnatal mood disorders? Second, among women with antenatal depression, can risk-guided care that tailors the intensity of treatment improve outcomes? Third, can risk-guided care achieve better overall mental health outcomes and improve resource efficiency for the health system overall? Such work is particularly critical in low-resource settings with limited mental health resources. Shaped by our collaborators with lived experience and guided by theory, we will apply advanced data science to four perinatal cohorts in low-resource countries to quantify the risk of perinatal mood disorder onset, early progression, and treatment non-response. We will then complete a randomized trial to test, compared to one-size-fits-all care, whether risk-guided perinatal care and follow-up improve outcomes and health system efficiency. This multi-country work will set the stage for a step- change in perinatal care to maximally impact mental health.
recipient: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

title: Identifying Depression Early in Adolescence for Maximising Prevention and Clinical Translation (IDEA-IMPACT)
description: Identifying Depression Early in Adolescence for Maximising Prevention and Clinical Translation (IDEA-IMPACT) aims to transform early identification and prevention of adolescent depression globally. Despite growing interest in early intervention, current approaches often lack precision in identifying and supporting youth before symptoms fully emerge. IDEA-IMPACT addresses this gap by advancing the Identifying Depression Early in Adolescence Risk Score (IDEA- RS), an empirically developed tool that aggregates 11 sociodemographic variables to estimate adolescents’ probability of developing depression within three years, independently of current symptoms. This tool has demonstrated beyond-chance discriminative ability across diverse settings on five continents. Recognising that effective prevention requires more than accurate prediction, IDEA-IMPACT emphasizes translating risk identification into actionable preventive interventions, guided by lived experience insights. Using advanced, context-sensitive methods, the project will begin by enhancing the generalisability of IDEA-RS across diverse settings. It will then broaden the scope of risk and outcome domains, as well as identify modifiable protective factors that buffer against depression among at-risk adolescents; analyse differential responses to existing interventions based on risk profiles; and co-design a new, low-intensity preventive intervention specifically tailored for high-risk adolescents. This comprehensive approach promotes youth engagement, equity, resilience-building, and sustainability in adolescent mental health globally.

title: Early Detection and Dynamic Relapse Monitoring in Bipolar Disorder: A Longitudinal Cohort Approach
description: This application represents a groundbreaking advance in the early detection and management of bipolar disorder (BD) by establishing the for the first time dynamic, time-varying predictive models tailored to BD and identified trajectories. Unlike traditional static approaches, BEACON will uniquely integrate longitudinal cohort data with routine clinical care data and with genomics, other -omics and experimental validation, enabling improved risk stratification. BEACON is built on four large, real-world population cohorts, with ongoing longitudinal follow-up that reflect diverse populations and healthcare settings, considerably enhancing both model development and validation. Throughout the development of the proposal, co-production with individuals with lived experience has shaped the research questions and initial design and this will continue throughout the delivery, evaluation, and implementation of the programme. The framework’s use of experimental approaches and multi-omics for putative causal pathway discovery marks a significant step toward interpretable, biologically informed modelling. Our team bridges data science, cellular modelling, precsion psychiatry, epidemiology, computational biology. This will enable future translational validation pioneering the first truly holistic and proactive model for BD care—offering unprecedented potential for early detection to reduce duration of untreated illness, delineate different trajectories of illness, feasibly prevent episodes, and transform relapse management.

title: Integration of a prediction tool for early detection and management of depression and anxiety among youth with HIV in Kenya
description: Over a quarter of youth living with HIV (YLH) have a common mental disorder (depression, anxiety or trauma symptoms), which significantly impact clinical outcomes by directly contributing to poor treatment adherence and subsequently poor viral suppression and mortality. Early detection of poor mental health has the potential to improve individual YLH treatment outcomes and reduce onward HIV transmission. Low-intensity mental health interventions are effective and scalable; however, these interventions are often used to manage YLH who are already symptomatic. Our proposal aims to: 1) leverage unique cohort datasets of ~2800 Kenyan YLH (15-24 years) to develop and validate a risk prediction model for early detection and detection of prevalent depression and anxiety symptoms among YLH, 2) co-design and pilot the delivery of a mental wellness intervention for YLH at high risk for depression and anxiety adapted using information from the prediction model, with the goal of early detection and management of depression and anxiety, and 3) extend follow-up to 3 years for ~500 YLH that received a brief psychological intervention to address depression, anxiety and trauma symptoms to identify predictors of long term treatment response and relapse.

title: FUTURE-D = Forecasting Depression Trajectories: Early Network-Guided Prediction of Severe and Persistent Disease Courses
description: FUTURE-D redefines early detection and intervention strategies for individuals at risk of severe and persistent depression by adopting a systems-level framework grounded in network science, dynamical systems, and control theory. The MACS and NESDA cohorts provide a unique foundation for modeling the dynamic evolution of neural, symptom, and psychosocial networks underlying severe and persistent depression. To validate and generalize our findings, we will leverage large, harmonized longitudinal datasets—UK Biobank, NAKO, and diverse treatment datasets. Using neuroimaging, digital phenotyping, and novel measures of lived experience, we aim to identify early warning signals of network destabilization predictive of an adverse disease course. A central innovation is to guide TMS interventions tailored to individual network trajectories and informed by robust Patient and Public Involvement. This paradigm shift moves from symptom-based reaction to mechanism-informed prevention, offering a precision mental health approach tailored to individual network trajectories. Early warning signals and individualized control targets will be developed and validated through a co-design process, with strong emphasis on real-world scalability and suitability in LMICs. These efforts will lay the groundwork for future clinical decision-support tools, enabling clinicians to tailor treatments and prevent adverse outcomes.

title: Funding for Global Health Partnerships (formerly THET) to provide the secretariat to the All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) on Global Health & Security.
description: GHP is seeking £10,000 from Wellcome to support its role as secretariat for the All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) on Global Health and Security. This contribution will strengthen how UK parliament engages with global health, ensuring parliamentarians have consistent access to expert insight, including LMIC perspectives, on the most pressing global health challenges. The APPG provides a cross-party forum for policymakers to examine the UK’s role in global health and security. As secretariat, GHP convenes experts, produces accessible briefings and reports, and ensures diverse perspectives inform parliamentary debate. Wellcome’s support will enable at least four meetings each year on priority global health themes, establish an Advisory Group and produce high-quality briefing materials for parliamentarians. To improve external understanding of the UK’s role in global health, GHP will also strengthen communications through dedicated website and social media channels. This work directly supports the promotion of themes central to Wellcome’s global health strategy, ensuring they receive sustained cross-party attention in parliament. This includes the Future of Global Health Initiatives process, antimicrobial resistance, mental health, global health equity, pandemic preparedness and climate health threats. Through this partnership, Wellcome can help create a more informed and effective policy environment for advancing Global Health and Security.

title: Advancing Adolescent Mental Health Science in Africa: Measurement, Mechanisms, and Meaning
description: The Africa Health Research Institute (AHRI) seeks to advance Adolescent Mental Health (AMH) science in Africa through (1) a core scientific project following up an existing cohort of 1536 adolescents to enrich measurement approaches of AMH outcomes and investigate the mechanisms driving them; and (2) an ecosystems’ strengthening initiative delivering open science assets and training opportunities. The scientific core aims to: 1.1 Use newly collected data (ages 18-24), and data-driven approaches, to build a contextually valid framework that captures, and situates mental disorders, within a full spectrum of AMH outcomes, across a range of dimensions ('Measurement'). 1.2 Harness the power of this individual-level data, augmenting it with longitudinal family and household surveillance data, to investigate the biological, psychological, and social mechanisms of, and pathways to, AMH outcomes ('Mechanisms'). 1.3 Co-create enriched understandings of measurements and mechanisms through lived experience engagement and nested qualitative cohorts ('Meaning'). The ecosystems’ strengthening aims to: 2.1 Contribute quality open science datasets, hosted within a trusted research environment. 2.2 Build AMH expertise, create opportunities for African researchers to use mental health data, and collaborate with continental partners on data use and training. Together, these will drive insights across AHRI’s AMH Research Strategy’s objectives and foster collaboration.

title: The IRL Trial: A school-based trial to reduce social media use and improve mental health among adolescents
description: We will trial an intervention that aims to reduce social media use among secondary school pupils in years 8, 9, and 10. This will be a parallel-arm cluster randomised trial in which school year groups are randomised at a 1:1 ratio to the intervention or a treatment-as-usual control condition. The intervention will entail a smartphone app that limits use of social media apps such as TikTok and Snapchat, using a coproduced combination of a daily ‘budget’ and a nighttime ‘curfew’. The primary study outcome will be self- reported anxiety, with secondary outcomes including sleep quality, time spent with friends and family, and bullying. All pupils will be eligible to participate, and we will focus on the subgroup with symptoms of anxiety at baseline. The focus on pupils with symptoms at baseline will demonstrate whether social media limitations can contribute to prevention at an early stage. The trial will also include qualitative research and quantitative mediation analysis to understand participants’ experience of the intervention and how it contributes to improved mental health. The research will be done in Bradford, UK.

title: Neuro-Immune Interactions in Heath and Disease - Investigating the Neuropathogenesis of Alphavirus Infections
description: Neurotropic alphaviruses cause severe disease in humans, and present a growing public health risk following climate change-driven increases in the ecological niche of their mosquito vectors. Alphavirus invasion of the central nervous system (CNS) can result in long-term neurological issues in adults, with observations of neurodevelopmental delays in perinatally infected children. Despite growing infection risks the mechanisms of alphavirus neuroinvasion, its neuropathological consequences, and resulting host immune responses are not well characterised. This is particularly relevant in foetal infections following vertical transmission in utero, where the impact of neuroinvasion on cortical development, progenitor dynamics, and cell fate decisions remain poorly understood. Using Sindbis virus (SINV), a prototypical alphavirus, this project aims to (i) elucidate the key cellular and molecular mechanisms underpinning alphavirus neuroinvasion and neuropathophysiology in developing brain, and (ii) provide insights into host immune responses to alphavirus infection and whether these are protective or pathologic. This work will achieve these aims by leveraging complementary in vitro and in vivo models (human ChP organoids, foetal brain tissue slices, immune cultures, zebrafish embryos), laying essential groundwork for the identification of potential molecular targets for future therapeutic interventions. Key Words: Sindbis virus, Choroid plexus, Cortical development, Neuroimmunology

title: Gut microbiome, immune function, and neuropsychiatric outcomes – examining causal relationships
description: Neuropsychiatric conditions represent a leading global health burden, with rising prevalence in younger populations and substantial treatment gaps despite existing pharmacological and psychological interventions. Emerging evidence implicates low-grade systemic inflammation, particularly elevated cytokines such as interleukin-6, as a potential causal contributor to a range of neuropsychiatric disorders including major depressive disorder and schizophrenia. The gut microbiome has gained attention as a modifiable factor influencing both neuropsychiatric risk and systemic immune activation. Altered microbial composition is consistently observed in individuals with neuropsychiatric conditions and is associated with gastrointestinal and immune dysregulation, suggesting a mechanistic pathway linking gut microbiota to brain health. However, causal relationships and underlying mechanisms remain poorly defined, as the literature is dominated by cross-sectional and observational studies. This PhD project aims to address these gaps using rigorous causal inference approaches to investigate the interplay between gut microbiota, immune function, and neuropsychiatric outcomes. Specific objectives include summarising existing evidence on gut-brain interactions, testing whether immune activation mediates the relationship between the gut microbiome and neuropsychiatric disorders, and evaluating the predictive potential of gut microbial profiles for neuropsychiatric conditions. Findings are expected to advance mechanistic understanding and inform novel preventative and therapeutic strategies.

title: Transposable element-gene chimeric transcripts in neural tissues: functional impacts on gene expression and behaviour and their regulatory control across model systems
description: Transposable elements (TEs), colloquially referred to as ‘jumping genes’, are repetitive mobile genetic elements capable of excising and inserting themselves throughout the genome. While historically dismissed as 'junk DNA', TEs constitute an extraordinary ~50% of the human genome. Together, TEs and other repetitive sequences represent the largest contributor to human genetic variation (1). Remarkably, approximately 4% of human genes incorporate transposon sequences as novel exons, and 75% of human lncRNAs contain segments of transposon origin (2). The impact of TEs extends beyond simple genome insertion; the resulting DNA, RNA and translation products can influence gene regulation, create novel coding structures, and affect chromosome stability. TE activation is increasingly recognised as a hallmark of neurodegenerative and psychiatric disorders, including Alzheimer’s disease, ALS, and schizophrenia (3). However, the molecular mechanisms governing TE-mediated variation in neural tissue remain poorly understood. This project aims to investigate how TE-gene chimeric transcripts in neural genes influence gene expression and behaviour. Using complementary model systems—Drosophila melanogaster and the parasitic nematode Strongyloides ratti—this research will characterise TE-derived chimeric mRNAs that form when intronic TEs introduce cryptic splice sites into neural genes. The comparative approach leverages distinct silencing mechanisms to identify universal and system-specific regulatory principles.

title: Integrated methods for drug discovery and repurposing in psychiatry: genomics, iPSC modelling, and pharmacogenetics
description: A major challenge in current psychiatric practice is that standard therapies fail for a subset of patients, with approximately 30% in both depression and schizophrenia. One symptom that stands out in these treatment-resistant cases is Anhedonia. Anhedonia (the reduced capacity to experience pleasure or pursue meaningful rewards) is a core, transdiagnostic symptom that appears across multiple psychiatric disorders including major depression, schizophrenia, and bipolar disorder. Its mechanisms remain unclear, and current medications only partly relieve anhedonic symptoms. Drug repurposing, guided by genetic evidence, enables identification of existing medications already approved for other conditions that may target relevant biological pathways in psychiatric disorders. However, no drug has been specifically developed for anhedonia. To address this unmet clinical need, our project will leverage GWAS and molecular QTL data to identify and prioritise druggable targets for anhedonia using cis- Mendelian randomisation and pharmacological annotation. Promising candidates will then be tested in human striatal-midbrain assembloids derived from induced pluripotent stem cells carrying schizophrenia-associated structural genetic variants, enabling mechanistic validation. Finally, our findings will be extended into patient populations using Triangulation WIthin a STudy framework that leverages multiple complementary causal inference methods to UK Biobank, assessing how genetic variation moderates patient response to antidepressants and antipsychotics.

title: Mechanisms for Sister Chromatid Cohesion Establishment at the Replication Fork
description: Sister chromatid cohesion describes the state of attachment between the two arms that constitute replicated chromosomes. It is crucial for accurate chromosome segregation during cell division and involves the topological entrapment of sister chromatids by the ring-shaped protein complex, cohesin. Two parallel pathways of cohesion establishment have been identified: de novo loading and conversion, both requiring DNA replication. However, their molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. This project will investigate how cohesin and the cohesin loading complex interact with the DNA replication machinery to generate cohesion, with a particular focus on the de novo loading pathway and comparisons between mitosis and meiosis. To this end, I will use a budding yeast model to identify these interactions via in vitro and in vivo methods, including co-IP with purified proteins and IP-MS. I will also characterise genome-wide cohesion patterns using sister-pore-C, a novel 3C sequencing method. By combining biochemical, structural, and functional investigations, this project will deliver insights into the mechanisms and roles of the cohesion establishment pathways. Anomalies in cohesion establishment can lead to abnormal chromosome segregation, which may manifest as cancer, infertility, developmental disorders, etc. Thus, my findings will contribute towards a fuller understanding of a fundamental step in cell division.

title: Four-year Basic Science PhD Programme
description: Mental health disorders, particularly depression and anxiety, are leading causes of disability worldwide and a major public health challenge. In England, prevalence has risen, with disproportionate impacts on disadvantaged groups and substantial economic costs. Digital therapies, such as internet- delivered cognitive behavioural therapy (iCBT) via the SilverCloud platform, are now embedded within the National Health Service (NHS) Talking Therapies programme and prioritised by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE). However, health technology assessments (HTAs) often rely on average treatment effects, which obscure subgroup differences and risk reinforcing inequalities. This PhD will leverage causal machine learning (ML) methods to estimate heterogeneous treatment effects (HTEs) and strengthen the evidence base for HTAs of digital mental health interventions. The research has four objectives:- (1) Identify and synthesise doubly robust causal ML methods for HTE estimation; (2) Conduct simulation studies comparing performance with traditional causal inference approaches; (3) Implement a target trial emulation using NHS data to evaluate SilverCloud iCBT against low-intensity CBT comparators; and (4) Examine unmeasured spatial confounding, with ambition of extending current methods. By combining methodological work with a policy-relevant mental health case study, this research will generate subgroup-level evidence, inform NICE evaluations, and support equitable public health decision-making.

title: The impact of late diagnosis of autism and ADHD on long term educational and economic outcomes.
description: This PhD project aims to determine the impact of late diagnosis of autism and ADHD on long-term educational and economic outcomes. The project will utilise longitudinal data from the Millennium Cohort Study, National Pupil Database and HMRC records to determine the impact that being diagnosed later in childhood/early adulthood may have on educational attainment and progress and economic outcomes. From this, economic modelling will be undertaken to simulate the lifelong impact of receiving a diagnosis and/or appropriate support earlier in life - either using existing microsimulation models or building a new model (if necessary). The project will also aim to undertake qualitative research to ascertain insights into experiences of autistic and ADHD individuals, to provide context and greater understanding to any quantitative outputs. The project will endeavour to use qualitative methodologies that involve coproduction with those who are experts by experience.

title: Polypharmacy and the impact of antidepressants, antipsychotics and benzodiazepines on falls and fractures risks in older adults: a triangulation approach towards causal inference for the study of drug combinations
description: I aim to use evidence from different causal inference study designs that rely on different assumptions and have differing strengths and limitations to evaluate combination use of antidepressants, antipsychotics and benzodiazepines on risks of falls and fractures in older adults. This will include use of the target trial framework, an appropriate self-controlled method (e.g., case cross-over or self-controlled case series) and mendelian randomization. The target trial approach can clarify the causal question of interest and account for biases introduced by analysis decisions such as immortal time bias, whereas the self-controlled design can better control for time-invariant confounding because it is a within-individual design. Mendelian randomization can allow assessment of the on-target and off-target effects of drugs and their corresponding indications on falls and fractures. The population of interest is older adults aged 40 years and above who have prescription records of an antidepressant, antipsychotic and/or benzodiazepine. Confounding and selection bias will be accounted for using appropriate analysis methods. I anticipate that results from this study will inform clinical guidelines, improve geriatric and psychiatric care, and help provide patients with informed choice about medications.

title: The Role of Dissociative States in Shaping Self-Relating
description: Although typically conceptualised as a deficit or disordered state, ‘dissociation’ may also be associated with positive mental health outcomes when deployed strategically. We will examine whether dissociative states induced by 50% nitrous oxide (N2O) facilitate change in habitual maladaptive patterns of self-relating (self-criticism). The related drug, ketamine, facilitates adaptive belief change, including promoting changes in negative self-schemas in people with depression. Moreover, the strength of antidepressant effects of ketamine may be associated with acute dissociative effects. We hypothesise that the dissociative state induced by N2O will encourage updating of maladaptive self-related beliefs following a reappraisal task. We will explore the extent to which (i) cognitive ‘defusion’ and (ii) reappraisal via ‘distancing’ might explain the effects of N2O. A preliminary study will refine the reappraisal (self-compassion) task and drug administration protocol in healthy volunteers. A larger study will then test an optimised N2O-reappraisal protocol in people displaying binge-eating behaviours, a group expected to be enriched for the cognitive phenotype of interest (self-criticism). This work will advance our understanding of the strategic therapeutic use of dissociative drugs to enhance psychological treatments by promoting adaptive belief change.

title: SHANK3 in human interneuron development
description: Mutations in the synaptic scaffold SHANK3 are a major genetic cause of neurodevelopmental conditions, yet their impact on human cortical interneuron development is unknown. This project will define how SHANK3 loss alters the maturation and circuit integration of MGE-derived PV and SST interneurons using human stem-cell platforms. We will generate isogenic H9 hESC lines (WT and SHANK3-KO) carrying an LHX6-Citrine reporter to enrich post-mitotic interneuron precursors by FACS. Aim 1 (in vitro): a dorsal–ventral “raining” co-culture overlays SHANK3-KO Citrine⁺ interneurons onto WT EMX1-mScarlet cortical organoids to test cell-autonomous vs microenvironmental influences on migration, morphology and synaptic assembly. Aim 2 (in vivo): FACS-purified Citrine⁺ D45 precursors will be xenotransplanted into neonatal Rag2-/- mouse cortex to assess human-paced maturation and host integration. We will assess interneuron maturation and circuit integration across in-vitro raining and in- vivo xenografts: migration/positioning; subtype identity (SST/PV) with developmental markers (NKX2.1/LHX6/SOX6); morphology (soma size, dendritic/axonal complexity, spine density); synaptic assembly and Excitatory/Inhibitory balance via pre-/post-synaptic puncta (Synapsin, VGLUT1/2, VGAT, PSD95, Gephyrin) and human–mouse appositions; connectivity by puncta colocalisation analyses; transcriptional state by scRNA-seq; and, in later phases, intrinsic membrane properties and synaptic function by whole- cell patch-clamp.

title: Investigating the influence of the reproductive cycle on epilepsy and related behaviours across the life course in SYNGAP1-related disorder.
description: Women and girls remain underrepresented in neurodevelopmental research, despite recognition that hormonal cycles can significantly influence symptoms such as seizures and emotional regulation. The reproductive cycle is largely unexplored in patients with SYNGAP1 mutations in SYNGAP1-related disorder (SRD), a cause of monogenic neurodevelopmental disorders resulting in severe autism and intellectual disability. Epilepsy is a key comorbidity in SRD, which is present in approximately 93% of patients; absence seizures are the most prevalent epilepsy-type. Puberty and the reproductive cycle can influence seizure occurrence and affect symptoms, such as sensory sensitivities and executive function. It remains unclear how the reproductive cycle influences seizures and behaviours across the life course in SRD. In my PhD, I will study the relationship between the reproductive cycle and SRD symptoms, such as seizures, sleep, and behavioural phenotypes, in rat Syngap knockout models. I will determine if the oestrus cycle is abnormal in Syngap heterozygous females and whether seizures, sleep abnormalities, and spontaneous behaviour phenotypes correlate with the oestrus cycle. Finally, I will modulate the oestrus cycle to determine whether Syngap phenotypes can be rescued. Understanding the relationship between the reproductive cycle and related behavioural phenotypes could lead to refined treatments.

title: Beyond Diagnosis: Investigating How Biologically Informed Risk for Severe Mental Illness Shapes Cognitive Ageing in the General Population
description: Severe mental illnesses (SMIs) are chronic psychiatric disorders characterized by cognitive deficits, emotional distress, and functional impairment. Cognitive dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a core feature of SMIs, significantly impacting long-term outcomes. Recent research indicates that individuals with a high molecular risk for SMIs, even without a clinical diagnosis, exhibit elevated dementia risk and poorer cognitive performance. This suggests that biological liability to SMI, captured through genetic, epigenetic, proteomic, and metabolic markers, exists on a continuum influencing phenotypic changes in aging populations and contributing to early cognitive decline. Traditional categorical diagnostic frameworks often miss this subclinical variation. This project aims to model SMI liability as a continuous biological construct and investigate its association with cognitive aging and brain health. Utilizing multi-omic profiling, neuroimaging, and advanced statistical methods in large-scale population cohorts, we will identify cross-sectional and longitudinal patterns linking common and unique multi-omic risk for SMI with aging-related cognitive and neuroimaging outcomes. Ultimately, this work seeks to enhance the detection of subclinical cognitive vulnerability, enabling earlier identification, targeted interventions, and promotion of healthier aging across populations.

title: Interictal Epileptiform Discharges as Predictive Markers of Neurodevelopmental Outcomes in Early-Onset Epilepsy
description: This project will investigate whether interictal epileptiform discharges (IEDs), detected on electroencephalography (EEG), can serve as early markers of network instability and predictors of neurodevelopmental outcomes in early- onset epilepsy. Using the Edinburgh Paediatric Epilepsy Cohort (EPEC), a longitudinal dataset of children diagnosed before age five with linked EEG, clinical, video, and outcome data, we will characterise IED features (frequency, morphology, spatial distribution, sleep–wake modulation) and evaluate their association with long-term developmental outcomes. Analyses will integrate clinical moderators (aetiology, seizure onset, anti-seizure medication) and expressive behaviours (vocalisations, affective gestures) coded from videos, to test whether a multimodal approach improves early risk prediction. Outcomes will be modelled both categorically (diagnoses) and dimensionally (psychometric scores) considering the developmental heterogeneity. As an exploratory component, rat models will be used to determine whether IED-like activity and ASM exposure alter network synchrony and protein pathways. This cross-species approach will provide preliminary mechanistic insights into whether molecular changes linked to hyperexcitability point to targetable therapeutic pathways. By combining clinical data with mechanistic experimental work, this project aims to identify early markers of vulnerability and resilience in childhood epilepsy, laying the foundation for earlier risk stratification and targeted interventions. Keywords: Interictal epileptiform discharges, childhood epilepsy, EEG, proteomics, neurodevelopment

title: The impact of social safety nets on mental health outcomes and inequalities: a multi-method investigation
description: Mental ill health is a public health burden with consequences at individual and societal levels. The burden of mental ill health is unequally distributed across people with different sociodemographic characteristics. Improving mental health outcomes at the population level, as well as reducing inequalities in mental health, should therefore be considered important targets for mental health research. Social safety nets, which are primarily governmental programs providing financial or in-kind assistance for individuals in need, represent a potential approach for addressing these challenges. This PhD therefore will investigate how social safety nets are related to mental health outcomes and inequalities. This question will be researched using multiple methodological approaches, including large-scale analyses of country-level mental health in relation to social safety nets, a cross-country comparison of differential impacts of social safety nets on mental health, a social safety net-related policy evaluation, and an experimental behavioural study. The results from this PhD can contribute towards understanding the role of social safety nets, as well as informing policy-level interventions towards both improving population level mental health outcomes and reducing inequalities.

title: Internalized weight stigma: causes and consequences in young adulthood
description: Internalised weight stigma (IWS) is the belief that negative obesity-related stereotypes apply to oneself, often leading to reduced self-worth. Among higher-weight individuals, it is linked to worse mental health, disordered eating, and worse quality of life. In normal-weight and underweight individuals, it predicts disordered eating and drive for thinness and is thus relevant to mental health across the body weight range. "Much of the research on internalised weight stigma has been based on small, non-representative samples (e.g., participants recruited from weight loss groups, or undergraduate psychology students)". Therefore, the aetiology and risk factors for weight stigma internalisation, and its health and social consequences, are not well understood in the general population. Advancing current understanding of these relationships would help identify groups especially at risk of internalising weight stigma and could inform policy interventions to mitigate the effects of weight stigma. This project will use data from the population birth cohort survey Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC) to investigate if: A variety of social, health and psychological factors at different points in the life course are associated with IWS in adulthood. Internalised weight-stigma has a negative impact on health and social outcomes in young adulthood

title: Understanding the relationship between mental health and NEET status in young adults
description: 13% of UK 16-24-year-olds were classified as NEET (Not in Education, Employment, or Training) in December 2024, representing a growing economic and public health challenge. Young people experiencing NEET face elevated risks of mental health disorders, substance abuse, and suicide. While cross-sectional studies demonstrate associations between NEET and mental health problems, longitudinal evidence is needed to establish directionality. Understanding mediating mechanisms will inform interventions aimed at supporting young adults experiencing NEET or mental health problems. Additionally, we aim to explore whether certain longitudinal patterns of mental health (i.e. timing and duration of symptoms) confer greater NEET risk. Key Goals: Explore bidirectionality: Longitudinal modelling to assess whether mental health problems lead to NEET status, vice versa, or both. Identify mediating mechanisms: Examine potential mediators between mental health and NEET such as academic attainment, school attendance, self-esteem, and substance abuse. Map mental health trajectories: Growth mixture modelling will identify distinct longitudinal patterns of mental health symptoms and their associations with NEET, informing targeted interventions. Data: Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC) - birth cohort study with repeated measures of mental health and education/employment activity. Next Steps - longitudinal cohort study with repeated measures of mental health and focus on post- education transitions.

title: Sex Specific Differences in Psychedelic Therapies
description: Research examining the therapeutic potential of psychedelic substances has expanded rapidly in recent years. However, there is a distinct lack of research examining effects specific to women. This is especially pertinent given the gender imbalance in some mental health disorders such as depression, as well as the presence of female-specific disorders like premenstrual dysphoric disorder. Previous research has shown that ovarian hormones such as estrogen and progesterone upregulate 5HT-2A, the primary target of classic psychedelics. However, whether monthly cyclical changes to these hormones impact the acute psychedelic experience and subsequent therapeutic outcomes is currently unknown. The current research aims to address this gap through three strands of work. First, a scoping review of sex-based differences in current psychedelic research. Second, a two-arm experimental study in which health participants will receive a single, fixed dose of psilocybin to compare differences in acute psychedelic experiences and outcomes at two different stages of the menstrual cycle (follicular and luteal). Qualitative (interviews), quantitative (standardized psychometric subscales), and physiological data (EEG, heart rate, blood pressure) will be collected. Third, within this experimental cohort, we will conduct exploratory analysis of whether a single psilocybin session reduces self-reported premenstrual distress.

title: Reimagining Prevention Science: LGBTQ+ Collective Action to Prevent Depression and Anxiety in Urban Vietnam
description: This project investigates how LGBTQ+ communities in the Global South are forging new forms of care and activism amid high rates of depression, anxiety, and exclusion from both public health systems and heteronormative society. Existing interventions—individualised, clinical, and Global North-derived—are often inadequate in the face of structural discrimination. I ask: can community-led collective action prevent depression and anxiety among LGBTQ+ people? Focusing on LGBTQ+ networks in urban Vietnam—one of the most dynamic sites of queer solidarity in the Global South—I reimagine collective action as a pathway to mental health. I define it as 'voluntary group efforts to support mutual well-being and respond to structural discrimination.' I will (1) theorise how LGBTQ+ collective action emerges, unfolds, and shapes mental health through a grounded theory study, (2) model reciprocal dynamics between collective action and depression/anxiety using an observational cohort, and (3) co-adapt and evaluate a promising collective action-based intervention through participatory and realist methods. Bridging the social and health sciences, this project integrates qualitative and quantitative approaches into a unified, three-stage pipeline. It sheds light on a neglected field—LGBTQ+ mental health in the Global South—and offers a new blueprint for prevention science, centring empowerment and structural transformation where traditional systems have failed.

title: What should we target to treat depression? From receptors and circuits to remission.
description: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a debilitating condition with most existing treatments being slow-acting or ineffective for many patients or depressive symptoms. Ketamine has shown promise as a fast-acting antidepressant that alleviates symptoms within hours; however, its effects are short-lived and it poses risks of abuse, highlighting the need for safer, more precise and longer-lasting treatments. Using an established chronic stress model, which elicits depression-related phenotypes in rodents, my recent research shows that ketamine’s antidepressant action begins with the inhibition of somatostatin-expressing (Sst+) interneurons in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC)—identifying this heterogenous neuronal population as key initiators of antidepressant effects. Here, I will delineate the Sst+ subtypes initiating antidepressant effects, to determine the precise circuit mechanisms induced by antidepressants. Next, I will uncover how different Sst+ subtypes influence distinct depression-related behaviours to identify precise ways to alleviate specific symptoms by targeting these subtypes. I will also investigate how ketamine restores cell-type-specific, stress-induced changes, with the goal of modulating these pathways to prolong antidepressant outcomes. Ultimately, I aim to deepen our understanding of mPFC-mediated antidepressant mechanisms and the pathophysiology underlying depressive symptoms to support the development of novel, multi-target treatments with lasting effects for MDD patients.

title: Is the Individual the Clue in Prevention? Towards a New Personalised Understanding of Depression Prevention in Adolescents
description: Depression rates among adolescents and young adults have risen over the past two decades. Depression is difficult to treat, often requiring intensive intervention, and even then, relapse and recurrence mean the lives of those with first-onset depression may be permanently affected. This highlights the urgent need for effective onset prevention. However, efforts to develop such strategies have been limited, with some school-based interventions worsening symptoms. A key barrier is the lack of intensive, longitudinal research capturing the dynamic, person-specific processes that drive depression onset and how they can be targeted. Promising insights may come from integrating approaches from successful relapse-prevention interventions targeting similar mechanisms. Therefore, the aims of this study are to: 1. Identify person- specific psychological and behavioural risk processes contributing to depression onset. 2. Determine promising psychological intervention components targeting these processes. 3. Test whether these components modify risk processes and reduce depression risk. This research will use Ecological Momentary Assessment in a representative youth cohort to identify real-time predictors of first-onset depression. A component network meta-analysis and Delphi survey will isolate effective components, informing a conceptual framework for personalised prevention, to be tested in a randomised A-B-A design. Findings will inform personalised, evidence-based strategies to prevent youth depression.

title: How can social accountability mechanisms enhance community-led responses to climate-related health challenges in rural and urban Malawi?
description: Malawi and other African countries are increasingly facing extreme climate events, marked by heavy floods, extreme heat, droughts and consequent outbreaks of infectious diseases, food insecurity and mental illnesses. Limited interventions however exist to support vulnerable communities adapt to climate-related health challenges. Understanding local vulnerability, integrating experiential or indigenous knowledge and promoting community-led adaptation are essential to strengthen climate resilience. Despite efforts to promote community engagement in global health, many initiatives in low- and middle-income settings remain driven by researchers, government or non- government organisations, inadvertently reinforcing epistemic injustice. My previous research in Malawi has further revealed how power holders often employ community engagement to legitimise their agendas, rather than respond to community needs. Using Participatory Action Research (PAR), this research will co-design a novel approach of enabling communities to initiate dialogue and demand accountability from stakeholders to collectively adapt to climate- related health challenges. I will integrate participatory evaluation methods including citizen science ethnography, reflective workshops and in-depth interviews to enable community members to analyse their experiences of initiating dialogue with stakeholders to adapt to climate related-health challenges. Study outcomes shall contribute both methodologically and theoretically to enhance community-led adaptation to climate-related health challenges and epistemic justice.

title: The Developing Children’s Connectome Project (DCCP)
description: The Developing Children’s Connectome Project (DCCP) will establish a fundamental understanding of brain, cognitive and socio-emotional development by acquiring, in unprecedented detail, neuroimaging, cognitive, behavioural and socio-environmental data from a large cohort of children aged 6 to 12 years, that were already deeply phenotyped during fetal, neonatal and toddler stages as part of the Developing Human Connectome Project (dHCP). We will elucidate, at the individual level, how socio-environmental and clinical factors influence children’s longitudinal brain maturation, shaping resilience to known risks (i.e., perinatal events, psychiatric family history, socio- economic circumstances) and/or susceptibility to mental health problems, as they enter and progress through school. This new information will provide clinically meaningful evidence to guide well-being strategies supporting the development of all children. Overarching goals: to create the most comprehensive ultra-high field neuroimaging dataset to date spanning age 6 to 12 (n=548 children) (Aim 1) and explore dynamic associations between changes in brain structure/function and phenotypic heterogeneity (Aim 2); to study how perinatal brain features inform later brain trajectories into middle childhood (Aim 3); to precisely model, at the individual level, the factors defining differences in mental health vulnerability in childhood (Aim 4).

title: Sensitising brain MRI to cell type and shape
description: We propose to sensitise brain MRI to cell type numbers and shapes or morphologies. The goal in each case is to achieve cell specificity.
