We will do so by (1) enhancing diffusion MRS to provide tissue microstructure intracellularly to distinguish between neuronal, astrocyte, and microglia morphology, by (2) combining high resolution diffusion and quantitative MRI with 2D and 3D microscopy and spatial transcriptomics to generate models that can predict cell distribution, and by (3) developing novel molecular MRI contrasts that provide cell or molecule specific signatures read out through the widely used BOLD signal. Each of these three classes of methods will be important on their own, but it is in their integration that we expect to achieve cellular specificity and spatial resolution in vivo. At the end of the eight year project we will have significantly advanced our ability to use MRI as a cell-specific readout of brain architecture and provided key insights into how variation in the cellular architecture of the brain leads to variation in risk and resilience in mental health.

title: ARIADNE: ARtificial Intelligence-based Assessment to Detect iNdividuals with Emerging psychosis risk
description: The Clinical High Risk for Psychosis (CHR-P) state offers a vital chance to step in early and prevent the onset of psychosis. But right now, almost 9 out of 10 people in this phase are not identified in time. The best way to detect CHR-P individuals is with a specialist clinical interview. However, these interviews are long, require highly trained clinicians, and are only done in specialist services. Many people who are referred for these assessments do not actually meet CHR-P criteria, meaning a lot of time is spent on unnecessary interviews. Reports are also often difficult for patients to understand and are not always useful for research. To address these problems, we are developing ARIADNE - a new voice-based interview system powered by generative artificial intelligence. ARIADNE will be able to hold a natural conversation, ask the right questions, and produce clear, tailored reports for patients, clinicians, and researchers. This would make assessments faster, more accessible and more empowering for patients while supporting research and clinical care. In this project, we will demonstrate that it is secure, accurate, safe, ethical, acceptable and cost-effective. This will support medical device registration to facilitate ARIADNE helping young people access preventive care.

title: HAI-Team: Human–AI Teaming Therapeutic Companion for Torture Survivors with PTSD
description: Torture survivors with PTSD experience severe distress between weekly therapy sessions, yet no digital intervention supports this vulnerable, culturally diverse population. This programme develops a generative AI therapeutic companion providing continuous stabilisation and grounding support, co- designed with survivors. Working with Freedom from Torture (FfT), the UK's largest specialist treatment centre, we create a multilingual system bridging care gaps whilst maintaining primacy of human therapeutic relationships. The AI operates within a three-way loop: providing grounding support to clients, generating clinical reports, and adapting strategies based on therapist guidance. We deliver five outputs: a validated therapeutic companion with multi-agent architecture; ethical, privacy and security frameworks addressing survivor-specific threats; human-AI teaming methods for mental health; clinically validated datasets combining recordings, roleplay and synthetic dialogues; and multimodal affect recognition with edge deployment for on- device use. Our consortium—FfT, UCL, University of Hamburg, and CISPA—places survivor co-design at its core. Developing frameworks for the most vulnerable population first, we create methods transferable to other trauma contexts including interpersonal violence, forced displacement, and childhood maltreatment. Datasets, models, and toolkits will be openly released to advance trauma-informed AI research globally. Keywords: generative AI, PTSD, torture survivors, therapeutic companion, human-AI teaming, affect recognition, stabilisation, ethics, privacy.

title: Generative AI for Simulated Conversations: Preparing Frontline Workers and Volunteers to Support Youth with Anxiety and Depression
description: This 24-month project brings together Kids Help Phone (KHP)—Canada’s only 24/7 eMental Health service offering free, multilingual, confidential support to youth— and Toronto Metropolitan University (TMU), a leading institution known for community-engaged, equity-promoting innovation and education. Our project addresses the urgent need for scalable training solutions for frontline mental health providers through the co-development and evaluation of a generative AI system built on a multi-agent infrastructure. Key components include a conversation simulator and a performance assessor. The simulator, co-designed with youth and frontline providers will create realistic single-session counselling and crisis response text conversations of youth experiencing anxiety and depression. The performance assessor delivers real-time feedback to trainees that is grounded in KHP’s established supervision and quality assurance measures. Using a developmental evaluation approach, we will iteratively refine the prototype and assess its validity, usability, and acceptance. We will complete a pragmatic evaluation to assess the tool’s effectiveness on provider confidence, knowledge, skills, and retention, as well as its impact on youth anxiety and depression. We will also leverage an established partnership with Childline Trinidad and Tobago to explore tailoring the developed simulator and assessor to their context.

title: shamiriAI – Scalable, Culturally-Informed AI for Fidelity Feedback and Adaptive Training in Youth Mental Health
description: Training and supervising non-specialists to deliver evidence-based mental health interventions (“task-shifting”) is a promising strategy for closing the youth mental health treatment gap. However, scaling this approach is constrained by supervision bottlenecks, as traditional methods are labor- intensive and rely on scarce professionals. To address this, we’ve developed shamiriAI, an AI-augmented supervision tool for non-specialist lay-providers. shamiriAI processes session audio, using multilingual Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and prosodic analysis to generate structured feedback for supervisors. Operating within an "AI-in-the-loop" design, shamiriAI supplements—rather than replaces—supervisors, who remain the primary agents of supervision. Our proposal seeks to further develop, deploy, and rigorously evaluate shamiriAI through three aims: (1) Further develop shamiriAI through co-design to ensure a safe, contextually-grounded system with advanced multilingual ASR and prosodic modeling; (2) Conduct a comprehensive implementation science evaluation by deploying shamiriAI within training and supervision workflows of a task-shifted youth mental health program; and (3) Conduct a well-powered randomized non-inferiority trial (N=1,000 youth; N=20 lay providers) to test if AI-augmented supervision maintains clinical effectiveness while improving fidelity and cost-effectiveness. Outputs include open-source models and datasets, implementation guides, and peer-reviewed manuscripts. Ultimately, we hope to create a template for safe, contextually- grounded AI-augmented supervision in mental health programs globally.

title: Bridging the Treatment Gap with AI-Enhanced Supervision (BRIDGE-AI)
description: BRIDGE-AI aims to strengthen the quality and scalability of evidence-based psychological treatments in low-resource settings by designing and evaluating an AI-enabled supervision feedback tool for non-specialist counselors in India. Leveraging the CARE platform (an existing, validated AI-powered feedback tool) and over 4,000 Behavioral Activation therapy sessions delivered in Hindi by non-specialists, the study will: (1) Develop the BRIDGE-AI tool to identify key therapeutic techniques and generate timely, culturally-grounded feedback that helps counselors strengthen their practice and supervisors prioritize cases needing additional support; (2) Evaluate the tool’s acceptability, feasibility, and impact on counselor performance and patient outcomes through a pilot trial; and (3) Co-develop an ethical, participatory framework to ensure safe, transparent, and equitable integration into supervision systems. BRIDGE-AI integrates expertise in AI, ethics, lived experience, psychological science, quality-assured supervision, and global mental health to strengthen task-shared care in primary care settings in the Global South. The project combines participatory design with technical innovation to ensure the tool reflects local realities, strengthens therapy- quality measurement, and generates evidence on how AI can safely and effectively collaborate with non-specialist counselors and supervisors. Together, these efforts will lay the groundwork for scalable, trustworthy, and ethically governed quality-assurance systems in global mental health care.

title: Culturally Aligned Generative AI to Support Para-Counselors in Low-Resource Community Mental Health Settings
description: This project aims to develop culturally grounded generative AI tools to support para-counselors in Bangladesh who provide front-line mental health support for anxiety, depression, and psychosis. Para-counselors are often embedded in community-based services but work with limited training and diagnostic tools, leading to oversimplified or incorrect attributions (e.g., financial hardship as the cause of all distress). Our goal is to integrate a causal reasoning framework with large language models (LLMs) to help para- counselors understand their clients using explanatory models that are culturally and contextually appropriate and align better with client experiences and scientific understanding, thereby informing the development of culturally resonant care plans and intervention strategies. We adopt a rigorous, participatory approach: lived experience experts are embedded throughout the project lifecycle-as co-researchers, evaluators, advisory board members, and compensated co-designers-to shape tool functionality, language, and deployment strategy. During the research, we will build on data centered on people with lived experiences, develop a causal graph library reflecting local idioms of distress, and evaluate language and reasoning performance with stakeholders. The solution will be open source, interoperable with existing systems, and designed for future scaling across LMIC contexts. Long-term capacity-building with partner organizations will ensure sustainability and continuous improvement.

title: Generative AI for Identifying Mechanisms and Intervention Points in the Intergenerational Transmission of Anxiety
description: Understanding how anxiety is transmitted from parent to child remains one of the most important yet elusive challenges in clinical science. Parental anxiety profoundly shapes children’s emotional development, yet we lack tools to capture these processes as they unfold in real-world interactions. This is a critical knowledge gap and persistent barrier to developing effective interventions. RAISE-AI (Resilience Across Intergenerational Stresses and Emotional Health through AI-Enabled Discovery) applies generative AI to detect and explain how stress, worry, and fear pass between parents and children. We will develop models that identify when and how anxiety signals are transmitted through multimodal cues (e.g., language, prosody, facial affect, posture) during naturalistic interactions and evaluate these models for accuracy, interpretability, and fairness across racially, ethnically, and socioeconomically diverse families. Finally, we will generate outputs (e.g., summaries, real-time feedback) to inform pediatric anxiety prevention and treatment plans. If funded, RAISE-AI will reveal the mechanisms through which parental anxiety shapes children’s emotional responses and establish one of the first pediatric benchmarks for generative-AI performance in mental health. By translating subtle emotional signals into interpretable feedback, it will help providers support families and advance ethical, culturally responsive pediatric mental health interventions. Key Words: Anxiety; Parent-Child Interaction; Developmental Psychopathology

title: SYLFAEN-PSY: SYmptom Learning through Foundation models to Augment and ENhance measurement in PSYchosis
description: Dimensional symptom scales are sensitive measurements of the course of psychosis. While they are recommended for routinely monitoring psychotic symptoms, their use is inconsistent at best: Fewer than 30% of psychiatrists report even occasionally using them, while research studies often differ substantially in which and how many scales they assess, even when measuring the same symptoms. Thus, most people with psychotic disorders, either in the clinic or as research participants, only get their experiences partially translated (if at all) into quantitative dimensions. One main argument against dimensional scales is that they are lengthy to complete, and our project offers a pragmatic alternative. We will create a system, informed by lived experience and based on Large Language Models, to generate proxy measurements of psychotic symptoms by integrating multimodal data. These proxies will be validated against gold-standard scales in deeply characterised cohorts of individuals with psychotic disorders, and in research data from mental health NHS services. Through extensive assessments of uncertainty and bias, we will develop a new standard for AI-based information extraction and inference in mental health research, delivering a solution for assessing the experiences of people with psychosis at scale, and removing a long-standing barrier for symptom-based research.

title: GENSCORE Project: Leveraging Generative AI to adapt and enhance the scoring of widely used mental health assessment tools in low-resource context
description: In Nigeria where about 250 psychiatrists serve over 220 million people, contextually accurate mental health screening tools are not just beneficial, they are essential. Our GENSCORE Project aims to develop and validate a culturally grounded, multimodal AI platform/software to improve depression and anxiety screening for Pidgin English, Hausa, and Yoruba speakers in Nigeria. The project will build on our successful pilot to co-develop GENSCORE-DATA v2.0, one of Africa’s largest multilingual mental health dataset, and fine- tune GENSCORE-LLM v2.0 for culturally aligned interpretation. Our culturally relevant model, GENSCORE-LLM, will enable the development of contextually relevant mental health screening (GenPHQ and GenGAD) tools co-designed with people with lived experience and mental health experts. These tools will be integrated into an open-access, multimodal GENSCORE platform combining voice (audio) and self-reported text, facilitating real-time screening and decision support. The GENSCORE tools will undergo rigorous community and clinical validation and benchmarked against SCID-5-CV assessments among 990 participants in language-specific sites: Lagos State (Pidgin English), Abuja, FCT (Hausa) and Oyo State (Yoruba). Robust ethical, governance, and safety frameworks will ensure fairness, data sovereignty, and responsible AI use, with broad national and international dissemination.

title: STELLAR – Steering-Vector Enhanced LLM Agents for Realistic Digital Twins in Mental Health
description: The scarcity of mental health training resources worldwide creates critical shortages in qualified health workers. Complex psychiatric presentations make it difficult for trainees to gain sufficient clinical exposure. To address these gaps, we propose STELLAR (Steering-Vector Enhanced LLM Agents for Realistic Digital Twins in Mental Health), AI-powered patient simulations using Large Language Models enhanced with Conceptors – advanced steering vectors enabling precise control over model outputs – to create realistic digital patient twins with controllable psychiatric symptoms for scalable clinician training. We leverage Conceptors to encode specific symptom constructs (Anxious/misery, Psychosis, Behavioral/externalizing, Fear) with scalable intensity and combinability, surpassing traditional prompting. We will develop Conceptors using the Philadelphia Neurodevelopmental Cohort, a community sample of 9,500+ individuals with comprehensive psychiatric assessments and diagnostic criteria. A key innovation is Conceptor shareability. Once validated, symptom-specific Conceptors can be distributed to other institutions, accelerating training and collaborative research. Primary applications include: (1) interdisciplinary clinical training through safe interactions with diverse patient presentations; (2) validation of language-based diagnostic tools against reproducible digital twin presentations before clinical deployment. This collaboration unites clinical expertise for symptom annotation with AI capabilities for Conceptor development. STELLAR will be tested by an experienced clinical team with global reach and diverse stakeholder input.

title: AURORA: Adaptive Understanding through Real-time Observation, Reporting, and Assistance
description: Depression acuity can rapidly shift, yet weekly assessments detect change slowly and often unreliably, delaying treatment personalization and compounding disability. AURORA (Adaptive Understanding through Real-time Observation, Reporting, and Assistance) pairs passive sensing with voice- native, conversational GenAI check-ins to capture rich context plus objective multimodal signals. This enables sensitive, safe, and equitable measurement—the foundation for just-in-time adaptive interventions that address stakeholder concerns about privacy, context, and the risk of dehumanizing, metric-driven care. AURORA’s passive triggers launch brief, adaptive audio-visual assessments of depressive symptoms and provide psychoeducation and CBT-inspired engagement prompts/cues, while collecting high-quality audio–visual signals and lived context. The result is an actionable, valid depressive symptom measurement that can individualize treatment. Following development and refinement, we will evaluate AURORA in a pragmatic cluster-randomized trial of 1,000 patients through 100 clinician dyads across 4 continents. With an international team of researchers and lived experience experts, we leverage our strengths in GenAI, digital phenotyping, global clinical studies, ethics, and advanced analytical methods. We aim to: (1) Develop AURORA; (2) Validate AURORA as a psychometrically robust, responsive, and fair measurement system for depression; (3) Demonstrate engagement, acceptability, and clinical utility; and (4) Explore AURORA’s impact on clinical outcomes relative to treatment-as-usual.

title: AI4You(th): Advancing Generative AI for Personalised and Collaborative Youth Mental Health Care
description: The global youth mental health (YMH) crisis demands scalable, effective solutions, yet current care models remain insufficiently engaging and effective. Critical barriers include limited personalisation, reduced youth agency in collaborative decision-making, and poor care continuity. Generative AI has the potential to address these challenges. However, key limitations prevent clinical translation: LLMs cannot reason longitudinally over evolving clinical contexts; lack frameworks for ensuring safety, youth agency, and evidence-informed decision-making; and operate as standalone tools disconnected from face-to-face care. This project will address these limitations through SensAI, a multi-stakeholder AI collaborator that supports young people with depression and anxiety and their clinicians to enhance personalisation, agency, and continuity in YMH. We will: (1) develop novel methods for longitudinal LLM reasoning using personalised knowledge graphs; (2) produce the first YMH-specific constitutional principles that enable LLMs to deliver safe, agency-supportive, and evidence-aligned guidance; (3) integrate these methods into SensAI, an AI collaborator that supports young people and clinicians across the care journey; and (4) evaluate SensAI’s feasibility, safety, and preliminary effectiveness of through a pilot randomised controlled trial. Co-designed with young people and clinicians, this research will establish the foundational methods and evidence required for future generative AI applications to transform YMH care.

title: Human-in-the-loop Evaluation of Assisted Depression Screening (HEADS)
description: We develop and evaluate HEADS (Human-in-the-loop Evaluation of Assisted Depression Screening), a multilingual, modular, interpretable, HIL, LLM-based automated pipeline for clinical depression diagnosis (DSM-5) and severity (PHQ-9) in diverse clinical populations. Psychiatrists will collect data via QuickSCID-5 and PHQ-9, with adaptive sampling across languages, genders, comorbidity. HEADS has individually trainable modules: (i) Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) supporting five languages (Kannada, Hindi, Bengali, Assamese, English); (ii) Domain-sensitive translation (Indic to English); (iii) Inference module providing contextual summaries, DSM-5 diagnoses, PHQ-9 score-bands, reasoning and confidence scores. Key deliverables: (a) HEADS solution; (b) de-identified datasets: 4500 Indic language clinical interviews; native-language transcripts and English translations; DSM-5 diagnosis, PHQ-9 scores, clinical reasoning by psychiatrists; 6000 synthetic English transcripts simulating edge cases; (c) well-documented pipelines for eliciting clinical reasoning from psychiatrists in Chain-of-Thought format and synthetic data generation for training diagnostic models. The key goal is to create safe (HIL), scalable, non-intrusive automated system to help non-specialists measure depression in culturally diverse populations, potentially addressing mental health gaps due to shortage of psychiatrists, underdiagnosis or misdiagnosis, with lived experience experts embedded at all stages of study, who will also co-design bias and safety analysis protocols. Keywords: Depression, Culturally-sensitive care, Human-in-the-loop, Generative-AI, Automatic Speech Recognition
recipient: National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro Sciences

title: FarajaMH: Culturally Adapted Generative AI Model for Mental Health Screening in Kenya and Tanzania; Leveraging Longitudinal Data, Clinical Notes and Conversational Chats
description: This project aims to build, validate, and ethically evaluate a bilingual (English and Swahili) generative AI (FarajaMH) model for screening of depression, anxiety, and psychosis (DAP) through natural language interactions. The project combines research and lived experiences to address the lack of culturally attuned tools for early screening and referral in Kenya and Tanzania. The word Faraja means “comfort” in Swahili, symbolising the project’s goal of creating a compassionate GenAI model that will recognize DAP, expressed in everyday metaphors. FarajaMH is a model trained with mental health conversational chats, clinical notes, audio and textual screening data from Health Demographic and Surveillance Systems (HDSS), for screening DAP from sampled populations in Kenya and Tanzania. It will be evaluated and validated entirely within a controlled research environment, testing its screening accuracy, usability, and safety. The expected outcomes include (1) a harmonised multimodal data repository of mental health information mapped to the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership Common Data Model (OMOP CDM); (2) a bilingual generative AI model for screening for DAP; (3) a mental-health data catalogue and visual analytics dashboard; and (4) publications and conference presentations on GenAI in mental health in East-African context.
recipient: African Population and Health Research Centre

title: Evaluating the Real-World Effectiveness and Scalability of METRA for Adolescents in Conflict-Affected Contexts Across Syria, Iraq, and Afghanistan
description: Adolescents exposed to war, violence, and displacement in crisis-affected regions face high rates of psychological distress and trauma, yet have limited access to effective mental health care. To address this gap, our team developed METRA (Memory Training for Recovery-Adolescent); a brief, low- intensity scalable early intervention that can be delivered by trained local community health workers and educators. The program is culturally adaptable and designed for low-resource settings. We have conducted five clinical trials with adolescents aged 10–19 in Afghanistan, Iraq and Pakistan. Results show METRA is feasible, acceptable, and associated with improvements in PTSD, depression and anxiety symptoms. All sessions were delivered by trained non- specialists, demonstrating the intervention’s potential for scale. METRA was found to be cost-effective compared to individual trauma-informed interventions. We are now aiming to evaluate METRA in real-world conditions through the Wellcome Trust’s Impact Phase. Our objectives in the Foundation Phase are to further strengthen partnerships and pathways to implementation and scale for the Impact Phase. The Impact Phase will assess the effectiveness, scalability, and implementation of METRA in three diverse conflict-affected settings (Iraq, Afghanistan and Syria). The research will contribute robust evidence for early mental health interventions for adolescents affected by crises in LMICs.

title: Improving mental health among Ugandan and Ghanaian adolescents through a school-based sleep health intervention: Better Sleep, Better Health
description: Insomnia can cause depression and anxiety in adolescents. Cognitive behavior therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is an effective early intervention for depression and anxiety. Focusing on improving sleep can offer a non-stigmatising pathway to improve mental health, but CBT-I is not widely used due to lack of awareness of the importance of sleep for mental health, shortage of trained providers and non-existence of scalable resource-efficient delivery models. We will address the evidence gap of how to deliver CBT-I at scale to adolescents in Africa. In the Foundation Phase, we will build a partnership to design and evaluate scalable CBT-I-based interventions to improve the mental health of secondary school students in Africa. Objectives: 1) To establish a sustainable equitable partnership among researchers, implementation partners, lived- experience experts, WHO and the Ministries of Health and Education in Uganda and Ghana. 2) To adapt a CBT-I-based intervention to ensure scalability and sustainability in Uganda and Ghana, guided by May’s General Theory of Implementation and feasibility case-series. 3) To co-design a cluster- randomised controlled trial to evaluate the implementation, effectiveness, cost-effectiveness and sustainability of these CBT-I-based interventions to reduce depression and anxiety among secondary school students in Uganda and Ghana, using the RE-AIM evaluation framework.
recipient: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine

title: Data-Augmented quality improvement With lived experience engagement in early iNtervention for anxiety and depression (DAWN)
description: DAWN (Data-Augmented quality improvement With lived experience engagement in early iNtervention for anxiety and depression) aims to strengthen delivery-at- scale of the Early Adolescent Skills for Emotions (EASE) intervention for 10-15-year-olds in humanitarian settings in Lebanon, Nepal, and Uganda. These countries combine high adolescent mental health burden, humanitarian emergencies, government commitment to psychosocial integration, and experience involving persons with lived experience of mental health conditions (PLWEs) in mental health training and supervision. Foundational phase activities include establishing consortium governance, mapping policies, theory-of-change workshops, stakeholder consultation, and forming adolescent advisory groups to co-develop a hybrid type 2 trial protocol for the impact phase. The full trial will compare three arms: i) care-as-usual, ii) standard EASE, and iii) EASE+. EASE+ is an implementation strategy integrating youth co-leadership and competency-based, data-driven training and supervision using the WHO-UNICEF EQUIP platform. Co-primary outcomes for the hybrid type-2 include depression- anxiety symptoms (clinical effectiveness) and attendance (reach in the RE- AIM/PRISM implementation science framework), as well as cost-effectiveness and active ingredient mediation analyses. Lived-experience expertise is actively evaluated throughout DAWN. By embedding lived-experience leadership and data- driven systems within humanitarian settings, DAWN will create a scalable model, advancing Wellcome’s priorities on early intervention, equity, and lasting impact.

title: Blended delivery of cognitive-behavioural therapy for repetitive negative thought within mental health support teams in schools as scalable early intervention for anxiety and depression
description: Repetitive negative thought (RNT)—including worry, rumination, overthinking—is increasingly common in young people and contributes significantly to the onset and maintenance of anxiety and depression in youth. Reducing RNT is a well- established active therapeutic ingredient. Multiple randomized controlled trials show that cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT) focused on RNT effectively reduces and prevents RNT, anxiety, and depression in youth. However, this intervention is not yet widely accessible. This project aims to scale up CBT-for-RNT by adapting it for integration into Mental Health Support Teams (MHSTs), which are expanding to all schools in England. We will adapt group-based and supported digital formats aligned with current service delivery models. In the Foundation phase, our key goals are to co-adapt the intervention for MHSTs, map implementation and sustainability pathways, and design a definitive trial to evaluate effectiveness and cost-effectiveness, to be conducted in the Impact phase. We hypothesize that CBT-for-RNT will be more effective and cost-effective than treatment-as-usual. Young people with lived experience will play a central role in shaping research questions, co- designing intervention adaptations, and informing implementation strategies. This project will deliver scalable, economical, and impactful early interventions for common mental health problems in young people, with potential to transform school-based mental health support globally.

title: Transforming Early Psychosis Care through Supported Employment and Education in Peru
description: Supported employment and education can transform early psychosis care by helping young people recover through work and study. This project will launch Peru’s first national implementation of the Individual Placement and Support (IPS) model for youth with early psychosis. The Foundation Phase (Year 1) will build a multi-sector partnership across health, labour, and education to co- adapt IPS—an evidence-based model that integrates vocational and educational recovery into mental health care. Co-designed with young people, caregivers, employers, lived-experience leaders, and policymakers, this phase will ensure cultural and contextual fit, and sustainability. It will: (1) establish governance through a Steering Committee and Youth Lived-Experience Advisory Panel; (2) deliver IPS co-adaptation workshops and develop Spanish manuals and training materials; (3) create an employer and education engagement framework and inclusion toolkit; and (4) design a hybrid effectiveness–implementation trial protocol, public and patient involvement plans, and dissemination strategies. The Impact Phase (Years 2–6) will evaluate IPS within Peru’s community mental-health network, assessing effects on education, employment, functioning, and recovery, and examining implementation feasibility and cost- effectiveness. Findings will guide a national scale-up roadmap co-produced with government and lived-experience partners, including validated implementation tools, and financing mechanisms. Keywords: Early psychosis; Supported employment; Early intervention services; Lived experience co- production.

title: Y-MIND Africa: A Multi-Country Hybrid Type 2 Implementation-Effectiveness Stepped-Wedge Trial of a Scalable Psychological Intervention for Depression Among Adolescents and Young People.
description: Depression and anxiety often begin during the teenage years, especially around age 15. While effective and affordable treatments exist, many young people in low- and middle-income countries still struggle to access the support they need. The Y-MIND intervention helps adolescents/young people aged 15-24 years re-engage in meaningful activities and build problem-solving skills. It is delivered by trained lay counselors making it accessible through trusted community spaces. From the outset, adolescents/young people in Ghana and Zimbabwe helped shape the Y-MIND intervention – identifying what matters to them, ensuring the language felt real, and making activities practical and relevant to their daily lives. Adolescents/young people who participated in the early stages of Y-MIND have voiced their strong support for bringing this program to others like them. Together, we now plan to expand Y-MIND to four countries across West (Ghana, Burkina Faso), East (Kenya), and Southern Africa (Zimbabwe), in both English- and French-speaking communities. Through the INDEPTH Network – comprising health research centres that operate Health and Demographic Surveillance Systems across Africa, Asia and Oceania, we will partner with schools, communities, and adolescents/young people to test real- world delivery models, assess costs and resources, and co-design a sustainable scale-up plan rooted in equity and youth leadership.

title: Improving mental health among UK adolescents through a school-based sleep intervention
description: This project will prepare to test the efficacy, cost-effectiveness, and scalable delivery of a sleep intervention to treat adolescent depression and anxiety by building on an established, evidence-based sleep programme, utilising existing school mental health delivery structures, and by strengthening links with implementing partners. The sleep need in young people with mental health problems is high, unmet, and likely to impact on ability to benefit from other interventions. Sleep interventions have proven efficacy to improve symptoms of anxiety and depression alongside broader positive impacts on mental health and functioning. We will address the key knowledge gap of how to implement a sleep intervention across Mental Health Support Teams in Schools (MHSTs) in the UK. We have 3 objectives: 1) To create a sustainable partnership between researchers, stakeholders, and implementation partners. 2) To generate study protocols for the intervention and trial design, as well as co-designing effective recruitment, measurement, and data collection processes. 3) To prepare for a cluster-randomised controlled trial of a Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I) programme “The Better Sleep Programme” on depression and anxiety in MHSTs. These foundational activities will establish a sustainable school-based model for improving mental health, designed and fit for future scale-up.

title: Scaling up Problem Management Plus to Young Adults experiencing marginalization in Lebanon and Palestine – a initiative by and for young adults
description: Our proposal focuses on young adults-YA (18-30 years old) with symptoms of anxiety or depression, living in contexts of war, uncertainty, displacement in Lebanon and Palestine. YA exhibit higher rates of mental health distress than younger peers but are rarely the focus of interventions. Contexts of war/uncertainty/displacement increase distress. Yet, there are not enough licensed mental health providers to meet needs. We want to implement Problem Management Plus (PM+), an early-intervention community-based psychological intervention. PM+ works to decrease anxiety and depression by using strategies like problem-solving, stress management, taking action, and strengthening social support. A unique aspect of our application: YA without current distress will be trained to give PM+ to their peers. Our implementation partners include government mental health programs, a UN agency, NGOs that provide mental health programs, and Justice for Mental Health, a lived/living experience NGO in Lebanon. We will use the Foundation phase to include a Palestinian lived experience organization. This range of implementation partners will help us understand what works best to scale-up PM+. Plans for meaningful involvement of persons with lived experience will be developed by lived experience NGOs. The Foundation phase builds trusting relationships amongst the whole team and co-designs the impact phase.

title: A lost generation? Scaling iPDT to transform mental health outcomes for young people (age 16-25) in the UK
description: NHS-Talking Therapies (NHS-TT) is among the largest mental health service providers in the UK, receiving 1.82 million referrals in 2023/24. Yet the 16–25-year-old group has the poorest outcomes of all those referred to NHS-TT. Our vision is to improve engagement and outcomes for young people aged 16-25 seeking help with low mood. We aim for a stepped change in reach, impact, equity and sustainability by integrating an evidence-based, scalable digital intervention, designed by and for young people, into NHS-TT. During the Foundation Phase we will partner with key stakeholders, including young people, researchers, NHS services, policymakers, technology and implementation scientists to understand and plan how to embed internet-based psychodynamic therapy (iPDT), an evidence-based, guided self-help programme, into NHS-TT. The aim is to overcome barriers to young people receiving effective help. Working with our partners we will plan the Impact Phase to: (1) evaluate whether iPDT leads to higher levels of engagement, retention and impact in young people referred to NHS-TT services, (2) collect data to determine iPDT’s economic impact, including reduced onward referrals to higher-cost services, and (3) develop detailed plans for implementation and scalability. This project is a real-world transformation initiative with a clear route to sustained impact.

title: Cluster-randomised hybrid type 2 effectiveness-implementation trial and economic evaluation of a school-based problem-solving intervention for adolescent depression and anxiety: Co-design and trial preparation in Rajasthan, India
description: Adolescent depression and anxiety are prevalent in India but effective early interventions are scarce. Problem-solving is a common component of evidence- based programmes for both conditions, teaching individuals to identify tractable stressors, generate solutions, and test chosen options. Prior research in New Delhi showed that “Step 1,” a low-cost, school-based problem- solving intervention, reduced mental health symptoms, including internalising difficulties, up to 12-month follow-up. This proposal’s Foundation Phase will adapt Step 1 for secondary schools in Rajasthan, India’s largest state. Intervention materials, supervision and training will be updated for local relevance. We will also co-design a foundational implementation support package, build local partnerships, and finalise a trial protocol to enable rigorous evaluation of experimental implementation strategies. The Impact Phase will test two discrete implementation strategies using a type 2 hybrid effectiveness–implementation trial with a 2×2 factorial design. One comparison will examine the original multi-session programme against a single-session version that has potential to increase efficiency and reach. The other will compare delivery by external lay counsellors versus delivery by existing school staff to assess outcomes across workforce models. Findings will establish scalable, sustainable approaches for delivering Step 1 and inform broader implementation of early mental health interventions across India and beyond.

title: Towards a Scalable Early Intervention System for Youth Depression and Anxiety in Indonesia.
description: This Foundation Award will establish research and delivery infrastructure for a scalable, culturally adapted early intervention programme for adolescent depression and anxiety in Indonesia. Co-led with young people and lived experience contributors, the programme prioritises inclusive design, creative engagement, and community-based delivery. This preparatory work will enable a future impact study to expand early access to Behavioural Activation (BA)—a WHO-recommended psychological intervention that targets inactivity and avoidance, core mechanisms of depression and anxiety. BA’s simplicity, adaptability, and strong evidence base make it well-suited for delivery by trained lay health workers in low-resource settings, ensuring feasibility and sustainability. Three work packages will guide this foundation programme: WP1 (Empower) will build inclusive research capacity through training, translated resources, and digital tools to support meaningful participation. WP2 (Prepare) will co-develop youth-informed research infrastructure using creative methods and plan stigma-reduction strategies. WP3 (Develop) will strengthen strategic partnerships and collaborative governance. We will also identify culturally relevant, age-appropriate screening tools for early detection of depression and anxiety, ensuring practicality in low-resource contexts. Lived experience leadership will shape all stages, with arts-based activities—such as youth-led films, exhibitions, and plans for a co-created serial drama—amplifying youth voices, reducing stigma, and promoting help- seeking.

title: Scaling delivery of Narrative Exposure Therapy (NET) and the NETFacts community model for young survivors of gender-based violence in Guinea
description: The adolescent mental health burden is increasing, particularly among survivors of gender-based violence (GBV), who face a higher risk of Post- Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD). In Guinea, where 48% of people are under 18, GBV is pervasive and existing support focuses on physical health. Our previous work revealed major gaps in mental health care due to a lack of trained professionals. Addressing this will enable early intervention, which is critical to improve long-term mental health outcomes for young people. The proposed solution is training local practitioners in Narrative Exposure Therapy (NET), a scalable trauma-focused treatment effective in low-resource settings, and its community-based variant, NETfacts. NETfacts offers individual treatment with community reconciliation, reducing stigma and improving long-term outcomes. This study will test if NET/NETfacts provides an effective, low-cost, scalable intervention for young GBV survivors in Guinea. Our partnership—UCL, UNFPA, CJFLG, Guinean Health Ministry, vivo (NETfacts developers) and Universities of Conakry and Konstanz —will develop and evaluate this approach. During the Foundation Phase, the team, youth with lived experience, and stakeholders will co-design the adapted intervention for Guinea, the implementation and scale-up plan using UNFPA/CJFLG’s networks and a robust methodology to assess effectiveness and economic feasibility.

title: Teacher-Delivered Short-Term Group-Based Cognitive Behavioural Therapy Programme to Tackle Depression in Adolescents in West Africa (Ghana, Nigeria & Sierra Leone)
description: Adolescent depression poses a substantial public health burden in West Africa. This study aims to scale up a school-based, teacher-delivered group Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (group-CBT) programme for adolescents (aged 13–18) with early-stage depression (PHQ-9 ≥ 10), building on interventions that have been developed and evaluated for efficacy by the Centre for Child and Adolescent Mental Health (CCAMH), University of Ibadan. The implementation of the intervention in Ghana, Nigeria, and Sierra Leone will be led by CCAMH alumni who set up pioneering CAMH services in these countries. Teachers will be trained to deliver manualized, five-session group-CBT programme focusing on psychoeducation, behavioural activation, cognitive restructuring, spiritual integration, and relaxation techniques. This is a hybrid effectiveness–implementation study. The foundation phase will focus on co- adapting the intervention using the ADAPT-ITT framework and engaging stakeholders, including implementation partners and persons with lived experiences, to foster sustainable partnerships and strengthen capacity for the subsequent impact phase. Multisectoral implementation partnerships and economic evaluation models will be developed. The impact phase features a cluster-randomized controlled trial to assess clinical effectiveness, cost- effectiveness, fidelity, acceptability and appropriateness. This study will provide a scalable, evidence-based model to tackle adolescent depression in West Africa.
recipient: College of Medicine, University of Ibadan

title: RISE (Regional Implementation and Scale-up of Early Adolescent Skills for Emotions)
description: We propose to scale-up WHO–UNICEF endorsed Early Adolescent Skills for Emotions-EASE programme across Pakistan’s four provincial tertiary child and adolescent mental health(CAMH) facilities. Building on strong efficacy evidence from two RCTs(Pakistan and Jordan), we will evaluate EASE’s real- world clinical, implementation and cost-effectiveness compared with Enhanced Treatment as Usual using a Hybrid-Type-I trial design. EASE will be delivered by supervised postgraduate psychiatry and psychology residents, enabling rapid CAMH workforce expansion by integration in established and structured training, supervision and delivery pathways. Alongside the trial, to ensure integration and scale-up, co-designed by our Lived-Experience (LE) experts we will a)nationally, establish a government-endorsed Hub of Excellence for CAMH to coordinate scale-up; b)regionally, host a Collaborative Learning Group and Regional Fellowship Programme in eight CAMHSAN countries (Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan, Sri Lanka); and c)globally, co-develop a digital learning and knowledge-exchange hub using The Global Health Network(TGHN)’s Pathway to Impact framework to facilitate scale- up of CAMH psychotherapies and build scalable, youth-centred implementation capacity. LE youth will be embedded and co-lead governance, evaluation, and implementation, ensuring RISE delivers scalable, sustainable early intervention systems across Pakistan and South Asia. Keywords: EASE, active ingredients, implementation, (cost)-effectiveness evaluation, LE experts, task-shifting, regional and global scaling.

title: Pamoja Furaha: Integrating Group Interpersonal Therapy into maternal-child health services for perinatal adolescents in Kenya
description: Adolescent pregnancy rates remain high in Kenya, at approximately 20% of adolescents age 14-19. This group has disproportionately high risk of developing perinatal (pregnancy through first year after delivery) depression. We aim to develop and evaluate a perinatal depression treatment for adolescent girls age 14-19, integrated into maternal-child health services in Western Kenya. Our proposed intervention, Pamoja Furaha, includes (1) universal depression screening, (2) lay-delivered group interpersonal therapy, (3) measurement-based care, and (4) a bundle of implementation strategies to facilitate successful real-world implementation. Our team is comprised of Kenyan researchers in maternal-child health and mental health, a representative from Kenya’s national Ministry of Health, and experts in perinatal psychiatry, epidemiology and implementation science in the US. Foundation Phase: We will hold participatory workshops with national and county Ministries of Health, healthcare facility leadership, and lived experience experts, to formalize partnerships, agree on shared goals and priorities, and co-develop implementation strategies. Impact Phase: We will conduct an effectiveness-implementation hybrid cluster-randomized trial in 20 maternal-child health facilities in Homa Bay County. This low cost scalable package could extend across maternal-child health clinics throughout Kenya to improve mental health of adolescents and their infants.

title: Co-Creating and Scaling a Tailored, Lay-Delivered Group Cognitive-Behavioural Therapy (G-CBT) Intervention for Depression Among Young People Living with HIV (YPLHIV) in Cameroon: A Hybrid Implementation-Effectiveness Study
description: This proposal, led by the Clinton Health Access Initiative (CHAI) Cameroon in collaboration with the National AIDS Control Commission (NACC), the Directorate of Health Promotion, and an association of lived-experience experts, aims to adapt and scale a lay-delivered Group Cognitive-Behavioural Therapy (G-CBT) model to strengthen the management of depression among young people living with HIV (YPLHIV, aged 15–24 years) in Cameroon. The project will unfold in two linked phases. The Foundation Phase will establish coordination structures, assess evidence and site readiness, and co-create and culturally adapt the G-CBT model with youth and lived-experience experts. This phase will culminate in an implementation package—comprising an intervention manual, facilitator training curriculum, supervision and fidelity-monitoring tools, and a finalized protocol to guide the Impact Phase. The Impact Phase will assess the clinical effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, and scalability of the adapted model through a Hybrid Type II cluster-randomised trial, guided by RE-AIM and CFIR frameworks. Expected outcomes include improved depression management, better ART adherence and retention, and enhanced psychosocial wellbeing. The project will yield a validated implementation toolkit, a costed scale-up model, and policy-ready evidence to integrate depression care into youth-friendly HIV services in Cameroon. Keywords: Depression, Adolescents, HIV, Mental Health, G-CBT, Implementation Research, Cameroon

title: GENSCORE Project: Leveraging Generative AI to adapt and enhance the scoring of widely used mental health assessment tools in low-resource context
description: In Nigeria where about 250 psychiatrists serve over 220 million people, contextually accurate mental health screening tools are not just beneficial, they are essential. Our GENSCORE Project aims to develop and validate a culturally grounded, multimodal AI platform/software to improve depression and anxiety screening for Pidgin English, Hausa, and Yoruba speakers in Nigeria. The project will build on our successful pilot to co-develop GENSCORE-DATA v2.0, one of Africa’s largest multilingual mental health dataset, and fine- tune GENSCORE-LLM v2.0 for culturally aligned interpretation. Our culturally relevant model, GENSCORE-LLM, will enable the development of contextually relevant mental health screening (GenPHQ and GenGAD) tools co-designed with people with lived experience and mental health experts. These tools will be integrated into an open-access, multimodal GENSCORE platform combining voice (audio) and self-reported text, facilitating real-time screening and decision support. The GENSCORE tools will undergo rigorous community and clinical validation and benchmarked against SCID-5-CV assessments among 990 participants in language-specific sites: Lagos State (Pidgin English), Abuja, FCT (Hausa) and Oyo State (Yoruba). Robust ethical, governance, and safety frameworks will ensure fairness, data sovereignty, and responsible AI use, with broad national and international dissemination.

title: Interlinked burdens: Understanding the diabetes-depression syndemic in continental Africa
description: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) and depression are major global health challenges that often co-occur, leading to worse outcomes and increasing health system burdens. In Africa, both conditions are rising rapidly, yet their interplay remains poorly understood - particularly among African-ancestry populations, who are underrepresented in biomedical research and often present with distinct disease phenotypes. This fellowship aims to uncover shared biological and psychosocial mechanisms linking T2D and depression in African settings, generating foundational insights to inform future interventions. Building on my leadership in studies such as the Generation Malawi Birth Cohort and DepGen Africa, I will use rich, harmonised data from Malawi and other African countries to explore interactions between biological systems, social environments, and lived experiences. The programme comprises three work packages: (1) identify shared metabolic and inflammatory signatures using large-scale metabolomics; (2) investigate causal pathways through genetic analyses, including Mendelian randomisation; and (3) apply qualitative methods to understand how individuals experience comorbidity and navigate care. This interdisciplinary, discovery-focused research will advance our understanding of a critical but understudied public health challenge. Through a tailored training and mentorship programme, it will also support my development as a leading African scientist at the intersection of physical and mental health.

title: From Industry to Inequality: Mental Health in the Wake of Deindustrialisation
description: This project will establish the impact of historical deindustrialisation on contemporary mental health and wellbeing in the UK, using the case study of the city of Sunderland in the post-industrial North East of England. This region possesses a significant industrial legacy, having been a global leader in coal mining, shipbuilding, and associated industries. It also contains significant health inequalities relating to mental health, including the highest rates of adolescent self-harm and the highest levels of heavy alcohol use and substance-related deaths in England. This research will explore and explain how the process of deindustrialisation in the latter half of the 20th century contributed to poorer mental health outcomes today, not only among those directly impacted by the loss of industrial employment, but also their families, descendants, and those in the wider community. This qualitative inquiry will involve affected communities at all stages, utilising oral history interviews with older residents, a programme of peer research led by community members, and participatory workshops with residents of different generations. Together, these complementary strands of research will create a holistic picture of how historic deindustrialisation has impacted contemporary mental health outcomes, and how further harm might be prevented through policy change and community action.

title: Personalised REcommenDations for preventIng reCurrenT Urinary tract infections and esTimation of pharmacologIcal option effectiveness (PREDICT-rUTI)
description: Recurrent urinary tract infections (rUTIs) affect millions of women globally and are one of the most common reasons for repeated antibiotic use. These infections significantly impact women’s well-being and quality-of-life. They also drive repeated healthcare visits, urine sampling, and antibiotic prescribing, contributing to health service expenditure and antibiotic resistance. Despite the major personal and societal impacts, most rUTIs are treated reactively, with limited clinical evidence to support proactive, personalised prevention of repeated infections. This research aims to inform personalised prevention of rUTIs using real-world data. Inspired by four women with lived experience, it will address four questions: 1\. How effective are current pharmacological options for preventing rUTIs? 2\. Which women are likely to develop rUTIs? 3\. Which women with rUTIs are at highest risk of further infections? 4\. Which women will benefit from which specific pharmacological option for preventing rUTIs? To answer these, I will address four objectives: 1\. Evaluate the effectiveness of three preventive options: vaginal oestrogen, methenamine hippurate, and antibiotics. 2\. Develop three prediction models estimating: the risk of rUTIs, risk of recurrence, and individual response to prevention. 3\. Externally validate these models. 4\. Explore implementation through stakeholder engagement and user-testing. Keywords: recurrent UTIs, prediction tools, primary care

title: ‘It didn’t just kill them at sea’: an oral history of health and wellbeing in British fishing communities, c.1960 – present.
description: The health and wellbeing of coastal communities dependent on fishing is inextricably linked to the health and wellbeing of the seas. Over the last 70 years, environmental changes and governance measures linked to declining fish stocks have piled pressure onto an industry long characterised by dangerous working conditions and precarious employment, with health implications for coastal communities throughout the world. In Britain, the decline of the fishing industry since the 1950s has contributed to a coastal health crisis, whilst severing longstanding connections to the sea for many communities. This project places oral history and community engagement methodologies at its core, asking those who have lived and worked in British fishing communities about the impact of changing oceanic health on individual and community health and wellbeing. The project will seek to understand how the health risks of a dangerous trade changed over time, how these have been managed and remembered within communities across generations, and how processes of deindustrialisation and disconnection with the seas have affected community wellbeing over the long term. The project places communities at the heart of questions about their health and wellbeing, with historical change as the mechanism for enabling them to shape their own narratives.

title: Models of functional maturation in human cortical microcircuits
description: The human brain undergoes substantial developmental changes from childhood to adulthood, but the underlying biophysical mechanisms and their implications for cognitive maturation remain unclear. This computational neuroscience project addresses this gap using a unique multi-modal dataset of >1,100 patch- clamp recordings from human supragranular pyramidal neurons spanning a large age range (0.9-55 years). The main goal is to understand how developmental shifts in neuronal biophysical properties influence information processing and learning in human cortex. The approach uses a new Python toolbox that allows gradient-based optimization of biophysically detailed neural models. The project has three integrated phases: first, developing age-specific biophysical models of individual cortical neurons; second, constructing circuit models by connecting these detailed neurons through biologically realistic synapse models fitted to multi-patch synaptic recordings from human cortex; and third, integrating these components into larger networks trained on cognitive tasks to compare learning dynamics between children and adults. This represents the first application of gradient-based optimization to human cortical data across development. The project has the potential of providing insights into critical periods when neurodevelopmental disorders emerge, effectively bridging computational modeling with human developmental neurobiology.

title: Vinegar as Biotechnology: a practice-based study
description: Vinegar is a catalyst for medical innovation. In medieval alchemy, vinegar was considered a ‘vegetal mercury’, used to transform metals into gold. Vinegar was associated with the Alchemical Androgyne: a symbol of the perfect fusion of opposites, represented as a bi-gendered angelic figure. The melancholy humour was classified as ‘vinegary’. In medieval medicine, vinegar was a common ingredient in curative drinks and surgery. These recipes express the understanding that bodies and their emotions are fluid, and capable of material change. Today, popular healthcare remedies recommend drinking vinegar for its ‘hormone balancing’ effects, echoing premodern discourses of ‘humoral balance’. The term ‘humoral regulation’ is still used to describe hormonal treatments. I will explore this relationship between medieval medicine and alchemy, and present-day endocrinology. As a medieval biotechnology, vinegar was used for bodily transmutation. My experiences as a psychiatric and gender- clinic patient give me first-hand understanding of current medical treatments which alter the hormonal and chemical conditions within the body. Viewing these experiences through the lens of the medieval past, I will provide new conceptual and sociological narratives of endocrinological and psychiatric healthcare. This study will enable hormonal and psychiatric treatments to be better understood as forms of dynamic physical transformation.

title: Building a Global Knowledge & Connection Platform for Mental Health Innovators
description: Thank you for the invitation to apply for a Wellcome Discretionary Award. This proposal aims to expand Hemingway from an emerging community and publication into a global knowledge and connection infrastructure for mental health innovators. Hemingway already brings together people across research, clinical practice, industry, lived-experience and policy. But they still lack a reliable way to learn from each other in real time, access diverse perspectives, and build on emerging evidence rather than working in isolation. These gaps slow the development and spread of approaches that could meaningfully improve population mental health. The project delivers three major enhancements: Hemingway Sessions: Weekly, structured discussions where practitioners, researchers, and lived-experience contributors share insight on topics such as clinical models, safety, implementation, and evaluation. Hemingway Chapters: Local groups in global hubs that strengthen collaboration, peer support, and the practical exchange of experience. Hemingway Guides: Co- created, high-quality resources that translate collective insight into practical frameworks to support better decisions and avoid common pitfalls. Topics include care model design, business model design, user engagement, fundraising, etc. Together, these activities will create a more connected and better-informed community of innovators. By doing so, promising ideas will develop more efficiently and reach the people who need them.

title: African mental health community mobilisation: Influencing the 7th Ministerial Summit
description: The 7th Global Ministerial Mental Health Summit—the first to be hosted in Africa—offers a pivotal opportunity to advance rights‑based, person‑centred mental health reform across the continent. Yet lived experience advocates, who are essential to shaping effective and locally grounded solutions, remain underrepresented in global policy spaces. Strengthening their leadership is critical to ensuring that government commitments reflect real community needs and drive sustainable system change. This initiative will enable meaningful, well‑supported participation of African lived experience leaders throughout the Summit process. Through the Global Mental Health Action Network (GMHAN), which connects nearly 10,000 members worldwide and has a strong African base, we will convene a diverse Short‑Term Action Group chaired by lived experience advocates; deliver regional capacity‑building workshops in English and French; and provide travel grants, safeguarding, and logistical support for participation in WHO regional consultations and the Summit itself. We will also co‑host a high‑level Side Event on lived-experience advocacy and research and produce communications outputs that amplify African‑led narratives. By mobilising advocates, strengthening networks, and elevating lived experience leadership, this initiative will ensure that African voices shape Summit outcomes and drive long‑term progress toward inclusive, rights‑based mental health systems across the continent.

title: Youth Mental Health Hub at SXSW London 2026
description: The Child Mind Institute, in partnership with Wellcome Trust, proposes to deliver the inaugural Youth Mental Health Hub at SXSW London 2026: a curated platform for spotlighting practical, evidence-informed approaches to youth mental health. Embedded within a major international forum spanning technology, media, culture, and public conversation, the Hub will bring greater visibility and coherence to youth mental health programming across the week. Through 4-7 linked sessions and related engagement activities, the Hub will convene contributors from clinical care, science, technology, sport, media, and lived experience to examine approaches that can strengthen prevention, early support, family and community resilience, and public understanding. Working topics include family resilience, sport- and community- based pathways to support, responsible uses of AI, mental health in the media, and youth mental health in contexts of conflict and recovery. The project will produce a distinctive youth mental health presence at SXSW London, foster exchange among UK, U.S., and international partners, and generate a post-event summary to support further dissemination and collaboration.

title: Coordinating decision-making and the cell cycle: the role of signal dynamics
description: A limited set of signalling molecules drive embryonic cells to self-organise, pattern tissues and construct the entire body plan. Mutations that corrupt accurate signal interpretation are common drivers of human disease, however, embryonic development remains highly robust to these perturbations. Using a combination of quantitative imaging approaches and optogenetics, my aim is to uncover the basic design principles of dynamic signal interpretation and understand how the embryo coordinates tissue growth and cell decision-making, using Ras-Erk signalling in craniofacial patterning as a paradigm. Tissues that contribute to craniofacial development display differential sensitivity to the same perturbed signal in a family of developmental disorders, known as RASopathies. I will combine imaging approaches with whole embryo single-cell RNA-seq to determine what aspects of craniofacial development (signalling, gene expression, cell numbers) are sensitive to perturbation in the context of disease. Our ability to investigate the role of signal dynamics in embryonic development and disease has been limited by technology. However, I and others have pioneered new biosensors that enable the tracking of single-cell signalling and decision-making in vivo. Using zebrafish and Drosophila embryos as optically accessible models, I will reveal how tissues interpret normal and corrupted signals and identify buffering mechanisms that safeguard development.

title: The Night Shift 1850-Present: Re-imagining Sleep, Work and Wellbeing for Healthcare Professionals in English and Scottish Hospitals
description: Night Shift aims to radically re-imagine sleep work and wellbeing for healthcare professionals working at night on the general hospital ward in England and Scotland. Complimenting a burgeoning field of clinical and epidemiological research on healthcare fatigue, the project will reveal the ways in which long-standing working cultures and professional identities have normalized unsafe and unsustainable working conditions. Working across medical, environmental and labour histories, the project will provide the first systematic history of the British hospital at night. By drawing on cutting edge research in the studies of the night, sleep and everyday temporalities, Night Shift will also deliver a new framework to understand the lived experience of night shift work in the hospital. The project team will bring historical insights into conversation with contemporary challenges through semi-structured interviews and Participatory Action Research (PAR) with night shift workers. This interdisciplinary work will feed into better policy and practice supported by partnerships with three NHS Foundation Trusts in the North East of England, as well as the charity sector. Over five and a half years, the project team will deliver an ambitious programme of academic, public engagement and policy outputs, including an exhibition at the Royal College of Nursing (RCN).

title: Addressing everyday ethical tensions in global mental health task-sharing
description: Global Mental Health task-sharing (GMH-TS) involves redistributing tasks from mental health specialists to community-based health workers, or to lay “helpers”. It is heralded globally as a flagship innovation that increases access to effective and contextually appropriate mental healthcare. In everyday practice GMH-TS generates ethical tensions embedded in the epistemic, relational, and moral demands of delivering mental healthcare in local communities. These ethical tensions both motivate the unique strengths of GMH- TS, whilst raising potential distress and harms for those engaging with this form of care. Currently, GMH-TS lacks robust empirical and conceptual understandings, and practice-based approaches, to recognise and respond to such ethical tensions. I will address this through empirical bioethics research co-developed with collaborators in Pakistan and Ethiopia. Ethnographic and qualitative research will explore the ethical tensions arising in three diverse GMH-TS case studies: (1) individual manualised psychosocial support intervention, (2) expert-by-experience peer-support groups, and (3) religious and traditional healer collaborative care with specialists. Research will examine the ethical values GMH-TS embodies and invokes, the ‘goods’ it offers, and the suffering it provokes. This study will transform our understanding and practice of GMH-TS by generating significant theoretical advances, and developing practice-based resources for responding to the ethical tensions GMH-TS creates.

title: Constructive Conversations Pilot Project: Mental Health, Artificial Intelligence and Religious Communities
description: This project pioneers and evaluates a new way of fostering constructive conversations between researchers and religious communities, to have positive impact on researchers while benefitting the religious communities and giving them a voice. We will adapt the Participatory Futures Dialogue (PFD) approach to cover sensitive scientific topics, with three modules: scientific information, societal issues, and religious issues. Multiple religious issues modules can be produced to enable interaction with different religious communities. This pilot will look at AI and mental health, engaging with UK Jewish and Christian communities. This approach is scalable to other scientific topics, regions and religions in future. We will examine the implications of emerging AI technologies for mental health, with particular attention to ethical, clinical and psychosocial dimensions as understood within religious contexts. Religious communities play a significant role in mental health and wellbeing support, yet remain underexplored in current AI and mental health research. Through constructive conversations with AI researchers, this project will investigate how faith communities understand and engage with both generic AI tools and AI-mediated mental health tools in pursuit of wellbeing, asking how theology shapes responses to automation, care and vulnerability, and how these perspectives can inform responsible, culturally sensitive deployment of AI.
recipient: The Faraday Institute for Science and Religion

title: Trust Talks!: Constructive Conversations about health and creative adaptation to climate change
description: Trust Talks! offers an innovative approach to facilitate constructive conversations in low-income communities in Northwest England through meaningful collaboration with community organisations. The project responds to the Wellcome Trust priority areas of climate and health by focusing on the theme of “Health, well-being and creative adaptation to climate change”. The underpinning principles behind Trust Talks! are collaboration community organisation through the provision of decision-making power and financial resources to those with the greatest proximity to communities and low trust in institutions, to co-design constructive conversations. Previous research has revealed dominant narratives about a lack of agency in climate change and adaptation. The use of psychosocial tools offers an innovative way to facilitate new, exploratory ways of thinking, challenging taken-for-granted assumptions about the roles of science, research, and climate change and create space for envisioning an optimistic future. The Climate Psychology Alliance (CPA) will use innovative methods to facilaite conversations between communities and researchers, enabling people to not only explore fears and uncertainties about the ecological crisis, but also to aspirations and hopes. It will explore the sense of possibility and science for envisioning optimistic futures, exploring solutions, adaptations, and mitigation that are perceived as feasible within people’s daily lives.

title: Are measures of attachment and attachment-relevant caregiving helpful or unhelpful to assessments of child mental health and safeguarding needs?
description: The NICE Guidelines on Child Attachment (2016) highlighted the lack of empirical evidence for or against the value of assessments of attachment/attachment-relevant caregiving in clinical and child welfare practice, and urged the need for further research. A recent international consensus statement on attachment and applied practice further listed this as a key research priority (Forslund et al. 2022). There have also been stakeholder concerns about assessments discriminating against families based on sociodemographic factors and child neurodiversity. In partnership with families and practitioners, our study will evaluate whether assessments of attachment can improve the sensitivity and specificity of assessments for child mental health and welfare. 5-8 year old participants will be drawn from the consent-to-recontact register of Child & Adolescent Mental Health Services. Families will receive assessments of attachment/attachment-relevant caregiving. Co-production will help us examine the acceptability of the assessments to children and caregivers with cultural competence and ethical integrity. Using follow-up administrative data, we will assess the sensitivity and specificity of assessments of attachment/attachment-relevant caregiving compared to other concurrent information. We will examine whether assessments are confounded by sociodemographic factors and child neurodiversity. $2.5m in matched funding from the Canadian Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council will support dissemination and impact.

title: The cognitive mapping of uncertainty by integrated neuromodulation in the hippocampus
description: In a constantly changing environment, the brain must store and update information in a way that depends on uncertainty. The hippocampus is central to this continual process but relies on inputs that signpost new information and regulate the extent to which it is incorporated in future estimates. Our central hypothesis proposes that this signposting is performed by functionally overlapping neuromodulator systems interacting in an integrated fashion to signal different types of error and uncertainty. This signal enables appropriate updating of memories stored in the hippocampus providing realistic expectations on which to base decision making in uncertain situations, a fundamental process whose disruption is a core feature of multiple psychiatric disorders. To test these models, we will measure where and when neuromodulation by acetylcholine, dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin occurs in the hippocampus during spatial navigation tasks in mice designed to manipulate the type and degree of error and uncertainty. These findings will inform a novel theoretical framework which will be iteratively refined by experiments to selectively manipulate neuromodulator release and downstream targets, providing mechanisms for how neuromodulators integrate to modify observable hippocampal representations of space. Ultimately this project will fundamentally reappraise the principles of neuromodulation and its therapeutic potential.

title: PATHS – Psychedelics as Therapeutics: Harm Reduction and Safety
description: We are world leaders in researching substance use development, psychedelic pharmacology, and drug stigma, but we do not yet know precisely how millions of vulnerable people worldwide are using psychedelics as medicines outside formal medical systems — nor how to make this safer. This is urgent: individuals experiencing mental health crises are using psychedelics in unregulated settings lacking therapeutic support and safeguards, facing risks from uncertain supply, criminal networks, exploitation, and poorly-processed difficult experiences. Marginalised populations bear disproportionate risks. For many, the choice is understood as ‘legally dead or illegally alive’. This UK-focused discovery programme, through unprecedented partnerships with hard- to-reach communities — cluster headache patients, police using psychedelics for occupational trauma, festival crisis intervention providers — will investigate emergent, informal therapeutic psychedelic use outside legal and medical jurisdictions during the critical transitional period before anticipated approval. We will deliver a paradigmatic step-change in psychedelic harm reduction scholarship by shifting focus from institutional clinical trials to lay therapeutic practices. We will discover what harms users encounter, and evaluate which community-led innovations work or fail. Understanding these practices and consolidating fragmented grassroots knowledge will have transformative potential for the lives, health, and wellbeing of those driven to engage in therapeutic psychedelic use.

title: A Physiotherapy-Led Service for Postnatal Women with Vaginal Prolapse
description: Vaginal prolapse is a bulge or a feeling of heaviness in the vagina. Up to 43% of women report severe symptoms at one year after childbirth. A prolapse can stop women doing normal activities and can interfere with emptying the bladder or bowel and can affect a woman’s sex life. Women with a prolapse are five times more likely to have postnatal depression. There are however problems for postnatal women: 1) Poorly designed care pathways can result in multiple trips to the doctor before being referred for pelvic floor muscle exercise, and again for a pessary. This causes frustration, delays treatment and wastes appointments. 2) Postnatal women with prolapse are not always offered a pessary. Interviews and a survey showed 82% of GPs will not offer a pessary. This is because a pessary is more often used to treat prolapse in older women and GPs lack training in fitting pessaries. A service designed by and for women with prolapse could provide more treatment options and allow women to make better-informed choices. This research aims to improve health outcomes for postnatal women by testing if a new service for postnatal women with prolapse is feasible and acceptable to women.
